req.text:
You write transcripts of realistic video calls between strangers for a fully synthetic research dataset set in the UK. The study, in order (from its published design): a short puzzle task done alone; first impressions of the others' webcam photos; then a series of three-minute, one-on-one video calls in rounds, each person meeting the others in their group; after each call a short survey.

Call shape (from the original study's numbers): a call is cut off by a three-minute timer. A typical call has about 30 turns (most between 20 and 39) and about 570 words in total (most between 440 and 682); half of all turns are 12 words or fewer, and a quarter are 24 or more. Short acknowledgements ("yeah", "mm") count as turns too. So aim for about 570 words in about 30 turns: alongside the quick back-and-forth, people often talk in longer stretches (explaining their job, telling a story), and those long turns carry much of the call.

Guide to British conversational English (use it for how people talk; it is a description of speech, not a script):
How British people talk in casual conversation. This is a paraphrase of published descriptions of spoken British English; sources are in SOURCES.md. Use these features lightly and only where they fit the person. Never use them as a caricature.

- **Fillers.** British speakers hesitate with "erm" and "er". Women and younger speakers lean towards "erm".
- **Hedges.** "Sort of" is everywhere and steady. "Kind of" is spreading, and younger speakers use it more.
- **Politeness words.** "Please", "thank you", "thanks" and "sorry" mostly mean what they say. "Sorry" also works as a repair word (to correct yourself, or to ask someone to repeat) and can be ironic.
- **Tags at the end of a sentence.** "You know", "right", "okay", "yeah", "do you know what I mean". Among young Londoners, "innit" and "you get me" are rising. Tags depend on age and region only, never on ethnicity.
- **Echoing.** In an engaged conversation people pick up and re-use parts of each other's words.
- **Regional words and grammar** (from a recent dialect survey):
  - A bread roll is a "barm" in the North West (Manchester to Liverpool and western Lancashire), a "cob" around Nottinghamshire, a "bap" in Staffordshire, the West Midlands and North Wales, and a "batch" in Liverpool and Coventry.
  - Around Liverpool an ice lolly can be a "lolly ice".
  - The evening meal is "tea" in the North West, North East and Yorkshire, and "dinner" in the South East and London. Some people say both.
  - "Yous" or "youse" for plural "you" is common in the North East (Newcastle, Teesside), Liverpool and Scotland, less so in Manchester, and rare in York, Leeds and Sheffield.
  - "Give it me" is normal in the North West and West Midlands and widely accepted in Sheffield and York; it fades south of Birmingham, Coventry and Leicester.
  - "You was" is widely used, historically Northern and now found as far south as London.
- **Everyday British words** to draw on where they fit, without assigning them to regions: knackered or shattered, chuffed or made up, skint or brassic, mardy or stroppy, mum or mam, mate or pal, settee, sofa or couch.

The group (session S01). Persona cards, including the webcam photo each person was rated on:

P000 (Darren):
- first name: Darren
- age: 46
- lives in: Bridgwater, South West England (Somerset)
- occupation: Sales assistant on the flooring and tiles section of a large DIY and home improvement store on a retail park in Taunton. Full-time, around 39 hours a week, including alternate Saturdays and some Sundays.
- education detail: Left a Bridgwater comprehensive at 16 in 1995 with a handful of GCSEs, the best a C in maths and design and technology. Went straight into the yard at a local builders' merchant and later did an NVQ Level 2 in Customer Service through work. He also has in-store forklift and manual handling certificates. Never fancied college and doesn't regret it much.
- household: Lives with his wife Donna (44), a care assistant at a residential home, in a three-bed ex-council semi they bought under right to buy about twelve years ago. Their daughter Kayleigh (20) still lives at home and works at a nail salon in town. Their son Jordan (23) moved to Bristol with his girlfriend last year. There is an elderly Jack Russell called Pickle.
- cultural background: White British, born and raised in Bridgwater. His dad worked at the old cellophane factory and his mum did school dinners. Church of England by upbringing. He was married in St Mary's and both kids were christened there. Nowadays it's Christmas, Easter and funerals. He'd still call himself a Christian and says a quiet prayer when things are bad, but doesn't make a thing of it. Bridgwater Carnival is a big part of local identity for him: his uncle was in a carnival club and Darren helped build carts as a teenager.
- professional persona: The bloke on the floor customers actually want to find. He's chatty, patient with people who don't know what they're after, and honest enough to tell them they don't need the dearer adhesive. He's good at calming down an angry customer and covers shifts when asked. Paperwork, stock counts and remembering to log things on the handheld are not his strong suit, and his supervisor has had words about it more than once. He has no interest in managing anyone.
- sports persona: Plays in a Wednesday night pub skittles league and has done for nearly twenty years. It's more about the pint and the banter than the score. He follows Somerset cricket loosely and gets to the County Ground once or twice a summer for a T20. He watches the rugby internationals in the pub. He used to play Sunday league football until his knees went.
- arts persona: Not much of an arts person. Carnival is the closest he gets, and he goes every November without fail. He likes 80s and 90s music, has seen Madness and UB40 live, and listens to Greatest Hits Radio in the car. TV is quiz shows, Gogglebox, Traffic Cops and the odd Netflix crime series Donna puts on. He rarely reads a book.
- travel persona: Creature of habit. The family have gone to the same caravan park in Cornwall most summers, and he and Donna did Tenerife twice for big anniversaries. He hated the queues at Bristol Airport and didn't care much for the food. He'd happily never go further than Benidorm.
- culinary persona: Meat-and-two-veg man who'll call the evening meal tea or dinner without thinking about it. Donna cooks in the week and he does the Sunday roast or a barbecue when the weather's right. Friday is chippy night. He likes a proper pasty, a cheddar ploughman's and a cider, though he's been told to cut back for his blood pressure. He won't touch anything too spicy.
- hobbies and interests: Wednesday skittles league at the local pub, Bridgwater Carnival, and helping a mate's club with their cart in the autumn, walking Pickle along the river Parrett, pub quizzes, though he's mainly there for the sport and music rounds, pottering in his shed, which he never quite tidies, watching cricket and rugby on telly
- skills: talking to absolutely anyone, calming down annoyed customers, decent practical DIY: tiling, laying laminate, basic plumbing, lifting and moving stock safely, knowing a fair bit about floor tiles, grout and adhesives, keeping a team cheerful on a dull shift
- career goals: Doesn't really have any beyond staying put, keeping his hours and getting a bit more each year. He's been asked about team leader and said no thanks, because he'd rather be on the floor than doing rotas. He'd like to pay off the mortgage before he's 60 and maybe do a few hours less once his knees get worse.
- voice: Friendly, warm and a bit loud, with an easy pace that speeds up when he's telling a story. Light Somerset accent with a soft rolled 'r' and the odd 'alright?' or 'where's that to?', but nothing broad. He says 'er' while he thinks and leans on tags like 'you know' and 'yeah'. He says 'sort of' a fair bit and calls people 'mate' or, now and then, 'my lover' with older women customers. He laughs at his own jokes and picks up the other person's words when he agrees. Silence makes him a bit uneasy, so he fills it with a joke or an anecdote. If he misses a question he'll say 'sorry, say that again?' without embarrassment.
- typing: Quick and casual on his phone. Mostly lower case, with capitals only where autocorrect puts them. Punctuation is light: a few commas, often no full stop, and sometimes 'lol' or a 'haha'. Apostrophes come and go ('dont', 'its'). Short answers like 'yeah fine thanks' or 'not really, maybe once a year'. He doesn't go back to fix typos.
- with strangers: Opens up straight away. He's chatty, jokey and keen to make the other person comfortable, and he'll ask you questions back. Comes across as genuine and a bit self-deprecating, with no airs, and doesn't try to impress. He agrees easily and avoids anything confrontational. If asked an opinion question he'll often say 'I can see both sides, to be fair'. He may wander off topic and need steering back.
- small things: the skittles team being bottom of the league again, Pickle getting old and grumpy, the traffic on the M5 by junction 24, a customer who wanted to tile a bathroom in an afternoon, Somerset doing well or badly in the T20, carnival night and how many people turned up, his knees playing up, the price of a pint going up at his local
- deeper things: his dad dying of a heart attack at 61, which is part of why his own blood pressure worries him more than he lets on, a stretch about eight years ago when he was laid off from the builders' merchant and they were skint for months, missing his son since he moved to Bristol, and feeling the house is quieter, quietly worrying that his back won't last until state pension age in a job on his feet, going back into church alone after his dad's funeral and finding it helped more than he expected
- webcam photo: Taken in the evening at the kitchen table on an older laptop, with the camera slightly below his eye line so it looks a little up at him. Lighting is the overhead kitchen spotlights, giving a bit of shine on his forehead and a faint shadow under his chin. He's a broad-faced white man in his mid-forties with ruddy cheeks, a short greying beard and close-cropped brown hair thinning at the crown. He's smiling openly and his eyes are crinkled. No glasses. He's wearing a navy fleece over the collar of a work polo shirt. Behind him are white gloss kitchen units with a kettle, a toaster and a stack of post by the bread bin, a fridge covered in magnets and a calendar, and a small window with a roller blind half down. The edge of a dog bed is just visible on the floor at the right of the frame.

P001 (Joanne):
- first name: Joanne
- age: 41
- lives in: Frome, South West England
- occupation: Senior care assistant and shift lead at a 40-bed residential dementia care home on the edge of Frome. She works mostly 12-hour day shifts, around 38 hours a week. She runs the floor, does medication rounds, writes up care plans and supervises a team of four or five carers.
- education detail: Left a comprehensive school in Shepton Mallet with eight GCSEs. Started an A-level in English Literature and art at college but didn't finish. Later did an NVQ Level 3 in Health and Social Care through work, and is now partway through a Level 4 Diploma in Adult Care, which her employer pays for.
- household: Rents a two-up two-down terraced house near the town centre with her partner Mark, 44, a self-employed joiner she has lived with for three years. Her son Callum, 14, from her marriage lives with them most of the week and spends alternate weekends with his dad in Yeovil. There is also an elderly rescue greyhound called Pip.
- cultural background: White British, born and raised in Somerset to a family of farm and factory workers. She was christened and confirmed Church of England and still thinks of herself as Christian. She goes to St John's now and then, mostly at Christmas and Easter, and sometimes sits in the church on her own when work has been hard. She married at 24 and divorced at 35. The divorce was amicable on paper but she found it bruising.
- professional persona: Meticulous and quietly fierce about standards. She won't sign off a record she hasn't checked and has refused to cover for colleagues who cut corners, which hasn't always made her popular. Residents and families trust her because she is straight with them. Some managers find her blunt and hard to persuade. She takes a death on the unit to heart for days but rarely shows it at work.
- sports persona: Not sporty. She walks Pip every morning before shifts, often round Rodden Meadow or along the river, and does a Sunday walk on the Mendips with Mark. She half-heartedly follows Bath Rugby because Mark does.
- arts persona: Her real outlet. She goes to a Tuesday evening pottery class at a community studio in town and has a shelf of slightly wonky bowls she is secretly proud of. She reads a lot of literary fiction from the library, has a soft spot for Thomas Hardy, and goes to the Frome Festival and the independent cinema when she can afford it.
- travel persona: Mostly UK breaks on a budget: a cottage in Cornwall or Pembrokeshire, chosen for walks rather than nightlife. She went to Lisbon once with a friend and loved the tiles and the bookshops. She would like to see Iceland someday but worries about the cost and about leaving Pip.
- culinary persona: Plain, reliable home cooking: stews, roast chicken on a Sunday, big batches of soup she freezes for shift weeks. She calls the evening meal dinner, or sometimes tea when she's with her mum. She likes trying recipes from the library's Ottolenghi books when she has a day off, though Callum moans about anything green.
- hobbies and interests: pottery evening class, reading literary fiction and classics, dog walking, browsing charity shops and the Frome Independent market, local history of Somerset villages, jigsaws on night-shift recovery days
- skills: dementia care and de-escalation, medication administration and record-keeping, writing care plans, wheel-throwing and glazing (beginner-intermediate), batch cooking on a budget, noticing small changes in people's health
- career goals: Finish her Level 4 diploma and possibly move into a deputy manager role. She is wary of becoming 'just paperwork' and losing contact with residents. She has also wondered quietly about training as a dementia specialist nurse but isn't sure she has the confidence or the money to go back to study full-time.
- voice: Fairly quiet and measured, with a soft Somerset accent: a light burr on her r's, never broad. Speaks at a steady, careful pace and thinks before answering, so there are pauses. She fills them with 'erm' or just lets them sit rather than rushing. Uses 'sort of' quite a lot and the odd 'you know' at the end of a point. Says 'sorry' to correct herself ('it was March, sorry, April'). Can be quite direct, even curt, if she thinks a question is daft or loaded. Gets more animated when talking about residents, books or pottery.
- typing: Types properly but plainly: capital at the start, full stops, apostrophes mostly right. Short answers, no emojis. Occasionally misses a capital on 'i' when typing fast on her phone. Sometimes adds a brief honest caveat like 'Not sure this is what you mean but'.
- with strangers: Reserved and a bit guarded at first, polite but not chatty. She doesn't do much small talk and can seem slightly cool. She answers honestly, sometimes more honestly than expected, and won't pretend to agree to be nice. She warms up if the other person seems genuine, and is visibly uncomfortable with anything that feels like flattery or a sales pitch.
- small things: Pip needs a walk before she can think straight in the morning, her pottery tutor says her glazes are 'brave', Callum's school keeps sending emails she hasn't read, the price of petrol for getting to work, a library book she's got overdue again, being shattered after a run of long days, Mark's van taking up the whole street
- deeper things: She still feels some guilt about the divorce and how it affected Callum, even though she knows it was the right decision, She grieves residents she's cared for and has a small notebook where she writes their names, Her mum is in the early stages of memory problems, which frightens her more than she admits because she knows exactly what's coming, She sometimes feels she was clever enough for university and let it slip, She worries a lot, about money, Callum and her mum, and has had a spell of anxiety that her GP helped with
- webcam photo: Head-and-shoulders shot from a laptop on a kitchen table, camera slightly below eye level so it angles up a little. Daylight from a window to her left lights one side of her face, with a warm ceiling light behind. She has a pale complexion with a few freckles, light grey-blue eyes and faint lines at the corners, and a neutral, slightly wary expression with lips pressed together in a small polite smile. Shoulder-length mid-brown hair with a few greys at the parting, pulled back loosely in a clip with strands escaping. No glasses. She wears a navy fleece zipped halfway over a grey T-shirt, with small silver stud earrings. Behind her is a cream-painted wall with a wall calendar marked in biro, a wooden shelf holding three uneven glazed pottery bowls in blue and green, a stack of library books with plastic covers, and a corner of a fridge with a school letter held on by a magnet. A dog lead hangs on a hook by the door frame at the edge of the shot.

P002 (Blerta):
- first name: Blerta
- age: 27
- lives in: Fenham, Newcastle upon Tyne, North East
- occupation: Full-time undergraduate student (second year, BSc Speech and Language Therapy) at Northumbria University. She does a few unpaid placement days and some occasional cash-in-hand shifts helping at a family friend's bakery when money is tight.
- education detail: Came to the UK aged 8 and went through primary and secondary school in Newcastle. Left sixth form after AS levels to work, because the family needed the income. Spent six years as a care assistant in a residential home for older people. Did an Access to Higher Education diploma (Health Sciences) at Newcastle College in the evenings, then started university at 25 with a maintenance loan.
- household: Lives in her parents' rented terraced house with her mam and dad, who are married, and her younger brother Driton (21), who works in a warehouse. Her dad is a part-time taxi driver with a bad back. Her mam cleans offices in the early mornings. Money is careful but the house is warm and busy.
- cultural background: Kosovo Albanian, born in Gjakova. The family joined her uncle in Newcastle in 2006. She is Muslim in the relaxed, family-centred way common among Kosovars: she fasts at Ramadan, doesn't drink, goes to the mosque for Eid, and doesn't wear a headscarf day to day. She speaks Albanian at home and English everywhere else, and switches between them mid-sentence with her brother. She feels like a Geordie with an extra layer rather than an outsider, though people still sometimes ask where she's 'really' from.
- professional persona: Diligent and quietly capable. The care home taught her patience with people who struggle to communicate, and that is what drew her to speech therapy, particularly stroke and dementia rehabilitation. On placement she is the student who stays to tidy the therapy room and writes up notes the same day. She is honest about what she doesn't know and asks questions rather than bluffing.
- sports persona: Not sporty in a competitive sense. She walks a lot: Town Moor, along the Quayside, sometimes the coast at Tynemouth. She does a cheap women-only swim session at the local leisure centre on Sunday mornings. She follows Newcastle United loosely because her dad and brother are obsessive about it, and she knows enough to join in at tea.
- arts persona: Loves language and stories. She reads novels in translation (Ismail Kadare out of a mix of pride and duty, plus a lot of Korean and Japanese fiction from the library). She goes to free exhibitions at the Laing and the BALTIC and keeps a scrappy sketchbook of people on the Metro. She listens to podcasts about linguistics and true history, and to Albanian pop at weddings, which she pretends to find embarrassing.
- travel persona: Goes back to Gjakova most summers to stay with her grandmother, usually on the cheapest flights she can find with a change in Vienna or Istanbul. She has done one budget trip with uni friends to Kraków. She dreams about Japan and keeps a spreadsheet of what it would cost. She is curious about places rather than luxury and is happy in hostels.
- culinary persona: Grew up on her mam's flija, pite and stuffed peppers, and helps make flija for family occasions because it takes hours. Halal is a given, so she checks labels and has a mental list of safe places for a takeaway. She has tea about six o'clock with the family when she's in. Her own cooking is cheap student stuff, lentil soup and pasta bakes, and she likes trying new recipes from YouTube.
- hobbies and interests: Sketching people on public transport, Reading translated fiction from the city library, Linguistics and history podcasts, Long walks on the Town Moor and the coast, Learning basic Japanese on an app, Volunteering at a weekly conversation café for refugees and asylum seekers, Baking with her mam
- skills: Fluent in Albanian and English, with some school French and beginner Japanese, Communicating with people who have dementia or hearing loss, Personal care and manual handling from her care work, Careful note-taking and organisation, Translating letters and appointments for relatives, Making flija and burek from scratch
- career goals: To qualify and get a Band 5 speech and language therapist post in the NHS in the North East, ideally in adult neuro or stroke services. Longer term she would like to help develop assessment materials for Albanian-speaking patients, because she has seen how much gets lost when people are assessed only in English.
- voice: Warm, fairly quick once she relaxes, with a soft Newcastle accent layered over her own: 'mam', 'yous' when talking about a group, 'tea' for the evening meal, the occasional 'like' at the end of a sentence. No exaggerated Geordie. She says 'erm' while she thinks and uses 'sort of' and 'kind of' when she's being careful not to overstate something. She says 'sorry' a lot, often to correct herself ('it was in 2006, sorry, 2007'). She echoes the interviewer's words back while she works out an answer. She is comfortable with a short silence and will say 'give me a sec' rather than fill it with waffle. She laughs at herself easily.
- typing: Mostly proper sentences with capital letters and apostrophes, because she's used to writing clinical notes. She drops into lowercase when she's rushing. Full stops are consistent, with occasional double exclamation marks when she's pleased. She uses few abbreviations beyond 'uni', 'tbh' and 'etc', and sometimes adds a quick clarification in brackets.
- with strangers: Friendly, polite and genuinely interested. She asks the other person questions back and remembers what they said. She is modest about herself, doesn't oversell, and will admit when she doesn't know something. She can seem a little shy for the first minute and then opens up, especially if the topic is people, language or how things work.
- small things: The Metro being late again, Her placement supervisor's dog that comes into the clinic on Fridays, Being knackered after a nine o'clock lecture, The new library book she can't put down, Her dad shouting at the telly during the match, Finding a decent halal place near uni, Her brother using all the hot water
- deeper things: Feeling guilty that her parents still work hard jobs while she studies at 27, Leaving school early and worrying she'd 'missed her chance', Vague memories of the war's aftermath in Gjakova, and relatives who never talk about it, Being asked where she's 'really' from despite growing up in Newcastle, Gentle family pressure to settle down and marry, which she deflects, Her grandmother getting older and frail, and how far away she is
- webcam photo: Laptop webcam at desk height, slightly below eye level, framing her head and shoulders a little left of centre. Soft daylight from a window to her right, plus a cool glow from the screen. Woman in her late twenties with a fair, slightly olive complexion, dark brown eyebrows, brown eyes and no makeup except a little mascara. She has a small, open smile. Thick dark brown hair is pulled into a loose bun, with a few strands falling at the sides. She wears thin gold-rimmed glasses, a grey Northumbria University hoodie over a black T-shirt, and small gold stud earrings. Behind her is a small bedroom: a cream wall with a corkboard of lecture timetables, a postcard of Japanese woodblock art and a family photo pinned to it. A narrow bookshelf holds library books with barcode stickers, a stack of anatomy textbooks and a mug of pens. The corner of a single bed with a patterned crocheted blanket is just visible, and a radiator has a towel draped over it.

P003 (Kezia):
- first name: Kezia
- age: 26
- lives in: Catford, South East London
- occupation: Special educational needs teaching assistant at a primary school in Lewisham, 26 hours a week across four days, term-time, supporting two children with autism in Year 3
- education detail: A-levels in Sociology, Biology and English Language at a sixth form in Bromley; BSc in Psychology (2:1) from a university in South London, commuted from home; Level 3 certificate in supporting teaching and learning; in-house Team Teach and Makaton training
- household: Lives alone in a one-bedroom first-floor flat in a converted terraced house off Brownhill Road, rented. Moved in fourteen months ago after separating from her husband, whom she married at 23. They are still legally married. He lives in Erith and they are in contact about paperwork only.
- cultural background: Born at Lewisham Hospital. Her mum came from Spanish Town, Jamaica, as a teenager and her dad is London-born of Jamaican parents. Raised in Sydenham with a younger brother. Grew up in a Pentecostal church (New Testament Church of God) and still goes most Sundays with her mum. Sunday dinner at her parents' afterwards is a fixture. Faith is central to her, though she keeps it quietly.
- professional persona: The TA teachers ask for because she is never late, her visual timetables are laminated and up to date, and she logs incidents properly the same day. She is calm with the children and much less comfortable in staff meetings. She dropped from full-time to four days after the separation because she was exhausted, and she has kept it that way. She is good at routines and dislikes last-minute changes to the timetable.

req.text:
You write transcripts of realistic video calls between strangers for a fully synthetic research dataset set in the UK. The study, in order (from its published design): a short puzzle task done alone; first impressions of the others' webcam photos; then a series of three-minute, one-on-one video calls in rounds, each person meeting the others in their group; after each call a short survey.

Call shape (from the original study's numbers): a call is cut off by a three-minute timer. A typical call has about 30 turns (most between 20 and 39) and about 570 words in total (most between 440 and 682); half of all turns are 12 words or fewer, and a quarter are 24 or more. Short acknowledgements ("yeah", "mm") count as turns too. So aim for about 570 words in about 30 turns: alongside the quick back-and-forth, people often talk in longer stretches (explaining their job, telling a story), and those long turns carry much of the call.

Guide to British conversational English (use it for how people talk; it is a description of speech, not a script):
How British people talk in casual conversation. This is a paraphrase of published descriptions of spoken British English; sources are in SOURCES.md. Use these features lightly and only where they fit the person. Never use them as a caricature.

- **Fillers.** British speakers hesitate with "erm" and "er". Women and younger speakers lean towards "erm".
- **Hedges.** "Sort of" is everywhere and steady. "Kind of" is spreading, and younger speakers use it more.
- **Politeness words.** "Please", "thank you", "thanks" and "sorry" mostly mean what they say. "Sorry" also works as a repair word (to correct yourself, or to ask someone to repeat) and can be ironic.
- **Tags at the end of a sentence.** "You know", "right", "okay", "yeah", "do you know what I mean". Among young Londoners, "innit" and "you get me" are rising. Tags depend on age and region only, never on ethnicity.
- **Echoing.** In an engaged conversation people pick up and re-use parts of each other's words.
- **Regional words and grammar** (from a recent dialect survey):
  - A bread roll is a "barm" in the North West (Manchester to Liverpool and western Lancashire), a "cob" around Nottinghamshire, a "bap" in Staffordshire, the West Midlands and North Wales, and a "batch" in Liverpool and Coventry.
  - Around Liverpool an ice lolly can be a "lolly ice".
  - The evening meal is "tea" in the North West, North East and Yorkshire, and "dinner" in the South East and London. Some people say both.
  - "Yous" or "youse" for plural "you" is common in the North East (Newcastle, Teesside), Liverpool and Scotland, less so in Manchester, and rare in York, Leeds and Sheffield.
  - "Give it me" is normal in the North West and West Midlands and widely accepted in Sheffield and York; it fades south of Birmingham, Coventry and Leicester.
  - "You was" is widely used, historically Northern and now found as far south as London.
- **Everyday British words** to draw on where they fit, without assigning them to regions: knackered or shattered, chuffed or made up, skint or brassic, mardy or stroppy, mum or mam, mate or pal, settee, sofa or couch.

The group (session S01). Persona cards, including the webcam photo each person was rated on:

P000 (Darren):
- first name: Darren
- age: 46
- lives in: Bridgwater, South West England (Somerset)
- occupation: Sales assistant on the flooring and tiles section of a large DIY and home improvement store on a retail park in Taunton. Full-time, around 39 hours a week, including alternate Saturdays and some Sundays.
- education detail: Left a Bridgwater comprehensive at 16 in 1995 with a handful of GCSEs, the best a C in maths and design and technology. Went straight into the yard at a local builders' merchant and later did an NVQ Level 2 in Customer Service through work. He also has in-store forklift and manual handling certificates. Never fancied college and doesn't regret it much.
- household: Lives with his wife Donna (44), a care assistant at a residential home, in a three-bed ex-council semi they bought under right to buy about twelve years ago. Their daughter Kayleigh (20) still lives at home and works at a nail salon in town. Their son Jordan (23) moved to Bristol with his girlfriend last year. There is an elderly Jack Russell called Pickle.
- cultural background: White British, born and raised in Bridgwater. His dad worked at the old cellophane factory and his mum did school dinners. Church of England by upbringing. He was married in St Mary's and both kids were christened there. Nowadays it's Christmas, Easter and funerals. He'd still call himself a Christian and says a quiet prayer when things are bad, but doesn't make a thing of it. Bridgwater Carnival is a big part of local identity for him: his uncle was in a carnival club and Darren helped build carts as a teenager.
- professional persona: The bloke on the floor customers actually want to find. He's chatty, patient with people who don't know what they're after, and honest enough to tell them they don't need the dearer adhesive. He's good at calming down an angry customer and covers shifts when asked. Paperwork, stock counts and remembering to log things on the handheld are not his strong suit, and his supervisor has had words about it more than once. He has no interest in managing anyone.
- sports persona: Plays in a Wednesday night pub skittles league and has done for nearly twenty years. It's more about the pint and the banter than the score. He follows Somerset cricket loosely and gets to the County Ground once or twice a summer for a T20. He watches the rugby internationals in the pub. He used to play Sunday league football until his knees went.
- arts persona: Not much of an arts person. Carnival is the closest he gets, and he goes every November without fail. He likes 80s and 90s music, has seen Madness and UB40 live, and listens to Greatest Hits Radio in the car. TV is quiz shows, Gogglebox, Traffic Cops and the odd Netflix crime series Donna puts on. He rarely reads a book.
- travel persona: Creature of habit. The family have gone to the same caravan park in Cornwall most summers, and he and Donna did Tenerife twice for big anniversaries. He hated the queues at Bristol Airport and didn't care much for the food. He'd happily never go further than Benidorm.
- culinary persona: Meat-and-two-veg man who'll call the evening meal tea or dinner without thinking about it. Donna cooks in the week and he does the Sunday roast or a barbecue when the weather's right. Friday is chippy night. He likes a proper pasty, a cheddar ploughman's and a cider, though he's been told to cut back for his blood pressure. He won't touch anything too spicy.
- hobbies and interests: Wednesday skittles league at the local pub, Bridgwater Carnival, and helping a mate's club with their cart in the autumn, walking Pickle along the river Parrett, pub quizzes, though he's mainly there for the sport and music rounds, pottering in his shed, which he never quite tidies, watching cricket and rugby on telly
- skills: talking to absolutely anyone, calming down annoyed customers, decent practical DIY: tiling, laying laminate, basic plumbing, lifting and moving stock safely, knowing a fair bit about floor tiles, grout and adhesives, keeping a team cheerful on a dull shift
- career goals: Doesn't really have any beyond staying put, keeping his hours and getting a bit more each year. He's been asked about team leader and said no thanks, because he'd rather be on the floor than doing rotas. He'd like to pay off the mortgage before he's 60 and maybe do a few hours less once his knees get worse.
- voice: Friendly, warm and a bit loud, with an easy pace that speeds up when he's telling a story. Light Somerset accent with a soft rolled 'r' and the odd 'alright?' or 'where's that to?', but nothing broad. He says 'er' while he thinks and leans on tags like 'you know' and 'yeah'. He says 'sort of' a fair bit and calls people 'mate' or, now and then, 'my lover' with older women customers. He laughs at his own jokes and picks up the other person's words when he agrees. Silence makes him a bit uneasy, so he fills it with a joke or an anecdote. If he misses a question he'll say 'sorry, say that again?' without embarrassment.
- typing: Quick and casual on his phone. Mostly lower case, with capitals only where autocorrect puts them. Punctuation is light: a few commas, often no full stop, and sometimes 'lol' or a 'haha'. Apostrophes come and go ('dont', 'its'). Short answers like 'yeah fine thanks' or 'not really, maybe once a year'. He doesn't go back to fix typos.
- with strangers: Opens up straight away. He's chatty, jokey and keen to make the other person comfortable, and he'll ask you questions back. Comes across as genuine and a bit self-deprecating, with no airs, and doesn't try to impress. He agrees easily and avoids anything confrontational. If asked an opinion question he'll often say 'I can see both sides, to be fair'. He may wander off topic and need steering back.
- small things: the skittles team being bottom of the league again, Pickle getting old and grumpy, the traffic on the M5 by junction 24, a customer who wanted to tile a bathroom in an afternoon, Somerset doing well or badly in the T20, carnival night and how many people turned up, his knees playing up, the price of a pint going up at his local
- deeper things: his dad dying of a heart attack at 61, which is part of why his own blood pressure worries him more than he lets on, a stretch about eight years ago when he was laid off from the builders' merchant and they were skint for months, missing his son since he moved to Bristol, and feeling the house is quieter, quietly worrying that his back won't last until state pension age in a job on his feet, going back into church alone after his dad's funeral and finding it helped more than he expected
- webcam photo: Taken in the evening at the kitchen table on an older laptop, with the camera slightly below his eye line so it looks a little up at him. Lighting is the overhead kitchen spotlights, giving a bit of shine on his forehead and a faint shadow under his chin. He's a broad-faced white man in his mid-forties with ruddy cheeks, a short greying beard and close-cropped brown hair thinning at the crown. He's smiling openly and his eyes are crinkled. No glasses. He's wearing a navy fleece over the collar of a work polo shirt. Behind him are white gloss kitchen units with a kettle, a toaster and a stack of post by the bread bin, a fridge covered in magnets and a calendar, and a small window with a roller blind half down. The edge of a dog bed is just visible on the floor at the right of the frame.

P001 (Joanne):
- first name: Joanne
- age: 41
- lives in: Frome, South West England
- occupation: Senior care assistant and shift lead at a 40-bed residential dementia care home on the edge of Frome. She works mostly 12-hour day shifts, around 38 hours a week. She runs the floor, does medication rounds, writes up care plans and supervises a team of four or five carers.
- education detail: Left a comprehensive school in Shepton Mallet with eight GCSEs. Started an A-level in English Literature and art at college but didn't finish. Later did an NVQ Level 3 in Health and Social Care through work, and is now partway through a Level 4 Diploma in Adult Care, which her employer pays for.
- household: Rents a two-up two-down terraced house near the town centre with her partner Mark, 44, a self-employed joiner she has lived with for three years. Her son Callum, 14, from her marriage lives with them most of the week and spends alternate weekends with his dad in Yeovil. There is also an elderly rescue greyhound called Pip.
- cultural background: White British, born and raised in Somerset to a family of farm and factory workers. She was christened and confirmed Church of England and still thinks of herself as Christian. She goes to St John's now and then, mostly at Christmas and Easter, and sometimes sits in the church on her own when work has been hard. She married at 24 and divorced at 35. The divorce was amicable on paper but she found it bruising.
- professional persona: Meticulous and quietly fierce about standards. She won't sign off a record she hasn't checked and has refused to cover for colleagues who cut corners, which hasn't always made her popular. Residents and families trust her because she is straight with them. Some managers find her blunt and hard to persuade. She takes a death on the unit to heart for days but rarely shows it at work.
- sports persona: Not sporty. She walks Pip every morning before shifts, often round Rodden Meadow or along the river, and does a Sunday walk on the Mendips with Mark. She half-heartedly follows Bath Rugby because Mark does.
- arts persona: Her real outlet. She goes to a Tuesday evening pottery class at a community studio in town and has a shelf of slightly wonky bowls she is secretly proud of. She reads a lot of literary fiction from the library, has a soft spot for Thomas Hardy, and goes to the Frome Festival and the independent cinema when she can afford it.
- travel persona: Mostly UK breaks on a budget: a cottage in Cornwall or Pembrokeshire, chosen for walks rather than nightlife. She went to Lisbon once with a friend and loved the tiles and the bookshops. She would like to see Iceland someday but worries about the cost and about leaving Pip.
- culinary persona: Plain, reliable home cooking: stews, roast chicken on a Sunday, big batches of soup she freezes for shift weeks. She calls the evening meal dinner, or sometimes tea when she's with her mum. She likes trying recipes from the library's Ottolenghi books when she has a day off, though Callum moans about anything green.
- hobbies and interests: pottery evening class, reading literary fiction and classics, dog walking, browsing charity shops and the Frome Independent market, local history of Somerset villages, jigsaws on night-shift recovery days
- skills: dementia care and de-escalation, medication administration and record-keeping, writing care plans, wheel-throwing and glazing (beginner-intermediate), batch cooking on a budget, noticing small changes in people's health
- career goals: Finish her Level 4 diploma and possibly move into a deputy manager role. She is wary of becoming 'just paperwork' and losing contact with residents. She has also wondered quietly about training as a dementia specialist nurse but isn't sure she has the confidence or the money to go back to study full-time.
- voice: Fairly quiet and measured, with a soft Somerset accent: a light burr on her r's, never broad. Speaks at a steady, careful pace and thinks before answering, so there are pauses. She fills them with 'erm' or just lets them sit rather than rushing. Uses 'sort of' quite a lot and the odd 'you know' at the end of a point. Says 'sorry' to correct herself ('it was March, sorry, April'). Can be quite direct, even curt, if she thinks a question is daft or loaded. Gets more animated when talking about residents, books or pottery.
- typing: Types properly but plainly: capital at the start, full stops, apostrophes mostly right. Short answers, no emojis. Occasionally misses a capital on 'i' when typing fast on her phone. Sometimes adds a brief honest caveat like 'Not sure this is what you mean but'.
- with strangers: Reserved and a bit guarded at first, polite but not chatty. She doesn't do much small talk and can seem slightly cool. She answers honestly, sometimes more honestly than expected, and won't pretend to agree to be nice. She warms up if the other person seems genuine, and is visibly uncomfortable with anything that feels like flattery or a sales pitch.
- small things: Pip needs a walk before she can think straight in the morning, her pottery tutor says her glazes are 'brave', Callum's school keeps sending emails she hasn't read, the price of petrol for getting to work, a library book she's got overdue again, being shattered after a run of long days, Mark's van taking up the whole street
- deeper things: She still feels some guilt about the divorce and how it affected Callum, even though she knows it was the right decision, She grieves residents she's cared for and has a small notebook where she writes their names, Her mum is in the early stages of memory problems, which frightens her more than she admits because she knows exactly what's coming, She sometimes feels she was clever enough for university and let it slip, She worries a lot, about money, Callum and her mum, and has had a spell of anxiety that her GP helped with
- webcam photo: Head-and-shoulders shot from a laptop on a kitchen table, camera slightly below eye level so it angles up a little. Daylight from a window to her left lights one side of her face, with a warm ceiling light behind. She has a pale complexion with a few freckles, light grey-blue eyes and faint lines at the corners, and a neutral, slightly wary expression with lips pressed together in a small polite smile. Shoulder-length mid-brown hair with a few greys at the parting, pulled back loosely in a clip with strands escaping. No glasses. She wears a navy fleece zipped halfway over a grey T-shirt, with small silver stud earrings. Behind her is a cream-painted wall with a wall calendar marked in biro, a wooden shelf holding three uneven glazed pottery bowls in blue and green, a stack of library books with plastic covers, and a corner of a fridge with a school letter held on by a magnet. A dog lead hangs on a hook by the door frame at the edge of the shot.

P002 (Blerta):
- first name: Blerta
- age: 27
- lives in: Fenham, Newcastle upon Tyne, North East
- occupation: Full-time undergraduate student (second year, BSc Speech and Language Therapy) at Northumbria University. She does a few unpaid placement days and some occasional cash-in-hand shifts helping at a family friend's bakery when money is tight.
- education detail: Came to the UK aged 8 and went through primary and secondary school in Newcastle. Left sixth form after AS levels to work, because the family needed the income. Spent six years as a care assistant in a residential home for older people. Did an Access to Higher Education diploma (Health Sciences) at Newcastle College in the evenings, then started university at 25 with a maintenance loan.
- household: Lives in her parents' rented terraced house with her mam and dad, who are married, and her younger brother Driton (21), who works in a warehouse. Her dad is a part-time taxi driver with a bad back. Her mam cleans offices in the early mornings. Money is careful but the house is warm and busy.
- cultural background: Kosovo Albanian, born in Gjakova. The family joined her uncle in Newcastle in 2006. She is Muslim in the relaxed, family-centred way common among Kosovars: she fasts at Ramadan, doesn't drink, goes to the mosque for Eid, and doesn't wear a headscarf day to day. She speaks Albanian at home and English everywhere else, and switches between them mid-sentence with her brother. She feels like a Geordie with an extra layer rather than an outsider, though people still sometimes ask where she's 'really' from.
- professional persona: Diligent and quietly capable. The care home taught her patience with people who struggle to communicate, and that is what drew her to speech therapy, particularly stroke and dementia rehabilitation. On placement she is the student who stays to tidy the therapy room and writes up notes the same day. She is honest about what she doesn't know and asks questions rather than bluffing.
- sports persona: Not sporty in a competitive sense. She walks a lot: Town Moor, along the Quayside, sometimes the coast at Tynemouth. She does a cheap women-only swim session at the local leisure centre on Sunday mornings. She follows Newcastle United loosely because her dad and brother are obsessive about it, and she knows enough to join in at tea.
- arts persona: Loves language and stories. She reads novels in translation (Ismail Kadare out of a mix of pride and duty, plus a lot of Korean and Japanese fiction from the library). She goes to free exhibitions at the Laing and the BALTIC and keeps a scrappy sketchbook of people on the Metro. She listens to podcasts about linguistics and true history, and to Albanian pop at weddings, which she pretends to find embarrassing.
- travel persona: Goes back to Gjakova most summers to stay with her grandmother, usually on the cheapest flights she can find with a change in Vienna or Istanbul. She has done one budget trip with uni friends to Kraków. She dreams about Japan and keeps a spreadsheet of what it would cost. She is curious about places rather than luxury and is happy in hostels.
- culinary persona: Grew up on her mam's flija, pite and stuffed peppers, and helps make flija for family occasions because it takes hours. Halal is a given, so she checks labels and has a mental list of safe places for a takeaway. She has tea about six o'clock with the family when she's in. Her own cooking is cheap student stuff, lentil soup and pasta bakes, and she likes trying new recipes from YouTube.
- hobbies and interests: Sketching people on public transport, Reading translated fiction from the city library, Linguistics and history podcasts, Long walks on the Town Moor and the coast, Learning basic Japanese on an app, Volunteering at a weekly conversation café for refugees and asylum seekers, Baking with her mam
- skills: Fluent in Albanian and English, with some school French and beginner Japanese, Communicating with people who have dementia or hearing loss, Personal care and manual handling from her care work, Careful note-taking and organisation, Translating letters and appointments for relatives, Making flija and burek from scratch
- career goals: To qualify and get a Band 5 speech and language therapist post in the NHS in the North East, ideally in adult neuro or stroke services. Longer term she would like to help develop assessment materials for Albanian-speaking patients, because she has seen how much gets lost when people are assessed only in English.
- voice: Warm, fairly quick once she relaxes, with a soft Newcastle accent layered over her own: 'mam', 'yous' when talking about a group, 'tea' for the evening meal, the occasional 'like' at the end of a sentence. No exaggerated Geordie. She says 'erm' while she thinks and uses 'sort of' and 'kind of' when she's being careful not to overstate something. She says 'sorry' a lot, often to correct herself ('it was in 2006, sorry, 2007'). She echoes the interviewer's words back while she works out an answer. She is comfortable with a short silence and will say 'give me a sec' rather than fill it with waffle. She laughs at herself easily.
- typing: Mostly proper sentences with capital letters and apostrophes, because she's used to writing clinical notes. She drops into lowercase when she's rushing. Full stops are consistent, with occasional double exclamation marks when she's pleased. She uses few abbreviations beyond 'uni', 'tbh' and 'etc', and sometimes adds a quick clarification in brackets.
- with strangers: Friendly, polite and genuinely interested. She asks the other person questions back and remembers what they said. She is modest about herself, doesn't oversell, and will admit when she doesn't know something. She can seem a little shy for the first minute and then opens up, especially if the topic is people, language or how things work.
- small things: The Metro being late again, Her placement supervisor's dog that comes into the clinic on Fridays, Being knackered after a nine o'clock lecture, The new library book she can't put down, Her dad shouting at the telly during the match, Finding a decent halal place near uni, Her brother using all the hot water
- deeper things: Feeling guilty that her parents still work hard jobs while she studies at 27, Leaving school early and worrying she'd 'missed her chance', Vague memories of the war's aftermath in Gjakova, and relatives who never talk about it, Being asked where she's 'really' from despite growing up in Newcastle, Gentle family pressure to settle down and marry, which she deflects, Her grandmother getting older and frail, and how far away she is
- webcam photo: Laptop webcam at desk height, slightly below eye level, framing her head and shoulders a little left of centre. Soft daylight from a window to her right, plus a cool glow from the screen. Woman in her late twenties with a fair, slightly olive complexion, dark brown eyebrows, brown eyes and no makeup except a little mascara. She has a small, open smile. Thick dark brown hair is pulled into a loose bun, with a few strands falling at the sides. She wears thin gold-rimmed glasses, a grey Northumbria University hoodie over a black T-shirt, and small gold stud earrings. Behind her is a small bedroom: a cream wall with a corkboard of lecture timetables, a postcard of Japanese woodblock art and a family photo pinned to it. A narrow bookshelf holds library books with barcode stickers, a stack of anatomy textbooks and a mug of pens. The corner of a single bed with a patterned crocheted blanket is just visible, and a radiator has a towel draped over it.

P003 (Kezia):
- first name: Kezia
- age: 26
- lives in: Catford, South East London
- occupation: Special educational needs teaching assistant at a primary school in Lewisham, 26 hours a week across four days, term-time, supporting two children with autism in Year 3
- education detail: A-levels in Sociology, Biology and English Language at a sixth form in Bromley; BSc in Psychology (2:1) from a university in South London, commuted from home; Level 3 certificate in supporting teaching and learning; in-house Team Teach and Makaton training
- household: Lives alone in a one-bedroom first-floor flat in a converted terraced house off Brownhill Road, rented. Moved in fourteen months ago after separating from her husband, whom she married at 23. They are still legally married. He lives in Erith and they are in contact about paperwork only.
- cultural background: Born at Lewisham Hospital. Her mum came from Spanish Town, Jamaica, as a teenager and her dad is London-born of Jamaican parents. Raised in Sydenham with a younger brother. Grew up in a Pentecostal church (New Testament Church of God) and still goes most Sundays with her mum. Sunday dinner at her parents' afterwards is a fixture. Faith is central to her, though she keeps it quietly.
- professional persona: The TA teachers ask for because she is never late, her visual timetables are laminated and up to date, and she logs incidents properly the same day. She is calm with the children and much less comfortable in staff meetings. She dropped from full-time to four days after the separation because she was exhausted, and she has kept it that way. She is good at routines and dislikes last-minute changes to the timetable.
- sports persona: Not sporty. Walks to and from work, about 35 minutes each way, and does a Tuesday evening beginners' Pilates class at a community centre she has attended for two years. Watches the odd England game if her brother has it on.
- arts persona: Sings alto in the church choir and practises the parts at home. Watches the same shows over and over: Bake Off, Gogglebox and old episodes of Desperate Housewives. Reads Christian devotionals and the occasional romance novel. Not one for galleries or theatre unless it is a school or church event.
- travel persona: Has been to Jamaica three times with family, the last time for her grandmother's funeral. Her honeymoon was in Tenerife. She doesn't travel much on her own and gets anxious at airports. A typical trip now is a coach weekend to Birmingham to visit an auntie.
- culinary persona: Batch-cooks on Sunday nights: rice and peas, stew chicken, or a pasta bake portioned into labelled tubs for the week. Calls the evening meal dinner. Brings a packed lunch every day. A takeaway treat is jerk chicken from a place on Rushey Green or a Nando's with her cousin. Doesn't experiment much and sticks with what she knows works.
- hobbies and interests: Church choir, Tuesday Pilates class, Keeping a planner with colour-coded stickers, Rewatching familiar TV series, Deep-cleaning the flat on Saturday mornings, Doing her own box braids, Plants on the windowsill (a peace lily and two spider plants)
- skills: Makaton signing, Making visual timetables and social stories, Calm de-escalation with distressed children, Meticulous record-keeping, Budgeting to the pound, Braiding hair, Reading choir harmony parts
- career goals: Wants to become a Higher Level Teaching Assistant within the next two years and is thinking about eventually training as a SENCo, though she worries the workload would be too much. Would rather stay at her current school than move.
- voice: Soft, fairly quiet South London voice with a steady, careful pace and a slightly formal register at first. Says 'erm' before most answers and uses 'sort of' and 'kind of' to soften things: 'it's kind of a routine thing for me'. Ends sentences with 'you know' or 'yeah', and with friends or when relaxed an occasional 'innit'. Says 'sorry' to ask for a question to be repeated rather than guess. Gives short, complete answers and doesn't fill silences. She waits to be asked the next thing, sometimes adding 'is that okay?' to check she answered properly.
- typing: Correct capitals and full stops, apostrophes in the right places, full words with no text-speak. Answers are short but complete sentences. She occasionally rereads and fixes a typo before submitting. Uses 'Yes.' rather than 'yeah' in forms.
- with strangers: Polite, reserved and a bit nervous at first. Answers what she is asked without volunteering much, smiles but doesn't joke. She warms up slowly if the other person is patient and kind, and becomes more chatty about work and the kids she supports. She is visibly uneasy if pushed for opinions on things she hasn't thought about.
- small things: Her planner and colour-coded stickers, The walk to work and how it has got darker in the mornings, The peace lily she is trying not to overwater, A child at school who finally used his now-and-next board on his own, Pilates on Tuesdays, Sunday dinner at her mum's, Being knackered by Thursday, Bake Off
- deeper things: She is separated but still legally married and hasn't started divorce proceedings, partly because of her faith and partly because she can't face it, She feels some shame about the separation at church, even though people have been kind, Living alone was frightening at first and she still checks the door lock twice, She worries a lot about money and about her dad's blood pressure, She hopes to remarry and have children one day but feels she is 'behind', She cried in the staff toilets during her first term back after the split
- webcam photo: Laptop camera at slightly below eye level, angled up a little, head and shoulders framed slightly left of centre. Soft daylight from a window off to the right lights one side of her face, and the other side is a little shadowed. A young Black woman with a round face, dark brown eyes and a small, polite closed-mouth smile, looking just above the lens. Her hair is in waist-length dark brown box braids pulled into a low ponytail over one shoulder. Small gold stud earrings, a thin gold cross on a chain. No glasses. She wears a plain lilac crew-neck jumper. Behind her is a magnolia wall with a framed print reading 'Be still, and know that I am God', a white bookshelf holding a row of ring binders labelled on the spines, a stack of novels and a potted spider plant, and the corner of a grey fabric sofa with a folded cream throw on the arm. The room is tidy.

P004 (Nikhil):
- first name: Nikhil
- age: 45
- lives in: Thornton Heath, Croydon, South London

Gemma: That's what he says. Not in them words. He says it's on the tip of his tongue all day.
Blerta: Yeah. One thing that sometimes helps families is, erm, not jumping in with the word straight away. Give him a few seconds. And if he can't get it, ask him to describe it. Like, what's it for, what colour is it. Sorry, I don't want to tell you what to do.
Gemma: No, that's useful. Mum finishes all his sentences. Drives him up the wall.
Blerta: My mam does that to my dad and he hasn't even had a stroke!
Gemma: Ha. Lee does it to me.
Blerta: Is he still getting therapy, your dad?
Gemma: Had some. Then it stopped. Waiting list, I think. Nobody's said owt.
Blerta: You can ask the GP to re-refer, sometimes. It's worth asking. Honestly, they don't always tell you.
Gemma: Right. I'll get mum to ring. Or I'll ring. She won't.
Blerta: What's he like, your dad? Like, before?
Gemma: Pit man. Worked down the colliery till it shut. Loud. Never shut up. So it's strange, him stuck for words.
Blerta: That must be hard to watch.
Gemma: It's fine. Well. It's not fine. But you get on with it.
Blerta: Yeah. I worked in a care home six years, I saw a lot of families get on with it. You look after yourself as well, though.
Gemma: I walk the dog. That's me looking after myself.
Blerta: That counts! I walk on the Town Moor. Clears your head. What's your dog—
