req.text:
You write transcripts of realistic video calls between strangers for a fully synthetic research dataset set in the UK. The study, in order (from its published design): a short puzzle task done alone; first impressions of the others' webcam photos; then a series of three-minute, one-on-one video calls in rounds, each person meeting the others in their group; after each call a short survey.

Call shape (from the original study's numbers): a call is cut off by a three-minute timer. A typical call has about 30 turns (most between 20 and 39) and about 570 words in total (most between 440 and 682); half of all turns are 12 words or fewer, and a quarter are 24 or more. Short acknowledgements ("yeah", "mm") count as turns too. So aim for about 570 words in about 30 turns: alongside the quick back-and-forth, people often talk in longer stretches (explaining their job, telling a story), and those long turns carry much of the call.

Guide to British conversational English (use it for how people talk; it is a description of speech, not a script):
How British people talk in casual conversation. This is a paraphrase of published descriptions of spoken British English; sources are in SOURCES.md. Use these features lightly and only where they fit the person. Never use them as a caricature.

- **Fillers.** British speakers hesitate with "erm" and "er". Women and younger speakers lean towards "erm".
- **Hedges.** "Sort of" is everywhere and steady. "Kind of" is spreading, and younger speakers use it more.
- **Politeness words.** "Please", "thank you", "thanks" and "sorry" mostly mean what they say. "Sorry" also works as a repair word (to correct yourself, or to ask someone to repeat) and can be ironic.
- **Tags at the end of a sentence.** "You know", "right", "okay", "yeah", "do you know what I mean". Among young Londoners, "innit" and "you get me" are rising. Tags depend on age and region only, never on ethnicity.
- **Echoing.** In an engaged conversation people pick up and re-use parts of each other's words.
- **Regional words and grammar** (from a recent dialect survey):
  - A bread roll is a "barm" in the North West (Manchester to Liverpool and western Lancashire), a "cob" around Nottinghamshire, a "bap" in Staffordshire, the West Midlands and North Wales, and a "batch" in Liverpool and Coventry.
  - Around Liverpool an ice lolly can be a "lolly ice".
  - The evening meal is "tea" in the North West, North East and Yorkshire, and "dinner" in the South East and London. Some people say both.
  - "Yous" or "youse" for plural "you" is common in the North East (Newcastle, Teesside), Liverpool and Scotland, less so in Manchester, and rare in York, Leeds and Sheffield.
  - "Give it me" is normal in the North West and West Midlands and widely accepted in Sheffield and York; it fades south of Birmingham, Coventry and Leicester.
  - "You was" is widely used, historically Northern and now found as far south as London.
- **Everyday British words** to draw on where they fit, without assigning them to regions: knackered or shattered, chuffed or made up, skint or brassic, mardy or stroppy, mum or mam, mate or pal, settee, sofa or couch.

The group (session S08). Persona cards, including the webcam photo each person was rated on:

P034 (Bianca):
- first name: Bianca
- age: 20
- lives in: Wolverhampton, West Midlands
- occupation: Full-time second-year undergraduate student studying Accounting and Finance at the University of Wolverhampton. She isn't working at the moment. She did a few months of seasonal stock-room shifts at a retail park last winter but gave them up to focus on her course.
- education detail: Came to the UK aged eight and went through a local primary and secondary school in Wolverhampton. She got decent GCSEs and A-levels in Maths, Business and Psychology at a sixth form college. Now in her second year of a BA (Hons) in Accounting and Finance, commuting to the city campus by bus.
- household: Rents a small one-bedroom flat above a row of shops in Bilston with her boyfriend Kyle, 22, who works shifts at a distribution warehouse off the M6. They moved in together about a year ago, mostly because it worked out cheaper than both living with family. Her mum and younger brother live about fifteen minutes away.
- cultural background: Born in Craiova, Romania. She moved to Wolverhampton with her mum, who came for work in care homes, and her stepdad joined later. She speaks Romanian with her mum and grandmother on video calls but thinks in English now and would describe herself as 'basically from Wolves'. Not religious. Her nan in Romania is Orthodox and she'll go along to church at Easter if she's visiting, but only for the food afterwards. She doesn't make a big deal of her background unless asked.
- professional persona: Practical and quietly ambitious. She picked accounting because it pays and the jobs don't go away, not out of passion. She's steady rather than a high-flyer. She hands work in on time but doesn't overdo it, and she's good at working out what the marker actually wants. In group projects she's the easy-going one who doesn't argue but makes sure her name is on the parts that look good.
- sports persona: Not sporty. She goes to a budget gym near the flat two or three evenings a week, mostly treadmill and machines with headphones in, and likes that nobody talks to her there. She'll watch Wolves highlights if Kyle has them on but couldn't name more than a few players.
- arts persona: Mostly TV and phone. She binge-watches crime dramas and reality shows, follows a few makeup and 'clean girl' aesthetic accounts, and listens to whatever's on her Spotify daily mix. She hasn't been to a gallery since a school trip and doesn't feel she's missing much.
- travel persona: Goes back to Romania most summers to see her nan, flying from Birmingham. She has done one cheap girls' holiday to Magaluf and wants something nicer next time. She likes the idea of Dubai or somewhere with a good hotel more than backpacking. She is good at finding deals and will happily bend baggage rules.
- culinary persona: Cooks simple stuff: pasta, stir-fries, air-fryer chicken. Her mum sends her home with sarmale and ciorbă in tubs. She and Kyle get a Chinese or a Nando's on Fridays. Calls the evening meal tea or dinner interchangeably and a bread roll a bap without thinking about it. Sweet tooth, always has chocolate in the cupboard.
- hobbies and interests: watching crime and reality TV, makeup and skincare, gym sessions on her own, scrolling TikTok and Instagram, finding discount codes and resale bargains on Vinted, occasional nights out in Birmingham with two close friends, video calls with her nan
- skills: fluent in English and Romanian, Excel and basic bookkeeping software, budgeting and spotting a good deal, staying calm when things go wrong, doing her own nails and brows, getting along with almost anyone without much fuss
- career goals: Wants to get a placement year at an accountancy firm in Birmingham, qualify through ACCA or similar, and be earning properly by her mid-twenties. She'd like to own a house before thirty and have 'nice stuff', and is fairly open that money is the main motivation.
- voice: Quiet, fairly flat and unhurried. She speaks clearly in a light Wolverhampton/Black Country accent, with no trace of Romanian unless she's saying a Romanian word. Her answers are short and to the point, often starting with 'erm' or 'yeah, so'. She uses 'kind of' and 'like' quite a bit and occasionally ends with 'do you know what I mean' or 'yeah'. She'll say things like 'give it me' or 'we was going to' without noticing. Silence doesn't bother her. She'll just wait for the next question rather than fill the gap, and she sometimes needs a prompt to expand. Polite and agreeable, says 'sorry, what was that?' if she mishears.
- typing: Mostly lowercase, no capital at the start, and often no full stop at the end. Apostrophes are usually dropped ('dont', 'im', 'its'). She uses common abbreviations like 'tbh', 'idk' and 'bc', and gives short answers of a few words unless the box clearly needs more. The occasional 'lol' sneaks in.
- with strangers: Reserved but pleasant. She doesn't volunteer much at first and can come across as a bit detached or bored, though she's actually fine. She agrees easily and won't challenge the interviewer, and she warms up a little if the topic is something practical like money, uni or TV. She's not anxious and doesn't seem to worry about saying the wrong thing.
- small things: the bus into uni being late again, Kyle's night shifts meaning she has the flat to herself, a new skincare product she got half price, what she's currently binging on Netflix, being knackered after a seminar day, her mum sending her home with too much food, assignment deadlines piling up
- deeper things: she doesn't really remember much about Romania and sometimes feels odd being 'foreign' on paper, she sees the flat with Kyle as more practical than romantic and isn't sure it's forever, growing up with her mum working long care shifts made her determined never to be skint, she's a bit closer to her nan than to her stepdad, she sometimes stretches the truth on forms or applications and doesn't feel particularly guilty about it
- webcam photo: Head-and-shoulders shot from a laptop webcam slightly below eye level, so the angle looks up a little at her chin. The light comes from a window off to her left, with a faint blue tint from the screen on her face. She has a pale complexion, light freckles across her nose, groomed brows and a neutral, slightly unimpressed expression with her mouth closed. Her dark blonde hair is scraped back into a claw clip with a few loose strands at the front. She wears small gold hoop earrings, no glasses, and an oversized grey hoodie. Behind her is a magnolia wall with a cheap white floating shelf holding a scented candle, a few makeup palettes and a framed photo of her and Kyle. To the right edge of the frame is part of a grey fabric settee with a crumpled fleece throw and a phone charger cable trailing over the arm.

P035 (Lee):
- first name: Lee
- age: 50
- lives in: Hucknall, Nottinghamshire, East Midlands
- occupation: Quality technician at an aerospace components supplier on an industrial estate near Hucknall. He does dimensional inspection of machined parts on a CMM, writes up non-conformance reports and keeps the calibration records in order. He supervises two junior inspectors on days.
- education detail: Left a comprehensive in Bulwell at 16 with GCSEs, mostly Cs and a B in maths. Did an engineering apprenticeship with a BTEC National in Mechanical Engineering. Later did an HNC part-time at college in Nottingham, paid for by his employer in his late twenties. He has done various internal courses since, including Lean, root cause analysis and GD&T.
- household: Lives with his wife Karen (49, part-time receptionist at a GP surgery) in a three-bed semi they bought in 2001. Their son Ryan (24) moved out two years ago to a flat in Arnold with his girlfriend. Their daughter Megan (20) is at university in Sheffield and comes back some weekends and for the holidays. Ryan's old room is now Lee's 'office', mostly used for paperwork and the occasional Teams call.
- cultural background: White British, born and raised in north Nottingham. His dad worked at a colliery until the pits closed and then went on the buses; his mum worked in a hosiery factory. Christian, Church of England. He goes to the parish church with Karen at Christmas, Easter and Remembrance Sunday, and sometimes helps with setting up chairs for the harvest supper. He doesn't talk about faith much but considers himself a believer in a quiet, steady way.
- professional persona: Thorough, reliable and slightly pedantic about procedure. He is the one people go to when an audit is coming because his records are always up to date. He has been with the same firm for nineteen years, and with one earlier firm before that. He prefers to deal with problems by email so there is a paper trail, and he dislikes meetings that run over. He is fair with the junior inspectors but doesn't socialise much at work beyond the Christmas do, where he leaves early.
- sports persona: Notts County supporter from childhood, though he goes to Meadow Lane only a handful of times a season now and mostly follows on the radio or the app. He played Sunday league cricket for a village side until his early forties. Now he walks most evenings, about three miles on a fixed loop, and logs it on his phone.
- arts persona: Not much interested. He watches police dramas and documentaries about engineering or the war on telly. He likes 70s and 80s rock (Status Quo, Dire Straits) in the car. He reads the odd thriller on holiday, usually one Karen has finished.
- travel persona: Creature of habit. The family has gone to the same static caravan park near Mablethorpe for years, and now it's the two of them for a week in summer. They had one trip to Majorca for their 25th anniversary, which he enjoyed more than he expected but hasn't pushed to repeat. He plans routes and packing well in advance.
- culinary persona: Plain food. He has a cooked breakfast on Saturdays and a Sunday roast. Karen does most weekday cooking, but he does a decent chilli and is in charge of the barbecue. He takes a ham cob and an apple to work most days. Not keen on spicy or 'fancy' food; he'll have a chicken korma at most.
- hobbies and interests: Allotment, which he has had for twelve years, kept very tidy, with a written planting plan, Coarse fishing at a local lake, usually alone, early on a Sunday, Washing and maintaining the car, Doing the crossword and sudoku in the paper, Following Notts County, Evening walks
- skills: Precision measurement and CMM programming, Technical report writing and record keeping, Basic DIY: tiling, fitting shelves, plumbing in a washing machine, Vegetable growing, Spreadsheets in Excel, including the household budget
- career goals: Mostly to see out his working life where he is, ideally stepping up to quality lead when his manager retires in a couple of years. He has thought about retiring at 62 if the pension sums add up, and has a spreadsheet for it. He is not interested in moving firms or retraining.
- voice: Quiet, measured and fairly slow. He answers what is asked and stops, often with short answers that he'll expand only if prompted. Mild Nottingham accent with a flat, unhurried tone. He says 'cob' for a bread roll and will occasionally say 'mardy' or 'me duck' to people he knows, but not to strangers on a call. He uses 'er' before a considered answer and 'sort of' as a hedge, plus 'to be fair' and 'I'd say'. He is comfortable with silence and won't rush to fill it, and he may simply wait for the next question. He is precise with numbers and dates, and will correct himself ('sorry, it was 2014, not 2013').
- typing: Proper capitals and full stops, apostrophes in the right places, and no text-speak. Answers are short and complete, often one or two sentences. He occasionally uses brackets to add a detail. No emojis or exclamation marks.
- with strangers: Polite, reserved and a bit wary at first. He comes across as serious rather than unfriendly, gives straight answers without small talk, and seems keen to do things properly and on time. He warms slightly if the topic is practical, like his job, the allotment or fishing, but never becomes chatty.
- small things: The runner beans have done well this year, Traffic on the A611 in the morning, County's latest result, Having to recalibrate a gauge at work, Saturday breakfast, The caravan booking for next summer, Getting the car through its MOT
- deeper things: His dad died of a lung condition linked to the pits, and he thinks about his own health more than he lets on, He feels a bit lost since the kids left and the house is quiet, He worries quietly about Megan living away in Sheffield, He was turned down for a promotion ten years ago and still feels it was unfair, He finds church services a calm place, even if he wouldn't say so
- webcam photo: Laptop webcam, slightly below eye level, so the shot angles a little up at him. Daylight comes from a window to his left, with the ceiling light also on, giving even but slightly flat light. Head and shoulders, centred. A man of 50 with a lean face and close-cropped greying brown hair, thinning on top. Clean-shaven with a faint shadow. Thin silver-framed reading glasses. Neutral, attentive expression, lips closed, a slight crease between the brows. He is wearing a navy quarter-zip fleet-style fleece over a pale blue collared shirt. Behind him is a magnolia wall with a framed photo of two young adults at a graduation, a wall calendar from a local garden centre with dates written in biro, and a white flat-pack bookshelf. On the shelf are ring binders labelled by year, a small stack of fishing magazines and a Notts County mug holding pens.

P036 (Jasmine):
- first name: Jasmine
- age: 32
- lives in: Plymouth, South West England
- occupation: Co-owner and managing director of two franchised bubble tea outlets in Plymouth city centre. She works about 12 hours a week, mostly on rotas, stock orders, supplier calls and checking the books. A full-time shift supervisor handles the day-to-day.
- education detail: Finished secondary school (SPM, then STPM) in Ipoh, Malaysia. Moved to the UK at 18 and took a BSc in Business Management at the University of Plymouth, graduating with a 2:1 in 2014. Has done food hygiene and franchise operations courses since. No postgraduate study, and no interest in any.
- household: Rents a three-bed new-build semi in Plymstock with her partner Tom, 35, a marine engineer at Devonport. They've been together seven years and aren't married. Neither feels much need to be. No children. They have a grey British Shorthair called Biscuit.
- cultural background: Malaysian Chinese, born and raised in Ipoh, Perak. Her parents run a small hardware shop there and her older brother lives in Kuala Lumpur. She grew up speaking Cantonese at home and Malay and English at school. She was raised loosely Buddhist-Taoist through her grandparents but has no religion herself and only keeps the family side of Chinese New Year. She got British citizenship in 2022 and thinks of Plymouth as home now, though she calls Malaysia 'back home' when talking about family.
- professional persona: Practical and money-focused. She opened the first unit in 2019 with savings, a loan from her dad and Tom as guarantor, then added a second in 2022. She likes being the boss and having 'Director' on Companies House, but doesn't want to work long hours if she doesn't have to. She's good at haggling with suppliers and landlords and isn't shy about pushing for a better deal. She'll take a shortcut on paperwork if she thinks nobody will check. Staff find her fair but brisk.
- sports persona: Goes to a PureGym three times a week, mostly treadmill and weights machines, headphones in. She isn't sporty in a team sense. She'll go to Home Park with Tom a couple of times a season for the atmosphere and a pint, but couldn't name many Argyle players. Does the odd 5k charity run if a friend asks.
- arts persona: Not really an arts person. She watches Netflix and reality TV (Love Island, Selling Sunset, Married at First Sight Australia) and the occasional Korean drama her mum recommends. Listens to whatever's on Spotify's Today's Top Hits in the car. She's been to the Theatre Royal for a musical once or twice, usually because someone bought tickets for a birthday.
- travel persona: Flies back to Malaysia roughly every 18 months to two years for two or three weeks, usually via Doha. Otherwise she likes easy, comfortable holidays: all-inclusive in Tenerife or Turkey, a long weekend in London for shopping and a nice dinner. Not interested in backpacking or 'finding herself'. She likes a good hotel and a pool.
- culinary persona: Cooks simple home-style Chinese and Malaysian dishes a few times a week: rice, stir-fried veg, steamed fish, curry chicken when she can be bothered. She buys from the Oriental supermarket near the city centre and complains that you can't get proper Ipoh bean sprout chicken or decent char kway teow in Plymouth. Tom cooks roasts and pasta. Calls the evening meal 'dinner'. Likes a Sunday carvery more than she lets on.
- hobbies and interests: gym sessions with podcasts or playlists, reality TV and Netflix bingeing, browsing and buying skincare, mostly Korean and Japanese brands, Vinted and eBay for selling clothes she's bored of, keeping an eye on property prices on Rightmove, weekend walks on Plymouth Hoe or out at Wembury with Tom, video calls with her mum on Sundays
- skills: supplier negotiation, staff rota planning and basic HR, bookkeeping in Xero, fluent Cantonese, Malay and English, reading a lease and spotting a bad clause, stock forecasting for a small food business, confident haggling generally
- career goals: Wants to open a third unit, possibly in Exeter, without increasing her own hours much. Longer term she'd like to own a couple of buy-to-let flats so the money comes in without her being there. She'd happily sell the franchise units for a good price in five or ten years. She isn't interested in climbing a corporate ladder. She wants to be comfortable and in charge of her own time.
- voice: Clear, fairly quick, matter-of-fact. Her accent is mostly Malaysian English softened by 14 years in the South West: slightly clipped consonants, some Malaysian rhythm. She's picked up British phrasing like 'to be fair', 'sort of', 'proper busy' and 'I'm knackered'. Uses 'erm' when thinking, ends points with 'yeah' or 'you know'. Says 'sorry?' if she didn't catch something, without fuss. Doesn't fill silences nervously. She'll just wait or say 'yeah, that's it really'. Occasionally lets a 'lah' slip when she's relaxed or laughing, then carries on as if nothing happened. Gives short, direct answers unless asked about money, business or something she has a firm opinion on.
- typing: Quick and practical. Usually starts with a capital, but often drops full stops at the end and skips apostrophes ('dont', 'im', 'its fine'). Uses 'tbh', 'ok' and 'thx'. Rarely uses emojis in forms. Answers are short, sometimes a single phrase, unless the question is about work.
- with strangers: Friendly enough but businesslike and a bit guarded at first. She's confident, doesn't get flustered, and isn't trying hard to be liked. Can come across as slightly blunt or pleased with herself when she mentions owning a business. She warms up if the conversation turns to something practical she knows about. Not much for small talk about feelings or abstract ideas.
- small things: the cat knocking things off the kitchen counter, how much the parking costs in the city centre, a new skincare serum she's trying, the gym being packed in January, staff calling in sick on a Saturday, the Oriental supermarket running out of her usual soy sauce brand, rain on the Hoe ruining a weekend walk, a Vinted sale that went for more than she expected
- deeper things: Her dad still talks about the loan as if she owes him the business, and it gets under her skin, Her cousins in Singapore earn far more than she does and she quietly keeps score, She isn't sure she wants children, and Tom's mum keeps hinting, She doesn't really miss Malaysia day to day and sometimes feels guilty that she doesn't, She and Tom have never bothered to marry and she's not sure she ever will, partly because she likes keeping her finances separate, She worried more than she admitted when one unit nearly closed during a slow winter
- webcam photo: Laptop webcam at roughly eye level, slightly off-centre, showing head and shoulders. The light comes mostly from a window to her left, so the right side of her face is a little shadowed and there's a faint warm cast from a ceiling light. East Asian woman in her early thirties with straight black shoulder-length hair tucked behind one ear and light, neat makeup. She has a slight, composed half-smile, looking directly into the camera. No glasses. She wears a plain dusky-pink crewneck sweatshirt with small gold stud earrings. Behind her is a light grey painted wall in an open-plan kitchen-diner. A white IKEA shelf holds a small potted snake plant, a stack of three folders labelled in marker, and a jar of chopsticks. To the right, the edge of a grey L-shaped sofa is visible with a mustard cushion, and on the sofa arm a grey cat is half out of frame. A wall calendar with handwritten shift notes hangs slightly crooked near the doorway.

P037 (Gareth):
- first name: Gareth
- age: 44
- lives in: Walthamstow, London
- occupation: Structural engineer (associate level) at a mid-sized engineering consultancy in Farringdon, mostly working on residential conversions and mid-rise commercial refurbishments
- education detail: Grew up in Bromley and went to a comprehensive there. Did A-levels in maths, physics and geography, then a MEng in Civil Engineering at the University of Nottingham. Became a chartered engineer (MIStructE) in his early thirties. He passed the exam on the second attempt, which he puts down to not bothering to revise properly the first time.
- household: Lives alone in a rented one-bedroom first-floor flat in a converted Victorian terrace off Hoe Street. Never married. He had a long relationship through most of his thirties that ended about five years ago. He has no children and no pets. The landlord has been promising to fix the bathroom extractor fan for two years.
- cultural background: White British, born in Farnborough Hospital and raised in Bromley in south-east London. His dad was a heating engineer and his mum was a school receptionist. He was baptised and confirmed Church of England. He still calls himself Christian and goes to a carol service most Christmases with his mum, but otherwise doesn't attend. He has a younger sister in Sevenoaks with two kids. He supports Crystal Palace out of family habit rather than real passion.
- professional persona: Competent and quick at the technical side. He's good at spotting what will actually fail and what's just overcautious. He is less good at paperwork: his timesheets are always late and his calc packages get tidied up at the last minute. He's known for being blunt with architects and contractors. Some clients like that, and a couple have asked for someone else. He doesn't get rattled on site or in difficult meetings, so he tends to get sent to the awkward jobs. He mentors graduates, but in a 'work it out and then come and ask me' way.
- sports persona: Played five-a-side every Wednesday until he did his knee in at 39. Now he mostly watches. He'll go to Selhurst Park a few times a season with an old school mate and watches the rest in the pub. He has a gym membership he uses maybe twice a month, and he cycles along the Lea some weekends when the weather's decent.
- arts persona: Not a big gallery person, though he likes architecture and will happily wander round the Barbican or look at old warehouse conversions. req.text:
You write transcripts of realistic video calls between strangers for a fully synthetic research dataset set in the UK. The study, in order (from its published design): a short puzzle task done alone; first impressions of the others' webcam photos; then a series of three-minute, one-on-one video calls in rounds, each person meeting the others in their group; after each call a short survey.

Call shape (from the original study's numbers): a call is cut off by a three-minute timer. A typical call has about 30 turns (most between 20 and 39) and about 570 words in total (most between 440 and 682); half of all turns are 12 words or fewer, and a quarter are 24 or more. Short acknowledgements ("yeah", "mm") count as turns too. So aim for about 570 words in about 30 turns: alongside the quick back-and-forth, people often talk in longer stretches (explaining their job, telling a story), and those long turns carry much of the call.

Guide to British conversational English (use it for how people talk; it is a description of speech, not a script):
How British people talk in casual conversation. This is a paraphrase of published descriptions of spoken British English; sources are in SOURCES.md. Use these features lightly and only where they fit the person. Never use them as a caricature.

- **Fillers.** British speakers hesitate with "erm" and "er". Women and younger speakers lean towards "erm".
- **Hedges.** "Sort of" is everywhere and steady. "Kind of" is spreading, and younger speakers use it more.
- **Politeness words.** "Please", "thank you", "thanks" and "sorry" mostly mean what they say. "Sorry" also works as a repair word (to correct yourself, or to ask someone to repeat) and can be ironic.
- **Tags at the end of a sentence.** "You know", "right", "okay", "yeah", "do you know what I mean". Among young Londoners, "innit" and "you get me" are rising. Tags depend on age and region only, never on ethnicity.
- **Echoing.** In an engaged conversation people pick up and re-use parts of each other's words.
- **Regional words and grammar** (from a recent dialect survey):
  - A bread roll is a "barm" in the North West (Manchester to Liverpool and western Lancashire), a "cob" around Nottinghamshire, a "bap" in Staffordshire, the West Midlands and North Wales, and a "batch" in Liverpool and Coventry.
  - Around Liverpool an ice lolly can be a "lolly ice".
  - The evening meal is "tea" in the North West, North East and Yorkshire, and "dinner" in the South East and London. Some people say both.
  - "Yous" or "youse" for plural "you" is common in the North East (Newcastle, Teesside), Liverpool and Scotland, less so in Manchester, and rare in York, Leeds and Sheffield.
  - "Give it me" is normal in the North West and West Midlands and widely accepted in Sheffield and York; it fades south of Birmingham, Coventry and Leicester.
  - "You was" is widely used, historically Northern and now found as far south as London.
- **Everyday British words** to draw on where they fit, without assigning them to regions: knackered or shattered, chuffed or made up, skint or brassic, mardy or stroppy, mum or mam, mate or pal, settee, sofa or couch.

He would like to do a big trip to South America during a summer holiday.
- culinary persona: A keen, slightly showy cook. He does a proper Sunday roast, makes his own focaccia, and owns a Le Creuset he's very proud of. He likes trying new restaurants and keeps a running list from Instagram and Jay Rayner reviews. Walthamstow's food scene suits him: Eat17, the Thursday market, small plates in Blackhorse Road. He calls the evening meal 'dinner'. He knows a bit about wine, or acts like he does.

- career goals: To become an assistant head within two years, then deputy, then head of his own school by his early forties. He has also thought about moving into a trust-level role or consultancy, where the money is better. He sometimes talks about writing a popular history book or doing a podcast. He likes the idea of being 'known' for something.
- voice: Fast, warm and confident, with an Essex-to-London estuary accent. He drops some t's and says 'fink' only occasionally when relaxed. He talks easily and at length, tells anecdotes, and laughs at his own jokes a bit. He uses 'sort of' and 'you know' a lot. He says 'mate' even to people he's just met. He sometimes ends a point with 'do you know what I mean?' and occasionally says 'innit', half-ironically, picked up from the kids at school. He fills pauses with 'er' rather than letting them sit, and hates silence on a call. He'll jump in to fill a gap or ask the interviewer a question back. He picks up the interviewer's words and reuses them to build rapport. He says 'sorry' mostly as a repair word, as in 'sorry, what I mean is...'.
- typing: Quick and fairly tidy, because he's a teacher and notices errors. He uses capitals at the start of sentences and gets apostrophes right. He sometimes skips the final full stop. He uses dashes and the odd exclamation mark. He uses abbreviations like 'tbh', 'e.g.' and 'etc' but not text-speak. His answers tend to be longer than needed, with a bit of personality, for example: 'Probably the theatre tbh - we try to go every couple of months'.
- with strangers: Instantly friendly and easy to talk to. He asks your name, uses it, finds something in common, and makes a joke within the first minute. He's very likeable on first meeting, and most people come away thinking he's great company. req.text:
You write transcripts of realistic video calls between strangers for a fully synthetic research dataset set in the UK. The study, in order (from its published design): a short puzzle task done alone; first impressions of the others' webcam photos; then a series of three-minute, one-on-one video calls in rounds, each person meeting the others in their group; after each call a short survey.

Call shape (from the original study's numbers): a call is cut off by a three-minute timer. A typical call has about 30 turns (most between 20 and 39) and about 570 words in total (most between 440 and 682); half of all turns are 12 words or fewer, and a quarter are 24 or more. Short acknowledgements ("yeah", "mm") count as turns too. So aim for about 570 words in about 30 turns: alongside the quick back-and-forth, people often talk in longer stretches (explaining their job, telling a story), and those long turns carry much of the call.

Guide to British conversational English (use it for how people talk; it is a description of speech, not a script):
How British people talk in casual conversation. This is a paraphrase of published descriptions of spoken British English; sources are in SOURCES.md. Use these features lightly and only where they fit the person. Never use them as a caricature.

- **Fillers.** British speakers hesitate with "erm" and "er". Women and younger speakers lean towards "erm".
- **Hedges.** "Sort of" is everywhere and steady. "Kind of" is spreading, and younger speakers use it more.
- **Politeness words.** "Please", "thank you", "thanks" and "sorry" mostly mean what they say. "Sorry" also works as a repair word (to correct yourself, or to ask someone to repeat) and can be ironic.
- **Tags at the end of a sentence.** "You know", "right", "okay", "yeah", "do you know what I mean". Among young Londoners, "innit" and "you get me" are rising. Tags depend on age and region only, never on ethnicity.
- **Echoing.** In an engaged conversation people pick up and re-use parts of each other's words.
- **Regional words and grammar** (from a recent dialect survey):
  - A bread roll is a "barm" in the North West (Manchester to Liverpool and western Lancashire), a "cob" around Nottinghamshire, a "bap" in Staffordshire, the West Midlands and North Wales, and a "batch" in Liverpool and Coventry.
  - Around Liverpool an ice lolly can be a "lolly ice".
  - The evening meal is "tea" in the North West, North East and Yorkshire, and "dinner" in the South East and London. Some people say both.
  - "Yous" or "youse" for plural "you" is common in the North East (Newcastle, Teesside), Liverpool and Scotland, less so in Manchester, and rare in York, Leeds and Sheffield.
  - "Give it me" is normal in the North West and West Midlands and widely accepted in Sheffield and York; it fades south of Birmingham, Coventry and Leicester.
  - "You was" is widely used, historically Northern and now found as far south as London.
- **Everyday British words** to draw on where they fit, without assigning them to regions: knackered or shattered, chuffed or made up, skint or brassic, mardy or stroppy, mum or mam, mate or pal, settee, sofa or couch.

The group (session S06). Persona cards, including the webcam photo each person was rated on:

P025 (Karen):
- first name: Karen
- age: 51
- lives in: Stourbridge, West Midlands
- occupation: Repairs and Maintenance Operations Manager at a mid-sized housing association covering the Black Country. She runs three supervisors and about forty operatives and contractors, and owns response times, complaints and the budget.
- education detail: Left a comprehensive in Dudley with A-levels in Business Studies, English and Geography. She started as an admin assistant at the council housing office at 18, did an HNC in Business part-time in her twenties, and later took a Level 5 CMI Diploma in Management and Leadership paid for by her employer. She often notes she has no degree and has managed people who do.
- household: Lives with her husband Steve, 54, a self-employed electrician, in a four-bed 1970s detached house on the Pedmore side of Stourbridge. Their son Callum, 20, is in his second year at university in Leeds and comes home for holidays. Their daughter Jess, 23, lives with her boyfriend in Wolverhampton. They have an elderly Border terrier called Biscuit.
- cultural background: White British, born and raised in Netherton near Dudley. Her dad worked at a foundry and her mum did school dinners. She was brought up Church of England and was christened and married at the same church. Now she goes mainly at Christmas, Easter and for funerals, but calls herself Christian and means it, in a private way. She feels firmly Black Country rather than Brummie and corrects people who mix them up.
- professional persona: Direct, numbers-focused and impatient with excuses. She is good in a crisis, but she takes the stress home and lies awake going over things. Her staff find her fair but hard to please, and she won't pretend a bad job is a good one. She dislikes jargon from head office and long meetings that could have been an email. She is fiercely protective of her own team against senior management, while being openly critical of them in private.
- sports persona: Not sporty. She walks Biscuit most evenings and at weekends goes round the Clent Hills with Steve. She did a Couch to 5K a few years ago and stopped when her knee flared up. She follows Wolves loosely because Steve and Callum do, and gets more wound up at the telly than either of them.
- arts persona: Likes crime dramas and anything with a strong female lead, such as Happy Valley and Line of Duty. She will happily rewatch Gavin and Stacey. She reads crime thrillers on holiday and very little otherwise. She cries at films and is a bit embarrassed by it. She goes to the panto at the Grand in Wolverhampton most years with her daughter, now as a tradition.
- travel persona: One week abroad a year, usually Spain or Portugal, all-inclusive or a villa with friends. She gets anxious about flights and connections and over-plans, with printed boarding passes as a backup. She did a Rhine river cruise for their 25th anniversary and loved it more than she expected. She dislikes airports, delays and anyone who stands up the second the plane lands.
- culinary persona: Competent, unfussy home cook: roast on Sundays, spag bol, chilli, curries from a jar livened up. They call the evening meal 'tea' as often as 'dinner'. A chip shop tea on Fridays when nobody can be bothered. She is cutting down on salt on doctor's advice and resents it. She likes a glass of rosé at the weekend, and on a Saturday it's a bacon bap from the café in town.
- hobbies and interests: Dog walking on the Clent Hills, Crime dramas and true crime podcasts on the commute, Garden pots and hanging baskets in summer, Charity shop browsing for homeware, Quiz night at the local pub once a month with friends, Family history, on and off, mostly her dad's side
- skills: Managing contractors and chasing them hard, Budget tracking in Excel, Handling complaints and angry tenants without losing her rag (at work, anyway), Writing a sharp email, Organising family events and holidays down to the detail, Decorating and wallpapering, learned out of necessity
- career goals: Wants to make Head of Property Services before she's 55, mainly for the pension. She is half-tempted to apply externally because she thinks she's been overlooked twice. She is also wary of the extra stress given her blood pressure and sleep. Long-term she wants to go part-time at 60 and have time with grandchildren, if Jess ever gets on with it.
- voice: Mid-pace, clear, quite clipped when she's making a point and slower when she's thinking. She has a light Black Country accent that softens in work mode and gets broader when she's annoyed or laughing. She says 'erm' while she gathers her thoughts and uses 'sort of' a fair bit. 'You know' comes out when she wants agreement. Occasional local touches like 'give it me' or calling a roll a bap, never laid on. She'll say 'sorry, what was the question again?' if she's gone off on one. She doesn't like silence and will fill it, often with a slightly sharp aside. She is quick to say when she thinks a question is badly worded.
- typing: Mostly proper sentences with capitals and full stops, because she types work emails all day. Apostrophes are usually right. She gets terse when hurried, with short answers, the odd 'n/a', and sometimes 'tbh'. No emojis in a form. She occasionally uses double exclamation marks when irritated, and sometimes adds a pointed comment in an 'any other comments' box.
- with strangers: Polite but businesslike at first, with no gushing. She sizes people up quickly. If she thinks something is pointless or patronising she'll say so, politely but plainly. She warms up if the other person is straightforward and has a sense of humour. She can seem a bit guarded or sharp, but underneath she's often nervous about doing it 'right'.
- small things: Biscuit needs his teeth done and the vet's quoted a fortune, The traffic on the A491 was a nightmare again, Callum hasn't rung in a week, They've finally had the kitchen done, She can't get a GP appointment for love nor money, Head office have brought in another new system nobody asked for, Steve has left his van parked across the drive again
- deeper things: She's been on blood pressure tablets for two years and worries she'll end up like her dad, who had a stroke at 63, Perimenopause has wrecked her sleep and sometimes her confidence at work, and she hasn't told anyone there, She still feels guilty she wasn't there enough when the kids were little because of work, She fell out with her younger sister over their mum's care and they barely speak, She sometimes wonders if she'd have gone further with a degree, and it still stings, She prays when she's frightened, mostly about the kids, and doesn't really talk about it
- webcam photo: Head-and-shoulders shot from a laptop on a desk, angled slightly upward so the ceiling's edge shows. Natural daylight comes from a window to her left, lighting that side of her face, with the other side a little shadowed. She has a round-ish face and fair skin with some redness across the cheeks. Her expression is neutral to faintly sceptical, mouth closed and one eyebrow slightly raised. Her shoulder-length hair is highlighted ash blonde, with darker roots showing, tucked behind one ear. She wears rectangular black-framed reading glasses, a navy knit cardigan over a white top and a small gold cross on a chain. Behind her is a spare bedroom used as an office: magnolia walls, a white Ikea bookcase with lever-arch files, a few paperbacks and a framed photo of two young adults at a graduation. A cream radiator sits under the window, with a dog bed just visible in the bottom corner of the frame.

P026 (Usman):
- first name: Usman
- age: 30
- lives in: Ilford, East London
- occupation: Chartered accountant (audit senior manager) at a mid-sized accountancy firm near Liverpool Street
- education detail: BSc Accounting and Finance from a university in Lahore, then an MSc in Accounting from a London university after moving to the UK at 22; qualified as an ACA chartered accountant through his firm's training scheme
- household: Lives with his wife Hira, 28, a hospital pharmacist, in a two-bedroom rented flat off Cranbrook Road. They have been married three years and have no children yet. His older brother and his family live ten minutes away in Gants Hill.
- cultural background: Born and raised in Lahore, Pakistan, in a middle-class Punjabi family; his father ran a small textiles business. Came to London for his master's and stayed for work. A practising Sunni Muslim who prays regularly, goes to the local mosque for Jummah when his schedule allows, and fasts during Ramadan. Speaks Punjabi and Urdu at home with family, mostly English with Hira day to day. Now a British citizen, but still thinks of Lahore as home in some ways.
- professional persona: Steady, careful auditor who has worked at the same firm since qualifying. Mainly works on manufacturing and logistics clients. Known for being straight with clients and for not cutting corners. Juniors find him approachable. He doesn't chase the spotlight and is a bit uncomfortable with the networking side of the job. Hybrid working: three days in the office, two from home.
- sports persona: Lifelong cricket fan. Follows Pakistan closely and stays up for matches in other time zones. Plays in a Sunday-league tape-ball and softball cricket group in Valentines Park through the summer. Not into football beyond knowing the Premier League table from office chat. Goes on a brisk walk most evenings.
- arts persona: Not much of an arts person. Watches the same few things: cricket highlights, the odd Pakistani drama that Hira puts on, and action films at the Ilford cinema. Listens to nasheeds and Quran recitation on the commute, plus old Nusrat Fateh Ali Khan because his dad played it. Hasn't been to a gallery since a uni trip and doesn't feel he's missing anything.
- travel persona: Travel mostly means going back to Lahore once a year, usually for a wedding or Eid, to see his parents. He and Hira did Umrah together two years ago, which he counts as the most important trip of his life. One holiday to Istanbul because friends recommended it. Prefers places where he knows the food is halal and he knows what to expect.
- culinary persona: Likes the food he grew up with: his mum's karahi, daal chawal, and parathas at the weekend. He can cook a decent chicken karahi and makes it most Fridays. Eats on Ilford Lane or in Green Street with his brother. At work he sticks to the same meal deal or a chicken wrap from the same place. Not adventurous. He'll try something new if Hira insists, but usually orders what he had last time.
- hobbies and interests: Sunday cricket in Valentines Park, watching Pakistan cricket matches, evening walks, helping out at the mosque on Ramadan iftar rotas, keeping the household budget in a spreadsheet, FIFA on the PlayStation with his nephew
- skills: Financial audit and IFRS reporting, Excel and data analysis tools, Fluent Urdu and Punjabi, Supervising and training junior staff, Decent medium-pace bowler, Cooking a few Pakistani home dishes well
- career goals: Wants to make director at his current firm within five or six years rather than jump around. Mainly cares about stability, a good salary to buy a house in Redbridge, and being able to support his parents. Not interested in starting his own thing.
- voice: Polite, measured and fairly quiet, with a Lahori accent softened by eight years in London. Speaks at an even pace, a bit slower when he's thinking. Uses 'er' when he hesitates and says 'sort of' and 'you know' now and then. Says 'dinner' for the evening meal and 'mate' with colleagues. Doesn't use slang much. Answers questions directly and then stops. He's comfortable with a short silence and will wait rather than fill it. Sometimes says 'sorry, can you say that again?' if the line is unclear.
- typing: Mostly proper sentences with a capital at the start, full stops sometimes dropped at the end. Uses apostrophes correctly out of habit from work. Short answers, no emojis. Occasionally 'n/a' or 'approx'. Might write 'Yes, about 2 years' rather than anything longer.
- with strangers: Courteous and a little reserved at first. Shakes hands, remembers your name, asks one polite question back. Comes across as sincere and modest. He won't oversell himself and may undersell his job. Warms up once cricket, food or family comes up, but doesn't overshare.
- small things: The Central line being rammed in the mornings, His Sunday cricket game got rained off again, Hira's shift pattern at the hospital, Picking up meat from the halal butcher on Ilford Lane, Busy season at work from January to March, His nephew beating him at FIFA, Staying up till 3am for a Pakistan match
- deeper things: He feels guilty being so far from his ageing parents and worries about his father's diabetes, He and Hira have been hoping for children and it hasn't happened yet, He sometimes feels he doesn't fully belong in Lahore or London anymore, Saving for a house deposit while sending money home is a strain he doesn't talk about, His faith is what keeps him steady when work gets stressful
- webcam photo: Laptop webcam at eye level, slightly off-centre, lit by daylight from a window to his left with an overhead ceiling light on. Head and shoulders in frame. A man with light brown skin, short neatly trimmed black hair, and a short tidy beard. Brown eyes, no glasses, a small polite closed-mouth smile. Wearing a plain navy quarter-zip jumper over a white collared shirt. Behind him is a magnolia wall with a framed Arabic calligraphy print in gold on black, a white IKEA bookshelf holding accountancy study manuals, a few box files and a small cricket trophy, and a folded prayer mat on the lower shelf. The corner of a grey radiator is visible at bottom right.

P027 (Callum):
- first name: Callum
- age: 28
- lives in: Long Eaton, East Midlands
- occupation: Leading hand joiner at a small heritage joinery firm in Beeston that makes and restores sash windows, doors and staircases, mostly for period houses and some listed buildings. He splits his time between the workshop and fitting on site, and runs a two-person fitting crew.
- education detail: GCSEs at a comprehensive in Long Eaton. Then a Level 2 and Level 3 Diploma in Site Carpentry and Bench Joinery at college in Nottingham, done alongside a four-year apprenticeship. Since then he has done short courses in traditional timber repair and lime work, and is partway through a self-funded online course in architectural history.
- household: Lives with his mum and dad, who have been married for 33 years, in a three-bed 1930s semi in Long Eaton. He moved back three years ago to save for a deposit after a flatshare in Nottingham ended. He pays rent to his parents, does most of the DIY around the house and cooks a couple of nights a week. His older sister lives in Derby with her partner.
- cultural background: White British, born and raised in Long Eaton. His dad is a retired lorry driver and his mum works part-time on reception at a GP surgery. He was brought up non-religious and is still not religious, though he is happy to look round any church for the roof timbers. He is working-class in background, with a strong sense of craft pride from his granddad, who was a cabinet maker in the town when furniture making was big round there.
- professional persona: Methodical and quietly exacting. He measures twice, labels every component and keeps a notebook for each job with sketches and timings. Clients like him because he explains what he is doing without talking down to them. Apprentices like him because he doesn't shout. He regularly works 50 to 55 hours a week, more when a job is behind, and doesn't make a fuss about it. He stays calm when something goes wrong on site and just works out the fix.
- sports persona: Not a big sports fan. He follows Derby County loosely because his dad does and will go to the odd game with him. He keeps fit through the job and long walks, and does some wild swimming at a lake near Attenborough in summer with a couple of mates.
- arts persona: Very wide tastes. He listens to a lot of music on the van radio and on headphones in the workshop, everything from old soul to ambient electronic stuff to folk. He goes to gigs at Rock City and smaller places in Nottingham. He reads a lot, mainly non-fiction about buildings, design and history, but also some science fiction. He likes galleries, especially anything to do with design, and has been to Nottingham Contemporary a few times on his own.
- travel persona: Saves up for one proper trip a year and plans it carefully. He chooses places for the buildings: he has done Copenhagen, Porto and Kraków, and wants to go to Japan to see traditional timber joinery. Within the UK he likes weekend trips to places like York, Lincoln and the Peak District villages, usually by train or in his old Skoda.
- culinary persona: A decent, curious home cook. He'll follow a recipe from a cookbook exactly the first time, then adjust it. He makes curries from scratch, does a good slow-cooked ragù and has been learning to make Japanese dishes. Lunch on site is a cob from the bakery or a packed lunch he made the night before. He calls the evening meal both tea and dinner depending on who he's talking to.
- hobbies and interests: Making small furniture pieces in his dad's garage workshop (currently a walnut side table), Visiting old churches, mills and country houses to look at the woodwork, Reading about architecture and design history, Gigs and discovering new music, Wild swimming in summer, Long walks in the Peak District, Cooking new cuisines, Film photography with a secondhand camera
- skills: Traditional bench joinery and sash window restoration, Reading technical drawings and producing his own setting-out drawings, Hand-cut joints (mortise and tenon, dovetails), Running a small crew and training apprentices, Talking clients through options and estimates, Basic CAD for joinery drawings, Cooking from scratch, Driving a van and organising site logistics
- career goals: To move into a workshop foreman role within a couple of years, then eventually set up his own small heritage joinery business doing high-quality restoration and bespoke pieces. In the short term he wants to finish his architectural history course and save enough for a deposit on a terrace somewhere near Long Eaton or Beeston.
- voice: Relaxed and fairly steady pace, with a light East Midlands accent: flattened vowels and some dropped t's, nothing heavy. He tends to think before answering and uses 'er' or 'sort of' while he does: 'it's sort of a balance, really'. He says 'mate' casually and the occasional 'mardy' or 'knackered', and he'll ask 'you know what I mean?' when explaining something technical. He doesn't rush to fill silences. He's happy to pause, then come back with a considered answer. He echoes the question back sometimes ('what would I change? er, probably...'). He says 'sorry' to ask for a repeat if the line drops.
- typing: Tidy for a quick form. He uses capital letters at the start of sentences and full stops, and gets apostrophes right. He writes short, clear sentences and rarely uses abbreviations beyond 'etc' or 'approx'. He sometimes puts in a dash to add an afterthought. No emojis.

You write transcripts of realistic video calls between strangers for a fully synthetic research dataset set in the UK. The study, in order (from its published design): a short puzzle task done alone; first impressions of the others' webcam photos; then a series of three-minute, one-on-one video calls in rounds, each person meeting the others in their group; after each call a short survey.

Call shape (from the original study's numbers): a call is cut off by a three-minute timer. A typical call has about 30 turns (most between 20 and 39) and about 570 words in total (most between 440 and 682); half of all turns are 12 words or fewer, and a quarter are 24 or more. Short acknowledgements ("yeah", "mm") count as turns too. So aim for about 570 words in about 30 turns: alongside the quick back-and-forth, people often talk in longer stretches (explaining their job, telling a story), and those long turns carry much of the call.

Guide to British conversational English (use it for how people talk; it is a description of speech, not a script):
How British people talk in casual conversation. This is a paraphrase of published descriptions of spoken British English; sources are in SOURCES.md. Use these features lightly and only where they fit the person. Never use them as a caricature.

- **Fillers.** British speakers hesitate with "erm" and "er". Women and younger speakers lean towards "erm".
- **Hedges.** "Sort of" is everywhere and steady. "Kind of" is spreading, and younger speakers use it more.
- **Politeness words.** "Please", "thank you", "thanks" and "sorry" mostly mean what they say. "Sorry" also works as a repair word (to correct yourself, or to ask someone to repeat) and can be ironic.
- **Tags at the end of a sentence.** "You know", "right", "okay", "yeah", "do you know what I mean". Among young Londoners, "innit" and "you get me" are rising. Tags depend on age and region only, never on ethnicity.
- **Echoing.** In an engaged conversation people pick up and re-use parts of each other's words.
- **Regional words and grammar** (from a recent dialect survey):
  - A bread roll is a "barm" in the North West (Manchester to Liverpool and western Lancashire), a "cob" around Nottinghamshire, a "bap" in Staffordshire, the West Midlands and North Wales, and a "batch" in Liverpool and Coventry.
  - Around Liverpool an ice lolly can be a "lolly ice".
  - The evening meal is "tea" in the North West, North East and Yorkshire, and "dinner" in the South East and London. Some people say both.
  - "Yous" or "youse" for plural "you" is common in the North East (Newcastle, Teesside), Liverpool and Scotland, less so in Manchester, and rare in York, Leeds and Sheffield.
  - "Give it me" is normal in the North West and West Midlands and widely accepted in Sheffield and York; it fades south of Birmingham, Coventry and Leicester.
  - "You was" is widely used, historically Northern and now found as far south as London.
- **Everyday British words** to draw on where they fit, without assigning them to regions: knackered or shattered, chuffed or made up, skint or brassic, mardy or stroppy, mum or mam, mate or pal, settee, sofa or couch.
