req.text:
You write transcripts of realistic video calls between strangers for a fully synthetic research dataset set in the UK. The study, in order (from its published design): a short puzzle task done alone; first impressions of the others' webcam photos; then a series of three-minute, one-on-one video calls in rounds, each person meeting the others in their group; after each call a short survey.

Call shape (from the original study's numbers): a call is cut off by a three-minute timer. A typical call has about 30 turns (most between 20 and 39) and about 570 words in total (most between 440 and 682); half of all turns are 12 words or fewer, and a quarter are 24 or more. Short acknowledgements ("yeah", "mm") count as turns too. So aim for about 570 words in about 30 turns: alongside the quick back-and-forth, people often talk in longer stretches (explaining their job, telling a story), and those long turns carry much of the call.

Guide to British conversational English (use it for how people talk; it is a description of speech, not a script):
How British people talk in casual conversation. This is a paraphrase of published descriptions of spoken British English; sources are in SOURCES.md. Use these features lightly and only where they fit the person. Never use them as a caricature.

- **Fillers.** British speakers hesitate with "erm" and "er". Women and younger speakers lean towards "erm".
- **Hedges.** "Sort of" is everywhere and steady. "Kind of" is spreading, and younger speakers use it more.
- **Politeness words.** "Please", "thank you", "thanks" and "sorry" mostly mean what they say. "Sorry" also works as a repair word (to correct yourself, or to ask someone to repeat) and can be ironic.
- **Tags at the end of a sentence.** "You know", "right", "okay", "yeah", "do you know what I mean". Among young Londoners, "innit" and "you get me" are rising. Tags depend on age and region only, never on ethnicity.
- **Echoing.** In an engaged conversation people pick up and re-use parts of each other's words.
- **Regional words and grammar** (from a recent dialect survey):
  - A bread roll is a "barm" in the North West (Manchester to Liverpool and western Lancashire), a "cob" around Nottinghamshire, a "bap" in Staffordshire, the West Midlands and North Wales, and a "batch" in Liverpool and Coventry.
  - Around Liverpool an ice lolly can be a "lolly ice".
  - The evening meal is "tea" in the North West, North East and Yorkshire, and "dinner" in the South East and London. Some people say both.
  - "Yous" or "youse" for plural "you" is common in the North East (Newcastle, Teesside), Liverpool and Scotland, less so in Manchester, and rare in York, Leeds and Sheffield.
  - "Give it me" is normal in the North West and West Midlands and widely accepted in Sheffield and York; it fades south of Birmingham, Coventry and Leicester.
  - "You was" is widely used, historically Northern and now found as far south as London.
- **Everyday British words** to draw on where they fit, without assigning them to regions: knackered or shattered, chuffed or made up, skint or brassic, mardy or stroppy, mum or mam, mate or pal, settee, sofa or couch.

P050 (Jago):
- first name: Jago
- age: 23
- lives in: Truro, South West (Cornwall)
- occupation: Full-time final-year undergraduate in Film at Falmouth University (Penryn campus), commuting from his parents' house. Picks up Saturday shifts behind the bar at a busy pub in Truro town centre and the odd paid camera-assist day on local wedding and corporate shoots.
- education detail: GCSEs and A levels (Media Studies, English Literature, Psychology) at a Truro sixth-form college. Took two years out after college working bar and front-of-house jobs, including a summer season in a Newquay surf hostel. Now in the third year of a BA (Hons) Film, making a short documentary about Cornish gig rowing clubs for his final project.
- household: Lives in his parents' semi-detached house on an estate on the edge of Truro. His mum is an office manager at a GP surgery and his dad is a site supervisor for a building firm; they've been married 27 years. His younger sister Tamsin, 19, is away at university in Leeds and comes home in the holidays. He has the box-room-turned-edit-suite and pays a small amount of board when he's flush.
- cultural background: White British, Cornish born and bred, from a family that has been in and around Truro and Redruth for generations. Non-religious; his nan still goes to chapel at Christmas and he'll go along to keep her happy. Feels quite Cornish in a relaxed way. He likes the flag at rugby and the pasty jokes, and he gets wound up about second-home prices, but he isn't into the politics of it. Grew up on surfing, beach parties and his dad's old indie CDs.
- professional persona: Pitches himself as a filmmaker-slash-content-person, and his LinkedIn and Instagram bios are a bit grander than his CV. He's genuinely good at getting people to talk on camera and at talking his way onto shoots. He's well liked on group projects for keeping morale up, though tutors have noticed he sometimes lets others do the boring logistics and then fronts the presentation. He networks hard at every screening and festival.
- sports persona: Surfs at Perranporth and Gwithian when the swell's decent, mostly in autumn and spring when it's quieter. Plays five-a-side on a Wednesday with old college mates. Follows the Cornish Pirates rugby casually and watches the Six Nations in the pub. Rowed a few seasons of gig rowing as a teenager and has gone back to it a bit through his documentary.
- arts persona: Watches films constantly and has opinions about everything from A24 releases to old Ken Loach. Loves Mark Jenkin's Cornish films, especially Bait. Goes to gigs at the Hall for Cornwall and smaller venues in Falmouth, and helped run visuals for a mate's band. Listens to a mix of indie, UK garage revival and whatever's trending on TikTok, and he'll admit to the last one.
- travel persona: Interrailed around Europe for five weeks at 20 on hostel bunks and a credit card he's still paying off. Lisbon and Berlin are his favourites. Did a cheap ski week in Bulgaria with the five-a-side lot. Wants to do South America or Japan after graduating and talks about it like it's already booked.
- culinary persona: Eats whatever his mum cooks and is grateful for it, roast on Sundays especially. Can do a decent carbonara and a show-off Thai green curry when he has people over. Strong views on where the best pasty in Truro is. Lives on meal deals and campus coffee during the week, and is partial to a late-night chippy after shifts.
- hobbies and interests: Surfing, Shooting and editing short films and reels, Five-a-side football, Gigs and festivals (Boardmasters most summers, usually on a crew or wristband blag), Film podcasts, Vintage clothes shopping in Falmouth charity shops, Gig rowing (lapsed, recently back), Pub quizzes, where he's the film and music round guy
- skills: Camera operation (Sony FX3, gimbals), Editing in Premiere Pro and DaVinci Resolve, Interviewing and putting people at ease on camera, Bar work and cocktail making, Social media content and short-form video, Talking his way into places, Basic drone flying (has his flyer ID)
- career goals: Wants to work in documentary or branded content, ideally directing, and imagines his own production company within five years. Realistically he's hoping a Bristol production house will take him on as a runner or junior editor after graduating. He's quietly entered his final project into a couple of short film festivals and hopes one picks it up so he can put 'official selection' on everything.
- voice: Chatty, warm and quick. He leans in and fills the space easily. Soft West Country accent, more noticeable when he's relaxed or talking about home, but he doesn't overdo it. Says 'proper' as an intensifier ('it was proper good'), 'mate' a lot, and 'like' and 'kind of' as hedges, plus the odd 'erm' when he's actually thinking rather than performing. Ends points with 'yeah?' or 'do you know what I mean'. Picks up the other person's phrasing and runs with it. Rarely lets a silence sit. He jumps in with a joke or a 'sorry, go on' if he's talked over someone. He tells stories with a bit of embellishment.
- typing: Fast and casual, mostly lowercase with occasional capitals for names. Drops apostrophes sometimes ('dont', 'its') but not always. Uses 'tbh', 'ngl' and 'lol' in informal boxes. Long run-on answers in open text fields with dashes and commas instead of full stops. Will write more than asked if the question interests him.
- with strangers: Instantly friendly and easy to talk to. Asks questions back, finds common ground fast and makes people laugh. Comes across as confident and a bit charming. A sharper listener might notice he steers things towards his projects and drops in small humblebrags. He's agreeable and avoids friction, so he tends to say what he thinks people want to hear.
- small things: The surf at Perranporth was rubbish this weekend, Just finished a double shift at the pub and he's knackered, His mum's roast and how he'll never move out at this rate, The train between Truro and Penryn being cancelled again, A film he watched last night that he wants everyone to see, Saving up for a new lens, His mate's band's gig on Friday, Getting soaked on the bus stop walk
- deeper things: Feels a bit behind his school mates who went straight to uni and are now working in London, Worries the documentary won't be as good as he's been telling everyone, Has around two grand on a credit card from travelling that his parents don't know about, Admits he sometimes inflates his experience on applications and is slightly anxious about being found out, Wants to leave Cornwall for his career but feels guilty about it and loves home, His grandad was a tin miner's son and he'd love to make something about that side of the family one day
- webcam photo: Laptop webcam at a slightly low angle, framing him from mid-chest up, a little off-centre to the left. Lit mainly by a window to his right, so one side of his face is brighter, with a faint blue glow from a second monitor. Fair skin with some leftover tan and a few freckles across the nose, light stubble, and a wide easy grin mid-laugh, eyes creased. Sandy-brown hair, longish on top and pushed back, a bit salty and messy. No glasses. Wearing a faded mustard vintage crewneck sweatshirt over a white T-shirt, with wired earphones trailing from one ear. Behind him is a small box room: a white wall with a Bait film poster and a cork board pinned with call sheets and festival wristbands. A shelf holds a camera body, a couple of lenses and a gimbal, with a surfboard sock hanging off the corner. A slightly unmade single bed with a navy duvet is just visible in the bottom right.

P051 (Claire):
- first name: Claire
- age: 46
- lives in: Faversham, Kent, South East England
- occupation: Co-owner and director of a small interior design and refurbishment studio in Canterbury. She works about 12 hours a week, mostly client pitches and design sign-offs, while her business partner runs day-to-day operations.
- education detail: A-levels in Art, English and History at a grammar school in Maidstone. BA in Fine Art from Kingston University. She later did a part-time evening diploma in interior design, which she admits she 'scraped through'.
- household: Lone parent in a rented-then-bought Victorian terrace near the creek, with her two children: a son aged 15 and a daughter aged 11. She divorced about five years ago, and the children see their dad, who lives in Whitstable, every other weekend. There is also an elderly, badly behaved terrier called Moss.
- cultural background: White British, born and raised in Kent. Her dad was a surveyor and her mum a primary school teacher. She was brought up Church of England and still calls herself Christian. She goes to the parish church at Christmas and Easter and likes the building and the hymns more than the theology. Comfortably middle class, a bit bohemian in taste, and not especially sentimental about tradition.
- professional persona: Strong on ideas and on reading what a client actually wants, weak on follow-through. She is good in the room with clients, decisive about colour, materials and layout, and quite blunt when she thinks a client's idea is naff. She deliberately cut her hours after the divorce and lets her partner handle invoices, scheduling and suppliers. She is aware she would be a nightmare without someone organised beside her.
- sports persona: Not sporty in any organised sense. She walks Moss along the Saxon Shore Way and the marshes most mornings and swims in the sea at Tankerton in summer, occasionally into October. She has no interest in watching football and gets mildly irritated when her son has it on.
- arts persona: Her strongest area. She goes to the Turner Contemporary in Margate regularly and to London galleries a few times a year. She still paints occasionally, big loose abstracts, and leaves them half-finished in the spare room. She reads widely and messily, with several books on the go at once. She likes odd films and slow TV dramas, and goes to the occasional gig at the Booking Hall in Dover.
- travel persona: Prefers unplanned trips. She books last-minute and once forgot to check passport expiry dates and nearly missed a ferry. She loves Lisbon, rural France and the Italian lakes. With the kids it's usually a gîte or a cheap flight somewhere warm. She has a vague ambition to do a long solo trip to Japan once her daughter is older.
- culinary persona: An enthusiastic but chaotic cook. She makes big pots of things, like dal, ragù or a tagine, with whatever's in the fridge, and rarely follows a recipe exactly. Dinner is often late. She shops at the Faversham market and the Macknade food hall when she can afford to, and Aldi when she can't be bothered. She likes a glass of red with dinner.
- hobbies and interests: painting (sporadically), sea swimming, galleries and contemporary art, rummaging at antiques and reclamation yards, reading literary fiction and design books, walking the dog on the marshes, listening to podcasts about architecture
- skills: spatial and colour sense, pitching to clients, spotting good pieces at salvage yards, staying calm in a crisis, quick, rough sketching, talking tradespeople down on price
- career goals: Nothing grand. She wants to keep the studio ticking over on low hours while the kids are at home, take on fewer but more interesting projects, and maybe eventually step back into a creative-director role and sell her share. She has half a plan to do a residency or a proper painting course one day.
- voice: Southern English, educated, relaxed, with no strong regional accent. She speaks at a medium-quick pace and trails off when she's thinking. She uses 'erm' and 'sort of' a fair bit and says 'you know' at the end of points. She is direct to the point of bluntness, saying things like 'no, I don't really think that's true' without softening much. Silence doesn't bother her at all: she'll sit and think, then answer properly rather than fill the gap. Words like 'knackered' and 'naff' come out naturally, and she calls the evening meal 'dinner'. She occasionally drifts off topic and pulls herself back with 'sorry, what was the question?'
- typing: Fast and careless. Mostly lowercase, with an occasional capital at the start. Commas instead of full stops, and she sometimes misses apostrophes ('dont', 'its'). Short answers with the odd typo she doesn't correct. Rarely uses abbreviations apart from 'tbh' now and then.
- with strangers: Friendly enough but not eager to please. She comes across as confident, a bit dry, and unbothered by what the stranger thinks of her. She will disagree openly and ask a pointed question back. Some people find her refreshing, others a little brusque. She is curious about interesting topics and visibly bored by box-ticking ones.
- small things: Moss rolling in something revolting on the marshes, the Saturday market in Faversham, her son eating everything in the fridge, a decent mid-century sideboard she found at a reclamation yard, the water temperature at Tankerton, having to sort out school forms she's forgotten about, an exhibition she saw in Margate
- deeper things: The divorce was more of a relief than a heartbreak, and she sometimes feels she ought to feel guiltier about that than she does., She worries a little that her disorganisation makes life harder for the kids, especially her daughter, who is very tidy., She gave up on being a 'proper artist' in her twenties and still isn't sure if that was sensible or cowardly., Money is fine but not as secure as people assume. req.text:
You write transcripts of realistic video calls between strangers for a fully synthetic research dataset set in the UK. The study, in order (from its published design): a short puzzle task done alone; first impressions of the others' webcam photos; then a series of three-minute, one-on-one video calls in rounds, each person meeting the others in their group; after each call a short survey.

Call shape (from the original study's numbers): a call is cut off by a three-minute timer. A typical call has about 30 turns (most between 20 and 39) and about 570 words in total (most between 440 and 682); half of all turns are 12 words or fewer, and a quarter are 24 or more. Short acknowledgements ("yeah", "mm") count as turns too. So aim for about 570 words in about 30 turns: alongside the quick back-and-forth, people often talk in longer stretches (explaining their job, telling a story), and those long turns carry much of the call.

Guide to British conversational English (use it for how people talk; it is a description of speech, not a script):
How British people talk in casual conversation. This is a paraphrase of published descriptions of spoken British English; sources are in SOURCES.md. Use these features lightly and only where they fit the person. Never use them as a caricature.

- **Fillers.** British speakers hesitate with "erm" and "er". Women and younger speakers lean towards "erm".
- **Hedges.** "Sort of" is everywhere and steady. "Kind of" is spreading, and younger speakers use it more.
- **Politeness words.** "Please", "thank you", "thanks" and "sorry" mostly mean what they say. "Sorry" also works as a repair word (to correct yourself, or to ask someone to repeat) and can be ironic.
- **Tags at the end of a sentence.** "You know", "right", "okay", "yeah", "do you know what I mean". Among young Londoners, "innit" and "you get me" are rising. Tags depend on age and region only, never on ethnicity.
- **Echoing.** In an engaged conversation people pick up and re-use parts of each other's words.
- **Regional words and grammar** (from a recent dialect survey):
  - A bread roll is a "barm" in the North West (Manchester to Liverpool and western Lancashire), a "cob" around Nottinghamshire, a "bap" in Staffordshire, the West Midlands and North Wales, and a "batch" in Liverpool and Coventry.
  - Around Liverpool an ice lolly can be a "lolly ice".
  - The evening meal is "tea" in the North West, North East and Yorkshire, and "dinner" in the South East and London. Some people say both.
  - "Yous" or "youse" for plural "you" is common in the North East (Newcastle, Teesside), Liverpool and Scotland, less so in Manchester, and rare in York, Leeds and Sheffield.
  - "Give it me" is normal in the North West and West Midlands and widely accepted in Sheffield and York; it fades south of Birmingham, Coventry and Leicester.
  - "You was" is widely used, historically Northern and now found as far south as London.
- **Everyday British words** to draw on where they fit, without assigning them to regions: knackered or shattered, chuffed or made up, skint or brassic, mardy or stroppy, mum or mam, mate or pal, settee, sofa or couch.

P056 (Joanne):
- first name: Joanne
- age: 46
- lives in: Bolton, North West England
- occupation: Senior software developer for a payroll and HR software supplier. She maintains an old payroll system used by several councils and NHS trusts. She works from home four days a week, and on the fifth she goes into the office in Salford Quays.
- education detail: A-levels in maths, computing and physics at a sixth-form college in Bolton, then a BSc in Computer Science at the University of Salford. No postgraduate study. She has done a couple of company-paid certifications she only half finished the coursework for.
- household: Lives with her husband Mark (49), a service engineer for a boiler and heating firm, in a 1930s semi in Heaton that they bought in 2006. No children. Her widowed mum lives fifteen minutes away in Farnworth.
- cultural background: White British, born and raised in Bolton. Her dad was an electrician and her mum worked part-time in a building society. She was the first in her family to go to university. She was brought up nominally Church of England but has no religion and never really thought about it much. She is solidly Northern in outlook and suspicious of anything that seems like London fuss.
- professional persona: Twenty-odd years in the same niche, much of it with the same codebase. Colleagues see her as the person who actually understands how the old payroll engine works, and that gives her a lot of slack. She is bright and quick at diagnosing problems once she gets going, but she procrastinates badly. She leaves documentation half-written and does her best work in a panic the night before a release. She dislikes stand-ups, new frameworks and anything labelled 'transformation'. In meetings she can be curt and doesn't sugar-coat it when she thinks a plan is daft. She worries privately and a lot about being found out as disorganised, or made redundant if the system is ever replaced.
- sports persona: Not sporty at all. She watches Bolton Wanderers results come in because Mark and her late dad follow or followed them, but she rarely goes to the Toughsheet. She walks the dog round Moss Bank Park at weekends when she can be bothered. She tried a Couch to 5K app twice and gave up both times in week three.
- arts persona: Not one for galleries or theatre. She watches the same things repeatedly: reruns of Only Connect, Line of Duty, old episodes of Coronation Street with her mum, and crime dramas on ITVX. She listens to the same 90s indie and Britpop she liked at college, like Oasis, Pulp and The Charlatans, and rarely seeks out anything new. She reads the odd crime paperback on holiday.
- travel persona: A creature of habit. Most years it's the same apartment in Puerto Pollensa, Majorca, in September, plus a long weekend in the Lake District or a static caravan near Abersoch. She gets anxious flying and about getting to the airport on time. Mark handles the booking and passports because she would leave it too late. She has no interest in city breaks or anywhere 'adventurous'.
- culinary persona: Plain food. Mark cooks more than she does. Tea in the week is often something quick like chilli, jacket potatoes, a stir-fry from a kit or a chippy on Fridays. She likes a meat and potato pie from a proper bakery and a bacon barm on a Saturday. She won't eat seafood beyond fish and chips and finds tasting menus pretentious. She drinks too much tea and has a glass of white wine most weekend nights.
- hobbies and interests: Doing the daily Wordle and the Guardian quick crossword, though she never gets round to the cryptic, Walking their cocker spaniel, Bramble, Rewatching familiar TV box sets, Playing the same few mobile puzzle games, Pottering in the back garden without much of a plan, mostly letting it go wild
- skills: Debugging and maintaining legacy code, mainly COBOL-adjacent payroll logic, SQL and some C#, Understanding UK payroll rules: tax codes, NI, pension auto-enrolment, Spotting what is actually broken in a system quickly, Mental arithmetic, Getting a lot done very fast under deadline pressure
- career goals: Mostly to stay put. She would like to keep her current role until early retirement in her late fifties, without being pushed into management or retrained on whatever replaces the old system. She is quietly worried that the company's cloud migration will make her redundant. She has thought vaguely about contracting but hasn't done anything about it.
- voice: Quiet, fairly flat delivery with a mild Bolton accent: short 'a' in 'bath' and 'grass', and some dropped 'h's when relaxed. She speaks at a moderate pace, a bit clipped, and gives short answers unless asked to expand. She says 'erm' while she thinks and uses 'sort of' quite a bit. Occasionally she ends with 'do you know what I mean' or 'yeah'. Regional usage comes out naturally rather than performed: 'tea' for the evening meal, 'barm', and now and then 'give it me'. Joanne: Hiya.
Tomas: Hello. Tomas.
Joanne: Joanne. Bolton.

Tomas: Yes. Gary is good. He talks sense. You?
Joanne: Software. I look after a payroll system. Councils, NHS trusts, that sort of thing.
Tomas: Payroll. Okay. Then I have question. Is true overtime is taxed more? Guys at work say they don't take extra shift because tax takes everything.
Joanne: No. That's a myth, everyone says it. Your tax gets worked out on the month, so if you do loads of overtime one month the system sort of assumes you earn that every month, and it takes more. But it's cumulative, so it evens out over the year. If you've paid too much, it comes back to you in the next few months. The only real thing is if it actually pushes you over about fifty grand for the year, then that bit's at forty percent.
Tomas: So they are wrong.
Joanne: They're wrong, yeah. Unless you're on a week one or month one code. Then it doesn't even out, you'd have to sort it with HMRC.
Tomas: How I know which code?
Joanne: It's on your payslip. If there's a W1 or an M1 or an X after it, that's the one. If it's just 1257L you're fine.
Tomas: I check tonight. I keep all payslips in folder. And spreadsheet.
Joanne: Course you do. You're more organised than me. I can't find my reading glasses half the time.
Tomas: They are on your head in photo.
Joanne: Ha. They're probably on my head now an' all. Yeah. They are.
Tomas: You have dog, I think. The lead, in photo.
Joanne: Bramble. Cocker spaniel. She's daft. Gets in the bins every day, ate a loaf on Tuesday, bag and all.
Tomas: Dogs are expensive, no? Food, vet, insurance.
Joanne: Don't. Insurance went up again. Mark sorts that, my husband.
Tomas: You must call and ask for lower. Always. They don't give if you don't ask.
Joanne: That's what Gary said.
Tomas: Gary is right.
Joanne: You two'd get on. What do you do on your days off, then?
Tomas: Walk around Willen Lake. Fix bikes. Watch basketball late, Lithuanian team.
Joanne: I don't know anything about basketball.
Tomas: Is okay. Nobody here knows. In Lithuania is like football here. More.
Joanne: Mark's like that with Bolton Wanderers. Sits watching the scores come in like it's life or death.
Tomas: Is life or death. Žalgiris lose again on Thursday. I am angry two days.
Joanne: Two days. That's about what Mark does, do you know what I mean.

=== CALL C0123 ===
Gary: Now then.
Adam: Hi. Adam. Shipley, near Bradford.

Adam: Er, yeah. Word's got round, then.

Adam: Er, some of them are alright, to be fair. They just need showing.
Gary: Hm. Maybe. What d'you do, then, new stone or old?
Adam: Old, mostly. Repairs on sandstone, chapels, mills, terraces. Cutting new blocks to match and fixing them in, repointing in lime.
Gary: Lime. I'd have thought cement were stronger.
Adam: It is stronger, that's the problem. Er, if the mortar's harder than the stone, the stone takes all the movement and the water. So it cracks and the face blows instead of the joint. You want the joint to be the weak bit, so you can rake it out and do it again in fifty years.
Gary: Never thought of it like that.
Adam: Most people don't. You see it everywhere round Bradford, terraces done in cement in the eighties.
Gary: I put an extension on ours, back in the day. Brick, mind, not stone. Did it myself with a mate. Twenty year and not a crack in it.
Adam: That's good going. Brick's a lot more forgiving, mind.
Gary: You what? Laid it level, that's what. You doing football, you a City man?
Adam: Bradford City, yeah. Go with my dad, a few home games a season.
Gary: Notts County. We've had our share of rubbish an' all.
Adam: Ha. City's been a bit rubbish this year. I mostly go for my dad, really. He's semi-retired now, it's our thing.
Gary: That's right, that. My lad set me up a stream, but it's not the same as going.
Adam: No. The pies are better at the ground.
Gary: Pies are better at ours. What did your dad do?
Adam: Lorry driver. Thirty-odd years.
Gary: Mine were at the pit, Linby, till it shut. Then nothing for years. Taught me to keep money put by.
Adam: Yeah. I'm trying. Saving for a house, I'm back at my mum and dad's.
Gary: Nowt wrong with that. Get it paid off quick, that's the trick. I'll have mine done in two year.
Adam: That's good going.
Gary: You do any work on the side? I do fences, sheds, cash.
Adam: Er, a bit. Neighbours' walls now and then. Mostly I'm sketching stone in a notebook, if I'm honest. Not very profitable.
Gary: Ha. No. Do the walls, then.

=== CALL C0124 ===
Callum: Hey! Hiya, can you hear me alright?
Elira: Hi! Yeah, hi, I'm Elira.
Callum: Callum. Birmingham.
Elira: Oh my God, Callum. Sorry, my boyfriend's called Callum, so this is going to be weird for me. Gary already asked if it was you.
Callum: Ha, no, I can confirm I'm not your boyfriend. What did Gary say about me?
Elira: Erm, he said you talked about his steel for ten minutes. And that you were a nice enough lad. Which I think from Gary is quite high praise?
Callum: Nice enough lad. I'll take that, honestly, I thought he hated me. I did go on about his beam a bit. He said six metres and my brain just went.
Elira: What do you do, then, that a beam does that to you?
Callum: Structural engineer. Graduate, so I'm doing the chartership thing. Mostly residential, concrete and steel frames. Basically I'm the person who tells the architect their lovely cantilever's not happening.
Elira: Ha, that sounds quite satisfying, though.
Callum: A bit too satisfying, apparently. It came up in my review. What about you, you're London, right?
Elira: Walthamstow, yeah. I'm between jobs, I took voluntary redundancy from a property management company, so I'm applying for office manager stuff. And doing a bookkeeping course. Sorry, I've said that sentence about five times today, it's starting to sound rehearsed.
Callum: Nah, it's fine. Property management, so you'd have had all the defects on the new-build blocks?
Elira: Oh, all of it. Damp, mostly. Every tenant ringing about damp, and the developer saying it's just people drying washing indoors.
Callum: Which, to be fair, is half of it. Ventilation's rubbish in loads of those blocks, you know? Trickle vents taped over, extractor fans that do nothing. I've got an airer in my spare room right now, so I'm part of the problem.
Elira: Ha, everyone is. Do you like Birmingham? I've only been once, for a wedding.
Callum: Love it, honestly. People sleep on it. I'm in Stirchley, it's all little bakeries and a brilliant wine shop now, it's basically turned into Walthamstow.
Elira: That's so funny, that's exactly what people say about Walthamstow. Would you ever move to London?
Callum: Er. Maybe. Some of the practices I'd love to work for are there. It's kind of a live conversation at home, Hannah's job's in Birmingham, so.
Elira: Oh, yeah, that's hard. And honestly, the rent alone, we pay a fortune for a one-bed above a shop.
Callum: What does your Callum do?
Elira: Sound technician, theatres and events. So he comes in at midnight after a get-out and I'm asleep. But he gets free tickets, so I've seen loads of musicals I'd never pay for.
Callum: Okay, what's the best one?
Elira: Erm, honestly, anything funny. I can't do the really heavy dramas, I just sit there wanting it to end. Is that bad?
Callum: No, that's fair. I'm the opposite, I drag Hannah to really slow films on Mubi and she falls asleep. Last one was a lighthouse keeper, three hours, barely any talking. It was overrated, to be fair, even I'll admit that.
Elira: Three hours! She deserves a medal. What do you do for fun that isn't a sad lighthouse?
Callum: Cooking, mostly. I've got a sourdough starter, Hannah named it Gerald. Fresh pasta at weekends. Five-a-side, and I'm getting back into bouldering after I did my finger.
Elira: Gerald! I love that. I'm trying to learn my mum's pite, it's an Albanian pastry, really thin layers. Mine always tears.
Callum: Is it like filo, rolled out by hand?
Elira: By hand, with a long thin rolling pin, my mum does it on the kitchen table. Mine ends up looking like a map.
Callum: Ha. It's probably the resting. You want the dough really soft and then leave it ages. Do you rest it?
Elira: Sorry, rest it how long?
Callum: Like an hour, under a bit of oil. Then it stretches instead of tearing, right?
Elira: I do about ten minutes. Okay, I'm telling my mum a man from Birmingham fixed her recipe.
Callum: Don't tell her that, she'll never forgive me.

You write transcripts of realistic video calls between strangers for a fully synthetic research dataset set in the UK. The study, in order (from its published design): a short puzzle task done alone; first impressions of the others' webcam photos; then a series of three-minute, one-on-one video calls in rounds, each person meeting the others in their group; after each call a short survey.

Call shape (from the original study's numbers): a call is cut off by a three-minute timer. A typical call has about 30 turns (most between 20 and 39) and about 570 words in total (most between 440 and 682); half of all turns are 12 words or fewer, and a quarter are 24 or more. Short acknowledgements ("yeah", "mm") count as turns too. So aim for about 570 words in about 30 turns: alongside the quick back-and-forth, people often talk in longer stretches (explaining their job, telling a story), and those long turns carry much of the call.

Guide to British conversational English (use it for how people talk; it is a description of speech, not a script):
How British people talk in casual conversation. This is a paraphrase of published descriptions of spoken British English; sources are in SOURCES.md. Use these features lightly and only where they fit the person. Never use them as a caricature.

- **Fillers.** British speakers hesitate with "erm" and "er". Women and younger speakers lean towards "erm".
- **Hedges.** "Sort of" is everywhere and steady. "Kind of" is spreading, and younger speakers use it more.
- **Politeness words.** "Please", "thank you", "thanks" and "sorry" mostly mean what they say. "Sorry" also works as a repair word (to correct yourself, or to ask someone to repeat) and can be ironic.
- **Tags at the end of a sentence.** "You know", "right", "okay", "yeah", "do you know what I mean". Among young Londoners, "innit" and "you get me" are rising. Tags depend on age and region only, never on ethnicity.
- **Echoing.** In an engaged conversation people pick up and re-use parts of each other's words.
- **Regional words and grammar** (from a recent dialect survey):
  - A bread roll is a "barm" in the North West (Manchester to Liverpool and western Lancashire), a "cob" around Nottinghamshire, a "bap" in Staffordshire, the West Midlands and North Wales, and a "batch" in Liverpool and Coventry.
  - Around Liverpool an ice lolly can be a "lolly ice".
  - The evening meal is "tea" in the North West, North East and Yorkshire, and "dinner" in the South East and London. Some people say both.
  - "Yous" or "youse" for plural "you" is common in the North East (Newcastle, Teesside), Liverpool and Scotland, less so in Manchester, and rare in York, Leeds and Sheffield.
  - "Give it me" is normal in the North West and West Midlands and widely accepted in Sheffield and York; it fades south of Birmingham, Coventry and Leicester.
  - "You was" is widely used, historically Northern and now found as far south as London.
- **Everyday British words** to draw on where they fit, without assigning them to regions: knackered or shattered, chuffed or made up, skint or brassic, mardy or stroppy, mum or mam, mate or pal, settee, sofa or couch.

The group (session S10). Persona cards, including the webcam photo each person was rated on:

P044 (Gareth):
- first name: Gareth
- age: 36
- lives in: Wrexham, North Wales
- occupation: Administrative assistant in the transport and scheduling office of a building supplies distributor on the Wrexham Industrial Estate. He books deliveries, updates the dispatch spreadsheet and chases paperwork with drivers, Monday to Friday, about 37.5 hours a week.
- education detail: Went to a local comprehensive and left with GCSEs, then did a year of an IT BTEC at Coleg Cambria (then Yale College) and didn't finish it. He has picked up everything else on the job, plus a couple of mandatory health and safety e-learning certificates.
- household: Lives with his wife Kerry, a healthcare assistant at the Maelor hospital who works shifts, in a two-bed semi they've been renting for six years on an estate on the edge of town. No children. They have a Staffordshire bull terrier called Dot.
- cultural background: White Welsh, born and raised in Wrexham. His parents still live about ten minutes away. He understands a bit of Welsh from school but doesn't speak it. He isn't religious. He was christened, but the family only went to chapel for funerals. He has always lived locally and has no particular wish to move.
- professional persona: Gets the job done well enough but leaves things until the last minute and relies on the dispatch manager reminding him. He's known as easy-going and unflappable when a lorry doesn't turn up, because he doesn't panic. He's less good at keeping his inbox under control. He keeps his head down, doesn't go to the Christmas do if he can help it, and has been in the same role for nine years.
- sports persona: Supports Wrexham AFC the way his dad did and watches most matches on the telly. He gets to the Racecourse a few times a season, usually with his dad or his brother-in-law. He doesn't play anything himself any more. Five-a-side stopped about eight years ago. He walks Dot round the block most evenings because she needs it.
- arts persona: Not much interest. Watches whatever's on with Kerry: crime dramas, quiz shows, the odd Netflix series she's picked. He'll rewatch films he already likes rather than try new ones. Listens to the same indie and Britpop his mates liked at school, mostly in the car.
- travel persona: Holidays are a week somewhere familiar. They go back to the same caravan park near Abersoch most summers, and every couple of years Kerry books a package deal to Tenerife. He's happy to let her plan it. He's been abroad maybe six times and doesn't feel he's missing out.
- culinary persona: Plain food. Chips, a chicken curry, pie, a bacon bap on a Saturday morning. He can do a fry-up and spag bol and that's about it. When Kerry's on a late, tea is often a takeaway or something from the freezer. He doesn't like anything too spicy or anything he can't name.
- hobbies and interests: Watching Wrexham AFC, Football games on the PlayStation, usually online with the same two mates from school, Walking the dog, Watching quiz shows with Kerry, The odd pint at the local on a Friday
- skills: Keeping calm when deliveries go wrong, Excel to a basic level, mainly filters and copying formulas, Knows the local road network and delivery routes well, Fixing minor things on the PlayStation and home Wi-Fi, Getting on quietly with drivers who are in a bad mood
- career goals: Nothing specific. He'd take a bump in pay if a senior admin or dispatch coordinator role came up without him having to apply too hard, but he's comfortable where he is. He mainly wants the job to stay steady so he and Kerry can eventually put a deposit down on a house.
- voice: Quiet, fairly flat, unhurried North Wales accent. Short answers unless pushed. Says 'erm' or 'er' before most replies and uses 'sort of' a lot. Occasionally says 'aye' or 'yeah, fair enough'. Ends sentences with 'you know' or 'I dunno, really'. Doesn't fill silences. He'll let a pause sit and wait for the next question rather than add more. Not nervous, just not chatty. Might say 'sorry, say that again?' if the line drops.
- typing: Mostly lowercase, no full stops at the end, apostrophes often missing (dont, im, its). Short answers, sometimes just one or two words. Uses 'n/a' or 'dunno' rather than leave a box blank. Occasional typo he doesn't go back to fix.
- with strangers: Polite but reserved, and slightly hard to draw out. Not unfriendly, just doesn't volunteer much and looks a bit like he's waiting for it to be over. Relaxed rather than awkward. Warms up a little if football or the dog comes up.
- small things: Dot chewed through the TV remote cable last week, The industrial estate traffic is a nightmare at half four, Wrexham's results at the weekend, Kerry's on nights this week so he's been living on oven chips, Needs to sort the car's MOT and keeps forgetting, Bacon bap from the van outside work on a Friday
- deeper things: They've been trying for a baby for a couple of years and it hasn't happened. He's mostly fine about it but knows Kerry isn't, He sometimes wonders if he should have finished college, but doesn't dwell on it, His dad had a heart scare last year and he's been going round more since, Saving for a house deposit feels like it's taking forever on two ordinary wages
- webcam photo: Head-and-shoulders shot from a laptop webcam placed slightly below eye level, so the camera looks up a little at his chin. Lighting comes mainly from a ceiling light, flat and slightly yellow, with the left side of his face a bit brighter from a window out of frame. He has a round, clean-shaven face with light stubble along the jaw, short mousy brown hair clipped at the sides and a bit flat on top, and pale skin. No glasses. His expression is neutral, mouth closed, eyes looking just below the camera at the screen. He's wearing a navy crew-neck sweatshirt with a small faded logo on the chest. Behind him is a magnolia living-room wall with a framed canvas print of the couple's wedding day slightly off-centre, a grey fabric settee with a crumpled throw over one arm, and the edge of a dog bed on the floor. A PlayStation controller is on the settee cushion, and a Wrexham AFC scarf is draped over the top of a door partly visible on the right.

P045 (Joanne):
- first name: Joanne
- age: 42
- lives in: Sutton-in-Ashfield, East Midlands
- occupation: Kitchen assistant at a primary school, about 25 hours a week in term time: prepping veg, serving dinners, washing up and wiping down the hall after lunch
- education detail: Left the local comprehensive at 16 with five GCSEs, including English and Art. Has a Level 2 Food Hygiene certificate through work. Has done a couple of free short online courses for fun, one on local history and one on drawing.
- household: Rents a two-bed terraced house with her partner Gary (45, a forklift driver at a distribution warehouse off the M1). They have been together eleven years and never got round to marrying, and have no children together. Gary's grown-up daughter visits now and then. They have an elderly tabby cat called Moss.
- cultural background: White British, born and raised in Nottinghamshire. Her dad worked down the pit until the closures and her mum did shifts at a hosiery factory. She was brought up Methodist and still goes to the local chapel most months and at Christmas and Easter. Her faith is quiet and practical rather than something she talks about much. Close to her mum, who lives ten minutes away.
- professional persona: Reliable and honest at work. She's the one who points out when the till float is a pound over, and she won't take leftover food home without asking. Gets on with the kids and remembers which ones have allergies. She doesn't push herself forward, and she worries a bit when Ofsted or a new cook manager is due. Has done the job about eight years and likes that it fits around term time.
- sports persona: Not sporty. Walks most days, usually round the reservoir or the old railway trails, and sometimes does a weekend parkrun walk with a friend. Watches the odd bit of Wimbledon. Gary follows Mansfield Town and she'll go to a match once a season to keep him company.
- arts persona: This is her real interest. She sketches and does watercolours at the kitchen table, mostly birds, trees and local buildings. She borrows a lot from the library: historical novels, folk tales and books about local mining history. She loves period dramas and documentaries and has been to the art gallery in Nottingham several times on her own. She's a bit shy about calling herself arty.
- travel persona: On a tight budget. Holidays are usually a static caravan at Skegness or Mablethorpe, or a cheap week in Wales. She went abroad twice, to Spain and Majorca, and would love to see Rome or Iceland someday. She enjoys day trips to places like Southwell Minster, Hardwick Hall and the Peak District, and always looks up the history beforehand.
- culinary persona: Plain home cooking she's good at: stews, cottage pie, a Sunday roast, cheese and onion cob for lunch. Occasionally she tries a new recipe from the telly, like a Thai curry or a shakshuka, to Gary's mild suspicion. Bakes for chapel coffee mornings. Calls the evening meal tea.
- hobbies and interests: watercolour and pencil sketching, library books, especially historical fiction, walking on the old railway trails, birdwatching from the back garden, local and family history, chapel coffee mornings, period dramas and nature documentaries, charity shop browsing
- skills: food prep and kitchen hygiene, working fast at busy lunchtimes, patience with young children, drawing and watercolour, budgeting on a low income, baking, keeping a house running
- career goals: Mostly content. She'd like a few more hours or a step up to assistant cook if one came up, but doesn't want the stress of running a kitchen. Quietly wonders about doing an evening art class or a course in something like teaching assistant work, but worries she's left it too late and isn't clever enough, which isn't true.
- voice: Warm, fairly quiet, a mild Notts accent. Moderate pace that speeds up a little when she's nervous. Uses 'erm' a fair bit and 'sort of' to soften things. Says 'you know' at the end of sentences. Might call someone 'duck' once she's relaxed, and uses words like 'mardy', 'cob' and 'me mum'. Apologises easily: 'sorry, that's not what you asked, is it'. In silences she tends to fill the gap with a small laugh or 'I don't know if that makes sense', then waits to be prompted again.
- typing: Mostly lower case with a capital at the start. Commas and the odd full stop, sometimes no final full stop. Apostrophes mostly right but sometimes dropped (dont, im). Few abbreviations beyond 'tbh' now and then. Short answers, and occasionally a second sentence adding an honest caveat.
- with strangers: Polite, a little reserved and self-deprecating at first. She worries about saying the wrong thing or not being helpful enough. She warms up quickly if the other person is friendly, and becomes chatty and thoughtful, especially on anything to do with art, nature or history. She's very straight and won't exaggerate to sound good.
- small things: Moss the cat sleeping on the radiator shelf, the blue tits nesting in the box Gary put up, what the kids at school won't eat (anything green), a library book she's halfway through, the price of a weekly shop, a walk round the reservoir at the weekend, her mum's knees playing up, the new Tesco self-checkouts annoying her
- deeper things: Feeling she never had the chance to do art properly and that it's too late, Worrying about money if Gary's warehouse cuts shifts, Sadness at not having children, which she's mostly made peace with, Her dad's death six years ago and the way the mining towns changed, Her faith being a comfort when she gets anxious at night, Being a bit hurt when people assume she isn't bright because of her job
- webcam photo: Laptop webcam at slightly below eye level, angled up a little, on a kitchen table. Daylight comes from a window to her left and gives soft, slightly uneven light. A woman in her early forties fills the middle of the frame from the chest up, with a fair complexion, light freckles and faint lines around her eyes. She has a small, slightly nervous smile. Her shoulder-length mid-brown hair has a few grey strands and is tied back loosely, with bits falling at the front. She wears a navy hooded sweatshirt over a white t-shirt, small silver stud earrings and no glasses. Behind her are pale magnolia walls, a wall calendar from a local takeaway with dates written in biro, a wooden shelf holding a few cookbooks, a jar of paintbrushes and a small framed watercolour of a robin, a kettle and a toaster on the worktop, and the top of a fridge with magnets and a school lunch menu pinned to it.

P046 (Imran):
- first name: Imran
- age: 47
- lives in: Huddersfield, Yorkshire and The Humber
- occupation: Part-time IT support technician, about 12 hours a week, split between a small accountancy firm in the town centre and a dental practice in Lindley. He looks after their laptops, printers, backups and Microsoft 365 accounts.
- education detail: GCSEs at a comprehensive in Huddersfield, then a BTEC National Diploma in IT at Huddersfield Technical College, followed by a part-time HNC in Computing. He later took CompTIA A+ and a Microsoft 365 administrator certificate through evening and online study in his thirties.
- household: He lives with his partner Saima, 44, a teaching assistant at a local primary school, in a three-bed semi in Birkby. They had a nikah three years ago but haven't done a civil registration yet, which he's been meaning to sort out. His two children from his first marriage, Zain (17) and Aleena (14), live with their mum in Dewsbury. They stay with him every other weekend and come round for tea on Wednesdays.
- cultural background: Born in Huddersfield to parents from the Mirpur district of Pakistan. His dad came over in the late 1960s and worked nights in a textile mill, and his mum raised four children. He is British Pakistani and a practising Muslim, quietly so. He prays most of his daily prayers, goes to Friday prayers when work allows and fasts in Ramadan. He speaks Pahari-Pothwari and some Urdu with older relatives and English everywhere else. His mum died in 2020. His dad, now 79, lives ten minutes away with Imran's younger brother.
- professional persona: He spent nearly twenty years full-time in IT support, mostly at a college and then a logistics firm, and was a team leader for a while. Four years ago he cut his hours right down, partly after the divorce and his mum's death, and partly to be around for his dad's hospital appointments and for the kids. He is methodical and patient with non-technical staff. He documents everything, keeps a password-managed log for each client and labels cables. He'd rather fix a problem properly once than patch it twice. He doesn't like selling himself and gets most work by word of mouth.
- sports persona: A lifelong Yorkshire cricket follower. He played as a batsman in the Huddersfield league in his twenties and early thirties and now watches more than he plays, sometimes at Headingley with his son. He walks most days, often up to Castle Hill or along the canal, and tracks his steps carefully. Not a big football fan, though he keeps half an eye on Huddersfield Town results.
- arts persona: He listens to Nusrat Fateh Ali Khan and old qawwali in the car, along with some 90s British music from his college days, like Oasis, The Verve and Cornershop. He reads popular history, especially about the Partition and the Second World War, and gets through a book a month on his Kindle. He doesn't really go to galleries or the theatre.
- travel persona: He has visited Pakistan several times for family weddings and to see relatives, most recently in 2022. He did Umrah with his mum in 2019, which he holds very dear. Otherwise he prefers UK breaks: the Lake District, Whitby, the Yorkshire Dales. He plans trips well in advance, with a printed itinerary and booked parking. He doesn't enjoy flying much and gets anxious about connections.
- culinary persona: He cooks a reliable chicken karahi and his mum's tarka dal, which the kids ask for on Wednesday nights. Saima does more of the everyday cooking, but he does Saturday breakfast for the household: eggs, parathas, chai. He shops at the big halal butcher on the same day each week. He likes a fish and chip tea at the seaside and has a sweet tooth for jalebi and Yorkshire parkin alike.
- hobbies and interests: Refurbishing old laptops and giving them to families at the local mosque and the kids' schools, Walking around Castle Hill and the Colne Valley, Following Yorkshire County Cricket, Reading popular history, Keeping a tidy vegetable patch in the back garden (tomatoes, chillies, coriander), Watching cricket highlights and documentaries with his son
- skills: Windows and Microsoft 365 administration, Network and printer troubleshooting, Hardware repair and refurbishment, Clear step-by-step explanation for non-technical people, Meticulous record-keeping and spreadsheets, Conversational Pahari-Pothwari and basic Urdu, Cooking family-sized curries
- career goals: He isn't chasing promotion. He'd like to gradually take on two or three more small-business clients so he can go up to about 20 hours once his dad's needs are clearer, while keeping Wednesdays and the kids' weekends free. He has thought about formally setting up as a sole trader with a proper website but keeps putting off the self-promotion side.
- voice: Quiet, measured and polite, with a soft West Yorkshire accent: flat vowels, 'tea' for the evening meal, the odd 'nowt' or 'reckon'. He thinks before answering, often starting with 'Er...' or 'Well, it's sort of...', and his answers are fairly short unless the topic is something he knows well, like computers, cricket or his kids, when he opens up more. He says 'sorry' readily, sometimes to correct himself ('sorry, I mean the other one'). He ends points with 'you know' or 'if that makes sense'. He doesn't fill silences himself. He waits, and might say 'Is that alright?' to check he's answered properly.
- typing: Careful and correct. Proper capital letters, full stops, correct apostrophes, and usually complete sentences even in quick boxes. He rarely abbreviates beyond 'e.g.' or 'IT'. He sometimes reads back and corrects a typo before submitting. No emojis.
- with strangers: Courteous, a bit reserved and eager not to give the wrong answer. He comes across as kind and trustworthy rather than chatty. He'll ask a clarifying question rather than guess, and he warms up noticeably once he's put at ease or the conversation turns practical.
- small things: The dental practice's printer that 'jams if you look at it wrong', Getting his step count in on the canal path, Whether Yorkshire will get through to the knockout stages this season, His chillies finally coming through in the greenhouse, Doing Wednesday tea for the kids, Saturday morning parathas, Traffic on the A62 into Huddersfield
- deeper things: The divorce eight years ago and feeling he let his children down, even though they're close now, Missing his mum, and how much the Umrah trip with her means to him now, Worry about his dad's heart condition and who'll look after him long-term, Feeling a bit 'between' worlds: very Yorkshire, very Muslim, never quite fully either in some rooms, Wanting to make his relationship with Saima official legally and not having got round to it, Quiet anxiety about money since dropping his hours
- webcam photo: Laptop webcam, slightly below eye level, so the view looks a little upward at him. He sits centred at a dining table, head and shoulders in frame. Soft daylight comes from a window off to the left, leaving the right side of his face a little shadowed. He's a South Asian man with light-brown skin, short black hair greying at the temples, and a neatly trimmed short beard flecked with grey. He wears thin black rectangular glasses and has a polite, slightly tentative half-smile. He's in a navy quarter-zip jumper over a white collared shirt. Behind him is a magnolia-painted wall with a framed black-and-gold Arabic calligraphy piece (Ayat al-Kursi) hung a little to the right. Below it is a low pine bookshelf holding a row of labelled ring binders, a few paperbacks, a small potted plant and a phone charging cable. The edge of a white radiator is visible at the bottom left.

P047 (Abdirahman):
- first name: Abdirahman
- age: 27
- lives in: Leicester, East Midlands
- occupation: Vehicle maintenance technician at a commercial van fleet depot on an industrial estate off the A6, where he services and repairs delivery vans. Full-time, roughly 40 hours a week, with an early shift pattern and the odd Saturday morning. Since last year he has been the senior tech on his shift, so he signs off other people's jobs and shows the apprentices what to do.
- education detail: Went to secondary school in Leicester and left with GCSEs, mostly passes, with maths his best subject. Did a Level 3 Light Vehicle Maintenance and Repair apprenticeship through a local college while working at a fast-fit garage. Has since added a few manufacturer and electric-vehicle safety courses through work.
- household: Rents a two-bed terraced house in the Belgrave area with his partner, Hodan, who works as a pharmacy dispenser. They had a nikah at the mosque two years ago but have not legally registered the marriage yet. They keep meaning to sort it out. No children yet. His mum and two younger sisters live about ten minutes' drive away.
- cultural background: Born in Rotterdam to Somali parents. The family moved to Leicester when he was eight, like a lot of Dutch-Somali families did around then. He speaks Somali with his mum, English everywhere else, and has a bit of rusty Dutch he barely uses now. Muslim and fairly steady about it. He prays when he can, goes to Friday prayers if his shift allows and fasts in Ramadan, but he doesn't make a big show of it. He feels thoroughly Leicester and doesn't think about identity much.
- professional persona: Reliable and fair at work rather than flashy. Good at finding faults and patient with the apprentices. He never pretends a van is fixed when it isn't, and the managers trust him for that. The weak spot is admin. His job sheets are often late or half-filled, and the supervisor chases him about it. He doesn't get rattled by breakdowns or angry drivers. He just gets on with it.
- sports persona: Plays five-a-side on Wednesday nights with lads from work and from the area, at the same pitches he's used for years. Follows Leicester City and watches most matches at his cousin's house or on his phone. Not into fitness for its own sake and has never set foot in a gym class.
- arts persona: Not much interest. Listens to whatever's on the radio in the workshop and some Somali music his mum plays. Watches the odd film if Hodan picks it. Has no interest in galleries or theatre and would say so politely.
- travel persona: Has been back to the Netherlands a couple of times to see relatives, and once to Hargeisa for a family wedding. Beyond that he isn't fussed about travelling. He'd rather have a week off at home. Hodan wants a holiday in Turkey and he'll probably go along with it.
- culinary persona: Eats the same few things and is happy with that: rice and goat, suqaar, pasta, chicken from the halal takeaway near work. Grabs a chicken cob or a meal deal at lunch. Hodan does most of the cooking. His job is making tea with plenty of cardamom and sugar.
- hobbies and interests: five-a-side football, watching Leicester City, playing FIFA/EA FC online with his cousins, tinkering with his own car, an old Honda Civic, YouTube videos of car repairs
- skills: diagnosing engine and electrical faults, using diagnostic software, training apprentices, speaking Somali, staying calm under pressure
- career goals: Wants to get his EV qualifications to the higher level, because he can see that's where the work is going. He might go for workshop supervisor eventually if it comes up, though he'd rather avoid the paperwork. He's vaguely thought about doing mobile mechanic work on the side but hasn't done anything about it.
- voice: Quiet, unhurried Leicester voice, with nothing very marked in it. Fairly short answers unless asked something about cars or football, when he says a bit more. Uses 'erm' and 'sort of' now and then, and ends some sentences with 'you know' or 'yeah'. Says 'mate' to men and would say 'cob' for a bread roll without thinking. Doesn't mind silence at all and won't rush to fill it. He just waits for the next question. Polite and says 'sorry, what was that?' if he mishears.
- typing: Mostly lowercase and minimal punctuation, with no full stop at the end. Sometimes skips apostrophes ('dont', 'im'). Uses 'tbh' and 'idk' occasionally. Answers are short and plain, sometimes just a few words. He doesn't go back to fix typos.
- with strangers: Reserved but friendly. He comes across as calm, decent and a bit hard to read at first. He answers honestly and doesn't try to impress. He won't pretend to know things he doesn't, and he's easy to get on with once he warms up a little.
- small things: the van he fixed today that had three different faults, being knackered after an early shift, Leicester's league position, his Civic needing a new clutch, five-a-side getting rained off, Hodan making him watch a series he doesn't follow, the price of fuel
- deeper things: his dad went back to Somalia years ago and they barely speak, he and Hodan haven't legally registered their marriage and his mum keeps nagging about it, he feels a bit responsible for his younger sisters, sometimes worries he'll be doing the same job at 50, though it doesn't keep him up at night
- webcam photo: Laptop webcam at slightly below eye level, angled up a little, so the shot shows his head and shoulders with some ceiling visible. Evening light from a ceiling bulb gives a warm yellowish cast, with a faint glare on his forehead. He is a slim Black man with a short neat beard and short, closely cut dark hair, faded at the sides. His expression is neutral and relaxed, with a small polite half-smile. No glasses. He wears a navy work polo shirt with a small embroidered company logo on the chest. Behind him is a magnolia-painted living room wall with a framed piece of Arabic calligraphy slightly off-centre. The corner of a grey fabric sofa is visible on the left, with a folded prayer mat over its arm. On the right, a phone charger cable hangs from a socket near a radiator draped with a hi-vis jacket.

P048 (Gareth):
- first name: Gareth
- age: 36
- lives in: Chelmsford, East of England
- occupation: Senior travel consultant at an independent tailor-made travel agency in Chelmsford city centre, specialising in high-end trips to Japan, South-East Asia and Southern Africa. He works full-time, about 40 hours a week including one Saturday in three, on a basic salary plus commission.
- education detail: A-levels in Geography, History and Spanish at a sixth form college in Colchester, then a BA in Geography from the University of Leicester. He has an ABTA travel consultant certificate and several destination specialist qualifications from tourism boards.
- household: Lives alone in a rented two-bedroom flat in a converted Victorian building near Chelmsford station. He and his wife separated about fourteen months ago after eight years of marriage. They have no children and the divorce paperwork is in progress but not finalised. She kept their house in Witham and he moved out.
- cultural background: White British, born and raised in Colchester. His dad was a quantity surveyor and his mum was a primary school deputy head. He has an older sister in St Albans. Not religious and never really was; he went to church at Christmas as a kid and that was it. Comfortably middle class, and he has always been quietly keen on moving up a rung.
- professional persona: Very organised and very good at his job. He builds itineraries down to transfer times and keeps a spreadsheet of every hotel he has seen in person. He is persuasive with clients and good at steering them towards the more expensive option, and he is not above overstating how 'exclusive' something is if it closes a sale. He takes pride in being the top earner in the office and keeps an eye on everyone else's figures. Colleagues find him reliable but slightly calculating.
- sports persona: Runs three or four times a week along the Chelmer towpath and logs everything on Strava. He did his first marathon (Manchester) two years ago and is training for a sub-3:30. He follows Formula 1 closely and is not bothered about football, which he is happy to admit.
- arts persona: Reads widely: narrative non-fiction, translated Japanese fiction, travel writing. He goes to exhibitions in London a few times a year, mostly photography and design. He likes the film programme at the Mercury Theatre in Colchester and watches subtitled dramas on streaming services. He has a decent eye for photography and takes a mirrorless camera on every trip.
- travel persona: Travel is central to his life and part of his job. He goes on regular fam trips, which are subsidised hosted trips for agents, and he is not shy about using them for upgrades. He has been to Japan five times and loves Kyoto in November. Since the separation he travels solo: a long-haul trip each year plus city breaks to places like Lisbon, Copenhagen and Ljubljana. He plans meticulously but leaves a day or two blank for wandering.
- culinary persona: A capable, precise cook who enjoys technique. He weighs ingredients, has a carbon steel wok and makes his own ramen broth at weekends. He calls his evening meal 'dinner'. On weekdays he batch-cooks so he isn't eating rubbish. He likes natural wine, though he is a bit performative about it, and keeps a list of restaurants he wants to try in London.
- hobbies and interests: distance running and marathon training, travel photography and editing in Lightroom, Japanese cooking, learning Japanese on an app and with a weekly online tutor, Formula 1, reading travel writing and translated fiction, planning trips in spreadsheets

req.text:
You write transcripts of realistic video calls between strangers for a fully synthetic research dataset set in the UK. The study, in order (from its published design): a short puzzle task done alone; first impressions of the others' webcam photos; then a series of three-minute, one-on-one video calls in rounds, each person meeting the others in their group; after each call a short survey.

Call shape (from the original study's numbers): a call is cut off by a three-minute timer. A typical call has about 30 turns (most between 20 and 39) and about 570 words in total (most between 440 and 682); half of all turns are 12 words or fewer, and a quarter are 24 or more. Short acknowledgements ("yeah", "mm") count as turns too. So aim for about 570 words in about 30 turns: alongside the quick back-and-forth, people often talk in longer stretches (explaining their job, telling a story), and those long turns carry much of the call.

Guide to British conversational English (use it for how people talk; it is a description of speech, not a script):
How British people talk in casual conversation. This is a paraphrase of published descriptions of spoken British English; sources are in SOURCES.md. Use these features lightly and only where they fit the person. Never use them as a caricature.

- **Fillers.** British speakers hesitate with "erm" and "er". Women and younger speakers lean towards "erm".
- **Hedges.** "Sort of" is everywhere and steady. "Kind of" is spreading, and younger speakers use it more.
- **Politeness words.** "Please", "thank you", "thanks" and "sorry" mostly mean what they say. "Sorry" also works as a repair word (to correct yourself, or to ask someone to repeat) and can be ironic.
- **Tags at the end of a sentence.** "You know", "right", "okay", "yeah", "do you know what I mean". Among young Londoners, "innit" and "you get me" are rising. Tags depend on age and region only, never on ethnicity.
- **Echoing.** In an engaged conversation people pick up and re-use parts of each other's words.
- **Regional words and grammar** (from a recent dialect survey):
  - A bread roll is a "barm" in the North West (Manchester to Liverpool and western Lancashire), a "cob" around Nottinghamshire, a "bap" in Staffordshire, the West Midlands and North Wales, and a "batch" in Liverpool and Coventry.
  - Around Liverpool an ice lolly can be a "lolly ice".
  - The evening meal is "tea" in the North West, North East and Yorkshire, and "dinner" in the South East and London. Some people say both.
  - "Yous" or "youse" for plural "you" is common in the North East (Newcastle, Teesside), Liverpool and Scotland, less so in Manchester, and rare in York, Leeds and Sheffield.
  - "Give it me" is normal in the North West and West Midlands and widely accepted in Sheffield and York; it fades south of Birmingham, Coventry and Leicester.
  - "You was" is widely used, historically Northern and now found as far south as London.
- **Everyday British words** to draw on where they fit, without assigning them to regions: knackered or shattered, chuffed or made up, skint or brassic, mardy or stroppy, mum or mam, mate or pal, settee, sofa or couch.

Karen: Can't sack volunteers. That's the trouble. I just end up doing it all myself, then I'm short with them.
Tomasz: Short is good. You tell them, they come next time.
Karen: Sometimes. Sometimes they don't come back at all. Then I feel bad.
Tomasz: Don't feel bad. Work is work. Look, I get people swear at me fifty times a day, I sleep like baby.
Karen: Lucky you.
Tomasz: What you do apart from shop?
Karen: Sewing, mostly. Mending, upcycling. Walking on the Quantocks. Garden, tomatoes.
Tomasz: Tomatoes, my wife's mum in Poland, whole garden, tomatoes, cucumbers, she makes pickles. Me, I do barbecue. That's it.
Karen: Right.
Tomasz: You sell your sewing? Online, eBay, Vinted? Listen, there's money in it. Upcycle, you put nice photos, you sell for double.
Karen: I keep meaning to. Never get round to it.
Tomasz: You must! Start this week. I tell you, if I can sew, I would be rich. You have the product, you just need sales. That's me, sales.
Karen: (laughs) Are you offering?
Tomasz: For ten per cent, why not? Listen, first thing, photos, good light —

=== CALL C0046 ===
Darren: Alright? Darren. Can you hear me?

Darren: Bridgwater, Somerset. Nice to meet you.
Abena: You too. I noticed the starlings on your calendar. Is that local to you?
Darren: Yeah, Ham Wall, on the Levels. That one's bought, but I photograph them myself. Got into photography about five years ago, saved up for a second-hand Fuji. The Levels, the murmurations, Hinkley from a distance at dusk.
Abena: Hinkley? The power station?
Darren: Yeah, the construction. Sounds daft, but at dusk, with the cranes all lit up across the water, it's sort of beautiful. Industrial, you know? People think Bridgwater's just a place you drive past, but there's stuff there.
Abena: No, it doesn't sound daft at all. There's a long tradition of that, painting factories and industry. The light on something ugly can be the most interesting thing.
Darren: That's it, that's exactly it. The light on something ugly. I'll be using that.
Abena: (laughs) Please do. Do you show them anywhere?
Darren: Local Facebook group mostly. One of the murmurations got a couple of hundred likes. Others, not so much. Bit gutting when you've stood out there two hours.
Abena: Erm, I think likes are a strange way to judge it. Some of the best work I've seen gets very little attention. Have you thought about printing them?
Darren: Not really. Wouldn't know where to start.
Abena: A local library or café will often hang work. It's sort of how many people start.
Darren: Huh. Might look into that. What do you do, then?
Abena: Interior design, part-time, for a studio in Dulwich.
Darren: Oh, nice. I'm tiling our downstairs loo at the moment, myself. We own the place, ex-council semi, so I do all the DIY. Laminate, shelves, the lot.
Abena: Well done. Tiling is harder than people think. What tiles?
Darren: Plain white, metro ones. Cheap, Wickes. Kerry wanted grey.
Abena: White metro is safe. Have you thought about a coloured grout? A dark one with white tiles can look very smart, and it hides the dirt in a toilet.
Darren: Dark grout. Never even thought of that. Hides the dirt, that's a selling point with an eight-year-old in the house.
Abena: (laughs) Exactly. Practical and pretty.
Darren: So you do posh houses, then?
Abena: Some. Period houses mostly, Victorian. I've done one for someone quite well known, but I'm not allowed to say.
Darren: Go on.
Abena: No. (laughs) But honestly, the small jobs are often more satisfying. Someone who's saved up for one room.
Darren: Fair enough. I'm a machine operator, packaging, at a food plant. Shifts.
Abena: That must take real concentration.
Darren: It does, yeah. Most people don't get that. Changeovers, fault codes —

=== CALL C0047 ===
