req.text:
You write transcripts of realistic video calls between strangers for a fully synthetic research dataset set in the UK. The study, in order (from its published design): a short puzzle task done alone; first impressions of the others' webcam photos; then a series of three-minute, one-on-one video calls in rounds, each person meeting the others in their group; after each call a short survey.

Call shape (from the original study's numbers): a call is cut off by a three-minute timer. A typical call has about 30 turns (most between 20 and 39) and about 570 words in total (most between 440 and 682); half of all turns are 12 words or fewer, and a quarter are 24 or more. Short acknowledgements ("yeah", "mm") count as turns too. So aim for about 570 words in about 30 turns: alongside the quick back-and-forth, people often talk in longer stretches (explaining their job, telling a story), and those long turns carry much of the call.

Guide to British conversational English (use it for how people talk; it is a description of speech, not a script):
How British people talk in casual conversation. This is a paraphrase of published descriptions of spoken British English; sources are in SOURCES.md. Use these features lightly and only where they fit the person. Never use them as a caricature.

- **Fillers.** British speakers hesitate with "erm" and "er". Women and younger speakers lean towards "erm".
- **Hedges.** "Sort of" is everywhere and steady. "Kind of" is spreading, and younger speakers use it more.
- **Politeness words.** "Please", "thank you", "thanks" and "sorry" mostly mean what they say. "Sorry" also works as a repair word (to correct yourself, or to ask someone to repeat) and can be ironic.
- **Tags at the end of a sentence.** "You know", "right", "okay", "yeah", "do you know what I mean". Among young Londoners, "innit" and "you get me" are rising. Tags depend on age and region only, never on ethnicity.
- **Echoing.** In an engaged conversation people pick up and re-use parts of each other's words.
- **Regional words and grammar** (from a recent dialect survey):
  - A bread roll is a "barm" in the North West (Manchester to Liverpool and western Lancashire), a "cob" around Nottinghamshire, a "bap" in Staffordshire, the West Midlands and North Wales, and a "batch" in Liverpool and Coventry.
  - Around Liverpool an ice lolly can be a "lolly ice".
  - The evening meal is "tea" in the North West, North East and Yorkshire, and "dinner" in the South East and London. Some people say both.
  - "Yous" or "youse" for plural "you" is common in the North East (Newcastle, Teesside), Liverpool and Scotland, less so in Manchester, and rare in York, Leeds and Sheffield.
  - "Give it me" is normal in the North West and West Midlands and widely accepted in Sheffield and York; it fades south of Birmingham, Coventry and Leicester.
  - "You was" is widely used, historically Northern and now found as far south as London.
- **Everyday British words** to draw on where they fit, without assigning them to regions: knackered or shattered, chuffed or made up, skint or brassic, mardy or stroppy, mum or mam, mate or pal, settee, sofa or couch.

The group (session S05). Persona cards, including the webcam photo each person was rated on:

P019 (Tomasz):
- first name: Tomasz
- age: 44
- lives in: Walsall, West Midlands
- occupation: Outbound telesales agent at a call centre on a business park near Junction 10 of the M6. He sells business energy and water contracts to small firms like takeaways, garages and hair salons, on a low basic wage plus commission.
- education detail: Finished a technikum (technical secondary school) in Poland in automotive mechanics, with the Polish maturity exam. He has no UK qualifications apart from a forklift licence from his warehouse years and the in-house sales training certificates the company hands out.
- household: Lives with his wife Agnieszka, who works shifts as a care assistant in a residential home, and their 15-year-old son Kacper, who goes to the local secondary. They rent a three-bed semi from a private landlord off the Wolverhampton Road and have been there about eight years.
- cultural background: Born and raised in a mid-sized town near Bydgoszcz in northern Poland. He came to the UK in 2006 at 26, first doing agency warehouse work in Wednesbury, then delivery driving, then moving into telesales about nine years ago when he realised he could out-talk most people. Catholic by upbringing. He goes to the Polish Mass at Christmas and Easter mainly because Agnieszka wants to, and for the food afterwards. He has British citizenship and says he is not going back, though his mum and brother are still in Poland.
- professional persona: Competitive and target-driven. He knows exactly where he sits on the leaderboard every day and will tell you, often rounding up. He is good at opening a call and not letting the other person off the line, and he isn't bothered by people swearing at him or hanging up. He thinks most of the training is rubbish and says so in team meetings, which has got him a couple of informal warnings. He gets on with whichever team leader leaves him alone. His paperwork is done properly enough to get paid and no more than that.
- sports persona: Watches football more than he plays it. He follows Lech Poznań from childhood and has a soft spot for Wolves because a mate took him to Molineux in his first year here. He plays five-a-side on Thursday nights with a mixed Polish and English group at a leisure centre, where he is loud, argues every decision and doesn't pass much. He likes a bet on the football and darts on his phone.
- arts persona: Not much interest. He watches Netflix crime series and action films with Agnieszka, and scrolls YouTube for car reviews and Polish comedy clips. He hasn't been to a museum or the theatre since a school trip and doesn't see the point. Music is Polish radio hits and whatever is on in the car.
- travel persona: Drives or flies back to Poland once or twice a year to see his mum, usually from Birmingham Airport to Gdańsk. They had one all-inclusive week in Turkey two summers ago, which he liked mostly for the buffet and the pool bar. He isn't interested in sightseeing and would rather go somewhere hot and do nothing.
- culinary persona: Agnieszka does most of the cooking: pierogi, schabowy, soups on Sunday. He does the barbecue in summer and treats it as his job. Lunch at work is a meal deal or a bacon bap from the van on the industrial estate. Friday is often a chippy or kebab. He buys Polish sausage and beer from the Polish shop on Caldmore Green.
- hobbies and interests: Cars, especially German ones. He drives a nine-year-old BMW 3 Series on finance and keeps it very clean, Five-a-side football on Thursdays, Football betting accumulators, Barbecues in the back garden with mates, Watching boxing and MMA on pay-per-view, Car boot sales on Sunday mornings, looking for tools to resell
- skills: Cold calling and handling objections, Basic car maintenance: brakes, oil, bulbs, Forklift driving, Fluent Polish, good working English, Haggling, Fast at the call centre CRM system
- career goals: Wants to move into a field sales job with a company car and a better commission structure, or become a team leader, though he has been passed over once and blames favouritism. He half-seriously talks about starting his own business brokering energy contracts but hasn't done anything about it. Mostly he wants more money and to be seen to be winning.
- voice: Confident and fast, with a clear Polish accent and a few West Midlands bits picked up over the years. He says 'bap', 'give it me', 'mate' and 'tara' and doesn't think about it. Sometimes he drops an article ('I was at shop') or uses Polish-style word order when he's speeding up. He starts sentences with 'Listen,' or 'Look,' and finishes with 'you know?' or 'yeah?'. He rarely hesitates, but when he does it's a short 'er'. He doesn't leave silences. He fills them himself with an opinion or a story about a sale, and if a question bores him he answers briefly and moves on. When he hasn't heard something he says 'Sorry?' bluntly. He talks over people a bit without meaning it as rude.
- typing: Quick and minimal. Mostly lowercase, with a capital for names sometimes. Few full stops, and commas used as all-purpose breaks. He often leaves out apostrophes ('dont', 'its ok') and sometimes leaves out articles. He uses 'ok', 'yes', 'no idea' and an occasional 'lol'. A typical answer is one line unless the topic is money or cars, in which case it runs on.
- with strangers: Instantly chatty and friendly on the surface, with a firm handshake energy even on a call. He asks what you do and works out within a minute whether you are useful or interesting. He likes to show he knows things and can come across as a bit boastful or salesy. He is blunt in his opinions about the government, prices and lazy people. He isn't easily offended and doesn't apologise much. Some people find him good fun, others find him too much.
- small things: His team hit target last month and he 'carried them', Price of diesel and insurance in Walsall, The bacon bap van on the estate does the best one around, Kacper spends too long on the PlayStation, Wolves' last result and the referee's mistakes, Got a good drill set at the car boot for a fiver, The M6 at Junction 10 is always a nightmare
- deeper things: His dad drank a lot and died when Tomasz was 19, and he left Poland partly to get away from all that, He sends money to his mum every month and his brother doesn't, which they have fallen out over, He worries quietly that he'll still be renting at 60, He feels English people sometimes treat him as a cheap Polish worker and it makes him want to prove them wrong, He is proud Kacper speaks perfect English but annoyed his Polish is getting worse, He has some credit card debt Agnieszka doesn't know the full size of
- webcam photo: Laptop webcam shot from slightly below, laptop on a kitchen table, head and shoulders filling most of the frame. Lit by the overhead kitchen light and a bit of grey daylight from a window to the left, so the left side of his face is brighter. He has a broad face, short dark-blond hair clipped close at the sides and thinning a little at the front, light stubble and pale blue eyes. He is looking straight into the camera with a half-grin, chin slightly up. No glasses. He wears a navy quarter-zip work fleece with a small company logo on the chest over a grey T-shirt. Behind him are white gloss kitchen cupboards, a kettle and a toaster on a laminate worktop, a roll of kitchen towel, a Lech Poznań calendar pinned to the side of a cupboard, and a small wooden crucifix hanging above the doorway into the hall, which is partly out of frame on the right.

P020 (Abena):
- first name: Abena
- age: 53
- lives in: Herne Hill, South London
- occupation: Part-time interior design consultant for a small residential design studio in Dulwich. She works about two short days a fortnight, mostly client consultations, mood boards and sourcing fabrics and furniture.
- education detail: BA in Fine Art from a university in Kumasi, Ghana. After moving to London she took a part-time diploma in interior design in her early thirties, then a few short courses in colour and lighting.
- household: Lives with her husband Kwame, 56, a finance director at a housing association, in a three-bedroom Victorian terrace they bought in 2004. Their two children, a daughter of 26 and a son of 23, have both moved out. The daughter lives in Manchester and the son in a flatshare in Peckham. No pets.
- cultural background: Born and raised in Accra, Ghana, in a Fante-speaking family, and came to London at 25 to join Kwame, who was already working here. She has been a British citizen for over twenty years. She is Christian and attends a Ghanaian Methodist congregation in South London most Sundays, though she treats it as much as community as worship. She speaks Fante and Twi with family and English everywhere else.
- professional persona: Calm and unhurried with clients. She is good at reading what people actually want under what they say they want. She steers clients towards pricier, better-quality pieces without them feeling pushed, and she is not above mentioning that she has done a house 'for someone quite well known' when it helps. She likes the part-time arrangement because it keeps the work interesting rather than a grind.
- sports persona: Not sporty. She walks a lot, round Brockwell Park most mornings, and does a Pilates class once a week at a studio on Railton Road. She watches the Ghana national team when there's a tournament on, mostly because Kwame does.
- arts persona: This is her main interest. She goes to the Dulwich Picture Gallery and the South London Gallery regularly and has a Tate membership. She follows contemporary African artists closely and has bought a couple of small pieces herself. She also reads widely, mostly literary fiction and design history.
- travel persona: Goes back to Ghana every year or two, usually around Christmas. She prefers small, characterful hotels to big resorts and plans trips around galleries and markets: Lisbon, Marrakech, Copenhagen. Kwame does the bookings; she does the itinerary.
- culinary persona: Cooks Ghanaian food at home most weeks, especially light soup, jollof and kontomire stew, but is curious and will try anything. She likes eating out somewhere a bit special and notices the interiors as much as the food. She calls the evening meal dinner.
- hobbies and interests: Visiting galleries and exhibitions, Collecting small artworks and ceramics, Reading literary fiction, Morning walks in Brockwell Park, Weekly Pilates, Browsing antique and vintage furniture shops, Watching design and property programmes
- skills: Colour and spatial planning, Sourcing furniture and fabrics, Negotiating prices with suppliers, Sketching and mood-board making, Speaking Fante and Twi, Staying composed under pressure
- career goals: No big ambitions to expand. She would like to take on a few private clients of her own alongside the studio work, ideally period-house renovations, and perhaps one day help curate a small exhibition of Ghanaian design.
- voice: Measured, low-key and fairly quiet, with a soft Ghanaian lilt underneath decades of South London English. She speaks at an even pace and thinks before answering, often starting with 'erm' or 'well'. She uses 'sort of' as a hedge now and then and sometimes ends with 'you know'. Her tone is polite and warm without being effusive. She is comfortable with silence and will simply wait, or say 'let me think' rather than fill the gap. She rarely raises her voice or gets animated, except a little when talking about art.
- typing: Types in proper sentences with capitals at the start and correct apostrophes. She often skips the full stop at the end of a short answer. No text-speak, and she rarely uses exclamation marks. Answers are brief and to the point.
- with strangers: Reserved and pleasant at first, a little hard to read. She is polite, listens well and doesn't overshare. She comes across as composed and quietly confident, sometimes slightly cool, but kind if you need help or get something wrong. She warms up noticeably if the conversation turns to art, design or Ghana.
- small things: The Pilates teacher keeps changing the class time, A lovely mid-century sideboard she spotted in a shop in Crystal Palace, Her son never answers his phone, The rain has been relentless this week, She's halfway through a novel her book-loving friend recommended, Church harvest is coming up and she's been roped into decorating
- deeper things: She gave up a more serious painting career when the children were small and sometimes wonders what she'd have made of it, She finds the gap between how she's treated as a Black woman in some upmarket shops and how her clients treat her quietly funny, and uses it to her advantage, Her mother in Accra is getting frail and she is weighing how much time to spend there, She doesn't feel especially devout, and goes to church mostly for the people and the singing, She enjoys being comfortably off and doesn't feel guilty about it
- webcam photo: Head-and-shoulders shot from a laptop on a dining table, camera slightly below eye level. Soft daylight comes from a window to her left, so the right side of her face is a little shadowed. She is a Black woman in her early fifties with a calm, closed-mouth half-smile and steady eye contact with the camera. Her short natural hair is neatly shaped and greying at the temples. She wears tortoiseshell reading glasses pushed up on her head, small gold stud earrings and a loose mustard-yellow linen shirt. Behind her is a sage-green painted wall with a framed abstract print in ochre and indigo, a tall white shelf holding art books and a few handmade ceramic vases, and a trailing pothos plant on the top shelf. The edge of a brass floor lamp is visible on the right.

P021 (Karen):
- first name: Karen
- age: 43
- lives in: Taunton, South West England
- occupation: Shop manager of a hospice charity shop on a high street, around 25 hours a week across four days. She runs the rota for about twenty volunteers, prices donations, handles the till reconciliation and stock targets, and reports to an area manager.
- education detail: Left school at 16 with GCSEs from a comprehensive in Bridgwater. Did a retail apprenticeship at a shoe shop chain, later an NVQ Level 3 in Retail Management through a previous employer. No degree and no plans for one.
- household: Lives alone in a two-bedroom Victorian terrace she bought eleven years ago with a small inheritance from her nan towards the deposit. She has no pets, though she has thought about getting a cat for years. Never married. Had one long relationship in her late twenties and early thirties that ended badly.
- cultural background: White British, born and raised in Somerset. Her family were Methodist, and she still goes to the local Methodist chapel maybe twice a month, more around Christmas and Easter. For her it is more about routine and the people than strong doctrine. Her mum is widowed and still lives in Bridgwater. She has one older brother in Yeovil with two teenage kids.
- professional persona: Competent, organised enough, and quietly proud that her shop hits its targets. She is blunt with volunteers who don't pull their weight and can come across as sharp. Afterwards she worries she's upset someone and replays it at night. She dislikes the head office emails full of buzzwords. She went part-time after a stressful full-time stint managing a discount chain store and doesn't miss the stress.
- sports persona: Not sporty in a team sense. She swims lengths at the leisure centre early on her days off because it's quiet then. She half-follows Somerset county cricket because her dad used to take her, and has the radio on in the summer.
- arts persona: Reads crime novels, mostly Ann Cleeves and Peter James, many picked up from the shop's book shelves. Watches British detective dramas and the Great British Sewing Bee. Not a theatre or gallery person. She went to a craft fair in Wells and found it overpriced.
- travel persona: Gets anxious about flying so mostly holidays in the UK: a week in a cottage in north Cornwall most years, and once a coach tour to the Lake District with her mum. She went to Tenerife with friends at 30 and spent half of it worrying about the hotel safe.
- culinary persona: Plain, sensible cooking. She batch-cooks chilli and shepherd's pie on Sundays and freezes portions. Most Sundays she has a roast dinner at her mum's. Likes a cream tea but thinks people argue about jam-or-cream-first far too much. Drinks too much tea and the occasional cider.
- hobbies and interests: upcycling and mending clothes on her sewing machine, walking on the Quantocks, usually alone, growing tomatoes and runner beans in her small back garden, crime novels, jigsaws in winter
- skills: pricing second-hand goods quickly, sewing and alterations, volunteer rota planning, cash handling and basic bookkeeping, spotting designer labels in donation bags
- career goals: Mostly wants stability. She'd take an area manager role only if it stayed part-time, which she doubts it would. Sometimes she thinks about selling upcycled clothes online on the side but hasn't got round to it.
- voice: Quiet, measured, slightly guarded at first. She has a soft Somerset accent with a bit of a rolled 'r', but nothing exaggerated. Uses 'erm' when thinking and 'sort of' a lot. Says 'dinner' for her evening meal and 'proper' now and then ('proper knackered'). Answers are short until she warms up, and then she can be quite opinionated and dry. Sometimes adds 'you know' at the end. Silence makes her a bit uneasy, so she'll fill it with 'sorry, was that what you meant?' rather than wait.
- typing: Mostly lowercase with a capital at the start of the first sentence and sometimes not after. Uses apostrophes correctly most of the time. Ends sentences with full stops or nothing. Occasionally types 'tbh' or 'dont know'. Short answers, no emojis.
- with strangers: Reserved and a little wary. She doesn't do small talk well, gives brief answers and doesn't ask much back. She can sound curt without meaning to. If a topic touches something she knows about (charity shops, sewing, Somerset) she opens up and becomes more direct and funny.
- small things: the weird things people donate, like a full set of false teeth once, parking in town being a nightmare, her tomatoes doing well or not, volunteers who never turn up on Saturdays, being shattered after a stock delivery day, what she's reading
- deeper things: her dad dying suddenly when she was 35 and how much she still misses him, worrying about her mum getting older and being the one nearby to look after her, the ex who left and how she's not sure she wants to try again, lying awake worrying about things she said at work, feeling her faith matters more to her than she lets on
- webcam photo: Laptop webcam at a slight upward angle, framing her from mid-chest up, slightly off-centre to the left. Lighting is a mix of grey daylight from a window to her right and a warm ceiling bulb, leaving one side of her face a little shadowed. She has a pale, lightly freckled face and a neutral, slightly wary expression with her lips pressed together. Shoulder-length mid-brown hair with a few greys, tucked behind one ear. Wearing a navy fleece zip-top over a grey T-shirt, no glasses, small silver stud earrings. Behind her is a small back sitting room: magnolia wall, a pine bookshelf with paperbacks and a jigsaw box on top, a sewing machine under a fabric cover on a side table, and a framed photo of an older man in a cricket cap. Part of a beige sofa with a crocheted throw is visible in the lower right corner.

P022 (Darren):
- first name: Darren
- age: 36
- lives in: Bridgwater, South West
- occupation: Machine operator on a packaging line at a food manufacturing plant on the edge of town. Works a four-on, four-off shift pattern of days and nights, averaging about 42 hours a week.
- education detail: Left secondary school in Bridgwater with seven GCSEs, mostly Cs, with a B in history. Did a year of a BTEC in engineering at college, then left for paid work. Has since done an NVQ Level 2 in Performing Manufacturing Operations through work, plus a counterbalance forklift ticket and food hygiene Level 2.
- household: Lives with his wife Kerry, 35, a part-time receptionist at a dental practice. They have a son, Alfie, aged 8, and an elderly Staffordshire bull terrier called Bruno. Home is a three-bed ex-council semi they bought six years ago. He is quietly proud they own it and mentions it more than he probably should.
- cultural background: White British, born and raised in Somerset. His dad worked at the old cellophane factory and his mum did school dinners. Christian in the Church of England sense: christened, married at St Mary's, goes at Christmas and for Alfie's school services. === CALL C0048 ===
Tomasz: Hello! Tomasz, from Walsall. You're Abena, yeah?

Tomasz: Okay, okay, I don't push. Little bit, maybe. So where you find furniture? Shops, auctions?
Abena: Vintage and antique shops mostly. Some suppliers. There's a mid-century sideboard in Crystal Palace I keep going back to see. Teak. Nine hundred pounds.
Tomasz: Nine hundred! For cupboard? Listen, you go in, you don't look at it. You look at something else. Then you ask, what about that one, by the way, and you say six, cash. They say no, you walk to the door. They call you back. Every time. I do this at car boot every Sunday, I get drill set for a fiver last week.

req.text:
You write transcripts of realistic video calls between strangers for a fully synthetic research dataset set in the UK. The study, in order (from its published design): a short puzzle task done alone; first impressions of the others' webcam photos; then a series of three-minute, one-on-one video calls in rounds, each person meeting the others in their group; after each call a short survey.

Call shape (from the original study's numbers): a call is cut off by a three-minute timer. A typical call has about 30 turns (most between 20 and 39) and about 570 words in total (most between 440 and 682); half of all turns are 12 words or fewer, and a quarter are 24 or more. Short acknowledgements ("yeah", "mm") count as turns too. So aim for about 570 words in about 30 turns: alongside the quick back-and-forth, people often talk in longer stretches (explaining their job, telling a story), and those long turns carry much of the call.

Guide to British conversational English (use it for how people talk; it is a description of speech, not a script):
How British people talk in casual conversation. This is a paraphrase of published descriptions of spoken British English; sources are in SOURCES.md. Use these features lightly and only where they fit the person. Never use them as a caricature.

- **Fillers.** British speakers hesitate with "erm" and "er". Women and younger speakers lean towards "erm".
- **Hedges.** "Sort of" is everywhere and steady. "Kind of" is spreading, and younger speakers use it more.
- **Politeness words.** "Please", "thank you", "thanks" and "sorry" mostly mean what they say. "Sorry" also works as a repair word (to correct yourself, or to ask someone to repeat) and can be ironic.
- **Tags at the end of a sentence.** "You know", "right", "okay", "yeah", "do you know what I mean". Among young Londoners, "innit" and "you get me" are rising. Tags depend on age and region only, never on ethnicity.
- **Echoing.** In an engaged conversation people pick up and re-use parts of each other's words.
- **Regional words and grammar** (from a recent dialect survey):
  - A bread roll is a "barm" in the North West (Manchester to Liverpool and western Lancashire), a "cob" around Nottinghamshire, a "bap" in Staffordshire, the West Midlands and North Wales, and a "batch" in Liverpool and Coventry.
  - Around Liverpool an ice lolly can be a "lolly ice".
  - The evening meal is "tea" in the North West, North East and Yorkshire, and "dinner" in the South East and London. Some people say both.
  - "Yous" or "youse" for plural "you" is common in the North East (Newcastle, Teesside), Liverpool and Scotland, less so in Manchester, and rare in York, Leeds and Sheffield.
  - "Give it me" is normal in the North West and West Midlands and widely accepted in Sheffield and York; it fades south of Birmingham, Coventry and Leicester.
  - "You was" is widely used, historically Northern and now found as far south as London.
- **Everyday British words** to draw on where they fit, without assigning them to regions: knackered or shattered, chuffed or made up, skint or brassic, mardy or stroppy, mum or mam, mate or pal, settee, sofa or couch.

P044 (Gareth; transcript label: Gareth A):
- first name: Gareth
- age: 36
- lives in: Wrexham, North Wales
- occupation: Administrative assistant in the transport and scheduling office of a building supplies distributor on the Wrexham Industrial Estate. He books deliveries, updates the dispatch spreadsheet and chases paperwork with drivers, Monday to Friday, about 37.5 hours a week.
- education detail: Went to a local comprehensive and left with GCSEs, then did a year of an IT BTEC at Coleg Cambria (then Yale College) and didn't finish it. He has picked up everything else on the job, plus a couple of mandatory health and safety e-learning certificates.
- household: Lives with his wife Kerry, a healthcare assistant at the Maelor hospital who works shifts, in a two-bed semi they've been renting for six years on an estate on the edge of town. No children. They have a Staffordshire bull terrier called Dot.
- cultural background: White Welsh, born and raised in Wrexham. His parents still live about ten minutes away. He understands a bit of Welsh from school but doesn't speak it. He isn't religious. He was christened, but the family only went to chapel for funerals. He has always lived locally and has no particular wish to move.
- professional persona: Gets the job done well enough but leaves things until the last minute and relies on the dispatch manager reminding him. He's known as easy-going and unflappable when a lorry doesn't turn up, because he doesn't panic. He's less good at keeping his inbox under control. He keeps his head down, doesn't go to the Christmas do if he can help it, and has been in the same role for nine years.
- sports persona: Supports Wrexham AFC the way his dad did and watches most matches on the telly. He gets to the Racecourse a few times a season, usually with his dad or his brother-in-law. He doesn't play anything himself any more. Five-a-side stopped about eight years ago. He walks Dot round the block most evenings because she needs it.
- arts persona: Not much interest. Watches whatever's on with Kerry: crime dramas, quiz shows, the odd Netflix series she's picked. He'll rewatch films he already likes rather than try new ones. Listens to the same indie and Britpop his mates liked at school, mostly in the car.
- travel persona: Holidays are a week somewhere familiar. They go back to the same caravan park near Abersoch most summers, and every couple of years Kerry books a package deal to Tenerife. He's happy to let her plan it. He's been abroad maybe six times and doesn't feel he's missing out.
- culinary persona: Plain food. Chips, a chicken curry, pie, a bacon bap on a Saturday morning. He can do a fry-up and spag bol and that's about it. When Kerry's on a late, tea is often a takeaway or something from the freezer. He doesn't like anything too spicy or anything he can't name.
- hobbies and interests: Watching Wrexham AFC, Football games on the PlayStation, usually online with the same two mates from school, Walking the dog, Watching quiz shows with Kerry, The odd pint at the local on a Friday
- skills: Keeping calm when deliveries go wrong, Excel to a basic level, mainly filters and copying formulas, Knows the local road network and delivery routes well, Fixing minor things on the PlayStation and home Wi-Fi, Getting on quietly with drivers who are in a bad mood
- career goals: Nothing specific. He'd take a bump in pay if a senior admin or dispatch coordinator role came up without him having to apply too hard, but he's comfortable where he is. He mainly wants the job to stay steady so he and Kerry can eventually put a deposit down on a house.
- voice: Quiet, fairly flat, unhurried North Wales accent. Short answers unless pushed. Says 'erm' or 'er' before most replies and uses 'sort of' a lot. Occasionally says 'aye' or 'yeah, fair enough'. Ends sentences with 'you know' or 'I dunno, really'. Doesn't fill silences. He'll let a pause sit and wait for the next question rather than add more. Not nervous, just not chatty. Might say 'sorry, say that again?' if the line drops.
- typing: Mostly lowercase, no full stops at the end, apostrophes often missing (dont, im, its). Short answers, sometimes just one or two words. Uses 'n/a' or 'dunno' rather than leave a box blank. Occasional typo he doesn't go back to fix.
- with strangers: Polite but reserved, and slightly hard to draw out. Not unfriendly, just doesn't volunteer much and looks a bit like he's waiting for it to be over. Relaxed rather than awkward. Warms up a little if football or the dog comes up.
- small things: Dot chewed through the TV remote cable last week, The industrial estate traffic is a nightmare at half four, Wrexham's results at the weekend, Kerry's on nights this week so he's been living on oven chips, Needs to sort the car's MOT and keeps forgetting, Bacon bap from the van outside work on a Friday
- deeper things: They've been trying for a baby for a couple of years and it hasn't happened. He's mostly fine about it but knows Kerry isn't, He sometimes wonders if he should have finished college, but doesn't dwell on it, His dad had a heart scare last year and he's been going round more since, Saving for a house deposit feels like it's taking forever on two ordinary wages
- webcam photo: Head-and-shoulders shot from a laptop webcam placed slightly below eye level, so the camera looks up a little at his chin. Lighting comes mainly from a ceiling light, flat and slightly yellow, with the left side of his face a bit brighter from a window out of frame. He has a round, clean-shaven face with light stubble along the jaw, short mousy brown hair clipped at the sides and a bit flat on top, and pale skin. No glasses. His expression is neutral, mouth closed, eyes looking just below the camera at the screen. He's wearing a navy crew-neck sweatshirt with a small faded logo on the chest. Behind him is a magnolia living-room wall with a framed canvas print of the couple's wedding day slightly off-centre, a grey fabric settee with a crumpled throw over one arm, and the edge of a dog bed on the floor. A PlayStation controller is on the settee cushion, and a Wrexham AFC scarf is draped over the top of a door partly visible on the right.

P045 (Joanne; transcript label: Joanne):
- first name: Joanne
- age: 42
- lives in: Sutton-in-Ashfield, East Midlands
- occupation: Kitchen assistant at a primary school, about 25 hours a week in term time: prepping veg, serving dinners, washing up and wiping down the hall after lunch

Quietly wonders about doing an evening art class or a course in something like teaching assistant work, but worries she's left it too late and isn't clever enough, which isn't true.
- voice: Warm, fairly quiet, a mild Notts accent. Moderate pace that speeds up a little when she's nervous. Uses 'erm' a fair bit and 'sort of' to soften things. Says 'you know' at the end of sentences. Might call someone 'duck' once she's relaxed, and uses words like 'mardy', 'cob' and 'me mum'. Apologises easily: 'sorry, that's not what you asked, is it'. In silences she tends to fill the gap with a small laugh or 'I don't know if that makes sense', then waits to be prompted again.
- typing: Mostly lower case with a capital at the start. Commas and the odd full stop, sometimes no final full stop. Apostrophes mostly right but sometimes dropped (dont, im). Few abbreviations beyond 'tbh' now and then. Short answers, and occasionally a second sentence adding an honest caveat.
- with strangers: Polite, a little reserved and self-deprecating at first. She worries about saying the wrong thing or not being helpful enough. She warms up quickly if the other person is friendly, and becomes chatty and thoughtful, especially on anything to do with art, nature or history. She's very straight and won't exaggerate to sound good.

- webcam photo: Laptop webcam at slightly below eye level, angled up a little, on a kitchen table. Daylight comes from a window to her left and gives soft, slightly uneven light. A woman in her early forties fills the middle of the frame from the chest up, with a fair complexion, light freckles and faint lines around her eyes. She has a small, slightly nervous smile. Her shoulder-length mid-brown hair has a few grey strands and is tied back loosely, with bits falling at the front. She wears a navy hooded sweatshirt over a white t-shirt, small silver stud earrings and no glasses. Behind her are pale magnolia walls, a wall calendar from a local takeaway with dates written in biro, a wooden shelf holding a few cookbooks, a jar of paintbrushes and a small framed watercolour of a robin, a kettle and a toaster on the worktop, and the top of a fridge with magnets and a school lunch menu pinned to it.

P046 (Imran; transcript label: Imran):
- first name: Imran
- age: 47
- lives in: Huddersfield, Yorkshire and The Humber

- skills: Windows and Microsoft 365 administration, Network and printer troubleshooting, Hardware repair and refurbishment, Clear step-by-step explanation for non-technical people, Meticulous record-keeping and spreadsheets, Conversational Pahari-Pothwari and basic Urdu, Cooking family-sized curries
- career goals: He isn't chasing promotion. req.text:
You write transcripts of realistic video calls between strangers for a fully synthetic research dataset set in the UK. The study, in order (from its published design): a short puzzle task done alone; first impressions of the others' webcam photos; then a series of three-minute, one-on-one video calls in rounds, each person meeting the others in their group; after each call a short survey.

Call shape (from the original study's numbers): a call is cut off by a three-minute timer. A typical call has about 30 turns (most between 20 and 39) and about 570 words in total (most between 440 and 682); half of all turns are 12 words or fewer, and a quarter are 24 or more. Short acknowledgements ("yeah", "mm") count as turns too. So aim for about 570 words in about 30 turns: alongside the quick back-and-forth, people often talk in longer stretches (explaining their job, telling a story), and those long turns carry much of the call.

Guide to British conversational English (use it for how people talk; it is a description of speech, not a script):
How British people talk in casual conversation. This is a paraphrase of published descriptions of spoken British English; sources are in SOURCES.md. Use these features lightly and only where they fit the person. Never use them as a caricature.

- **Fillers.** British speakers hesitate with "erm" and "er". Women and younger speakers lean towards "erm".
- **Hedges.** "Sort of" is everywhere and steady. "Kind of" is spreading, and younger speakers use it more.
- **Politeness words.** "Please", "thank you", "thanks" and "sorry" mostly mean what they say. "Sorry" also works as a repair word (to correct yourself, or to ask someone to repeat) and can be ironic.
- **Tags at the end of a sentence.** "You know", "right", "okay", "yeah", "do you know what I mean". Among young Londoners, "innit" and "you get me" are rising. Tags depend on age and region only, never on ethnicity.
- **Echoing.** In an engaged conversation people pick up and re-use parts of each other's words.
- **Regional words and grammar** (from a recent dialect survey):
  - A bread roll is a "barm" in the North West (Manchester to Liverpool and western Lancashire), a "cob" around Nottinghamshire, a "bap" in Staffordshire, the West Midlands and North Wales, and a "batch" in Liverpool and Coventry.
  - Around Liverpool an ice lolly can be a "lolly ice".
  - The evening meal is "tea" in the North West, North East and Yorkshire, and "dinner" in the South East and London. Some people say both.
  - "Yous" or "youse" for plural "you" is common in the North East (Newcastle, Teesside), Liverpool and Scotland, less so in Manchester, and rare in York, Leeds and Sheffield.
  - "Give it me" is normal in the North West and West Midlands and widely accepted in Sheffield and York; it fades south of Birmingham, Coventry and Leicester.
  - "You was" is widely used, historically Northern and now found as far south as London.
- **Everyday British words** to draw on where they fit, without assigning them to regions: knackered or shattered, chuffed or made up, skint or brassic, mardy or stroppy, mum or mam, mate or pal, settee, sofa or couch.

The group (session S10). Persona cards, including the webcam photo each person was rated on:

P044 (Gareth; transcript label: Gareth A):
- first name: Gareth
- age: 36
- lives in: Wrexham, North Wales
- occupation: Administrative assistant in the transport and scheduling office of a building supplies distributor on the Wrexham Industrial Estate. He books deliveries, updates the dispatch spreadsheet and chases paperwork with drivers, Monday to Friday, about 37.5 hours a week.

- household: Lives with his wife Kerry, a healthcare assistant at the Maelor hospital who works shifts, in a two-bed semi they've been renting for six years on an estate on the edge of town. No children. They have a Staffordshire bull terrier called Dot.

req.text:
You write transcripts of realistic video calls between strangers for a fully synthetic research dataset set in the UK. The study, in order (from its published design): a short puzzle task done alone; first impressions of the others' webcam photos; then a series of three-minute, one-on-one video calls in rounds, each person meeting the others in their group; after each call a short survey.

Call shape (from the original study's numbers): a call is cut off by a three-minute timer. A typical call has about 30 turns (most between 20 and 39) and about 570 words in total (most between 440 and 682); half of all turns are 12 words or fewer, and a quarter are 24 or more. Short acknowledgements ("yeah", "mm") count as turns too. So aim for about 570 words in about 30 turns: alongside the quick back-and-forth, people often talk in longer stretches (explaining their job, telling a story), and those long turns carry much of the call.

Guide to British conversational English (use it for how people talk; it is a description of speech, not a script):
How British people talk in casual conversation. This is a paraphrase of published descriptions of spoken British English; sources are in SOURCES.md. Use these features lightly and only where they fit the person. Never use them as a caricature.

- **Fillers.** British speakers hesitate with "erm" and "er". Women and younger speakers lean towards "erm".
- **Hedges.** "Sort of" is everywhere and steady. "Kind of" is spreading, and younger speakers use it more.
- **Politeness words.** "Please", "thank you", "thanks" and "sorry" mostly mean what they say. "Sorry" also works as a repair word (to correct yourself, or to ask someone to repeat) and can be ironic.
- **Tags at the end of a sentence.** "You know", "right", "okay", "yeah", "do you know what I mean". Among young Londoners, "innit" and "you get me" are rising. Tags depend on age and region only, never on ethnicity.
- **Echoing.** In an engaged conversation people pick up and re-use parts of each other's words.
- **Regional words and grammar** (from a recent dialect survey):
  - A bread roll is a "barm" in the North West (Manchester to Liverpool and western Lancashire), a "cob" around Nottinghamshire, a "bap" in Staffordshire, the West Midlands and North Wales, and a "batch" in Liverpool and Coventry.
  - Around Liverpool an ice lolly can be a "lolly ice".
  - The evening meal is "tea" in the North West, North East and Yorkshire, and "dinner" in the South East and London. Some people say both.
  - "Yous" or "youse" for plural "you" is common in the North East (Newcastle, Teesside), Liverpool and Scotland, less so in Manchester, and rare in York, Leeds and Sheffield.
  - "Give it me" is normal in the North West and West Midlands and widely accepted in Sheffield and York; it fades south of Birmingham, Coventry and Leicester.
  - "You was" is widely used, historically Northern and now found as far south as London.
- **Everyday British words** to draw on where they fit, without assigning them to regions: knackered or shattered, chuffed or made up, skint or brassic, mardy or stroppy, mum or mam, mate or pal, settee, sofa or couch.

The group (session S10). Persona cards, including the webcam photo each person was rated on:

P044 (Gareth; transcript label: Gareth A):
- first name: Gareth
- age: 36
- lives in: Wrexham, North Wales
- occupation: Administrative assistant in the transport and scheduling office of a building supplies distributor on the Wrexham Industrial Estate. He books deliveries, updates the dispatch spreadsheet and chases paperwork with drivers, Monday to Friday, about 37.5 hours a week.
- education detail: Went to a local comprehensive and left with GCSEs, then did a year of an IT BTEC at Coleg Cambria (then Yale College) and didn't finish it. He has picked up everything else on the job, plus a couple of mandatory health and safety e-learning certificates.
- household: Lives with his wife Kerry, a healthcare assistant at the Maelor hospital who works shifts, in a two-bed semi they've been renting for six years on an estate on the edge of town. No children. They have a Staffordshire bull terrier called Dot.
- cultural background: White Welsh, born and raised in Wrexham. His parents still live about ten minutes away. He understands a bit of Welsh from school but doesn't speak it. He isn't religious. He was christened, but the family only went to chapel for funerals. He has always lived locally and has no particular wish to move.
- professional persona: Gets the job done well enough but leaves things until the last minute and relies on the dispatch manager reminding him. He's known as easy-going and unflappable when a lorry doesn't turn up, because he doesn't panic. He's less good at keeping his inbox under control. He keeps his head down, doesn't go to the Christmas do if he can help it, and has been in the same role for nine years.
- sports persona: Supports Wrexham AFC the way his dad did and watches most matches on the telly. He gets to the Racecourse a few times a season, usually with his dad or his brother-in-law. He doesn't play anything himself any more. Five-a-side stopped about eight years ago. He walks Dot round the block most evenings because she needs it.
- arts persona: Not much interest. Watches whatever's on with Kerry: crime dramas, quiz shows, the odd Netflix series she's picked. He'll rewatch films he already likes rather than try new ones. Listens to the same indie and Britpop his mates liked at school, mostly in the car.
- travel persona: Holidays are a week somewhere familiar. They go back to the same caravan park near Abersoch most summers, and every couple of years Kerry books a package deal to Tenerife. He's happy to let her plan it. He's been abroad maybe six times and doesn't feel he's missing out.
- culinary persona: Plain food. Chips, a chicken curry, pie, a bacon bap on a Saturday morning. He can do a fry-up and spag bol and that's about it. When Kerry's on a late, tea is often a takeaway or something from the freezer. He doesn't like anything too spicy or anything he can't name.
- hobbies and interests: Watching Wrexham AFC, Football games on the PlayStation, usually online with the same two mates from school, Walking the dog, Watching quiz shows with Kerry, The odd pint at the local on a Friday
- skills: Keeping calm when deliveries go wrong, Excel to a basic level, mainly filters and copying formulas, Knows the local road network and delivery routes well, Fixing minor things on the PlayStation and home Wi-Fi, Getting on quietly with drivers who are in a bad mood
- career goals: Nothing specific. He'd take a bump in pay if a senior admin or dispatch coordinator role came up without him having to apply too hard, but he's comfortable where he is. He mainly wants the job to stay steady so he and Kerry can eventually put a deposit down on a house.
- voice: Quiet, fairly flat, unhurried North Wales accent. Short answers unless pushed. Says 'erm' or 'er' before most replies and uses 'sort of' a lot. Occasionally says 'aye' or 'yeah, fair enough'. Ends sentences with 'you know' or 'I dunno, really'. Doesn't fill silences. He'll let a pause sit and wait for the next question rather than add more. Not nervous, just not chatty. Might say 'sorry, say that again?' if the line drops.
- typing: Mostly lowercase, no full stops at the end, apostrophes often missing (dont, im, its). Short answers, sometimes just one or two words. Uses 'n/a' or 'dunno' rather than leave a box blank. Occasional typo he doesn't go back to fix.
- with strangers: Polite but reserved, and slightly hard to draw out. Not unfriendly, just doesn't volunteer much and looks a bit like he's waiting for it to be over. Relaxed rather than awkward. Warms up a little if football or the dog comes up.
- small things: Dot chewed through the TV remote cable last week, The industrial estate traffic is a nightmare at half four, Wrexham's results at the weekend, Kerry's on nights this week so he's been living on oven chips, Needs to sort the car's MOT and keeps forgetting, Bacon bap from the van outside work on a Friday
- deeper things: They've been trying for a baby for a couple of years and it hasn't happened. He's mostly fine about it but knows Kerry isn't, He sometimes wonders if he should have finished college, but doesn't dwell on it, His dad had a heart scare last year and he's been going round more since, Saving for a house deposit feels like it's taking forever on two ordinary wages
- webcam photo: Head-and-shoulders shot from a laptop webcam placed slightly below eye level, so the camera looks up a little at his chin. Lighting comes mainly from a ceiling light, flat and slightly yellow, with the left side of his face a bit brighter from a window out of frame. He has a round, clean-shaven face with light stubble along the jaw, short mousy brown hair clipped at the sides and a bit flat on top, and pale skin. No glasses. His expression is neutral, mouth closed, eyes looking just below the camera at the screen. He's wearing a navy crew-neck sweatshirt with a small faded logo on the chest. Behind him is a magnolia living-room wall with a framed canvas print of the couple's wedding day slightly off-centre, a grey fabric settee with a crumpled throw over one arm, and the edge of a dog bed on the floor. A PlayStation controller is on the settee cushion, and a Wrexham AFC scarf is draped over the top of a door partly visible on the right.

P045 (Joanne; transcript label: Joanne):
- first name: Joanne
- age: 42
- lives in: Sutton-in-Ashfield, East Midlands
- occupation: Kitchen assistant at a primary school, about 25 hours a week in term time: prepping veg, serving dinners, washing up and wiping down the hall after lunch
- education detail: Left the local comprehensive at 16 with five GCSEs, including English and Art. Has a Level 2 Food Hygiene certificate through work. Has done a couple of free short online courses for fun, one on local history and one on drawing.
- household: Rents a two-bed terraced house with her partner Gary (45, a forklift driver at a distribution warehouse off the M1). They have been together eleven years and never got round to marrying, and have no children together. Gary's grown-up daughter visits now and then. They have an elderly tabby cat called Moss.
- cultural background: White British, born and raised in Nottinghamshire. Her dad worked down the pit until the closures and her mum did shifts at a hosiery factory. She was brought up Methodist and still goes to the local chapel most months and at Christmas and Easter. Her faith is quiet and practical rather than something she talks about much. Close to her mum, who lives ten minutes away.
- professional persona: Reliable and honest at work. She's the one who points out when the till float is a pound over, and she won't take leftover food home without asking. Gets on with the kids and remembers which ones have allergies. She doesn't push herself forward, and she worries a bit when Ofsted or a new cook manager is due. Has done the job about eight years and likes that it fits around term time.
- sports persona: Not sporty. Walks most days, usually round the reservoir or the old railway trails, and sometimes does a weekend parkrun walk with a friend. Watches the odd bit of Wimbledon. Gary follows Mansfield Town and she'll go to a match once a season to keep him company.
- arts persona: This is her real interest. She sketches and does watercolours at the kitchen table, mostly birds, trees and local buildings. She borrows a lot from the library: historical novels, folk tales and books about local mining history. She loves period dramas and documentaries and has been to the art gallery in Nottingham several times on her own. She's a bit shy about calling herself arty.
- travel persona: On a tight budget. Holidays are usually a static caravan at Skegness or Mablethorpe, or a cheap week in Wales. She went abroad twice, to Spain and Majorca, and would love to see Rome or Iceland someday. She enjoys day trips to places like Southwell Minster, Hardwick Hall and the Peak District, and always looks up the history beforehand.
- culinary persona: Plain home cooking she's good at: stews, cottage pie, a Sunday roast, cheese and onion cob for lunch. Occasionally she tries a new recipe from the telly, like a Thai curry or a shakshuka, to Gary's mild suspicion. Bakes for chapel coffee mornings. Calls the evening meal tea.
- hobbies and interests: watercolour and pencil sketching, library books, especially historical fiction, walking on the old railway trails, birdwatching from the back garden, local and family history, chapel coffee mornings, period dramas and nature documentaries, charity shop browsing
- skills: food prep and kitchen hygiene, working fast at busy lunchtimes, patience with young children, drawing and watercolour, budgeting on a low income, baking, keeping a house running
- career goals: Mostly content. She'd like a few more hours or a step up to assistant cook if one came up, but doesn't want the stress of running a kitchen. Quietly wonders about doing an evening art class or a course in something like teaching assistant work, but worries she's left it too late and isn't clever enough, which isn't true.
- voice: Warm, fairly quiet, a mild Notts accent. Moderate pace that speeds up a little when she's nervous. Uses 'erm' a fair bit and 'sort of' to soften things. Says 'you know' at the end of sentences. Might call someone 'duck' once she's relaxed, and uses words like 'mardy', 'cob' and 'me mum'. Apologises easily: 'sorry, that's not what you asked, is it'. In silences she tends to fill the gap with a small laugh or 'I don't know if that makes sense', then waits to be prompted again.
- typing: Mostly lower case with a capital at the start. Commas and the odd full stop, sometimes no final full stop. Apostrophes mostly right but sometimes dropped (dont, im). Few abbreviations beyond 'tbh' now and then. Short answers, and occasionally a second sentence adding an honest caveat.
- with strangers: Polite, a little reserved and self-deprecating at first. She worries about saying the wrong thing or not being helpful enough. She warms up quickly if the other person is friendly, and becomes chatty and thoughtful, especially on anything to do with art, nature or history. She's very straight and won't exaggerate to sound good.
- small things: Moss the cat sleeping on the radiator shelf, the blue tits nesting in the box Gary put up, what the kids at school won't eat (anything green), a library book she's halfway through, the price of a weekly shop, a walk round the reservoir at the weekend, her mum's knees playing up, the new Tesco self-checkouts annoying her
- deeper things: Feeling she never had the chance to do art properly and that it's too late, Worrying about money if Gary's warehouse cuts shifts, Sadness at not having children, which she's mostly made peace with, Her dad's death six years ago and the way the mining towns changed, Her faith being a comfort when she gets anxious at night, Being a bit hurt when people assume she isn't bright because of her job
- webcam photo: Laptop webcam at slightly below eye level, angled up a little, on a kitchen table. Daylight comes from a window to her left and gives soft, slightly uneven light. A woman in her early forties fills the middle of the frame from the chest up, with a fair complexion, light freckles and faint lines around her eyes. She has a small, slightly nervous smile. Her shoulder-length mid-brown hair has a few grey strands and is tied back loosely, with bits falling at the front. She wears a navy hooded sweatshirt over a white t-shirt, small silver stud earrings and no glasses. Behind her are pale magnolia walls, a wall calendar from a local takeaway with dates written in biro, a wooden shelf holding a few cookbooks, a jar of paintbrushes and a small framed watercolour of a robin, a kettle and a toaster on the worktop, and the top of a fridge with magnets and a school lunch menu pinned to it.

P046 (Imran; transcript label: Imran):
- first name: Imran
- age: 47
- lives in: Huddersfield, Yorkshire and The Humber
- occupation: Part-time IT support technician, about 12 hours a week, split between a small accountancy firm in the town centre and a dental practice in Lindley. He looks after their laptops, printers, backups and Microsoft 365 accounts.
- education detail: GCSEs at a comprehensive in Huddersfield, then a BTEC National Diploma in IT at Huddersfield Technical College, followed by a part-time HNC in Computing. He later took CompTIA A+ and a Microsoft 365 administrator certificate through evening and online study in his thirties.
- household: He lives with his partner Saima, 44, a teaching assistant at a local primary school, in a three-bed semi in Birkby. They had a nikah three years ago but haven't done a civil registration yet, which he's been meaning to sort out. His two children from his first marriage, Zain (17) and Aleena (14), live with their mum in Dewsbury. They stay with him every other weekend and come round for tea on Wednesdays.
- cultural background: Born in Huddersfield to parents from the Mirpur district of Pakistan. His dad came over in the late 1960s and worked nights in a textile mill, and his mum raised four children. He is British Pakistani and a practising Muslim, quietly so. He prays most of his daily prayers, goes to Friday prayers when work allows and fasts in Ramadan. He speaks Pahari-Pothwari and some Urdu with older relatives and English everywhere else. His mum died in 2020. His dad, now 79, lives ten minutes away with Imran's younger brother.
- professional persona: He spent nearly twenty years full-time in IT support, mostly at a college and then a logistics firm, and was a team leader for a while. Four years ago he cut his hours right down, partly after the divorce and his mum's death, and partly to be around for his dad's hospital appointments and for the kids. He is methodical and patient with non-technical staff. He documents everything, keeps a password-managed log for each client and labels cables. He'd rather fix a problem properly once than patch it twice. He doesn't like selling himself and gets most work by word of mouth.
- sports persona: A lifelong Yorkshire cricket follower. He played as a batsman in the Huddersfield league in his twenties and early thirties and now watches more than he plays, sometimes at Headingley with his son. He walks most days, often up to Castle Hill or along the canal, and tracks his steps carefully. Not a big football fan, though he keeps half an eye on Huddersfield Town results.
- arts persona: He listens to Nusrat Fateh Ali Khan and old qawwali in the car, along with some 90s British music from his college days, like Oasis, The Verve and Cornershop. He reads popular history, especially about the Partition and the Second World War, and gets through a book a month on his Kindle. He doesn't really go to galleries or the theatre.
- travel persona: He has visited Pakistan several times for family weddings and to see relatives, most recently in 2022. He did Umrah with his mum in 2019, which he holds very dear. Otherwise he prefers UK breaks: the Lake District, Whitby, the Yorkshire Dales. He plans trips well in advance, with a printed itinerary and booked parking. He doesn't enjoy flying much and gets anxious about connections.
- culinary persona: He cooks a reliable chicken karahi and his mum's tarka dal, which the kids ask for on Wednesday nights. Saima does more of the everyday cooking, but he does Saturday breakfast for the household: eggs, parathas, chai. He shops at the big halal butcher on the same day each week. He likes a fish and chip tea at the seaside and has a sweet tooth for jalebi and Yorkshire parkin alike.
- hobbies and interests: Refurbishing old laptops and giving them to families at the local mosque and the kids' schools, Walking around Castle Hill and the Colne Valley, Following Yorkshire County Cricket, Reading popular history, Keeping a tidy vegetable patch in the back garden (tomatoes, chillies, coriander), Watching cricket highlights and documentaries with his son
- skills: Windows and Microsoft 365 administration, Network and printer troubleshooting, Hardware repair and refurbishment, Clear step-by-step explanation for non-technical people, Meticulous record-keeping and spreadsheets, Conversational Pahari-Pothwari and basic Urdu, Cooking family-sized curries
- career goals: He isn't chasing promotion. He'd like to gradually take on two or three more small-business clients so he can go up to about 20 hours once his dad's needs are clearer, while keeping Wednesdays and the kids' weekends free. He has thought about formally setting up as a sole trader with a proper website but keeps putting off the self-promotion side.
- voice: Quiet, measured and polite, with a soft West Yorkshire accent: flat vowels, 'tea' for the evening meal, the odd 'nowt' or 'reckon'. He thinks before answering, often starting with 'Er...' or 'Well, it's sort of...', and his answers are fairly short unless the topic is something he knows well, like computers, cricket or his kids, when he opens up more. He says 'sorry' readily, sometimes to correct himself ('sorry, I mean the other one'). He ends points with 'you know' or 'if that makes sense'. He doesn't fill silences himself. He waits, and might say 'Is that alright?' to check he's answered properly.

req.text:
You write transcripts of realistic video calls between strangers for a fully synthetic research dataset set in the UK. The study, in order (from its published design): a short puzzle task done alone; first impressions of the others' webcam photos; then a series of three-minute, one-on-one video calls in rounds, each person meeting the others in their group; after each call a short survey.

Call shape (from the original study's numbers): a call is cut off by a three-minute timer. A typical call has about 30 turns (most between 20 and 39) and about 570 words in total (most between 440 and 682); half of all turns are 12 words or fewer, and a quarter are 24 or more. Short acknowledgements ("yeah", "mm") count as turns too. So aim for about 570 words in about 30 turns: alongside the quick back-and-forth, people often talk in longer stretches (explaining their job, telling a story), and those long turns carry much of the call.

Guide to British conversational English (use it for how people talk; it is a description of speech, not a script):
How British people talk in casual conversation. This is a paraphrase of published descriptions of spoken British English; sources are in SOURCES.md. Use these features lightly and only where they fit the person. Never use them as a caricature.

- **Fillers.** British speakers hesitate with "erm" and "er". Women and younger speakers lean towards "erm".
- **Hedges.** "Sort of" is everywhere and steady. "Kind of" is spreading, and younger speakers use it more.
- **Politeness words.** "Please", "thank you", "thanks" and "sorry" mostly mean what they say. "Sorry" also works as a repair word (to correct yourself, or to ask someone to repeat) and can be ironic.
- **Tags at the end of a sentence.** "You know", "right", "okay", "yeah", "do you know what I mean". Among young Londoners, "innit" and "you get me" are rising. Tags depend on age and region only, never on ethnicity.
- **Echoing.** In an engaged conversation people pick up and re-use parts of each other's words.
- **Regional words and grammar** (from a recent dialect survey):
  - A bread roll is a "barm" in the North West (Manchester to Liverpool and western Lancashire), a "cob" around Nottinghamshire, a "bap" in Staffordshire, the West Midlands and North Wales, and a "batch" in Liverpool and Coventry.
  - Around Liverpool an ice lolly can be a "lolly ice".
  - The evening meal is "tea" in the North West, North East and Yorkshire, and "dinner" in the South East and London. Some people say both.
  - "Yous" or "youse" for plural "you" is common in the North East (Newcastle, Teesside), Liverpool and Scotland, less so in Manchester, and rare in York, Leeds and Sheffield.
  - "Give it me" is normal in the North West and West Midlands and widely accepted in Sheffield and York; it fades south of Birmingham, Coventry and Leicester.
  - "You was" is widely used, historically Northern and now found as far south as London.
- **Everyday British words** to draw on where they fit, without assigning them to regions: knackered or shattered, chuffed or made up, skint or brassic, mardy or stroppy, mum or mam, mate or pal, settee, sofa or couch.

req.text:
You write transcripts of realistic video calls between strangers for a fully synthetic research dataset set in the UK. The study, in order (from its published design): a short puzzle task done alone; first impressions of the others' webcam photos; then a series of three-minute, one-on-one video calls in rounds, each person meeting the others in their group; after each call a short survey.

Call shape (from the original study's numbers): a call is cut off by a three-minute timer. A typical call has about 30 turns (most between 20 and 39) and about 570 words in total (most between 440 and 682); half of all turns are 12 words or fewer, and a quarter are 24 or more. Short acknowledgements ("yeah", "mm") count as turns too. So aim for about 570 words in about 30 turns: alongside the quick back-and-forth, people often talk in longer stretches (explaining their job, telling a story), and those long turns carry much of the call.

Guide to British conversational English (use it for how people talk; it is a description of speech, not a script):
How British people talk in casual conversation. This is a paraphrase of published descriptions of spoken British English; sources are in SOURCES.md. Use these features lightly and only where they fit the person. Never use them as a caricature.

- **Fillers.** British speakers hesitate with "erm" and "er". Women and younger speakers lean towards "erm".
- **Hedges.** "Sort of" is everywhere and steady. "Kind of" is spreading, and younger speakers use it more.
- **Politeness words.** "Please", "thank you", "thanks" and "sorry" mostly mean what they say. "Sorry" also works as a repair word (to correct yourself, or to ask someone to repeat) and can be ironic.
- **Tags at the end of a sentence.** "You know", "right", "okay", "yeah", "do you know what I mean". Among young Londoners, "innit" and "you get me" are rising. Tags depend on age and region only, never on ethnicity.
- **Echoing.** In an engaged conversation people pick up and re-use parts of each other's words.
- **Regional words and grammar** (from a recent dialect survey):
  - A bread roll is a "barm" in the North West (Manchester to Liverpool and western Lancashire), a "cob" around Nottinghamshire, a "bap" in Staffordshire, the West Midlands and North Wales, and a "batch" in Liverpool and Coventry.
  - Around Liverpool an ice lolly can be a "lolly ice".
  - The evening meal is "tea" in the North West, North East and Yorkshire, and "dinner" in the South East and London. Some people say both.
  - "Yous" or "youse" for plural "you" is common in the North East (Newcastle, Teesside), Liverpool and Scotland, less so in Manchester, and rare in York, Leeds and Sheffield.
  - "Give it me" is normal in the North West and West Midlands and widely accepted in Sheffield and York; it fades south of Birmingham, Coventry and Leicester.
  - "You was" is widely used, historically Northern and now found as far south as London.
- **Everyday British words** to draw on where they fit, without assigning them to regions: knackered or shattered, chuffed or made up, skint or brassic, mardy or stroppy, mum or mam, mate or pal, settee, sofa or couch.

P044 (Gareth; transcript label: Gareth A):
- first name: Gareth
- age: 36
- lives in: Wrexham, North Wales
- occupation: Administrative assistant in the transport and scheduling office of a building supplies distributor on the Wrexham Industrial Estate. He books deliveries, updates the dispatch spreadsheet and chases paperwork with drivers, Monday to Friday, about 37.5 hours a week.
- education detail: Went to a local comprehensive and left with GCSEs, then did a year of an IT BTEC at Coleg Cambria (then Yale College) and didn't finish it. He has picked up everything else on the job, plus a couple of mandatory health and safety e-learning certificates.
- household: Lives with his wife Kerry, a healthcare assistant at the Maelor hospital who works shifts, in a two-bed semi they've been renting for six years on an estate on the edge of town. No children. They have a Staffordshire bull terrier called Dot.
- cultural background: White Welsh, born and raised in Wrexham. His parents still live about ten minutes away. He understands a bit of Welsh from school but doesn't speak it. He isn't religious. He was christened, but the family only went to chapel for funerals. He has always lived locally and has no particular wish to move.
- professional persona: Gets the job done well enough but leaves things until the last minute and relies on the dispatch manager reminding him. He's known as easy-going and unflappable when a lorry doesn't turn up, because he doesn't panic. He's less good at keeping his inbox under control. He keeps his head down, doesn't go to the Christmas do if he can help it, and has been in the same role for nine years.
- sports persona: Supports Wrexham AFC the way his dad did and watches most matches on the telly. He gets to the Racecourse a few times a season, usually with his dad or his brother-in-law. He doesn't play anything himself any more. Five-a-side stopped about eight years ago. He walks Dot round the block most evenings because she needs it.
- arts persona: Not much interest. Watches whatever's on with Kerry: crime dramas, quiz shows, the odd Netflix series she's picked. He'll rewatch films he already likes rather than try new ones. Listens to the same indie and Britpop his mates liked at school, mostly in the car.
- travel persona: Holidays are a week somewhere familiar. They go back to the same caravan park near Abersoch most summers, and every couple of years Kerry books a package deal to Tenerife. He's happy to let her plan it. He's been abroad maybe six times and doesn't feel he's missing out.
- culinary persona: Plain food. Chips, a chicken curry, pie, a bacon bap on a Saturday morning. He can do a fry-up and spag bol and that's about it. When Kerry's on a late, tea is often a takeaway or something from the freezer. He doesn't like anything too spicy or anything he can't name.
- hobbies and interests: Watching Wrexham AFC, Football games on the PlayStation, usually online with the same two mates from school, Walking the dog, Watching quiz shows with Kerry, The odd pint at the local on a Friday
- skills: Keeping calm when deliveries go wrong, Excel to a basic level, mainly filters and copying formulas, Knows the local road network and delivery routes well, Fixing minor things on the PlayStation and home Wi-Fi, Getting on quietly with drivers who are in a bad mood
- career goals: Nothing specific. He'd take a bump in pay if a senior admin or dispatch coordinator role came up without him having to apply too hard, but he's comfortable where he is. He mainly wants the job to stay steady so he and Kerry can eventually put a deposit down on a house.
- voice: Quiet, fairly flat, unhurried North Wales accent. Short answers unless pushed. Says 'erm' or 'er' before most replies and uses 'sort of' a lot. Occasionally says 'aye' or 'yeah, fair enough'. Ends sentences with 'you know' or 'I dunno, really'. Doesn't fill silences. He'll let a pause sit and wait for the next question rather than add more. Not nervous, just not chatty. Might say 'sorry, say that again?' if the line drops.
- typing: Mostly lowercase, no full stops at the end, apostrophes often missing (dont, im, its). Short answers, sometimes just one or two words. Uses 'n/a' or 'dunno' rather than leave a box blank. Occasional typo he doesn't go back to fix.
- with strangers: Polite but reserved, and slightly hard to draw out. Not unfriendly, just doesn't volunteer much and looks a bit like he's waiting for it to be over. Relaxed rather than awkward. Warms up a little if football or the dog comes up.
- small things: Dot chewed through the TV remote cable last week, The industrial estate traffic is a nightmare at half four, Wrexham's results at the weekend, Kerry's on nights this week so he's been living on oven chips, Needs to sort the car's MOT and keeps forgetting, Bacon bap from the van outside work on a Friday
- deeper things: They've been trying for a baby for a couple of years and it hasn't happened. He's mostly fine about it but knows Kerry isn't, He sometimes wonders if he should have finished college, but doesn't dwell on it, His dad had a heart scare last year and he's been going round more since, Saving for a house deposit feels like it's taking forever on two ordinary wages
- webcam photo: Head-and-shoulders shot from a laptop webcam placed slightly below eye level, so the camera looks up a little at his chin. Lighting comes mainly from a ceiling light, flat and slightly yellow, with the left side of his face a bit brighter from a window out of frame. He has a round, clean-shaven face with light stubble along the jaw, short mousy brown hair clipped at the sides and a bit flat on top, and pale skin. No glasses. His expression is neutral, mouth closed, eyes looking just below the camera at the screen. He's wearing a navy crew-neck sweatshirt with a small faded logo on the chest. Behind him is a magnolia living-room wall with a framed canvas print of the couple's wedding day slightly off-centre, a grey fabric settee with a crumpled throw over one arm, and the edge of a dog bed on the floor. A PlayStation controller is on the settee cushion, and a Wrexham AFC scarf is draped over the top of a door partly visible on the right.

P045 (Joanne; transcript label: Joanne):
- first name: Joanne
- age: 42
- lives in: Sutton-in-Ashfield, East Midlands
- occupation: Kitchen assistant at a primary school, about 25 hours a week in term time: prepping veg, serving dinners, washing up and wiping down the hall after lunch

Call shape (from the original study's numbers): a call is cut off by a three-minute timer. A typical call has about 30 turns (most between 20 and 39) and about 570 words in total (most between 440 and 682); half of all turns are 12 words or fewer, and a quarter are 24 or more. Guide to British conversational English (use it for how people talk; it is a description of speech, not a script):
How British people talk in casual conversation. This is a paraphrase of published descriptions of spoken British English; sources are in SOURCES.md. Use these features lightly and only where they fit the person. Never use them as a caricature.

- **Fillers.** British speakers hesitate with "erm" and "er". Women and younger speakers lean towards "erm".
- **Hedges.** "Sort of" is everywhere and steady. "Kind of" is spreading, and younger speakers use it more.
- **Politeness words.** "Please", "thank you", "thanks" and "sorry" mostly mean what they say. "Sorry" also works as a repair word (to correct yourself, or to ask someone to repeat) and can be ironic.
- **Tags at the end of a sentence.** "You know", "right", "okay", "yeah", "do you know what I mean". Among young Londoners, "innit" and "you get me" are rising. Tags depend on age and region only, never on ethnicity.
- **Echoing.** In an engaged conversation people pick up and re-use parts of each other's words.
- **Regional words and grammar** (from a recent dialect survey):
  - A bread roll is a "barm" in the North West (Manchester to Liverpool and western Lancashire), a "cob" around Nottinghamshire, a "bap" in Staffordshire, the West Midlands and North Wales, and a "batch" in Liverpool and Coventry.

  - "You was" is widely used, historically Northern and now found as far south as London.
