req.text:
You write transcripts of realistic video calls between strangers for a fully synthetic research dataset set in the UK. The study, in order (from its published design): a short puzzle task done alone; first impressions of the others' webcam photos; then a series of three-minute, one-on-one video calls in rounds, each person meeting the others in their group; after each call a short survey.

Call shape (from the original study's numbers): a call is cut off by a three-minute timer. A typical call has about 30 turns (most between 20 and 39) and about 570 words in total (most between 440 and 682); half of all turns are 12 words or fewer, and a quarter are 24 or more. Short acknowledgements ("yeah", "mm") count as turns too. So aim for about 570 words in about 30 turns: alongside the quick back-and-forth, people often talk in longer stretches (explaining their job, telling a story), and those long turns carry much of the call.

Guide to British conversational English (use it for how people talk; it is a description of speech, not a script):
How British people talk in casual conversation. This is a paraphrase of published descriptions of spoken British English; sources are in SOURCES.md. Use these features lightly and only where they fit the person. Never use them as a caricature.

- **Fillers.** British speakers hesitate with "erm" and "er". Women and younger speakers lean towards "erm".
- **Hedges.** "Sort of" is everywhere and steady. "Kind of" is spreading, and younger speakers use it more.
- **Politeness words.** "Please", "thank you", "thanks" and "sorry" mostly mean what they say. "Sorry" also works as a repair word (to correct yourself, or to ask someone to repeat) and can be ironic.
- **Tags at the end of a sentence.** "You know", "right", "okay", "yeah", "do you know what I mean". Among young Londoners, "innit" and "you get me" are rising. Tags depend on age and region only, never on ethnicity.
- **Echoing.** In an engaged conversation people pick up and re-use parts of each other's words.
- **Regional words and grammar** (from a recent dialect survey):
  - A bread roll is a "barm" in the North West (Manchester to Liverpool and western Lancashire), a "cob" around Nottinghamshire, a "bap" in Staffordshire, the West Midlands and North Wales, and a "batch" in Liverpool and Coventry.
  - Around Liverpool an ice lolly can be a "lolly ice".
  - The evening meal is "tea" in the North West, North East and Yorkshire, and "dinner" in the South East and London. Some people say both.
  - "Yous" or "youse" for plural "you" is common in the North East (Newcastle, Teesside), Liverpool and Scotland, less so in Manchester, and rare in York, Leeds and Sheffield.
  - "Give it me" is normal in the North West and West Midlands and widely accepted in Sheffield and York; it fades south of Birmingham, Coventry and Leicester.
  - "You was" is widely used, historically Northern and now found as far south as London.
- **Everyday British words** to draw on where they fit, without assigning them to regions: knackered or shattered, chuffed or made up, skint or brassic, mardy or stroppy, mum or mam, mate or pal, settee, sofa or couch.

P068 (Neil; transcript label: Neil):
- first name: Neil
- age: 52
- lives in: Basingstoke, South East England
- occupation: Chartered civil engineer (asset engineer) for a regional water utility, looking after pumping stations and sewer networks across north Hampshire
- education detail: A levels in Maths, Physics and Geography at a sixth-form college in Reading. BEng in Civil Engineering from the University of Portsmouth. Became chartered with the Institution of Civil Engineers in his late twenties.
- household: Lives with his wife Karen, 51, a part-time practice manager at a GP surgery, in a four-bedroom 1990s detached house on an estate in Chineham. Their two children have left home. Their daughter, 24, is a physio in Southampton, and their son, 21, is finishing a degree in Nottingham. The son's room is still kept as it was.
- cultural background: White British, born and raised in Reading. His dad was an electrician and his mum worked in a building society. Church of England. He and Karen go to their local parish church at Christmas and Easter and for the odd harvest festival. He was confirmed as a teenager and still thinks of himself as Christian, but he doesn't talk about it much. Middle-of-the-road and settled. He has lived within thirty miles of where he grew up for his whole life.
- professional persona: Steady and dependable. He has been with the same utility for nineteen years, and colleagues come to him because he knows where everything is buried, sometimes literally. He prefers proven methods to new approaches and is quietly sceptical of consultants and rebrands. He doesn't get rattled when a pump station floods at 2am or a project slips. He writes clear, plain reports, gets his work done in standard hours and logs off at about half five. He is good with the site operatives and contractors because he is fair and doesn't throw his weight around.
- sports persona: Lifelong Reading FC supporter. He went to Elm Park as a boy with his dad and now goes to the odd home game, but mostly follows the results. He watches the cricket when it's on, especially the Test matches. He used to play five-a-side and gave it up in his forties after a calf strain. Now he walks a lot and does a bit of golf at a municipal course about once a month with two old colleagues. He plays off a high handicap and doesn't mind.
- arts persona: Not really his thing. He reads the odd thriller on holiday, Lee Child or similar. He watches whatever Karen puts on, police dramas and quiz shows mainly, and he likes Only Connect and University Challenge. He has been to the theatre in London a handful of times, always for Karen's birthday. Music is the classic rock and 80s stuff he grew up with, Dire Straits and Queen, on in the car.
- travel persona: Creature of habit. They have been going to the same part of Cornwall, near Padstow, most summers for fifteen years. They do one week abroad every couple of years, usually somewhere in Spain or Portugal they have been before. He's not keen on long-haul flights or 'adventure' holidays. He drives everywhere if he can.
- culinary persona: Plain, traditional food. Roast on a Sunday, which he usually cooks: chicken or beef, never anything fancy. He is happy with shepherd's pie, a curry from the local takeaway on Fridays, and fish and chips in Cornwall. He doesn't like overly spicy food or 'messed about' dishes. He calls the evening meal dinner. He drinks bitter at the pub and the occasional glass of red with a roast.
- hobbies and interests: Gardening, mainly keeping the lawn tidy and growing tomatoes and runner beans in raised beds, Walking the family's Labrador, Bramble, along the Basingstoke Canal, Following Reading FC and Test cricket, Pottering in the garage and fixing things around the house, Quiz shows, especially Only Connect, Monthly round of golf with old work mates
- skills: Hydraulic modelling and drainage design, Reading and checking engineering drawings, Managing contractors and site safety, Basic DIY, plumbing and electrics, Staying calm in a crisis, Excel spreadsheets, a lot of them
- career goals: No big ambitions left. He'd like to stay in his current role, perhaps mentor a couple of the graduate engineers, and retire at around 60 or 62 if the pension allows. He has turned down moving into senior management twice because he didn't fancy the meetings.
- voice: Mild South East accent, Thames Valley rather than London, unremarkable. Measured, fairly slow pace. He says 'er' rather than 'erm' when thinking and uses 'sort of' a fair bit. He gives short, practical answers and doesn't elaborate unless asked. He is happy to sit in silence while he thinks, and he doesn't rush to fill gaps. He might say 'yeah, fair enough' or 'that's about it really' to close an answer. He is polite, says 'sorry, could you repeat that?' if he mishears, and thanks the interviewer at the end.
- typing: Proper sentences with capitals and full stops, and apostrophes in the right place. He's a bit brief and sometimes leaves off the last full stop. No emojis or text-speak, though he will write 'etc' and use '&' occasionally. He checks his answer once before submitting.
- with strangers: Reserved but friendly enough. He comes across as a decent, unflappable, slightly quiet bloke. He doesn't volunteer much at first and answers what he's asked. He is easy-going and agreeable, unlikely to argue or push back, and warms up a bit if the conversation turns to something practical like football, the garden or the dog.
- small things: The dog needed walking before the call, Reading lost again at the weekend, The tomatoes have come on well this year, Roadworks on the A33 making the commute a pain, Karen's got him watching a new detective series, Booked Cornwall again for August
- deeper things: His dad died of a stroke five years ago and he still thinks about how quick it was, He feels the house is quiet since the kids left and he misses his son more than he lets on, He sometimes wonders if he should have pushed himself more in his career, but mostly he's content, His faith is a quiet thing for him. He prays occasionally and found the church a comfort at his dad's funeral, He is a bit worried about his mum, who is 79 and living alone in Reading
- webcam photo: Head-and-shoulders framing from a laptop webcam, slightly below eye level, so the camera looks up a little at his chin. Lighting comes from a window to his left, giving soft daylight on one side of his face with the other side a bit shadowed. A white man in his early fifties with a broad, slightly ruddy face, light stubble and short greying brown hair receding at the temples. Neutral, mildly pleasant expression with a faint closed-mouth smile. Rimless glasses. He is wearing a navy quarter-zip fleece over a pale blue collared shirt. Behind him is a spare bedroom used as a home office: magnolia walls, a white flat-pack bookcase holding ring binders labelled with project codes, a few paperback thrillers and a framed photo of two young adults at a graduation. A cream radiator sits under the window edge, and a folded ironing board leans against the wall in the corner.

- first name: Hodan
- age: 29
- lives in: Wembley, Brent, North West London
- occupation: Senior pharmacy technician in the aseptic and dispensary unit of an NHS hospital in North West London, full-time at around 37.5 hours plus occasional weekend rota cover
- education detail: GCSEs and A-levels (Chemistry, Biology, Business) at a Brent sixth form. Now part-way through an accredited medicines management and accuracy checking qualification.

Grew up between Somali at home and London English at school. Muslim and practising in her own way: she prays when she can fit it in, fasts at Ramadan, wears a hijab, and goes to the mosque mainly for Eid and family occasions. - travel persona: Has been back to Hargeisa twice, once as a teenager and once with Idris at five. Prefers organised, efficient trips: Dubai with her cousins, a long weekend in Istanbul. She researches prices obsessively and boasts a bit about the deals she gets. Wants to take Idris to Disneyland Paris next year and has a savings pot for it.

Likes a nice brunch spot and will judge it on Instagram-worthiness as much as taste. Makes proper Somali tea with cardamom and is snobby about anyone else's.
- hobbies and interests: Weight training and tracking her lifts, Budgeting and side savings pots, plus reading money-saving forums, True-crime documentaries, Organising family events such as Eid get-togethers and cousins' weddings, Sorting and reselling Idris's outgrown clothes and toys online, Trying new brunch places with her two closest friends
- skills: Aseptic preparation and final accuracy checking, Stock control and pharmacy systems, Rota planning and supervising junior technicians, Spreadsheets and data-keeping, Fluent Somali and English, Negotiating, from shift swaps to car prices, Running a household tightly on a budget
- career goals: Wants a Band 6 lead technician post within two years, ideally in medicines optimisation, where the pay and the status are better and the hours less chaotic. Has thought about retraining as a pharmacist through a part-time degree once Idris is older, but mainly cares about being the one in charge and earning properly.
- voice: Fast, confident London English with a light Somali family influence only in names and the odd word with her mum. She talks a lot and fills silences herself rather than waiting. Uses "erm" briefly when she's choosing her words, "kind of" and "like" as hedges, and ends points with "you know" or, among friends, an occasional "innit". Says "you was" now and then casually. Interrupts, then says "sorry, go on" without really meaning to stop. Laughs loudly. Gets clipped and flat when she thinks a question is pointless. She'll say so straight out: "that's a bit of a weird question, but fine."
- typing: Quick and mostly lowercase, with a capital at the start only if autocorrect does it. Apostrophes are hit and miss ("dont", "its"). Uses commas instead of full stops and drops the final full stop. Abbreviations like "tbh", "idk" and "bc", and digits instead of words ("2 kids no 1" style errors are rare because she rereads). Answers are short unless she has an opinion, then she writes a block.

She soon sizes people up and can be dismissive if she thinks someone's slow or wasting her time. She's not unpleasant, but she doesn't soften things or flatter. She'll happily talk about herself and her achievements, and asks fewer questions back.
- small things: Idris's football club kit costing a fortune, The Jubilee line being down again, Having done her lifts at 6am before work, A brunch place in Kensal Rise that she says is overrated, Her mum's cardamom tea being better than anything you can buy, Sorting the rota while everyone else complains about it, Getting a parking fine she's appealing on principle
- deeper things: Having Idris at 21 and feeling she had to prove everyone wrong, which still drives her, Resentment that Idris's dad gets to be the fun parent on holidays, Aunties' constant comments about marriage, and not knowing if she even wants it, Barely remembering Hargeisa but feeling judged as not Somali enough there and not British enough here, Worrying her mum is getting older and she relies on her too much, Knowing people at work find her hard to like, and mostly deciding she doesn't care
- webcam photo: Laptop webcam, slightly below eye level, framing her from mid-chest up and a little off-centre to the left. Evening light from a ceiling bulb gives a warm cast, with a cooler glow on one cheek from the screen. Dark brown skin, defined eyebrows, light makeup with a nude lip, and a direct, slightly amused half-smile. A black jersey hijab is wrapped neatly, with no hair visible. She wears a grey zip-up hoodie with the hospital trust's lanyard still around her neck, and small gold stud earrings just visible at the hijab edge. No glasses. Behind her is a pale grey living-room wall with a framed school photo of a smiling boy in a red jumper, and a wall calendar covered in colour-coded handwriting. A corner of a dark grey sofa shows a folded laundry pile on the arm. A wooden shelf holds a small Qur'an stand, a plant in a white pot and a stack of children's books.

req.text:
You write transcripts of realistic video calls between strangers for a fully synthetic research dataset set in the UK. The study, in order (from its published design): a short puzzle task done alone; first impressions of the others' webcam photos; then a series of three-minute, one-on-one video calls in rounds, each person meeting the others in their group; after each call a short survey.

Call shape (from the original study's numbers): a call is cut off by a three-minute timer. A typical call has about 30 turns (most between 20 and 39) and about 570 words in total (most between 440 and 682); half of all turns are 12 words or fewer, and a quarter are 24 or more. Short acknowledgements ("yeah", "mm") count as turns too. So aim for about 570 words in about 30 turns: alongside the quick back-and-forth, people often talk in longer stretches (explaining their job, telling a story), and those long turns carry much of the call.

Guide to British conversational English (use it for how people talk; it is a description of speech, not a script):
How British people talk in casual conversation. This is a paraphrase of published descriptions of spoken British English; sources are in SOURCES.md. Use these features lightly and only where they fit the person. Never use them as a caricature.

- **Fillers.** British speakers hesitate with "erm" and "er". Women and younger speakers lean towards "erm".
- **Hedges.** "Sort of" is everywhere and steady. "Kind of" is spreading, and younger speakers use it more.
- **Politeness words.** "Please", "thank you", "thanks" and "sorry" mostly mean what they say. "Sorry" also works as a repair word (to correct yourself, or to ask someone to repeat) and can be ironic.
- **Tags at the end of a sentence.** "You know", "right", "okay", "yeah", "do you know what I mean". Among young Londoners, "innit" and "you get me" are rising. Tags depend on age and region only, never on ethnicity.
- **Echoing.** In an engaged conversation people pick up and re-use parts of each other's words.
- **Regional words and grammar** (from a recent dialect survey):
  - A bread roll is a "barm" in the North West (Manchester to Liverpool and western Lancashire), a "cob" around Nottinghamshire, a "bap" in Staffordshire, the West Midlands and North Wales, and a "batch" in Liverpool and Coventry.
  - Around Liverpool an ice lolly can be a "lolly ice".
  - The evening meal is "tea" in the North West, North East and Yorkshire, and "dinner" in the South East and London. Some people say both.
  - "Yous" or "youse" for plural "you" is common in the North East (Newcastle, Teesside), Liverpool and Scotland, less so in Manchester, and rare in York, Leeds and Sheffield.
  - "Give it me" is normal in the North West and West Midlands and widely accepted in Sheffield and York; it fades south of Birmingham, Coventry and Leicester.
  - "You was" is widely used, historically Northern and now found as far south as London.
- **Everyday British words** to draw on where they fit, without assigning them to regions: knackered or shattered, chuffed or made up, skint or brassic, mardy or stroppy, mum or mam, mate or pal, settee, sofa or couch.

The group (session S17). Persona cards, including the webcam photo each person was rated on:

P084 (Craig; transcript label: Craig):
- first name: Craig
- age: 48
- lives in: Woodley, near Reading, South East England
- occupation: Associate structural engineer at a mid-sized engineering consultancy in central Reading, working mainly on commercial and residential refurbishment schemes
- education detail: BSc in Civil Engineering from the University of Natal in Durban, completed in 1999. Chartered Engineer (CEng) and Member of the Institution of Structural Engineers since 2008, after qualifying through the UK route.
- household: Lives alone in a three-bedroom 1970s semi in Woodley that he kept after his divorce four years ago. His daughter, 15, lives with her mum in Earley and stays with him every other weekend and one evening a week. The spare room is mostly her room.
- cultural background: Born and raised in Durban, South Africa, in an English-speaking white family. His parents became Bahá'ís in the 1970s and brought him up in the faith. He still describes himself as Bahá'í and goes to the occasional local gathering, particularly around Naw-Rúz in March. He keeps it low-key and practical rather than devout, and doesn't drink, which he puts down partly to upbringing and partly to habit. He came to the UK at 24 on a work visa, intending to stay two years, and is now a British citizen. His parents are still in Durban and his younger sister is in Perth, Australia.
- professional persona: Steady and reliable, the engineer people go to when they want a straight answer on whether a beam will take the load. He works long hours, usually 50 to 55 a week, mostly because project deadlines stack up and he'd rather finish things than leave them hanging. He's not interested in office politics or networking events. He gets on fine with the team but doesn't socialise much beyond the odd leaving do. He prefers proven methods and gets mildly irritated by new software rollouts that change things for the sake of it.
- sports persona: Lifelong rugby follower who supports the Springboks and watches every test, usually alone at home with the TV loud. He watches Premiership rugby casually too. He cycles on his own on weekend mornings, the same few loops out towards Wargrave and Henley, and does a gym session twice a week before work at a budget gym near the office.
- arts persona: Not much of one. He listens to the same rock he liked in his twenties: Bon Jovi, Dire Straits, a bit of Johnny Clegg from home. He watches crime dramas and documentaries about engineering or the war. He hasn't been to a gallery or theatre in years, apart from his daughter's school productions, which he attends without fail.
- travel persona: He goes back to Durban roughly every 18 months to see his parents, usually over Christmas or the Easter break. Beyond that he takes one week abroad a year, normally the Algarve or Crete, at the same type of hotel. He doesn't see the point of city breaks and isn't drawn to anywhere he hasn't been.
- culinary persona: Plain, dependable cooking: a small rotation of stir-fries, chicken and rice, pasta bake and steak. He braais on a gas barbecue in the garden whenever the weather allows, including in October, and buys boerewors from a South African shop online. He has a weakness for rusks with his morning coffee and makes his own biltong in a homemade drying box in the garage.
- hobbies and interests: Solo road cycling on weekend mornings, Watching rugby, especially the Springboks, Making biltong, Odd jobs and DIY around the house, Keeping the garden tidy, mainly the lawn, Watching crime dramas
- skills: Structural calculations and design using standard industry software, Reviewing contractor drawings and spotting problems quickly, Basic plumbing, electrics and carpentry, Bike maintenance, Cooking on a braai, Staying calm when site issues go wrong
- career goals: No grand ambitions. He'd accept a director-level role if it were offered, but won't chase it. His main aim is to keep the work steady, pay off the mortgage in about eight years, help his daughter through university, and maybe cut down to four days a week in his mid-fifties.
- voice: A South African accent softened by 24 years in Berkshire. Flat vowels still come through on some words, and he occasionally says 'ja' instead of 'yeah' without noticing. He speaks at a measured pace, in fairly short sentences, and gets to the point. He uses 'er' when thinking and the odd 'sort of' as a hedge. He calls the evening meal 'dinner'. He isn't bothered by silence on a call; he'll wait for the next question rather than fill the gap. When he's unsure what's being asked he'll say 'sorry, what was that?' rather than guess.
- typing: Proper capitals and full stops, apostrophes correct, no abbreviations or emojis. Answers are short and literal, often one sentence, and he rarely adds extra detail unless a field explicitly asks him to explain.
- with strangers: Polite, reserved and a bit dry. He answers what he's asked without volunteering much and doesn't do much small talk, but he isn't cold. He'll crack a deadpan joke now and then. Some people read him as unbothered or hard to read at first.
- small things: The traffic on the A329(M) in the mornings, Whether the Springboks squad is any good this year, His latest batch of biltong, A loop he cycled at the weekend, Work being busy, as usual, Needing to sort out the guttering
- deeper things: The divorce was mostly about him working too much and not talking enough, and he accepts some of that, He worries a little about his parents getting older so far away, He sometimes wonders whether he should have gone back to South Africa, but doesn't think he'd fit there now either, His faith is more a habit and a link to his parents than something he thinks hard about, Weekends without his daughter can feel very quiet
- webcam photo: Head-and-shoulders shot from a laptop camera slightly below eye level, so the view is a little upward. Lighting is mainly a ceiling light plus daylight from a window off to the left, which leaves the right side of his face a touch shadowed. He has a broad, weathered face with light stubber growth, short greying brown hair cut close at the sides and receding at the temples, and a neutral expression with a faint polite half-smile. No glasses. He wears a navy quarter-zip fleece over a grey T-shirt. Behind him is a magnolia wall in a small spare-room office with a white IKEA bookshelf holding ring binders, a few engineering reference books, a framed photo of a teenage girl, and a small Springboks mug used as a pen pot. A road bike helmet hangs on a hook near the door frame at the edge of the image.

P085 (Lauren; transcript label: Lauren):
- first name: Lauren
- age: 33
- lives in: Chaddesden, Derby, East Midlands
- occupation: Currently out of work and looking. Until about five months ago she was a group exercise and fitness instructor at a council-run leisure centre in Derby. Her post went when the centre's management was handed to a new operator and the class timetable was cut. She picks up the odd cash-in-hand cover class at a small community gym and is signing on while she applies for instructor and activity coordinator jobs.
- education detail: GCSEs at a comprehensive in Derby. BTEC National Diploma in Sport at a local college. She started a dance degree at the University of Derby, left part-way through the first year, then did a Level 2 Gym Instructor and Level 3 Personal Trainer qualification in her mid-twenties. She has an Exercise to Music certificate and keeps saying she'll renew her first aid.
- household: Rents a two-bed terraced house with her partner Ryan, 35, a forklift driver at a distribution warehouse near East Midlands Airport. They've been together seven years and aren't married. Ryan's shifts mean they often eat at different times. They have one cat, a fat grey rescue called Biscuit. Her mum lives about ten minutes away in Spondon.
- cultural background: White British, born and raised in Derby. Her mum worked in school catering and her dad drove for a parcels firm before he retired. She isn't religious and nobody in the family has really been churchy, apart from weddings and her nan's funeral. She's very much a Derby person: she knows everyone's cousin, goes to Rams matches with her dad now and then, and has a strong opinion about which Greggs is best.
- professional persona: Brilliant at the front of a studio. She's loud, encouraging, remembers everyone's name and has a knack for getting nervous beginners and older regulars to come back. She's weaker on the admin side: forgetting to log attendance, submitting timesheets late, letting her CPD lapse. She took the redundancy harder than she lets on and worries about money. She's applying for jobs in bursts, ten one evening and then nothing for a week.
- sports persona: Very active and genuinely fit. She teaches or does Zumba, step and circuits, and goes to a Saturday parkrun at Markeaton Park when she can drag herself up. She'd rather do something fun and social than follow a structured training plan, and has started and abandoned several 'proper' running programmes. She watches Derby County with her dad and shouts at the telly.
- arts persona: A former dancer who still loves it. She watches musicals whenever she can afford to, at Derby Theatre or the Nottingham Theatre Royal, and has a soft spot for anything with big choreography. She went through a phase of doing pottery evenings and says she'd go back. She listens to a lot of 2000s pop and musical soundtracks, and likes trying odd new things at local festivals.
- travel persona: Loves going away but rarely plans it. She does cheap last-minute deals from East Midlands Airport to Spain or the Greek islands with Ryan or the girls, and has done Benidorm twice and Crete once. She'd like to do something more adventurous, like Thailand or Iceland, and spends a lot of time looking at it online. At the moment it's more weekends at a Skegness caravan with her mum.
- culinary persona: An enthusiastic but chaotic cook. She'll try any recipe from TikTok or a Pinch of Nom book, then improvise when she's missing half the ingredients. With Ryan's shifts it's often a quick pasta or a cob with something in it. She loves trying new street food at markets and makes a decent Sunday dinner when her mum comes round, though her mum still does the gravy.
- hobbies and interests: Dance and dance-fitness classes, Parkrun at Markeaton Park, Musical theatre and watching cast recordings on YouTube, Charity shop rummaging, especially for retro clothes, Pottery taster evenings (on and off), Reality TV, particularly Strictly and Love Island, Trying new cafes and street food stalls, Looking after Biscuit the cat
- skills: Leading group exercise classes to music, Putting nervous people at ease quickly, Choreographing simple routines, Basic personal training and programme writing, Customer service and reception cover, Social media posting for a small gym's page, Chatting with literally anyone
- career goals: Get back into steady instructor work, ideally with more hours and more security than before. Longer term she'd love to run her own dance-fitness classes for women and older adults in community halls around Derby. She knows she'd need to get her head round the business and paperwork side, and keeps meaning to look into a start-up course through the job centre.
- voice: Warm, chatty and fast, with a Derby accent that's noticeable but not broad. She sometimes says 'me mum' and occasionally calls people 'duck' if she warms to them. She uses 'erm' quite a lot when thinking and 'sort of' and 'kind of' as she goes, and ends sentences with 'you know' or 'do you know what I mean'. She laughs easily, often mid-sentence, and picks up the interviewer's words and runs with them. She hates silence and will fill a pause with a tangent, sometimes stopping herself with 'sorry, I'm going off on one'. She can get a bit emotional if money or the job loss comes up, but tends to brush it off with a joke.
- typing: Quick and casual. Usually lowercase, with a capital for the first word if autocorrect does it. Apostrophes are hit and miss ('dont', 'im', but 'it's' when her phone fixes it). She uses lots of commas or no punctuation at all, the occasional 'lol', and sometimes an exclamation mark or a smiley. She uses abbreviations like 'tbh', 'prob' and 'cos'. Answers are often longer than needed because she adds context.
- with strangers: Instantly friendly and easy to talk to. She'll ask how your day's going and mean it. She overshares a little, apologises for rambling, and is quick to agree and reassure. She can come across as a bit scattered, losing track of the original question, but people tend to like her straight away.
- small things: Biscuit knocking things off the windowsill, Ryan's night shifts meaning she's tiptoeing round in the mornings, Having a cheese cob for lunch again, Parkrun being freezing on Saturday, Something daft that happened on Love Island, A charity shop find, like a 90s windbreaker for three quid, Her mum ringing her three times a day, Being knackered after covering a class
- deeper things: Feeling a bit lost and embarrassed since losing her job, especially telling people she's signing on, Money being tight and quietly worrying about rent going up, Still sometimes regretting dropping out of the dance degree, Wondering whether she and Ryan will ever get married or have kids, and not being sure what she wants, Her dad's health worrying her lately, Feeling like she's good with people but rubbish at being organised, and that holding her back
- webcam photo: Head-and-shoulders shot from a laptop on a kitchen table, angled slightly upwards so the ceiling light is visible at the top edge. Light comes from a window to her left, so one side of her face is brighter. She has a round, open face, light freckles across her nose and a big smile showing her teeth. Her mid-length dark blonde hair is scraped back into a high messy ponytail with a few loose strands. She's wearing a black zip-up sports hoodie, half undone, over a bright pink vest top, and small silver hoop earrings. No glasses. Behind her is a white kitchen wall with a calendar from a local Chinese takeaway, a magnetic whiteboard with a half-wiped shopping list, a kettle and a stack of mugs on the counter, and part of a fridge covered in magnets. On the right edge, a grey cat is curled on a chair.

P086 (Bethany; transcript label: Bethany):
- first name: Bethany
- age: 27
- lives in: Pontefract, Yorkshire and The Humber
- occupation: Not currently in paid work. She trained and worked as a florist, but the independent flower shop she worked at in Castleford closed about eighteen months ago and she hasn't had a job since. She does occasional unpaid flowers for friends' and family's weddings and does online surveys for pocket money.
- education detail: GCSEs at a comprehensive in Pontefract. Level 2 and Level 3 diplomas in floristry at a further education college in Wakefield, done part-time while working in the shop. She started an online Level 3 course in wedding planning but never finished it.
- household: Lives with her husband Craig (29), a shift supervisor at a distribution warehouse off the M62, in a two-bedroom ex-council semi they bought three years ago. No children yet. They have an anxious rescue whippet called Mabel. Craig's job and pay are what keep them in a C1 household.
- cultural background: White British, born and raised in West Yorkshire. Her mum is a dinner lady and her dad drove for a builders' merchant until his knees went. Her grandad worked at one of the local pits before the closures, which still comes up at family dos. She isn't religious. She got married at the registry office in Wakefield with a do afterwards at a local cricket club. She's close to her mum and her younger sister, who live ten minutes away.
- professional persona: Careful and gentle with customers. At the shop she was the one who dealt with sympathy flowers, because she was patient with people who were upset. She's good with her hands and has a decent eye for colour, but she's disorganised with orders, paperwork and invoices, and the old owner used to do all that side. Being out of work has knocked her confidence. She finds job interviews and phoning places very stressful, and she tends to put applications off.
- sports persona: Not sporty. She walks Mabel round the park and along the lanes most days, but slowly. She went to a beginners' Pilates class twice and stopped going because she felt self-conscious. Craig watches rugby league (Castleford Tigers) and she sometimes sits with him for it.
- arts persona: Likes pretty, hands-on things rather than galleries. She follows florists and pressed-flower artists on Instagram and Pinterest. She watches comfort telly like Bake Off and Gilmore Girls rewatches, and she reads cosy mysteries on her Kindle. She went to Yorkshire Sculpture Park once with her sister and liked the walk more than the sculptures.
- travel persona: A homebody who gets anxious about travelling. Holidays are usually a static caravan at Filey or a cottage in the Dales that takes dogs. She's been abroad a few times: Benidorm with friends at 19, and Tenerife for the honeymoon, which she enjoyed but was nervous about flying for. She'd like to see Amsterdam for the flower markets but hasn't got round to planning it.
- culinary persona: Plain home cooking. Tea is things like spag bol, chicken fajitas from a kit, sausage and mash, or a chippy tea on Fridays. Sunday dinner at her mum's most weeks, with Yorkshire puddings. She bakes when she's stressed, mostly traybakes and banana bread from Instagram recipes, though they don't always turn out. She drinks a lot of tea and the odd pink gin.
- hobbies and interests: pressing flowers and making little framed pieces for friends, walking the dog, baking traybakes, cosy mystery novels, rewatching comfort TV shows, scrolling florist and home decor accounts, tending a few pots and a small raised bed in the back garden, jigsaw puzzles in winter
- skills: floristry (bouquets, buttonholes, sympathy arrangements), colour matching, calming down upset or nervous people, basic baking, plant care, patient with animals
- career goals: Vague and a bit stalled. She'd like to do wedding and funeral flowers from home as a small business one day, but the thought of setting up a website, doing the accounts and putting herself out there puts her off. In the meantime she's half-heartedly looking at part-time jobs in garden centres or supermarket floral departments.
- voice: Quiet, soft West Yorkshire accent: short vowels in 'bath' and 'grass', and flattened 'u' in words like 'love' and 'mum'. She talks fairly slowly and often trails off at the end of sentences. She says 'erm' a lot and hedges with 'sort of' and 'I don't know, it's just...'. She'll say 'tea' for her evening meal, 'mum', and occasionally 'love' or 'you was' without thinking. She apologises often ('sorry, that probably doesn't make sense') and will agree with the interviewer to be nice. She doesn't fill silences herself. She waits, or gives a little laugh, and needs gentle prompts to expand. She opens up a bit more when talking about flowers or the dog.
- typing: Mostly lowercase, with capitals only sometimes at the start. Few full stops, and she'll string things together with commas or 'and'. Apostrophes are often missing ('dont', 'im', 'its'). Short answers. She uses the odd 'lol' or 'tbh', and sometimes ends with '...' if she's unsure. No emojis in a form.
- with strangers: Shy and polite, slightly nervous at first, smiles a lot and keeps answers short. She's very agreeable and won't contradict anyone, so she can come across as having fewer opinions than she really has. Warm once she relaxes. She'll ask the other person if they're alright and thank them more than once.
- small things: Mabel being scared of the bin lorry, what she's having for tea, it being freezing again, a cosy murder mystery she's halfway through, the peonies in her garden coming through, Sunday dinner at her mum's, Craig being on nights this week, a banana bread that sank in the middle
- deeper things: She feels guilty and a bit useless about not working while Craig does long shifts, She gets bad anxiety and has thought about seeing the GP about it but keeps putting it off, She's unsure whether she wants children soon, and people keep asking, She was really upset when the flower shop closed, because it felt like her place, She worries she's not organised enough to ever run her own business
- webcam photo: Head-and-shoulders shot from a laptop camera angled slightly upward, so the ceiling corner is visible. Soft, slightly grey daylight from a window to her left, leaving the right side of her face a little shadowed. She is a young white woman with a round face, light freckles, pale skin and minimal makeup, smiling slightly with closed lips and looking a bit shy, eyes just off the camera. Shoulder-length mousy blonde hair is pulled back in a loose claw clip, with strands falling around her face. No glasses. She wears an oversized sage-green knitted jumper and has a small silver necklace. Behind her is a magnolia-painted wall in a small living room. A grey fabric settee is partly visible with a mustard throw over the arm, and a whippet curled up asleep on a cushion. A white shelf on the wall holds two small framed pressed-flower pictures, a trailing pothos plant and a candle in a jar. A wedding photo in a silver frame sits slightly out of focus at the edge of the frame.

P087 (Darren; transcript label: Darren):
- first name: Darren
- age: 43
- lives in: Castleford, Yorkshire and The Humber
- occupation: Maintenance joiner for a housing association, covering council and social housing stock across the Wakefield district: doors, windows, kitchen units, floorboards, fencing, boarding up after break-ins
- education detail: Left a comprehensive in Castleford at 16 with a handful of GCSEs (C in Maths, D in English). Did a joinery apprenticeship with a small local firm and got his NVQ Level 2, then Level 3 in Site Carpentry at Wakefield College in his early twenties. Has a CSCS card and keeps meaning to do an asbestos awareness refresher before it lapses.
- household: Lives alone in a two-bed ex-council terrace he bought in 2011. The back bedroom is half spare room, half dumping ground for tools, a dismantled bike and boxes from his mam's house. No pets, though he sometimes feeds next door's cat.
- cultural background: White British, born in Pontefract hospital and raised in Castleford. His dad was a miner at Glasshoughton until the pit closed, then drove vans, and died when Darren was 29. His mam was a dinner lady and died three years ago. He has one older sister, Joanne, in Normanton with two teenage kids. He was christened and confirmed Church of England and calls himself Christian. He goes to church at Christmas, for funerals and sometimes on the anniversary of his mam's death. He says he believes 'in something', and saying a quick prayer when he's worried feels natural to him, though he'd never bring it up unprompted. Rugby league town through and through.
- professional persona: Good with his hands and quick at the actual job, but disorganised with everything around it. Job sheets get filled in late, the van is a tip, and he's lost more than one set of tenants' keys down the side of the seat. He won't cut corners or claim hours he hasn't worked, and he's openly scornful of lads who do. He is blunt with supervisors and has a reputation for moaning about management, the scheduling system and 'whoever designed these uPVC frames'. Tenants generally like him because he's straight with them. He worries more than he lets on about getting a complaint or being blamed when something goes wrong.
- sports persona: Lifelong Castleford Tigers fan with an on-and-off season ticket at the Jungle. He gets genuinely wound up during matches and can be in a mood for a day after a bad loss. He played amateur rugby league as a teenager until he did his shoulder in. Now he walks a bit and occasionally plays five-a-side, though he finds excuses not to go if it's raining. He watches darts on telly.
- arts persona: Not a gallery person. He listens to Absolute 80s and Radio 2 in the van and likes Oasis, The Verve and older stuff his dad played, like Elvis Costello and Status Quo. He'll admit to welling up at films, especially anything about fathers and sons. He watches a lot of crime dramas and true-crime documentaries on his own in the evenings.
- travel persona: Doesn't travel much and gets anxious about flying, mostly the airport side of it. He's done a few lads' holidays to Tenerife and Magaluf in his twenties and a week in Benidorm with his sister's family a few years back. He prefers a caravan at Filey or a few nights in the Dales. He keeps saying he'll go to Krakow because a mate went and loved it, but he never books it.
- culinary persona: Plain eater. His tea is often something quick: oven chips and a pie, beans on toast, a chippy tea on Fridays. He can do a decent Sunday dinner but rarely bothers just for himself. He goes to Joanne's for Sunday dinner most weeks. He's partial to a bacon sandwich from the café by the trading estate and drinks too much tea with two sugars. Bitter or lager at the club, nothing fancy.
- hobbies and interests: Castleford Tigers, Pottering in his shed making things out of offcuts, like bird boxes and a bench for his sister, Fishing at a pond near Fairburn Ings a few times a summer, True-crime documentaries and police dramas, Pub quiz at the working men's club, though he isn't a regular, Half-heartedly restoring an old mountain bike
- skills: Second-fix and first-fix joinery, Hanging doors and fitting locks, Fitting kitchens, Reading people quickly when he knocks on a door, Basic plumbing and tiling, picked up on the job, Driving a van round Wakefield back streets without a satnav
- career goals: Mostly to keep his job steady until retirement and avoid getting stuck on the out-of-hours rota. He has vaguely thought about going self-employed, but he knows he'd be hopeless at the invoicing and it frightens him. He'd quite like a supervisor role for the money, but he doesn't think he'd suit telling people what to do, and he 'can't be doing with the meetings'.
- voice: West Yorkshire accent: flat vowels and some dropped 'the' ('going t' shop' comes out occasionally). He sometimes says 'it were' rather than 'it was', but it's not heavy. He says 'tea' for his evening meal and 'mam' for his mother. He uses 'er' a lot when he's thinking and 'sort of' when he's unsure, and ends points with 'you know' or 'do you know what I mean'. His pace is moderate, but he speeds up and gets a bit sharp when something annoys him, like management or the cost of living. If there's a silence he'll fill it with a short 'yeah... anyway' or wait it out uneasily. When he realises he's sounded harsh he'll say 'sorry, I'm just being a grump'. He says 'mate' and 'pal' and calls himself 'knackered' most evenings.
- typing: Mostly lowercase, with the occasional capital at the start. Few commas, and he often runs sentences together with no full stop at the end. He drops apostrophes ('dont', 'im', 'its'). Short answers, and if he's irritated he'll repeat a word or add 'tbh'. He sometimes types 'ok' or 'yeah' as a whole answer. He spells his own trade words fine but makes the odd slip like 'there' for 'their'.
- with strangers: Guarded and a bit gruff at first, not rude but not putting on a show. He answers what he's asked honestly and doesn't try to make himself sound better than he is. He can come across as grumpy or sceptical, especially if questions feel pointless or corporate. If the other person is down to earth he softens quite a lot and will talk more than he meant to. He'll sometimes reveal worries quite openly once he's going.
- small things: The van's heater has been broken since October, Cas lost again at the weekend and the ref was a disgrace, Fuel prices, He's been meaning to sort the guttering at the back for months, He tried a new chippy and it weren't as good as the old one, Next door's cat keeps coming in through the back door, His knees ache after a day of kneeling on floors
- deeper things: He still hasn't cleared all his mam's things and can't bring himself to open some of the boxes, He worries about getting ill living on his own and nobody noticing, and checks lumps and moles more than he'd admit, He was with a woman called Kerry for seven years in his thirties and thought they'd marry; she left, and he still thinks about it, He gets lonely in the evenings and sometimes rings Joanne just to have someone to talk to, He feels he has a temper like his dad's and doesn't like that about himself, He prays sometimes, usually when he's anxious about money or health
- webcam photo: A laptop webcam shot from slightly below, as the laptop sits on a low coffee table, so the framing catches his chin and neck and cuts off the top of his head. The light is a warm ceiling bulb from above plus a cooler glow from the screen on his face, leaving mild shadows under his eyes. He's a white man in his early forties with a broad, slightly ruddy face, short mousy-brown hair clipped at the sides and thinning on top, and two or three days of stubble with some grey in it. No glasses. His expression is neutral to faintly wary, with a slight frown of concentration and his mouth closed. He's wearing a navy work fleece with a small embroidered housing association logo, half-zipped over a grey T-shirt. Behind him is a magnolia wall with a slightly wonky framed photo of an older woman and two children at the seaside. Below it is part of a brown leather settee with a crumpled Castleford Tigers throw over the arm. On the left edge the corner of a radiator is visible with a pair of socks drying on it, and a mug sits on the windowsill in front of drawn beige curtains.

P088 (Callum; transcript label: Callum):
- first name: Callum
- age: 21
- lives in: Plymouth, South West England

=== CALL C0173 ===
Danuta: Hello! Hello, can you hear me? Oh good, there you are. I'm Danuta.
Craig: Hi, Danuta. Craig. Yes, I can hear you fine.
Danuta: Lovely. So we have three minutes, no? I never know what to say in three minutes, I talk too much, so you stop me. Have you had your tea yet?
Craig: Not yet, no. I'll have dinner after this. Probably chicken and rice.
Danuta: Chicken and rice, very good, very healthy. I had a late shift yesterday so today I am off, I made pierogi at the weekend, sixty of them, all in the freezer now. So tonight is easy, just boil.
Craig: Sixty. That's commitment.
Danuta: My husband says I cook for an army, but then my son comes from Manchester with his little girl and they all disappear, you know? Where are you from, Craig? Your accent, it's not from here, I think.
Craig: No. Durban originally. South Africa. I've been here about twenty-four years though. I'm in Woodley, near Reading.
Danuta: Oh, South Africa! So far. I am from Poland, near Rzeszów, but I live in Preston now nearly twenty years. So we are both, how do you say, from somewhere else.
Craig: Ja, that's about right.
Danuta: And what work you do? I guessed from your photo, I think engineer, with the books and the folders.
Craig: That's right, actually. Structural engineer. Mostly refurbishment jobs. Old buildings, checking whether they'll stand up when people knock walls out.
Danuta: Ha, I was right! I'm proud of myself. I work at the hospital, I clean the wards. Eleven years on the same two wards. Everybody knows me, the nurses, the patients. I like it, but my knees, after an early shift, oh.
Craig: I can imagine. That's a lot of time on your feet.
Danuta: All day walking, mopping. But I like to talk to the old ones, the lonely ones, you know? Some of them nobody visits. Sorry, I talk too much.
Craig: No, that's fine. Someone's got to.
Danuta: And your family, they are still in South Africa?
Craig: My parents are, yes. In Durban. My sister's in Australia. I've got a daughter here, she's fifteen. That's her in the photo behind me.
Danuta: She's beautiful. Fifteen, oh, difficult age, no? My daughter at fifteen, I don't want to remember. Now she's in Poland again, I miss her very much.
Craig: Ja. It's hard, being far from people. I go back to see my folks every eighteen months or so. They're getting on a bit.
Danuta: My mother is eighty-four. I go every summer. Every time I leave I think, maybe last time, you know? It's not easy.
Craig: No. It's not.
Danuta: But then, phone calls every evening! Video, now, with my granddaughter, she says Polish words to me. So that helps.
Craig: That's good. My parents aren't great with video calls. Lots of foreheads.
Danuta: Ha! Yes, my mother too, only her ear I see!
Craig: Do you cook South African food? Sorry, I mean, do you cook much from home? Polish food?
Danuta: All the time! Gołąbki, żurek at Easter, poppy-seed cake at Christmas. And you, you have special food from Durban?
Craig: I make biltong. Dried meat. I built a drying box in the garage. The latest batch is nearly ready, actually.
Danuta: You built a box for meat! This is very engineer. My Tadeusz would love that, he—

=== CALL C0174 ===
Callum: Alright? Can you hear me yeah?

Callum: Nah, you're alright. Yeah, second year, business and management. And I work at a pub on the Barbican, glass collecting, pot washing, that sort of thing. Weekends mostly.
Lauren: Oh, nice. Do you get good tips?
Callum: Sometimes, yeah. Had a stag do in last weekend, they were proper generous, like. Bunged me a twenty for basically just being there.
Lauren: Twenty quid! That's amazing. I used to be a fitness instructor, at the leisure centre, but erm, they changed who runs it and they cut loads of classes, so my job sort of went. So I'm, you know, looking. I do the odd cover class. Signing on, the glamorous life.

Callum: That's quite cool, actually. I've got a gym membership. I use it, like, in bursts.
Lauren: Everyone does! Three weeks keen and then gone. I can always tell.
Callum: Yeah, nah, that's me exactly, caught out. What else d'you get up to, then?
Lauren: Erm, charity shops, I'm obsessed. I got a nineties windbreaker last week for three quid, proper retro, all purple and teal.
Callum: Three quid? Mate, you need to be flipping that. I do Vinted, trainers mostly. Got some Jordans the other week, made forty quid on them.
Lauren: Shut up, forty quid?
Callum: Yeah, I've got a bit of a system going. Buy cheap, clean them up, sell. A nineties windbreaker, people'd go mad for that.
Lauren: I'm not selling it though, I look amazing in it! Sorry, I'm going off on one. But that's actually a good shout, like, the ones I don't wear.
Callum: You should, honestly. Easy money. You could do, like, a whole retro page.
Lauren: Maybe. Me boyfriend Ryan'd be chuffed, he says the spare room's just bags of clothes now. So what do you wanna do after uni?
Callum: Erm, kind of sales, maybe. Or start something. Haven't really worked it out yet, I'll be—

=== CALL C0175 ===
Darren: Hello? Is it on?
Bethany: Hiya. Yeah, I think so. I can see you.
Darren: Right. Good. Darren. Not done one of these before.
Bethany: Me neither. I'm Bethany. Sorry, I'm a bit nervous.
Darren: You're alright. It's only three minutes, love. Where are you, then?
Bethany: Pontefract.
Darren: Pontefract? Give over. I'm Castleford. Born in Pontefract hospital, actually.
Bethany: Oh, no way. That's... that's mad, that. I worked in Castleford, at a flower shop. On the main road down near the precinct.
Darren: Not the one that shut? Little independent place?
Bethany: Yeah. That one. About eighteen month ago now.
Darren: I knew it. I used to drive past it in the van every day. Shame, that. It were a nice shop.
Bethany: It was. It was sort of my place, you know. I've not really found anything since, so I'm just... erm, looking. Sort of.
Darren: It's hard round here. Everything's shutting. What did you do there, then? Bouquets and that?
Bethany: Yeah, bouquets, weddings, buttonholes. And I did a lot of the sympathy flowers, for funerals. People are upset when they come in, and I didn't mind. I'd just let them talk.
Darren: Takes a certain kind of person, that. When me mam died, the lass who did the flowers were dead kind. Made a big difference, actually.
Bethany: I'm sorry about your mam.
Darren: Ah, it's three year ago now. Anyway. What about you, are you married? Sorry, saw the photo.
Bethany: Yeah, I am. My husband's called Craig. He'd like you, I think. He's Cas Tigers mad. I saw your throw in your photo.
Darren: Ha, did you? Good man. Is he going Sunday?
Bethany: He's on nights this week, so I don't know. I sit with him when he watches it on telly. I don't really understand it.
Darren: Neither do the refs, half the time. Last week were a disgrace. Sorry, I'm just being a grump.
Bethany: No, that's alright. He says the same thing every week.
Darren: I'm a joiner, by the way. Housing association. Doors, windows, kitchens, boarding up. All over Wakefield district.
Bethany: Oh, that's handy. Our back door sticks all the time. Mabel, that's our dog, she's a whippet, she's scared of it. She's scared of everything, really. The bin lorry especially.
Darren: Is that her on the settee in the back?
Bethany: Yeah, that's her. She just sleeps all day.
Darren: Lucky her. Your door'll be the frame dropping. Probably the hinges, nine times out of ten. Easy fix.
Bethany: Really? Craig keeps saying he'll look at it.
Darren: They all say that. I've been saying I'll do me own guttering since October.
Bethany: Ha. I do little pressed flowers, framed ones, for people. I could swap you one for...

The study, in order (from its published design): a short puzzle task done alone; first impressions of the others' webcam photos; then a series of three-minute, one-on-one video calls in rounds, each person meeting the others in their group; after each call a short survey.

Call shape (from the original study's numbers): a call is cut off by a three-minute timer. A typical call has about 30 turns (most between 20 and 39) and about 570 words in total (most between 440 and 682); half of all turns are 12 words or fewer, and a quarter are 24 or more. Short acknowledgements ("yeah", "mm") count as turns too. So aim for about 570 words in about 30 turns: alongside the quick back-and-forth, people often talk in longer stretches (explaining their job, telling a story), and those long turns carry much of the call.

Guide to British conversational English (use it for how people talk; it is a description of speech, not a script):
How British people talk in casual conversation. This is a paraphrase of published descriptions of spoken British English; sources are in SOURCES.md. Use these features lightly and only where they fit the person. Never use them as a caricature.

- **Fillers.** British speakers hesitate with "erm" and "er". Women and younger speakers lean towards "erm".
- **Hedges.** "Sort of" is everywhere and steady. "Kind of" is spreading, and younger speakers use it more.
- **Politeness words.** "Please", "thank you", "thanks" and "sorry" mostly mean what they say. "Sorry" also works as a repair word (to correct yourself, or to ask someone to repeat) and can be ironic.
- **Tags at the end of a sentence.** "You know", "right", "okay", "yeah", "do you know what I mean". Among young Londoners, "innit" and "you get me" are rising. Tags depend on age and region only, never on ethnicity.
- **Echoing.** In an engaged conversation people pick up and re-use parts of each other's words.
- **Regional words and grammar** (from a recent dialect survey):
  - A bread roll is a "barm" in the North West (Manchester to Liverpool and western Lancashire), a "cob" around Nottinghamshire, a "bap" in Staffordshire, the West Midlands and North Wales, and a "batch" in Liverpool and Coventry.
  - Around Liverpool an ice lolly can be a "lolly ice".
  - The evening meal is "tea" in the North West, North East and Yorkshire, and "dinner" in the South East and London. Some people say both.
  - "Yous" or "youse" for plural "you" is common in the North East (Newcastle, Teesside), Liverpool and Scotland, less so in Manchester, and rare in York, Leeds and Sheffield.
  - "Give it me" is normal in the North West and West Midlands and widely accepted in Sheffield and York; it fades south of Birmingham, Coventry and Leicester.
  - "You was" is widely used, historically Northern and now found as far south as London.
- **Everyday British words** to draw on where they fit, without assigning them to regions: knackered or shattered, chuffed or made up, skint or brassic, mardy or stroppy, mum or mam, mate or pal, settee, sofa or couch.

You write transcripts of realistic video calls between strangers for a fully synthetic research dataset set in the UK. The study, in order (from its published design): a short puzzle task done alone; first impressions of the others' webcam photos; then a series of three-minute, one-on-one video calls in rounds, each person meeting the others in their group; after each call a short survey.

Call shape (from the original study's numbers): a call is cut off by a three-minute timer. A typical call has about 30 turns (most between 20 and 39) and about 570 words in total (most between 440 and 682); half of all turns are 12 words or fewer, and a quarter are 24 or more. Short acknowledgements ("yeah", "mm") count as turns too. So aim for about 570 words in about 30 turns: alongside the quick back-and-forth, people often talk in longer stretches (explaining their job, telling a story), and those long turns carry much of the call.

Guide to British conversational English (use it for how people talk; it is a description of speech, not a script):
How British people talk in casual conversation. This is a paraphrase of published descriptions of spoken British English; sources are in SOURCES.md. Use these features lightly and only where they fit the person. Never use them as a caricature.

- **Fillers.** British speakers hesitate with "erm" and "er". Women and younger speakers lean towards "erm".
- **Hedges.** "Sort of" is everywhere and steady. "Kind of" is spreading, and younger speakers use it more.
- **Politeness words.** "Please", "thank you", "thanks" and "sorry" mostly mean what they say. "Sorry" also works as a repair word (to correct yourself, or to ask someone to repeat) and can be ironic.
- **Tags at the end of a sentence.** "You know", "right", "okay", "yeah", "do you know what I mean". Among young Londoners, "innit" and "you get me" are rising. Tags depend on age and region only, never on ethnicity.
- **Echoing.** In an engaged conversation people pick up and re-use parts of each other's words.
- **Regional words and grammar** (from a recent dialect survey):
  - A bread roll is a "barm" in the North West (Manchester to Liverpool and western Lancashire), a "cob" around Nottinghamshire, a "bap" in Staffordshire, the West Midlands and North Wales, and a "batch" in Liverpool and Coventry.
  - Around Liverpool an ice lolly can be a "lolly ice".
  - The evening meal is "tea" in the North West, North East and Yorkshire, and "dinner" in the South East and London. Some people say both.
  - "Yous" or "youse" for plural "you" is common in the North East (Newcastle, Teesside), Liverpool and Scotland, less so in Manchester, and rare in York, Leeds and Sheffield.
  - "Give it me" is normal in the North West and West Midlands and widely accepted in Sheffield and York; it fades south of Birmingham, Coventry and Leicester.
  - "You was" is widely used, historically Northern and now found as far south as London.
- **Everyday British words** to draw on where they fit, without assigning them to regions: knackered or shattered, chuffed or made up, skint or brassic, mardy or stroppy, mum or mam, mate or pal, settee, sofa or couch.

P106 (Joanne; transcript label: Joanne):
- first name: Joanne
- age: 44
- lives in: St Helens, North West England
- occupation: Not currently in paid work. She left her job on a food-packing line at a warehouse in Haydock three years ago to look after her mum, who has early-stage dementia and lives four streets away. Before that she worked eleven years as a picker-packer and briefly as a cleaner at a primary school. She gets Carer's Allowance and does online survey panels for a bit of extra money.
- education detail: Left a local comprehensive at 16 with five GCSEs, including a C in English and a D in maths. Did a year of a childcare NVQ at college but didn't finish it. Has a food hygiene certificate and a forklift counterbalance licence from the warehouse, now lapsed.
- household: Lives with her husband Gary, 47, a multi-drop delivery driver, in a two-bed ex-council terrace they bought under right-to-buy from his late dad's estate. They have no children. There's an elderly tabby cat called Mabel. Her mum lives alone nearby, and her younger sister lives in Warrington.
- cultural background: White British, born and raised in St Helens to a working-class family. Her dad was a glassworks labourer who died when she was 30. She was christened Church of England and still calls herself Christian. She doesn't go to church except for funerals, Christmas Eve and her mum's harvest festival, but she prays privately when she's worried, which is often. She's local through and through and has never lived more than three miles from where she grew up.
- professional persona: A reliable, head-down worker who kept herself to herself. She was respected for never fiddling her hours or skiving, and disliked for telling supervisors straight when something was unfair or done wrong. She'd rather be on her own on a task than in a team. Caring for her mum has become her full-time job: medication, appointments, chasing the GP and social services. She does it carefully but gets frustrated and short with the system.
- sports persona: Not sporty. She goes for walks round Sherdley Park or Taylor Park most mornings, partly to clear her head. She'll have the rugby league on in the background because Gary follows St Helens (Saints), but she isn't bothered herself beyond knowing the score.
- arts persona: Watches a lot of telly: crime dramas, Escape to the Country, old Coronation Street episodes. Reads paperback psychological thrillers from the library and charity shops. She doesn't go to the theatre or gigs because crowds put her on edge. She did once go to see Take That in Manchester with her sister and found it overwhelming.
- travel persona: Rarely goes abroad. She's been to Tenerife twice and Majorca once with Gary, and was anxious about the flights both times. She prefers a caravan in North Wales (Prestatyn or Rhyl) or a few days in the Lake District, somewhere quiet. She hasn't been away overnight since her mum's diagnosis because she worries something will happen.
- culinary persona: Plain home cooking. Tea is on the table about half five for when Gary gets in: chilli, spag bol, a roast on Sunday, scouse in winter, and chippy on Fridays. She does her mum's shopping and meals as well. She buys budget-range stuff and is careful with money. She likes a chip barm and a brew. She doesn't really drink, just a Baileys at Christmas.
- hobbies and interests: morning walks in the park, reading thrillers from the library, word searches and crosswords in the puzzle magazines, watching crime dramas, online survey panels, looking after the cat, keeping her small back yard tidy with pots of geraniums
- skills: managing medication schedules and appointments, budgeting on a tight income, plain cooking for two households, methodical, careful form-filling, basic forklift and warehouse stock work, being blunt and persistent on the phone with the council or GP surgery when she has to
- career goals: No real career ambitions at the moment. Her mum comes first. She has vaguely thought she might go back to warehouse or cleaning work, part-time, if her mum goes into a home, but she feels guilty even thinking about that. She would like a bit more money coming in and not to have to rely on benefits.
- voice: Quiet and a bit flat, with a mild St Helens accent: not strongly Scouse, more Lancashire-edged. Fairly short answers to start with. She says 'erm' a lot, especially at the start of an answer, and uses 'sort of' as a hedge. She'll say 'tea' for her evening meal and 'me mum' sometimes. She's honest to the point of being blunt ('No, I didn't like it, to be honest') and doesn't do fake enthusiasm. Long silences make her uncomfortable, so she'll either fill them with 'yeah... that's it really' or just wait awkwardly. If she's asked something she doesn't understand she says 'sorry, what d'you mean?' rather than guess. She gets slightly more talkative if the topic is her mum or something that's annoyed her.
- typing: Mostly lowercase. She sometimes capitalises the first word and 'I', but not consistently. Minimal punctuation, often no full stop at the end. Apostrophes are hit and miss ('dont', 'its', but 'I'm' sometimes from autocorrect). Short, literal answers. She'll write 'dont know' or 'not sure to be honest' rather than make something up, and occasionally adds a line of explanation if she thinks the question is unfair.
- with strangers: Reserved, wary and a bit nervous. She doesn't chat for the sake of it and can come across as cold or curt at first. She's polite but won't flatter, and if she disagrees she says so plainly. She's very straight and doesn't exaggerate. It takes a while for her to warm up, and she may visibly relax once she realises nobody's judging her.
- small things: Mabel the cat being sick on the settee again, the price of the big shop going up at Asda, the buses being rubbish since they changed the timetable, Gary working late on his rounds before Christmas, finishing a library book she guessed the ending of, the weather stopping her walk, having to ring the surgery at 8am to get an appointment
- deeper things: She worries constantly that her mum will fall or wander off while she's not there, and she sleeps badly, She hasn't spoken properly to her sister in over a year because she feels her sister doesn't pull her weight with their mum, She and Gary tried for children for years, and it didn't happen. She doesn't really talk about it, She still misses her dad and gets upset around the anniversary, She sometimes feels lonely and invisible since she stopped working, but doesn't want to burden anyone, She feels guilty about the times she's lost her temper with her mum
- webcam photo: Slightly low-angle shot from an older laptop sitting on a kitchen table, framing her from the chest up, a little off-centre to the left. Lighting is flat and greyish from a window to her right with net curtains, plus a ceiling light making her face a bit shiny. She has a pale, slightly tired-looking face, faint lines around the eyes, and no makeup apart from a bit of mascara. Her expression is neutral to wary, mouth closed, eyebrows slightly raised. Shoulder-length mousy brown hair with a few greys, scraped back into a low ponytail with some loose strands. She's wearing a navy zip-up fleece over a grey T-shirt. No glasses. Behind her: a magnolia wall with a calendar from a local Chinese takeaway showing scribbled appointments, a wall clock, part of a white kitchen cupboard, a kettle and a mug tree on the counter, and the edge of a fridge with magnets and a pharmacy leaflet stuck on it.

P107 (Shazia; transcript label: Shazia):
- first name: Shazia
- age: 40
- lives in: Blackburn, North West England
- occupation: Not currently working. She started a Level 2 childcare course at Blackburn College at 17 but stopped going partway through the second term. She has no qualifications since then apart from a food hygiene certificate from the warehouse.
- household: Lives in a rented two-up two-down terraced house in the Audley area with her partner Imran, 44, who drives a taxi. Her widowed mum lives three streets away with Shazia's younger brother and his family, and Shazia goes round most days.
- cultural background: Born in a village near Mirpur in Azad Kashmir and moved to Lancashire as a teenager when her dad got work here. She speaks Pahari-Potwari with her mum and aunties, English with Imran a lot of the time, and reads basic Urdu. She is a practising Muslim but not strict about it. She prays when she can, fasts in Ramadan and wears a headscarf out of the house. She feels like she belongs to Blackburn more than anywhere else, though she wouldn't put it that way.
- professional persona: At work she kept her head down and did the job without chatting much. She doesn't like being told what to do twice and could be short with supervisors she felt were picking on her. She was often late for shifts and lost one agency job over timekeeping. She has no real interest in a career. Work has always been about money and getting out of the house.
- sports persona: Doesn't do any sport. She tried a women-only swimming session at the leisure centre a few years back on her GP's advice, went three times and stopped. Imran watches cricket and Blackburn Rovers, and she has it on in the background without following it.
- arts persona: Watches Pakistani dramas on YouTube most evenings, the long family ones, and gets properly upset at them. She liked art at school and still doodles on the backs of envelopes but would never call it anything. She doesn't go to galleries, the theatre or concerts.
- travel persona: Has been back to Pakistan four or five times for weddings and a funeral, always with family, and finds the journey exhausting and stressful. Otherwise she has barely travelled: a day at Blackpool now and then, and once a weekend in Birmingham for a cousin's mehndi. Airports make her anxious. She isn't bothered about holidays abroad.
- culinary persona: Cooks everyday Pakistani food without measuring: saalan, daal and chapatis, with a big pot of something on the hob most days. Imran likes it hot, so she cooks it hot. She makes tea at half seven-ish, or whenever Imran's in. On bad days it's oven chips, or a barm from the corner shop with a samosa stuffed in it. She drinks a lot of sugary chai.
- hobbies and interests: Pakistani TV dramas on YouTube, scrolling Facebook and TikTok, mainly recipe and family-gossip type videos, doing online surveys for small amounts of money, doodling and colouring-in books, on and off, looking after a couple of potted plants on the windowsill, sitting with her mum and aunties
- skills: cooking for large numbers at family events, cleaning quickly and thoroughly when she gets going, speaking Pahari-Potwari and Punjabi, reading some Urdu, packing and picking in a warehouse, threading eyebrows, which she does for relatives
- career goals: Nothing firm. She sometimes says she might do a bit of part-time cleaning again or help in her cousin's clothes shop if her back gets better. Mostly she wants her benefits sorted out without hassle and enough money not to worry about the electric.
- voice: Quiet and fairly flat, with a Blackburn/East Lancashire accent and slightly Pahari-shaped vowels on some words. She gives short answers at a steady, slowish pace. She says 'erm' a lot before answering and uses 'sort of' and 'you know' as softeners. She calls her mum 'mum' and says 'tea' for the evening meal. She'll say 'I'm knackered' or 'I was proper skint that month' and sometimes uses 'give it me'. She doesn't fill silences herself; she waits for the next question. If something annoys her she gets blunter rather than louder. Asked to repeat something, she says 'sorry?'
- typing: Mostly lower case, often with no capital at the start or on 'i'. Hardly any punctuation beyond the odd full stop or a run of '...'. She usually drops apostrophes ('dont', 'cant', 'im'). Spelling is phonetic in places ('definatly', 'alot') and she uses 'u' and 'ur' sometimes. Answers are short, a few words to one line.
- with strangers: Reserved and a bit guarded at first. She doesn't smile much on camera and can seem uninterested or slightly grumpy. She answers what she's asked and no more, and if a question feels nosy or pointless she says so plainly. She warms a little if the person is patient and not patronising.
- small things: her back playing up after carrying shopping, the bins not being collected on their street again, a drama she's watching where the mother-in-law is awful, Imran working late shifts on Fridays and Saturdays, chai with too much sugar, the price of gas and electric, her mum's knees, that she forgot her GP appointment last week
- deeper things: that she and Imran never registered the marriage and she sometimes worries what that means for her if something happens to him, that they wanted children and it hasn't happened, and the aunties don't let it drop, she's been on and off antidepressants for anxiety since her dad died six years ago, she feels she wasted chances when she left college and blames herself for it, she sometimes feels she doesn't properly belong here or back in Pakistan
- webcam photo: A slightly low-angle shot from a laptop balanced on her knees, framing her head and shoulders a bit off-centre to the left. Light comes from a window to her right with net curtains, so one side of her face is brighter, and a ceiling light adds a yellowish tint. She has a round face, light brown skin, dark eyes with faint shadows under them and a neutral, slightly tired expression with her lips closed. She wears a loosely wrapped black jersey headscarf with a little dark hair showing at the front, and a maroon zip-up fleece over a patterned kameez. She has no glasses. Behind her is a grey fabric settee with a crocheted throw over the back, a cream wall with a framed gold-and-black Ayat al-Kursi calligraphy print, a wall clock, and the edge of a doorway into a narrow hallway with a coat hanging on a hook.
