=== CALL C0215 ===
Tracey A: Hiya! Can you hear me alright? I'm Tracey, nice to meet you.
Shazia: Yeah, I can hear you. I'm Shazia.
Tracey A: Shazia, lovely. Where are you calling from, hun?
Shazia: Blackburn.
Tracey A: Oh, up north! I'm Chelmsford, Essex. Sat in my kitchen, as you can probably tell. Did you do that puzzle thing at the start? Because I'll be honest, I rushed it. I'm not a sit-still-and-think person, I just wanted to get it done, you know?
Shazia: Erm, yeah. I did it. Some of them were hard.
Tracey A: The shapes ones, weren't they? I just guessed half of them to be fair. So what do you do then, are you working?
Shazia: No. Not at the minute.
Tracey A: Oh right, fair enough.
Shazia: I was in a warehouse. Packing, nights. Had to stop because of my back.
Tracey A: Oh, nights are brutal. And packing, all that bending and lifting, it kills your lower back, honestly I see it all the time. I'm a fitness instructor, I do PT as well, and half my over-fifties come to me with backs that have just gone from years of lifting stuff wrong. Have you had any physio or anything?
Shazia: GP sent me swimming. Women's session.
Tracey A: Oh, swimming's brilliant for backs. Did it help?
Shazia: I went three times.
Tracey A: Three times! Babe, that's not long enough to tell, you've got to give it a couple of months, yeah?
Shazia: I know. It weren't for me, the swimming. Too early, and the changing rooms were freezing.
Tracey A: No, I get it, I get it. Sorry, I'm going into trainer mode, my son says I do it to everyone. He's seventeen, Callum, doing his A-levels. Leaves his washing on the floor, drives me mad. Have you got kids?
Shazia: No.
Tracey A: Oh, okay.
Shazia: Just me and my husband. My mum's round the corner, I'm there most days.
Tracey A: Oh, that's nice, being close. I don't see my mum enough to be honest, since my dad passed. She's still in Basildon and with the A12 traffic it's a nightmare getting over there. I should go more. What's he do then, your husband?
Shazia: He drives a taxi.
Tracey A: Oh, he must have some stories, I bet! Late nights though.
Shazia: Fridays and Saturdays, yeah. He's out till three, four.
Tracey A: So what do you do with yourself evenings when he's out? Feet up, telly?
Shazia: Erm, I watch dramas. Pakistani ones on YouTube.
Tracey A: Oh, are they good? I'm the same with Netflix, all the true crime stuff. And The Traitors, did you watch The Traitors?
Shazia: No. I don't really watch English stuff. The dramas, they go on for ages, like forty episodes. There's one now with a mother-in-law who's horrible to the girl, honest, I shout at the screen.
Tracey A: Ha! Oh, I love that. That's me with Gogglebox. So you cook as well, I bet, proper home cooking?
Shazia: Yeah. Saalan, daal, chapatis. Every day nearly.
Tracey A: See, I'm rubbish at all that. I meal prep on a Sunday, chicken, rice, boxes in the fridge. Very boring. Then at the weekend I go out for an Italian and undo it all with Prosecco.
Shazia: Mine's not healthy. Imran likes it hot, lots of oil.
Tracey A: Well, it's what you enjoy, isn't it? Life's too short. Do you get out for walks with your back, or is that bad as well?
Shazia: Bit. To my mum's and the shop.
Tracey A: Even that's something, honestly, walking's the best thing you can do. I do Parkrun a couple of times a month, I did the London Marathon once, and I swear it's...

=== CALL C0216 ===
Callum: Hello, er, can you see me alright?
Joanne: Yeah. Yeah, I can.
Callum: Good stuff. I'm Callum. I'm in Taunton, down in Somerset.
Joanne: Joanne. St Helens.
Callum: St Helens, right. Rugby league, isn't it?
Joanne: Yeah. My husband's Saints mad. I'm not bothered, I just know the score.
Callum: Ha, fair. I'm a bit like that with the cricket. I go to the County Ground but I'm mostly there for the cider, you know.
Joanne: Yeah.
Callum: So, er, what do you do, Joanne?
Joanne: I'm not working at the minute. I look after me mum. She's got dementia, early stages, so it's sort of a full-time thing now.
Callum: Oh, sorry. That must be hard work.
Joanne: It is, yeah. I was in a warehouse eleven years, food packing in Haydock. I gave it up three years ago. She lives four streets away, so I'm back and forth all day. Tablets, appointments, ringing the surgery at eight o'clock to get through. You spend half your life on hold.
Callum: Is it like, they don't call you back sort of thing?
Joanne: They don't. Or they ring when I'm at hers and I can't answer. I'm blunt with them now. I weren't before, but you have to be.
Callum: Yeah, I bet. My mum'd be the same. Sorry, I'm not comparing, I just mean she'd be like a dog with a bone.
Joanne: No, it's alright. What do you do?
Callum: I'm a joiner. Windows, doors, repairs on old houses mostly. We're doing this big Victorian one at the minute, and when we took the panelling off, the original shutters were still in there, folded back into the walls. Nobody'd known for, like, a hundred years. Proper lovely they are, still work and everything. I was dead chuffed. Sorry, I'm going on.
Joanne: No, that's interesting. Me dad was at the glassworks. He liked old things like that.
Callum: Pilkington's?
Joanne: Yeah.
Callum: Oh nice. Old glass is lovely, the wavy stuff in sashes. We try and save it when we can. Is your dad still about?
Joanne: No, he died when I was thirty.
Callum: Ah. Sorry.
Joanne: It's alright. Long time ago now.
Callum: Yeah.
Joanne: Do you live on your own, then?
Callum: Er, no. Back at my mum and stepdad's, to be honest. Split up with my girlfriend a couple of years back, gave up the flat. Thirty and in my old bedroom. Not where I thought I'd be, but they're good about it. My stepdad's the one got me into wood, so I've taken half his garage over.
Joanne: Nowt wrong with that. Better than paying some landlord.
Callum: That's what my mum says. Meant to be saving. Going alright, sort of.
Joanne: I've never lived more than three mile from where I grew up, so I can't talk.
Callum: Do you get away at all?
Joanne: Not since me mum's diagnosis. We used to go to a caravan in Prestatyn. I worry something'll happen if I'm not there.
Callum: Yeah, that makes sense. Wales is nice though, I camp in Wales a fair bit. You'll get back there.
Joanne: Maybe. That puzzle at the start, did you finish it?
Callum: Not really, no. The shapes ones did my head in.
Joanne: Me too. I like a word search, me. That was something else.
Callum: Ha, yeah. Give me a set of drawings and I'm fine, but those little...

req.text:
You write transcripts of realistic video calls between strangers for a fully synthetic research dataset set in the UK. The study, in order (from its published design): a short puzzle task done alone; first impressions of the others' webcam photos; then a series of three-minute, one-on-one video calls in rounds, each person meeting the others in their group; after each call a short survey.

Call shape (from the original study's numbers): a call is cut off by a three-minute timer. A typical call has about 30 turns (most between 20 and 39) and about 570 words in total (most between 440 and 682); half of all turns are 12 words or fewer, and a quarter are 24 or more. Short acknowledgements ("yeah", "mm") count as turns too. So aim for about 570 words in about 30 turns: alongside the quick back-and-forth, people often talk in longer stretches (explaining their job, telling a story), and those long turns carry much of the call.

Guide to British conversational English (use it for how people talk; it is a description of speech, not a script):
How British people talk in casual conversation. This is a paraphrase of published descriptions of spoken British English; sources are in SOURCES.md. Use these features lightly and only where they fit the person. Never use them as a caricature.

- **Fillers.** British speakers hesitate with "erm" and "er". Women and younger speakers lean towards "erm".
- **Hedges.** "Sort of" is everywhere and steady. "Kind of" is spreading, and younger speakers use it more.
- **Politeness words.** "Please", "thank you", "thanks" and "sorry" mostly mean what they say. "Sorry" also works as a repair word (to correct yourself, or to ask someone to repeat) and can be ironic.
- **Tags at the end of a sentence.** "You know", "right", "okay", "yeah", "do you know what I mean". Among young Londoners, "innit" and "you get me" are rising. Tags depend on age and region only, never on ethnicity.
- **Echoing.** In an engaged conversation people pick up and re-use parts of each other's words.
- **Regional words and grammar** (from a recent dialect survey):
  - A bread roll is a "barm" in the North West (Manchester to Liverpool and western Lancashire), a "cob" around Nottinghamshire, a "bap" in Staffordshire, the West Midlands and North Wales, and a "batch" in Liverpool and Coventry.
  - Around Liverpool an ice lolly can be a "lolly ice".
  - The evening meal is "tea" in the North West, North East and Yorkshire, and "dinner" in the South East and London. Some people say both.
  - "Yous" or "youse" for plural "you" is common in the North East (Newcastle, Teesside), Liverpool and Scotland, less so in Manchester, and rare in York, Leeds and Sheffield.
  - "Give it me" is normal in the North West and West Midlands and widely accepted in Sheffield and York; it fades south of Birmingham, Coventry and Leicester.
  - "You was" is widely used, historically Northern and now found as far south as London.
- **Everyday British words** to draw on where they fit, without assigning them to regions: knackered or shattered, chuffed or made up, skint or brassic, mardy or stroppy, mum or mam, mate or pal, settee, sofa or couch.

The group (session S19). Persona cards, including the webcam photo each person was rated on:

P096 (Gareth; transcript label: Gareth):
- first name: Gareth
- age: 51
- lives in: Darwen, Lancashire, North West England
- occupation: Senior Countryside Ranger for a borough council's countryside and green spaces team. He supervises two rangers and a rota of volunteers, and looks after moorland paths, woodland, a reservoir walk and school visits.
- education detail: Left a Blackburn comprehensive at 16 with GCSEs, then did a National Diploma in Countryside Management at Myerscough College near Preston. In his thirties he did a part-time Foundation Degree in Environmental Conservation while working. He has also picked up chainsaw, first aid, brushcutter and outdoor-leader certificates along the way.
- household: Lives with his wife Helen, 50, a part-time practice manager at a GP surgery, in a three-bed stone-built semi on the edge of town. Their two children have moved out: Ellie, 24, teaches primary in Leeds, and Sam, 21, is in his last year at uni in Manchester. They have no pets since the old collie died two years ago, and they keep talking about getting another.
- cultural background: White British, born and raised in Blackburn. His dad was a fitter at a paper mill and his mum worked in a school kitchen. He was brought up Church of England and still goes to the parish church most months and at Christmas and Easter, more for the community and the hymns than out of strong doctrine. His family voted Labour, and he is quietly pragmatic about politics now. He has a strong sense of Lancashire mill-town identity but isn't precious about it.
- professional persona: Has worked for the council for 22 years and before that did seasonal estate work. He is good with the public and especially good with volunteers and school groups, and can get a quiet ten-year-old talking about newts. He is fair, doesn't take credit, and will own up when something's gone wrong. He is less keen on the paperwork side, with risk assessments and budget spreadsheets often done at the last minute. He is frustrated by funding cuts but tends to look for workarounds rather than moan.
- sports persona: A lifelong Blackburn Rovers fan who goes to a few home games a season with Sam when he can, and follows the rest on the radio. He walks constantly for work and fell-walks on weekends. He played Sunday league football until his early forties and now does the odd local fell race, finishing comfortably mid-pack. He watches cricket in the summer when Lancashire are on.
- arts persona: Sings tenor in a community choir that meets on Tuesday nights in a church hall, doing a mix of folk, gospel and the occasional pop arrangement. He listens to a lot of folk and Americana and gets to gigs in Manchester a few times a year. He reads widely, mostly nature writing, history and some crime novels. He takes decent photos of wildlife on an older DSLR and posts them on a local Facebook group.
- travel persona: Mostly UK holidays: the Lakes, Northumberland, the Scottish Highlands, and one memorable fortnight on Skye. Helen and he did a long-planned trip to Norway's fjords for their 25th anniversary. He likes trips with walking and a decent pub at the end. He is curious about Iceland and the Pyrenees and doesn't fancy beach resorts.
- culinary persona: Tea is the evening meal and is usually around six. He does most of the weekend cooking: big pans of chilli, curries, and a hotpot when it's cold. He is happy with a barm cake from the bakery for lunch on a work day. He likes trying new things when they eat out, enjoys real ale, drinks moderately and has a soft spot for Eccles cakes.
- hobbies and interests: choir singing (tenor), fell walking and the occasional fell race, wildlife photography, birdwatching, especially upland birds, following Blackburn Rovers, folk and Americana music, reading nature writing and local history, pub quizzes with mates
- skills: leading groups outdoors and managing volunteers, dry-stone walling and path repair, chainsaw and brushcutter use (certified), first aid, identifying birds by song, talking to all sorts of people and calming tense situations, basic carpentry, cooking for a crowd
- career goals: No big ambitions to move up into management because he'd hate being stuck at a desk. He'd like to keep the ranger service funded until he retires, maybe push through a long-talked-about woodland restoration project, and train up the younger rangers properly. He sometimes thinks about part-time work with a wildlife trust after 60.
- voice: Warm, friendly and relaxed, with a moderate Lancashire accent: flat vowels and the odd dropped 'h', but easy to follow. He talks at a steady pace and speeds up when he's enthusiastic about something like birds or the choir. He uses 'erm' and 'er' a fair bit, and 'sort of' when he's working out a thought. He ends sentences with 'you know' or 'do you know what I mean' now and then. Regional bits come out naturally: 'tea' for the evening meal, 'barm', 'give it me', and occasionally 'mate' or 'pal' with people he's warmed to. He's happy to sit through a short silence, and sometimes he fills it with a light joke or asks the other person a question back.
- typing: Quick and practical. He usually starts with a capital but sometimes forgets, uses full stops loosely, and gets apostrophes mostly right but drops them in a hurry ('dont', 'its'). He uses the odd 'tbh' or 'etc' and writes short, plain answers. He might add a friendly 'cheers' or a smiley if there's a comment box.
- with strangers: Comes across as open, approachable and genuinely interested. He asks follow-up questions, laughs easily and puts people at ease quickly. He is modest about himself and quick to praise others. He's not guarded, though he moves on from anything too personal with a joke rather than a refusal.
- small things: saw a pair of stonechats on the moor this morning, the car park at work's been flooded again, choir's doing a Christmas concert in the church hall, Rovers were rubbish on Saturday, Helen's got him doing Wordle every morning, had a barm from the bakery near the depot for lunch, trying to talk Helen into another dog, son's coming home for Sunday dinner at the weekend
- deeper things: his dad died of mesothelioma linked to the mill, and it's part of why he cares about outdoor work and health, he misses having the kids at home more than he lets on, he worries his job might be cut in the next round of council savings, his faith is quieter now, but he finds singing in church grounding, he once talked a distressed man down near the reservoir, still thinks about it, and doesn't tell many people
- webcam photo: Head-and-shoulders shot from a laptop on a dining table, with the camera angled slightly upward. Soft daylight comes from a window to his left, so the right side of his face is a little shadowed. He is a broad-faced man with a weathered, ruddy complexion, short greying brown hair cropped close at the sides, a neat salt-and-pepper beard and crow's feet. He has a relaxed, warm half-smile and is looking just off-camera. He wears no glasses and has on a dark green fleece zipped halfway over a grey t-shirt. Behind him is a magnolia wall with a framed photo of a moorland landscape and a stone tower on the skyline, and part of a pine bookcase with paperbacks, a pair of binoculars and a small potted plant. In the corner of the frame a radiator has a pair of walking socks drying on it.

P097 (Harriet; transcript label: Harriet):
- first name: Harriet
- age: 21
- lives in: Walthamstow, London
- occupation: Full-time undergraduate student (final year, BA History at Queen Mary University of London)
- education detail: A levels in History, English Literature and Biology (A, A, B) from a state comprehensive in St Albans. Now in the third year of a BA in History at Queen Mary, writing a dissertation on women's lodging houses in Victorian East London. She is behind on the dissertation and has already had one extension.
- household: Rents a one-bedroom flat above a nail bar off Hoe Street with her boyfriend, Callum (24), a junior data analyst at an insurance firm in the City. They've been together almost three years and moved in together last September. Callum pays the larger share of the rent and her parents top up her side. They're not engaged, and she gets a bit awkward when relatives ask.
- cultural background: White British, born in Watford and raised in St Albans. Her dad is a chartered surveyor and her mum is a deputy head at a primary school. She was brought up Church of England: Sunday school, confirmed at 13, and the youth group was a big part of her early teens. She still calls herself Christian and means it quietly. She prays now and then, goes to the parish church with her parents at Christmas and Easter, and has been meaning to find a church in Walthamstow for over a year without getting round to it. Comfortably middle-class, and fairly aware of it.
- professional persona: Works one or two shifts a week at a secondhand bookshop in Walthamstow Village for pocket money. Customers like her because she'll tell them straight that a book isn't worth the price. At uni she's bright but disorganised: a good seminar contributor when she's done the reading, which is about half the time. She doesn't network and finds it slightly embarrassing when people do.
- sports persona: Not sporty. She walks a lot, round Lloyd Park and along the Walthamstow Wetlands, and did a term of uni netball in first year before drifting off. She'll watch the Women's Euros or Wimbledon if they're on, but doesn't follow anything week to week.
- arts persona: Reads constantly but chaotically, usually three novels on the go, a lot of them from the shop. She likes Sarah Waters and Elizabeth Strout. She goes to the William Morris Gallery because it's round the corner, and to cheap matinees at the Barbican with a uni friend. Music-wise she listens to whatever's on her Release Radar, plus a lot of Phoebe Bridgers when she's revising. She doesn't make art herself.
- travel persona: Family holidays in Cornwall and a few trips to France and Spain growing up. She did a week in Lisbon with Callum last summer and loved it. She's never been further than Europe and isn't desperate to. She'd rather go somewhere slowly than tick places off.
- culinary persona: Callum does most of the proper cooking. Her repertoire is pasta bakes, a decent dhal and toast with things on it. She calls the evening meal dinner. She has a weakness for the Turkish bakeries on the high street and the market, and she'll happily eat cereal for dinner when he's out. She's vaguely trying to eat less meat for money and ethics reasons, but isn't strict about it.
- hobbies and interests: Reading novels, especially historical fiction, Walking round the Wetlands and Epping Forest edges, Charity shop browsing, Cryptic crosswords with Callum (badly), Local history of East London, Watching Great British Bake Off and old episodes of Gilmore Girls
- skills: Archival research and close reading of primary sources, Clear, plain essay writing (when she actually starts), Patient with customers and older people, Basic French, Good at finding cheap books and things secondhand
- career goals: Honestly unsure. She has half an idea about archives or museum work, maybe a master's in archive and records management, but she hasn't looked at application deadlines yet. Teaching gets suggested by her mum a lot and she's not ruled it out. She cares more about doing something useful and not hateful than about money or status.
- voice: Soft, southern, middle-class English with a slight London flattening she's picked up since moving. She speaks quite quietly and fairly slowly, and starts answers with "erm" and "I mean". She hedges a lot with "sort of" and "kind of" and "I don't know, like…", and will say "sorry, what was the question?" if she's drifted. She doesn't really use "innit"; sometimes she tags with "yeah" or "if that makes sense". When there's a silence she won't rush to fill it, which can feel slightly awkward. Then she'll give a very direct, honest answer, sometimes more candid than expected, like "no, I haven't actually done that, I just said I would."
- typing: Mostly lowercase, quick and a bit sloppy. Apostrophes are usually there, but she sometimes misses capital letters for names. She uses commas more than full stops and rarely finishes with a full stop. Occasional "tbh", "idk" and "ngl". Answers are short unless the question is about something she cares about, then they run on.
- with strangers: Reserved and a little shy at first. She's polite, says sorry and thank you a lot, and doesn't push herself forward. She comes across as genuine and unshowy. She won't exaggerate or try to impress, and she'll admit not knowing things. She warms up gradually, especially if the conversation turns to books, history or where she lives.
- small things: Her dissertation is due in May and she's 'about a third of the way through, maybe less', The nail bar downstairs makes the stairwell smell of acetone, She found a first edition of a Barbara Pym novel at the shop for £2, The Victoria line being down again, Callum's sourdough starter, which he's named, She keeps meaning to get a library card for Walthamstow library
- deeper things: She feels guilty that her parents still help with rent while she's not working very hard at uni, Her faith matters to her more than she lets on to uni friends, and she misses having a church community, She sometimes wonders if she moved in with Callum too young, though she's happy, She struggles to start work and suspects it might be more than laziness, but hasn't spoken to anyone about it, Her grandmother, who she was close to, died in her second year, and that's partly why she fell behind
- webcam photo: Laptop webcam shot, slightly below eye level so the frame tilts up a little, taken in the evening under a warm overhead bulb with a cooler glow from the screen on her face. She's centred, framed from mid-chest up, sitting at a small wooden table. Pale skin with some redness on her cheeks, a light scattering of freckles, no visible make-up. Light brown hair, shoulder length, pushed behind her ears and a bit flat on top. She wears round tortoiseshell glasses and a slightly polite, half-smile with her eyes looking just off-camera at the screen. She has on an oversized dark green knitted jumper with the sleeves pulled over her hands. Behind her is a magnolia wall with a cheap white IKEA bookcase crammed with paperbacks stacked both upright and sideways, a mug of pens on one shelf and a small trailing pothos. To the right, part of a radiator with a tea towel draped over it, and the corner of a window with a grey blind half-down. A tote bag hangs off the back of a door in the far left of the frame.

Bright daylight from patio doors to her right lights that side of her face; the other side is a little shadowed. She has a light tan, neatly shaped dark brows and light makeup, and gives a polite closed-mouth smile. Her shoulder-length hair is highlighted honey blonde, straightened, and tucked behind one ear. She wears a fitted navy V-neck knit jumper and small gold hoop earrings. No glasses. Behind her are glossy grey handleless kitchen units, a white quartz worktop with a chrome boiling-water tap, a pampas grass arrangement in a tall white vase, a canvas print reading 'Home' in gold script, and the edge of a dog bed with a beige cockapoo curled in it on the floor near the patio doors.

- age: 27
- lives in: Chelmsford, East of England
- occupation: General manager of a cocktail bar and small-plates restaurant in Chelmsford city centre, part of a regional hospitality group with five sites across Essex and Hertfordshire. - skills: reading a room and handling difficult customers, motivating and keeping hold of young staff, cocktail making, event planning and selling private hire, networking with suppliers and reps, talking her way into upgrades or a better table, social media marketing for the venue

She sometimes daydreams about opening her own bar with a friend, although she knows she'd need someone else to do the money side. She'd like to be seen as one of the rising names in the group and have a bit of a profile locally.
- voice: Fast, bright and chatty, with a mild Essex/South East accent: some glottal stops, 'innit' very occasionally and only jokingly, and 'like' and 'literally' used a lot. She doesn't sit in silence well and will fill a pause with a story or a joke, sometimes answering a slightly different question than the one asked. She says 'sorry, what was that?' if the line drops, and uses an ironic 'sorry' when she's mid-rant.

She uses 'lol', 'tbh', 'x' out of habit even in forms, and 'sooo' with extra letters. Commas are sparse, she ends with no full stop or with '!!', and she makes the odd autocorrect slip she doesn't fix.
- with strangers: Instantly friendly and makes you feel like you've known her for ages. She asks you questions back, compliments you, and finds something in common within a minute. She is a bit of a performer and likes to come across as successful and fun, so she'll mention being a GM fairly early. - cultural background: White British, born and raised in Exeter, and her parents are both from Devon. She is Church of England and goes to the family's local parish church most Sundays. - arts persona: Not hugely into galleries or anything experimental. She loves big West End musicals and has seen Wicked twice, once in London and once on tour at Plymouth. She watches Strictly and Bake Off with her mum every series. She sang in the school choir and occasionally joins the church choir at Christmas and Easter. She mostly listens to pop and her musicals playlist.
- travel persona: Prefers familiar places done well. Growing up there were family holidays to Cornwall (St Ives, Padstow) every year, and a fortnight in Menorca most summers. She makes the same three or four dinners on rotation when it's her turn: spaghetti bolognese, chicken fajitas, a tuna pasta bake. - hobbies and interests: Netball (club team), Running along the estuary trail, Walking the dog on Dartmoor at weekends, Musicals, Strictly Come Dancing and Bake Off, Helping with the church children's group, Planning and stationery (bullet journal), Pub quizzes with friends
- skills: Lesson planning and classroom organisation, Managing groups of young children, Safeguarding awareness (trained through church and PGCE), Netball coaching basics (Level 1 coaching certificate), Time management, Customer service from café work, Confident with spreadsheets and Google Classroom
- career goals: To get an Early Career Teacher post in a Devon primary school for September, ideally Key Stage 1 and ideally within half an hour of home. Longer term she'd like to become a phase leader or SENCo, stay in the area, buy a house nearby and keep playing netball. She has no plans to move to London.

Fillers are mostly 'erm', and she hedges with 'sort of' and, a bit more often, 'kind of'. She uses tags like 'yeah' and 'do you know what I mean?'. She says 'sorry' a lot, both genuinely and as a repair ('sorry, I mean the Year 2 class'). She'll use words like 'knackered' and 'chuffed'. She can't really sit in silence. If there's a pause she'll fill it with 'erm, does that answer it?' or add an example. She tends to echo the interviewer's words back when thinking ('what would I do differently... erm').

She's very straightforward and doesn't exaggerate or show off. If she doesn't know something or has no strong view, she says so. Shoulder-length dark blonde hair is pulled back in a loose ponytail with a few strands falling at the front. No glasses. - first name: Karim
- age: 45
- lives in: Hall Green, Birmingham, West Midlands

- education detail: Moved to Birmingham from Basra, Iraq, aged 14. Did GCSEs and A-levels at a comprehensive and sixth form in Sparkhill. - cultural background: Iraqi Arab, born in Basra. The family left in the early 1990s and arrived in Birmingham via Jordan in 1994. He is a practising Muslim in a relaxed, personal way. He goes to Friday prayers when work allows, fasts in Ramadan and doesn't drink. He is curious about other faiths and philosophies and happily argues about them. He speaks Iraqi Arabic at home with his mum and mostly English with his kids, who reply to her Arabic in English. He considers himself a Brummie first when abroad and an Iraqi first when someone in Birmingham asks where he's 'really' from.
- professional persona: The ideas person in a company run by two cautious brothers who own it. He's good at spotting what's coming next, like a Turkish snack brand before it took off, or selling to the new dessert cafés and student areas, and at charming buyers. He's poor at the follow-through. His inbox runs into the thousands, he signs off documents he's skimmed, and he relies heavily on his operations manager, Bev, to chase the detail. He works 50 to 55 hours a week, often on the phone in the car between suppliers. Nothing seems to rattle him, whether it's a lorry stuck at Dover or a big client walking, and junior staff find that reassuring. The owners sometimes find it worrying.
- sports persona: Follows Aston Villa, and has done since a schoolmate dragged him to Villa Park in 1995. He gets to a few home games a season when he can get a ticket off his cousin. He plays five-a-side on Tuesday nights in a works league when he remembers his trainers, and he's not very good. He watches the odd bit of cricket because his son got into it.
- arts persona: A very wide, unsystematic appetite. He reads translated fiction, history and popular science, often three books on the go and none finished quickly. He loves old Iraqi maqam recordings and also Jazz, and goes to Symphony Hall a couple of times a year, sometimes on his own. He likes Brutalist buildings and is still annoyed they knocked down the old Central Library. He takes street photography on his phone around Digbeth and posts it to an Instagram account with about 200 followers.
- travel persona: Restless and curious rather than organised. He'll book a long weekend in Lisbon or Istanbul with a week's notice and work it out when he gets there. Family summers are usually Dina's planning, often Turkey or visiting her relatives in Amman. He went back to Basra once, in 2019, and found it both familiar and completely strange. He wants to do Japan before he's fifty.
- culinary persona: Dina is the better everyday cook. He does weekend projects, like slow lamb, his mum's dolma (badly, according to his mum) and attempts at sourdough that have mostly failed. Work gives him early access to new products, so he brings random jars home for the family to test. He eats a lot of bacon-less breakfast baps from the café near the warehouse. He likes trying the new places on the Ladypool Road and in Digbeth, and he calls it 'tea' or 'dinner' depending on who he's talking to.
- hobbies and interests: Phone street photography, mostly of buildings and markets, Reading history and translated novels, Old Arabic music and jazz records, Five-a-side football, inconsistently, Watching Aston Villa, Podcasts on philosophy and economics during long drives, Pottering at food markets and new restaurants
- skills: Negotiating with suppliers and buyers in English and Arabic, Spotting food trends early, Staying calm in a crisis, Building rapport quickly with almost anyone, Pitching ideas to sceptical bosses, Fluent Iraqi Arabic, decent Levantine Arabic, Basic photo editing on his phone
- career goals: Half-serious about starting his own business, maybe a small import brand or a café-deli, within the next five years. He knows he'd need a business partner who loves spreadsheets. In the meantime he'd like a minority stake in the current company, which he's hinted at but never formally asked for.
- voice: Birmingham accent, softened, with a slight Arabic rhythm on some vowels and on names and food words. Relaxed, medium-fast, conversational, and he goes off on tangents. He says 'sort of' and 'you know' a lot, and the odd 'er' when he's thinking. He calls people 'mate' fairly freely. Regional bits come out naturally, like 'give it me' and 'bap', but nothing heavy. He uses 'to be honest' as a lead-in. He doesn't mind silence at all. He'll just say 'hang on, let me think about that' and take his time, or fill it with a joke if the other person seems uncomfortable. He laughs easily, including at himself.
- typing: Fast and sloppy. Mostly lowercase, with a capital only if autocorrect does it. Apostrophes are often missing ('dont', 'im'). He uses commas instead of full stops, a lot of 'tbh' and 'etc', and occasionally a typo he doesn't bother fixing. Answers are short unless the topic interests him, and then he writes a paragraph with no line breaks.
- with strangers: Warm, chatty and quickly informal. He asks the other person questions back and gets curious about the study itself. He's comfortable sharing opinions, a bit too willing to wander off topic, and unbothered by awkward or personal questions. He comes across as easygoing and confident, occasionally a bit scattered, like he's taking the call between two other things, which he often is.
- small things: He's late for most things and blames the M5, His car is full of product samples, Villa's latest result, Whatever book he's halfway through, His daughter teaching him TikTok, The café near the warehouse does the best egg bap in Smethwick, He keeps meaning to paint the hallway, He got a parking ticket last week for forgetting to pay, His five-a-side team lost again
- deeper things: Memories of leaving Basra as a boy and the year in Amman before Birmingham, His dad died in 2016 and he wishes he'd asked him more about his life, Feeling slightly between two places, never fully Iraqi or fully English, He knows his disorganisation has cost him promotions, and Dina carries a lot of the household admin, He worries a little that his kids won't keep their Arabic, His faith matters to him more privately than people assume, His quiet frustration at being 'the ideas guy' in someone else's business
- webcam photo: Laptop webcam, slightly below eye level, so the angle looks up a little. Evening light from a warm desk lamp on the left and the cool glow of the screen on his face. A man in his mid-forties with light olive-brown skin and short dark hair greying at the temples and thinning a bit at the crown. He has a neatly trimmed short beard with grey flecks and rectangular black-framed reading glasses pushed slightly down his nose. He is half-smiling with eyebrows raised, as if mid-sentence. He wears a navy quarter-zip jumper over a white collared shirt, open at the neck. Behind him is a small spare-room office: a white IKEA bookcase crammed with paperbacks stacked both upright and sideways, a framed black-and-white photo of an old Basra street, a cardboard box of product samples on the floor with Arabic and Turkish labels visible, a folded prayer mat on the top shelf, and a Villa scarf hung over the corner of the door. The magnolia wall has a patch of unfinished paint testers on it.

req.text:
You write transcripts of realistic video calls between strangers for a fully synthetic research dataset set in the UK. The study, in order (from its published design): a short puzzle task done alone; first impressions of the others' webcam photos; then a series of three-minute, one-on-one video calls in rounds, each person meeting the others in their group; after each call a short survey.

Call shape (from the original study's numbers): a call is cut off by a three-minute timer. A typical call has about 30 turns (most between 20 and 39) and about 570 words in total (most between 440 and 682); half of all turns are 12 words or fewer, and a quarter are 24 or more. Short acknowledgements ("yeah", "mm") count as turns too. So aim for about 570 words in about 30 turns: alongside the quick back-and-forth, people often talk in longer stretches (explaining their job, telling a story), and those long turns carry much of the call.

Guide to British conversational English (use it for how people talk; it is a description of speech, not a script):
How British people talk in casual conversation. This is a paraphrase of published descriptions of spoken British English; sources are in SOURCES.md. Use these features lightly and only where they fit the person. Never use them as a caricature.

- **Fillers.** British speakers hesitate with "erm" and "er". Women and younger speakers lean towards "erm".
- **Hedges.** "Sort of" is everywhere and steady. "Kind of" is spreading, and younger speakers use it more.
- **Politeness words.** "Please", "thank you", "thanks" and "sorry" mostly mean what they say. "Sorry" also works as a repair word (to correct yourself, or to ask someone to repeat) and can be ironic.
- **Tags at the end of a sentence.** "You know", "right", "okay", "yeah", "do you know what I mean". Among young Londoners, "innit" and "you get me" are rising. Tags depend on age and region only, never on ethnicity.
- **Echoing.** In an engaged conversation people pick up and re-use parts of each other's words.
- **Regional words and grammar** (from a recent dialect survey):
  - A bread roll is a "barm" in the North West (Manchester to Liverpool and western Lancashire), a "cob" around Nottinghamshire, a "bap" in Staffordshire, the West Midlands and North Wales, and a "batch" in Liverpool and Coventry.
  - Around Liverpool an ice lolly can be a "lolly ice".
  - The evening meal is "tea" in the North West, North East and Yorkshire, and "dinner" in the South East and London. Some people say both.
  - "Yous" or "youse" for plural "you" is common in the North East (Newcastle, Teesside), Liverpool and Scotland, less so in Manchester, and rare in York, Leeds and Sheffield.
  - "Give it me" is normal in the North West and West Midlands and widely accepted in Sheffield and York; it fades south of Birmingham, Coventry and Leicester.
  - "You was" is widely used, historically Northern and now found as far south as London.
- **Everyday British words** to draw on where they fit, without assigning them to regions: knackered or shattered, chuffed or made up, skint or brassic, mardy or stroppy, mum or mam, mate or pal, settee, sofa or couch.

The group (session S21). Persona cards, including the webcam photo each person was rated on:

P108 (Gemma; transcript label: Gemma):
- first name: Gemma
- age: 36
- lives in: Beeston, Nottinghamshire, East Midlands
- occupation: Pharmacy technician (part-time, about 24 hours a week over three days) in the dispensary at a large NHS hospital in Nottingham. She checks prescriptions, does medicines reconciliation on the wards and trains new starters.
- education detail: GCSEs and A-levels in Biology, Chemistry and English at a sixth form in Long Eaton. She started a Biomedical Science degree at Sheffield Hallam and left after the first year. Later she did a BTEC/NVQ Level 3 in Pharmaceutical Science through work and became a GPhC-registered pharmacy technician at 27. She has since done an accredited checking technician course.
- household: Semi-detached three-bed house in Beeston, which she shares with her husband Rob (38, a quantity surveyor for a regional construction firm) and their daughter Isla (6, Year 2 at the local primary). Her mum lives ten minutes away in Chilwell and does two school pick-ups a week.
- cultural background: White British, born and raised in the Nottingham area to a family that worked in local factories and offices. Her dad was a Raleigh fitter before it moved and later drove for a brewery. She was brought up Methodist and still goes to a Methodist church in Beeston most Sundays, where she sings with the music group and helps on the toddler group rota. Her faith is warm and practical rather than preachy. She is very much a Nottingham person: she supports Forest loosely because her dad did, and she says 'cob' without thinking about it.
- professional persona: Meticulous and calm at the bench, chatty everywhere else. She is known for colour-coded checklists and for spotting the dosing error everyone else missed. Ward nurses like her because she explains things without making them feel stupid. She gets visibly upset when something nearly goes wrong, then writes it up properly and wants the process fixed. Newer techs come to her first.
- sports persona: She plays in a back-to-netball group on Wednesday evenings and has a loud on-court voice. She does the occasional parkrun at Highfields, mostly for the social side. She watches Forest on the telly with Rob but gets more nervous than he does and sometimes leaves the room.
- arts persona: She has sung since school and now sings in the church music group and a community choir that does pop arrangements. She goes to musicals at the Theatre Royal whenever she can get a deal and cries at all of them. She has recently got into pottery night classes and has a shelf of slightly wonky mugs.
- travel persona: She prefers UK breaks: a cottage in the Peak District, Norfolk caravan weeks with her mum, and Center Parcs with friends. She plans everything on a shared spreadsheet. Before Isla she went on a couple of trips to Spain and a girls' weekend in Amsterdam. She would love to do Italy properly one day.
- culinary persona: A confident home cook who batch cooks on Sundays and labels everything in the freezer. Tea in their house is usually something like a chicken traybake, a veggie chilli or pasta bake. She bakes a lot for church and work, especially lemon drizzle and millionaire's shortbread. She is trying to eat less meat after a documentary got to her.
- hobbies and interests: community choir and church music group, back-to-netball, pottery classes, baking for church coffee mornings, musical theatre, true-crime and medical podcasts, organising the school PTA tombola, growing tomatoes and herbs in the back garden
- skills: accuracy checking of dispensed medicines, training and mentoring junior staff, explaining medical stuff in plain English, organising events and rotas, singing (alto), baking, keeping a group chat going
- career goals: She wants to move up to a Band 5 or 6 lead technician role in medicines optimisation, ideally still part-time while Isla is at primary school. She has thought about going back to do a pharmacist degree but worries about the cost and time. She would like to do more training and education work.
- voice: Bright, fast and warm, with a fairly light Nottingham accent: flat vowels and 'me' for 'my' sometimes. She will occasionally say 'duck' to someone she has warmed to, and words like 'mardy' and 'cob' slip in naturally. She uses 'erm' a lot when she is thinking and says 'sort of' constantly. She tags with 'do you know what I mean?' and 'yeah'. She laughs easily, often at herself. She uses 'sorry' to backtrack ('it was Tuesday, sorry, Wednesday'). She is uncomfortable with silence and will fill it with a little explanation or a joke, then apologise for rambling.
- typing: Proper capitals and full stops almost always, and apostrophes correct because it bothers her when they aren't. She sometimes uses exclamation marks to sound friendly ('Yes happy to!'). Abbreviations are minimal: maybe 'etc' or 'approx'. She occasionally adds a short extra sentence of context nobody asked for.

She is a bit anxious about doing it right, so she checks whether she has understood the question. She is warm but not pushy, and very polite.
- small things: the school run and Isla's latest obsession (currently dinosaurs and loom bands), Rob's terrible attempts at DIY, the tram works and traffic on the A52, a lemon drizzle that sank in the middle, being knackered after a long dispensary shift, choir learning a new song for a summer concert, a bargain at the Beeston market, her mum's dog, a mardy old Jack Russell called Pip

She has a round, friendly face, a light smattering of freckles and minimal makeup, and she is smiling widely with her mouth slightly open as if mid-word. Her shoulder-length mid-brown hair is pulled back in a loose clip, with a few strands falling at the front. She wears a navy cardigan over a striped Breton top, with a small silver cross on a fine chain visible at her neck. No glasses. Behind her are white kitchen wall units, a fridge covered in children's drawings and a school letter held by magnets, a wall calendar with handwritten entries, and a wonky glazed mug holding pens on the worktop. A folded tea towel hangs on the oven door.

- first name: Karen

Meal planning has never worked for her, so she's often in Tesco at half six working out what to make.

- voice: Warm, chatty and informal, with a light southern English accent from the Hampshire commuter belt. Mostly standard grammar, with the odd 'you was' slipping in. She talks at a moderate-to-quick pace and wanders off topic, then catches herself: 'sorry, where was I?' She uses 'erm' a fair bit, 'sort of' and 'to be honest' a lot, and ends sentences with 'you know' or 'yeah'. She says 'knackered', 'shattered' and 'mate'. She laughs easily, including at herself. If there's a silence she fills it, usually with a small apology or a 'that's probably not what you wanted, is it?'

She has a round, friendly face, light freckles, a little mascara and no other obvious make-up. She has a broad, slightly sheepish smile, as if she's just said 'can you see me okay?'. Her shoulder-length dark blonde hair has visible darker roots and is pulled back in a loose clip with a few strands falling forward. No glasses. She's wearing a navy cardigan over a pale grey T-shirt, with a lanyard from work still around her neck and the badge turned the wrong way. Behind her is a small kitchen with cream units. On the worktop sit a kettle, a stack of unopened post, a fruit bowl holding two bananas and a phone charger, and a pile of school letters. A fridge on the right is covered in magnets, a Callum school photo and a takeaway menu. A ginger cat's tail is just visible on a chair in the bottom corner.

- age: 21
- lives in: Sunderland, North East England

Might add a slightly sarcastic aside in brackets.

Not especially warm or reassuring, and can be blunt or mildly sarcastic if a question seems pointless. Opens up noticeably if the conversation touches on something creative or strange, and then can be surprisingly thoughtful and articulate. Likely to quietly judge the other person's taste.
- small things: her bus to work being late again, a new fineliner pen she's obsessed with, a horror film she watched last night that was 'actually dead good', Kayla nicking her hoodies, selling a jacket on Vinted for three times what she paid, the office printer jamming, being knackered after a day of phone calls, the sea looking nice at Roker, her nana's cat

Pale skin with some redness on her cheeks and a couple of spots on her chin. Neutral, slightly wary expression with lips closed, looking just above the camera. Dark brown hair dyed black at the ends, shoulder length, scraped back into a loose claw clip with strands falling forward. Thin black eyeliner, small silver hoop in each ear and a tiny stud in her left nostril. No glasses. Wearing an oversized faded grey hoodie with a small cartoon moth print. Behind her is a pale lilac wall with pinned-up ink drawings and postcards, a slightly peeling poster for a horror film, the fairy lights draped over a wonky shelf holding manga volumes, a jar of pens and a ceramic skull ornament. - occupation: Senior care assistant at a 48-bed residential care home for older people, working full-time (about 40 hours a week across a rota of long days, including some weekends)

She makes pierogi in big batches for the freezer, along with gołąbki and a proper Sunday rosół, but she does roast dinners too and is proud of her Yorkshire puddings. She shops at Aldi and the Polish shop in town. She bakes for colleagues' birthdays and brings in cakes for the residents' tea afternoons.
- hobbies and interests: Daily dog walks around Ninesprings and Yeovil Country Park, Thursday Zumba class with work friends, Batch cooking and baking, especially Polish recipes from her mum, Video calls with her mum and sister, Helping with the church's coffee mornings when she's off, Growing tomatoes and herbs in pots on the patio, Watching Strictly and Bake Off with Mark
- skills: Personal care and moving and handling, Medication administration and record-keeping, Supporting people living with dementia, Calming anxious relatives, Mentoring new care staff, Bilingual in Polish and English, sometimes interpreting informally for Polish families, Cooking for large groups, Planning and organising rotas and events
- career goals: She is thinking about applying for a deputy or team leader role at the home, or training as a nursing associate if she can get funding and fit the study around shifts. She is slightly nervous about the academic writing part, but her manager keeps encouraging her. Either way, she wants to stay in care work with older people.
- voice: Fluent, quick and friendly, with a clear Polish accent that has softened over the years. She occasionally drops 'the' or 'a', or puts a word in an unusual order when she's speaking fast, but she's easy to follow. Her English has picked up a lot from colleagues and from Mark: 'knackered', 'chuffed', 'sort of', 'bless him', 'you know'. She uses 'erm' when searching for a word, and once in a while says something in Polish under her breath, laughs, and translates it. She talks with her hands and laughs a lot. She tends to fill silences herself, often by asking the other person a question back or saying 'sorry, I talk too much, yeah?' She is polite and says thank you often.
- typing: Types properly with capitals and full stops most of the time, because she is used to writing care notes. Apostrophes are usually right, though she sometimes misses one in a hurry ('dont', 'its'). She rarely uses abbreviations beyond 'ok' and 'etc'. She occasionally adds a smiley ':)' even in a form. Now and then there is a small article slip or a Polish-style word order, for example 'I am working in care home 12 years'.
- with strangers: Instantly warm and chatty. She makes people feel at ease and asks about them as much as she talks about herself. She's open and honest, doesn't show off, and will happily admit when she doesn't know something. Underneath the sociable surface she can be a bit anxious about doing things 'right', so she might ask whether her answer was what you wanted.
- small things: Biscuit refusing to walk in the rain, Being knackered after three long days in a row, A resident who calls her 'Agnes' and sings to her, The price of the weekly shop at Aldi, Making pierogi with her mum over video call, Zumba being 'more laughing than dancing', Mark being useless with the washing machine settings, Traffic on the A303 when they go anywhere, The Polish shop running out of good bread
- deeper things: She and Mark tried for children for several years and it didn't happen. They've mostly made peace with it, but it still hurts sometimes, especially at family events back home., She worries about her mum getting older in Poland while she looks after other people's parents in England., She felt unsettled and less welcome after the Brexit vote, even though she had already been here years. Applying for settled status made her anxious., Losing residents she has cared for a long time affects her more than she shows at work., Her faith helps her a lot. She prays for residents and lights candles for them at church., She sometimes feels between two places: too English for her old friends in Poland, still 'the Polish one' here.

Daylight comes from a window to her left, so the left side of her face is brighter, and a ceiling light adds a warm tone. She has a round, open face with light skin, rosy cheeks and a few faint lines at the corners of her eyes. She is mid-smile with her eyebrows slightly raised, as if she has just said hello. Shoulder-length dark blonde hair is pulled back in a loose ponytail, with a few strands loose around her face. She wears no glasses, small gold stud earrings and a thin gold chain with a small cross. Her clothing is a navy zip-up fleece over a plain grey T-shirt. Behind her is a fitted kitchen with white cupboards and a grey worktop, a kettle and a toaster, a wooden utensil pot, a fridge-freezer with a few magnets, a calendar and a printed shift rota held up on it, and a small potted basil plant on the windowsill. P112 (Ioana; transcript label: Ioana):
- first name: Ioana
- age: 25
- lives in: Burnt Oak, North West London (London Borough of Barnet)
- occupation: Lettings and property administrator at an independent estate agency in Edgware, full-time, Monday to Friday plus one Saturday a month, about 40 hours a week
- education detail: Came to London from Romania at 11. Did GCSEs and A-levels (Business, Maths, Romanian) at a comprehensive in Barnet. Started a Business Management degree at Middlesex University but left after the first year because she disliked the group work and was paying for it herself. Currently working through an AAT Level 3 accounting qualification in the evenings, paid for partly by her employer.
- household: Rents a one-bedroom flat above a shop on Burnt Oak Broadway with her boyfriend of four years, Liam (27, English, from Enfield), who works as an electrician's mate. Not married and no plans to rush it. Her mum, stepdad and younger brother live a 15-minute bus ride away in Colindale.
- cultural background: Born in Cluj-Napoca, Romania. Her mum moved to London first for cleaning and care work, and Ioana and her brother followed when she was 11. She grew up bilingual. She speaks Romanian with family and English everywhere else, and her English is now essentially North London. She was raised Romanian Orthodox and still calls herself Christian. She goes to church at Easter and Christmas and sometimes for a family memorial service, mostly for her mum's sake, though she does find the Easter midnight service moving. She has dual citizenship and goes back to Cluj every year or two to see her grandmother.
- professional persona: The person in the office who actually knows where everything is. She handles tenancy agreements, deposit registrations, gas safety certificate reminders, referencing and landlord statements. She is careful and fast, and she gets irritated when negotiators promise tenants things without checking. She doesn't do the office chat much and eats lunch at her desk with headphones in. Her manager trusts her completely with compliance deadlines but has twice had to tell her to 'soften' her emails to landlords.
- sports persona: Not sporty. She walks a lot, usually around Stanmore Common or Mill Hill at weekends, partly for her head. She tried a gym membership and cancelled it after three months because the place was too crowded and loud. She half-watches football when Liam has Spurs on but doesn't care who wins.
- arts persona: Reads crime and psychological thrillers on her Kindle on the bus. Watches Scandinavian and British detective series, usually on her own because Liam talks through them. Doesn't go to galleries or gigs much, as crowds wear her out, though she went to the Sky Garden and the Tate Modern when her cousin visited. She likes making neat, slightly obsessive photo albums on her phone.
- travel persona: Mostly trips back to Romania, flying Wizz Air from Luton, with a week at her grandmother's and a couple of days in Cluj with old school friends. She and Liam did a cheap week in Crete last year. She plans trips months ahead with a spreadsheet and gets anxious at airports, so she arrives very early.
- culinary persona: Cooks most evenings because she doesn't trust Liam with anything beyond pasta. She makes a mix of Romanian food her mum taught her (ciorbă, sarmale at Christmas, mămăligă) and normal London weeknight dinners like stir fries and fajitas. She does a weekly Lidl shop with a list and meal plans on a Sunday. She has a sensitive stomach, so she avoids very spicy food and too much coffee.
- hobbies and interests: true crime podcasts, crime and thriller novels, long weekend walks on Stanmore Common, organising and budgeting apps, jigsaw puzzles (1000-piece, done on a board on the coffee table), keeping houseplants alive, detective dramas
- skills: fluent in Romanian and English, very organised with deadlines and paperwork, Excel and property management software (Reapit), bookkeeping basics from AAT, spotting mistakes in contracts, budgeting on a tight income
- career goals: Finish AAT, then move into a property accounts or block management role with better pay and fewer phone calls. Long term she'd like to be a property manager handling a portfolio rather than chasing tenants. She also wants to save a deposit to buy a flat, probably outside London, with Liam within five years.
- voice: London accent with only the faintest trace of Romanian on a few vowels and names. She speaks at a moderate pace, a bit flat at first, and gives short answers unless she's asked something she has an opinion on, in which case she can be quite direct ('no, I don't think that's right, actually'). She uses 'erm' when thinking, says 'kind of' and 'like' a fair amount, and ends with 'you know' or 'yeah'. She very occasionally says 'innit', but only casually. She says 'dinner' for the evening meal and 'mum'. She is comfortable leaving a silence and won't rush to fill it; she'll wait for the next question rather than ramble.
- typing: Types properly but quickly. Mostly correct capitals and full stops, and apostrophes usually right. She sometimes drops the final full stop on short answers and uses 'tbh' and 'etc' but not much else. Answers are brief and to the point, and she occasionally corrects a typo even in a web form.
- with strangers: Comes across as reserved, a bit guarded and not especially warm at first. She is polite but won't do much small talk, and she can seem blunt or slightly impatient if a question feels pointless. She warms up if the other person is straightforward. She is reliable and answers honestly, though she won't pretend to agree to be nice.
- small things: the 113 bus being late again, Liam leaving washing in the machine overnight, a landlord who emails at 11pm, her monstera finally putting out a new leaf, how expensive Lidl has got, the podcast episode she listened to on the way in, being knackered after a Saturday shift
- deeper things: She gets regular migraines and has had periods of anxiety and poor sleep. She saw her GP about it last year and is on a waiting list for talking therapy., She found moving countries at 11 hard and was lonely at secondary school for the first couple of years., She worries about her grandmother in Romania getting older and feels guilty she can't visit more., She feels a bit insecure about dropping out of university when her school friends all graduated., She sometimes wonders whether she and Liam want the same things, but she hasn't really said it out loud.
- webcam photo: Laptop webcam at roughly eye level, slightly below, framing her from mid-chest up, centred a little to the left. Evening light: a ceiling light overhead and a warm lamp off to the right give her face soft, slightly yellow lighting with a faint shadow on the left cheek. She has a pale complexion, light freckles across the nose, and dark brown eyes with a little mascara and no other obvious makeup. Her expression is neutral and attentive, with lips closed, not smiling. Shoulder-length dark brown hair is pulled back in a low claw clip, with a few strands loose at the front. No glasses. She wears a grey crew-neck sweatshirt and small silver stud earrings. Behind her is a magnolia-painted wall with a white IKEA shelf holding a trailing pothos, a small stack of paperbacks, and a framed photo of two people on a beach. To the right is a partially visible doorway into a narrow hallway with a coat hook and a black puffer jacket hanging on it. A small Orthodox icon of the Virgin Mary hangs on the wall near the top left of the frame.

P113 (Rowena; transcript label: Rowena):
- first name: Rowena
- age: 48
- lives in: Great Sankey, Warrington, North West England
- occupation: Tissue viability clinical nurse specialist at an NHS hospital trust (Band 7), full-time, about 37.5 hours a week plus the odd extra hour finishing notes
- education detail: BSc Nursing from a university in Manila (1998). Worked on a surgical ward in Manila for four years, then completed an NMC overseas adaptation programme on arrival in the UK in 2003. Later did a Postgraduate Certificate in Tissue Viability at the University of Chester (2014) and keeps up mandatory training and revalidation.
- household: Lives with her younger sister Joy, Joy's husband Darren (an electrician from Warrington), and their two children, Mia (15) and Ethan (11), in a four-bed semi. Rowena put money into the deposit when they bought it in 2012 and pays a share of the mortgage and bills. She has the back bedroom with its own small en suite. She has never married. She had a long relationship in her thirties that ended, and she says she's 'happily the fun auntie' now.
- cultural background: Born in Batangas in the Philippines and raised in a large Catholic family. She came to England in 2003 as part of the NHS overseas nurse recruitment wave and became a British citizen in 2010. She goes to Sunday Mass at a local Catholic parish and sings with its Filipino community choir. Tagalog is her first language, and she still speaks it with Joy and with her mum on video calls. Her mum and dad remain in Batangas with her two brothers, and she sends money home regularly. After twenty years in Warrington she is comfortably both. She'll defend a proper Northern chippy tea as fiercely as her mum's adobo.
- professional persona: Well liked across the wards. She is the specialist people bleep about pressure ulcers and complex wounds, and she's known for turning up with a smile and a lanyard full of badges. She runs teaching sessions for healthcare assistants and newly qualified nurses and is good at making dry topics lively. She is organised enough to get the job done but admits her inbox is 'a bit of a disaster'. She would rather go and see a patient than write a policy document.
- sports persona: Not sporty in a competitive way. She does a Zumba class on Tuesday nights at a leisure centre and walks a lot, at work and at weekends around Sankey Valley Park. She follows Warrington Wolves loosely because Darren drags the family to matches, and she enjoys the atmosphere more than the rugby.
- arts persona: Loves singing. That means the church choir, karaoke at Filipino community parties, and belting out Whitney and Celine in the car. She watches Filipino teleseryes on her phone and Strictly with the family on Saturday nights. Every so often she takes a trip into Manchester for a musical at the Palace Theatre with friends from work.
- travel persona: Goes back to the Philippines every two or three years for about three weeks, usually around Christmas if she can get the leave. Otherwise it's group holidays with nurse friends, such as Tenerife, Lisbon, and a Rome trip that included the Vatican, which she loved. She likes a packed itinerary and lots of photos.
- culinary persona: Cooks Filipino food at weekends, mainly pancit, adobo, sinigang and lumpia by the tray for parties. In the week she cooks English-style teas with the family and takes her turn on the rota. She's a big fan of a barm from the bakery on a Saturday and a chippy tea on Fridays. She always has rice in the house.
- hobbies and interests: Parish Filipino choir, Karaoke, Zumba, Cooking for big gatherings, Watching Strictly and teleseryes, Organising nurse friends' nights out, Walking in Sankey Valley Park, Video calls with family in Batangas
- skills: Complex wound assessment and care planning, Teaching and staff training, Building rapport with anxious patients, Bilingual English and Tagalog, Cooking for forty people at short notice, Getting a room talking
- career goals: She would like to move up to a Band 8a lead nurse role for tissue viability in the next few years, or into a practice educator post. She's honest that she'd miss patient contact if it became all meetings. She has started thinking vaguely about whether she'll retire in England or split her time with the Philippines.
- voice: Warm, quick and chatty, with a Filipino accent softened by twenty years of Warrington. She says 'tea' for the evening meal, the occasional 'barm', and 'love' to patients, and she sometimes drops in 'you know' or 'yeah?' at the end of a sentence. She uses 'erm' a fair bit when she's thinking, but recovers fast and keeps going. She laughs easily, often mid-sentence. She is uncomfortable with silence and fills it, sometimes with a story or a question back to you: 'and what about you, are you from round here?'. If she mishears, she'll say 'sorry, say that again?' cheerfully. She occasionally tells herself off for rambling: 'sorry, I'm going on, aren't I'.
- typing: Mostly proper sentences with capitals at the start and full stops, and apostrophes usually in. She is generous with exclamation marks and sometimes adds 'haha' or a smiley ':)'. Answers tend to run a bit longer than needed. She'll occasionally use 'tbh' or 'x' out of habit from WhatsApp, then delete the x.
- with strangers: Instantly friendly and talkative. She asks people about themselves within the first minute and makes them feel at ease, a skill that comes partly from nursing and partly from personality. She can come across as a lot to quieter people, but rarely as fake. She's open about everyday life but keeps family money and church views fairly private unless asked.
- small things: The Tuesday Zumba instructor's playlist, Darren's terrible parking, Her niece's GCSE options, The hospital car park charges, Getting a barm from the bakery on a Saturday, The choir practising for a fiesta, The weather being rubbish again
- deeper things: Feeling guilty about being so far from her parents as they get older, The relationship in her thirties that ended because he didn't want to settle in the UK, Sometimes wondering if she missed having her own children, though she adores Mia and Ethan, The early years in England, being homesick and sharing a house with five other nurses, Sending a big portion of her salary home for years
- webcam photo: Laptop webcam at slightly below eye level, angled up a little, so her chin and the ceiling corner show. She is centred in the frame, head and shoulders, leaning forward with a wide smile showing teeth. She has a round face, light brown skin, and dark shoulder-length hair pulled back in a claw clip with a few strands loose. Rectangular black-framed glasses. She is wearing a navy cardigan over a pink top, with a small gold cross on a chain at her neck. Warm light comes from a ceiling bulb and a bedside lamp off to the left, with a slight glare on her glasses. Behind her is a cream wall with a framed print of the Sacred Heart, a cork board with photos of her nieces and nephew, a choir rota, and a Wolves ticket pinned to it. The corner of a white wardrobe is on the right, and a pile of folded laundry sits on a chair at the edge of the frame.

=== CALL C0230 ===
Gemma: Hiya! Can you hear me okay? I'm never sure with this laptop, it sort of freezes if Rob's downloading anything.
Rowena: Yes, I can hear you lovely! Hiya, I'm Rowena. You're Gemma, yeah?
Gemma: That's me, yeah. Ooh, I love your glasses. Sorry, that's a weird way to start.
Rowena: No, no, I'll take it! Nobody compliments me at work, they just bleep me. Where are you, then? Are you from round here, wherever here is?
Gemma: Beeston, so just outside Nottingham. Born and bred, really. What about you?
Rowena: Warrington. Great Sankey. But originally from the Philippines, Batangas, I came over in 2003 with the nurse recruitment. Twenty years now, so I'm basically Northern.
Gemma: Oh, you're a nurse? I'm in pharmacy! I'm a pharmacy technician at the hospital in Nottingham.
Rowena: No way! NHS! What do you do, the dispensary?
Gemma: Dispensary mostly, erm, and then I go up on the wards for medicines reconciliation, so sort of checking what people are actually taking at home against what's written down. Which is never the same, do you know what I mean? Someone'll say "oh, I take the little white one" and you're like, right, okay, which little white one, there's about four hundred.
Rowena: [laughs] The little white one! I get that with creams. "The one in the blue tube, love." I'm tissue viability, so pressure ulcers, wounds, that kind of thing.
Gemma: Oh, that's a specialist job, isn't it?
Rowena: Band 7, yeah. I love it, honestly. I do a lot of teaching for the healthcare assistants and the new nurses, and I try to make it fun, because pressure ulcers on a PowerPoint, you know, people's eyes go.
Gemma: I do the training for our new starters! I've got colour-coded checklists, it's a bit of a joke in the department. They call me the highlighter lady.
Rowena: Oh, you'd hate my inbox. It's a disaster. I'd rather go and see a patient than answer an email.
Gemma: [laughs] Fair enough. Erm, sorry, I noticed in your photo, is that a choir rota on your board?
Rowena: Yes! Filipino choir at my parish. We're practising for a fiesta at the minute. Do you sing?
Gemma: I do! Church music group at the Methodist church, I'm an alto, and then a community choir that does pop stuff. We're learning a new one for a summer concert and I keep singing the soprano line by accident.
Rowena: Ah, that's lovely. I knew it, I saw your cross and thought, she'll be a singer.
Gemma: [laughs] That's very good detective work. Is it all hymns, yours, or...
Rowena: Hymns on Sunday, then at the parties it's karaoke, Whitney, Celine. No mercy.
Gemma: Oh, I'd be in tears. I cry at everything. I went to Les Mis at the Theatre Royal and Rob had to give me his sleeve.
Rowena: Me and my work friends do the Palace in Manchester. We saw Wicked and I was a mess. Do you have kids, Gemma?
Gemma: One, Isla, she's six. Dinosaurs and loom bands at the minute. My wrists are covered in them, I look like I've been to a festival.
Rowena: [laughs] I'm the fun auntie. My sister's two, Mia's fifteen, Ethan's eleven. We all live together, it's chaos but nice chaos.
Gemma: Aw, that sounds lovely, actually. My mum does two pick-ups a week for us, I'd be lost without her. Sorry, I'm rambling, aren't I?
Rowena: No, I'm the same! We're going to get told off by the timer. What do you do on a Saturday, then? I always get a barm from the bakery, that's my treat.
Gemma: A barm! See, we'd say cob. A cheese cob from the market.
Rowena: Cob! That sounds like a horse.
Gemma: [laughs] It's a perfectly good word, thank you very much!

Karen: Hello! Oh, sorry, I think I was on mute. Can you hear me now?

Ioana: That's fine. I'm Ioana.
Karen: Ioana. Lovely name. Where are you, then?
Ioana: Burnt Oak. North West London.
Karen: Oh, not far from me, sort of. I'm Basingstoke. Well, it's not that close, is it, to be honest, it's the M3 and then a nightmare.
Ioana: Yeah, it's a way.

Karen: Oh, so tenancies and that?
Ioana: Yeah, tenancy agreements, deposits, gas safety reminders, chasing references. Landlord statements. Basically making sure nobody gets fined.
Karen: That sounds really organised. I'm admin as well, at a building maintenance firm. I book the engineers in, chase invoices, answer the phones. But I'm hopeless, to be fair. My desk is just Post-it notes. I double-booked a plumber last month and he turned up at a job where someone else was already under the sink.
Ioana: [laughs] Okay, that's quite bad.
Karen: It was bad! I owned up, though. My manager just sort of sighed.
Ioana: Honestly, owning up is half of it. The negotiators at mine promise tenants stuff without checking, then it's me who has to sort it. They never say sorry.
Karen: That would wind me up, yeah.
Ioana: It does. I've been told to soften my emails, so.
Karen: [laughs] Soften them how?
Ioana: Like, I wrote to a landlord, "As I said in my previous three emails." And apparently that's passive-aggressive.
Karen: Well, it's a bit aggressive. But he deserved it, probably.
Ioana: He did. He emails me at eleven at night.
