req.text:
You write transcripts of realistic video calls between strangers for a fully synthetic research dataset set in the UK. The study, in order (from its published design): a short puzzle task done alone; first impressions of the others' webcam photos; then a series of three-minute, one-on-one video calls in rounds, each person meeting the others in their group; after each call a short survey.

Call shape (from the original study's numbers): a call is cut off by a three-minute timer. A typical call has about 30 turns (most between 20 and 39) and about 570 words in total (most between 440 and 682); half of all turns are 12 words or fewer, and a quarter are 24 or more. Short acknowledgements ("yeah", "mm") count as turns too. So aim for about 570 words in about 30 turns: alongside the quick back-and-forth, people often talk in longer stretches (explaining their job, telling a story), and those long turns carry much of the call.

Guide to British conversational English (use it for how people talk; it is a description of speech, not a script):
How British people talk in casual conversation. This is a paraphrase of published descriptions of spoken British English; sources are in SOURCES.md. Use these features lightly and only where they fit the person. Never use them as a caricature.

- **Fillers.** British speakers hesitate with "erm" and "er". Women and younger speakers lean towards "erm".
- **Hedges.** "Sort of" is everywhere and steady. "Kind of" is spreading, and younger speakers use it more.
- **Politeness words.** "Please", "thank you", "thanks" and "sorry" mostly mean what they say. "Sorry" also works as a repair word (to correct yourself, or to ask someone to repeat) and can be ironic.
- **Tags at the end of a sentence.** "You know", "right", "okay", "yeah", "do you know what I mean". Among young Londoners, "innit" and "you get me" are rising. Tags depend on age and region only, never on ethnicity.
- **Echoing.** In an engaged conversation people pick up and re-use parts of each other's words.
- **Regional words and grammar** (from a recent dialect survey):
  - A bread roll is a "barm" in the North West (Manchester to Liverpool and western Lancashire), a "cob" around Nottinghamshire, a "bap" in Staffordshire, the West Midlands and North Wales, and a "batch" in Liverpool and Coventry.
  - Around Liverpool an ice lolly can be a "lolly ice".
  - The evening meal is "tea" in the North West, North East and Yorkshire, and "dinner" in the South East and London. Some people say both.
  - "Yous" or "youse" for plural "you" is common in the North East (Newcastle, Teesside), Liverpool and Scotland, less so in Manchester, and rare in York, Leeds and Sheffield.
  - "Give it me" is normal in the North West and West Midlands and widely accepted in Sheffield and York; it fades south of Birmingham, Coventry and Leicester.
  - "You was" is widely used, historically Northern and now found as far south as London.
- **Everyday British words** to draw on where they fit, without assigning them to regions: knackered or shattered, chuffed or made up, skint or brassic, mardy or stroppy, mum or mam, mate or pal, settee, sofa or couch.

The group (session S15). Persona cards, including the webcam photo each person was rated on:

P073 (Rhys; transcript label: Rhys):
- first name: Rhys
- age: 37
- lives in: Caerphilly, South Wales
- occupation: Senior video editor and motion graphics designer at a mid-sized marketing and production agency in Cardiff, mostly corporate films, social ads and the odd S4C-adjacent job. Regularly works 50 to 55 hours a week around client deadlines.
- education detail: BA in Media Production from the University of South Wales (Treforest campus), plus a few short online courses in After Effects and colour grading he never quite finished but lists anyway.
- household: Lives with his wife, Ffion, a primary school teacher, in a three-bed semi on a 2000s estate on the edge of Caerphilly. No children yet. It's a 'maybe in a couple of years' conversation that keeps getting pushed back. They have an anxious rescue whippet called Moss.
- cultural background: Born and raised in Ystrad Mynach to a bus driver dad and a mum who worked in a school office. White Welsh, English-speaking at home. He did Welsh at school and understands more than he lets on but won't speak it in front of fluent speakers. Not religious; his nan was chapel but he hasn't been inside one since her funeral. Quietly proud of being from the Valleys, though he likes people to know he 'does creative work in Cardiff'.
- professional persona: Talented and fast in the edit suite, with a good eye for pacing and colour. Disorganised with file naming, timesheets and admin, and leans on a producer colleague to keep him on track. Avoids client calls where he can and prefers to send a cut and let the work speak. He's been known to round his hours up and to take a bit more credit for a concept than was strictly his. He's easy to work with, rarely argues back on notes, and quietly stews about bad feedback for days.
- sports persona: Not sporty, but he follows Wales in the Six Nations with his dad and gets genuinely tense watching. Walks Moss up Caerphilly Mountain most weekends, and bought an expensive road bike during lockdown that mostly sits in the garage.
- arts persona: Watches a lot of arthouse and world cinema, keeps a Letterboxd account and is a bit precious about it. Likes ambient and electronic music (Boards of Canada, Gruff Rhys's solo stuff, Jon Hopkins). Collects vintage film posters and second-hand photo books, and occasionally does experimental short edits for himself that he never shows anyone.
- travel persona: Prefers city breaks with good food and galleries: Copenhagen, Lisbon, Berlin. Gets anxious about flights and airport timings and lets Ffion plan everything. Likes a nice hotel more than he admits, and will happily spend money to avoid hostels or anything 'rough'.
- culinary persona: An enthusiastic but chaotic cook who leaves the kitchen wrecked. Does elaborate weekend projects like ramen broth or slow-cooked lamb and lives on meal deals and coffee during deadline weeks. He'll happily pay for a tasting menu in Cardiff to post about. He calls the evening meal 'tea' at his mam's and 'dinner' at home.
- hobbies and interests: arthouse and world cinema, film poster collecting, ambient and electronic music, walking the dog on Caerphilly Mountain, cooking ambitious weekend meals, photography with an old Olympus film camera, half-finished personal video projects
- skills: Premiere Pro and After Effects, DaVinci Resolve colour grading, visual storytelling and pacing, basic sound design, film photography, being calm and patient with difficult clients by email
- career goals: Wants to be seen as a 'proper' creative rather than a corporate editor, ideally as a creative director or with his own small studio and his name on the credits. He's vague about how to get there and hasn't updated his showreel in two years. He also likes the idea of the salary and status bump more than the extra responsibility.
- voice: Quiet, fairly soft-spoken South Walian accent, a bit more neutral at work than with family. Medium-slow pace with plenty of 'erm' and 'sort of' while he works out what he wants to say. He occasionally says 'tidy' or 'now in a minute' without thinking, and says 'mam' about his mum. Polite, with plenty of 'yeah, no, that's fair'. He tends to echo the question back ('what do I find stressful... erm') to buy time. He's uncomfortable with silence and fills it with a nervous little laugh or 'sorry, I'm rambling'. He warms up and talks faster once the topic is film or food.
- typing: Mostly lowercase and quick, with capitals usually missing at the start. He drops apostrophes in 'dont' and 'im' but not always consistently. Few full stops, more commas and the odd '...'. Uses 'tbh' and 'prob', and makes typos he doesn't go back to fix.
- with strangers: Reserved and slightly awkward at first, giving short answers and lots of nodding. He comes across as gentle, likeable and agreeable, never confrontational. If you show interest in what he does he opens up and can be a bit keen to mention his clients or a job he 'basically led'. He picks up on other people's moods and worries afterwards about how he came across.
- small things: Moss the whippet is scared of the wheelie bins, the A469 traffic into Cardiff, a film he watched at Chapter Arts Centre, having a pint of coffee by 9am on deadline days, the bike in the garage he keeps meaning to use, Wales losing again and his dad texting him about it, needing a new monitor for the home office
- deeper things: Worries he's a bit of a fraud creatively and is scared of being found out, Has health anxiety despite being perfectly well, and googles symptoms late at night, Feels guilty and a bit relieved every time the kids conversation with Ffion gets postponed, Envies uni friends who moved to London and 'made it', and sometimes exaggerates his own work to keep up, Still gets upset about his nan dying, and kept her chapel hymn book, Knows the long hours are partly avoidance, because being busy stops him thinking
- webcam photo: Laptop webcam at a slight upward angle, framing him from mid-chest up and a little off-centre to the left. Soft daylight comes from a window to his right, so the left side of his face is a touch shadowed, with a faint blue glow from a second monitor. He has short dark brown hair, slightly messy on top, and a neat but overdue beard with a few grey hairs at the chin. He's wearing black rectangular-framed glasses. Expression: a polite, slightly tight closed-mouth smile, eyes looking just below the camera at the screen. He wears a plain charcoal crewneck sweatshirt. Behind him is a white-painted spare bedroom used as an office: a framed vintage Polish film poster in red and black on the wall, a tall bookshelf with photo books, a few DVDs and a small Olympus film camera on top, and a rolled-up yoga mat leaning against it. A grey dog bed is partly visible in the lower right corner, and a pair of over-ear headphones hangs on a hook by the door.

P074 (Martin; transcript label: Martin):
- first name: Martin
- age: 55
- lives in: Taunton, Somerset, South West England
- occupation: Former secondary school geography teacher. He left teaching two years ago on a stress-related absence that became early retirement, and now does occasional exam invigilation at a local college during the summer and winter exam seasons.
- education detail: A-levels at a sixth form in Yeovil, a BSc in Geography from Plymouth Polytechnic (as it still was then), and a PGCE from Exeter. He has done no formal study since, apart from compulsory safeguarding and first-aid refreshers.
- household: Lives with his wife Karen, 53, a teaching assistant at a primary school, in a 1970s semi-detached house on the edge of town. Their two children are grown up: a son in Bristol and a daughter in Cardiff. There is an elderly, overweight Labrador called Biscuit.
- cultural background: White British, born and raised in Somerset to a father who worked at a dairy and a mother who did school dinners. He is Church of England and goes to the parish church at Christmas, Easter and the odd Sunday when Karen persuades him. He holds his faith quietly but sincerely, mostly as a sense of right and wrong rather than doctrine. He is very rooted in the West Country and slightly suspicious of anything that feels too London.
- professional persona: He was a popular, chatty, slightly chaotic teacher. Students liked him for his stories and his bluntness. Management found him hard work: marking was late, lesson plans were scribbled the morning of, and he argued in staff meetings. He would never fudge data or cover up a mistake, and he said so loudly when others did. The pressure of inspections and paperwork wore him down badly in his last few years.
- sports persona: A lifelong Somerset cricket supporter. He goes to a few County Championship days at the County Ground each season with a flask and strong opinions. He watches rugby on telly, Bath mostly, and shouts at it. He played village cricket until his knees gave out in his forties, and these days he walks the dog along the canal, which is about as athletic as it gets.
- arts persona: Loves a pub folk night and knows a lot of old songs he will sing given half a chance. He reads thrillers and local history, half-finishes a lot of books, and watches nature documentaries and panel shows. He went to Glastonbury twice in his twenties and still tells stories about it.
- travel persona: Mostly UK holidays: Cornwall, Pembrokeshire, the Lake District once. He and Karen take a fortnight in Spain or Portugal every couple of years. He hates the airport bit and gets anxious about connections, but he is great company once he is there. He would like to see Norway's fjords but keeps not booking it.
- culinary persona: Enjoys cooking a big Sunday roast and a decent chilli but makes a mess of the kitchen. He drinks local cider and the odd real ale. He is supposed to be cutting back on sugar and bread for his diabetes and is not very good at it. He calls the evening meal 'tea' or 'dinner' depending on mood.
- hobbies and interests: Watching Somerset County Cricket, Folk music and pub sing-arounds, Local history, especially the Somerset Levels and the Monmouth Rebellion, Walking the dog on the Bridgwater and Taunton Canal, Pub quizzes (he is the team's geography and sport man), Half-hearted vegetable growing on a raised bed
- skills: Talking to a room of teenagers and holding their attention, Map reading and explaining landscape and weather, Quiz trivia, Basic first aid, Telling a good story, Singing, loudly and roughly in tune
- career goals: No real career ambitions now. He would like enough invigilation and maybe some tutoring to top up his pension and get him out of the house. He has vaguely thought about volunteering as a guide at a local museum or heritage site but has not filled in the form.
- voice: Warm, quite loud, talks a lot and fast once he gets going. His West Country accent is soft but present: a slightly rolled 'r', the odd 'proper' as an intensifier ('proper knackered', 'proper job'), and occasionally 'gert' as a joke. He says 'er' rather than 'erm' and uses 'sort of' and 'you know' as tags. He will interrupt and disagree bluntly ('no, see, that's not right though'), then soften it with a laugh or 'sorry, go on'. He rarely leaves a silence and fills it with an anecdote. He gets audibly emotional talking about his kids or his old students.
- typing: Quick and sloppy. Mostly lowercase, with a capital 'I' about half the time. Commas are scarce and he uses dots between thoughts... like that. He drops apostrophes sometimes ('dont', 'its'), makes the occasional typo he does not fix, uses no text-speak beyond 'tbh' and 'etc', and writes answers longer than the box needs.
- with strangers: Friendly and talkative straight away, with jokes and tangents, and he will share more than expected. He can come across as opinionated and a bit contrary, and will tell you if he thinks a question is daft. He is obviously honest and unpretentious, and plays down any expertise. People tend to like him while also wishing he would get to the point.
- small things: Biscuit the Labrador needing a trip to the vet for his ears, Somerset's bowling attack this season, The roadworks on the A358, The pub quiz team losing by one point again, Runner beans going stringy because he forgot to pick them, Karen's school putting on a nativity
- deeper things: Leaving teaching felt like being pushed out, and he still has a sense of failure and anger about it, He was diagnosed with type 2 diabetes three years ago and worries about his health more than he admits, He misses the kids being at home and gets low on quiet weekdays, His dad died of a heart attack at 62, and he thinks about that number, He feels guilty that Karen is still working while he is not, He finds church comforting at funerals and wishes he went more but feels a bit of a fraud
- webcam photo: Head-and-shoulders shot from a laptop on a dining table, angled slightly upward so the ceiling light is visible at the top of the frame. The light is warm overhead lamplight mixed with grey daylight from a window to his left. He has a round, ruddy face with a broad smile mid-sentence and crinkled eyes. His short, thinning grey hair is receding at the front, with grey stubble. He wears gold-rimmed reading glasses pushed slightly down his nose and a navy fleece over a checked shirt collar. Behind him is a magnolia wall with a framed Ordnance Survey map of Exmoor, a wooden bookcase crammed with paperbacks and a Somerset CCC mug on one shelf, a wall calendar from a local vet, and part of a brown leather settee with a folded tartan throw. A Labrador's tail is just visible at the bottom right of the frame.

req.text:
You write transcripts of realistic video calls between strangers for a fully synthetic research dataset set in the UK. The study, in order (from its published design): a short puzzle task done alone; first impressions of the others' webcam photos; then a series of three-minute, one-on-one video calls in rounds, each person meeting the others in their group; after each call a short survey.

Call shape (from the original study's numbers): a call is cut off by a three-minute timer. A typical call has about 30 turns (most between 20 and 39) and about 570 words in total (most between 440 and 682); half of all turns are 12 words or fewer, and a quarter are 24 or more. Short acknowledgements ("yeah", "mm") count as turns too. So aim for about 570 words in about 30 turns: alongside the quick back-and-forth, people often talk in longer stretches (explaining their job, telling a story), and those long turns carry much of the call.

Guide to British conversational English (use it for how people talk; it is a description of speech, not a script):
How British people talk in casual conversation. This is a paraphrase of published descriptions of spoken British English; sources are in SOURCES.md. Use these features lightly and only where they fit the person. Never use them as a caricature.

- **Fillers.** British speakers hesitate with "erm" and "er". Women and younger speakers lean towards "erm".
- **Hedges.** "Sort of" is everywhere and steady. "Kind of" is spreading, and younger speakers use it more.
- **Politeness words.** "Please", "thank you", "thanks" and "sorry" mostly mean what they say. "Sorry" also works as a repair word (to correct yourself, or to ask someone to repeat) and can be ironic.
- **Tags at the end of a sentence.** "You know", "right", "okay", "yeah", "do you know what I mean". Among young Londoners, "innit" and "you get me" are rising. Tags depend on age and region only, never on ethnicity.
- **Echoing.** In an engaged conversation people pick up and re-use parts of each other's words.
- **Regional words and grammar** (from a recent dialect survey):
  - A bread roll is a "barm" in the North West (Manchester to Liverpool and western Lancashire), a "cob" around Nottinghamshire, a "bap" in Staffordshire, the West Midlands and North Wales, and a "batch" in Liverpool and Coventry.
  - Around Liverpool an ice lolly can be a "lolly ice".
  - The evening meal is "tea" in the North West, North East and Yorkshire, and "dinner" in the South East and London. Some people say both.
  - "Yous" or "youse" for plural "you" is common in the North East (Newcastle, Teesside), Liverpool and Scotland, less so in Manchester, and rare in York, Leeds and Sheffield.
  - "Give it me" is normal in the North West and West Midlands and widely accepted in Sheffield and York; it fades south of Birmingham, Coventry and Leicester.
  - "You was" is widely used, historically Northern and now found as far south as London.
- **Everyday British words** to draw on where they fit, without assigning them to regions: knackered or shattered, chuffed or made up, skint or brassic, mardy or stroppy, mum or mam, mate or pal, settee, sofa or couch.

The group (session S14). Persona cards, including the webcam photo each person was rated on:

P068 (Neil; transcript label: Neil):
- first name: Neil
- age: 52
- lives in: Basingstoke, South East England
- occupation: Chartered civil engineer (asset engineer) for a regional water utility, looking after pumping stations and sewer networks across north Hampshire
- education detail: A levels in Maths, Physics and Geography at a sixth-form college in Reading. BEng in Civil Engineering from the University of Portsmouth. Became chartered with the Institution of Civil Engineers in his late twenties.
- household: Lives with his wife Karen, 51, a part-time practice manager at a GP surgery, in a four-bedroom 1990s detached house on an estate in Chineham. Their two children have left home. Their daughter, 24, is a physio in Southampton, and their son, 21, is finishing a degree in Nottingham. The son's room is still kept as it was.
- cultural background: White British, born and raised in Reading. His dad was an electrician and his mum worked in a building society. Church of England. He and Karen go to their local parish church at Christmas and Easter and for the odd harvest festival. He was confirmed as a teenager and still thinks of himself as Christian, but he doesn't talk about it much. Middle-of-the-road and settled. He has lived within thirty miles of where he grew up for his whole life.
- professional persona: Steady and dependable. He has been with the same utility for nineteen years, and colleagues come to him because he knows where everything is buried, sometimes literally. He prefers proven methods to new approaches and is quietly sceptical of consultants and rebrands. He doesn't get rattled when a pump station floods at 2am or a project slips. He writes clear, plain reports, gets his work done in standard hours and logs off at about half five. He is good with the site operatives and contractors because he is fair and doesn't throw his weight around.
- sports persona: Lifelong Reading FC supporter. He went to Elm Park as a boy with his dad and now goes to the odd home game, but mostly follows the results. He watches the cricket when it's on, especially the Test matches. He used to play five-a-side and gave it up in his forties after a calf strain. Now he walks a lot and does a bit of golf at a municipal course about once a month with two old colleagues. He plays off a high handicap and doesn't mind.
- arts persona: Not really his thing. He reads the odd thriller on holiday, Lee Child or similar. He watches whatever Karen puts on, police dramas and quiz shows mainly, and he likes Only Connect and University Challenge. He has been to the theatre in London a handful of times, always for Karen's birthday. Music is the classic rock and 80s stuff he grew up with, Dire Straits and Queen, on in the car.
- travel persona: Creature of habit. They have been going to the same part of Cornwall, near Padstow, most summers for fifteen years. They do one week abroad every couple of years, usually somewhere in Spain or Portugal they have been before. He's not keen on long-haul flights or 'adventure' holidays. He drives everywhere if he can.
- culinary persona: Plain, traditional food. Roast on a Sunday, which he usually cooks: chicken or beef, never anything fancy. He is happy with shepherd's pie, a curry from the local takeaway on Fridays, and fish and chips in Cornwall. He doesn't like overly spicy food or 'messed about' dishes. He calls the evening meal dinner. He drinks bitter at the pub and the occasional glass of red with a roast.
- hobbies and interests: Gardening, mainly keeping the lawn tidy and growing tomatoes and runner beans in raised beds, Walking the family's Labrador, Bramble, along the Basingstoke Canal, Following Reading FC and Test cricket, Pottering in the garage and fixing things around the house, Quiz shows, especially Only Connect, Monthly round of golf with old work mates
- skills: Hydraulic modelling and drainage design, Reading and checking engineering drawings, Managing contractors and site safety, Basic DIY, plumbing and electrics, Staying calm in a crisis, Excel spreadsheets, a lot of them
- career goals: No big ambitions left. He'd like to stay in his current role, perhaps mentor a couple of the graduate engineers, and retire at around 60 or 62 if the pension allows. He has turned down moving into senior management twice because he didn't fancy the meetings.
- voice: Mild South East accent, Thames Valley rather than London, unremarkable. Measured, fairly slow pace. He says 'er' rather than 'erm' when thinking and uses 'sort of' a fair bit. He gives short, practical answers and doesn't elaborate unless asked. He is happy to sit in silence while he thinks, and he doesn't rush to fill gaps. He might say 'yeah, fair enough' or 'that's about it really' to close an answer. He is polite, says 'sorry, could you repeat that?' if he mishears, and thanks the interviewer at the end.
- typing: Proper sentences with capitals and full stops, and apostrophes in the right place. He's a bit brief and sometimes leaves off the last full stop. No emojis or text-speak, though he will write 'etc' and use '&' occasionally. He checks his answer once before submitting.
- with strangers: Reserved but friendly enough. He comes across as a decent, unflappable, slightly quiet bloke. He doesn't volunteer much at first and answers what he's asked. He is easy-going and agreeable, unlikely to argue or push back, and warms up a bit if the conversation turns to something practical like football, the garden or the dog.
- small things: The dog needed walking before the call, Reading lost again at the weekend, The tomatoes have come on well this year, Roadworks on the A33 making the commute a pain, Karen's got him watching a new detective series, Booked Cornwall again for August
- deeper things: His dad died of a stroke five years ago and he still thinks about how quick it was, He feels the house is quiet since the kids left and he misses his son more than he lets on, He sometimes wonders if he should have pushed himself more in his career, but mostly he's content, His faith is a quiet thing for him. He prays occasionally and found the church a comfort at his dad's funeral, He is a bit worried about his mum, who is 79 and living alone in Reading
- webcam photo: Head-and-shoulders framing from a laptop webcam, slightly below eye level, so the camera looks up a little at his chin. Lighting comes from a window to his left, giving soft daylight on one side of his face with the other side a bit shadowed. A white man in his early fifties with a broad, slightly ruddy face, light stubble and short greying brown hair receding at the temples. Neutral, mildly pleasant expression with a faint closed-mouth smile. Rimless glasses. He is wearing a navy quarter-zip fleece over a pale blue collared shirt. Behind him is a spare bedroom used as a home office: magnolia walls, a white flat-pack bookcase holding ring binders labelled with project codes, a few paperback thrillers and a framed photo of two young adults at a graduation. A cream radiator sits under the window edge, and a folded ironing board leans against the wall in the corner.

P069 (Hodan; transcript label: Hodan):
- first name: Hodan
- age: 29
- lives in: Wembley, Brent, North West London
- occupation: Senior pharmacy technician in the aseptic and dispensary unit of an NHS hospital in North West London, full-time at around 37.5 hours plus occasional weekend rota cover
- education detail: GCSEs and A-levels (Chemistry, Biology, Business) at a Brent sixth form. Level 3 Diploma in Principles and Practices for Pharmacy Technicians and the work-based NVQ, completed through a trainee post while her son was a toddler. GPhC registered. Now part-way through an accredited medicines management and accuracy checking qualification.
- household: Lone parent in a two-bedroom housing association flat near Wembley Park with her son Idris, aged 8. Never married. Idris's father lives in Leicester and sees him some school holidays. Her mum lives a ten-minute bus ride away and does most school pickups on Hodan's late shifts.
- cultural background: Born in Hargeisa, Somaliland, and came to London aged six with her mum and two older brothers, joining an uncle already in Brent. Grew up between Somali at home and London English at school. Muslim and practising in her own way: she prays when she can fit it in, fasts at Ramadan, wears a hijab, and goes to the mosque mainly for Eid and family occasions. She is close to her extended family but openly irritated by aunties' opinions on her being unmarried, and she doesn't pretend otherwise.
- professional persona: Precise, fast and slightly feared. She runs the dispensary checking rota, keeps her own spreadsheet of error near-misses, and has no patience for people who cut corners or talk rather than do. She's good at making herself visible to managers. She volunteers for audits and the projects that get noticed, and is quick to point out when a success was hers. Junior technicians find her blunt but learn a lot. She negotiates hard over shifts and banding and has already pushed through one regrading.
- sports persona: Goes to a women-only gym session in Harrow three mornings a week before work, mostly weights and the rowing machine. She tracks everything in an app and gets competitive about her numbers. Watches Arsenal with her brothers, mostly for the arguing.
- arts persona: Not much of a gallery person. Listens to Afrobeats, UK rap and old Somali songs her mum plays. Binges true-crime documentaries and reality competition shows, and has firm views on who deserved to win. Took Idris to a West End musical for his birthday and quietly loved it.
- travel persona: Has been back to Hargeisa twice, once as a teenager and once with Idris at five. Prefers organised, efficient trips: Dubai with her cousins, a long weekend in Istanbul. She researches prices obsessively and boasts a bit about the deals she gets. Wants to take Idris to Disneyland Paris next year and has a savings pot for it.
- culinary persona: Batch-cooks on Sundays: rice with spiced lamb, suqaar, pasta bakes Idris will actually eat. Calls the evening meal dinner. Halal-strict at home, a bit choosy about it out. Likes a nice brunch spot and will judge it on Instagram-worthiness as much as taste. Makes proper Somali tea with cardamom and is snobby about anyone else's.
- hobbies and interests: Weight training and tracking her lifts, Budgeting and side savings pots, plus reading money-saving forums, True-crime documentaries, Organising family events such as Eid get-togethers and cousins' weddings, Sorting and reselling Idris's outgrown clothes and toys online, Trying new brunch places with her two closest friends
- skills: Aseptic preparation and final accuracy checking, Stock control and pharmacy systems, Rota planning and supervising junior technicians, Spreadsheets and data-keeping, Fluent Somali and English, Negotiating, from shift swaps to car prices, Running a household tightly on a budget
- career goals: Wants a Band 6 lead technician post within two years, ideally in medicines optimisation, where the pay and the status are better and the hours less chaotic. Has thought about retraining as a pharmacist through a part-time degree once Idris is older, but mainly cares about being the one in charge and earning properly.
- voice: Fast, confident London English with a light Somali family influence only in names and the odd word with her mum. She talks a lot and fills silences herself rather than waiting. Uses "erm" briefly when she's choosing her words, "kind of" and "like" as hedges, and ends points with "you know" or, among friends, an occasional "innit". Says "you was" now and then casually. Interrupts, then says "sorry, go on" without really meaning to stop. Laughs loudly. Gets clipped and flat when she thinks a question is pointless. She'll say so straight out: "that's a bit of a weird question, but fine."
- typing: Quick and mostly lowercase, with a capital at the start only if autocorrect does it. Apostrophes are hit and miss ("dont", "its"). Uses commas instead of full stops and drops the final full stop. Abbreviations like "tbh", "idk" and "bc", and digits instead of words ("2 kids no 1" style errors are rare because she rereads). Answers are short unless she has an opinion, then she writes a block.
- with strangers: Warm and chatty in the first minute, quick to make a joke, and comes across as very sure of herself. She soon sizes people up and can be dismissive if she thinks someone's slow or wasting her time. She's not unpleasant, but she doesn't soften things or flatter. She'll happily talk about herself and her achievements, and asks fewer questions back.
- small things: Idris's football club kit costing a fortune, The Jubilee line being down again, Having done her lifts at 6am before work, A brunch place in Kensal Rise that she says is overrated, Her mum's cardamom tea being better than anything you can buy, Sorting the rota while everyone else complains about it, Getting a parking fine she's appealing on principle
- deeper things: Having Idris at 21 and feeling she had to prove everyone wrong, which still drives her, Resentment that Idris's dad gets to be the fun parent on holidays, Aunties' constant comments about marriage, and not knowing if she even wants it, Barely remembering Hargeisa but feeling judged as not Somali enough there and not British enough here, Worrying her mum is getting older and she relies on her too much, Knowing people at work find her hard to like, and mostly deciding she doesn't care
- webcam photo: Laptop webcam, slightly below eye level, framing her from mid-chest up and a little off-centre to the left. Evening light from a ceiling bulb gives a warm cast, with a cooler glow on one cheek from the screen. Dark brown skin, defined eyebrows, light makeup with a nude lip, and a direct, slightly amused half-smile. A black jersey hijab is wrapped neatly, with no hair visible. She wears a grey zip-up hoodie with the hospital trust's lanyard still around her neck, and small gold stud earrings just visible at the hijab edge. No glasses. Behind her is a pale grey living-room wall with a framed school photo of a smiling boy in a red jumper, and a wall calendar covered in colour-coded handwriting. A corner of a dark grey sofa shows a folded laundry pile on the arm. A wooden shelf holds a small Qur'an stand, a plant in a white pot and a stack of children's books.

P070 (Joanne; transcript label: Joanne):
- first name: Joanne
- age: 48
- lives in: Batley, West Yorkshire (Yorkshire and The Humber)
- occupation: Upholsterer. She has been self-employed for nine years, working from a rented unit on a small industrial estate. She reupholsters armchairs, dining chairs, headboards and the odd vintage settee, and does some contract work for a pub chain and two care homes.
- education detail: Left secondary school in Dewsbury at 16 with GCSEs including a B in Art and a C in Maths. Did a two-year apprenticeship at a furniture manufacturer in Heckmondwike with an NVQ Level 2, later Level 3, in upholstery. Took an evening bookkeeping course at the local college when she went self-employed.
- household: Lives with her husband Darren (50), a maintenance fitter at a food factory, in a three-bed semi they have owned for 19 years. Their son Lewis (23) moved to Leeds two years ago and comes back most Sundays for his tea. They have an elderly Border terrier called Mabel.
- cultural background: White British and West Yorkshire through and through. Her dad worked in a textile mill until it closed and her mum was a school dinner lady. She was brought up loosely C of E but hasn't been to church since her wedding and describes herself as 'not religious, just decent, hopefully'. She has a big extended family within a few miles, and Saturday mornings often mean a quick call round to her mum's.
- professional persona: Meticulous and proud of her work. She measures twice, keeps every receipt, and quotes honestly even when it loses her a job. She won't cut corners on springing or webbing because 'it's somebody's nan's chair'. Customers like her because she's chatty and straight with them. She frets privately about late payments and slow months, and puts money aside every month for her tax bill.
- sports persona: Not sporty in a competitive sense. She walks Mabel every morning before work and goes to a Tuesday night Zumba class at the community centre with her sister-in-law, mostly for the laugh. She follows the rugby league a bit because Darren does and will go to the odd Batley Bulldogs game.
- arts persona: She has a good eye for fabric and colour and loves looking at textiles in heritage houses and museums. She watches a lot of telly: The Repair Shop (which she critiques), Gogglebox and crime dramas. She sings along loudly to 90s pop in the workshop and went to see Take That with her friends last year.
- travel persona: Usually takes a week in a caravan or cottage on the Yorkshire coast (Filey or Whitby), plus one sunshine holiday every couple of years, generally Spain or Majorca. She plans holidays well in advance with a spreadsheet and gets anxious about flights and connections. She'd like to see Italy properly one day.
- culinary persona: Plain, reliable home cooking. Tea is on the table at six: shepherd's pie, chilli, a roast on Sundays with proper Yorkshire puddings she's quietly competitive about. She batch-cooks and freezes on Sunday afternoons. She likes a curry out in Dewsbury or Bradford for birthdays and will have a glass of rosé on a Friday.
- hobbies and interests: Dog walking with Mabel, Tuesday Zumba class, Charity-shop and car-boot hunting for old chairs to restore, Watching The Repair Shop and Gogglebox, Keeping the front garden tidy, hanging baskets in summer, Quizzes at the local pub once a month with friends, Following Batley Bulldogs loosely
- skills: Traditional and modern upholstery (springing, stuffing, buttoning, piping), Pattern cutting and fabric matching, Industrial sewing machine operation and basic maintenance, Accurate quoting and bookkeeping, Customer relations and plain-speaking advice, Organising and planning (household calendar keeper)
- career goals: To keep the business steady and debt-free until she's ready to wind down. She'd like to take on an apprentice in the next few years and pass on what she knows properly, because she worries the trade is dying out. She sometimes thinks about running weekend beginner upholstery workshops but worries she's not 'a teacher'.
- voice: Warm, quick and talkative, with a West Yorkshire accent: flat vowels, 'love' now and then, 'tea' for the evening meal, 'mum' not 'mam'. She uses 'erm' when thinking and 'sort of' a lot ('it's sort of a mid-century style'), and finishes points with 'you know' or 'do you know what I mean'. Says 'sorry' to correct herself mid-sentence ('it were Tuesday — sorry, Wednesday'). Occasionally uses 'were' for 'was' when relaxed. She dislikes silence and will fill a pause with a little laugh or 'anyway, I'm rambling'. If asked something she doesn't know, she says so straight out rather than guessing.
- typing: Proper sentences with capital letters and full stops, apostrophes in the right places; she checks before submitting. Occasionally starts with 'Hi' even in a form. Uses 'etc' and the odd '!' but no text abbreviations. Short answers are still complete sentences, e.g. 'I'd say fairly satisfied, but it depends on the month to be honest.'
- with strangers: Friendly and open almost immediately. She asks questions back and makes small jokes about herself. Underneath she is a bit anxious about doing it 'right', so she might check she's understood a question or apologise for going off on a tangent. She comes across as genuine, unpretentious and trustworthy.
- small things: Mabel has started snoring louder than Darren, A customer brought in a 1960s armchair still with the original label, The price of fabric has gone up again, Zumba was a laugh but her knees felt it, Lewis is coming for his tea Sunday, She's trying to cut back on biscuits at the workshop, The hanging baskets need watering every day in this weather
- deeper things: She worries about her mum, who's 76 and getting forgetful, She sometimes feels she missed out by not going to college properly and is quietly proud her son went to university, A difficult year when the business nearly folded during the pandemic and she barely slept, She feels the trade is undervalued and gets upset when people expect cheap rush jobs, She and Darren are still close, and she says marrying him was the best decision she ever made, She cries easily at films and sad news and is a bit embarrassed about it
- webcam photo: Laptop webcam shot from slightly below eye level, taken at her kitchen table in the early evening. Warm overhead light and some daylight from a window to her left. Head and shoulders are centred, slightly close to the camera. She has a round, friendly face with light freckles, faint lines at the eyes, and a wide open smile showing her teeth. Her shoulder-length dark blonde hair has visible lighter highlights and is pulled back loosely in a clip, with a few strands loose. She wears red-framed reading glasses pushed up on her head and a navy zip-up fleece over a grey T-shirt. Behind her is a cream kitchen wall with a calendar covered in handwritten notes, a magnetic knife rack, and the edge of a white fridge with photos and a dog-shaped magnet. A small window ledge holds a potted basil plant and a mug. The tip of a dog bed is just visible in the bottom corner.

P071 (Jibin; transcript label: Jibin):
- first name: Jibin
- age: 43
- lives in: Bradley Stoke, near Bristol, South West England
- occupation: Senior systems engineer (embedded software) at an aerospace and defence supplier in Filton
- education detail: BTech in Electronics and Communication Engineering from an engineering college in Kottayam, Kerala; MSc in Embedded Systems from a university in the south of England, completed after moving to the UK at 24; chartered engineer status gained in his thirties
- household: Lives in a four-bedroom new-build detached house with his wife Liza (41, a ward manager at Southmead Hospital, also from Kerala) and their two children, Aaron (12) and Ann (9). His mother visits from Kerala for a few months most years.

Came to the UK on a student visa in 2005, stayed on through work visas and is now a British citizen. Speaks Malayalam at home with Liza and his mother, English with the kids, who reply almost entirely in English. The family attends a Malayalam-language Mass held monthly at a Catholic church in Bristol, and an English Mass at their local parish the other Sundays. He goes more out of habit, family duty and community connection than deep devotion, though he would not say that at church.
- professional persona: Technically strong and knows it. Works on flight-control software verification and is the person people go to when a test rig behaves oddly. - sports persona: Grew up mad about cricket and still follows India closely, watching Test matches on his phone at odd hours. Watches Somerset occasionally at Taunton with a couple of Malayali friends. Plays badminton on Thursday evenings at a leisure centre in a mixed group, where he is competitive and argues line calls. Took up running during lockdown and does Saturday parkrun at Little Stoke now and then, mostly because his GP mentioned his cholesterol.
- arts persona: Not a gallery person. Watches Malayalam films on streaming services with Liza, and is quite opinionated about which recent ones are overrated. Likes old Malayalam film songs in the car. Will sit through the kids' school concerts but checks his phone. Reads the odd thriller or popular science book on holiday.

Otherwise does short European holidays: Algarve, Tenerife, a Christmas markets trip to Kraków. Likes to plan the itinerary himself and gets irritable when plans slip. Has firm views on which Bristol Indian restaurants are 'not real Kerala food'. Drinks a beer or a whisky with friends at weekends. Does a big shop at Tesco Extra and a monthly run to an Asian grocer on Stapleton Road.
- hobbies and interests: Badminton on Thursday nights, Following Indian cricket and the IPL, Occasional parkrun, Tinkering with home automation: smart thermostat, Raspberry Pi projects, Keeping the car clean (a fairly new BMW 3 Series he is pleased with), Reading tech and finance news, checking his investment ISA more often than is useful, Malayali association events, mainly Onam and Christmas
- skills: C and C++ for embedded systems, Software verification and test for safety-critical systems (DO-178C), Debugging hardware-software integration problems, Python scripting for test automation, Reading contracts and payslips very carefully, Barbecuing and making a Kerala beef fry, Fluent Malayalam, good Hindi, fluent English
- career goals: Wants to move into a principal engineer or technical lead role within the next two to three years, partly for the money and partly because he feels he is overdue. You write transcripts of realistic video calls between strangers for a fully synthetic research dataset set in the UK. The study, in order (from its published design): a short puzzle task done alone; first impressions of the others' webcam photos; then a series of three-minute, one-on-one video calls in rounds, each person meeting the others in their group; after each call a short survey.

Call shape (from the original study's numbers): a call is cut off by a three-minute timer. A typical call has about 30 turns (most between 20 and 39) and about 570 words in total (most between 440 and 682); half of all turns are 12 words or fewer, and a quarter are 24 or more. Short acknowledgements ("yeah", "mm") count as turns too. So aim for about 570 words in about 30 turns: alongside the quick back-and-forth, people often talk in longer stretches (explaining their job, telling a story), and those long turns carry much of the call.

Guide to British conversational English (use it for how people talk; it is a description of speech, not a script):
How British people talk in casual conversation. This is a paraphrase of published descriptions of spoken British English; sources are in SOURCES.md. Use these features lightly and only where they fit the person. Never use them as a caricature.

- **Fillers.** British speakers hesitate with "erm" and "er". Women and younger speakers lean towards "erm".
- **Hedges.** "Sort of" is everywhere and steady. "Kind of" is spreading, and younger speakers use it more.
- **Politeness words.** "Please", "thank you", "thanks" and "sorry" mostly mean what they say. "Sorry" also works as a repair word (to correct yourself, or to ask someone to repeat) and can be ironic.
- **Tags at the end of a sentence.** "You know", "right", "okay", "yeah", "do you know what I mean". Among young Londoners, "innit" and "you get me" are rising. Tags depend on age and region only, never on ethnicity.
- **Echoing.** In an engaged conversation people pick up and re-use parts of each other's words.
- **Regional words and grammar** (from a recent dialect survey):
  - A bread roll is a "barm" in the North West (Manchester to Liverpool and western Lancashire), a "cob" around Nottinghamshire, a "bap" in Staffordshire, the West Midlands and North Wales, and a "batch" in Liverpool and Coventry.
  - Around Liverpool an ice lolly can be a "lolly ice".
  - The evening meal is "tea" in the North West, North East and Yorkshire, and "dinner" in the South East and London. Some people say both.
  - "Yous" or "youse" for plural "you" is common in the North East (Newcastle, Teesside), Liverpool and Scotland, less so in Manchester, and rare in York, Leeds and Sheffield.
  - "Give it me" is normal in the North West and West Midlands and widely accepted in Sheffield and York; it fades south of Birmingham, Coventry and Leicester.
  - "You was" is widely used, historically Northern and now found as far south as London.
- **Everyday British words** to draw on where they fit, without assigning them to regions: knackered or shattered, chuffed or made up, skint or brassic, mardy or stroppy, mum or mam, mate or pal, settee, sofa or couch.

req.text:
You write transcripts of realistic video calls between strangers for a fully synthetic research dataset set in the UK. The study, in order (from its published design): a short puzzle task done alone; first impressions of the others' webcam photos; then a series of three-minute, one-on-one video calls in rounds, each person meeting the others in their group; after each call a short survey.

Call shape (from the original study's numbers): a call is cut off by a three-minute timer. A typical call has about 30 turns (most between 20 and 39) and about 570 words in total (most between 440 and 682); half of all turns are 12 words or fewer, and a quarter are 24 or more. Short acknowledgements ("yeah", "mm") count as turns too. So aim for about 570 words in about 30 turns: alongside the quick back-and-forth, people often talk in longer stretches (explaining their job, telling a story), and those long turns carry much of the call.

Guide to British conversational English (use it for how people talk; it is a description of speech, not a script):
How British people talk in casual conversation. This is a paraphrase of published descriptions of spoken British English; sources are in SOURCES.md. Use these features lightly and only where they fit the person. Never use them as a caricature.

- **Fillers.** British speakers hesitate with "erm" and "er". Women and younger speakers lean towards "erm".
- **Hedges.** "Sort of" is everywhere and steady. "Kind of" is spreading, and younger speakers use it more.
- **Politeness words.** "Please", "thank you", "thanks" and "sorry" mostly mean what they say. "Sorry" also works as a repair word (to correct yourself, or to ask someone to repeat) and can be ironic.
- **Tags at the end of a sentence.** "You know", "right", "okay", "yeah", "do you know what I mean". Among young Londoners, "innit" and "you get me" are rising. Tags depend on age and region only, never on ethnicity.
- **Echoing.** In an engaged conversation people pick up and re-use parts of each other's words.
- **Regional words and grammar** (from a recent dialect survey):
  - A bread roll is a "barm" in the North West (Manchester to Liverpool and western Lancashire), a "cob" around Nottinghamshire, a "bap" in Staffordshire, the West Midlands and North Wales, and a "batch" in Liverpool and Coventry.
  - Around Liverpool an ice lolly can be a "lolly ice".
  - The evening meal is "tea" in the North West, North East and Yorkshire, and "dinner" in the South East and London. Some people say both.
  - "Yous" or "youse" for plural "you" is common in the North East (Newcastle, Teesside), Liverpool and Scotland, less so in Manchester, and rare in York, Leeds and Sheffield.
  - "Give it me" is normal in the North West and West Midlands and widely accepted in Sheffield and York; it fades south of Birmingham, Coventry and Leicester.
  - "You was" is widely used, historically Northern and now found as far south as London.
- **Everyday British words** to draw on where they fit, without assigning them to regions: knackered or shattered, chuffed or made up, skint or brassic, mardy or stroppy, mum or mam, mate or pal, settee, sofa or couch.

The group (session S16). Persona cards, including the webcam photo each person was rated on:

P079 (Tomasz; transcript label: Tomasz):
- first name: Tomasz
- age: 37
- lives in: Exeter, South West England
- occupation: Full-time mature undergraduate (BA Archaeology, second year) who also works about 22 hours a week as a machine operator on a packing line at a food manufacturing plant on an industrial estate on the edge of Exeter, mostly weekend and evening shifts
- education detail: Finished technical secondary school (technikum) in mechanics in Lublin, Poland. Did one year of a history degree there before dropping out and moving to the UK at 22. Took an Access to HE course at Exeter College in his mid-thirties and is now a second-year Archaeology student at the University of Exeter, funded by a student loan and his shift work.
- household: Lives with his wife Hannah, 35, who is British and works as a hospital pharmacist at the Royal Devon and Exeter. They have no children and rent a two-bedroom terraced house in St Thomas, Exeter. Her salary carries most of the household. The spare room is half study and half where the laundry ends up.
- cultural background: Born and raised in Lublin, eastern Poland, in a Catholic family. His dad was a bus mechanic and his mum worked in a school canteen. He came to Exeter in 2009 because a friend had factory work lined up, and he stayed. He met Hannah at a pub quiz in 2014 and they married in 2017, with a church service in Poland and a registry office do in Devon. He still calls himself Catholic. He goes to the Polish Mass now and then, more at Christmas and Easter, and mostly because it matters to his mum. He speaks Polish on the phone home every Sunday and English everywhere else.
- professional persona: Has been in factory and warehouse work for fifteen years: packing, forklift, then running and minding machines on a line. He's good with the machines but not much of a stickler for paperwork, and he admits his checklists are sometimes filled in afterwards. He's quiet on shift, gets on with it, and is known as the one who can clear a jam without calling an engineer. At university he is the older bloke at the back of the seminar who doesn't say much, but whose essays are interesting and usually handed in on the deadline night.
- sports persona: Not sporty in a team sense. He walks a lot, mostly long rambling walks on Dartmoor or along the Exe estuary, usually alone or with Hannah. He follows Polish football loosely and will watch a Poland international in the pub. Otherwise he couldn't tell you the Premier League table.
- arts persona: Reads widely and erratically. He has three or four books on the go at once, a mix of history, odd non-fiction about landscapes and some Polish science fiction (Lem, mainly). He likes documentaries and slow European films. He goes to the RAMM museum in Exeter more than anyone reasonably should. He doesn't play an instrument but listens to old Polish rock and ambient stuff while studying.
- travel persona: Goes back to Lublin once or twice a year, usually driving the long way or flying from Bristol. He prefers trips with something old to look at: they did Orkney for the Neolithic sites and want to do Crete. He doesn't plan much and books things last minute, which annoys Hannah.
- culinary persona: Cooks Polish food when he has the energy, like żurek, pierogi at Christmas and bigos that lasts a week. Otherwise it's pasta and whatever's in the fridge. He shops at the Polish shop on Cowick Street for proper bread and kiełbasa. He's picked up a fondness for a Devon cream tea, though he still argues about cream-first.
- hobbies and interests: walking on Dartmoor and looking at stone rows and hut circles, local history and old maps, reading Stanisław Lem and popular history, documentaries, metal detecting rules and debates (he's thought about it but never bought a detector), visiting museums, Sunday phone calls with family in Poland
- skills: operating and troubleshooting packing machinery, forklift licence (counterbalance), bilingual Polish and English, basic GIS mapping from his course, reading landscapes and old field boundaries, patient, careful listening
- career goals: Would like to get into field archaeology or heritage work after his degree, ideally with a commercial archaeology unit or something like the National Trust in Devon or Cornwall. He knows the pay is poor and that he'll be nearly 40 starting out. He's vague on the details and hasn't really looked into a master's yet, but he wants to be out of factory work within a couple of years.
- voice: Fluent, fairly relaxed English with a clear Polish accent, softened by fifteen years in Devon. He speaks at a steady, slightly slow pace and thinks before answering. He uses 'erm' a fair bit and 'sort of' as a hedge, and sometimes says 'you know' at the end of a point. He occasionally drops an article or puts a word in an unusual order when he's tired, and corrects himself with 'sorry, I mean...'. He has picked up 'mate', 'knackered' and 'proper' without thinking about it. He doesn't fill silences. He'll just wait, or say 'yeah... I don't know' and leave it there. He warms up and talks more if the topic is history or landscapes.
- typing: Mostly lowercase and quick. He capitalises names and 'I' inconsistently, and often leaves apostrophes out (dont, its, im). He uses commas instead of full stops and rarely ends with a full stop at all. Answers are short unless the question interests him, and then he writes a long run-on paragraph. He makes the odd typo and doesn't go back to fix it.
- with strangers: Reserved and a bit guarded at first. He's polite and gives short answers, and he doesn't ask much back early on. He's not unfriendly, just quiet, and comes across as thoughtful rather than shy. A dry sense of humour shows up after ten minutes or so. He opens up noticeably if you ask about something he's curious about.
- small things: the night shift last week was knackering because a machine kept jamming, he's behind on an essay about Bronze Age burial practices, the Polish shop ran out of the good rye bread, it rained the whole walk on Saturday but he didn't mind, Hannah's on lates this week so he's been eating toast for dinner, he still hasn't sorted out the spare room, the buses into campus are always late
- deeper things: he feels a bit embarrassed being a student at 37 with younger classmates and a wife who earns far more than him, he worries he left it too late and the archaeology plan is a fantasy, dropping out of university in Poland still bothers him, and his dad never quite understood why he left, he and Hannah have talked about children and haven't decided, and it's a sore point sometimes, his faith is more about family and habit than belief now, and he hasn't told his mum that, after Brexit he felt for a while that he didn't belong anywhere, and he only applied for settled status at the last minute
- webcam photo: Laptop webcam at a slight upward angle, so the framing is from mid-chest up and a bit of ceiling shows at the top. Light comes from a window to his left, giving soft daylight on one side of his face, with the other side a little shadowed. He has a broad, pale face with light stubber-length brown stubble and short dark-blond hair that's slightly messy, as if he's run a hand through it. He wears thin rectangular black-framed glasses. His expression is neutral and attentive, with a faint polite half-smile and his eyes looking at the screen just below the camera. He's wearing a faded navy hoodie with the cord missing on one side. Behind him is the spare room: a white wall with a cheap pine bookshelf crammed with paperbacks, some lying flat on top of others, a few in Polish, and a stack of library books with University of Exeter barcode stickers. An Ordnance Survey Dartmoor map is pinned to the wall with a corner curling. A clothes airer with a couple of T-shirts on it is partly visible at the right edge of the frame, and a mug sits on the shelf at shoulder height.

P080 (Lorraine; transcript label: Lorraine A):
- first name: Lorraine
- age: 43
- lives in: Wednesbury, West Midlands
- occupation: Not currently in paid work; until about eighteen months ago she was a sewing machinist at a small upholstery and soft-furnishings firm in Darlaston, which shut down. She signs up for online surveys for a bit of extra money.

- household: Lives in a three-bed ex-council semi with her husband Gary (46), an HGV fitter at a haulage depot near the M6, and their son Kieran (15), who is in Year 10. They also have an elderly Staffie cross called Bella.
- cultural background: White British, born and raised in the Black Country. Her parents still live two streets away in Wednesbury; her dad worked in a foundry and her mum did cleaning jobs. Not religious, though she was christened and married in a register office. Her family is close in a bickering way and she sees her mum most days.

She had little patience for supervisors and fell out with one manager for good. She hasn't looked hard for a new job. She's half-heartedly applied for a couple of warehouse and school kitchen jobs and finds application forms and interviews stressful. She worries about money more than she lets on, but she also can't face starting somewhere new with people she doesn't know.

- arts persona: Watches a lot of telly: soaps (Coronation Street, EastEnders), true crime documentaries, and reality shows she claims to hate but watches anyway. Doesn't read much beyond magazines and Facebook. Has no interest in theatre or galleries. She did like drawing at school and sometimes still doodles on the backs of envelopes.
- travel persona: Prefers places she knows. They've had caravan holidays in Wales (Tenby, Prestatyn) for years and went to Tenerife twice. She gets nervous about flying and airports and would happily go back to the same caravan park every year. Gary is the one who suggests anywhere new.

Doesn't like spicy food or trying new places, and gets irritated if Kieran turns his nose up at what she's made.
- hobbies and interests: Walking the dog by the canal, Soaps and true crime documentaries, Scrolling local Facebook groups and occasionally arguing in the comments, Altering and mending clothes on her old Singer, Scratchcards now and then, Doing online surveys
- skills: Fast, accurate industrial and domestic sewing, Pattern adjustment and alterations, Knowing exactly what things cost and where they're cheapest, Spotting when someone's being fobbed off and calling it out, Driving (has a licence, drives Gary's old Corsa)
- career goals: Nothing ambitious. She'd like something part-time and local, ideally on her own doing alterations from home, but she hasn't done anything to set it up. Mostly she wants enough money coming in that she stops lying awake about bills.
- voice: A mild Black Country/West Midlands accent, broadly local but not broad dialect. Medium-quick when she's annoyed or on a topic she cares about, slower and flatter when she's unsure. Says 'erm' a lot at the start of answers and uses 'sort of' as a hedge. Says things like 'give it me', 'tea' for her evening meal, 'bap' for a roll, 'our Kieran', 'me mum', and sometimes 'you was'. Ends sentences with 'you know' or 'do you know what I mean'. Gives short answers to questions she sees as pointless and can be blunt, saying 'I don't see what that's got to do with anything' or 'that's a daft question, sorry'. Lets silences hang rather than filling them, then might add a sudden worried afterthought.
- typing: Mostly lower case and often no capital at the start. Few full stops, with commas or nothing between thoughts. Apostrophes are hit and miss ('dont', 'its' for it's). Uses 'tbh', 'idk' and 'lol' occasionally. Answers are short and to the point, sometimes just 'no' or 'not really'. When something bothers her she writes a longer, run-on paragraph.
- with strangers: Guarded and a bit prickly at first, and can come across as unfriendly or bored. She doesn't do much small talk, answers what she's asked and no more, and is quick to say if she thinks something's a waste of time. She's visibly nervous underneath, fidgeting and checking whether she's 'doing it right'. She warms up a little if the other person seems straightforward and not posh or patronising, but she never gushes.
- small things: Bella the dog needing letting out mid-call, The price of electric and food shopping going up, Something annoying a neighbour has done with their bins or parking, What happened on Corrie last night, Kieran leaving his stuff everywhere, Popping round to her mum's, The weather and whether it's worth taking the washing out
- deeper things: She feels lost since the firm shut and misses having somewhere to be, though she wouldn't put it that way, She lies awake worrying about money and whether Gary's job is safe, She has a long-running fallout with her younger sister that she's never got over, She worries a lot about Kieran, about his mates, his phone and whether he's happy, and cries more than anyone would guess, She sometimes thinks she wasted her chance at the fashion course
- webcam photo: Laptop webcam, slightly below face level so the angle looks up a little. She's sitting on a settee in a front room, framed from mid-chest up and a bit off-centre to the left. Light comes from a window to her right with net curtains, so that side of her face is brighter and the other side is in mild shadow. White woman in her early forties with a fair, slightly flushed complexion and fine lines around her eyes. Her expression is neutral to wary, lips pressed together, eyebrows slightly raised as if waiting to be told what to do. Shoulder-length dyed dark-brown hair with a little grey showing at the parting, pulled back in a loose clip with strands falling at the front. No glasses. She's wearing a grey zip-up hoodie over a black T-shirt and small silver hoop earrings. Behind her is a magnolia wall with a large canvas print of a family photo (her, a man and a teenage boy on a beach), part of a wall-mounted TV at the edge of the frame, a beige throw over the back of the settee, and the top of a dog's head with brown and white fur resting on a cushion beside her.

P081 (Colin; transcript label: Colin):
- first name: Colin
- age: 71
- lives in: Worthing, South East England
- occupation: Retired joiner and carpenter (worked in the trade for about 45 years, mostly self-employed, finished up around 66)
- education detail: Left a secondary modern in Shoreham at 16; did a four-year apprenticeship with a local building firm and got his City & Guilds in carpentry and joinery at day release. - household: Lives with his wife Maureen (69, retired school receptionist) in a 1930s semi they bought in 1986. - arts persona: Likes jazz, mostly the older stuff like Dave Brubeck and Miles Davis, which he got into through a mate in the seventies, and he'll listen to anything once. - travel persona: Late starter. Barely went abroad until his forties, but now loves it. Has been to Spain several times, including a trip to Granada he still talks about, and did a coach tour of Portugal. Prefers wandering about a town with no fixed plan to organised itineraries, which occasionally leads to missed trains. Would like to see Japan 'before the knees go', mainly for the wooden temples and the joinery.

- skills: Carpentry and joinery, including staircases and sash window repair, Woodturning, General DIY and fixing things for neighbours, Patient teaching of practical skills, A bit of conversational Spanish, Getting on with almost anyone
- career goals: None really. He's happily retired. He'd like to spend more time teaching woodwork, maybe at a men's shed or volunteering with a youth project, and has 'been meaning to look into it' for about two years. Mostly wants to keep healthy, travel a bit more and be around for the grandkids.

Colin: Hello, mate. Colin, down in Worthing. Can you hear me alright?

Tomasz: I'm doing it at thirty-seven, so. Maybe it's never too late. Or maybe it is, I'll tell you in two years.
Colin: Ha. What got you into it, then?
Tomasz: Erm, it's a long answer. In Lublin there's the old town and a castle on the hill, and my grandmother used to take me round and tell me who was killed where, which for a child is very exciting. I started history at university there, then I left, came here for factory work, and I thought, okay, that's finished. Fifteen years. Then Hannah, my wife, she sort of pushed me to do the Access course at the college. And now I'm here.
Colin: That's not a long answer, that's a good answer.
Tomasz: Thank you. You were a builder?
Colin: Joiner. Kitchens, staircases, doors. My favourite was old sash windows, though, restoring them. You open one up and you can see how some bloke did it in eighteen-ninety, and he did it better than me, usually.
Tomasz: That's archaeology too, a bit. Reading a building.
Colin: Is it? I'll put it on my CV.
Tomasz: Really. In old buildings they look at how the timber was cut, the tool marks, and it helps to date it.
Colin: Tool marks, yeah. I did a job on a church roof once, years ago, and you could see the adze marks on the beams, every one a bit different. Somebody's whole week, that beam.
Tomasz: Mm. Somebody's whole life, maybe, that roof.
Colin: That's it. That's why I want to see Japan, the old wooden temples. Before the knees go.
Tomasz: Hannah wants Crete. Knossos. I want it too, but she wants the beach as well.
Colin: Oh, you can do both. We did Granada, the Alhambra. I've never seen anything like it. All that carved plaster, it's like lace.
Tomasz: When were you there?
Colin: Ooh, er, let me think. Twenty-twelve? Thirteen? Not the most organised with dates. We missed the train back to Málaga, I remember that.
Tomasz: I don't plan either. I book everything last minute. Hannah gets very angry.
Colin: Maureen too. Thirty-odd years she's been angry, and I've still not learnt.
Tomasz: Good. So there's no hope for me. That's relaxing.
Colin: Ha, none at all, mate. What are you reading at the minute, apart from all the uni stuff?
Tomasz: Lem, again. Polish science fiction. And a book about old field boundaries, which sounds boring, but it's not.
Colin: I'd read that. I've got three library books on the go and I'll finish one, if I'm lucky.
Tomasz: I have four. I think the library is worried about me.
Colin: They'll send someone round. What's the field boundary one, is it —

You write transcripts of realistic video calls between strangers for a fully synthetic research dataset set in the UK. The study, in order (from its published design): a short puzzle task done alone; first impressions of the others' webcam photos; then a series of three-minute, one-on-one video calls in rounds, each person meeting the others in their group; after each call a short survey.

Call shape (from the original study's numbers): a call is cut off by a three-minute timer. A typical call has about 30 turns (most between 20 and 39) and about 570 words in total (most between 440 and 682); half of all turns are 12 words or fewer, and a quarter are 24 or more. Short acknowledgements ("yeah", "mm") count as turns too. So aim for about 570 words in about 30 turns: alongside the quick back-and-forth, people often talk in longer stretches (explaining their job, telling a story), and those long turns carry much of the call.

Guide to British conversational English (use it for how people talk; it is a description of speech, not a script):
How British people talk in casual conversation. This is a paraphrase of published descriptions of spoken British English; sources are in SOURCES.md. Use these features lightly and only where they fit the person. Never use them as a caricature.

- **Fillers.** British speakers hesitate with "erm" and "er". Women and younger speakers lean towards "erm".
- **Hedges.** "Sort of" is everywhere and steady. "Kind of" is spreading, and younger speakers use it more.
- **Politeness words.** "Please", "thank you", "thanks" and "sorry" mostly mean what they say. "Sorry" also works as a repair word (to correct yourself, or to ask someone to repeat) and can be ironic.
- **Tags at the end of a sentence.** "You know", "right", "okay", "yeah", "do you know what I mean". Among young Londoners, "innit" and "you get me" are rising. Tags depend on age and region only, never on ethnicity.
- **Echoing.** In an engaged conversation people pick up and re-use parts of each other's words.
- **Regional words and grammar** (from a recent dialect survey):
  - A bread roll is a "barm" in the North West (Manchester to Liverpool and western Lancashire), a "cob" around Nottinghamshire, a "bap" in Staffordshire, the West Midlands and North Wales, and a "batch" in Liverpool and Coventry.
  - Around Liverpool an ice lolly can be a "lolly ice".
  - The evening meal is "tea" in the North West, North East and Yorkshire, and "dinner" in the South East and London. Some people say both.
  - "Yous" or "youse" for plural "you" is common in the North East (Newcastle, Teesside), Liverpool and Scotland, less so in Manchester, and rare in York, Leeds and Sheffield.
  - "Give it me" is normal in the North West and West Midlands and widely accepted in Sheffield and York; it fades south of Birmingham, Coventry and Leicester.
  - "You was" is widely used, historically Northern and now found as far south as London.
- **Everyday British words** to draw on where they fit, without assigning them to regions: knackered or shattered, chuffed or made up, skint or brassic, mardy or stroppy, mum or mam, mate or pal, settee, sofa or couch.

You write transcripts of realistic video calls between strangers for a fully synthetic research dataset set in the UK. The study, in order (from its published design): a short puzzle task done alone; first impressions of the others' webcam photos; then a series of three-minute, one-on-one video calls in rounds, each person meeting the others in their group; after each call a short survey.

Call shape (from the original study's numbers): a call is cut off by a three-minute timer. A typical call has about 30 turns (most between 20 and 39) and about 570 words in total (most between 440 and 682); half of all turns are 12 words or fewer, and a quarter are 24 or more. Short acknowledgements ("yeah", "mm") count as turns too. So aim for about 570 words in about 30 turns: alongside the quick back-and-forth, people often talk in longer stretches (explaining their job, telling a story), and those long turns carry much of the call.

Guide to British conversational English (use it for how people talk; it is a description of speech, not a script):
How British people talk in casual conversation. This is a paraphrase of published descriptions of spoken British English; sources are in SOURCES.md. Use these features lightly and only where they fit the person. Never use them as a caricature.

- **Fillers.** British speakers hesitate with "erm" and "er". Women and younger speakers lean towards "erm".
- **Hedges.** "Sort of" is everywhere and steady. "Kind of" is spreading, and younger speakers use it more.
- **Politeness words.** "Please", "thank you", "thanks" and "sorry" mostly mean what they say. "Sorry" also works as a repair word (to correct yourself, or to ask someone to repeat) and can be ironic.
- **Tags at the end of a sentence.** "You know", "right", "okay", "yeah", "do you know what I mean". Among young Londoners, "innit" and "you get me" are rising. Tags depend on age and region only, never on ethnicity.
- **Echoing.** In an engaged conversation people pick up and re-use parts of each other's words.
- **Regional words and grammar** (from a recent dialect survey):
  - A bread roll is a "barm" in the North West (Manchester to Liverpool and western Lancashire), a "cob" around Nottinghamshire, a "bap" in Staffordshire, the West Midlands and North Wales, and a "batch" in Liverpool and Coventry.
  - Around Liverpool an ice lolly can be a "lolly ice".
  - The evening meal is "tea" in the North West, North East and Yorkshire, and "dinner" in the South East and London. Some people say both.
  - "Yous" or "youse" for plural "you" is common in the North East (Newcastle, Teesside), Liverpool and Scotland, less so in Manchester, and rare in York, Leeds and Sheffield.
  - "Give it me" is normal in the North West and West Midlands and widely accepted in Sheffield and York; it fades south of Birmingham, Coventry and Leicester.
  - "You was" is widely used, historically Northern and now found as far south as London.
- **Everyday British words** to draw on where they fit, without assigning them to regions: knackered or shattered, chuffed or made up, skint or brassic, mardy or stroppy, mum or mam, mate or pal, settee, sofa or couch.

Craig: Hi. Craig.

Bethany: Pontefract. In Yorkshire. Sorry, I keep saying "in Yorkshire" like nobody knows where it is.
Craig: I didn't, to be honest. I'm in Woodley. Near Reading.
Bethany: Oh, right. Down south.
Craig: Ja. Originally South Africa, though. Durban.
Bethany: I thought your accent were different. That's a long way.
Craig: It is. Twenty-four years ago now.
Bethany: My husband's called Craig, actually. So that's, erm... that's easy to remember.
Craig: Good. Saves you writing it down.
Bethany: Ha. What do you do?
Craig: Structural engineer. Mostly refurbishment. Checking old buildings will stay up when people change them.
Bethany: Oh. That sounds really clever. I was a florist. The shop closed, so I'm not working at the minute.
Craig: Sorry to hear that. Was it a big shop?
Bethany: No, just a little one in Castleford. The man I spoke to earlier, Darren, he knew it. He used to drive past it.
Craig: I had Darren as well. Joiner. He wasn't keen on uPVC frames.
Bethany: Ha, no. He told me our back door's probably the hinges. Craig's been saying he'll look at it for ages.
Craig: He's probably right. Hinges drop, the door catches on the frame. Usually a few screws and some packing. Half an hour, if you've got the right screwdriver.
Bethany: Really? I might just do it myself, then. I'll look it up.
Craig: You'll be fine. Take a photo before you start, so you know how it went back.
Bethany: That's a good idea. Thank you.
Craig: Do you still do flowers at all? For yourself?
Bethany: Erm, a bit. I've got a little raised bed in the back. The peonies are coming through now, I check them every morning, which is a bit sad. And I press flowers and frame them. Them on the shelf behind me are mine.
Craig: They're nice. I thought they were bought.
Bethany: Everyone keeps saying that. Thank you. What do you do, when you're not working?
Craig: Cycle on Saturday mornings. Watch rugby. Cut the lawn more often than it needs. My daughter says I'm obsessed with it.
Bethany: How old is she?
Craig: Fifteen. She's in the school play next month. I go to all of them. I don't understand most of them, but I go.
Bethany: Aw, that's lovely. She'll remember that, you know. My dad came to everything when I was little. Even the rubbish nativity where I was a sheep.
Craig: Sounds like a strong performance.
Bethany: Ha, I had one line. Baa. I think I forgot it.
Craig: Easy to do under pressure. What are you having for dinner?
Bethany: Tea? Erm, sausage and mash. I've said that to everybody now, I'll have to actually make it.
Craig: Ja, I'm committed to chicken and rice. I've told three people.
Bethany: Ha. We'll both have to stick to it, then. Have you got far to go after this, or are you—

=== CALL C0182 ===

Darren: Sorry to hear that. Hope he's alright.
Lauren: Yeah, he's... we don't really know yet, they're doing tests. Anyway! Sorry, didn't mean to go there.
