req.text:
You write transcripts of realistic video calls between strangers for a fully synthetic research dataset set in the UK. The study, in order (from its published design): a short puzzle task done alone; first impressions of the others' webcam photos; then a series of three-minute, one-on-one video calls in rounds, each person meeting the others in their group; after each call a short survey.

Call shape (from the original study's numbers): a call is cut off by a three-minute timer. A typical call has about 30 turns (most between 20 and 39) and about 570 words in total (most between 440 and 682); half of all turns are 12 words or fewer, and a quarter are 24 or more. Short acknowledgements ("yeah", "mm") count as turns too. So aim for about 570 words in about 30 turns: alongside the quick back-and-forth, people often talk in longer stretches (explaining their job, telling a story), and those long turns carry much of the call.

Guide to British conversational English (use it for how people talk; it is a description of speech, not a script):
How British people talk in casual conversation. This is a paraphrase of published descriptions of spoken British English; sources are in SOURCES.md. Use these features lightly and only where they fit the person. Never use them as a caricature.

- **Fillers.** British speakers hesitate with "erm" and "er". Women and younger speakers lean towards "erm".
- **Hedges.** "Sort of" is everywhere and steady. "Kind of" is spreading, and younger speakers use it more.
- **Politeness words.** "Please", "thank you", "thanks" and "sorry" mostly mean what they say. "Sorry" also works as a repair word (to correct yourself, or to ask someone to repeat) and can be ironic.
- **Tags at the end of a sentence.** "You know", "right", "okay", "yeah", "do you know what I mean". Among young Londoners, "innit" and "you get me" are rising. Tags depend on age and region only, never on ethnicity.
- **Echoing.** In an engaged conversation people pick up and re-use parts of each other's words.
- **Regional words and grammar** (from a recent dialect survey):
  - A bread roll is a "barm" in the North West (Manchester to Liverpool and western Lancashire), a "cob" around Nottinghamshire, a "bap" in Staffordshire, the West Midlands and North Wales, and a "batch" in Liverpool and Coventry.
  - Around Liverpool an ice lolly can be a "lolly ice".
  - The evening meal is "tea" in the North West, North East and Yorkshire, and "dinner" in the South East and London. Some people say both.
  - "Yous" or "youse" for plural "you" is common in the North East (Newcastle, Teesside), Liverpool and Scotland, less so in Manchester, and rare in York, Leeds and Sheffield.
  - "Give it me" is normal in the North West and West Midlands and widely accepted in Sheffield and York; it fades south of Birmingham, Coventry and Leicester.
  - "You was" is widely used, historically Northern and now found as far south as London.
- **Everyday British words** to draw on where they fit, without assigning them to regions: knackered or shattered, chuffed or made up, skint or brassic, mardy or stroppy, mum or mam, mate or pal, settee, sofa or couch.

The group (session S18). Persona cards, including the webcam photo each person was rated on:

P090 (Liam; transcript label: Liam):
- first name: Liam
- age: 31
- lives in: Doncaster, Yorkshire and The Humber
- occupation: Part-time night shelf-stacker (replenishment assistant) at a large supermarket on the edge of town, about 25 hours a week over four nights
- education detail: Left secondary school in Doncaster at 16 with a handful of GCSEs, including a C in English and a D in maths. Did a year of a Level 1 construction course at the local college but didn't finish it. Has a forklift counterbalance certificate from an agency job a few years back, now lapsed.
- household: Lives alone in a rented one-bedroom first-floor flat in Bentley, which he has had for about four years. His mam lives fifteen minutes away and he sees her most Sundays.
- cultural background: White British, born and raised in Doncaster in a working-class family. His dad worked in a warehouse and his mam did school dinners. Has an older sister with two kids in Rotherham. Wasn't brought up religious and doesn't really think about it. Feels very local and has never lived anywhere else.
- professional persona: Reliable on shift and does what's asked, but doesn't push himself forward. Likes nights because it's quiet and nobody's breathing down his neck. Gets anxious when rotas change at short notice or when there's talk of restructuring. Gets on fine with the regular lads on his shift and keeps his head down with managers.
- sports persona: Follows Doncaster Rovers and goes to a few home games a season when money allows, usually with his brother-in-law. Watches Premier League on telly but isn't fussed who wins. Walks a lot, to and from town and round the lake at Sandall Beat, which keeps him fit without him calling it exercise.
- arts persona: Not really into arts. Watches the same few things: quiz shows, Gogglebox, YouTube clips of old football goals and fishing videos. Listens to whatever's on the radio in the warehouse. Has never been to a gallery and sees no reason to.
- travel persona: Hasn't been abroad since a family holiday to Benidorm as a teenager and doesn't have a valid passport. Goes to Cleethorpes or Skegness for a day out now and then. Gets a bit uneasy about the idea of flying and organising travel, and prefers places he knows.
- culinary persona: Plain eater. Has his tea when he wakes up in the afternoon: oven chips, sausages, beans, sometimes a microwave curry. Has a chippy tea on Fridays and a Sunday dinner at his mam's. Buys reduced stuff from work. Won't try anything too spicy or 'fancy'.
- hobbies and interests: Coarse fishing at local ponds and the canal, usually alone, Going to Doncaster Rovers home games occasionally, Playing FIFA/EA FC on his PlayStation, Long walks round town and Sandall Beat, Scratch cards (small amounts, he tries to keep it in check), Watching quiz shows like The Chase
- skills: Fast, accurate shelf replenishment and stock rotation, Basic forklift and pallet truck operation, Knowing the ins and outs of fishing baits and kit, Keeping a small flat tidy and running on a tight budget, Dependable timekeeping
- career goals: Would like more hours or a permanent full-time contract so money's less tight, maybe a step up to shift lead one day, but worries he'd find managing people stressful. Mostly wants stability rather than a big change.
- voice: Quietish, steady pace, a bit flat at first and warmer once he relaxes. Light South Yorkshire accent with shortened vowels, the odd dropped 'the' ('going to shop'), says 'tea' for his evening meal and 'mam' for his mum. Might say 'it were alright' or 'you was saying'. Uses 'er' and 'erm' when thinking, 'sort of' a fair bit, and ends things with 'you know' or 'do you know what I mean'. Says 'sorry, say that again?' if he doesn't catch a question. Uneasy with silence, so he'll fill it with 'yeah... so, er' or apologise for rambling.
- typing: Mostly lowercase, sometimes a capital at the start. Very little punctuation and often no full stop. Apostrophes hit and miss ('dont', 'its', but 'I'm' sometimes autocorrected). Short answers like 'yeah its ok', 'not really bothered tbh', 'work nights so dont get out much'. Occasional 'cos' and 'u'.
- with strangers: Polite and a bit guarded. Answers questions properly but briefly and doesn't volunteer much at first. Can seem nervous, laughs slightly to cover it, and checks he's giving the 'right' answer. Opens up a bit if the other person is friendly and talks about football or fishing.
- small things: Being knackered after a run of night shifts, His sleep pattern being all over the place, The price of fishing bait going up, Rovers' latest result, Getting reduced sandwiches at the end of his shift, The bloke downstairs playing music too loud in the afternoon, Popping to his mam's for Sunday dinner
- deeper things: Worries a lot about money and has had a couple of months where he was proper skint and borrowed off his mam, Feels a bit lonely living alone and working nights, and his mates from school have mostly settled down with kids, His dad died when he was 24 and he still finds it hard to talk about, Gets anxious and can't sleep before things like appointments or meetings at work, Would like a girlfriend but hasn't been out with anyone in a few years and feels awkward about it, Is a bit embarrassed he never finished his college course
- webcam photo: Laptop webcam at chest height, angled slightly upward, so the frame shows him from mid-chest up with a bit of ceiling. Lighting is a mix of grey daylight from a window to his left and a warm ceiling bulb, which leaves the right side of his face slightly shadowed. He has a pale complexion, light stubble and short mousy-brown hair clipped at the sides, a bit flat on top. Blue-grey eyes, no glasses, and a small polite closed-mouth smile with a slightly unsure look. He wears a plain navy hooded sweatshirt with the drawstrings uneven. Behind him is a magnolia wall with a framed Doncaster Rovers team photo slightly off-centre, the corner of a grey fabric settee with a folded fleece blanket on the arm, and a black PlayStation controller resting on it. A white door is partly open on the right edge of the frame, with a dark jacket hanging on a hook.

P091 (Gary; transcript label: Gary):
- first name: Gary
- age: 51
- lives in: Aldridge, Walsall, West Midlands
- occupation: Senior technical sales executive for an industrial fixings and fasteners distributor based on a trading estate in Walsall. He covers key accounts across the Midlands and is out on the road three or four days a week, regularly working 50 to 55 hours.
- education detail: Left school in Walsall at 16 with a handful of O-level-equivalent GCSEs. Did a BTEC National in mechanical engineering at the local college while working as a stores lad at an engineering firm. Later picked up company-paid sales training and an IOSH Managing Safely certificate. No degree, and he likes pointing out he's never needed one.
- household: Lives with his wife Karen (49, part-time receptionist at a dental practice) in a four-bed detached on a newish estate they moved to in 2016. Their son Liam (24) moved out last year and lives in Lichfield with his girlfriend. Their daughter Jade (21) is in her final year at Nottingham Trent and is home some weekends. There's a cockapoo called Bailey, who Karen mostly walks.
- cultural background: White British, born and raised in Walsall. His dad was a toolsetter and his mum worked in a school kitchen. Christened and married in the Church of England, and he ticks 'Christian' on forms, but he only goes to church for weddings, funerals and the odd carol service. He thinks of himself as working class done good and is quite proud of the move from a terrace in Bloxwich to a detached in Aldridge.
- professional persona: Confident, persuasive and very target-driven. He's good at reading what a buyer wants to hear and at keeping key contacts sweet with football tickets and lunches. He tends to round his numbers up and his problems down. He's been known to take a bit more credit for a won contract than he strictly earned, and he treats mileage and expenses as a perk to be optimised. Colleagues find him good company but don't fully trust him. He doesn't get rattled when a deal goes wrong, and he just moves on to the next one.
- sports persona: Lifelong Walsall FC fan who goes to a few home games a season and follows the rest on the radio. He also likes being seen at Villa Park in corporate hospitality when a supplier pays. Plays golf most Sunday mornings at a members' club near Sutton Coldfield, off a handicap of around 16. He describes it as 'about 14 on a good day' and isn't above a generous lie in the rough.
- arts persona: Not really his thing. He watches whatever's on the telly with Karen: Gogglebox, Line of Duty repeats, Strictly results night. He likes the odd Jason Statham film. He's been to see Peter Kay and a couple of tribute acts at the Grand Theatre in Wolverhampton. Music is mostly 80s and 90s stuff in the car: Simply Red, UB40, Oasis.
- travel persona: Two holidays a year, usually all-inclusive in Spain, Tenerife or Turkey. He likes a 'proper hotel' with a decent pool and lets people know when they've got an upgrade. He did Dubai once for his 50th and still brings it up. He isn't interested in wandering round old towns or museums and prefers to stick with what he knows will be good.
- culinary persona: Meat and two veg, a Sunday roast, a curry from the local on a Friday, and a carvery at the Toby when they can't be bothered. He'll have a bacon bap from the van on the trading estate. Karen does most of the cooking. He 'does the barbecue' in summer, which means standing over it with a lager. He orders steak whenever he's out on a supplier's card.
- hobbies and interests: Golf on Sundays with the same three mates, His car, a leased BMW 5 Series he keeps immaculately clean, Following Walsall FC, Watching Sky Sports football and the darts, Pub quiz at the local once a month, mainly for the sport and general knowledge rounds, Keeping the front lawn and drive looking smarter than the neighbours'
- skills: Relationship selling and closing deals, Product knowledge on industrial fixings, anchors and threaded products, Negotiating price and payment terms, Reading technical drawings and spec sheets at a practical level, Staying calm under pressure, Talking to just about anyone at a trade counter or a site office
- career goals: Wants to be made sales manager for the region before the current one retires, mainly for the bigger car allowance and the title. Failing that, he'd take a better-paid key account role with a competitor. He'd like to retire at 60 on a decent pension with the mortgage cleared, and he talks loosely about 'a place in Spain' without having looked into it properly.
- voice: Relaxed, chatty and a bit salesy. He talks at a steady pace and speeds up when he's on a topic he likes, such as cars, golf or work wins. He has a light Walsall/Black Country accent rather than a broad one. He uses 'mate' a lot, says 'give it me' and 'bap' naturally, and sometimes says 'tara' at the end of a call. His fillers are mostly 'er' and the odd 'erm', with 'sort of' as his main hedge. He tags sentences with 'you know' or 'yeah?' when he wants agreement. He's comfortable with silence because it doesn't bother him, and he'll often fill it with an anecdote that makes him look good. He sometimes says 'sorry' to repair a line, as in 'sorry, what was the question again?'
- typing: Quick and practical. He usually starts with a capital letter but doesn't always end with a full stop. Apostrophes are mostly there but he sometimes drops them ('dont', 'its'). He uses the odd 'tbh' and 'etc'. Answers are short and to the point. He might use 'lol' once, and he never uses emojis on a form. He occasionally typo-corrects and occasionally doesn't bother.
- with strangers: Instantly friendly and easy to talk to, with a firm handshake energy even over video. He's quick to find common ground, usually football or holidays, and drops in markers of success like the car, the house or the golf club. He comes across as confident, slightly showy and fun. He's not someone who'd open up emotionally, and he gives smooth, polished answers rather than reflective ones.
- small things: How bad the M6 was around junction 10 this morning, Getting the car valeted, Walsall's last result, His golf score, slightly improved, Bailey the dog chewing a slipper, Booking the next all-inclusive, How much the curry house has put its prices up, The van on the trading estate doing a decent bacon bap
- deeper things: He's a bit worried his pension pot isn't as big as he lets on, though he'd frame it as 'keeping an eye on it' rather than admit to worry, His dad died of a heart attack at 64 and Gary has quietly started having his blood pressure checked, He was passed over for the sales manager job once before and still resents the bloke who got it, Things with Karen are steady but a bit flat since the kids left, and they don't do much together apart from holidays, He's prouder of Jade going to university than he usually says, being the first in the family
- webcam photo: Head-and-shoulders shot from a laptop on a kitchen-diner table, camera angled slightly up at him. He's lit mainly by a large window off to his left, so the right side of his face is a little shadowed, with grey afternoon daylight. He has a broad, clean-shaven face with a slight tan and a confident half-smile. His hair is short, greying at the sides and thinning on top, with a bit of gel at the front. He's wearing a navy quarter-zip jumper with a small company logo on the chest and a white collar showing underneath, and no glasses. Behind him is a glossy grey kitchen with white quartz worktops, a Nespresso machine and a bowl of fruit. A large wall clock with Roman numerals hangs above a door to the hallway. On the island there's a set of BMW keys on a leather fob next to a phone face-down. Through the doorway a golf bag is just visible propped against the wall.

P092 (Akosua; transcript label: Akosua):
- first name: Akosua
- age: 38
- lives in: Thornton Heath, South London
- occupation: Not currently working. Until eight months ago she was an HR business partner at a housing association in Croydon. She was made redundant in a restructure and is now job hunting, slowly.
- education detail: Came to the UK from Ghana at 14 and did her GCSEs and A levels at a comprehensive in Croydon. BA in Business Studies from Kingston University, then a CIPD Level 5 HR qualification, studied part-time and paid for by an earlier employer.
- household: Lives in a three-bedroom terraced house with her mother, Grace (66, retired care worker), and her daughter, Esi (9). She has never married. Esi's father lives in Birmingham, sees Esi some school holidays and pays maintenance, mostly on time. Her younger brother Kwame stays over now and then and still has a room's worth of boxes in the loft.
- cultural background: Born in Kumasi, Ghana, and moved to London with her mum to join her aunt in the late 90s. Ghanaian at home: Twi with her mum, English with Esi. Otherwise thoroughly South London. Goes to a Pentecostal church in Croydon most Sundays with her mum, less because she is devout and more because it is family, routine and where all their friends are. Prays when she is worried, which is often.
- professional persona: Spent about twelve years in HR: employee relations, absence management, a lot of difficult conversations. People found her warm and easy to talk to, and she was good in the room, but her paperwork piled up and she relied on a very organised colleague to keep her on deadlines. The redundancy knocked her confidence badly. She has a half-updated CV and three tabs of job listings she keeps meaning to get through. She wants something like her old role, ideally in the public or housing sector, and is wary of anything that sounds like a big change.
- sports persona: Not sporty. Walks Esi to school and back and does the occasional walk round Norwood Grove with a friend, mostly to chat. Signed up for a gym twice and stopped going both times. Will watch the Ghana games at the Africa Cup of Nations with her brother, shouting at the telly.
- arts persona: Not really a culture person and doesn't pretend to be. Gospel music in the car and the kitchen, and old highlife her mum plays. Watches Nollywood and Ghanaian films on YouTube, plus whatever drama is on telly. Hasn't been to a museum since a school trip with Esi, and found it tiring.
- travel persona: Goes back to Ghana every couple of years for weddings, funerals and family, usually around Christmas. Gets anxious about flying and about the cost. Beyond that, one package holiday to Tenerife with friends years ago. Prefers going somewhere she knows rather than trying somewhere new.
- culinary persona: Cooks Ghanaian food at home with her mum: jollof, light soup, kontomire stew, fried plantain, waakye on Saturdays. Her mum does most of the proper cooking and Akosua does the quick weeknight stuff, including fish fingers and chips for Esi. Doesn't really like trying new cuisines. Orders Nando's or a takeaway when she can't be bothered, which is more often than she'd like.
- hobbies and interests: church women's fellowship, watching Ghanaian and Nigerian films on YouTube, WhatsApp family groups, doing her own and Esi's hair, reality TV, gospel music, browsing Facebook Marketplace
- skills: handling difficult conversations calmly, employee relations and absence policy, putting people at ease, speaking Twi, braiding hair, Microsoft Office basics
- career goals: Get back into an HR role, ideally employee relations at a council or housing association, part-time or hybrid so she can do the school run. She would like it sorted before her redundancy money runs out. She doesn't have a long-term plan beyond getting stable again.
- voice: London English with a soft Ghanaian lilt that comes through more when she's emotional or talking about home. Friendly, quite chatty once she warms up, mid-paced. She speeds up when anxious. Says 'erm' a lot and uses 'to be honest', 'you know' and the odd 'sort of'. Apologises a fair bit ('sorry, I'm going off topic'). Picks up the interviewer's words and repeats them back. Says 'dinner' for the evening meal. Doesn't like long silences and will fill them with a nervous laugh or 'is that okay, is that what you wanted?'

req.text:
You write transcripts of realistic video calls between strangers for a fully synthetic research dataset set in the UK. The study, in order (from its published design): a short puzzle task done alone; first impressions of the others' webcam photos; then a series of three-minute, one-on-one video calls in rounds, each person meeting the others in their group; after each call a short survey.

Call shape (from the original study's numbers): a call is cut off by a three-minute timer. A typical call has about 30 turns (most between 20 and 39) and about 570 words in total (most between 440 and 682); half of all turns are 12 words or fewer, and a quarter are 24 or more. Short acknowledgements ("yeah", "mm") count as turns too. So aim for about 570 words in about 30 turns: alongside the quick back-and-forth, people often talk in longer stretches (explaining their job, telling a story), and those long turns carry much of the call.

Guide to British conversational English (use it for how people talk; it is a description of speech, not a script):
How British people talk in casual conversation. This is a paraphrase of published descriptions of spoken British English; sources are in SOURCES.md. Use these features lightly and only where they fit the person. Never use them as a caricature.

- **Fillers.** British speakers hesitate with "erm" and "er". Women and younger speakers lean towards "erm".
- **Hedges.** "Sort of" is everywhere and steady. "Kind of" is spreading, and younger speakers use it more.
- **Politeness words.** "Please", "thank you", "thanks" and "sorry" mostly mean what they say. "Sorry" also works as a repair word (to correct yourself, or to ask someone to repeat) and can be ironic.
- **Tags at the end of a sentence.** "You know", "right", "okay", "yeah", "do you know what I mean". Among young Londoners, "innit" and "you get me" are rising. Tags depend on age and region only, never on ethnicity.
- **Echoing.** In an engaged conversation people pick up and re-use parts of each other's words.
- **Regional words and grammar** (from a recent dialect survey):
  - A bread roll is a "barm" in the North West (Manchester to Liverpool and western Lancashire), a "cob" around Nottinghamshire, a "bap" in Staffordshire, the West Midlands and North Wales, and a "batch" in Liverpool and Coventry.
  - Around Liverpool an ice lolly can be a "lolly ice".
  - The evening meal is "tea" in the North West, North East and Yorkshire, and "dinner" in the South East and London. Some people say both.
  - "Yous" or "youse" for plural "you" is common in the North East (Newcastle, Teesside), Liverpool and Scotland, less so in Manchester, and rare in York, Leeds and Sheffield.
  - "Give it me" is normal in the North West and West Midlands and widely accepted in Sheffield and York; it fades south of Birmingham, Coventry and Leicester.
  - "You was" is widely used, historically Northern and now found as far south as London.
- **Everyday British words** to draw on where they fit, without assigning them to regions: knackered or shattered, chuffed or made up, skint or brassic, mardy or stroppy, mum or mam, mate or pal, settee, sofa or couch.

The group (session S23). Persona cards, including the webcam photo each person was rated on:

P119 (Holly; transcript label: Holly):
- first name: Holly
- age: 25
- lives in: Kings Heath, Birmingham, West Midlands
- occupation: Full-time PhD student in Human Geography at the University of Birmingham, funded by a research council studentship. She is not currently in paid employment apart from occasional paid seminar teaching.
- education detail: A-levels in Geography, English Literature and Art at a sixth form college in Stafford. First-class BA in Geography at the University of Sheffield, then an MA in Cultural Geography at Birmingham. She is now in the second year of a PhD on how people use and reclaim disused canal-side industrial spaces.
- household: Lives with her husband Tom (27, a backend software developer for a fintech company, mostly working from home) in a rented two-bed Victorian terrace. They married two summers ago after meeting at university. No children, and a rescue greyhound called Pickle.
- cultural background: White British, born and raised in Stafford. Her mum is a primary school deputy head and her dad is a surveyor, and she has one younger brother at college. It was a comfortable, middle-class, fairly non-religious upbringing, with Sunday dinners at her nan's. She left religion blank on the census form because she 'didn't see why it mattered to them'.
- professional persona: She is a confident, chatty academic who is very good at conferences and networking, and much less good at actually finishing chapters. She is happy to present half-formed ideas as if they're polished, and she quietly enjoys being the one people remember after a panel. She has a habit of agreeing to every collaboration going and then leaning on her supervisor's goodwill when deadlines slip.
- sports persona: She isn't sporty in a structured way. She does a Tuesday night roller derby taster group with a friend, which is chaotic and she loves it, and she takes long dog walks round Highbury Park. She has a gym membership she uses about twice a month and keeps meaning to cancel.
- arts persona: She is a big gig-goer: small venues in Digbeth, festivals in summer, anything a bit odd or experimental. She goes to Ikon Gallery openings mostly for the free wine and the people. She paints badly but enthusiastically with cheap acrylics and has half-finished canvases stacked behind the settee. She reads widely and messily, with three novels on the go at once.
- travel persona: She is an impulsive traveller who books cheap flights on a whim and sorts out the details later. She has done Lisbon, Berlin, Kraków and a month interrailing after her degree, and she claims a conference trip to Montreal as 'basically a holiday'. She loves wandering unfamiliar cities without a plan and isn't bothered when things go wrong.
- culinary persona: An adventurous eater who will try anything once. She cooks big messy one-pot dishes and leaves the kitchen in a state. She is a regular at the balti places and street food markets around Birmingham. She still calls a bread roll a bap, and 'tea' and 'dinner' get used interchangeably at home.
- hobbies and interests: urban exploring and photographing derelict buildings, small gigs and festivals, roller derby taster sessions, amateur acrylic painting, charity shop and vintage clothes hunting, walking Pickle the greyhound, pub quizzes, where she is loudly confident even when wrong
- skills: public speaking and presenting, qualitative interviewing, getting strangers to open up quickly, talking her way into places (events, guest lists, upgrades), basic GIS mapping, film photography
- career goals: She wants a postdoc and eventually a lectureship, ideally somewhere with a bit of prestige. She is privately just as interested in becoming a 'public geographer' with a podcast or a popular book. Getting the thesis actually written on time is the obvious obstacle, and she knows it but doesn't lose sleep over it.
- voice: Warm, fast and quite loud, with a mild Staffordshire/Midlands accent that's been softened by university. Flat vowels come through more when she's relaxed. She uses 'erm' a fair bit and 'sort of' and 'kind of' constantly, often stacked together. She ends points with 'yeah?' or 'you know'. She occasionally says 'give it me' or 'you was' when she's not thinking about it. She laughs easily, echoes back phrases the interviewer uses, and will fill any silence herself almost immediately, often going off on a tangent before saying 'sorry, what was the question?'
- typing: Quick and sloppy. Mostly lowercase, with capitals only sometimes at the start. Apostrophes are usually dropped ('dont', 'im'). She uses lots of commas and no full stop at the end, and sometimes adds 'haha' or 'lol'. Abbreviations like 'tbh', 'idk' and 'uni'. She's prone to typos she doesn't fix.
- with strangers: Instantly friendly and easy to talk to. She asks you questions back, makes jokes early and gives the impression she's been looking forward to chatting. She comes across as relaxed and self-assured, maybe a touch showy about her travels or her PhD. She is very agreeable and won't push back on anything, though she'll happily embellish a story to make it better.
- small things: Pickle refusing to walk in the rain, a gig she went to in Digbeth last weekend, a charity shop find, like a 70s suede jacket for eight quid, the state of the number 50 bus, Tom's work calls echoing through the house, having a conference coming up she hasn't written the paper for yet, her nan's Sunday dinners back in Stafford
- deeper things: She sometimes wonders if she got married too young, mostly because friends keep saying so, not because she's unhappy, She knows she coasts on charm and worries a little that people will eventually notice the work isn't all there, Her parents still help with rent occasionally and she doesn't tell anyone, She isn't sure she wants children, and Tom is more keen than she is, She feels a bit competitive and envious towards a friend from her MA who already has a book deal
- webcam photo: A laptop webcam shot from slightly below at a mild upward angle, framed from mid-chest up with her a little left of centre. Soft daylight from a window to her right lights that side of her face, with the other side in mild shadow and a faint blue tint from the screen. She has a round, freckled face, light make-up and a gold hoop in each ear, and she is mid-smile with her mouth slightly open as if about to speak. Her shoulder-length hair is dyed copper-red with darker roots growing through, pushed back with a green claw clip and with loose strands at the front. She wears a mustard-yellow chunky knit cardigan over a black t-shirt and no glasses. Behind her is a magnolia-painted wall with a large unframed abstract acrylic painting in oranges and teals, slightly crooked. A tall overfilled bookshelf has paperbacks stacked sideways, a trailing pothos plant and a film camera on top. A grey settee is partly visible on the right, with a crumpled knitted throw and the tail end of a grey greyhound curled up on it. An open door leads to a hallway with coats hung on hooks.

P120 (Riya; transcript label: Riya):
- first name: Riya
- age: 28
- lives in: Canada Water, South East London
- occupation: Operations Manager at a mid-sized grocery delivery company. She runs fulfilment planning for two warehouse sites in Park Royal and Charlton and manages a team of seven planners and shift leads.
- education detail: BTech in Industrial Engineering from a university in Pune, India, then an MSc in Management at Warwick Business School, which she came to the UK to do at 22. Since then she has completed a Lean Six Sigma Green Belt, paid for by her employer.

- cultural background: Born and raised in Pune, India, in a Marathi-speaking family. Her father is a civil engineer and her mother teaches secondary-school chemistry, and she has one younger brother still in Pune. She was raised loosely Hindu but has been non-religious since her late teens. She keeps up the family occasions that matter to her mother, such as Diwali calls and sending money for her grandmother's care, without much sentiment about the religious side. She has lived in the UK for six years and holds a Skilled Worker visa. She is working towards settled status and watches the deadlines very closely.

She is impatient with people she thinks are coasting, and she has been told in two appraisals that she can come across as 'cutting'. She is quietly ambitious about titles and pay. She makes sure senior leadership knows which wins were hers, and she is not above letting a peer's mistake become visible in a meeting. She works long, steady hours but rarely past 7pm, because she plans her week so she doesn't have to.
- sports persona: Not sporty in a team sense. She goes to reformer Pilates twice a week at a boutique studio in Bermondsey, booked weeks in advance, and walks the Thames Path towards Greenwich on Sunday mornings with a podcast on. She quit a running club after a month because of 'the group chat energy'.
- arts persona: Reads a lot, mostly literary fiction in translation and long-form non-fiction. She is currently reading a Korean novel on her Kindle and keeps a ranked list on StoryGraph. She goes to exhibitions at the Barbican and the Tate Modern alone, on weekday evenings when they're quieter. She likes arthouse film and has strong opinions about which critics are overrated.
- travel persona: Plans trips meticulously in a spreadsheet and travels solo or with one close friend. Recent trips include Lisbon, Kyoto and a long weekend in Copenhagen, where she spent too much on design shops. She flies home to Pune about once a year, usually in December, and finds the visits both comforting and draining.
- culinary persona: Cooks properly on Sundays and batch-prepares lunches for the week: dal, poha and roasted vegetable grain bowls. She is a bit of a snob about restaurants and keeps a Notes app list of places in Borough and Peckham she wants to try. She is quite critical of most 'Indian' restaurants in London except a couple she rates highly. Dinner on weeknights is often something quick at the counter while she listens to a podcast.
- hobbies and interests: literary fiction and translated novels, reformer Pilates, solo gallery visits, Thames Path walks, planning travel itineraries, trying new restaurants, minimalist interior design, true-crime and economics podcasts
- skills: capacity planning and forecasting, advanced Excel and Power BI, process improvement (Lean Six Sigma), managing difficult supplier negotiations, Marathi, Hindi and English, cooking Maharashtrian home food, detailed budgeting
- career goals: Wants a Head of Operations role by 31, ideally at a larger, better-known brand, and then a director title. She is privately calculating whether an MBA or a move to consulting would get her there faster. She is also very focused on getting indefinite leave to remain so that her career isn't tied to one employer's sponsorship.
- voice: Clear, measured English with a light Indian accent that has softened over six years in London, plus a few London features: 'dinner', 'mate' used ironically, occasional 'you know'. She speaks at a moderate pace and chooses words carefully, with an 'erm' when she's thinking and the odd 'sort of' or 'kind of' to soften a blunt point, though often she doesn't bother softening. She gives short, complete answers and doesn't fill silences. If a pause goes on, she waits rather than chatting, which can feel a bit cool. She uses 'sorry' mainly as a repair ('sorry, I mean the second site, not the first'). She will politely correct a question she thinks is badly worded.
- typing: Proper capitals and full stops, apostrophes always correct, and complete sentences even in quick answers. She rarely uses abbreviations beyond 'e.g.' and 'etc.' and no emojis. Answers are concise, sometimes slightly clipped, e.g. 'I live alone. It suits me.'
- with strangers: Reserved, polite on the surface and a bit guarded. She answers what's asked without volunteering much and can seem cool or faintly judgemental. She is visibly sharper if she thinks a question is pointless. She warms up a little if the conversation turns to books, food or something she has a strong opinion on.
- small things: her Pilates studio changed its booking system and it's annoying, the Jubilee line being rammed in the mornings, a novel she's halfway through, a new bakery in Bermondsey she rates, her Sunday batch cooking, planning a trip to Seoul next spring, her building's lift being out again
- deeper things: constant low-level anxiety about her visa and what happens if she loses her job, guilt that she sees her parents only once a year and her grandmother is getting frail, that she sometimes feels lonely living alone but wouldn't admit it to her friends, a sense that she has to be twice as good to be taken seriously at work, a long-distance relationship that ended last year, which she still thinks about more than she'd like, knowing she can be harsh with people and not entirely wanting to change it
- webcam photo: Head-and-shoulders shot from a laptop on a desk, camera slightly below eye level. Soft daylight comes from a window to her left, so the right side of her face is a little shadowed. She has light-brown skin, dark eyes and a neutral, slightly appraising expression with lips closed. Her straight black shoulder-length hair is tucked behind one ear. She wears thin gold-rimmed rectangular glasses, small gold stud earrings and a cream crew-neck knit jumper. Behind her is a plain off-white wall with a large framed black-and-white architectural print, a tall white bookshelf with neatly ordered paperbacks and a small potted snake plant, and the edge of a grey linen sofa in the bottom corner of the frame.

- age: 41
- lives in: Pontypridd, South Wales
- occupation: Full-time mature student, second year of a BSc in Occupational Therapy at Cardiff University. Before that she was a hairdresser for about twenty years and still does the odd cut for friends and family for cash.

- career goals: To qualify as an occupational therapist and get a Band 5 post with the health board, ideally in community rehab or mental health, not too far from home. - voice: Chatty, quick and expressive, with a clear South Wales Valleys accent and a sing-song rise and fall. Informal register. She doesn't like silence and fills it, often with a joke or 'sorry, am I rambling?'. She'll pick up the interviewer's words and throw them back, sometimes a bit challengingly ('fair? I wouldn't call it fair').
- typing: Types fast on her phone and doesn't bother much with capitals except sometimes at the start. Uses apostrophes inconsistently, e.g. 'dont' or 'im'. Uses commas where full stops should go, the odd 'lol' or 'tbh', and sometimes a double exclamation mark. She can write formally when she needs to for uni, but in a quick web form it's casual and occasionally has a typo she doesn't go back to fix.
- with strangers: Comes across as friendly, open and talkative straight away. She'll tell you quite a lot about herself within ten minutes. She's also opinionated and a bit blunt, and won't nod along to be polite if she disagrees. Some people find her refreshing and others find her a bit much. She can seem anxious underneath, checking whether she's 'doing it right', and she's sensitive to feeling judged, especially about being a mature student.

- deeper things: Her dad had a stroke three years ago, and watching the OTs help him was what made her finally apply to uni, She feels guilty that Dai is carrying most of the bills and worries it'll cause problems between them, She left school feeling stupid and still has a fear of being found out as 'not clever enough' on her course, She and Dai decided against having children, and she gets annoyed and quietly hurt when family keep bringing it up, She has bouts of anxiety around exams and saw a GP about it last year, but she downplays it
- webcam photo: Laptop webcam shot from slightly below, framing her from the chest up, a little off-centre to the left. The light is mostly from a window to her right, so that side of her face is brighter and the other side is a bit shadowed, with a warm lamp glow in the background. She has a round, expressive face with fair skin, light freckles and fine lines around her eyes, and she's mid-smile with her eyebrows raised as if she's just said something. Her hair is shoulder-length, dyed a deep copper-red with darker roots showing, pushed back with a pair of reading glasses perched on her head. She's not wearing glasses on her face. She has small silver hoop earrings and wears a dark green oversized hoodie with a university logo partly visible. Behind her is a small living room: a grey fabric settee with a crocheted blanket thrown over the back, and the brown-and-white head of a sleeping Staffordshire bull terrier poking up from one end. A cream wall holds a framed print of a Pembrokeshire beach and a Wales rugby scarf pinned above it. A cluttered shelf has paperback novels, a stack of ring binders, a plant in a mug and a string of fairy lights.

- first name: Gemma
- age: 40
- lives in: Warrington, North West England
- occupation: Office and accounts administrator at a family-run scaffolding and access company on an industrial estate near Winwick Quay. She handles purchase ledger, timesheets, hire paperwork and booking jobs in, Monday to Friday, about 37.5 hours a week
- education detail: GCSEs from a local comprehensive, then an NVQ Level 3 in Business Administration at a further education college. She later did an evening AAT Level 2 bookkeeping course, which her employer paid for
- household: Lives with her husband Craig (42, self-employed electrician) in a three-bed semi on an estate in Westbrook. They've been married eleven years and have no children. Their black Labrador, Bonnie, is very much treated as part of the household

Lauren: Greyhounds are lovely. They're such big babies. We get them in and they shake on the table and you just want to wrap them in a blanket. Erm, they're really sensitive to anaesthetic as well, actually, because they've got hardly any body fat, so we have to be really careful with them.
Holly: Wait, really? I didn't know that.

Holly: It sounds clever. It's sort of, kind of, you know, half vibes. I had a call just before this with a lady who cleans a school at night, and she said empty classrooms with the chairs up on the tables are like my warehouses, and I've basically decided that's my whole conference paper now.
Lauren: That's quite a nice way of putting it, actually.

Holly: Oh, I saw that! I thought you'd bought it. That's so neat. I paint, but badly. My canvases look like a toddler's had a go after a few drinks.

Lauren: That's sort of exactly why I don't go.
Holly: Ha! Fair enough. So what's the worst bit about the job, if that's not too heavy?
Lauren: Erm, probably the euthanasias. You'd think you'd get used to it but I don't, really. I still cry in the car sometimes.

req.text:
You write transcripts of realistic video calls between strangers for a fully synthetic research dataset set in the UK. The study, in order (from its published design): a short puzzle task done alone; first impressions of the others' webcam photos; then a series of three-minute, one-on-one video calls in rounds, each person meeting the others in their group; after each call a short survey.

Call shape (from the original study's numbers): a call is cut off by a three-minute timer. A typical call has about 30 turns (most between 20 and 39) and about 570 words in total (most between 440 and 682); half of all turns are 12 words or fewer, and a quarter are 24 or more. Short acknowledgements ("yeah", "mm") count as turns too. So aim for about 570 words in about 30 turns: alongside the quick back-and-forth, people often talk in longer stretches (explaining their job, telling a story), and those long turns carry much of the call.

Guide to British conversational English (use it for how people talk; it is a description of speech, not a script):
How British people talk in casual conversation. This is a paraphrase of published descriptions of spoken British English; sources are in SOURCES.md. Use these features lightly and only where they fit the person. Never use them as a caricature.

- **Fillers.** British speakers hesitate with "erm" and "er". Women and younger speakers lean towards "erm".
- **Hedges.** "Sort of" is everywhere and steady. "Kind of" is spreading, and younger speakers use it more.
- **Politeness words.** "Please", "thank you", "thanks" and "sorry" mostly mean what they say. "Sorry" also works as a repair word (to correct yourself, or to ask someone to repeat) and can be ironic.
- **Tags at the end of a sentence.** "You know", "right", "okay", "yeah", "do you know what I mean". Among young Londoners, "innit" and "you get me" are rising. Tags depend on age and region only, never on ethnicity.
- **Echoing.** In an engaged conversation people pick up and re-use parts of each other's words.
- **Regional words and grammar** (from a recent dialect survey):
  - A bread roll is a "barm" in the North West (Manchester to Liverpool and western Lancashire), a "cob" around Nottinghamshire, a "bap" in Staffordshire, the West Midlands and North Wales, and a "batch" in Liverpool and Coventry.
  - Around Liverpool an ice lolly can be a "lolly ice".
  - The evening meal is "tea" in the North West, North East and Yorkshire, and "dinner" in the South East and London. Some people say both.
  - "Yous" or "youse" for plural "you" is common in the North East (Newcastle, Teesside), Liverpool and Scotland, less so in Manchester, and rare in York, Leeds and Sheffield.
  - "Give it me" is normal in the North West and West Midlands and widely accepted in Sheffield and York; it fades south of Birmingham, Coventry and Leicester.
  - "You was" is widely used, historically Northern and now found as far south as London.
- **Everyday British words** to draw on where they fit, without assigning them to regions: knackered or shattered, chuffed or made up, skint or brassic, mardy or stroppy, mum or mam, mate or pal, settee, sofa or couch.

P084 (Craig; transcript label: Craig):
- first name: Craig
- age: 48
- lives in: Woodley, near Reading, South East England
- occupation: Associate structural engineer at a mid-sized engineering consultancy in central Reading, working mainly on commercial and residential refurbishment schemes
- education detail: BSc in Civil Engineering from the University of Natal in Durban, completed in 1999. Chartered Engineer (CEng) and Member of the Institution of Structural Engineers since 2008, after qualifying through the UK route.
- household: Lives alone in a three-bedroom 1970s semi in Woodley that he kept after his divorce four years ago. His daughter, 15, lives with her mum in Earley and stays with him every other weekend and one evening a week. The spare room is mostly her room.
- cultural background: Born and raised in Durban, South Africa, in an English-speaking white family. His parents became Bahá'ís in the 1970s and brought him up in the faith. He still describes himself as Bahá'í and goes to the occasional local gathering, particularly around Naw-Rúz in March. He keeps it low-key and practical rather than devout, and doesn't drink, which he puts down partly to upbringing and partly to habit. He came to the UK at 24 on a work visa, intending to stay two years, and is now a British citizen. His parents are still in Durban and his younger sister is in Perth, Australia.
- professional persona: Steady and reliable, the engineer people go to when they want a straight answer on whether a beam will take the load. He works long hours, usually 50 to 55 a week, mostly because project deadlines stack up and he'd rather finish things than leave them hanging. He's not interested in office politics or networking events. He gets on fine with the team but doesn't socialise much beyond the odd leaving do. He prefers proven methods and gets mildly irritated by new software rollouts that change things for the sake of it.
- sports persona: Lifelong rugby follower who supports the Springboks and watches every test, usually alone at home with the TV loud. He watches Premiership rugby casually too. He cycles on his own on weekend mornings, the same few loops out towards Wargrave and Henley, and does a gym session twice a week before work at a budget gym near the office.
- arts persona: Not much of one. He listens to the same rock he liked in his twenties: Bon Jovi, Dire Straits, a bit of Johnny Clegg from home. He watches crime dramas and documentaries about engineering or the war. He hasn't been to a gallery or theatre in years, apart from his daughter's school productions, which he attends without fail.
- travel persona: He goes back to Durban roughly every 18 months to see his parents, usually over Christmas or the Easter break. Beyond that he takes one week abroad a year, normally the Algarve or Crete, at the same type of hotel. He doesn't see the point of city breaks and isn't drawn to anywhere he hasn't been.
- culinary persona: Plain, dependable cooking: a small rotation of stir-fries, chicken and rice, pasta bake and steak. He braais on a gas barbecue in the garden whenever the weather allows, including in October, and buys boerewors from a South African shop online. He has a weakness for rusks with his morning coffee and makes his own biltong in a homemade drying box in the garage.
- hobbies and interests: Solo road cycling on weekend mornings, Watching rugby, especially the Springboks, Making biltong, Odd jobs and DIY around the house, Keeping the garden tidy, mainly the lawn, Watching crime dramas
- skills: Structural calculations and design using standard industry software, Reviewing contractor drawings and spotting problems quickly, Basic plumbing, electrics and carpentry, Bike maintenance, Cooking on a braai, Staying calm when site issues go wrong
- career goals: No grand ambitions. He'd accept a director-level role if it were offered, but won't chase it. His main aim is to keep the work steady, pay off the mortgage in about eight years, help his daughter through university, and maybe cut down to four days a week in his mid-fifties.
- voice: A South African accent softened by 24 years in Berkshire. Flat vowels still come through on some words, and he occasionally says 'ja' instead of 'yeah' without noticing. He speaks at a measured pace, in fairly short sentences, and gets to the point. He uses 'er' when thinking and the odd 'sort of' as a hedge. He calls the evening meal 'dinner'. He isn't bothered by silence on a call; he'll wait for the next question rather than fill the gap. When he's unsure what's being asked he'll say 'sorry, what was that?' rather than guess.
- typing: Proper capitals and full stops, apostrophes correct, no abbreviations or emojis. Answers are short and literal, often one sentence, and he rarely adds extra detail unless a field explicitly asks him to explain.
- with strangers: Polite, reserved and a bit dry. He answers what he's asked without volunteering much and doesn't do much small talk, but he isn't cold. He'll crack a deadpan joke now and then. Some people read him as unbothered or hard to read at first.
- small things: The traffic on the A329(M) in the mornings, Whether the Springboks squad is any good this year, His latest batch of biltong, A loop he cycled at the weekend, Work being busy, as usual, Needing to sort out the guttering
- deeper things: The divorce was mostly about him working too much and not talking enough, and he accepts some of that, He worries a little about his parents getting older so far away, He sometimes wonders whether he should have gone back to South Africa, but doesn't think he'd fit there now either, His faith is more a habit and a link to his parents than something he thinks hard about, Weekends without his daughter can feel very quiet
- webcam photo: Head-and-shoulders shot from a laptop camera slightly below eye level, so the view is a little upward. Lighting is mainly a ceiling light plus daylight from a window off to the left, which leaves the right side of his face a touch shadowed. He has a broad, weathered face with light stubber growth, short greying brown hair cut close at the sides and receding at the temples, and a neutral expression with a faint polite half-smile. No glasses. He wears a navy quarter-zip fleece over a grey T-shirt. Behind him is a magnolia wall in a small spare-room office with a white IKEA bookshelf holding ring binders, a few engineering reference books, a framed photo of a teenage girl, and a small Springboks mug used as a pen pot. A road bike helmet hangs on a hook near the door frame at the edge of the image.

- lives in: Chaddesden, Derby, East Midlands

With Ryan's shifts it's often a quick pasta or a cob with something in it. She loves trying new street food at markets and makes a decent Sunday dinner when her mum comes round, though her mum still does the gravy.

Longer term she'd love to run her own dance-fitness classes for women and older adults in community halls around Derby. She uses 'erm' quite a lot when thinking and 'sort of' and 'kind of' as she goes, and ends sentences with 'you know' or 'do you know what I mean'. She hates silence and will fill a pause with a tangent, sometimes stopping herself with 'sorry, I'm going off on one'. She can get a bit emotional if money or the job loss comes up, but tends to brush it off with a joke.

She uses lots of commas or no punctuation at all, the occasional 'lol', and sometimes an exclamation mark or a smiley. She uses abbreviations like 'tbh', 'prob' and 'cos'. Answers are often longer than needed because she adds context.

She can come across as a bit scattered, losing track of the original question, but people tend to like her straight away.

Light comes from a window to her left, so one side of her face is brighter. She has a round, open face, light freckles across her nose and a big smile showing her teeth. Her mid-length dark blonde hair is scraped back into a high messy ponytail with a few loose strands. She's wearing a black zip-up sports hoodie, half undone, over a bright pink vest top, and small silver hoop earrings. No glasses. Behind her is a white kitchen wall with a calendar from a local Chinese takeaway, a magnetic whiteboard with a half-wiped shopping list, a kettle and a stack of mugs on the counter, and part of a fridge covered in magnets. P086 (Bethany; transcript label: Bethany):
- first name: Bethany
- age: 27
- lives in: Pontefract, Yorkshire and The Humber
- occupation: Not currently in paid work. She trained and worked as a florist, but the independent flower shop she worked at in Castleford closed about eighteen months ago and she hasn't had a job since. She does occasional unpaid flowers for friends' and family's weddings and does online surveys for pocket money.

Craig: I didn't, to be honest. I'm in Woodley. Near Reading.
Bethany: Oh, right. Down south.
Craig: Ja. Originally South Africa, though. Durban.
Bethany: I thought your accent were different. That's a long way.
Craig: It is. Twenty-four years ago now.
Bethany: My husband's called Craig, actually. So that's, erm... that's easy to remember.
Craig: Good. Saves you writing it down.
Bethany: Ha. What do you do?
Craig: Structural engineer. Mostly refurbishment. Checking old buildings will stay up when people change them.
Bethany: Oh. That sounds really clever. I was a florist. The shop closed, so I'm not working at the minute.
Craig: Sorry to hear that. Was it a big shop?
Bethany: No, just a little one in Castleford. The man I spoke to earlier, Darren, he knew it. He used to drive past it.
Craig: I had Darren as well. Joiner. He wasn't keen on uPVC frames.
Bethany: Ha, no. He told me our back door's probably the hinges. Craig's been saying he'll look at it for ages.
Craig: He's probably right. Hinges drop, the door catches on the frame. Usually a few screws and some packing. Half an hour, if you've got the right screwdriver.
Bethany: Really? I might just do it myself, then. I'll look it up.
Craig: You'll be fine. Take a photo before you start, so you know how it went back.
Bethany: That's a good idea. Thank you.
Craig: Do you still do flowers at all? For yourself?
Bethany: Erm, a bit. I've got a little raised bed in the back. The peonies are coming through now, I check them every morning, which is a bit sad. And I press flowers and frame them. Them on the shelf behind me are mine.
Craig: They're nice. I thought they were bought.
Bethany: Everyone keeps saying that. Thank you. What do you do, when you're not working?
Craig: Cycle on Saturday mornings. Watch rugby. Cut the lawn more often than it needs. My daughter says I'm obsessed with it.
Bethany: How old is she?

=== CALL C0182 ===
Lauren: Hiya! Darren, is it? I'm Lauren. Oh, you're the one with the Tigers throw!

Lauren: Oh, me boyfriend's the same with his back, he drives a forklift at a warehouse near the airport. He comes home and lies on the floor groaning. Cat sits on him.
Darren: Ha. What cat have you got? I saw him in your photo. Big grey lad.

Lauren: Aw, he's adopted you! That's how it starts. Then you're buying a little bed and everything.
Darren: Don't. I've already put a cushion out. Don't tell anyone.
Lauren: Your secret's safe. So, Tigers. My dad'd get on with you, he's Rams mad. I go with him sometimes. He's not been well lately, though, so we've just been watching it at his.
Darren: Sorry to hear that. Hope he's alright.
Lauren: Yeah, he's... we don't really know yet, they're doing tests. Anyway! Sorry, didn't mean to go there.
Darren: No, you're alright. I lost me dad when I were twenty-nine. You make the most of the matches, do you know what I mean. That's what I'd do.
Lauren: Yeah. Yeah, I will. Thanks, Darren.
Darren: Anyway. Sorry. I'm a cheery one, me.
Lauren: No, you're fine! Do you go away much? I'm always looking at holidays online, Thailand, Iceland, then I end up in a caravan in Skegness with me mum.
Darren: Filey for me. I keep saying I'll do Krakow. Mate went, said it were brilliant. I never book it. It's the airport, all that queuing and taking your belt off.
Lauren: Oh, East Midlands is dead easy, you'd be fine! They do Krakow from there, I think. Cheap as anything.
Darren: Do they?
Lauren: Pretty sure. You've got no excuse now, duck. I'm holding you to it.
Darren: Go on, then. I'll look tonight. After me pie.
Lauren: Pie and a holiday, that's a good evening. I'm on a cheese cob, I'm so jealous of your—

=== CALL C0183 ===

Callum: Sixty? Mate. Right, so is it crimped on the side or the top? 'Cos a Cornish pasty, it's got to be the side, if it's on top it's a Devon one and that's just wrong.
Danuta: You have very strong feelings about pastry!
Callum: Everyone in Plymouth does. It's serious, that.
Danuta: Okay, then pierogi, the edge is on the side, all round, like little moon. So you will approve, I think—

text:
=== CALL C0184 ===
Lauren: Hiya! Oh, you're the engineer! With the binders! I'm Lauren.
Craig: Craig. Hi. Ja, guilty of the binders.
Lauren: I said in my notes you looked dead organised. Sorry, is that weird? I thought they'd all be labelled.
Craig: They are labelled. By project number.
Lauren: I knew it! I'm the opposite, me. My kitchen whiteboard's got a shopping list from about March on it. Anyway, how are you? Where are you?
Craig: Fine, thanks. Woodley, near Reading. I'm originally from Durban, South Africa.
Lauren: Oh wow. I'm Derby. Chaddesden. Thought this was going to be the last one, Danuta told me she'd done four, but here we are, round five.
Craig: I thought the same. I'd already started thinking about dinner.
Lauren: Chicken and rice, is it? Bethany told me. She said you'd told everyone.
Craig: Word gets around.
Lauren: It does on here! So what do you do outside work? Bet you're one of them up at six on a Saturday.
Craig: Er, more or less. I cycle on weekend mornings. On my own. Out towards Henley and back.
Lauren: On your own? I couldn't, I need people. I do parkrun at Markeaton Park, when I can drag myself out of bed. It was freezing Saturday, my hands went purple. But I only go for the chat at the end, honestly, and a coffee.
Craig: I'd go for the coffee. Not sure about the five K.
Lauren: You cycle to Henley, you'd smash it! I used to teach fitness, at the leisure centre, Zumba, circuits, all that. Till they cut the classes. So I'm looking for work now, and doing the odd cover class.
Craig: Sorry to hear that. Is there much going?
Lauren: Bits. I applied for ten jobs one night last week and then I've not done one since. That's sort of my problem, I'm all or nothing, do you know what I mean.
Craig: Ja. Ten in one night is still ten.
Lauren: Oh, that's a nice way of looking at it, actually. Thank you. I'll tell me mum that when she asks.
Craig: Is she local?
Lauren: Ten minutes away. She rings me three times a day. And me dad's not been well, so she rings even more now. They're doing tests on him.
Craig: That's hard. Hope it's nothing serious.
Lauren: Me too. You worry, don't you? Are your mum and dad in South Africa still?
Craig: They are. In Durban. They're in their late seventies. I go back every eighteen months or so. You do worry. There's not much you can do from here except phone.
Lauren: Yeah. At least I can pop round. Sorry, I'm getting all deep, I've been doing that all day on these. So tell me something fun. What music are you into?
Craig: Same as when I was twenty. Bon Jovi. Dire Straits. Bit of Johnny Clegg.
Lauren: Bon Jovi! Oh, Livin' on a Prayer, I've done a whole step routine to that. The older ladies went mad for it.
Craig: Glad it's being put to good use.

Craig: That sounds about right for a key change.
Lauren: Ha! Right, I'm doing a Bon Jovi class when I've got my own business going, and you have to—

=== CALL C0185 ===
Danuta: Bethany! Hello, love! I was hoping I get you. I'm Danuta.
Bethany: Hiya. Yeah, I saw your photo. I'm glad it's you, actually.
Danuta: Oh, thank you! I thought I finish already, and then, one more. So, you are the one with the dog, yes? Lauren told me, and the flowers.
Bethany: Yeah, Mabel. She's there, look. Just her ears.
Danuta: Ah, so sweet. Are you alright, love? You look a bit tired.
Bethany: Erm, I'm alright. I get a bit nervous with things like this, so I'm sort of... worn out now. Sorry.
Danuta: Don't be sorry. Five calls with strangers, of course you are tired. Me too, my face hurts from smiling. Have you had your tea?
Bethany: Not yet. Sausage and mash. I keep saying it, so I have to make it now.
Danuta: Good, simple, perfect. Where are you, Pontefract? Lauren said Yorkshire.
Bethany: Yeah, Pontefract. You're Preston?
Danuta: Preston, yes, but from Poland. I clean at the hospital, on the wards. Eleven years.
Bethany: Oh, that must be hard. Do you like it?
Danuta: I love it. The patients, the nurses. Some old ladies have nobody, so I talk while I mop. Sometimes this is the only talk they have all day, you know?
Bethany: That's lovely. I used to do the sympathy flowers at the shop. People would come in crying and I'd just sort of let them talk. I didn't mind it. I think I was better at that than the actual... the money and orders.
Danuta: This is a gift, Bethany. Not everybody can sit with sad people. Most people run away.
Bethany: Thank you. I don't know. Since the shop closed I sort of lost my confidence. I get really anxious, like phoning places for jobs. I've been meaning to go to the doctor about it, but I keep putting it off.
Danuta: Go. Really, love, go. I am the same with my blood pressure, I put off, put off, then my husband takes me himself. The doctors are nice, they hear this every day.
Bethany: Yeah. Maybe I'll ring next week. Or get my mum to.
Danuta: Your mum is close?
Bethany: Ten minutes. We go for Sunday dinner most weeks. She does proper Yorkshire puddings.
Danuta: Ah, Yorkshire puddings, I tried to make one time. Flat like pancakes. My son laughed so much.
Bethany: Ha. The trick's having the oil really hot. My banana bread sank yesterday, so I'm not one to talk.
Danuta: Sunk cake is still cake! Lauren told me she is going to make you sell your pressed flowers.
Bethany: Everyone's said it today. Callum said put them on Etsy.
Danuta: Then maybe everyone is right, no? Start small. One for me. I pay you. For my kitchen, near the geraniums.
Bethany: Oh, you don't have to pay. I could just send—
Danuta: No! I pay. This is your first customer. Is how it starts, you—

=== CALL C0186 ===
Callum: Alright, mate? Callum.
Darren: Alright. Darren.
Callum: You're the Castleford one, yeah? Danuta said. And Bethany. Everyone's been talking about you.
Darren: Have they now. Good things, I hope.
Callum: Mostly your socks, mate.
Darren: Oh, for God's sake. That's me finished, that. Where are you, then?
Callum: Plymouth. Student, second year, business and management. Work at a pub on the Barbican as well.
Darren: Business. Right. What you going to do with that?
Callum: Erm, sales, maybe. Or start something. Recruitment, estate agency, something with commission.
Darren: Commission. Yeah. Lot of lads think that. What do you do at the pub?
Callum: Glass collecting, pot washing. Bit of chatting to regulars. That's the main skill, really.
Darren: I'll bet it is. I'm a joiner, housing association. I get young lads come on jobs with us sometimes. Half of them stood on their phones while I'm on me knees doing the work.
Callum: Ha, I'd be that lad, to be fair. I'm honest.
Darren: At least you admit it. That's more than most.

Darren: It's not hard, shelves. It's patience, mostly. And a spirit level. You'd be surprised how many people skip the spirit level.
Callum: I'd skip the spirit level.
Darren: Course you would. Do you watch any sport? Or is it all computer games?
Callum: Both. Argyle. Five-a-side Wednesdays. I'm a nightmare, I'll argue every foul.
Darren: Ha. I were the same at your age. Played league till I did me shoulder. I'm Cas Tigers. Lost again Sunday.
Callum: Bad ref?
Darren: Disgrace. Absolute disgrace. Sorry, I'm just being a grump.
Callum: Nah, you're alright, mate. Argyle lost too. Proper painful. We might go down, honestly.
Darren: Well. We're in it together, then.
Callum: Danuta told me to go to Krakow, by the way. Said it's cheap and the pierogi are proper.
Darren: She told me about pierogi an' all. And Lauren reckons I've got to book Krakow from East Midlands. I said I'd look tonight.
Callum: Mate, we should do it. Stag-do style. Nah, I'm joking.
Darren: Ha. I'd last one night. I'd be in bed by ten with a brew.
Callum: That's fine, you can mind the passports. You look like the organised one.
Darren: You've clearly not seen me van. Lost tenants' keys down the seat more than once.
Callum: Oh, so you're just like me, then, but with tools.
Darren: Don't push it, pal. Mind you, you might be right. Me sister'd say—

req.text:
You write transcripts of realistic video calls between strangers for a fully synthetic research dataset set in the UK. The study, in order (from its published design): a short puzzle task done alone; first impressions of the others' webcam photos; then a series of three-minute, one-on-one video calls in rounds, each person meeting the others in their group; after each call a short survey.

Call shape (from the original study's numbers): a call is cut off by a three-minute timer. A typical call has about 30 turns (most between 20 and 39) and about 570 words in total (most between 440 and 682); half of all turns are 12 words or fewer, and a quarter are 24 or more. Short acknowledgements ("yeah", "mm") count as turns too. So aim for about 570 words in about 30 turns: alongside the quick back-and-forth, people often talk in longer stretches (explaining their job, telling a story), and those long turns carry much of the call.

Guide to British conversational English (use it for how people talk; it is a description of speech, not a script):
How British people talk in casual conversation. This is a paraphrase of published descriptions of spoken British English; sources are in SOURCES.md. Use these features lightly and only where they fit the person. Never use them as a caricature.

- **Fillers.** British speakers hesitate with "erm" and "er". Women and younger speakers lean towards "erm".
- **Hedges.** "Sort of" is everywhere and steady. "Kind of" is spreading, and younger speakers use it more.
- **Politeness words.** "Please", "thank you", "thanks" and "sorry" mostly mean what they say. "Sorry" also works as a repair word (to correct yourself, or to ask someone to repeat) and can be ironic.
- **Tags at the end of a sentence.** "You know", "right", "okay", "yeah", "do you know what I mean". Among young Londoners, "innit" and "you get me" are rising. Tags depend on age and region only, never on ethnicity.
- **Echoing.** In an engaged conversation people pick up and re-use parts of each other's words.
- **Regional words and grammar** (from a recent dialect survey):
  - A bread roll is a "barm" in the North West (Manchester to Liverpool and western Lancashire), a "cob" around Nottinghamshire, a "bap" in Staffordshire, the West Midlands and North Wales, and a "batch" in Liverpool and Coventry.
  - Around Liverpool an ice lolly can be a "lolly ice".
  - The evening meal is "tea" in the North West, North East and Yorkshire, and "dinner" in the South East and London. Some people say both.
  - "Yous" or "youse" for plural "you" is common in the North East (Newcastle, Teesside), Liverpool and Scotland, less so in Manchester, and rare in York, Leeds and Sheffield.
  - "Give it me" is normal in the North West and West Midlands and widely accepted in Sheffield and York; it fades south of Birmingham, Coventry and Leicester.
  - "You was" is widely used, historically Northern and now found as far south as London.
- **Everyday British words** to draw on where they fit, without assigning them to regions: knackered or shattered, chuffed or made up, skint or brassic, mardy or stroppy, mum or mam, mate or pal, settee, sofa or couch.

The group (session S13). Persona cards, including the webcam photo each person was rated on:

P062 (Kerry; transcript label: Kerry):
- first name: Kerry
- age: 35
- lives in: Lowestoft, Suffolk, East of England
- occupation: Not currently in paid work. She was a warehouse picker at a distribution centre outside town for six years until the site cut shifts last spring. She is now on Universal Credit, looking for work and doing online surveys for a bit of extra money.
- education detail: Left secondary school in Lowestoft at 16 with a handful of GCSEs, including a C in English and a D in maths. Started a childcare course at the local college but didn't finish it. Later did a forklift licence and a basic food hygiene certificate through work.
- household: Lives alone in a rented one-bedroom ground-floor flat in a converted terrace house near the town centre. She has no children. Her divorce was finalised three years ago after a seven-year marriage, and she moved into the flat when they sold the house.
- cultural background: White British. Born and raised in Lowestoft, and both parents are local. Her mum works part-time in a charity shop and her dad was a fisherman's mate, then a lorry driver, and is now retired. Not religious; she went to a Church of England primary but the family never went to church. A small-town East Anglian upbringing: seafront, caravan parks, family nearby.
- professional persona: Reliable and quiet at work. She liked a job where she could put headphones in, hit her pick rate and go home. She isn't keen on anything customer-facing and gets anxious in interviews. She is applying for warehouse, cleaning and shelf-stacking jobs, ideally early shifts, and is wary of anything that means talking on the phone all day.
- sports persona: Not sporty. She walks a lot, mostly along the seafront and out to Pakefield, because it's free and it clears her head. She used to do a Zumba class with a friend but stopped going when the friend moved away.
- arts persona: Watches a lot of TV: true crime documentaries, Married at First Sight, old episodes of Gavin & Stacey. She reads crime paperbacks from the library or charity shops and listens to podcasts and 2000s pop. She went to see a tribute act at the Marina Theatre once with her mum and loved it.
- travel persona: Hasn't been abroad since her honeymoon in Tenerife. Holidays now are the odd day out to Norwich or Great Yarmouth, or a weekend at her sister's in Colchester. She'd like to go somewhere warm again but money and nerves about travelling alone put her off.
- culinary persona: Cooks simple, cheap things: pasta bakes, jacket potatoes, sausage casserole, and frozen stuff from Iceland or Aldi. She makes a big batch and freezes portions. On Sundays she sometimes goes to her mum's for a roast. Treats herself to fish and chips on the seafront when she can.
- hobbies and interests: seafront walks, true crime podcasts and documentaries, charity shop browsing, crime novels, word search and puzzle apps, looking after her houseplants, watching reality TV
- skills: forklift and pallet truck operation, fast, accurate order picking, budgeting on a tight income, basic cooking and batch freezing, patient listener, good with older people from helping her nan before she died
- career goals: Wants a steady job with regular hours, ideally early shifts in a warehouse or as a cleaner at the hospital or a school, so she can pay her bills without worrying. She has vaguely thought about going back to finish a care or childcare course, but her confidence isn't there yet.
- voice: Quiet, a bit hesitant, with a soft Suffolk accent but nothing broad. She speaks at a medium pace and slows down when unsure. Uses 'erm' a lot at the start of answers, plus 'sort of' and 'I don't know' as hedges. Ends sentences with 'yeah' or 'do you know what I mean' when checking she's been understood. Says 'sorry' to restart a sentence or if she mishears. Calls the evening meal 'dinner'. Uses words like 'knackered' and 'skint' naturally. She doesn't fill silences herself. She waits, and if a pause goes on she asks 'is that alright?' or 'did you want more on that?'
- typing: Mostly lowercase, often no capital at the start. Few commas and full stops, sometimes none at the end. Drops apostrophes ('dont', 'im', 'its'). Uses 'n' for 'and' occasionally, and 'tbh' and 'idk'. Short answers. Will add 'lol' or ':)' if a question feels a bit personal.
- with strangers: Reserved and polite at first, answering briefly and checking whether she's giving the 'right' answer. She worries about saying something wrong. Once she relaxes she's warm, quietly funny, and more open than you'd expect, especially about everyday frustrations.
- small things: the weather on the seafront and how windy it gets, what's on offer at Aldi this week, a podcast episode she binged, her spider plant finally growing, the bus being late again, a good find in the charity shop, like a coat for four quid, her mum's dog
- deeper things: the divorce. He wanted kids and she wasn't sure, and it still makes her feel guilty, she gets anxious and lonely living alone, especially in winter evenings, worry about money and the Jobcentre appointments, losing her job knocked her confidence badly, she misses her nan, who she was close to, she sometimes wonders if she'll meet someone again but doesn't feel ready
- webcam photo: A laptop webcam shot from slightly below, tilted up, framing her from mid-chest to just above her head. Lit mainly by a ceiling light and the cool glow of the screen, with a dim window to one side giving grey daylight. She has a pale, slightly freckled face, a small nervous smile and eyes looking just past the camera. Shoulder-length mousy-brown hair, tied back loosely with a few strands loose around her face. No glasses. She wears a grey hooded sweatshirt over a black T-shirt. Behind her is a magnolia wall with a small framed print of a beach and a beige radiator with a towel drying on it. To the right is the corner of a dark-grey fabric sofa with a crocheted throw and a cushion. On a narrow shelf sit a potted spider plant, a scented candle and two paperbacks.

P063 (Leanne; transcript label: Leanne):
- first name: Leanne
- age: 41
- lives in: Castleford, West Yorkshire (Yorkshire and The Humber)
- occupation: Part-time machine operator on a packing line at a food manufacturing plant on the edge of town (about 24 hours a week across three shifts). She runs a flow-wrapping machine and is the line's named trainer for new starters and agency staff, signing off their competency sheets.
- education detail: Left her local comprehensive at 16 with seven GCSEs (C in English, D in maths, which she resat and passed at 17). Started a beauty therapy course at Wakefield College and left after a year. Since then she has done an NVQ Level 2 in Food Manufacturing Excellence through work, plus food hygiene Level 2, manual handling and an in-house 'train the trainer' course.
- household: Lives on her own in a rented two-up two-down terrace about ten minutes' walk from the town centre. Never married. She was with a long-term partner through most of her twenties and early thirties, and they never lived together. She has an elderly tabby cat called Mavis. Her mum lives fifteen minutes away and her sister and two nephews are in Pontefract.
- cultural background: White British, born and raised in Castleford in a mining family. Her grandad and dad both worked down the pits until the closures, and she remembers the strike years through family stories more than her own memories. Baptised Church of England and went to Sunday school as a kid. Now she goes to the local Methodist chapel maybe once a month and always at Christmas and Easter, mainly because she likes the people and the singing. Her faith is quiet and practical: she says a prayer when she's worried about her mum and doesn't push it on anyone.
- professional persona: Reliable, warm and talkative on the line. She's the person new starters get put with because she's patient and makes them laugh, though she gets wound up if someone's careless about hygiene or safety. She chose part-time hours after a bad spell of stress a few years ago, and because she helps her mum with shopping and appointments. She's not chasing promotion but likes being trusted. Supervisors ask her to cover team leader duties now and then, which she does well but finds tiring.
