P164 (Callum; transcript label: Callum):
- first name: Callum
- age: 25
- lives in: St Helens, North West England
- occupation: Float line operator at a glass manufacturing plant, working a four-on, four-off rotating shift pattern of days and nights
- education detail: Left a local Catholic high school with GCSEs, including a B in English and a C in Maths. Did a Level 3 BTEC in Engineering at St Helens College, then joined the plant through a manufacturing apprenticeship at 19. Since then he has picked up a Level 2 NVQ in Performing Manufacturing Operations, forklift and overhead crane tickets, and an IOSH Managing Safely certificate the company paid for.
- household: Lives with his wife Megan, 25, a dental nurse, in a rented two-up two-down terrace in Sutton. They met at sixth-form college and married two years ago at their parish church, with the do at a rugby club function room. No kids yet. They have a rescue greyhound called Dolly and are saving for a deposit to buy somewhere with a proper garden.
- cultural background: White British, born and raised in St Helens. Both sides of the family go back generations in the town, with grandparents who worked at the pits and the glassworks. Brought up Catholic. He goes to Mass at Christmas, Easter and the odd Sunday with his mum, and he and Megan married in church. He calls his faith 'quiet but there' and isn't preachy about it. Rugby league is close to a family religion too.
- professional persona: Reliable, upbeat operator on the hot end of the float line. He monitors furnace and tin bath readings, checks ribbon thickness and flags defects. He's known for logging everything properly and leaving handovers tidy, which the older lads tease him about. He gets on with everyone from the cleaners to the shift managers and is the one who organises the crew's Christmas night out. He stays calm when there's a line break or a furnace alarm, and the team leader has started leaning on him to show new starters the ropes.
- sports persona: St Helens Saints season ticket holder with his dad and younger brother, in the same part of the ground for years. Plays five-a-side on Wednesdays when shifts allow and runs a 5k parkrun at Victoria Park most free Saturdays. He's chasing a sub-21-minute time and keeps a spreadsheet of his splits.
- arts persona: Curious more than arty. He's been round the Walker Art Gallery and Tate Liverpool more than once, usually dragging Megan or a mate along. He gets into history and architecture podcasts on the commute and reads non-fiction about engineering, the Industrial Revolution and space. He picked up an old acoustic guitar during lockdown and can manage a few Oasis and Arctic Monkeys songs at parties.
- travel persona: Uses the four-off days for cheap trips: Lake District walks, a weekend in Edinburgh, a bus tour of Snowdonia. Honeymooned in Croatia and loved it. He's teaching himself Spanish on Duolingo for a planned trip to Seville and Granada, and he'd rather wander a new city than lie by a pool.
- culinary persona: Proper tea is a big deal in their house. He does a decent scouse from his nan's recipe and has got into trying curries and stir-fries from YouTube. On nights he lives on a bacon barm and a flask of tea. Chippy on Fridays if they're both off. He's started batch cooking on Sundays to keep on top of the shifts and the budget.
- hobbies and interests: St Helens Saints and rugby league generally, Parkrun and five-a-side, History and science podcasts, Learning Spanish, Walking Dolly the greyhound round Sherdley Park, Pub quizzes, where he's the team captain at the local on Thursdays, Playing acoustic guitar badly but happily, DIY around the rented house within what the landlord allows
- skills: Float glass line operation and quality checks, Forklift and overhead crane operation, Health and safety reporting (IOSH), Training and buddying new starters, Calm under pressure during breakdowns, Basic Excel and spreadsheet tracking, Organising social events, Cooking on a budget
- career goals: Wants to make shift team leader in the next couple of years, then maybe move into a process technician or health and safety role. He has looked into the company sponsoring an HNC in manufacturing engineering. He wants something steady enough for a mortgage and kids, and he admits he'd get bored doing exactly the same job forever.
- voice: Chatty, warm and quick, with a St Helens accent that sits somewhere between Scouse and Wigan, though not heavy. He talks fast when he's enthused and slows down when he's explaining something technical. He says 'erm' when picking his words, and uses 'sort of' and 'to be fair' a lot, plus the odd 'do you know what I mean'. Says 'tea' for the evening meal, 'barm' for a roll and 'give it me', and occasionally 'yous' to a group. He says 'me mum' and calls people 'mate'. He's comfortable with silence on a call, but he usually fills it with a joke or a 'sorry, go on' if he's talked over someone. He echoes questions back while he thinks: 'what would I change? erm...'
- typing: Quick but fairly tidy. He capitalises the first word and usually ends with a full stop, but he drops apostrophes when rushing ('dont', 'im', 'its'). He uses 'n' for 'and' now and then, adds the occasional 'tbh' or 'lol', and spells everything right because he hates looking sloppy. Answers are short and to the point, sometimes with an extra sentence of detail he couldn't resist adding.
- with strangers: Instantly friendly and easy to talk to, the sort who asks you where you're from within two minutes and finds something in common. He's confident without being cocky, laughs easily and doesn't get flustered by odd questions. He's genuinely curious about other people's jobs and will ask follow-up questions. He's honest and straightforward, though he won't overshare about money or his marriage with someone he's just met.
- small things: Being knackered after a run of night shifts, Saints' latest result or a dodgy refereeing call, Dolly the greyhound being scared of the hoover, His parkrun time that week, A podcast he's just listened to about the Titanic or the Moon landings, Megan making him watch Love Island, The price of petrol for the drive to work, Getting a bacon barm from the van outside the plant
- deeper things: Feeling pressure to buy a house and start a family while rents keep going up, His grandad's lung problems from the pits, and why he takes safety so seriously, Occasionally wondering if he should have gone to university, given how much he likes learning, His faith being something he keeps privately but values, especially after his nan died last year, Worrying about automation at the plant, even though he tries to stay positive, Wanting to be a better dad than some of the lads he grew up around had
- webcam photo: Laptop webcam at chest height, angled slightly upward, in a small back bedroom used as a box room. It's daytime, and soft light comes from a window off to the left, so the left side of his face is brighter. A young white man with a broad, friendly face, light stubble and blue-grey eyes, mid-laugh with a wide open grin. His short light-brown hair is faded at the sides and slightly longer and messy on top. No glasses. He's wearing a navy St Helens Saints training top with the zip half down. Behind him is a magnolia wall with a framed wedding photo slightly off-centre, a cheap white flat-pack shelf holding a few paperbacks, a parkrun finisher token on a lanyard and a small wooden crucifix. An acoustic guitar leans against the wall in the right-hand corner. The edge of a clothes airer with work hi-vis trousers on it is just in frame at the bottom right.

P165 (Rebecca; transcript label: Rebecca):
- first name: Rebecca
- age: 33
- lives in: Exeter, South West England
- occupation: Veterinary surgeon at a mixed farm and small-animal practice on the edge of Crediton, Mid Devon. Her days are mostly cattle and sheep work (TB testing, calvings, herd health visits) plus some small-animal consults, with a share of the out-of-hours rota. She regularly works 50–60 hours a week.
- education detail: A-levels in Biology, Chemistry and English Literature at a state sixth form in Stroud. She then did the five-year BVSc at the University of Bristol, training at the Langford campus, and qualified at 24. Since then she has done CPD in cattle fertility and is part-way through a postgraduate certificate in dairy herd health, which she keeps meaning to finish.
- household: Rents a two-bed terraced house in St Thomas, Exeter, with her partner Dan (35), a self-employed carpenter who mostly does kitchens and boat interiors. They have been together seven years and aren't married. They talk about it now and then, but neither of them is in a hurry. Their household also includes Moss, a scruffy rescue lurcher who came in as a stray and never left.
- cultural background: White British. She grew up in Stroud, Gloucestershire, the eldest of two. Her mum was a primary school teaching assistant and her dad a postman, and there was a lot of folk music and Labour-leaning dinner-table arguing at home. No religion. Her parents weren't churchgoers and she has never felt the pull, though she likes old village churches for the architecture. She has lived in the South West her whole life apart from a few months working abroad, and thinks of herself as a West Country person more than any particular county.
- professional persona: Practical, cheerful and unflappable on calls. She is the vet who'll be laughing with a farmer in a freezing shed at 3am while she sorts out a difficult calving. Farmers trust her because she's straight with them about costs and prognoses and doesn't pretend to know things she doesn't. She's good with nervous new graduates and happy to talk them through things. Paperwork is her weak spot: clinical notes get done, but sometimes late in the evening on the sofa.
- sports persona: Rows pilot gigs with a club in Topsham, training twice a week when the rota allows and racing at local regattas in the summer. Swims in the sea at Exmouth or Dawlish Warren most of the year with a loose group of women from the club, and goes in a wetsuit only in the coldest months. She watches very little sport on telly, except the Six Nations at the pub.
- arts persona: Plays fiddle, badly by her own account but with enthusiasm, at a monthly folk session in a pub near the quay. She learned as a kid and picked it back up after vet school. She goes to gigs at Exeter Phoenix and the Cavern, loves a bit of weird theatre at festivals, and reads a lot of fiction in fits and starts: lately translated novels and nature writing. She has a Libby library app habit and a pile of half-finished paperbacks by the bed.
- travel persona: Spent four months after qualifying doing locum dairy work in the Waikato, New Zealand, and still talks about it. Prefers cheap, slightly chaotic trips: interrailing through Slovenia and Croatia, a walking week in the Picos de Europa, a long weekend in Glasgow for a music festival. Holidays are hard to arrange around the rota, so they often book last minute. She'd rather camp in a field than stay in a resort.
- culinary persona: A generous, messy cook who makes huge pots of dal, chilli or tagine on a Sunday so there's something for the late nights. Dan is the more careful cook and does the roasts. She loves a market and a farm shop, has opinions on clotted cream (cream first, sorry Cornwall), and once got very into sourdough before letting the starter die. They eat dinner late, often at nine or after.
- hobbies and interests: pilot gig rowing, year-round sea swimming, playing fiddle at folk sessions, reading translated fiction and nature writing, walking Moss on Haldon Forest and Woodbury Common, live music and small festivals, foraging, mainly wild garlic and blackberries, pub quizzes, where she is the animal and biology round person
- skills: large-animal medicine and surgery, including calvings and caesareans, explaining bad news to clients plainly but kindly, staying calm in emergencies, driving a 4x4 down terrible Devon lanes in the dark, basic fiddle and reading folk tunes by ear, talking to almost anyone, rowing technique and coxing a gig crew
- career goals: To finish the herd health certificate and move towards a more advisory role with dairy clients, focused on preventive medicine rather than firefighting. She'd like to become a partner or director in a smaller independent practice eventually, ideally one that isn't owned by a big corporate group, and to cut her hours down to something closer to human. She has also floated the idea of doing a stint with a veterinary charity overseas before she's forty.
- voice: Warm, quick and talkative, with a light West Country lilt from Gloucestershire. The R after vowels is softened rather than strong, and it comes out more when she's tired or laughing. She says 'erm' while she's thinking and uses 'sort of' and 'kind of' a lot, often stacked ('it was sort of, kind of a mess'). She ends points with 'you know?' or 'yeah?' and picks up the other person's words when she's engaged ('a good weekend? Yeah, a really good weekend actually'). She says 'knackered' constantly and 'proper' as an intensifier now and then ('proper cold'). She talks fast and goes off on tangents, but catches herself with a 'sorry, anyway' and comes back to the question. Silence doesn't bother her at all. She'll happily wait, or fill it with a joke, and she never sounds anxious about pauses.
- typing: Fast and mostly lowercase, starting with a capital only sometimes. Light punctuation: commas run sentences together, and full stops at the end are often missing. Apostrophes appear about half the time ('dont', 'its', but 'I'm' usually right). She uses 'tbh', 'lol', 'v' for 'very', and an occasional 'x' out of habit, which she then deletes. There are typos from typing on her phone in the car between visits, and she rarely goes back to fix them.
- with strangers: Instantly friendly and open. She asks questions back, makes self-deprecating jokes and fills any awkward moment without seeming to try. She's honest to the point of being blunt if asked for an opinion, but never in a mean way. She's not easily rattled or offended and comes across as relaxed, curious and fun to talk to. Some people find her a bit much at first because she talks so freely.
- small things: Moss stole a whole block of cheddar off the counter last week, the A377 to Crediton being a nightmare with tractors, being knackered after a night on call, the water at Exmouth being proper cold this time of year, a gig rowing race they lost by a boat length, a new album she's been playing on repeat in the car, Dan building a bookshelf she didn't ask for but loves, getting kicked by a heifer and having a bruise the size of a dinner plate
- deeper things: She is worried about burnout. Several friends from vet school have left the profession, and one died by suicide, which she still thinks about., She isn't sure she wants children, and she and Dan haven't fully talked it through., She feels guilty about how little she sees her parents in Stroud now her dad's knees are going., She's quietly frustrated about corporate takeovers of vet practices and what they do to pricing and to the farmers she works with., She sometimes wonders whether she'd have been happier in something creative, though she'd never actually leave vet work.
- webcam photo: A laptop webcam shot from slightly below, framing her from mid-chest up, a little off-centre to the left. Evening, lit mainly by a warm overhead pendant light with a cooler glow from the screen on her face. She has a round, freckled face with weathered cheeks, light brown eyes and a wide grin mid-laugh. Her dark blonde hair is scraped back in a messy ponytail with loose strands around her face. No glasses. She wears a navy fleece with a small embroidered vet practice logo over a grey t-shirt. Behind her is a small kitchen-diner: a pine dresser stacked with mismatched mugs, a wall calendar covered in biro scribbles, a fiddle case leaning against the wall, and a dog lead hanging from a hook. The corner of a grey dog bed with a brindle lurcher's back end in it is just visible at the bottom right.

P166 (Abena; transcript label: Abena):
- first name: Abena
- age: 18
- lives in: Chelmsford, East of England
- occupation: Full-time first-year undergraduate student (BSc Biomedical Science), with a few Saturday shifts at a high-street pharmacy counter
- education detail: Did GCSEs and A-levels (Biology, Chemistry, Psychology: A, B, A) at a sixth form college in Chelmsford. - household: Lives with her parents, who are married, in a three-bedroom semi on an estate on the edge of Chelmsford. Her dad, Kwabena, is a band 6 staff nurse on a ward at Broomfield Hospital. Her mum, Grace, is an admin supervisor in the council's housing team. She understands Twi well but answers her mum in English, which her mum teases her about. The family goes to a Ghanaian Methodist congregation in east London most Sundays, and she sings alto in the youth choir. Her faith matters to her quietly and personally. She prays when she's anxious, but she doesn't talk about it much outside church.
- professional persona: Careful, prepared and a bit nervous. At the pharmacy she triple-checks things and gets flustered if a customer is rude, but she's reliable and the manager trusts her to cash up. At uni she sits near the front, takes very full notes and rarely speaks in seminars unless she's sure of the answer.

She does fine-liner botanical drawings in a sketchbook. She also listens to a mix of gospel, Little Simz, Cleo Sol and old highlife her dad plays in the car.
- travel persona: Has been back to Ghana twice since moving, the last time at fifteen for her grandmother's funeral, which hit her hard. Otherwise she's done a church trip to Paris and day trips to Cambridge and the coast at Southend and Walton. She'd love to go to Japan and Iceland someday, but she worries about flying and about money.
- culinary persona: Her mum's cooking is the centre of home: jollof, light soup, kenkey and fish on Saturdays, waakye now and then. Abena can make a decent jollof and plantain herself, and she bakes banana bread when she's stressed. She calls the evening meal dinner. She has a soft spot for Greggs and for her uni's meal deal.
- hobbies and interests: reading literary fiction and sci-fi, fine-liner botanical sketching, singing alto in the church youth choir, watching science and history YouTube explainers, journalling, baking when stressed, houseplants (she has six and they all have names)
- skills: organised note-taking and revision planning, careful lab technique, drawing, understanding Twi, basic till and stock work, good at listening and remembering details people tell her
- career goals: Wants to work as a biomedical scientist in an NHS lab, possibly doing haematology because of sickle cell in the wider family. She's thinking about a master's later. Her dad would quietly love her to do medicine, and she feels guilty that she doesn't want to.
- voice: Soft-spoken, southern English with a light Essex/London edge, and Ghanaian intonation surfaces mostly when she's talking about family. Measured pace that speeds up when she's nervous or excited about a book. Uses 'erm' a lot at the start of answers and 'kind of' and 'like' as hedges. She tags things with 'you know?' or 'yeah' and occasionally says 'innit' with friends but almost never with strangers. Says 'sorry' to repair herself ('sorry, I mean the second one'). In silences she tends to wait, then fills the gap with an apology or 'I don't know if that makes sense'.
- typing: Writes quick answers in mostly lowercase but with correct apostrophes and reasonable punctuation, because she can't quite leave a typo. She'll go back and fix one. Occasionally uses 'tbh' or 'idk', and rarely uses emojis in a form. Answers are often slightly longer than needed, because she wants to be accurate.
- with strangers: Quiet, polite and a bit guarded at first. She smiles a lot and agrees easily to avoid friction, and she answers precisely but briefly. She warms up noticeably if the conversation touches books, science or something she cares about, and then she can talk for ages and then apologise for rambling.
- small things: the 100 bus being late again, her brother using all the hot water, a book she's halfway through, her monstera getting a new leaf, the meal deal at uni, being shattered after a Saturday shift, choir practice running over, her mum's jollof being better than anyone's
- deeper things: she still grieves her grandmother in Kumasi and wishes she'd visited more, she gets anxiety before exams and sometimes can't sleep for days, she feels caught between being Ghanaian and British and not fully either, she worries about disappointing her dad by not doing medicine, she has only a couple of close friends and sometimes feels lonely at uni living at home, her faith is how she copes when things feel too much
- webcam photo: Laptop webcam at slightly below eye level, angled up a little, in her bedroom in the early evening. Warm light from a desk lamp to her left mixes with grey daylight from a window off-frame on the right. She has a dark brown complexion and a round face, with a small, slightly unsure smile and her eyes looking just off the camera at the screen. Her hair is in shoulder-length box braids, pushed back behind her ears. She wears a grey Anglia Ruskin hoodie over a black T-shirt, a thin gold cross on a chain and no glasses. Behind her is a pale lilac wall with a printed revision timetable and a few botanical drawings pinned up with washi tape. There is a white IKEA shelf holding paperbacks, a trailing pothos and a small monstera in a pot. The corner of a neatly made bed with a mustard throw is just visible on the right.

P167 (Dominic; transcript label: Dominic):
- first name: Dominic
- age: 41
- lives in: Walthamstow, London
- occupation: Co-owner and managing director of a small post-production company in Soho (editing, colour grading and sound for adverts and some TV), managing a team of about 14
- education detail: A-levels at a comprehensive in Bexley, then a BA in Film Studies at the University of Kent. No formal management training. He started as a runner at a Soho facilities house at 22 and worked up through assistant editor and editor before co-founding his own company at 33.
- household: Rents the loft conversion in his older sister Claire's terraced house. Claire and her husband Rob are married and have two kids, aged 9 and 12. He moved in 'for a few months' after splitting with his partner of eleven years and selling their flat in Leyton. That was over two years ago. He pays rent, mostly eats out, and is out of the house a lot of the time.
- cultural background: Grew up in Bexleyheath in south-east London. His dad was a print-shop manager and his mum a school receptionist. He was christened and confirmed Church of England, and ticks 'Christian' on forms. He goes to a carol service at Christmas with his mum and that's about it. He calls it 'more heritage than belief really'. He has lived on the north-east side of the river since his late twenties and now thinks of himself as an East London person, which his family tease him about.
- professional persona: Good in the edit suite and good with clients who want something interesting. Bad at anything that involves a spreadsheet, a deadline he set himself, or remembering to reply to emails. He relies heavily on his business partner Priya and an office manager to keep the company solvent and compliant. He works long, irregular hours, often 10am to 10pm in a busy week, and likes being the one whose name goes on the pitch. - arts persona: This is where his real interest is. He goes to the cinema on his own a lot, mainly the Prince Charles, the BFI and the Curzon. He likes Korean thrillers, seventies American films and anything odd. He goes to gallery openings partly for the work and partly for the networking. He collects a few limited-run screen prints, which he can't really afford to keep buying. He listens to a lot of ambient and jazz-adjacent electronic music while working.
- travel persona: Prefers city breaks to beach holidays, usually alone or with one friend: Tokyo, Mexico City, Berlin for a weekend. He books late and pays more because of it, and has missed at least two flights. He likes a nice hotel and will stretch to one even when it doesn't really make sense.
- culinary persona: Doesn't really cook. In the week he eats lunch at his desk and dinner at whatever is open near the office. He likes going to new places, especially small-plates, natural wine and Japanese restaurants, and enjoys knowing about somewhere before it gets busy. At Claire's he'll occasionally make a big pasta for everyone on a Sunday and leave the kitchen in a state.
- hobbies and interests: Watching films, mostly on his own at independent cinemas, Collecting screen prints and film posters, Vinyl, mostly jazz and electronic reissues, Wandering round galleries and East London studios, Trying new restaurants, Occasional cycling
- skills: Video editing (Avid, Premiere, some DaVinci Resolve), Pitching creative ideas to clients, Staying calm in a crisis, Spotting talent in junior staff, Negotiating rates, Talking knowledgeably about film history
- career goals: He wants the company to win more long-form TV and documentary work, partly for the money and partly because it's more prestigious than adverts. He'd also like to get his name on a feature as a director or producer at some point. Privately he'd consider selling his stake to a bigger group if the offer was good. He hasn't mentioned that to Priya.
- voice: Quiet, fairly low and unhurried, with a light South-East London accent that's been sanded down by years of client meetings. Some glottal stops, and 'yeah' as an acknowledgement. He says 'sort of' a lot and the odd 'er' while he's thinking. He sometimes ends with 'you know' or 'if that makes sense'. He doesn't fill silences and is comfortable letting a pause sit, which can come across as slightly aloof. His answers are short unless the topic is film or work he's proud of, and then he goes on for a bit. He'd say 'dinner' for the evening meal and 'mate' to a man he's just met. He uses dry understatement rather than enthusiasm, e.g. 'it was alright actually' for something he loved.
- typing: Fast and careless. Mostly lowercase, occasionally capitalising the start of a sentence out of habit. He often drops apostrophes ('dont', 'its') and mostly skips full stops at the end. He uses commas rather than separate sentences, the odd 'tbh' or 'prob', and short answers. He doesn't go back to correct typos.

req.text:
You write transcripts of realistic video calls between strangers for a fully synthetic research dataset set in the UK. The study, in order (from its published design): a short puzzle task done alone; first impressions of the others' webcam photos; then a series of three-minute, one-on-one video calls in rounds, each person meeting the others in their group; after each call a short survey.

Call shape (from the original study's numbers): a call is cut off by a three-minute timer. A typical call has about 30 turns (most between 20 and 39) and about 570 words in total (most between 440 and 682); half of all turns are 12 words or fewer, and a quarter are 24 or more. Short acknowledgements ("yeah", "mm") count as turns too. So aim for about 570 words in about 30 turns: alongside the quick back-and-forth, people often talk in longer stretches (explaining their job, telling a story), and those long turns carry much of the call.

Guide to British conversational English (use it for how people talk; it is a description of speech, not a script):
How British people talk in casual conversation. This is a paraphrase of published descriptions of spoken British English; sources are in SOURCES.md. Use these features lightly and only where they fit the person. Never use them as a caricature.

- **Fillers.** British speakers hesitate with "erm" and "er". Women and younger speakers lean towards "erm".
- **Hedges.** "Sort of" is everywhere and steady. "Kind of" is spreading, and younger speakers use it more.
- **Politeness words.** "Please", "thank you", "thanks" and "sorry" mostly mean what they say. "Sorry" also works as a repair word (to correct yourself, or to ask someone to repeat) and can be ironic.
- **Tags at the end of a sentence.** "You know", "right", "okay", "yeah", "do you know what I mean". Among young Londoners, "innit" and "you get me" are rising. Tags depend on age and region only, never on ethnicity.
- **Echoing.** In an engaged conversation people pick up and re-use parts of each other's words.
- **Regional words and grammar** (from a recent dialect survey):
  - A bread roll is a "barm" in the North West (Manchester to Liverpool and western Lancashire), a "cob" around Nottinghamshire, a "bap" in Staffordshire, the West Midlands and North Wales, and a "batch" in Liverpool and Coventry.
  - Around Liverpool an ice lolly can be a "lolly ice".
  - The evening meal is "tea" in the North West, North East and Yorkshire, and "dinner" in the South East and London. Some people say both.
  - "Yous" or "youse" for plural "you" is common in the North East (Newcastle, Teesside), Liverpool and Scotland, less so in Manchester, and rare in York, Leeds and Sheffield.
  - "Give it me" is normal in the North West and West Midlands and widely accepted in Sheffield and York; it fades south of Birmingham, Coventry and Leicester.
  - "You was" is widely used, historically Northern and now found as far south as London.
- **Everyday British words** to draw on where they fit, without assigning them to regions: knackered or shattered, chuffed or made up, skint or brassic, mardy or stroppy, mum or mam, mate or pal, settee, sofa or couch.

req.text:
You write transcripts of realistic video calls between strangers for a fully synthetic research dataset set in the UK. The study, in order (from its published design): a short puzzle task done alone; first impressions of the others' webcam photos; then a series of three-minute, one-on-one video calls in rounds, each person meeting the others in their group; after each call a short survey.

Call shape (from the original study's numbers): a call is cut off by a three-minute timer. A typical call has about 30 turns (most between 20 and 39) and about 570 words in total (most between 440 and 682); half of all turns are 12 words or fewer, and a quarter are 24 or more. Short acknowledgements ("yeah", "mm") count as turns too. So aim for about 570 words in about 30 turns: alongside the quick back-and-forth, people often talk in longer stretches (explaining their job, telling a story), and those long turns carry much of the call.

Guide to British conversational English (use it for how people talk; it is a description of speech, not a script):
How British people talk in casual conversation. This is a paraphrase of published descriptions of spoken British English; sources are in SOURCES.md. Use these features lightly and only where they fit the person. Never use them as a caricature.

- **Fillers.** British speakers hesitate with "erm" and "er". Women and younger speakers lean towards "erm".
- **Hedges.** "Sort of" is everywhere and steady. "Kind of" is spreading, and younger speakers use it more.
- **Politeness words.** "Please", "thank you", "thanks" and "sorry" mostly mean what they say. "Sorry" also works as a repair word (to correct yourself, or to ask someone to repeat) and can be ironic.
- **Tags at the end of a sentence.** "You know", "right", "okay", "yeah", "do you know what I mean". Among young Londoners, "innit" and "you get me" are rising. Tags depend on age and region only, never on ethnicity.
- **Echoing.** In an engaged conversation people pick up and re-use parts of each other's words.
- **Regional words and grammar** (from a recent dialect survey):
  - A bread roll is a "barm" in the North West (Manchester to Liverpool and western Lancashire), a "cob" around Nottinghamshire, a "bap" in Staffordshire, the West Midlands and North Wales, and a "batch" in Liverpool and Coventry.
  - Around Liverpool an ice lolly can be a "lolly ice".
  - The evening meal is "tea" in the North West, North East and Yorkshire, and "dinner" in the South East and London. Some people say both.
  - "Yous" or "youse" for plural "you" is common in the North East (Newcastle, Teesside), Liverpool and Scotland, less so in Manchester, and rare in York, Leeds and Sheffield.
  - "Give it me" is normal in the North West and West Midlands and widely accepted in Sheffield and York; it fades south of Birmingham, Coventry and Leicester.
  - "You was" is widely used, historically Northern and now found as far south as London.
- **Everyday British words** to draw on where they fit, without assigning them to regions: knackered or shattered, chuffed or made up, skint or brassic, mardy or stroppy, mum or mam, mate or pal, settee, sofa or couch.

The group (session S29). Persona cards, including the webcam photo each person was rated on:

P153 (Tomasz; transcript label: Tomasz):
- first name: Tomasz
- age: 42
- lives in: Basingstoke, South East England
- occupation: Carpenter and kitchen fitter, employed full-time by a small fitted-kitchen firm based on an industrial estate on the edge of town. Usually works about 40 to 45 hours a week, going out to customers' houses across north Hampshire and Berkshire.
- education detail: Finished a technikum (vocational secondary school) in wood technology near Rzeszów in south-east Poland, which gave him a qualified joiner's certificate. Since moving to the UK he has done short courses, including CSCS card training and a manufacturer's worktop installation course. No university.
- household: Lives with his wife Claire, 39, who is English and works as a dispenser at a high-street pharmacy, and their son Oliver, 10. They own a three-bed semi on an estate in Brighton Hill that they bought in 2016, with a mortgage. Tomasz's van is parked outside.
- cultural background: Born and raised in a small town in Podkarpackie, Poland, in a Catholic family. His father was a lorry driver and his mother worked in a school kitchen. He came to England in 2006 at 24 with a friend, first doing labouring in Reading, then joinery work. He met Claire in 2010 through a mate from work. He is Catholic and goes to the Polish Mass in Reading now and then, reliably at Christmas and Easter, and Oliver did his First Communion there. He speaks Polish to his mum on video calls every Sunday and English at home. He feels settled here but still calls Poland 'home' without thinking about it.
- professional persona: Good with his hands and quietly proud of a clean scribe on a worktop or doors that hang straight. Customers like him because he is patient and doesn't argue, even when they change their minds halfway through a job. He is less good at the admin side. He forgets to photograph finished jobs for the company Instagram, his timesheets are late, and he once left a whole box of hinges at a customer's house. His boss tolerates it because the work itself is good.
- sports persona: Watches football rather than plays it. He follows the Polish national team and keeps a soft spot for Resovia from back home. Here he half-supports Arsenal because Claire's family do. He goes carp fishing at a lake near Alton maybe twice a month in summer, sometimes overnight with a bivvy. He doesn't go to a gym and says his job is enough.
- arts persona: Not much of a theatre or gallery person. He listens to a mix of Polish rock from his teens, like Dżem and Perfect, and whatever is on Heart in the van. He watches crime series on Netflix with Claire, and the occasional Polish film when one comes up. He likes woodworking videos on YouTube more than anything else.
- travel persona: Goes back to Poland most summers for two weeks to see his mum and sister, usually flying Ryanair from Stansted or Luton, though one year they drove. They had one beach holiday in Crete with Claire's parents. He'd like to take Oliver to the Tatra mountains properly, but he hasn't planned it, and Claire does most of the booking.
- culinary persona: Claire does most of the weekday cooking, but Tomasz makes Polish dishes at weekends: żurek at Easter, bigos in winter, and pierogi with his mum's recipe when he has patience, which isn't often. He gets things from the Polish shop on Winton Square. On site he lives on meal deals and coffee from the garage. He likes a barbecue in summer and is the one who stands over it.
- hobbies and interests: carp fishing, restoring old bikes in the garage, mostly for Oliver and his friends, watching woodworking and van-fitout videos on YouTube, Polish and Premier League football on TV, half-finished projects around the house, like a garden bench that's been 'nearly done' for a year, helping Oliver with Lego builds
- skills: fitting kitchens and worktops, including laminate and solid wood, hanging doors and first and second fix carpentry, reading drawings and measuring up, basic plumbing and electrics for appliance installs, within what he's allowed to do, fluent Polish and good working English, staying calm with difficult customers, fixing bikes
- career goals: Vaguely thinks about going self-employed one day doing bespoke fitted wardrobes and alcoves, because he knows that's where the money is. But he dislikes paperwork and chasing invoices, so the idea hasn't moved much in five years. Mostly he wants steady work, to pay down the mortgage, and not to wreck his knees before 55.
- voice: Calm, unhurried, fairly low voice with a clear Polish accent softened by 18 years in England. His grammar is mostly good, with small slips like dropping 'the' or 'a' now and then ('I went to shop', 'is good, yeah'). He uses 'er' rather than 'erm', and picked up 'sort of', 'mate', 'to be honest' and 'yeah, no' from building sites. He says 'dinner' for the evening meal. He gives short answers at first and doesn't rush to fill silences. He'll wait, then say something like 'yeah, er, I think so' or 'what else you want to know?' He laughs quietly at himself more than at others. He agrees easily but will say 'no, is not really like that' gently if something is wrong. When he's tired he sometimes says 'knackered'.
- typing: Mostly lowercase, starts sentences without capitals, and capitalises 'I' about half the time. Few commas, and full stops often missing at the end. Usually drops apostrophes ('dont', 'its', 'im'). He doesn't use text-speak much beyond 'ok' and the odd 'thx'. Answers are short and practical, with an occasional small grammar slip, for example 'i work in kitchens fitting, about 8 years same company'.
- with strangers: Polite, reserved and a bit hard to read at first. He is friendly but not chatty, and answers what he's asked without volunteering much. He comes across as easygoing and patient, the kind of person who won't complain if the call runs late. He warms up if the conversation turns to something practical he knows about, or to his son.
- small things: the van's sliding door sticks and he keeps meaning to get it looked at, traffic on the M3 in the mornings, a customer who changed her worktop colour three times, Oliver's football training on Saturday mornings, the Polish shop running out of good kiełbasa, a bike he found at the tip that just needed new brakes, the fishing lake being closed because of the weather, the price of timber going up
- deeper things: his dad died in 2019 and he couldn't get back in time; he still thinks about it, he worries a little about his mum living alone in Poland and whether she should come here, but she won't, after Brexit he applied for settled status and felt, for the first time, like a guest, he and Claire had wanted a second child but it didn't happen, and they don't talk about it much now, he sometimes feels he's 'not really Polish any more and not really English', his faith is quieter than his mother's, but he prays when things are bad
- webcam photo: Laptop webcam view from slightly below, the laptop set on a kitchen table, framing his head and shoulders a little off-centre to the left. Evening, lit by a warm ceiling light overhead and the cooler glow of the screen on his face. He has a broad face, light stubble with a few grey hairs at the chin, short light-brown hair clipped at the sides and thinning slightly at the front, and blue-grey eyes. No glasses. His expression is neutral and a little tired, mouth closed, with the faint start of a polite smile. He is wearing a navy work fleece with a small embroidered company logo on the chest, unzipped over a grey T-shirt. Behind him is a fitted kitchen with white gloss doors and a wood-effect laminate worktop. On the worktop are a kettle, a toaster, a fruit bowl with bananas and a stack of post. A child's school drawing and a takeaway menu are held to the fridge with magnets on the right edge of the frame, and a dark window shows a reflection of the ceiling light. A hi-vis vest hangs over the back of a chair partly visible beside him.

P154 (Rob; transcript label: Rob):
- first name: Rob
- age: 31
- lives in: Stockport (Edgeley), North West England
- occupation: Full-time mature student, second year of a BSc in Ecology and Wildlife Conservation at Manchester Metropolitan University. Before that he spent eight years in admin and clerical roles, latterly as a planning support officer at a local council. He does a few paid shifts in the summer as a bat and bird survey assistant for a small ecological consultancy.
- education detail: Went to a comprehensive in Stockport and did A-levels in Geography, Biology and English Language at a sixth form college. Started a degree at 18 but left after a term because he didn't feel ready. Went into office work, did an Access to HE course in Science part-time at 28, then started university full-time at 30 on a student loan, with savings to top it up.
- household: Rents a two-bed terraced house in Edgeley with his partner of six years, Hannah, who is a dental nurse. They aren't married and say they've 'never really seen the point yet'. The second bedroom is a box room he uses as a study. No kids. There's a rescue cat called Moss.
- cultural background: White British, born and raised in Stockport. His dad was a bus driver and his mum works in a school office. He has one older sister in Hazel Grove. Not religious, and neither were his parents in any real way. He's the first in the family to go to university, which he mentions matter-of-factly rather than proudly.
- professional persona: Organised in a practical, office-trained way, but not obsessive about it: he can run a spreadsheet and chase an email, though his notes are a bit chaotic. He is straightforward with lecturers and doesn't flatter anyone. He tends to be the calm one in group projects when deadlines bunch up. He left a steady council job because he was bored, and he says that plainly.
- sports persona: Not sporty in a team sense. He watches Stockport County when he can afford it and follows them loosely the rest of the time. Mostly he walks: long days in the Peak District, sometimes with a camera. He cycles to the station. He took up bouldering at a climbing wall in town last year and is middling at it.
- arts persona: Reads a lot, mostly nature writing and odd non-fiction, plus the occasional sci-fi novel. He likes documentaries and has a soft spot for old folk and ambient music. He goes to small gigs in Manchester a few times a year. He takes decent wildlife photos on a secondhand camera and has no interest in posting them much.
- travel persona: Travels cheaply and not often. He has done a few weeks on Mull and in the Highlands, a trip to the Netherlands with Hannah, and a student field trip to the Algarve that he loved. He wants to do a proper trip to Scandinavia or the Pyrenees for the wildlife. He's happier with a tent or a hostel than a resort.
- culinary persona: Decent everyday cook and does most of the tea during the week because his timetable is looser than Hannah's. Lots of one-pot things, curries and chilli. He's been trying to eat less meat for environmental reasons but doesn't make a thing of it. He likes a chippy barm and a pint at the weekend.
- hobbies and interests: hillwalking in the Peak District, birdwatching and bat detecting, wildlife photography, bouldering, nature writing and popular science books, following Stockport County, small music gigs, volunteering at a local nature reserve on occasional Saturdays
- skills: spreadsheets and data entry, species identification (birds, getting better at plants), using bat detectors and survey software, basic GIS mapping, writing clear emails and reports, staying calm under pressure, cooking on a budget
- career goals: Finish his degree with a good grade, then get a job as a field ecologist or in a wildlife trust, ideally in the North West so he and Hannah don't have to move. He'd consider a master's if he could fund it. He isn't fussed about money as long as the work is outdoors and means something.
- voice: Relaxed, mid-paced, light Stockport/Manchester accent without being broad. Says 'erm' when thinking, sometimes 'sort of' or 'kind of' to soften an opinion. Uses 'mate' casually, says 'tea' for the evening meal, and might say 'I was made up' or 'I'm knackered'. Answers honestly and fairly briefly, with the occasional dry joke. Totally fine with silence: he'll just wait, or say 'yeah, I think that's it really' rather than pad things out.
- typing: Quick and mostly lowercase, with capitals only for names now and then. Commas are sparse and full stops are often missing at the end. He usually gets apostrophes right in 'don't' and 'it's' but drops them when rushing ('im', 'thats'). He writes 'tbh' occasionally and otherwise avoids text abbreviations. Short, plain answers.
- with strangers: Easygoing and polite, not especially chatty to start but warms up quickly. Comes across as unpretentious and a bit dry. Doesn't try to impress, and will say 'I don't know, to be honest' rather than bluff. Seems steady and hard to rattle.
- small things: Moss the cat knocking stuff off his desk, trying to get the 7:40 train into Piccadilly, a barn owl he saw on a field trip, County's last result, doing the big shop at Aldi with Hannah, his secondhand camera lens, the damp in the back bedroom, the essay deadline that's coming up
- deeper things: dropping out of uni at 18 and feeling like he'd let himself down for years, money being genuinely tight since he gave up his salary, and feeling a bit guilty that Hannah covers more of the bills, being the first in his family at university and sometimes feeling older than everyone on his course, wondering whether he and Hannah will get married or have kids, and not being in a rush either way, how much being outdoors helped him when the office job made him feel flat
- webcam photo: Head-and-shoulders shot from a laptop camera, slightly below eye level so the ceiling corner shows. Daylight from a window on the left lights one side of his face, and the right side is a little shadowed. White man with a short light-brown beard and short, slightly messy mid-brown hair, no glasses. He has a mild, friendly half-smile and is looking just off-centre at the screen. He's wearing a faded dark green hoodie over a grey T-shirt. Behind him is a magnolia wall with a cork board pinned with lecture timetables, a printed OS map of the Dark Peak and a couple of photo postcards of birds. To the right is a cheap white bookshelf with field guides, paperbacks, a pair of binoculars and a pot plant. The top of a grey office chair is visible behind his shoulders, and a tabby cat's tail hangs over the edge of the shelf.

P155 (Neil; transcript label: Neil):
- first name: Neil
- age: 53
- lives in: Loughborough, East Midlands
- occupation: Site services manager at a mid-sized food packaging manufacturer on an industrial estate on the edge of Loughborough. He looks after maintenance, health and safety compliance and contractors, and has a team of six engineers and a facilities coordinator.
- education detail: Left school in Coalville with four O-levels and two A-levels (maths and physics). Did an HND in mechanical engineering at a polytechnic while on day release from his first maintenance job. Picked up NEBOSH and IOSH certificates through work. Finished an Open University BA in History in his forties, studying evenings over six years, mainly because he wanted to.
- household: Lives with his wife Julie, 51, a part-time practice manager at a GP surgery, in a 1960s three-bed semi they have owned for 22 years. Their daughter Hannah (25) lives in Sheffield and works for a housing association. Their son Tom (22) moved to Bristol last year. The house is noticeably quieter now and they are still getting used to it.
- cultural background: White British, born and raised in North West Leicestershire. His dad was a fitter at a mine that later closed, and his mum worked in a hosiery factory and then a school kitchen. He was brought up loosely Church of England but has no religion and doesn't think about it much. He has a strong attachment to the local landscape and industrial history: Charnwood, the old pit villages, the canals.
- professional persona: Methodical and calm. He is the person who reads the whole contract and keeps the maintenance log properly. He doesn't get rattled when a line goes down at 6am, and colleagues describe him as 'unflappable' and fair. req.text:
You write transcripts of realistic video calls between strangers for a fully synthetic research dataset set in the UK. The study, in order (from its published design): a short puzzle task done alone; first impressions of the others' webcam photos; then a series of three-minute, one-on-one video calls in rounds, each person meeting the others in their group; after each call a short survey.

Call shape (from the original study's numbers): a call is cut off by a three-minute timer. A typical call has about 30 turns (most between 20 and 39) and about 570 words in total (most between 440 and 682); half of all turns are 12 words or fewer, and a quarter are 24 or more. Short acknowledgements ("yeah", "mm") count as turns too. So aim for about 570 words in about 30 turns: alongside the quick back-and-forth, people often talk in longer stretches (explaining their job, telling a story), and those long turns carry much of the call.

Guide to British conversational English (use it for how people talk; it is a description of speech, not a script):
How British people talk in casual conversation. This is a paraphrase of published descriptions of spoken British English; sources are in SOURCES.md. Use these features lightly and only where they fit the person. Never use them as a caricature.

- **Fillers.** British speakers hesitate with "erm" and "er". Women and younger speakers lean towards "erm".
- **Hedges.** "Sort of" is everywhere and steady. "Kind of" is spreading, and younger speakers use it more.
- **Politeness words.** "Please", "thank you", "thanks" and "sorry" mostly mean what they say. "Sorry" also works as a repair word (to correct yourself, or to ask someone to repeat) and can be ironic.
- **Tags at the end of a sentence.** "You know", "right", "okay", "yeah", "do you know what I mean". Among young Londoners, "innit" and "you get me" are rising. Tags depend on age and region only, never on ethnicity.
- **Echoing.** In an engaged conversation people pick up and re-use parts of each other's words.
- **Regional words and grammar** (from a recent dialect survey):
  - A bread roll is a "barm" in the North West (Manchester to Liverpool and western Lancashire), a "cob" around Nottinghamshire, a "bap" in Staffordshire, the West Midlands and North Wales, and a "batch" in Liverpool and Coventry.
  - Around Liverpool an ice lolly can be a "lolly ice".
  - The evening meal is "tea" in the North West, North East and Yorkshire, and "dinner" in the South East and London. Some people say both.
  - "Yous" or "youse" for plural "you" is common in the North East (Newcastle, Teesside), Liverpool and Scotland, less so in Manchester, and rare in York, Leeds and Sheffield.
  - "Give it me" is normal in the North West and West Midlands and widely accepted in Sheffield and York; it fades south of Birmingham, Coventry and Leicester.
  - "You was" is widely used, historically Northern and now found as far south as London.
- **Everyday British words** to draw on where they fit, without assigning them to regions: knackered or shattered, chuffed or made up, skint or brassic, mardy or stroppy, mum or mam, mate or pal, settee, sofa or couch.

- education detail: GCSEs and A-levels (Biology, English, Geography) at a comprehensive and sixth form in Somerset. Diploma in Veterinary Nursing, gained while working at a practice. She later did short CPD courses in practice management and anaesthesia monitoring.

- cultural background: White British, born in Bridgwater and raised in Somerset. Her dad worked at the Hinkley Point power station and her mum was a school dinner lady. She apologises quickly ('sorry, I mean...') when she corrects herself. She doesn't fill silences herself. She waits, then gives a careful, honest answer, sometimes with a small nervous laugh. If a question touches on something emotional, her voice can go a bit tight.
- typing: Types properly even in a quick form: capital letters at the start of sentences, full stops, correct apostrophes. She rarely abbreviates beyond 'e.g.' or 'etc.'. Answers are short but complete, sometimes with a slightly formal phrasing. She occasionally adds a qualifying second sentence, like 'Not sure if that is what you meant.' No emojis, and the odd typo she goes back and fixes.
- with strangers: Reserved and polite, a bit nervous at first, and inclined to let the other person lead. She answers questions honestly rather than to impress, and won't exaggerate or claim knowledge she doesn't have. She warms up slowly if the person seems kind. She can be surprisingly frank once comfortable, but she is never loud or performative, and she would rather listen than talk.
- small things: the cat being sick on the hall rug again, how steep the walk up from the bus stop is, a robin that has started visiting the bird feeder, this month's book group novel, the ferry to Rotterdam being delayed by weather, Graham's new hobby of sourdough, the university car park being full by half eight, her sister's grandchildren in Utrecht
- deeper things: She still feels slightly foreign after thirty years and isn't sure where 'home' is., She has had periods of anxiety and once took several weeks off work with stress, which she found hard to admit., Her mother in Amersfoort is in the early stages of dementia, and she feels guilty living so far away., She worries a great deal about her daughter, who lives alone in Bristol., Her faith helped her through a miscarriage in her thirties that she rarely talks about., She sometimes wonders whether she gave up a more ambitious career when she moved to England.

Soft daylight comes from a window to her left, so the left side of her face is brighter, and a warm ceiling light is on. She has a pale, lightly lined face with a few freckles, no visible makeup apart from a little mascara, and a polite, slightly tentative closed-mouth smile. Her hair is shoulder-length, ash-blonde going grey, tucked behind one ear. She wears thin rectangular tortoiseshell reading glasses and a navy wool cardigan over a cream striped top, with a small silver cross on a fine chain just visible at her neckline. Behind her is a pale sage-green kitchen wall with a calendar from a Dutch bakery showing a canal scene, a wooden shelf with cookbooks and a blue-and-white Delft-style jug holding wooden spoons, and the edge of a window with a bird feeder visible outside. Part of a kettle and a tea towel hanging on an oven door are visible in the lower right corner.

P138 (Shahida; transcript label: Shahida):
- first name: Shahida
- age: 67
- lives in: Ilford, London (Redbridge, East London)
- occupation: Retired. Worked part-time for about fifteen years as a sales assistant in a ladies' clothing and fabric shop on Green Street, Upton Park, and stopped at 60 when her knees got bad. Not in paid work now.
- education detail: Passed her Matric (secondary school certificate) in Lahore and started her FA intermediate studies but left when she married at 20. Took ESOL evening classes at the adult college in Ilford in the early 1980s, plus a basic computer course at the library about ten years ago.
- household: Lives with her husband Tariq, 71, a retired minicab driver, in a three-bed semi in Newbury Park they have owned since 1994. Two sons and a daughter have all married and moved out. The elder son lives ten minutes away in Gants Hill and his children are dropped off after school two days a week.
- cultural background: Born in Lahore, Pakistan. Came to London in 1978 after marrying Tariq, whose family were already in East Ham. Sunni Muslim, prays regularly at home and goes to the local mosque's ladies' section for Eid and some Fridays. Punjabi is her first language, Urdu her second, and English is fluent for everyday life. She has made two trips to Pakistan in the last decade and did Umrah in 2017. Her world is family, the mosque network and a handful of long-standing neighbours.
- professional persona: Was a reliable, efficient shop worker. She was good at the till and at folding and stock, and firm with customers who tried to haggle too far. She was quite good at nudging people towards the dearer suit. She saw the job as money, not identity, and doesn't miss it except for the routine.
- sports persona: Not sporty at all. Walks to the shops on Cranbrook Road when her knees allow and does the chair exercises the physio gave her, mostly. Tariq watches cricket and she has it on in the background without following it.
- arts persona: Little interest. She watches Pakistani dramas on YouTube and ARY on the TV in the evenings, always the same kind of family drama. Has never been to a gallery or the theatre in London and doesn't see the point.
- travel persona: Travels for family and religion only: Lahore for weddings and funerals, and Umrah once. Doesn't care for holidays as such. Her son took them to Turkey once and she found it 'too much walking, food not right'. Prefers her own bed.
- culinary persona: Cooks every day, the same rotation she has done for forty years: daal, aloo gosht, chicken karahi, saag in winter, rotis made fresh. Halal only, buys meat from the same butcher on Ilford Lane. Doesn't experiment and is privately critical of her daughter-in-law's cooking. Has cut down on sugar because of her diabetes, grudgingly.
- hobbies and interests: Pakistani TV dramas on YouTube, keeping the house very clean and organised, sewing and altering clothes for family, looking after her grandchildren after school, WhatsApp family groups, doing online surveys for vouchers, looking after her front garden roses
- skills: sewing and tailoring alterations, household budgeting, which she tracks in a notebook, cooking large quantities for gatherings, bargaining and spotting a good deal, basic smartphone and tablet use, organising family events and dowry-style gift lists
- career goals: None in work terms. She wants to keep her health manageable, see the youngest grandchild through primary school, and get the bathroom redone before Tariq 'spends it on something stupid'. She does the surveys mainly for the Amazon vouchers.
- voice: Fluent, practical London-Asian English with a clear Punjabi-Urdu accent. She is quite clipped and to the point, with medium pace and short answers unless asked something about family or money. She uses the occasional 'erm' while thinking, and sometimes ends with 'you know' or 'okay?'. She says 'dinner' for the evening meal. She sometimes drops articles ('I went to doctor') or uses 'you was', but it is natural, not heavy. She doesn't fill silences. She'll just wait, or say 'that's it' when she's finished. Occasional Urdu word slips in ('acha', 'bas') when she's wrapping up.
- typing: Short answers, often all lower case or with a capital only at the start. She rarely uses commas, sometimes doubles up full stops ('yes..'). Apostrophes are often missing ('dont', 'its'). She writes numbers as digits. No abbreviations beyond 'ok'. Occasional typos she doesn't correct.
- with strangers: Polite but reserved, slightly guarded at first. She answers what's asked without volunteering much. She can come across as a bit blunt or unimpressed, and isn't trying to please the interviewer. She warms up a little if the topic touches on her grandchildren, her house or getting value for money.
- small things: the bus being late again on the 128, her knees in the cold weather, the price of lamb going up, picking the grandkids up from school, her neighbour's hedge growing over her side, the new Lidl, having to go for her diabetes check at the surgery, Tariq falling asleep in front of the cricket
- deeper things: She married young and didn't choose Tariq herself. It worked out, but she says it 'works because I run everything'., She resents that her younger sister in Lahore got to finish college, She is quietly proud the family owns their house outright and drops it into conversation with other aunties, She thinks her daughter married 'down' and hasn't fully forgiven it, She worries less about death than about who will look after Tariq if she goes first, She once kept cash from the shop till over a disputed wage and doesn't regret it
- webcam photo: Head-and-shoulders shot from a tablet propped slightly below face level on a dining table, so the camera looks a little up at her. Soft daylight comes from a window to her left, and the right side of her face is slightly shadowed. She is a South Asian woman in her late sixties with a round face, faint lines around the mouth and a neutral, slightly impatient expression. She is looking just past the camera. A loose cream chiffon dupatta covers most of her hair, showing grey-black hair at the hairline. She wears a maroon kameez with small embroidery at the neckline, thin gold earrings, and gold-rimmed reading glasses pushed up on her head. Behind her is a magnolia wall with a framed gold Arabic calligraphy print (Ayat al-Kursi) and a wall clock. To one side is the corner of a dark wood glass-fronted cabinet holding a dinner set and some brass ornaments. On the edge of the table is a plastic-covered tablecloth with a floral pattern.

P139 (Helen; transcript label: Helen):
- first name: Helen
- age: 41
- lives in: Otley, West Yorkshire (Yorkshire and The Humber)
- occupation: Archivist in a university special collections library in Leeds, part-time (three days a week, about 22 hours)
- education detail: Grew up in Keighley and went to the local comprehensive. BA in History at the University of York, then a postgraduate MA in Archives and Records Management at Liverpool. She is a registered member of the Archives and Records Association.
- household: Lives with her daughter Isla, 9, in a two-bedroom stone terrace near the centre of Otley. She was never married. She and Isla's dad split up when Isla was a toddler. He lives in Bradford and has Isla every other weekend, which mostly works without fuss. Her mum lives fifteen minutes away and does the Tuesday school pick-up.
- cultural background: White British, Yorkshire born and bred. She was raised Methodist and now goes to the parish church in Otley perhaps twice a month, more often around Advent and Easter. Her faith is quiet and private, more about the habit of reflection and the community than about doctrine. Her family is solidly working class. She was the first of them to go to university, and that still makes her mum a bit proud and a bit wary.
- professional persona: Careful and methodical, and happiest with a box of uncatalogued letters and a free afternoon. She does the cataloguing, the digitisation planning and some reading-room supervision. She dreads the termly show-and-tell sessions for students, but she prepares thoroughly and they usually go fine. Colleagues trust her judgement on tricky provenance questions. She answers emails thoughtfully rather than quickly.
- sports persona: Not sporty in any team sense. She walks a lot, mostly up the Chevin and along the Wharfe, often on her own early on a Sunday. She did a beginners' yoga course at the community centre and now follows videos at home instead because the class felt like too many people.
- arts persona: Reading is the big one. She likes translated fiction, mostly Scandinavian and Japanese, and nature writing. She has taught herself botanical drawing in pencil and watercolour and fills small sketchbooks with hedgerow plants. She likes choral music, especially evensong, and occasionally goes to a concert at Leeds Minster or Ripon Cathedral. She also goes to small exhibitions at the Hepworth Wakefield and the Henry Moore Institute, ideally on a quiet weekday.
- travel persona: Prefers slow, quiet trips. She has had several holidays in a rented cottage in Northumberland or on the Lleyn Peninsula with Isla. Before Isla she went alone to Kyoto and to the Lofoten Islands and still thinks about both. She would love to take Isla to Norway when she is older. She has no interest in resorts or city breaks with a packed itinerary.
- culinary persona: A practical, decent cook. Tea is usually something simple, like a lentil soup, a traybake or pasta, because she is shattered by six. She enjoys baking bread at the weekend and has had a sourdough starter going for three years. She is curious about Japanese home cooking and makes a passable miso soup. She will eat out at a quiet café but finds busy restaurants tiring.
- hobbies and interests: botanical drawing and watercolour, reading translated fiction and nature writing, walking the Chevin and the Wharfe valley, baking sourdough, learning Italian on an app, slowly, evensong and choral music, local history of Wharfedale mills
- skills: archival cataloguing and metadata standards, handling and assessing fragile documents, palaeography for 17th–19th century handwriting, careful, clear written communication, pencil and watercolour plant illustration, bread baking, organising a household on a tight timetable
- career goals: She wants to stay part-time while Isla is at primary school. Longer term she would like to lead a cataloguing project of her own, ideally on a collection of local women's letters or diaries, and perhaps write it up for a journal. She has no wish to manage a large team. She would take a senior archivist post if it kept her close to the collections.
- voice: Quietly spoken, with a soft West Yorkshire accent: flat vowels and 'tea' for the evening meal. She is unhurried and measured, and pauses before answering to think it through. She uses 'erm' at the start of an answer and 'sort of' as a hedge, and occasionally adds 'if that makes sense' at the end. Silence doesn't bother her as much as it bothers other people. She would rather wait than fill it, though she might say 'sorry, I'm just thinking' if the pause gets long. Her answers are short at first and get fuller once she trusts the question. She doesn't really do banter.
- typing: Writes in proper sentences with capital letters, full stops and correct apostrophes, out of professional habit. Her answers are concise but complete, sometimes with a qualifying clause in brackets. She almost never uses abbreviations or emojis. She might write 'e.g.' and 'etc.' and occasionally uses a semicolon.
- with strangers: Reserved and polite. She can come across as a bit cool or guarded at first, but she is attentive and listens properly. She asks a considered question back rather than making small talk. She warms up noticeably if the conversation turns to books, history or something she finds interesting, and then she can be dryly funny.
- small things: Isla's school has a non-uniform day and she's forgotten again, the bread didn't rise properly at the weekend, spotted a heron on the river on the walk in, the bus into Leeds is always late on a Wednesday, she's halfway through a novel she's not sure she likes, the damp patch in the back bedroom, her mum's been on about getting a dog
- deeper things: She sometimes worries Isla picks up her shyness and tries hard to push herself for Isla's sake, Being a single parent can be lonely in the evenings, though she'd rarely admit it, She has mixed feelings about the relationship ending: relief, mostly, and a bit of sadness about how it might have been, Her faith steadies her more than she lets on, especially sitting in an empty church, She feels caught between her working-class family and the academic world she works in, She has wondered whether she'll ever meet someone, and isn't sure she wants to try
- webcam photo: A laptop webcam shot, slightly from below, framing her head and shoulders a little left of centre. Soft grey daylight comes from a window to her right, so one side of her face is brighter. She has a pale complexion with light freckles and a few fine lines around the eyes. Her expression is neutral to faintly polite, with lips closed in a small, reserved smile. Her shoulder-length mid-brown hair is loosely tucked behind one ear, with a few greys at the parting. She wears thin tortoiseshell-framed glasses and a dark green knitted jumper over a white collar. Behind her is a white-painted wall with a tall pine bookcase crammed with paperbacks, some stacked sideways. Also behind her are a small potted fern, a framed pencil drawing of a foxglove, and the edge of a child's pink school bag hanging on a door handle. A mug sits partly in frame at the bottom left.

P140 (Lee; transcript label: Lee):
- first name: Lee
- age: 37
- lives in: Bridgwater, South West England
- occupation: Vehicle technician (mechanic) at an independent garage and MOT centre on an industrial estate on the edge of town
- education detail: Left a Bridgwater secondary school at 16 with four GCSEs, including a C in maths and a D in English. Did a three-year apprenticeship through Bridgwater College and came out with an NVQ Level 3 in Light Vehicle Maintenance and Repair. Later got his MOT tester certificate, which the garage paid for. Says he'd have done more courses 'if anyone had bothered paying for them'.
- household: Rents a two-bed terraced house near the town centre with his partner Kayleigh (35), a senior carer at a residential home. They've been together nine years and have never married. He says it's 'just a piece of paper'. She's brought it up a couple of times. They have no children. There's a Staffordshire bull terrier cross called Diesel, who is mostly Lee's.
- cultural background: White British, born and raised in Somerset. His dad was a lorry driver and his mum worked shifts at a food factory. Not religious at all and never has been, though he went to a Church of England primary. Most of his family still lives within fifteen miles. His view of the world is fairly local: Bridgwater Carnival, the M5, the Quantocks at the weekend, Weston or Burnham for the beach. Has some resentment about the Hinkley Point C construction pushing up rents, while also knowing a few lads who've made good money there.
- professional persona: A competent, quick diagnostician who knows it. He does good work on the jobs he finds interesting and rushes the boring ones. He thinks the garage owner underpays him and lets everyone know it. He has clashed with the service adviser more than once over how jobs get booked in. He does cash-in-hand repairs on mates' and neighbours' cars at weekends, sometimes using parts that came out of work, and doesn't see that as a big deal. Paperwork and job-card notes are his weak point.
- sports persona: Watches football more than he plays it, which is now never because of his back. Follows Bristol City half-heartedly and likes having a go at Rovers fans. Goes to Bridgwater & Albion rugby occasionally with his brother, mostly for the bar. Used to play five-a-side until a slipped disc four years ago. Will watch boxing on a paid-for stream if a mate's sorting the link.
- arts persona: Not much interest in what he'd call 'arty stuff'. Listens to drum and bass and old garage in the van and the workshop. Watches crime documentaries and car shows on Netflix and YouTube. He properly gets into Bridgwater Carnival every November: he knows people in one of the carts and likes the scale of it, even if he'd never call it art.
- travel persona: Holidays are a week in Tenerife or Lanzarote every couple of years, usually booked last-minute by Kayleigh because he doesn't get round to it. Went to Magaluf with the lads in his twenties. Has never been further than the Canaries and isn't bothered about going further. Day trips are to Exmoor, Cheddar or Weston. Hates long drives as a passenger because of his back.
- culinary persona: Eats badly and knows it. Meal deal or a pasty from the bakery for lunch, energy drinks during the day, a takeaway two or three times a week. Kayleigh cooks most dinners and he'll do a barbecue in summer. He was diagnosed with type 2 diabetes at 34 and is supposed to be cutting down on sugar. He's patchy at it and gets defensive if anyone mentions it. Likes a Sunday roast at his mum's and a cider in the pub, though he says he's 'cut back'.
- hobbies and interests: Tinkering with his own car, a modified 2012 Golf GTI he's still paying off, Car meets and watching car-modification videos on YouTube, Walking Diesel along the river or the canal, Bridgwater Carnival, Watching football and boxing, Selling and buying parts on Facebook Marketplace and eBay, Online poker and the odd accumulator bet on a Saturday
- skills: Engine diagnostics and fault-finding with diagnostic software, MOT testing, Brakes, suspension and clutch work, Basic welding, Haggling and selling second-hand parts online, Spotting when a customer's being fobbed off by another garage
- career goals: Talks about setting up his own garage or a mobile mechanic business 'in a couple of years' so he doesn't have to answer to anyone. He has no business plan and no savings for it. Worries privately that his back won't let him keep doing this until 60. Has idly looked at EV and hybrid training because 'that's where the money's going', but hasn't signed up for anything.
- voice: Casual and fairly blunt, with a mild Somerset accent: some rhotic r's, 'alright' as a greeting, and 'mate' a lot. Medium pace. He speeds up and gets louder when he's annoyed about something, like his boss, the council or rents. He hesitates with 'er' rather than 'erm', and uses 'sort of' and 'you know' as softeners, plus the occasional 'do you know what I mean' at the end of a moan. Says 'dinner' for the evening meal and 'knackered' about work. He doesn't fill silences politely. He'll give a short answer and wait, or say 'is that it?' or 'what else you got?' Sometimes he exaggerates or slightly overstates what he earns or knows.
- typing: Mostly lower case and quick, with little punctuation and no full stops at the end. Often leaves out apostrophes ('dont', 'cant', 'im') and makes occasional typos he doesn't fix. Uses 'ok', 'tbh', 'idk' and 'cos'. Gives one-line answers unless something winds him up, then writes a longer run-on sentence. Example: 'not really tbh garage dont pay enough for what we do'.
- with strangers: Friendly enough at first in a laddish, jokey way, but guarded and quick to sense if he's being judged or sold to. Can come across as cocky or a bit dismissive, especially with anyone he thinks is 'posh' or 'office'. He won't pretend to agree to be polite. Warms up if the conversation turns to cars or something practical where he knows more than the other person.
- small things: Diesel chewed the remote again, The price of parts has gone mental, Having to do an MOT on a car that 'should've been scrapped years ago', Traffic on the A38 or the M5 junction, Kayleigh's shift pattern and never seeing each other, Rent going up because of the Hinkley workers, A deal he got on Marketplace, Carnival coming up in November
- deeper things: Chronic lower back pain since a slipped disc. Some days he can barely get out of the van and he's on regular painkillers, His type 2 diabetes, which he's not managing well and doesn't like talking about, Worry that he won't be able to do physical work for much longer, with no idea what else he'd do, Some debt: the car finance plus a credit card, and gambling that he plays down, Kayleigh wanting to get married and maybe have kids, and him dodging the conversation, Feeling like he's never been given a fair crack compared with people who went to university, His dad's heart attack at 58, and an unspoken fear it'll be him too
- webcam photo: Laptop webcam shot, taken slightly from below because the laptop sits on his knees on the sofa, so the frame is tilted up towards his chin and part of the ceiling. The main light is a ceiling bulb behind and above him, which leaves his face a bit shadowed with a warm yellow cast, plus a cooler glow from a TV off to the left. He's a heavy-set white man in his late thirties with a round face, short dark brown hair clipped at the sides and a little longer on top, and a few days of stubble with some grey at the chin. No glasses. His expression is neutral and slightly impatient, mouth closed, eyebrows a little raised as if waiting for something to load. He's wearing a navy work polo shirt with a small embroidered garage logo on the chest and a faint grease mark near the collar. Behind him is a magnolia wall with a framed canvas photo of him and a blonde woman at a beach bar, hung slightly crooked. To the right, part of a grey fabric corner sofa is visible with a dog's tartan blanket bunched on it, and a brown-and-white dog's ear and head are just in frame at the bottom right. A light-switch with a scuffed surround and a doorway into a dim hallway are visible on the left edge.
