For Gemma–Riya, I'm building out their dynamic around colour-coded spreadsheets, holiday planning, and batch cooking Sundays, with Riya's cooler, more precise manner warming slightly over shared enthusiasm for Excel and organisation, while also touching on Gemma's AAT qualification and office manager role.

For Lauren–Ioana, I'm focusing on their quieter, more tired energy — late and evening shifts, comfortable silences, a shared love of cosy crime novels, Lauren's habit of apologising, and a mention of Ioana's caretaker's dog along with a slightly unflattering photo comment.

Now I'm adding small personal touches — Ioana asking after Biscuit, a mention of her cousin crashing on the sofa, a mushroom-and-trees tangent, Lauren's wonky cross-stitch cat versus Ioana's rough sketches, and Lauren reading on her Kindle — while aiming to keep each conversation around 30 turns and roughly 570 words before I start writing the full piece.

req.text:
You write transcripts of realistic video calls between strangers for a fully synthetic research dataset set in the UK. The study, in order (from its published design): a short puzzle task done alone; first impressions of the others' webcam photos; then a series of three-minute, one-on-one video calls in rounds, each person meeting the others in their group; after each call a short survey.

Call shape (from the original study's numbers): a call is cut off by a three-minute timer. A typical call has about 30 turns (most between 20 and 39) and about 570 words in total (most between 440 and 682); half of all turns are 12 words or fewer, and a quarter are 24 or more. Short acknowledgements ("yeah", "mm") count as turns too. So aim for about 570 words in about 30 turns: alongside the quick back-and-forth, people often talk in longer stretches (explaining their job, telling a story), and those long turns carry much of the call.

Guide to British conversational English (use it for how people talk; it is a description of speech, not a script):
How British people talk in casual conversation. This is a paraphrase of published descriptions of spoken British English; sources are in SOURCES.md. Use these features lightly and only where they fit the person. Never use them as a caricature.

- **Fillers.** British speakers hesitate with "erm" and "er". Women and younger speakers lean towards "erm".
- **Hedges.** "Sort of" is everywhere and steady. "Kind of" is spreading, and younger speakers use it more.
- **Politeness words.** "Please", "thank you", "thanks" and "sorry" mostly mean what they say. "Sorry" also works as a repair word (to correct yourself, or to ask someone to repeat) and can be ironic.
- **Tags at the end of a sentence.** "You know", "right", "okay", "yeah", "do you know what I mean". Among young Londoners, "innit" and "you get me" are rising. Tags depend on age and region only, never on ethnicity.
- **Echoing.** In an engaged conversation people pick up and re-use parts of each other's words.
- **Regional words and grammar** (from a recent dialect survey):
  - A bread roll is a "barm" in the North West (Manchester to Liverpool and western Lancashire), a "cob" around Nottinghamshire, a "bap" in Staffordshire, the West Midlands and North Wales, and a "batch" in Liverpool and Coventry.
  - Around Liverpool an ice lolly can be a "lolly ice".
  - The evening meal is "tea" in the North West, North East and Yorkshire, and "dinner" in the South East and London. Some people say both.
  - "Yous" or "youse" for plural "you" is common in the North East (Newcastle, Teesside), Liverpool and Scotland, less so in Manchester, and rare in York, Leeds and Sheffield.
  - "Give it me" is normal in the North West and West Midlands and widely accepted in Sheffield and York; it fades south of Birmingham, Coventry and Leicester.
  - "You was" is widely used, historically Northern and now found as far south as London.
- **Everyday British words** to draw on where they fit, without assigning them to regions: knackered or shattered, chuffed or made up, skint or brassic, mardy or stroppy, mum or mam, mate or pal, settee, sofa or couch.

The group (session S28). Persona cards, including the webcam photo each person was rated on:

P147 (Craig; transcript label: Craig):
- first name: Craig
- age: 35
- lives in: Hartlepool, North East England
- occupation: Bricklayer by trade, currently out of work. He was signed off with a lower back problem about eighteen months ago, is now on Universal Credit, and does online panel surveys for a bit of extra money.
- education detail: Left secondary school in Hartlepool at 16 with a handful of GCSEs, the best a C in maths. Did a Level 2 NVQ in bricklaying at the local college while on an apprenticeship with a small building firm, and later a CSCS card and a short first aid course through work.
- household: Lives with his mam (62, works part-time at a supermarket) and his younger brother Lee (29, warehouse shifts) in the terraced council house he grew up in. He moved back in after the divorce four years ago. His daughter Ellie, 9, stays over every other weekend and sleeps in the box room.
- cultural background: White British, born and raised in Hartlepool in a working-class family. His dad was a welder and passed away when Craig was in his twenties. Not religious, although he went to a Church of England primary school. Very rooted in the town; most of his mates are lads he went to school with.
- professional persona: Practical, steady and well liked on site. He was the one who kept the peace and never moaned about the weather. He took pride in a neat, level wall. Since the back trouble he has felt a bit at a loss without the routine of work. He is honest about what he can and can't do and would rather not overpromise.
- sports persona: Lifelong Hartlepool United fan. He used to have a season ticket and now goes when money allows, watching the rest down the pub or on his phone. He played Sunday league football until his late twenties. These days the most he does is walk the seafront on the physio's advice.
- arts persona: Not really into arts. He watches telly with his mam in the evenings: quiz shows, Gogglebox, the odd crime drama. He listens to whatever is on local radio or old Oasis and Arctic Monkeys in the car. He hasn't been to a gallery since a school trip.
- travel persona: He has been abroad a few times, to Spain and once to Turkey, all package holidays with his ex-wife. Since then it's been the odd caravan weekend at Whitby or in Northumberland with Ellie. He is happy enough close to home and isn't bothered about seeing the world.
- culinary persona: Plain, filling food. His mam does most of the cooking, and he has his tea around half five: mince and dumplings, a Sunday dinner, chips from the chippy on a Friday. He can do a fry-up and spag bol when Ellie is over. Not adventurous, and he wouldn't order something he can't pronounce.
- hobbies and interests: Following Hartlepool United, Walking along the seafront and the Headland, Fishing off the pier with his brother now and then, FIFA/EA FC on the PlayStation, Doing small DIY jobs for his mam and neighbours when his back allows, Taking his daughter to the park and the cinema
- skills: Bricklaying and blockwork, Reading basic building plans, General DIY: tiling, fixing fences, putting up shelves, Getting on with pretty much anyone, Keeping calm when other people are wound up
- career goals: He wants to get back into work but knows full-time bricklaying might be off the cards for his back. He's been half-thinking about a site supervisor or building maintenance role, or a CSCS-related course through the job centre. Mostly he wants something steady so he can get his own place and have Ellie over more.
- voice: Friendly, unhurried and fairly quiet at first, with a light Hartlepool/Teesside accent. Says 'mam', 'aye' now and then, occasionally 'yous' when talking about a group, and 'tea' for his evening meal. Uses 'er' and 'sort of' a fair bit, and ends things with 'you know' or 'like'. Answers are short to begin with and he warms up once he's comfortable. If there's a silence he'll fill it with a 'yeah... er' or a small laugh rather than leave it hanging. He tends to agree with the interviewer and say 'aye, fair enough' even when he's only half sure.
- typing: Mostly lowercase and rarely capitalises 'i'. Few full stops, with sentences run together with commas or nothing. Drops apostrophes ('dont', 'im', 'cant'). Short answers, sometimes 'not sure tbh' or 'yeah its alright'. Spelling is mostly fine, with the odd slip he doesn't go back and fix.
- with strangers: Polite and a bit reserved at first, a touch self-conscious about being out of work. He's easy-going and keen not to cause bother, so he goes along with things and apologises if he thinks he's given the 'wrong' answer. Once he relaxes he's warm and chatty, with a dry, self-deprecating sense of humour.
- small things: The weather coming in off the sea, How Pools are getting on this season, His mam's Sunday dinner, His back playing up after sitting too long, Ellie's school stuff or what film they last saw, The price of a pint going up, Lee coming in late off his shifts
- deeper things: Feeling a bit embarrassed to be 35 and back in his childhood bedroom, Worrying he won't be able to lay bricks again and not knowing what else he's good for, Missing his dad, especially at the football, The divorce being nobody's fault really. They just drifted, and he still gets on with his ex for Ellie's sake, Being skint most months and not wanting his mam to carry him, Occasional low days since the injury that he doesn't really talk about
- webcam photo: Laptop webcam at a slightly low angle, so the image looks up a little at his chin. Head and shoulders, slightly off-centre to the left. Light comes from a window to his right, leaving one side of his face a bit shadowed, plus the warm yellow glow of a ceiling light. Pale skin with a bit of redness on the cheeks, short dark brown hair clipped at the sides and slightly longer on top, and a few days' stubble. Brown eyes, no glasses. A slightly awkward, polite half-smile. He wears a plain navy hooded sweatshirt with the drawstrings uneven. Behind him is a magnolia living room wall with a framed school photo of a smiling girl in a red jumper and a small mirror. Part of a brown leather settee is visible, with a folded grey throw on the arm. A blue and white Hartlepool United scarf is draped over the top of a door just out of focus on the right.

P148 (Kerry; transcript label: Kerry):
- first name: Kerry
- age: 42
- lives in: Taunton, South West England
- occupation: Diagnostic radiographer at a large NHS hospital, mostly general X-ray and some CT shifts. Full-time, about 37.5 hours a week plus the odd on-call weekend.
- education detail: GCSEs and A-levels (Biology, Chemistry, PE) at a comprehensive and sixth form in Bridgwater; BSc (Hons) Diagnostic Radiography from a university in the South West, finished in 2003. Has since done in-house CT training and a short course in clinical supervision of students.
- household: Lives with her husband Darren (44, an electrician who runs his own small business) in a three-bed semi on a 1990s estate on the edge of Taunton. They have no children. They have a ten-year-old springer spaniel called Moss. Her mum lives about fifteen minutes away in Bridgwater, and Kerry pops round most Sundays.
- cultural background: White British, born and raised in Somerset. Her dad was a postman and her mum worked in a school kitchen. She was the first in her family to go to university, though she doesn't make a thing of it. She isn't religious and never really was, apart from school nativities. She is rooted in the area: most of her friends are from school, netball or work, and she has no real interest in moving anywhere else.
- professional persona: Calm, efficient and reliable. She is the one who gets the department list moving on a busy Monday. She is good with anxious or confused patients, chatty without wasting time. She is straight with colleagues and doesn't play politics, and she would rather tell a manager directly that a rota won't work than moan about it in the staff room. She supervises student radiographers and is known for being firm but fair, with checklists for everything. She likes protocols and gets quietly irritated when people cut corners.
- sports persona: Plays goal defence in a local women's netball league on Tuesday nights and has done on and off since her twenties. She does the Saturday parkrun most weeks, more for the coffee and chat afterwards than for her time, though she does keep a note of it. She watches the rugby with Darren, mostly Bath and the Six Nations, and is fairly loud about it.
- arts persona: Not really an arts person, and she'd say so. She likes a good crime drama on telly, anything with Line of Duty energy, and the odd big musical if a mate organises a trip to Bristol Hippodrome. She reads a bit on holiday, usually a thriller someone has lent her. She listens to Heart or Radio 2 in the car.
- travel persona: Creature of habit. They go to the same campsite near Bude most summers with friends, and have a week somewhere warm in Spain or the Canaries in the autumn, usually a place they've been before. She organises everything well in advance, with a spreadsheet for the packing list. She isn't bothered about city breaks or 'finding herself', and calls a good holiday 'sun, a pool and someone else cooking'.
- culinary persona: Plain, decent home cooking. She batch-cooks chilli and spag bol on a Sunday so there's dinner ready after long shifts. She does a roast most weekends, sometimes at her mum's. She isn't adventurous: she'll have a curry on a Friday from the same takeaway and always orders the same thing. Darren does the barbecue. She likes a cream tea, jam first because she's from this side of the Tamar, and will defend it.
- hobbies and interests: Netball league, Saturday parkrun, Walking the dog on the Quantocks, Watching rugby, Crime dramas and quiz shows, Pub quiz with the netball girls once a month, Keeping the garden tidy
- skills: Patient positioning and image quality checks, Calming nervous patients, Organising rotas and lists, Training and supervising students, Keeping cool under pressure, Planning trips and events for friends, Basic DIY (learned from Darren)
- career goals: Would like to move up to a Band 7 lead or superintendent radiographer post in the next few years, ideally running the general X-ray team. She has no interest in leaving clinical work entirely for management, or in changing career. She is happy to stay at the same hospital until she retires if the job's right.
- voice: Warm, quick and confident, with a fairly mild Somerset accent. It's mostly in the vowels and the odd rolled 'r', and gets stronger when she's laughing or talking about home. She occasionally says 'proper' as an intensifier ('it was proper busy') or 'lush' about food, but nothing exaggerated. She says 'dinner' for the evening meal. She uses 'erm' a bit when thinking but usually gets to the point fast, with tags like 'you know' and 'yeah'. She answers questions directly and sometimes jokes. Silence doesn't bother her much, but she tends to fill it with a quick 'is that what you're after?' or 'sorry, do you want more on that?'
- typing: Quick and practical. She mostly uses capitals at the start of sentences and full stops, sometimes skipping the final one. Apostrophes are usually right. She uses the odd 'tbh' or 'x' habit from texting, but not in a form. Answers are short and to the point. She won't write paragraphs unless asked, and might use a dash or two.
- with strangers: Friendly and easy to talk to, quick to put people at ease, likely to make a light joke early on. Open about everyday stuff but not oversharing. Honest and unpretentious, she'll say 'I don't really know much about that' rather than bluff. Comes across as capable, grounded and a bit no-nonsense.
- small things: Moss rolled in something on the Quantocks again, The hospital car park is a nightmare, Netball team lost by two goals on Tuesday, Got a PB at parkrun, only by eight seconds, Darren's van needs an MOT, Planning the Bude camping trip with friends, Watching the latest crime series everyone's on about, Her mum's knee is playing up
- deeper things: She and Darren tried for children for a few years in their thirties, then decided to stop. She's mostly at peace with it but doesn't talk about it often., Her dad died suddenly when she was twenty-nine, and she still thinks about how she took over sorting everything for her mum., She sometimes worries about burnout in her department and about staff shortages., Being the first in her family to go to uni still means more to her than she lets on.
- webcam photo: Head-and-shoulders shot from a laptop on a kitchen table, camera slightly below eye level. Soft daylight from a window to her left lights her face, with the right side in slight shadow. She has fair skin, light freckles, a few fine lines round her eyes, and an open, friendly half-smile, looking straight at the camera. Her shoulder-length dark blonde hair, with darker roots showing, is tucked behind one ear. She wears a navy hoodie with a small netball club logo, no glasses, and small silver studs. Behind her is a white kitchen with grey cabinets. On the counter are a kettle, a toaster and a fruit bowl with bananas. A wall calendar with handwritten shifts hangs by the fridge. A dog lead hangs on a hook by the back door, and a corner of a dog bed is just visible on the floor.

P149 (Gareth; transcript label: Gareth):
- first name: Gareth
- age: 47
- lives in: Basingstoke, South East England (Hampshire)
- occupation: Senior structural engineer at a mid-sized engineering consultancy in Basingstoke, mostly working on commercial and light-industrial buildings such as warehouses, retail units and the odd school extension. Hybrid: three days in the office, two at home.
- education detail: A-levels in Maths, Physics and Design Technology at a sixth-form college in Andover. BEng Civil Engineering at the University of Portsmouth, graduating in 1999. Became a Chartered Engineer (ICE) at 36, later than his peers, after putting off the paperwork for years.
- household: Lone parent household in a three-bed semi on an estate in Brighton Hill. He lives with his son Callum (15) and daughter Ellie (12). He and his wife Joanne separated about eighteen months ago and are still legally married. Divorce has been talked about but nobody has started it. Joanne rents a flat in Reading and has the kids every other weekend and one evening a week. The arrangement mostly works, though she organises more of it than he does.
- cultural background: White British, born in Andover. His father was a telecoms engineer for BT and his mother worked part-time in a building society. He has one older sister in Salisbury. He wasn't brought up religious and isn't now. He doesn't think about it much and ticks 'no religion' without hesitation. His tastes are ordinary middle-England: football on the telly, a takeaway on Friday, the same pub he has gone to for ten years.
- professional persona: Technically solid and trusted to get the numbers right, but not someone who chases work or manages people by choice. He is good at the calculations and the design checks. He is less good at keeping on top of admin: timesheets go in late, emails sit unanswered and his desk is a mess of marked-up drawings. Colleagues see him as reliable when it counts and calm under deadline pressure, because very little rattles him. He avoids client presentations where he can and lets the project director do the talking.
- sports persona: A Southampton FC supporter, inherited from his dad. He watches matches on TV and goes to St Mary's two or three times a season, usually with Callum. He played five-a-side until his late thirties and stopped when the group drifted apart. Now his exercise is walking the dog and the occasional bike ride along the canal, and he means to do more than he does.
- arts persona: Not much interest. He watches whatever is on: crime dramas, Top Gear repeats, and football highlights more than anything. He listens to the same handful of bands he liked at uni, like Oasis, Ocean Colour Scene and Stereophonics, mostly in the car. He hasn't been to a gallery or the theatre since a school panto with the kids years ago, and doesn't feel he's missing anything.
- travel persona: Prefers somewhere familiar. For years the family went to the same holiday park in Cornwall, and before that a few package holidays to Majorca and Lanzarote. Since the separation he has taken the kids to a caravan in Devon once. He has no wish to go anywhere far or unusual and finds the planning a hassle.
- culinary persona: Cooks plain, repeatable meals for the kids: spag bol, chilli, oven chips with chicken, jacket potatoes. He leans on a big Tesco shop and frozen stuff when the week gets away from him. Friday is takeaway night, usually Chinese or a Domino's. He calls the evening meal 'dinner'. He likes a pint of Doom Bar or Guinness and doesn't really drink wine.
- hobbies and interests: Watching Southampton FC, Walking the family's Labrador cross, Bonnie, Fiddling about with the car, mostly basic maintenance, Fantasy Premier League in a work mini-league, though he often forgets to change his team, The odd bike ride along the Basingstoke Canal, A quiet pint at his local on a Thursday when the kids are at their mum's
- skills: Structural analysis and design calcs (steel and concrete frames), Using structural design software such as Tekla and Robot, Reading and marking up drawings, Staying calm when things go wrong on site, Basic car maintenance, Batch-cooking a chilli that lasts three days
- career goals: Nothing ambitious. He would like to stay where he is, keep the hybrid days, and maybe make associate eventually if it comes to him without having to push. Mostly he wants work to stay steady while the kids get through school.
- voice: Quiet, low and fairly flat, with a neutral southern accent from Hampshire and a bit of glottal stop on words like 'bit' and 'lot'. Answers are short, often just 'yeah' or 'not really', and he rarely elaborates unless asked a direct follow-up. He uses 'er' before answering and 'sort of' as a hedge ('it's sort of fine, yeah'). He occasionally ends with 'you know' but doesn't pile up tags. Silence doesn't bother him at all. He'll let a pause sit rather than fill it, which can make interviewers jump in first. He says 'sorry, say that again?' if the line is bad. He isn't unfriendly, just economical.
- typing: Mostly lowercase, often no capital at the start. Short answers, sometimes just a few words. Full stops are inconsistent and he usually leaves the last one off. Apostrophes are often dropped ('dont', 'its'). The occasional 'tbh' or 'n/a', and the odd typo he doesn't go back to fix. Example: 'not really, i just do the big shop on a sunday mostly tesco'
- with strangers: Reserved and a bit hard to read at first. He is polite and answers what he's asked, but offers little and doesn't ask questions back. He comes across as calm, unflustered and a little closed. People sometimes mistake his flatness for boredom. He warms up slightly if the topic turns to football, the kids or something practical.
- small things: Bonnie the dog needing walking before it gets dark, Callum's GCSE options and whether he's actually revising, The A33 traffic and the roadworks near Chineham, Saints' last result, Forgetting it was non-uniform day at Ellie's school, The boiler making a noise he keeps meaning to get looked at, Friday takeaway being the highlight of the week
- deeper things: He and Joanne drifted apart over years, and he admits he wasn't really paying attention until she said she was going, Being the main parent wasn't something he expected, and he worries he's doing the bare minimum with the kids rather than doing it well, Neither of them has started the divorce, and he isn't sure whether that's practicality or him avoiding it, He sometimes feels he coasted through his career and got chartered late because he just didn't get round to it, His dad's health is getting worse and his sister handles most of it, which he feels a bit guilty about
- webcam photo: Laptop webcam on a kitchen-diner table, angled slightly upward so the frame catches his chin and the ceiling edge. He is lit mostly by the overhead kitchen spotlights, which give a flat, slightly yellow light with a faint shine on his forehead. He is a white man in his late forties with a broad face, light stubble and short, thinning mid-brown hair going grey at the sides, cut fairly short. No glasses. His expression is neutral, a little tired, mouth closed, looking just below the camera at the screen. He wears a navy crew-neck sweatshirt over a grey T-shirt. Behind him on the left is a white fridge-freezer covered in school letters, a takeaway menu and a Southampton FC fixtures magnet. To the right is a laminate worktop with a kettle, a toaster, a stack of post and a dog lead hanging on a cupboard handle. A clothes airer with school shirts on it stands partly in shot at the back near patio doors, and the doors show darkness outside.

P150 (Ryan; transcript label: Ryan):
- first name: Ryan
- age: 37
- lives in: Stockport, North West England
- occupation: General manager of a mid-sized bar and live music venue in Manchester's Northern Quarter, running a team of about 18 bar staff, two duty managers and the booking side
- education detail: GCSEs at a comprehensive in Stockport, then a BTEC National in Business at college. Started a Media Studies degree at Salford and left after the first year to work full-time in bars. Holds a personal licence (APLH) and has done various in-house management and health and safety courses.
- household: Since his divorce about eighteen months ago he lives in the spare room of his older sister Claire's semi in Heaton Moor, with her and her husband Mark. He pays them rent and keeps saying it's temporary. Their two kids are 9 and 12. He has no children of his own.
- cultural background: White British, born and raised in Stockport to a working-class family. His dad was a bus mechanic and his mum worked in a school kitchen. He was christened Church of England and ticks 'Christian' on forms, but he only goes to church for weddings, funerals and the odd carol service with his mum. Very Manchester in outlook. He has opinions about Oasis versus the Stone Roses and is a lifelong County fan who also goes to City.
- professional persona: A confident, front-of-house operator who is good at selling the venue, chasing promoters and getting bands booked. He likes being the face of the place and knows half the regulars by name. Staff call him a decent boss but blunt. He doesn't soften bad news, can be impatient with people who 'faff', and is comfortable bending a rule or two if it gets a result. He isn't great at the spreadsheet side of the job, but he gets it done because the owners check.
- sports persona: Season ticket at Edgeley Park, and he takes his nephew. Five-a-side on Wednesday nights, which he plays very competitively and moans about the ref in. He got into padel last year and won't stop talking about it.
- arts persona: Music is the big one. He goes to gigs several times a week, partly for work and partly not. His tastes are broad: post-punk, Afrobeat, jazz nights at Band on the Wall, and the occasional techno night at the Warehouse Project. He likes the Whitworth and HOME, and will go to a weird experimental theatre thing just to say he has. He reads in bursts, mostly music biographies and the odd novel someone recommends.
- travel persona: A restless traveller who prefers cities to resorts. He did Berlin and Lisbon with mates, went to Mexico City on his own after the divorce, and keeps a running list that includes Tokyo, Bogotá and Tbilisi. He books last-minute, hates organised tours, and likes to find the bar the locals go to.
- culinary persona: He'll try anything and likes to be seen as the one who knows the new places. He loves Rusholme curry houses, Ancoats small-plates places and Vietnamese on the Northern Quarter. At home he barely cooks because Claire does tea most nights, though he does a decent chilli and rates himself highly at barbecues. A bacon barm on a Saturday morning is non-negotiable.
- hobbies and interests: live music and DJing records at friends' parties, Stockport County, five-a-side and padel, collecting vinyl, mostly from Vinyl Exchange and Discogs, city breaks abroad, trying new restaurants, podcasts about music history and true crime
- skills: staff management and rota planning, booking and negotiating with promoters and agents, licensing and venue compliance, cash-up and stock control (does it, doesn't love it), talking his way into or out of most situations, basic sound and lighting setup, beat-matching on decks
- career goals: He wants to open his own place within five years, a smallish bar with a basement room for gigs. He's been talking to a mate with money about it. He likes the idea of being the owner rather than working for owners he thinks are less clued up than him. If that falls through, he'd take a move into festival or venue operations for a bigger group.
- voice: Fast, loud and fluent, with a broad but not thick Greater Manchester accent: flat vowels, 'bath' with a short a. He talks in long runs, interrupts himself with 'er' rather than 'erm', and tags things with 'you know' and 'do you know what I mean'. He uses 'mate' a lot, even to the interviewer, says 'tea' for the evening meal and 'barm' for a roll, and will say 'give it me'. He occasionally says 'you was', but not 'yous'. He's quick with a joke or a mild wind-up, and is blunt when he disagrees: 'nah, that's not right, that'. He hates silence and fills it immediately, usually by expanding his answer or asking a question back. Rarely says sorry except as a repair ('sorry, what was the question again?').
- typing: Quick and mostly lowercase. He capitalises proper names inconsistently, often skips apostrophes ('dont', 'im'), and uses commas instead of full stops so answers become one long run-on sentence. He's comfortable with 'tbh', 'lol' and 'prob'. He rarely goes back to fix typos and sometimes ends with a 'haha'.
- with strangers: Instantly chatty and at ease, sometimes a bit too much. He'll be on first-name terms within a minute and treats the conversation like a chat at the bar. He comes across as charming and self-assured, sometimes cocky. He tells good stories that make him look good, pushes back if he thinks a question is daft, and isn't shy about saying he's better at something than most people.
- small things: the five-a-side lads are useless at turning up on time, he's just got a new turntable cartridge, County's chances this season, a band he saw last week that 'nobody's heard of yet', the Metrolink being rammed, his nephew getting into football, a new Vietnamese place he's been to, being knackered after a late lock-up
- deeper things: the divorce from his ex-wife Jess, which he mostly blames on her but admits he was barely home, feeling a bit embarrassed living in his sister's spare room at 37, wondering if he's left it too late to have kids, his dad's heart scare two years ago, worry that the bar plan is all talk, having dropped out of uni and still feeling he has to prove he's clever
- webcam photo: Laptop webcam at roughly chest height, angled slightly upward. He's seated, framed from mid-chest up and a little off-centre to the left. Light comes from a window to his right, so that side of his face is brighter and the other side is in mild shadow. He's a white man in his late thirties with short dark brown hair faded at the sides and slightly longer and pushed back on top, a neat dark beard with a few grey hairs at the chin, and light stubble on the neck. No glasses. He's grinning with his mouth slightly open, mid-word, eyebrows raised. He's wearing a black crew-neck T-shirt with a faded gig poster print, partly hidden by an unzipped olive-green overshirt. Behind him is a small spare bedroom with pale grey walls. A single bed with a navy duvet is pushed against the back wall. Above it, two unframed gig posters are held up with Blu Tack. To the right is a low white flat-pack shelf holding about thirty vinyl records upright and a turntable with a clear dust cover. A Stockport County scarf is draped over the corner of the shelf, and a folded pile of laundry sits on the end of the bed.

P151 (Gemma; transcript label: Gemma):
- first name: Gemma
- age: 34
- lives in: Bloxwich, Walsall, West Midlands
- occupation: Shift operations manager at a regional parcel sorting depot off the M6 near Cannock. She runs the late shift of about forty sorters, drivers' loaders and two team leaders, working four long shifts a week
- education detail: GCSEs at a comprehensive in Walsall. Started an NVQ in business admin at college and didn't finish it. Later did a Level 3 Team Leading qualification and a forklift licence through work, and an in-house management course when she was promoted
- household: Lives with her husband Craig (36, a self-employed plasterer) in a two-bed ex-council semi they bought six years ago. No children yet. They have an elderly Staffordshire bull terrier called Dolly
- cultural background: White British, born and raised in Walsall. Her family has been in the Black Country for generations: her granddad worked at a lock factory in Willenhall and her mum was a dinner lady. She isn't religious and was only ever in church for weddings and christenings. She is close to her mum and her older sister, who live ten minutes away
- professional persona: She worked her way up from scanning parcels on the belt at 19 to running a shift, mostly because she was steady, fair and didn't panic in front of people. Staff trust her because she's straight with them, never takes credit for the team's numbers and won't massage figures for head office. She is weaker on the admin side. Rotas get finalised late, emails sit unanswered, and she relies on one of her team leaders to chase the paperwork. She finds the people side draining, especially disciplinaries, and takes it home with her
- sports persona: Not sporty. She walks Dolly round the park most mornings and went to a few Couch to 5K sessions with her sister before giving up. She'll have the Walsall or Wolves score on if Craig's watching, but isn't bothered herself
- arts persona: Watches a lot of telly with Craig: crime dramas, Bake Off, and any documentary about the Black Country or old factories. Reads the odd thriller on holiday. Likes 90s and 2000s indie and R&B and will happily listen to the same playlist for months. Hasn't been to a gig in a couple of years because crowds wear her out
- travel persona: One week in the sun a year, usually a quiet all-inclusive in Tenerife or Majorca, booked last-minute because neither of them gets round to it earlier. Also caravan weekends in Wales with her mum. She gets anxious about flights and airport security and likes having the paperwork printed even though she always forgets where she put it
- culinary persona: Evening meal is tea. Weeknights are simple stuff like chilli, pasta bakes and a chippy on Fridays. Craig does most of the cooking on her shift days. She loves a bacon bap from the van outside the depot and her mum's faggots and peas. She bakes occasionally for staff birthdays, usually a traybake she half-burns
- hobbies and interests: walking the dog, crime dramas and true-crime podcasts, jigsaw puzzles in winter, local history Facebook groups about old Walsall, pottering in the back garden, mainly pots and hanging baskets, quiz nights at the local pub with her sister
- skills: calm under pressure on a busy shift, forklift and reach truck licensed, reading people and noticing when someone's struggling, handling customer complaints over the phone, basic Excel for shift reports, though she'd rather not, first aid at work certified
- career goals: She'd like to move to a day-shift role so she sees more of Craig, maybe site training lead rather than anything higher. She has no interest in a regional manager job; it'd mean more meetings and more admin. They've talked about starting a family in the next couple of years and she worries about how that would fit with shifts
- voice: Quiet, fairly slow and careful, with a soft Black Country accent that comes out more when she relaxes. Plenty of 'erm' and 'sort of', and 'to be fair' and 'do you know what I mean' at the end of sentences. Says 'give it me' and 'bap' without thinking. She doesn't fill silences. She'll pause and wait for the next question, sometimes adding 'sorry, does that answer it?' She is honest when she doesn't know something and laughs a bit nervously at first
- typing: Mostly lowercase, with the odd capital at the start of an answer if her phone autocorrects it. Light punctuation, often no full stop at the end, sometimes 'dont' and 'im' without apostrophes. Short answers, occasionally 'tbh' or 'not sure'. Rarely more than a sentence or two unless something matters to her
- with strangers: Reserved and polite. She can come across as a bit shy or flat at first, gives short answers and doesn't volunteer much. She warms up if the other person is friendly and unhurried, and then she's warm, modest and quietly funny. She plays down her job ('I just run a shift really') and is visibly uncomfortable being praised
- small things: the depot being rammed in the run-up to Christmas, Dolly's dodgy hips and the vet bills, Craig leaving plaster dust all over the van, the bacon bap van at work, getting knackered after four late shifts in a row, the new Greggs that opened in town, a jigsaw she's been doing for three weeks, her sister roping her into a pub quiz
- deeper things: she still feels like a bit of a fraud as a manager because she never finished college, she lies awake after having to sack someone, she and Craig have been trying for a baby for a while and it's starting to get to her, her dad died when she was 22 and she still misses his advice about work, she gets anxious about money even though they're doing alright, because she remembers her mum being skint
- webcam photo: Laptop webcam shot from slightly below, as if the laptop is on her knees on the settee. Lit mostly by a ceiling light with a warm yellow cast, and a cooler glow from the screen on her face. Head and shoulders fill the frame, slightly off-centre to the left. Pale skin with some redness on the cheeks, light freckles, no makeup apart from a bit of mascara, faint tiredness under the eyes. A small, polite, slightly self-conscious closed-mouth smile. Mid-brown shoulder-length hair pulled back in a loose ponytail with a few strands falling at the front. Navy zip-up fleece with a small embroidered company logo on the chest over a grey t-shirt. No glasses, small silver stud earrings. Behind her is a light grey wall with a framed canvas print of the couple at a wedding. Below it is the top edge of a dark grey fabric settee with a mustard cushion, and a folded fleece blanket over the arm. On the right edge of the frame is part of a white bookshelf with a few paperbacks, a diffuser and a half-finished jigsaw box. The dog's brown ear and head are just visible at the bottom right corner

- age: 18
- lives in: Morriston, Swansea, South Wales
- occupation: Full-time first-year undergraduate student (BSc Business Management) at Swansea University, living at home. Works about eight hours a week on Saturdays at a sports clothing shop in the Quadrant shopping centre
- education detail: A-levels in Business (A), Economics (B) and Psychology (B) from a sixth-form college in Swansea. GCSE Welsh second language, which she says she has 'mostly lost'. Commutes to the Bay Campus by bus or gets a lift from her dad.
- household: Lives with her parents, who are married, and her 14-year-old brother in a three-bedroom semi in Morriston. Her dad is a senior staff nurse at Morriston Hospital and her mum works as a pharmacy technician. The family moved from Kochi in Kerala when Aleena was seven, after her dad was recruited through an NHS nursing scheme. Her grandmother stays with them for a few months most years.
- cultural background: Born in Kerala and raised in Swansea from age seven. Her family are Syro-Malabar Catholic and attend Mass at a parish that runs a monthly Malayalam service. There is also a lively Malayali community she sees at Onam and Christmas gatherings. She speaks Malayalam at home with her parents, though less fluently than she lets on, and English everywhere else. She thinks of herself as Swansea first and gets irritated when people assume she's from Cardiff or from 'England'. She goes to church mostly because her mum expects it, and she enjoys the social side more than the services.
- professional persona: Confident and quick to put herself forward. She volunteers to present in group projects and likes being the one who 'sorts things'. She is upfront about wanting money and status from her career. She gets impatient with slower teammates and will say so. At the shop she is good on the floor and hits her accessory add-on targets, and she is not above talking a customer into a more expensive pair of trainers.
- sports persona: Played netball through school and still turns out for a casual university team, mainly for the socials. Goes to the gym on campus two or three times a week, a bit erratically. Watches the Swans occasionally with her dad and brother but isn't really invested. She is far more competitive than she is sporty.
- arts persona: Not especially arty. Listens to a mix of UK rap, Afrobeats and whatever is big on TikTok, and occasionally Malayalam film songs when her mum puts them on in the car. Watches reality TV (Love Island, The Traitors) and has strong opinions about who deserves to win. Went to a couple of gigs in Cardiff last year.
- travel persona: Has been back to Kerala four times since moving, most recently the summer before last for a cousin's wedding. She enjoyed the attention and the shopping more than the relatives. Did a girls' trip to Tenerife after A-levels and wants to do Ibiza or Magaluf next summer. Not much interest in backpacking. She likes nice hotels and being able to post about them.
- culinary persona: Eats her mum's cooking at home (appam, fish curry, beef fry at weekends) and will complain if it's 'just rice and something again'. With friends it's Nando's, Greggs, or chips on Mumbles front. Can make about three things herself: pasta, cheesy chips and Maggi noodles. Calls the evening meal 'tea' or 'dinner' depending on who she's with.
- hobbies and interests: Going out in Wind Street with uni friends, Netball socials, Gym (inconsistently), Reselling trainers and clothes on Vinted and Depop, Reality TV, Doing her nails and trying new makeup, Group chats with a big friendship group, Mumbles and the seafront in summer
- skills: Selling and persuading, Speaking up in groups, Bilingual Malayalam/English (conversational Malayalam), Basic Excel and Canva from college projects, Spotting a bargain and flipping it for profit, Staying calm under pressure
- career goals: Wants to go into sales or recruitment after graduating, ideally somewhere with commission and a company car. She talks about moving to London or Manchester 'where the money is'. Has vaguely mentioned starting her own clothing resale business. Her parents would prefer pharmacy or nursing, and she has told them flatly that it isn't happening.
- voice: Fast, loud and confident, with a clear Swansea accent: the lilt, plus the odd 'tidy' or 'now in a minute'. She doesn't put it on. She drops into 'like' and 'kind of' a lot, uses 'erm' when she's thinking but rarely stalls for long, and ends points with 'yeah?' or 'do you know what I mean'. She uses 'sorry' mostly to cut back in or correct herself ('sorry, no, it was Tuesday'). She fills silences herself rather than waiting, sometimes with a joke, and will talk over the interviewer if she thinks she knows where the question is going. Blunt rather than rude. She'll say 'no, that's a bit of a stupid question' and laugh.
- typing: Mostly lowercase, quick and abbreviated: 'idk', 'tbh', 'ngl', 'rn'. Often skips apostrophes ('dont', 'im') but sometimes has them because of autocorrect. Little punctuation apart from the odd full stop or 'lol'. Short answers unless the topic interests her or annoys her, and then she writes a quick run-on rant.
- with strangers: Instantly chatty and at ease, with no shyness at all. She asks the other person questions back and makes jokes early. She can come across as a bit cocky or dismissive, especially if she thinks something is pointless, and she doesn't soften disagreement much. She isn't nervous about being judged and seems to enjoy having an audience.
- small things: The 4 bus is always late, Her manager at the shop scheduling her on the same Saturdays as the stocktake, Something she sold on Vinted for double what she paid, Her little brother being on his PlayStation all night, Her mum making her go to Mass on Sunday when she's hungover, Getting her nails done before a night out, Lectures at 9am being 'actually criminal', Who got dumped on Love Island this week
- deeper things: She feels she has to act more confident than she is about where she fits, since she isn't fully 'Keralan' to her cousins or fully Welsh to some people at school, Her parents' sacrifices come up a lot at home, and she finds the pressure annoying but also feels guilty about it, She thinks she's not as close to her friends as it looks, and that people like her more than they trust her, She's been seeing a boy from her course and hasn't told her parents, and wouldn't unless it got serious, She sometimes wonders whether she actually believes in God or just likes the community at church
- webcam photo: Laptop webcam shot from slightly below, framing her head and shoulders in the centre with some headroom. Lighting comes mainly from a window to her left, so that side of her face is brighter, with a warm ceiling light adding a yellow tint. She is a young South Asian woman with medium-brown skin, dark brown eyes and full eyebrows, wearing light makeup with mascara and a nude lip. She is half-smiling with one eyebrow slightly raised, as if mid-comment. Her long, straight black hair is pulled into a high claw clip with a few loose strands at the front. She has small gold hoop earrings and a thin gold chain with a small cross. She wears a grey cropped zip-up hoodie over a white top and no glasses. Behind her is a bedroom wall painted pale lilac, with a white wardrobe door partly open and clothes visible inside. A fairy-light strip runs along the top edge of the wall. A cork board holds a few photos, a festival wristband and a Swansea University lanyard. On the right edge of the frame is a corner of an unmade bed with a fluffy cream cushion.

req.text:
You write transcripts of realistic video calls between strangers for a fully synthetic research dataset set in the UK. The study, in order (from its published design): a short puzzle task done alone; first impressions of the others' webcam photos; then a series of three-minute, one-on-one video calls in rounds, each person meeting the others in their group; after each call a short survey.

Call shape (from the original study's numbers): a call is cut off by a three-minute timer. A typical call has about 30 turns (most between 20 and 39) and about 570 words in total (most between 440 and 682); half of all turns are 12 words or fewer, and a quarter are 24 or more. Short acknowledgements ("yeah", "mm") count as turns too. So aim for about 570 words in about 30 turns: alongside the quick back-and-forth, people often talk in longer stretches (explaining their job, telling a story), and those long turns carry much of the call.

Guide to British conversational English (use it for how people talk; it is a description of speech, not a script):
How British people talk in casual conversation. This is a paraphrase of published descriptions of spoken British English; sources are in SOURCES.md. Use these features lightly and only where they fit the person. Never use them as a caricature.

- **Fillers.** British speakers hesitate with "erm" and "er". Women and younger speakers lean towards "erm".
- **Hedges.** "Sort of" is everywhere and steady. "Kind of" is spreading, and younger speakers use it more.
- **Politeness words.** "Please", "thank you", "thanks" and "sorry" mostly mean what they say. "Sorry" also works as a repair word (to correct yourself, or to ask someone to repeat) and can be ironic.
- **Tags at the end of a sentence.** "You know", "right", "okay", "yeah", "do you know what I mean". Among young Londoners, "innit" and "you get me" are rising. Tags depend on age and region only, never on ethnicity.
- **Echoing.** In an engaged conversation people pick up and re-use parts of each other's words.
- **Regional words and grammar** (from a recent dialect survey):
  - A bread roll is a "barm" in the North West (Manchester to Liverpool and western Lancashire), a "cob" around Nottinghamshire, a "bap" in Staffordshire, the West Midlands and North Wales, and a "batch" in Liverpool and Coventry.
  - Around Liverpool an ice lolly can be a "lolly ice".
  - The evening meal is "tea" in the North West, North East and Yorkshire, and "dinner" in the South East and London. Some people say both.
  - "Yous" or "youse" for plural "you" is common in the North East (Newcastle, Teesside), Liverpool and Scotland, less so in Manchester, and rare in York, Leeds and Sheffield.
  - "Give it me" is normal in the North West and West Midlands and widely accepted in Sheffield and York; it fades south of Birmingham, Coventry and Leicester.
  - "You was" is widely used, historically Northern and now found as far south as London.
- **Everyday British words** to draw on where they fit, without assigning them to regions: knackered or shattered, chuffed or made up, skint or brassic, mardy or stroppy, mum or mam, mate or pal, settee, sofa or couch.

The group (session S26). Persona cards, including the webcam photo each person was rated on:

P135 (Joanne; transcript label: Joanne):
- first name: Joanne
- age: 50
- lives in: Taunton, South West England
- occupation: Not currently in paid work. Formerly a registered veterinary nurse for over twenty years, most recently head nurse at a mixed small-animal practice. She left three years ago because of a long-standing lower back problem and the shift work. She now does a few unpaid hours a week helping at a local cat rescue.
- education detail: GCSEs and A-levels (Biology, English, Geography) at a comprehensive and sixth form in Somerset. Diploma in Veterinary Nursing, gained while working at a practice. She later did short CPD courses in practice management and anaesthesia monitoring.
- household: Lives with her husband Martin (53), a chartered building surveyor with a regional firm, in a four-bedroom 1990s detached house on the edge of Taunton. Their son Callum (22) works in Bristol and comes back most weekends. Their daughter Ellie (19) is at university in Cardiff and is home in the holidays. They also have an elderly Border terrier called Biscuit and two rescue cats.
- cultural background: White British, born in Bridgwater and raised in Somerset. Her dad worked at the Hinkley Point power station and her mum was a school dinner lady. She is Church of England and goes to the local parish church about once or twice a month, more around Christmas and Harvest. She is on the flower rota and helps with the church's coffee mornings. Her faith is comfortable rather than intense: she says she 'believes in something' and likes the community side of church.
- professional persona: Practical and warm, and very good with anxious owners. She was the nurse people asked for when their pet was being put to sleep. She was organised enough to run a rota but never a stickler. She misses the team banter and having a role, and she still slips into 'nurse mode' when friends ask about their dogs. Her confidence took a knock when she stopped working, and she sometimes undersells what she did.
- sports persona: Not sporty. Her back means she gave up the Zumba class she loved. She now does a gentle Pilates class on Tuesday mornings and walks Biscuit along the canal or up on the Quantocks when her back allows. She watches Somerset cricket on the telly with Martin and enjoys the atmosphere at the County Ground once a summer, mostly for the picnic and a glass of Pimm's.
- arts persona: Loves a good drama series and reality TV, especially Strictly and The Great British Bake Off, and gets properly emotional at the results. She sings in a community choir that does pop and musical theatre numbers. She reads book-club novels on her Kindle and enjoys a trip to the Brewhouse Theatre or a touring musical in Bristol.
- travel persona: Prefers holidays that are relaxing and sociable over adventurous ones. They go to Cornwall or Pembrokeshire most years with the dog, plus one sunny week abroad, often Crete, Majorca or the Algarve. She gets anxious about flying and airport queues but loves it once she is there. She has a long-held wish to see the Northern Lights.
- culinary persona: A confident everyday cook: roasts, shepherd's pie, curries from a jar 'jazzed up', traybakes for church and choir. She calls the evening meal 'dinner' mostly, sometimes 'tea' when it is something quick. She likes a Sunday carvery at the pub and a cream tea, and has firm views on jam going first. Her treat is a glass or two of rosé on a Friday.
- hobbies and interests: community choir, gentle Pilates, dog walking on the Quantocks and along the canal, volunteering at a cat rescue, church flower rota and coffee mornings, Strictly Come Dancing and Bake Off, book club, baking traybakes, pottering in the garden with pots and hanging baskets
- skills: animal handling and basic veterinary care, calming distressed people, organising rotas and small events, baking for crowds, remembering everyone's names and news, first aid
- career goals: Not looking to go back to full-time nursing because of her back. She would like a part-time, sitting-down role that still involves animals or people, perhaps reception or client care at a practice, or a paid coordinator role at the rescue. She worries a bit about whether she is 'too out of the loop' now.
- voice: Chatty, warm and quite quick once she relaxes. She laughs easily and often apologises for 'waffling'. There is a soft West Country lilt with slightly rounded r's, but nothing broad. She uses 'erm' a fair bit and says 'sort of' and 'you know' often, and occasionally uses 'proper' as an intensifier ('it was proper lovely'). She echoes the interviewer's words back while thinking ('what would I do with it... erm, honestly?'). She cannot leave a silence alone for long and fills it with 'sorry, does that make sense?' or a little laugh. If a question touches on worries, she gets more animated and talks faster.
- typing: Mostly sentence case but inconsistent. She often forgets the capital at the start and sometimes gets 'i' wrong. She uses apostrophes correctly most of the time, ends sentences with exclamation marks, and uses '...' between thoughts. She types a full sentence or two rather than single words, e.g. 'not really... i do worry about it sometimes though!' She uses 'x' only with friends, never in a form. No text-speak beyond the odd 'tbh'.
- with strangers: Friendly and open almost immediately. She asks the other person questions back, notices if they seem tired and says so kindly. She comes across as lovely and a bit of a talker. She can over-share slightly when nervous and then apologise for it. She wants people to like her and gets flustered if she thinks she has given a 'wrong' answer.
- small things: Biscuit being a grumpy old man about the rain, the traffic on the M5 by Bridgwater, choir doing an ABBA medley for the summer concert, her hanging baskets not taking this year, Ellie ringing only when she needs money, a new café opening in town, being shattered after Pilates, the cost of the weekly shop going up

- webcam photo: Head-and-shoulders shot from a laptop on a kitchen table, angled slightly upward so the ceiling and a pendant light are partly visible. Daylight comes from a window to her left, giving soft, even light with a slight shadow on the right side of her face. She is a white woman in her fifties with a round, friendly face, light freckles and fine lines around her eyes. She has a wide, open smile showing her teeth and her head is tilted slightly. Her hair is shoulder-length, highlighted dark-blonde with some grey at the roots, pushed behind one ear. She wears red-framed reading glasses pushed up on her head, a teal knitted cardigan over a white T-shirt, and small silver hoop earrings. Behind her is a cream Shaker-style kitchen with a wooden worktop, a kettle, a bread bin, and a calendar on the wall covered in handwritten notes. On the windowsill sit a basil plant and a framed photo of two young adults. The corner of a dog bed with a tartan blanket is visible at the bottom right.

req.text:
You write transcripts of realistic video calls between strangers for a fully synthetic research dataset set in the UK. The study, in order (from its published design): a short puzzle task done alone; first impressions of the others' webcam photos; then a series of three-minute, one-on-one video calls in rounds, each person meeting the others in their group; after each call a short survey.

Call shape (from the original study's numbers): a call is cut off by a three-minute timer. A typical call has about 30 turns (most between 20 and 39) and about 570 words in total (most between 440 and 682); half of all turns are 12 words or fewer, and a quarter are 24 or more. Short acknowledgements ("yeah", "mm") count as turns too. So aim for about 570 words in about 30 turns: alongside the quick back-and-forth, people often talk in longer stretches (explaining their job, telling a story), and those long turns carry much of the call.

Guide to British conversational English (use it for how people talk; it is a description of speech, not a script):
How British people talk in casual conversation. This is a paraphrase of published descriptions of spoken British English; sources are in SOURCES.md. Use these features lightly and only where they fit the person. Never use them as a caricature.

- **Fillers.** British speakers hesitate with "erm" and "er". Women and younger speakers lean towards "erm".
- **Hedges.** "Sort of" is everywhere and steady. "Kind of" is spreading, and younger speakers use it more.
- **Politeness words.** "Please", "thank you", "thanks" and "sorry" mostly mean what they say. "Sorry" also works as a repair word (to correct yourself, or to ask someone to repeat) and can be ironic.
- **Tags at the end of a sentence.** "You know", "right", "okay", "yeah", "do you know what I mean". Among young Londoners, "innit" and "you get me" are rising. Tags depend on age and region only, never on ethnicity.
- **Echoing.** In an engaged conversation people pick up and re-use parts of each other's words.
- **Regional words and grammar** (from a recent dialect survey):
  - A bread roll is a "barm" in the North West (Manchester to Liverpool and western Lancashire), a "cob" around Nottinghamshire, a "bap" in Staffordshire, the West Midlands and North Wales, and a "batch" in Liverpool and Coventry.
  - Around Liverpool an ice lolly can be a "lolly ice".
  - The evening meal is "tea" in the North West, North East and Yorkshire, and "dinner" in the South East and London. Some people say both.
  - "Yous" or "youse" for plural "you" is common in the North East (Newcastle, Teesside), Liverpool and Scotland, less so in Manchester, and rare in York, Leeds and Sheffield.
  - "Give it me" is normal in the North West and West Midlands and widely accepted in Sheffield and York; it fades south of Birmingham, Coventry and Leicester.
  - "You was" is widely used, historically Northern and now found as far south as London.
- **Everyday British words** to draw on where they fit, without assigning them to regions: knackered or shattered, chuffed or made up, skint or brassic, mardy or stroppy, mum or mam, mate or pal, settee, sofa or couch.

req.text:
You write transcripts of realistic video calls between strangers for a fully synthetic research dataset set in the UK. The study, in order (from its published design): a short puzzle task done alone; first impressions of the others' webcam photos; then a series of three-minute, one-on-one video calls in rounds, each person meeting the others in their group; after each call a short survey.

Call shape (from the original study's numbers): a call is cut off by a three-minute timer. A typical call has about 30 turns (most between 20 and 39) and about 570 words in total (most between 440 and 682); half of all turns are 12 words or fewer, and a quarter are 24 or more. Short acknowledgements ("yeah", "mm") count as turns too. So aim for about 570 words in about 30 turns: alongside the quick back-and-forth, people often talk in longer stretches (explaining their job, telling a story), and those long turns carry much of the call.

Guide to British conversational English (use it for how people talk; it is a description of speech, not a script):
How British people talk in casual conversation. This is a paraphrase of published descriptions of spoken British English; sources are in SOURCES.md. Use these features lightly and only where they fit the person. Never use them as a caricature.

- **Fillers.** British speakers hesitate with "erm" and "er". Women and younger speakers lean towards "erm".
- **Hedges.** "Sort of" is everywhere and steady. "Kind of" is spreading, and younger speakers use it more.
- **Politeness words.** "Please", "thank you", "thanks" and "sorry" mostly mean what they say. "Sorry" also works as a repair word (to correct yourself, or to ask someone to repeat) and can be ironic.
- **Tags at the end of a sentence.** "You know", "right", "okay", "yeah", "do you know what I mean". Among young Londoners, "innit" and "you get me" are rising. Tags depend on age and region only, never on ethnicity.
- **Echoing.** In an engaged conversation people pick up and re-use parts of each other's words.
- **Regional words and grammar** (from a recent dialect survey):
  - A bread roll is a "barm" in the North West (Manchester to Liverpool and western Lancashire), a "cob" around Nottinghamshire, a "bap" in Staffordshire, the West Midlands and North Wales, and a "batch" in Liverpool and Coventry.
  - Around Liverpool an ice lolly can be a "lolly ice".
  - The evening meal is "tea" in the North West, North East and Yorkshire, and "dinner" in the South East and London. Some people say both.
  - "Yous" or "youse" for plural "you" is common in the North East (Newcastle, Teesside), Liverpool and Scotland, less so in Manchester, and rare in York, Leeds and Sheffield.
  - "Give it me" is normal in the North West and West Midlands and widely accepted in Sheffield and York; it fades south of Birmingham, Coventry and Leicester.
  - "You was" is widely used, historically Northern and now found as far south as London.
- **Everyday British words** to draw on where they fit, without assigning them to regions: knackered or shattered, chuffed or made up, skint or brassic, mardy or stroppy, mum or mam, mate or pal, settee, sofa or couch.

The group (session S29). Persona cards, including the webcam photo each person was rated on:

P153 (Tomasz; transcript label: Tomasz):
- first name: Tomasz
- age: 42
- lives in: Basingstoke, South East England
- occupation: Carpenter and kitchen fitter, employed full-time by a small fitted-kitchen firm based on an industrial estate on the edge of town. Usually works about 40 to 45 hours a week, going out to customers' houses across north Hampshire and Berkshire.
- education detail: Finished a technikum (vocational secondary school) in wood technology near Rzeszów in south-east Poland, which gave him a qualified joiner's certificate. Since moving to the UK he has done short courses, including CSCS card training and a manufacturer's worktop installation course. No university.
- household: Lives with his wife Claire, 39, who is English and works as a dispenser at a high-street pharmacy, and their son Oliver, 10. They own a three-bed semi on an estate in Brighton Hill that they bought in 2016, with a mortgage. Tomasz's van is parked outside.
- cultural background: Born and raised in a small town in Podkarpackie, Poland, in a Catholic family. His father was a lorry driver and his mother worked in a school kitchen. He came to England in 2006 at 24 with a friend, first doing labouring in Reading, then joinery work. He met Claire in 2010 through a mate from work. He is Catholic and goes to the Polish Mass in Reading now and then, reliably at Christmas and Easter, and Oliver did his First Communion there. He speaks Polish to his mum on video calls every Sunday and English at home. He feels settled here but still calls Poland 'home' without thinking about it.
- professional persona: Good with his hands and quietly proud of a clean scribe on a worktop or doors that hang straight. Customers like him because he is patient and doesn't argue, even when they change their minds halfway through a job. He is less good at the admin side. He forgets to photograph finished jobs for the company Instagram, his timesheets are late, and he once left a whole box of hinges at a customer's house. His boss tolerates it because the work itself is good.
- sports persona: Watches football rather than plays it. He follows the Polish national team and keeps a soft spot for Resovia from back home. Here he half-supports Arsenal because Claire's family do. He goes carp fishing at a lake near Alton maybe twice a month in summer, sometimes overnight with a bivvy. He doesn't go to a gym and says his job is enough.
- arts persona: Not much of a theatre or gallery person. He listens to a mix of Polish rock from his teens, like Dżem and Perfect, and whatever is on Heart in the van. He watches crime series on Netflix with Claire, and the occasional Polish film when one comes up. He likes woodworking videos on YouTube more than anything else.
- travel persona: Goes back to Poland most summers for two weeks to see his mum and sister, usually flying Ryanair from Stansted or Luton, though one year they drove. They had one beach holiday in Crete with Claire's parents. He'd like to take Oliver to the Tatra mountains properly, but he hasn't planned it, and Claire does most of the booking.
- culinary persona: Claire does most of the weekday cooking, but Tomasz makes Polish dishes at weekends: żurek at Easter, bigos in winter, and pierogi with his mum's recipe when he has patience, which isn't often. He gets things from the Polish shop on Winton Square. On site he lives on meal deals and coffee from the garage. He likes a barbecue in summer and is the one who stands over it.
- hobbies and interests: carp fishing, restoring old bikes in the garage, mostly for Oliver and his friends, watching woodworking and van-fitout videos on YouTube, Polish and Premier League football on TV, half-finished projects around the house, like a garden bench that's been 'nearly done' for a year, helping Oliver with Lego builds
- skills: fitting kitchens and worktops, including laminate and solid wood, hanging doors and first and second fix carpentry, reading drawings and measuring up, basic plumbing and electrics for appliance installs, within what he's allowed to do, fluent Polish and good working English, staying calm with difficult customers, fixing bikes
- career goals: Vaguely thinks about going self-employed one day doing bespoke fitted wardrobes and alcoves, because he knows that's where the money is. But he dislikes paperwork and chasing invoices, so the idea hasn't moved much in five years. Mostly he wants steady work, to pay down the mortgage, and not to wreck his knees before 55.
- voice: Calm, unhurried, fairly low voice with a clear Polish accent softened by 18 years in England. His grammar is mostly good, with small slips like dropping 'the' or 'a' now and then ('I went to shop', 'is good, yeah'). He uses 'er' rather than 'erm', and picked up 'sort of', 'mate', 'to be honest' and 'yeah, no' from building sites. He says 'dinner' for the evening meal. He gives short answers at first and doesn't rush to fill silences. He'll wait, then say something like 'yeah, er, I think so' or 'what else you want to know?' He laughs quietly at himself more than at others. He agrees easily but will say 'no, is not really like that' gently if something is wrong. When he's tired he sometimes says 'knackered'.
- typing: Mostly lowercase, starts sentences without capitals, and capitalises 'I' about half the time. Few commas, and full stops often missing at the end. Usually drops apostrophes ('dont', 'its', 'im'). He doesn't use text-speak much beyond 'ok' and the odd 'thx'. Answers are short and practical, with an occasional small grammar slip, for example 'i work in kitchens fitting, about 8 years same company'.
- with strangers: Polite, reserved and a bit hard to read at first. He is friendly but not chatty, and answers what he's asked without volunteering much. He comes across as easygoing and patient, the kind of person who won't complain if the call runs late. He warms up if the conversation turns to something practical he knows about, or to his son.
- small things: the van's sliding door sticks and he keeps meaning to get it looked at, traffic on the M3 in the mornings, a customer who changed her worktop colour three times, Oliver's football training on Saturday mornings, the Polish shop running out of good kiełbasa, a bike he found at the tip that just needed new brakes, the fishing lake being closed because of the weather, the price of timber going up
- deeper things: his dad died in 2019 and he couldn't get back in time; he still thinks about it, he worries a little about his mum living alone in Poland and whether she should come here, but she won't, after Brexit he applied for settled status and felt, for the first time, like a guest, he and Claire had wanted a second child but it didn't happen, and they don't talk about it much now, he sometimes feels he's 'not really Polish any more and not really English', his faith is quieter than his mother's, but he prays when things are bad
- webcam photo: Laptop webcam view from slightly below, the laptop set on a kitchen table, framing his head and shoulders a little off-centre to the left. Evening, lit by a warm ceiling light overhead and the cooler glow of the screen on his face. He has a broad face, light stubble with a few grey hairs at the chin, short light-brown hair clipped at the sides and thinning slightly at the front, and blue-grey eyes. No glasses. His expression is neutral and a little tired, mouth closed, with the faint start of a polite smile. He is wearing a navy work fleece with a small embroidered company logo on the chest, unzipped over a grey T-shirt. Behind him is a fitted kitchen with white gloss doors and a wood-effect laminate worktop. On the worktop are a kettle, a toaster, a fruit bowl with bananas and a stack of post. A child's school drawing and a takeaway menu are held to the fridge with magnets on the right edge of the frame, and a dark window shows a reflection of the ceiling light. A hi-vis vest hangs over the back of a chair partly visible beside him.

P154 (Rob; transcript label: Rob):
- first name: Rob
- age: 31
- lives in: Stockport (Edgeley), North West England
- occupation: Full-time mature student, second year of a BSc in Ecology and Wildlife Conservation at Manchester Metropolitan University. Before that he spent eight years in admin and clerical roles, latterly as a planning support officer at a local council. He does a few paid shifts in the summer as a bat and bird survey assistant for a small ecological consultancy.
- education detail: Went to a comprehensive in Stockport and did A-levels in Geography, Biology and English Language at a sixth form college. Started a degree at 18 but left after a term because he didn't feel ready. Went into office work, did an Access to HE course in Science part-time at 28, then started university full-time at 30 on a student loan, with savings to top it up.

- cultural background: White British, born and raised in Stockport. His dad was a bus driver and his mum works in a school office. He has one older sister in Hazel Grove. Not religious, and neither were his parents in any real way. He's the first in the family to go to university, which he mentions matter-of-factly rather than proudly.

Mostly he walks: long days in the Peak District, sometimes with a camera. He cycles to the station. He took up bouldering at a climbing wall in town last year and is middling at it.
- arts persona: Reads a lot, mostly nature writing and odd non-fiction, plus the occasional sci-fi novel. He likes documentaries and has a soft spot for old folk and ambient music. He goes to small gigs in Manchester a few times a year. He takes decent wildlife photos on a secondhand camera and has no interest in posting them much.
- travel persona: Travels cheaply and not often. He has done a few weeks on Mull and in the Highlands, a trip to the Netherlands with Hannah, and a student field trip to the Algarve that he loved. He wants to do a proper trip to Scandinavia or the Pyrenees for the wildlife. He's happier with a tent or a hostel than a resort.
- culinary persona: Decent everyday cook and does most of the tea during the week because his timetable is looser than Hannah's. Lots of one-pot things, curries and chilli. He's been trying to eat less meat for environmental reasons but doesn't make a thing of it. He likes a chippy barm and a pint at the weekend.
- hobbies and interests: hillwalking in the Peak District, birdwatching and bat detecting, wildlife photography, bouldering, nature writing and popular science books, following Stockport County, small music gigs, volunteering at a local nature reserve on occasional Saturdays
- skills: spreadsheets and data entry, species identification (birds, getting better at plants), using bat detectors and survey software, basic GIS mapping, writing clear emails and reports, staying calm under pressure, cooking on a budget
- career goals: Finish his degree with a good grade, then get a job as a field ecologist or in a wildlife trust, ideally in the North West so he and Hannah don't have to move. He'd consider a master's if he could fund it. He isn't fussed about money as long as the work is outdoors and means something.
- voice: Relaxed, mid-paced, light Stockport/Manchester accent without being broad. Says 'erm' when thinking, sometimes 'sort of' or 'kind of' to soften an opinion. Uses 'mate' casually, says 'tea' for the evening meal, and might say 'I was made up' or 'I'm knackered'. Answers honestly and fairly briefly, with the occasional dry joke. Totally fine with silence: he'll just wait, or say 'yeah, I think that's it really' rather than pad things out.
- typing: Quick and mostly lowercase, with capitals only for names now and then. Commas are sparse and full stops are often missing at the end. He usually gets apostrophes right in 'don't' and 'it's' but drops them when rushing ('im', 'thats'). He writes 'tbh' occasionally and otherwise avoids text abbreviations. Short, plain answers.
- with strangers: Easygoing and polite, not especially chatty to start but warms up quickly. Comes across as unpretentious and a bit dry. Doesn't try to impress, and will say 'I don't know, to be honest' rather than bluff. Seems steady and hard to rattle.
- small things: Moss the cat knocking stuff off his desk, trying to get the 7:40 train into Piccadilly, a barn owl he saw on a field trip, County's last result, doing the big shop at Aldi with Hannah, his secondhand camera lens, the damp in the back bedroom, the essay deadline that's coming up

- webcam photo: Head-and-shoulders shot from a laptop camera, slightly below eye level so the ceiling corner shows. Daylight from a window on the left lights one side of his face, and the right side is a little shadowed. White man with a short light-brown beard and short, slightly messy mid-brown hair, no glasses. He has a mild, friendly half-smile and is looking just off-centre at the screen. He's wearing a faded dark green hoodie over a grey T-shirt. Behind him is a magnolia wall with a cork board pinned with lecture timetables, a printed OS map of the Dark Peak and a couple of photo postcards of birds. To the right is a cheap white bookshelf with field guides, paperbacks, a pair of binoculars and a pot plant. The top of a grey office chair is visible behind his shoulders, and a tabby cat's tail hangs over the edge of the shelf.

- age: 53

- occupation: Site services manager at a mid-sized food packaging manufacturer on an industrial estate on the edge of Loughborough. He looks after maintenance, health and safety compliance and contractors, and has a team of six engineers and a facilities coordinator.
