req.text:
You write transcripts of realistic video calls between strangers for a fully synthetic research dataset set in the UK. The study, in order (from its published design): a short puzzle task done alone; first impressions of the others' webcam photos; then a series of three-minute, one-on-one video calls in rounds, each person meeting the others in their group; after each call a short survey.

Call shape (from the original study's numbers): a call is cut off by a three-minute timer. A typical call has about 30 turns (most between 20 and 39) and about 570 words in total (most between 440 and 682); half of all turns are 12 words or fewer, and a quarter are 24 or more. Short acknowledgements ("yeah", "mm") count as turns too. So aim for about 570 words in about 30 turns: alongside the quick back-and-forth, people often talk in longer stretches (explaining their job, telling a story), and those long turns carry much of the call.

Guide to British conversational English (use it for how people talk; it is a description of speech, not a script):
How British people talk in casual conversation. This is a paraphrase of published descriptions of spoken British English; sources are in SOURCES.md. Use these features lightly and only where they fit the person. Never use them as a caricature.

- **Fillers.** British speakers hesitate with "erm" and "er". Women and younger speakers lean towards "erm".
- **Hedges.** "Sort of" is everywhere and steady. "Kind of" is spreading, and younger speakers use it more.
- **Politeness words.** "Please", "thank you", "thanks" and "sorry" mostly mean what they say. "Sorry" also works as a repair word (to correct yourself, or to ask someone to repeat) and can be ironic.
- **Tags at the end of a sentence.** "You know", "right", "okay", "yeah", "do you know what I mean". Among young Londoners, "innit" and "you get me" are rising. Tags depend on age and region only, never on ethnicity.
- **Echoing.** In an engaged conversation people pick up and re-use parts of each other's words.
- **Regional words and grammar** (from a recent dialect survey):
  - A bread roll is a "barm" in the North West (Manchester to Liverpool and western Lancashire), a "cob" around Nottinghamshire, a "bap" in Staffordshire, the West Midlands and North Wales, and a "batch" in Liverpool and Coventry.
  - Around Liverpool an ice lolly can be a "lolly ice".
  - The evening meal is "tea" in the North West, North East and Yorkshire, and "dinner" in the South East and London. Some people say both.
  - "Yous" or "youse" for plural "you" is common in the North East (Newcastle, Teesside), Liverpool and Scotland, less so in Manchester, and rare in York, Leeds and Sheffield.
  - "Give it me" is normal in the North West and West Midlands and widely accepted in Sheffield and York; it fades south of Birmingham, Coventry and Leicester.
  - "You was" is widely used, historically Northern and now found as far south as London.
- **Everyday British words** to draw on where they fit, without assigning them to regions: knackered or shattered, chuffed or made up, skint or brassic, mardy or stroppy, mum or mam, mate or pal, settee, sofa or couch.

The group (session S23). Persona cards, including the webcam photo each person was rated on:

P119 (Holly; transcript label: Holly):
- first name: Holly
- age: 25
- lives in: Kings Heath, Birmingham, West Midlands
- occupation: Full-time PhD student in Human Geography at the University of Birmingham, funded by a research council studentship. She is not currently in paid employment apart from occasional paid seminar teaching.
- education detail: A-levels in Geography, English Literature and Art at a sixth form college in Stafford. First-class BA in Geography at the University of Sheffield, then an MA in Cultural Geography at Birmingham. She is now in the second year of a PhD on how people use and reclaim disused canal-side industrial spaces.
- household: Lives with her husband Tom (27, a backend software developer for a fintech company, mostly working from home) in a rented two-bed Victorian terrace. They married two summers ago after meeting at university. No children, and a rescue greyhound called Pickle.
- cultural background: White British, born and raised in Stafford. Her mum is a primary school deputy head and her dad is a surveyor, and she has one younger brother at college. It was a comfortable, middle-class, fairly non-religious upbringing, with Sunday dinners at her nan's. She left religion blank on the census form because she 'didn't see why it mattered to them'.
- professional persona: She is a confident, chatty academic who is very good at conferences and networking, and much less good at actually finishing chapters. She is happy to present half-formed ideas as if they're polished, and she quietly enjoys being the one people remember after a panel. She has a habit of agreeing to every collaboration going and then leaning on her supervisor's goodwill when deadlines slip.
- sports persona: She isn't sporty in a structured way. She does a Tuesday night roller derby taster group with a friend, which is chaotic and she loves it, and she takes long dog walks round Highbury Park. She has a gym membership she uses about twice a month and keeps meaning to cancel.
- arts persona: She is a big gig-goer: small venues in Digbeth, festivals in summer, anything a bit odd or experimental. She goes to Ikon Gallery openings mostly for the free wine and the people. She paints badly but enthusiastically with cheap acrylics and has half-finished canvases stacked behind the settee. She reads widely and messily, with three novels on the go at once.
- travel persona: She is an impulsive traveller who books cheap flights on a whim and sorts out the details later. She has done Lisbon, Berlin, Kraków and a month interrailing after her degree, and she claims a conference trip to Montreal as 'basically a holiday'. She loves wandering unfamiliar cities without a plan and isn't bothered when things go wrong.
- culinary persona: An adventurous eater who will try anything once. She cooks big messy one-pot dishes and leaves the kitchen in a state. She is a regular at the balti places and street food markets around Birmingham. She still calls a bread roll a bap, and 'tea' and 'dinner' get used interchangeably at home.
- hobbies and interests: urban exploring and photographing derelict buildings, small gigs and festivals, roller derby taster sessions, amateur acrylic painting, charity shop and vintage clothes hunting, walking Pickle the greyhound, pub quizzes, where she is loudly confident even when wrong
- skills: public speaking and presenting, qualitative interviewing, getting strangers to open up quickly, talking her way into places (events, guest lists, upgrades), basic GIS mapping, film photography
- career goals: She wants a postdoc and eventually a lectureship, ideally somewhere with a bit of prestige. She is privately just as interested in becoming a 'public geographer' with a podcast or a popular book. Getting the thesis actually written on time is the obvious obstacle, and she knows it but doesn't lose sleep over it.
- voice: Warm, fast and quite loud, with a mild Staffordshire/Midlands accent that's been softened by university. Flat vowels come through more when she's relaxed. She uses 'erm' a fair bit and 'sort of' and 'kind of' constantly, often stacked together. She ends points with 'yeah?' or 'you know'. She occasionally says 'give it me' or 'you was' when she's not thinking about it. She laughs easily, echoes back phrases the interviewer uses, and will fill any silence herself almost immediately, often going off on a tangent before saying 'sorry, what was the question?'
- typing: Quick and sloppy. Mostly lowercase, with capitals only sometimes at the start. Apostrophes are usually dropped ('dont', 'im'). She uses lots of commas and no full stop at the end, and sometimes adds 'haha' or 'lol'. Abbreviations like 'tbh', 'idk' and 'uni'. She's prone to typos she doesn't fix.
- with strangers: Instantly friendly and easy to talk to. She asks you questions back, makes jokes early and gives the impression she's been looking forward to chatting. She comes across as relaxed and self-assured, maybe a touch showy about her travels or her PhD. She is very agreeable and won't push back on anything, though she'll happily embellish a story to make it better.
- small things: Pickle refusing to walk in the rain, a gig she went to in Digbeth last weekend, a charity shop find, like a 70s suede jacket for eight quid, the state of the number 50 bus, Tom's work calls echoing through the house, having a conference coming up she hasn't written the paper for yet, her nan's Sunday dinners back in Stafford
- deeper things: She sometimes wonders if she got married too young, mostly because friends keep saying so, not because she's unhappy, She knows she coasts on charm and worries a little that people will eventually notice the work isn't all there, Her parents still help with rent occasionally and she doesn't tell anyone, She isn't sure she wants children, and Tom is more keen than she is, She feels a bit competitive and envious towards a friend from her MA who already has a book deal
- webcam photo: A laptop webcam shot from slightly below at a mild upward angle, framed from mid-chest up with her a little left of centre. Soft daylight from a window to her right lights that side of her face, with the other side in mild shadow and a faint blue tint from the screen. She has a round, freckled face, light make-up and a gold hoop in each ear, and she is mid-smile with her mouth slightly open as if about to speak. Her shoulder-length hair is dyed copper-red with darker roots growing through, pushed back with a green claw clip and with loose strands at the front. She wears a mustard-yellow chunky knit cardigan over a black t-shirt and no glasses. Behind her is a magnolia-painted wall with a large unframed abstract acrylic painting in oranges and teals, slightly crooked. A tall overfilled bookshelf has paperbacks stacked sideways, a trailing pothos plant and a film camera on top. A grey settee is partly visible on the right, with a crumpled knitted throw and the tail end of a grey greyhound curled up on it. An open door leads to a hallway with coats hung on hooks.

P120 (Riya; transcript label: Riya):
- first name: Riya
- age: 28
- lives in: Canada Water, South East London
- occupation: Operations Manager at a mid-sized grocery delivery company. She runs fulfilment planning for two warehouse sites in Park Royal and Charlton and manages a team of seven planners and shift leads.
- education detail: BTech in Industrial Engineering from a university in Pune, India, then an MSc in Management at Warwick Business School, which she came to the UK to do at 22. Since then she has completed a Lean Six Sigma Green Belt, paid for by her employer.
- household: Lives alone in a rented one-bedroom flat on the fourth floor of a 2010s block near Surrey Quays. She chose to live alone after two years of flatshares she describes as 'a nightmare of other people's dishes'. No pets.
- cultural background: Born and raised in Pune, India, in a Marathi-speaking family. Her father is a civil engineer and her mother teaches secondary-school chemistry, and she has one younger brother still in Pune. She was raised loosely Hindu but has been non-religious since her late teens. She keeps up the family occasions that matter to her mother, such as Diwali calls and sending money for her grandmother's care, without much sentiment about the religious side. She has lived in the UK for six years and holds a Skilled Worker visa. She is working towards settled status and watches the deadlines very closely.
- professional persona: Precise, demanding and very organised. Her colour-coded capacity models are known across the business. She is respected more than she is liked. She is impatient with people she thinks are coasting, and she has been told in two appraisals that she can come across as 'cutting'. She is quietly ambitious about titles and pay. She makes sure senior leadership knows which wins were hers, and she is not above letting a peer's mistake become visible in a meeting. She works long, steady hours but rarely past 7pm, because she plans her week so she doesn't have to.
- sports persona: Not sporty in a team sense. She goes to reformer Pilates twice a week at a boutique studio in Bermondsey, booked weeks in advance, and walks the Thames Path towards Greenwich on Sunday mornings with a podcast on. She quit a running club after a month because of 'the group chat energy'.
- arts persona: Reads a lot, mostly literary fiction in translation and long-form non-fiction. She is currently reading a Korean novel on her Kindle and keeps a ranked list on StoryGraph. She goes to exhibitions at the Barbican and the Tate Modern alone, on weekday evenings when they're quieter. She likes arthouse film and has strong opinions about which critics are overrated.
- travel persona: Plans trips meticulously in a spreadsheet and travels solo or with one close friend. Recent trips include Lisbon, Kyoto and a long weekend in Copenhagen, where she spent too much on design shops. She flies home to Pune about once a year, usually in December, and finds the visits both comforting and draining.
- culinary persona: Cooks properly on Sundays and batch-prepares lunches for the week: dal, poha and roasted vegetable grain bowls. She is a bit of a snob about restaurants and keeps a Notes app list of places in Borough and Peckham she wants to try. She is quite critical of most 'Indian' restaurants in London except a couple she rates highly. Dinner on weeknights is often something quick at the counter while she listens to a podcast.
- hobbies and interests: literary fiction and translated novels, reformer Pilates, solo gallery visits, Thames Path walks, planning travel itineraries, trying new restaurants, minimalist interior design, true-crime and economics podcasts
- skills: capacity planning and forecasting, advanced Excel and Power BI, process improvement (Lean Six Sigma), managing difficult supplier negotiations, Marathi, Hindi and English, cooking Maharashtrian home food, detailed budgeting
- career goals: Wants a Head of Operations role by 31, ideally at a larger, better-known brand, and then a director title. She is privately calculating whether an MBA or a move to consulting would get her there faster. She is also very focused on getting indefinite leave to remain so that her career isn't tied to one employer's sponsorship.
- voice: Clear, measured English with a light Indian accent that has softened over six years in London, plus a few London features: 'dinner', 'mate' used ironically, occasional 'you know'. She speaks at a moderate pace and chooses words carefully, with an 'erm' when she's thinking and the odd 'sort of' or 'kind of' to soften a blunt point, though often she doesn't bother softening. She gives short, complete answers and doesn't fill silences. If a pause goes on, she waits rather than chatting, which can feel a bit cool. She uses 'sorry' mainly as a repair ('sorry, I mean the second site, not the first'). She will politely correct a question she thinks is badly worded.
- typing: Proper capitals and full stops, apostrophes always correct, and complete sentences even in quick answers. She rarely uses abbreviations beyond 'e.g.' and 'etc.' and no emojis. Answers are concise, sometimes slightly clipped, e.g. 'I live alone. It suits me.'
- with strangers: Reserved, polite on the surface and a bit guarded. She answers what's asked without volunteering much and can seem cool or faintly judgemental. She is visibly sharper if she thinks a question is pointless. She warms up a little if the conversation turns to books, food or something she has a strong opinion on.
- small things: her Pilates studio changed its booking system and it's annoying, the Jubilee line being rammed in the mornings, a novel she's halfway through, a new bakery in Bermondsey she rates, her Sunday batch cooking, planning a trip to Seoul next spring, her building's lift being out again
- deeper things: constant low-level anxiety about her visa and what happens if she loses her job, guilt that she sees her parents only once a year and her grandmother is getting frail, that she sometimes feels lonely living alone but wouldn't admit it to her friends, a sense that she has to be twice as good to be taken seriously at work, a long-distance relationship that ended last year, which she still thinks about more than she'd like, knowing she can be harsh with people and not entirely wanting to change it
- webcam photo: Head-and-shoulders shot from a laptop on a desk, camera slightly below eye level. Soft daylight comes from a window to her left, so the right side of her face is a little shadowed. She has light-brown skin, dark eyes and a neutral, slightly appraising expression with lips closed. Her straight black shoulder-length hair is tucked behind one ear. She wears thin gold-rimmed rectangular glasses, small gold stud earrings and a cream crew-neck knit jumper. Behind her is a plain off-white wall with a large framed black-and-white architectural print, a tall white bookshelf with neatly ordered paperbacks and a small potted snake plant, and the edge of a grey linen sofa in the bottom corner of the frame.

P121 (Ceri; transcript label: Ceri):
- first name: Ceri
- age: 41
- lives in: Pontypridd, South Wales
- occupation: Full-time mature student, second year of a BSc in Occupational Therapy at Cardiff University. Before that she was a hairdresser for about twenty years and still does the odd cut for friends and family for cash.
- education detail: Left comprehensive school in Pontypridd at 16 with a handful of GCSEs and did an NVQ Level 3 in hairdressing at college. At 38 she did an Access to Higher Education Diploma (Health Science) at a further education college in the evenings, then got a place on the OT degree. She finds the academic writing hard but loves the anatomy and psychology modules.
- household: Lives with her partner of eleven years, Dai, a self-employed plumber, in a two-bed terraced house on a hill above the town centre. They've never married. - cultural background: White Welsh, born and raised in the Rhondda and Taff valleys in a working-class family. Her dad was a bus driver and her mam worked in a school canteen. - professional persona: On placement she's warm with patients and good at getting people talking, which she puts down to twenty years of salon chat. She's less patient with colleagues and lecturers. She'll question a decision she thinks is daft and doesn't always read the room before she does it. Gets anxious before assessments and over-prepares her notes, then talks fast when presenting. req.text:
You write transcripts of realistic video calls between strangers for a fully synthetic research dataset set in the UK. The study, in order (from its published design): a short puzzle task done alone; first impressions of the others' webcam photos; then a series of three-minute, one-on-one video calls in rounds, each person meeting the others in their group; after each call a short survey.

Call shape (from the original study's numbers): a call is cut off by a three-minute timer. A typical call has about 30 turns (most between 20 and 39) and about 570 words in total (most between 440 and 682); half of all turns are 12 words or fewer, and a quarter are 24 or more. Short acknowledgements ("yeah", "mm") count as turns too. So aim for about 570 words in about 30 turns: alongside the quick back-and-forth, people often talk in longer stretches (explaining their job, telling a story), and those long turns carry much of the call.

Guide to British conversational English (use it for how people talk; it is a description of speech, not a script):
How British people talk in casual conversation. This is a paraphrase of published descriptions of spoken British English; sources are in SOURCES.md. Use these features lightly and only where they fit the person. Never use them as a caricature.

- **Fillers.** British speakers hesitate with "erm" and "er". Women and younger speakers lean towards "erm".
- **Hedges.** "Sort of" is everywhere and steady. "Kind of" is spreading, and younger speakers use it more.
- **Politeness words.** "Please", "thank you", "thanks" and "sorry" mostly mean what they say. "Sorry" also works as a repair word (to correct yourself, or to ask someone to repeat) and can be ironic.
- **Tags at the end of a sentence.** "You know", "right", "okay", "yeah", "do you know what I mean". Among young Londoners, "innit" and "you get me" are rising. Tags depend on age and region only, never on ethnicity.
- **Echoing.** In an engaged conversation people pick up and re-use parts of each other's words.
- **Regional words and grammar** (from a recent dialect survey):
  - A bread roll is a "barm" in the North West (Manchester to Liverpool and western Lancashire), a "cob" around Nottinghamshire, a "bap" in Staffordshire, the West Midlands and North Wales, and a "batch" in Liverpool and Coventry.
  - Around Liverpool an ice lolly can be a "lolly ice".
  - The evening meal is "tea" in the North West, North East and Yorkshire, and "dinner" in the South East and London. Some people say both.
  - "Yous" or "youse" for plural "you" is common in the North East (Newcastle, Teesside), Liverpool and Scotland, less so in Manchester, and rare in York, Leeds and Sheffield.
  - "Give it me" is normal in the North West and West Midlands and widely accepted in Sheffield and York; it fades south of Birmingham, Coventry and Leicester.
  - "You was" is widely used, historically Northern and now found as far south as London.
- **Everyday British words** to draw on where they fit, without assigning them to regions: knackered or shattered, chuffed or made up, skint or brassic, mardy or stroppy, mum or mam, mate or pal, settee, sofa or couch.

req.text:
You write transcripts of realistic video calls between strangers for a fully synthetic research dataset set in the UK. The study, in order (from its published design): a short puzzle task done alone; first impressions of the others' webcam photos; then a series of three-minute, one-on-one video calls in rounds, each person meeting the others in their group; after each call a short survey.

Call shape (from the original study's numbers): a call is cut off by a three-minute timer. A typical call has about 30 turns (most between 20 and 39) and about 570 words in total (most between 440 and 682); half of all turns are 12 words or fewer, and a quarter are 24 or more. Short acknowledgements ("yeah", "mm") count as turns too. So aim for about 570 words in about 30 turns: alongside the quick back-and-forth, people often talk in longer stretches (explaining their job, telling a story), and those long turns carry much of the call.

Guide to British conversational English (use it for how people talk; it is a description of speech, not a script):
How British people talk in casual conversation. This is a paraphrase of published descriptions of spoken British English; sources are in SOURCES.md. Use these features lightly and only where they fit the person. Never use them as a caricature.

- **Fillers.** British speakers hesitate with "erm" and "er". Women and younger speakers lean towards "erm".
- **Hedges.** "Sort of" is everywhere and steady. "Kind of" is spreading, and younger speakers use it more.
- **Politeness words.** "Please", "thank you", "thanks" and "sorry" mostly mean what they say. "Sorry" also works as a repair word (to correct yourself, or to ask someone to repeat) and can be ironic.
- **Tags at the end of a sentence.** "You know", "right", "okay", "yeah", "do you know what I mean". Among young Londoners, "innit" and "you get me" are rising. Tags depend on age and region only, never on ethnicity.
- **Echoing.** In an engaged conversation people pick up and re-use parts of each other's words.
- **Regional words and grammar** (from a recent dialect survey):
  - A bread roll is a "barm" in the North West (Manchester to Liverpool and western Lancashire), a "cob" around Nottinghamshire, a "bap" in Staffordshire, the West Midlands and North Wales, and a "batch" in Liverpool and Coventry.
  - Around Liverpool an ice lolly can be a "lolly ice".
  - The evening meal is "tea" in the North West, North East and Yorkshire, and "dinner" in the South East and London. Some people say both.
  - "Yous" or "youse" for plural "you" is common in the North East (Newcastle, Teesside), Liverpool and Scotland, less so in Manchester, and rare in York, Leeds and Sheffield.
  - "Give it me" is normal in the North West and West Midlands and widely accepted in Sheffield and York; it fades south of Birmingham, Coventry and Leicester.
  - "You was" is widely used, historically Northern and now found as far south as London.
- **Everyday British words** to draw on where they fit, without assigning them to regions: knackered or shattered, chuffed or made up, skint or brassic, mardy or stroppy, mum or mam, mate or pal, settee, sofa or couch.

P169 (Gillian; transcript label: Gillian):
- first name: Gillian
- age: 52
- lives in: Bramhall, Stockport, North West England
- occupation: Optometrist, three days a week (about 22 hours) at a high-street opticians in Stockport town centre
- education detail: A-levels in Biology, Chemistry and Maths at a sixth form college in Stockport; BSc Optometry at UMIST/University of Manchester in the early 1990s; pre-registration year at an opticians in Altrincham; registered with the General Optical Council since then. Has done the minimum CPD needed and not much beyond it.
- household: Lives with her husband Martin (55), a regional sales director for an industrial flooring company, in a four-bed detached house they bought in 2004. Their son (24) lives in Leeds and their daughter (21) is at university in Nottingham. There is also a cockapoo called Bella.
- cultural background: White British, born and raised in Hazel Grove. Her dad was a quantity surveyor and her mum worked part-time at a building society. She was brought up nominally Church of England but has never been religious and says so plainly. She is firmly suburban South Manchester and quite attached to the idea that Bramhall is 'a nice area'. She reads the Daily Mail website and Mumsnet but would not admit to the second.
- professional persona: Competent at the core of the job: refractions, eye health checks and referrals. She is good at spotting things that need sending on, partly because she worries about missing something. She dropped to part-time when the kids were small and never went back to full-time. She dislikes the targets for selling glasses and add-ons, but she is not above steering people towards pricier lenses when the store manager is watching. Her paperwork and clinical notes run behind, and she leaves recall admin to the dispensing assistants. She has strong opinions about the younger optoms and the manager, mostly unflattering, and she shares them in the staff room.
- sports persona: Not sporty. She walks Bella round Bramhall Park most days and has had a gym membership at a local health club for years, though she mainly uses the pool and sauna. Martin watches Man City and she half-listens. She did a Couch to 5K once and stopped at week four.
- arts persona: Low interest. She watches a lot of telly: crime dramas, Married at First Sight, Strictly, and whatever is on ITV of an evening. She sees a musical at the Palace Theatre maybe once a year if a friend books it. She reads the odd psychological thriller on holiday and finds most 'arty' films boring and says so.
- travel persona: Creature of habit. They go to the same villa complex in the Algarve most summers, plus a city break now and then (Barcelona, Rome). She is a nervous flyer and gets anxious at airports, about passports especially. She likes a nice hotel and will mention it was a five-star. She has no interest in backpacking or anywhere 'difficult'.
- culinary persona: Cooks plain, familiar food: spag bol, chicken traybakes, a roast on Sunday. Tea is usually about half six. They get a takeaway on Fridays, usually Indian from the same place in Bramhall village. She likes eating out at chain-ish nice places and the local Italian, and enjoys a glass of Pinot Grigio or prosecco. She is not adventurous with food and is picky about restaurant service.
- hobbies and interests: Walking the dog in Bramhall Park, Watching reality TV and crime dramas, Browsing for handbags and homeware online, Swimming and the sauna at the health club, Doing up the house: she had the kitchen redone two years ago, WhatsApp group chats with a few old school friends
- skills: Eye examinations and refraction, Spotting signs of eye disease and making referrals, Explaining prescriptions to patients in plain terms, Driving (she does all the school-friend lifts to the Trafford Centre), Getting a refund or a discount when she complains
- career goals: None really ambitious. She wants to keep her three days, avoid being made to do Saturdays, and possibly drop to two days in a few years. She would like to retire at 60 if Martin's pension allows it. She grumbles about the job but has no plans to change.
- voice: Moderate pace with a light South Manchester accent, flat vowels, nothing broad. She says 'erm' when thinking and uses 'sort of' a lot. She sometimes finishes with 'you know' or 'do you know what I mean'. She calls the evening meal 'tea' and might say 'barm' without thinking. She says 'give it me' occasionally. Her register is quite clipped and guarded with strangers. She answers questions but doesn't elaborate unless it's a complaint or something that bothers her, and then she goes on. Silence makes her a bit uneasy, and she fills it with 'erm, yeah, that's it really' rather than adding more.
- typing: Quick and slightly careless. She usually starts with a capital but drops capitals mid-way. Apostrophes are hit and miss ('dont', 'its' for it's, though 'I'm' is usually right because of autocorrect on her phone). Commas go where full stops should be. She writes short answers and uses occasional 'tbh' and 'etc'. She doesn't use emojis in forms, and adds a '...' when she's annoyed.
- with strangers: A bit cool and wary at first, polite but not warm. She can come across as faintly judgemental or impatient, and she asks what the study is actually for. She warms up slightly if she can moan about something relatable, like the NHS, the cost of things or the neighbours. She makes sure to mention, casually, that she's an optometrist and lives in Bramhall.
- small things: Bella the cockapoo needs her nails doing and the groomer is 'daylight robbery', The neighbours' extension has blocked her light and she's still annoyed about it, The Indian takeaway on a Friday, Her new kitchen island, Parking in Stockport town centre being a nightmare, Being shattered after a Tuesday clinic, Watching Married at First Sight with a glass of wine, Her daughter needing money again
- deeper things: She gets health anxiety and lies awake worrying about lumps and headaches, and she googles symptoms constantly, She is worried Martin drinks too much and is heading for a heart attack like his dad, She feels a bit lost since both kids moved out and doesn't really know what to do with herself on her days off, She fell out with her sister over their mum's care and they've barely spoken in three years; she maintains it was entirely her sister's fault, She sometimes feels she coasted in her career and is privately envious of a university friend who went into ophthalmology research, Menopause has hit her hard with anxiety and poor sleep, and she's on HRT
- webcam photo: Laptop on a kitchen island, camera angled slightly upwards so the framing takes in her chin and the bottom of the ceiling spotlights. It is evening, with warm overhead spotlights and a cooler glow from the laptop screen on her face. She is a woman in her early fifties with shoulder-length highlighted blonde hair, blow-dried but a bit flat at the end of the day, with darker roots just visible. She wears tortoiseshell rectangular glasses, small gold stud earrings and light make-up. Her expression is neutral to slightly sceptical, lips pressed together, eyebrows a touch raised. She has on a navy fine-knit jumper with the sleeves pushed up. Behind her is a grey shaker-style kitchen with white quartz worktops, a chrome kettle, a Nespresso machine, a bowl of lemons, and a bottle of Pinot Grigio next to the hob. A wall calendar with scribbled appointments hangs slightly crooked by the fridge. Part of a dog bed and Bella's grey curly back are visible at the bottom right of the frame.

- hobbies and interests: Following Reading FC, Gym in the mornings, Barbecuing, Fantasy Premier League with lads from work, and he's competitive about it, Washing and valeting his car at weekends, Watching boxing on pay-per-view
- skills: Stock control and ordering, Forklift operation, Managing rotas and holiday cover, Handling difficult trade customers, Basic DIY, plastering and tiling, Reading a P&L report
- career goals: Wants an area manager role covering several branches within the next few years, mainly for the money and the company car. Worries he's not 'corporate' enough for it and resents the people he thinks get promoted for talking well in meetings. Isn't planning any more qualifications unless the company pays for them and it's a requirement.
- voice: Mid-to-quick pace with a Hampshire/South East accent: dropped t's, 'innit' never, 'mate' fairly often. Says 'dinner' for the evening meal. Uses 'sort of' and 'you know' as filler, with the occasional 'er' rather than 'erm' when he's thinking. Answers are short and a bit clipped, and he'll say plainly if he thinks a question is pointless ('not sure what you're after with that one, to be honest'). He doesn't like silence and fills it with a quick 'yeah, so...' or by asking if you're still there. When a topic touches on his son or money worries he slows down and gets quieter.
- typing: Mostly lowercase and rarely capitalises 'i'. Sometimes uses full stops, often doesn't. Apostrophes come and go ('dont', 'its', but 'I'm' when autocorrect catches it). How British people talk in casual conversation. This is a paraphrase of published descriptions of spoken British English; sources are in SOURCES.md. Use these features lightly and only where they fit the person. Never use them as a caricature.

- **Fillers.** British speakers hesitate with "erm" and "er". Women and younger speakers lean towards "erm".
- **Hedges.** "Sort of" is everywhere and steady. "Kind of" is spreading, and younger speakers use it more.
- **Politeness words.** "Please", "thank you", "thanks" and "sorry" mostly mean what they say. "Sorry" also works as a repair word (to correct yourself, or to ask someone to repeat) and can be ironic.
- **Tags at the end of a sentence.** "You know", "right", "okay", "yeah", "do you know what I mean". Among young Londoners, "innit" and "you get me" are rising. Tags depend on age and region only, never on ethnicity.
- **Echoing.** In an engaged conversation people pick up and re-use parts of each other's words.
- **Regional words and grammar** (from a recent dialect survey):
  - A bread roll is a "barm" in the North West (Manchester to Liverpool and western Lancashire), a "cob" around Nottinghamshire, a "bap" in Staffordshire, the West Midlands and North Wales, and a "batch" in Liverpool and Coventry.
  - Around Liverpool an ice lolly can be a "lolly ice".
  - The evening meal is "tea" in the North West, North East and Yorkshire, and "dinner" in the South East and London. Some people say both.
  - "Yous" or "youse" for plural "you" is common in the North East (Newcastle, Teesside), Liverpool and Scotland, less so in Manchester, and rare in York, Leeds and Sheffield.
  - "Give it me" is normal in the North West and West Midlands and widely accepted in Sheffield and York; it fades south of Birmingham, Coventry and Leicester.
  - "You was" is widely used, historically Northern and now found as far south as London.
- **Everyday British words** to draw on where they fit, without assigning them to regions: knackered or shattered, chuffed or made up, skint or brassic, mardy or stroppy, mum or mam, mate or pal, settee, sofa or couch.

req.text:
You write transcripts of realistic video calls between strangers for a fully synthetic research dataset set in the UK. The study, in order (from its published design): a short puzzle task done alone; first impressions of the others' webcam photos; then a series of three-minute, one-on-one video calls in rounds, each person meeting the others in their group; after each call a short survey.

Call shape (from the original study's numbers): a call is cut off by a three-minute timer. A typical call has about 30 turns (most between 20 and 39) and about 570 words in total (most between 440 and 682); half of all turns are 12 words or fewer, and a quarter are 24 or more. Short acknowledgements ("yeah", "mm") count as turns too. So aim for about 570 words in about 30 turns: alongside the quick back-and-forth, people often talk in longer stretches (explaining their job, telling a story), and those long turns carry much of the call.

Guide to British conversational English (use it for how people talk; it is a description of speech, not a script):
How British people talk in casual conversation. This is a paraphrase of published descriptions of spoken British English; sources are in SOURCES.md. Use these features lightly and only where they fit the person. Never use them as a caricature.

- **Fillers.** British speakers hesitate with "erm" and "er". Women and younger speakers lean towards "erm".
- **Hedges.** "Sort of" is everywhere and steady. "Kind of" is spreading, and younger speakers use it more.
- **Politeness words.** "Please", "thank you", "thanks" and "sorry" mostly mean what they say. "Sorry" also works as a repair word (to correct yourself, or to ask someone to repeat) and can be ironic.
- **Tags at the end of a sentence.** "You know", "right", "okay", "yeah", "do you know what I mean". Among young Londoners, "innit" and "you get me" are rising. Tags depend on age and region only, never on ethnicity.
- **Echoing.** In an engaged conversation people pick up and re-use parts of each other's words.
- **Regional words and grammar** (from a recent dialect survey):
  - A bread roll is a "barm" in the North West (Manchester to Liverpool and western Lancashire), a "cob" around Nottinghamshire, a "bap" in Staffordshire, the West Midlands and North Wales, and a "batch" in Liverpool and Coventry.
  - Around Liverpool an ice lolly can be a "lolly ice".
  - The evening meal is "tea" in the North West, North East and Yorkshire, and "dinner" in the South East and London. Some people say both.
  - "Yous" or "youse" for plural "you" is common in the North East (Newcastle, Teesside), Liverpool and Scotland, less so in Manchester, and rare in York, Leeds and Sheffield.
  - "Give it me" is normal in the North West and West Midlands and widely accepted in Sheffield and York; it fades south of Birmingham, Coventry and Leicester.
  - "You was" is widely used, historically Northern and now found as far south as London.
- **Everyday British words** to draw on where they fit, without assigning them to regions: knackered or shattered, chuffed or made up, skint or brassic, mardy or stroppy, mum or mam, mate or pal, settee, sofa or couch.

The group (session S30). Persona cards, including the webcam photo each person was rated on:

P159 (Sana; transcript label: Sana):
- first name: Sana
- age: 26
- lives in: Luton, East of England
- occupation: Currently out of work and job-hunting. Until about five months ago she was a nursery practitioner at a small private day nursery in Luton that closed down. She's applying for nursery, school and care assistant roles and does online research studies for a bit of extra money in the meantime.
- education detail: GCSEs at a secondary school in Luton, then a Level 2 and later a Level 3 Diploma in Early Years Education and Childcare at college. She started a part-time access course once but dropped it when she started working full time.
- household: Rents a two-bedroom terraced house in the Bury Park area with her partner Imran, 29, a delivery driver. They had a religious nikah two years ago but haven't done a civil registration yet. It's 'on the list'. No children yet. Her parents and younger siblings live about ten minutes' walk away, and she's round there most days.
- cultural background: Born in Mirpur, Azad Kashmir, Pakistan. She moved to Luton with her mum and brother at nine to join her dad, who already worked here. She grew up between Pahari/Punjabi at home and English at school, and speaks Urdu well enough for dramas and relatives on the phone. She's a practising Muslim in an everyday way: she prays when she can, fasts in Ramadan and goes to the mosque for Eid and the odd talk with her mum. She feels Lutonian more than anything, but gets homesick for a Pakistan she only half remembers.
- professional persona: Warm and patient with small children, and very attuned to when a child is upset. She takes it to heart when things go wrong, and still worries about whether the kids from the old nursery settled in their new places. At work she was dependable without being fussy. She did her observations and paperwork, just sometimes at the last minute. She doesn't push herself forward in meetings, but parents liked her because she remembered little details about their kids.
- sports persona: Not sporty. She walks a lot, round Wardown Park or to her mum's, and did a women-only swimming session for a while before it got moved to an awkward time. She'll half-watch cricket when Pakistan are playing because her dad and Imran have it on loud.
- arts persona: Watches Pakistani dramas on YouTube with her mum and gets properly invested, crying at the sad ones. She likes some Netflix stuff too, mainly reality and the odd Korean drama. She used to do mehndi designs for cousins and friends before weddings and is still asked to. She's quite good at it.
- travel persona: Has been back to Pakistan twice since moving, most recently for a cousin's wedding three years ago. She gets anxious about flying and about the whole trip going smoothly. She'd love to do Umrah with her mum one day and dreams vaguely of Istanbul. Otherwise trips are days out: Milton Keynes shopping, Southend, or London with friends.
- culinary persona: Cooks most evenings, mostly the dishes her mum taught her: chicken karahi, daal, aloo gobi and rotis, though she admits her rotis still aren't round. She tries TikTok recipes now and then, and pasta bakes have become a weeknight thing. She has a sweet tooth for gulab jamun and Krispy Kremes. Saturday nights are often a takeaway, burgers or peri-peri.
- hobbies and interests: Mehndi designs for family and friends' weddings, Pakistani and Korean dramas, Walking in Wardown Park, Following cooking and home organising accounts on TikTok and Instagram, Rearranging and decorating the house on a tight budget, Long phone calls with her best friend from college
- skills: Early years care, including safeguarding awareness and paediatric first aid (certificate needs renewing), Calming upset or anxious children, Henna/mehndi application, Fluent English and Pahari/Punjabi, good spoken Urdu, Home cooking for big family gatherings, Translating letters and appointments for older relatives
- career goals: Short term, she wants a stable nursery or school teaching-assistant job close to home, ideally with regular hours. Longer term she has thought about training as a SEN teaching assistant or even an early years teacher, but worries she isn't clever enough for a degree. She also likes the idea of running her own small childminding setup from home once they have a bigger place.
- voice: Soft, friendly and fairly quick when she's comfortable, slower and more careful at first. She has a south-east English accent with Luton features, and her vowels slip a bit more towards family speech when she's excited or talking about home. She uses 'erm' a lot, and 'like' and 'kind of' as hedges: 'it was kind of stressful, like, not gonna lie'. She ends thoughts with 'you know?' or 'yeah'. She says 'dinner' for the evening meal and 'shattered' when tired. She apologises quickly: 'sorry, what was the question again?' Silence makes her uneasy, so she'll fill it with a nervous laugh or 'I don't know if that makes sense'. She often echoes the interviewer's words before answering.
- typing: Mostly lowercase, sometimes capitalising the first word if her phone does it. Light punctuation, often no full stop at the end. Apostrophes come and go depending on autocorrect ('dont', 'it's'). She uses 'tbh', 'idk' and 'lol' sparingly, plus a lot of 'and' joining clauses. Answers are short unless a question touches something she cares about, then she writes more than needed.
- with strangers: Polite and a bit shy at first. She smiles a lot and checks she's doing it right. Once she relaxes she's chatty and warm and shares more than she intended, then worries afterwards that she overshared. She's sensitive to tone, so a brisk interviewer makes her quieter.
- small things: Her mum rang three times this morning about whether she's coming for dinner, The bus into town being late again, A mehndi booking she's got for a cousin's friend's wedding next month, Trying a new air fryer recipe that went wrong, Imran's long shifts and the van being in the garage, A drama she's watching where the mother-in-law is 'pure evil'
- deeper things: She feels guilty and anxious about being out of work and checks job sites every day, Worries about her dad's health since his diabetes got worse, Some relatives have opinions about her and Imran not having the civil registration done yet, and it bothers her more than she lets on, Feels caught between not fully belonging in Pakistan and sometimes not feeling fully accepted here, Would like children soon but is scared about money and housing, She still thinks about one little boy at the old nursery who had a hard home life and wonders if he's okay
- webcam photo: A laptop webcam shot from slightly below eye level, with her centred and close to the camera, cutting off at mid-chest. Soft daylight comes from a window off to her left, and the right side of her face is a little shadowed. She has a round face, warm brown skin and dark brown eyes. Her smile is slightly self-conscious and she's looking just above the lens. She wears a loosely draped dusky-pink jersey hijab with a little dark hair visible at the front, over a grey hoodie. No glasses, small gold stud earrings partly hidden. Behind her is a magnolia-painted wall with a framed Arabic calligraphy print in gold and black, a white IKEA-style shelf holding a few candles, a small plant and a stack of folded laundry, and the edge of a grey fabric sofa with a cream throw over its arm.

P160 (Darren; transcript label: Darren):
- first name: Darren
- age: 45
- lives in: King's Lynn, East of England
- occupation: Machine operator and line setter at a frozen vegetable processing plant on an industrial estate on the edge of town. He runs and adjusts the blanching and packing lines and works four-on, four-off twelve-hour shifts, plus regular overtime in pea and bean season, which usually takes him past 50 hours a week.
- education detail: Left a secondary school in King's Lynn at 16 with a handful of GCSEs, a B in Design and Technology and a C in Maths. He later did an NVQ Level 2 in Performing Manufacturing Operations through work. He also holds a counterbalance forklift licence and has done food hygiene and manual handling certificates, which he renews when asked.
- household: Lives alone in a rented two-bed terraced house in the Gaywood area. He has never married. There was a long relationship in his late twenties and early thirties that ended without much drama. No children and no pets. His mum lives about ten minutes away in a bungalow, and he does her garden and her odd jobs.
- cultural background: White British, Norfolk born and raised. His dad worked at the Campbell's soup factory before it closed, and his mum did shop work. He has no religion and doesn't think about it much. Christenings and funerals are 'just what you turn up for'. His values are fairly traditional working-town ones: pay your way, don't owe anyone, do the job properly.
- professional persona: Reliable, exact and quietly proud of keeping his line running with the least downtime on his shift. He's the one who logs every fault properly and won't sign off a changeover until the seals are right. He has no patience for agency staff who stand about, or for managers who 'come down from the office with a clipboard and no idea'. He says so to their faces, which has cost him a team leader role more than once. He has never lied on a timesheet or fiddled a temperature check, and people know it.
- sports persona: Goes to watch the King's Lynn Stars speedway on Wednesday nights when his shifts allow, and has done since he was a boy with his dad. He follows Norwich City on the radio and the telly but won't pay for a season ticket at the prices they charge now. He doesn't play anything himself these days. He walks a fair bit when he's fishing and reckons twelve hours on his feet is enough exercise.
- arts persona: Not really interested. He watches the odd action film or a documentary about engineering or the war, and listens to whatever's on Heart or KL.FM in the van. He saw Status Quo once at Sandringham and enjoyed it. He'd turn down a gallery or theatre without thinking twice and wouldn't pretend otherwise.
- travel persona: Rarely goes abroad. He's done Tenerife twice with mates in his thirties and found it 'too hot and too many people'. These days a break is a few days in a cheap static caravan at Hunstanton or Mundesley with his fishing gear, or a day out to the Lake District once a year on his own. He has a passport but it's close to running out and he's not fussed.
- culinary persona: Plain and practical. He batch-cooks chilli or a stew on his days off and portions it into tubs for the shift days. He calls the evening meal his dinner. He likes a proper fry-up on his first day off, fish and chips from the same chippy on a Friday, and Sunday dinner at his mum's when his rota lines up. He eats a lot of the factory's own frozen veg, half as a joke and half because it's good. He doesn't 'do' foreign food much beyond a curry.
- hobbies and interests: Coarse fishing on the Relief Channel and the Great Ouse, mostly bream and pike in winter, Watching King's Lynn Stars speedway, Doing his own servicing on his old Ford Transit Connect, Keeping his mum's garden tidy, Watching car restoration programmes, The odd pint at a quiet pub with one or two old school mates
- skills: Setting up and fault-finding on packing and blanching machinery, Forklift driving, Basic vehicle maintenance: brakes, oil, filters, bulbs, Basic DIY: tiling, fitting shelves, putting in a new tap, Keeping accurate records and checklists, Tying rigs and making up his own pike traces
- career goals: Not ambitious in the climbing sense. He'd take a maintenance technician role if the company paid for the electrical side of the training, because it's better money and fewer idiots to deal with. Mostly he wants to keep working steady, save enough to buy a small place of his own before he's fifty, and not have to rely on anyone.
- voice: Low, steady and fairly flat Norfolk accent, not broad but clearly local, with the odd 'that' instead of 'it' ('that was chucking it down'). Short sentences. He says 'er' rather than 'erm' when he's thinking, and 'sort of' now and then. He calls people 'mate' or 'boy' without thinking. He answers the question asked and stops. If there's a silence he leaves it rather than filling it, and if a question seems pointless he'll say 'not sure what you're after there, to be honest'. He gets a bit more talkative on fishing or machinery. He rarely says 'sorry' except to ask someone to repeat themselves.
- typing: Short and mostly correct. A capital at the start, usually a full stop at the end, few commas. He keeps apostrophes in 'don't' and 'it's' most of the time. No abbreviations beyond 'ok' and the odd 'n/a'. He won't write more than a line or two unless he has a point to make, and then it can come out blunt.
- with strangers: Guarded and a bit dry at first, with no small talk for its own sake. He comes across as straightforward and honest but not warm, and can seem curt or argumentative if he thinks something's daft. He's respectful if the other person is plain-speaking too. He won't flatter anyone and doesn't expect to be flattered.
- small things: Being knackered after a run of night shifts, The speedway result from Wednesday, What he caught at the weekend, or more often what he didn't, The price of diesel and his van's MOT, Agency lads not turning up at work, Doing his mum's hedge, The Friday chippy
- deeper things: Watching his dad struggle after the factory closed, and deciding then never to be caught out without savings, The relationship that ended because she wanted to move to Cambridge and he didn't. He doesn't regret it but thinks about it, Worry about what happens with his mum as she gets older, since he's the only one nearby, Knowing he rubs people up the wrong way and not really wanting to change it, Wanting a house in his own name and not to be renting at sixty
- webcam photo: A laptop webcam shot from slightly below. The laptop sits on a kitchen table, so the camera looks up a little at his chin. The main light is a window to his left, leaving one side of his face brighter and the other in mild shadow, with a ceiling light on as well. He has a broad, weathered face with a ruddy tinge across the cheeks and nose, light stubble, and short dark-blond hair clipped close at the sides and thinning on top. No glasses. His expression is neutral and slightly impatient, mouth closed, eyes looking just off the screen. He wears a navy hooded sweatshirt over a grey T-shirt. Behind him is a magnolia wall with a wall calendar from a local tackle shop, its days marked in biro, and a white plug-in clock. To one side there's the edge of a tall fridge-freezer with a takeaway menu held on by a magnet, and on the worktop next to it a kettle, a tea caddy and a folded hi-vis vest.

P161 (Abena; transcript label: Abena):
- first name: Abena
- age: 41
- lives in: Crawley, South East England
- occupation: Pharmacy technician at a community pharmacy in Crawley town centre, 24 hours a week over three days (Monday, Wednesday, Friday). - arts persona: Likes music more than anything: highlife and older Ghanaian gospel from her mum's house, plus Afrobeats, Burna Boy and some R&B from when she was in her twenties. - travel persona: Goes back to Ghana roughly every two or three years, usually over Christmas when flights are expensive, which annoys her every time. Took the kids to Accra and Kumasi last time. Otherwise travel is cheap and last minute: a long weekend in Bournemouth, a coach day trip to Brighton. Lives ten minutes from Gatwick and has never once flown anywhere on impulse, which she finds funny. Would like to do Dubai or Lisbon 'one day' but hasn't planned anything.
- culinary persona: Cooks Ghanaian food at weekends in big batches: light soup, jollof, groundnut soup, kontomire stew, waakye when she has the time. Buys ingredients from an African grocer in Crawley or stocks up when she's in Croydon. Weekday dinner is often fast and unglamorous: pasta, fish fingers, something from the freezer, chips from the place round the corner on Fridays. Calls the evening meal dinner. Not a baker. Kwame complains her jollof is too spicy and she doesn't change it.
- hobbies and interests: Ghanaian and gospel music, plus Afrobeats, Watching Nollywood/Ghanaian films and Netflix crime dramas, Long phone calls with her sister in Manchester and her mum in Kumasi, Church, fairly regularly, Hair: does her own braids and sometimes Efua's, Following Ghana in international football, Browsing Vinted and TK Maxx, buys more than she needs
- skills: Dispensing and checking prescriptions accurately under time pressure, Knowledge of common medications, interactions and dosing, Dealing firmly with difficult customers and surgery staff, Bilingual in English and Twi, Cooking Ghanaian dishes in large quantities, Braiding hair, Staying calm in a crisis, whether that's a child's injury or a shop emergency
- career goals: Vague more than ambitious. She has thought about the accuracy checking technician qualification, or moving into a hospital pharmacy job for better pay and the NHS pension, but she hasn't filled in the application. She'd go up to more hours once Efua starts secondary school. She has no interest in management: 'I'm not chasing people about rotas all day.'
- voice: Clear, fairly direct, medium pace. She speaks English with a Ghanaian accent softened by twenty-odd years in London and Sussex, so some vowels and the rhythm are West African and the vocabulary is plainly South East English. She'll say 'dinner', 'knackered', 'mum'. She uses 'erm' when she's thinking, and sometimes 'you know' or 'yeah?' at the end of a point. She doesn't fill silences and is comfortable letting a pause sit. If a question seems pointless she'll say so, politely but plainly: 'Sorry, what do you mean by that exactly?' She gives short answers unless the topic interests her, and then she gets animated and talks over herself a bit. She laughs easily at things she finds absurd but isn't trying to be liked.
- typing: Quick and a bit careless. Mostly lowercase, with a capital at the start only sometimes. She often skips apostrophes ('dont', 'im', 'its fine'). Light punctuation: commas run sentences together and there's rarely a full stop at the end. Occasional typos she doesn't correct ('teh', missing letters). Uses 'n/a' or 'dont know' rather than leaving fields blank. No emojis in forms.
- with strangers: Polite but not warm at first. She comes across as composed, a little guarded and slightly impatient if things are slow. She answers what's asked without padding and won't fake enthusiasm. If the person is straightforward she relaxes and can be quite funny and frank. She has no time for anything that feels condescending and will push back. She isn't nervous or apologetic and doesn't seem bothered about making a good impression.
- small things: Gatwick flight paths over the house and how you stop hearing them, Kwame being glued to his PlayStation, Efua's school wanting money for something again, Prescription mix-ups and customers who shout about waiting ten minutes, The price of plantain going up at the African shop, Rain, and her parking ticket in Crawley town centre, Church on Sunday running way over time, A Vinted bargain coat she got for twelve pounds
- deeper things: She and Daniel are still legally married because neither of them has sorted the paperwork, and partly because she hasn't decided how she feels about telling her mum it's final, Daniel cancelling his weekends with the kids, and how much that makes her angry on their behalf, Not finishing her biomedical science degree, and sometimes wondering where she'd be if she had, Her mum getting older in Kumasi and the question of who will look after her, Money being tight on part-time hours and never quite getting ahead, Feeling she holds grudges longer than she should, which her pastor has told her more than once
- webcam photo: Laptop webcam, slightly low angle looking up, framed from mid-chest up with a little space above her head. Evening light: a ceiling light overhead and a warm lamp off to the left of frame, so the left side of her face is brighter. The study, in order (from its published design): a short puzzle task done alone; first impressions of the others' webcam photos; then a series of three-minute, one-on-one video calls in rounds, each person meeting the others in their group; after each call a short survey.

Call shape (from the original study's numbers): a call is cut off by a three-minute timer. A typical call has about 30 turns (most between 20 and 39) and about 570 words in total (most between 440 and 682); half of all turns are 12 words or fewer, and a quarter are 24 or more. Short acknowledgements ("yeah", "mm") count as turns too. So aim for about 570 words in about 30 turns: alongside the quick back-and-forth, people often talk in longer stretches (explaining their job, telling a story), and those long turns carry much of the call.

Guide to British conversational English (use it for how people talk; it is a description of speech, not a script):
How British people talk in casual conversation. This is a paraphrase of published descriptions of spoken British English; sources are in SOURCES.md. Use these features lightly and only where they fit the person. Never use them as a caricature.

- **Fillers.** British speakers hesitate with "erm" and "er". Women and younger speakers lean towards "erm".
- **Hedges.** "Sort of" is everywhere and steady. "Kind of" is spreading, and younger speakers use it more.
- **Politeness words.** "Please", "thank you", "thanks" and "sorry" mostly mean what they say. "Sorry" also works as a repair word (to correct yourself, or to ask someone to repeat) and can be ironic.
- **Tags at the end of a sentence.** "You know", "right", "okay", "yeah", "do you know what I mean". Among young Londoners, "innit" and "you get me" are rising. Tags depend on age and region only, never on ethnicity.
- **Echoing.** In an engaged conversation people pick up and re-use parts of each other's words.
- **Regional words and grammar** (from a recent dialect survey):
  - A bread roll is a "barm" in the North West (Manchester to Liverpool and western Lancashire), a "cob" around Nottinghamshire, a "bap" in Staffordshire, the West Midlands and North Wales, and a "batch" in Liverpool and Coventry.
  - Around Liverpool an ice lolly can be a "lolly ice".
  - The evening meal is "tea" in the North West, North East and Yorkshire, and "dinner" in the South East and London. Some people say both.
  - "Yous" or "youse" for plural "you" is common in the North East (Newcastle, Teesside), Liverpool and Scotland, less so in Manchester, and rare in York, Leeds and Sheffield.
  - "Give it me" is normal in the North West and West Midlands and widely accepted in Sheffield and York; it fades south of Birmingham, Coventry and Leicester.
  - "You was" is widely used, historically Northern and now found as far south as London.
- **Everyday British words** to draw on where they fit, without assigning them to regions: knackered or shattered, chuffed or made up, skint or brassic, mardy or stroppy, mum or mam, mate or pal, settee, sofa or couch.

req.text:
You write transcripts of realistic video calls between strangers for a fully synthetic research dataset set in the UK. The study, in order (from its published design): a short puzzle task done alone; first impressions of the others' webcam photos; then a series of three-minute, one-on-one video calls in rounds, each person meeting the others in their group; after each call a short survey.

Call shape (from the original study's numbers): a call is cut off by a three-minute timer. A typical call has about 30 turns (most between 20 and 39) and about 570 words in total (most between 440 and 682); half of all turns are 12 words or fewer, and a quarter are 24 or more. Short acknowledgements ("yeah", "mm") count as turns too. So aim for about 570 words in about 30 turns: alongside the quick back-and-forth, people often talk in longer stretches (explaining their job, telling a story), and those long turns carry much of the call.

Guide to British conversational English (use it for how people talk; it is a description of speech, not a script):
How British people talk in casual conversation. This is a paraphrase of published descriptions of spoken British English; sources are in SOURCES.md. Use these features lightly and only where they fit the person. Never use them as a caricature.

- **Fillers.** British speakers hesitate with "erm" and "er". Women and younger speakers lean towards "erm".
- **Hedges.** "Sort of" is everywhere and steady. "Kind of" is spreading, and younger speakers use it more.
- **Politeness words.** "Please", "thank you", "thanks" and "sorry" mostly mean what they say. "Sorry" also works as a repair word (to correct yourself, or to ask someone to repeat) and can be ironic.
- **Tags at the end of a sentence.** "You know", "right", "okay", "yeah", "do you know what I mean". Among young Londoners, "innit" and "you get me" are rising. Tags depend on age and region only, never on ethnicity.
- **Echoing.** In an engaged conversation people pick up and re-use parts of each other's words.
- **Regional words and grammar** (from a recent dialect survey):
  - A bread roll is a "barm" in the North West (Manchester to Liverpool and western Lancashire), a "cob" around Nottinghamshire, a "bap" in Staffordshire, the West Midlands and North Wales, and a "batch" in Liverpool and Coventry.
  - Around Liverpool an ice lolly can be a "lolly ice".
  - The evening meal is "tea" in the North West, North East and Yorkshire, and "dinner" in the South East and London. Some people say both.
  - "Yous" or "youse" for plural "you" is common in the North East (Newcastle, Teesside), Liverpool and Scotland, less so in Manchester, and rare in York, Leeds and Sheffield.
  - "Give it me" is normal in the North West and West Midlands and widely accepted in Sheffield and York; it fades south of Birmingham, Coventry and Leicester.
  - "You was" is widely used, historically Northern and now found as far south as London.
- **Everyday British words** to draw on where they fit, without assigning them to regions: knackered or shattered, chuffed or made up, skint or brassic, mardy or stroppy, mum or mam, mate or pal, settee, sofa or couch.

P135 (Joanne; transcript label: Joanne):
- first name: Joanne
- age: 50
- lives in: Taunton, South West England
- occupation: Not currently in paid work. Formerly a registered veterinary nurse for over twenty years, most recently head nurse at a mixed small-animal practice. She left three years ago because of a long-standing lower back problem and the shift work. She now does a few unpaid hours a week helping at a local cat rescue.
- education detail: GCSEs and A-levels (Biology, English, Geography) at a comprehensive and sixth form in Somerset. Diploma in Veterinary Nursing, gained while working at a practice. She later did short CPD courses in practice management and anaesthesia monitoring.
- household: Lives with her husband Martin (53), a chartered building surveyor with a regional firm, in a four-bedroom 1990s detached house on the edge of Taunton. Their son Callum (22) works in Bristol and comes back most weekends. Their daughter Ellie (19) is at university in Cardiff and is home in the holidays. They also have an elderly Border terrier called Biscuit and two rescue cats.
- cultural background: White British, born in Bridgwater and raised in Somerset. Her dad worked at the Hinkley Point power station and her mum was a school dinner lady. She is Church of England and goes to the local parish church about once or twice a month, more around Christmas and Harvest. She is on the flower rota and helps with the church's coffee mornings. Her faith is comfortable rather than intense: she says she 'believes in something' and likes the community side of church.
- professional persona: Practical and warm, and very good with anxious owners. She was the nurse people asked for when their pet was being put to sleep. She was organised enough to run a rota but never a stickler. She misses the team banter and having a role, and she still slips into 'nurse mode' when friends ask about their dogs. Her confidence took a knock when she stopped working, and she sometimes undersells what she did.
- sports persona: Not sporty. Her back means she gave up the Zumba class she loved. She now does a gentle Pilates class on Tuesday mornings and walks Biscuit along the canal or up on the Quantocks when her back allows. She watches Somerset cricket on the telly with Martin and enjoys the atmosphere at the County Ground once a summer, mostly for the picnic and a glass of Pimm's.
- arts persona: Loves a good drama series and reality TV, especially Strictly and The Great British Bake Off, and gets properly emotional at the results. She sings in a community choir that does pop and musical theatre numbers. She reads book-club novels on her Kindle and enjoys a trip to the Brewhouse Theatre or a touring musical in Bristol.
- travel persona: Prefers holidays that are relaxing and sociable over adventurous ones. They go to Cornwall or Pembrokeshire most years with the dog, plus one sunny week abroad, often Crete, Majorca or the Algarve. She gets anxious about flying and airport queues but loves it once she is there. She has a long-held wish to see the Northern Lights.
- culinary persona: A confident everyday cook: roasts, shepherd's pie, curries from a jar 'jazzed up', traybakes for church and choir. She calls the evening meal 'dinner' mostly, sometimes 'tea' when it is something quick. She likes a Sunday carvery at the pub and a cream tea, and has firm views on jam going first. Her treat is a glass or two of rosé on a Friday.
- hobbies and interests: community choir, gentle Pilates, dog walking on the Quantocks and along the canal, volunteering at a cat rescue, church flower rota and coffee mornings, Strictly Come Dancing and Bake Off, book club, baking traybakes, pottering in the garden with pots and hanging baskets
- skills: animal handling and basic veterinary care, calming distressed people, organising rotas and small events, baking for crowds, remembering everyone's names and news, first aid
- career goals: Not looking to go back to full-time nursing because of her back. She would like a part-time, sitting-down role that still involves animals or people, perhaps reception or client care at a practice, or a paid coordinator role at the rescue. She worries a bit about whether she is 'too out of the loop' now.
- voice: Chatty, warm and quite quick once she relaxes. She laughs easily and often apologises for 'waffling'. There is a soft West Country lilt with slightly rounded r's, but nothing broad. She uses 'erm' a fair bit and says 'sort of' and 'you know' often, and occasionally uses 'proper' as an intensifier ('it was proper lovely'). She echoes the interviewer's words back while thinking ('what would I do with it... erm, honestly?'). She cannot leave a silence alone for long and fills it with 'sorry, does that make sense?' or a little laugh. If a question touches on worries, she gets more animated and talks faster.
- typing: Mostly sentence case but inconsistent. She often forgets the capital at the start and sometimes gets 'i' wrong. She uses apostrophes correctly most of the time, ends sentences with exclamation marks, and uses '...' between thoughts. She types a full sentence or two rather than single words, e.g. 'not really... i do worry about it sometimes though!' She uses 'x' only with friends, never in a form. No text-speak beyond the odd 'tbh'.
- with strangers: Friendly and open almost immediately. She asks the other person questions back, notices if they seem tired and says so kindly. She comes across as lovely and a bit of a talker. She can over-share slightly when nervous and then apologise for it. She wants people to like her and gets flustered if she thinks she has given a 'wrong' answer.
- small things: Biscuit being a grumpy old man about the rain, the traffic on the M5 by Bridgwater, choir doing an ABBA medley for the summer concert, her hanging baskets not taking this year, Ellie ringing only when she needs money, a new café opening in town, being shattered after Pilates, the cost of the weekly shop going up
- deeper things: grieving the loss of her career and feeling a bit invisible since stopping, chronic back pain and being on and off painkillers, which gets her down more than she lets on, worrying a lot about the children being away, especially Ellie living in a city, her mum's early signs of dementia and the guilt about not doing enough, anxiety that sometimes stops her sleeping, which she has never properly talked to her GP about, finding comfort in prayer at church even though she is not sure what she believes
- webcam photo: Head-and-shoulders shot from a laptop on a kitchen table, angled slightly upward so the ceiling and a pendant light are partly visible. Daylight comes from a window to her left, giving soft, even light with a slight shadow on the right side of her face. She is a white woman in her fifties with a round, friendly face, light freckles and fine lines around her eyes. She has a wide, open smile showing her teeth and her head is tilted slightly. Her hair is shoulder-length, highlighted dark-blonde with some grey at the roots, pushed behind one ear. She wears red-framed reading glasses pushed up on her head, a teal knitted cardigan over a white T-shirt, and small silver hoop earrings. Behind her is a cream Shaker-style kitchen with a wooden worktop, a kettle, a bread bin, and a calendar on the wall covered in handwritten notes. On the windowsill sit a basil plant and a framed photo of two young adults. The corner of a dog bed with a tartan blanket is visible at the bottom right.

P136 (Agnieszka; transcript label: Agnieszka):
- first name: Agnieszka
- age: 40
- lives in: Basingstoke, South East England
- occupation: Executive Assistant to the Chief Financial Officer at a mid-sized insurance company, managing his diary, board papers, travel and the finance team's office coordination
- education detail: Master's degree in Economics from the University of Rzeszów, Poland; later completed a CIPD-free but employer-funded Level 4 Diploma in Business Administration in the UK; English learned at school and polished through work

- cultural background: Born and raised in Rzeszów in south-east Poland and moved to the UK in 2007 at 23, first to Reading, where she worked in a hotel and then temped in offices. Roman Catholic and goes to the Polish Mass at a church in Basingstoke most Sundays. She takes Zosia to Polish Saturday school. She has lived here longer than she lived in Poland as an adult and feels 'from both places, a bit'. She took British citizenship in 2019, mostly for peace of mind after the Brexit vote, which unsettled her badly at the time.
- professional persona: Highly organised and quietly indispensable. She has worked for the same CFO for six years, knows how he likes his papers laid out and anticipates problems before they happen. Colleagues come to her to find out how things actually get done. She is diplomatic and warm but worries about mistakes more than she needs to, and will double-check a travel booking three times. She watched Iga Świątek's matches with real nerves and finds watching them stressful. Tomasz watches football and she half-watches with him.
- arts persona: Likes musicals and has seen Les Misérables in London twice. She cries easily at films and refuses to watch anything with an animal dying. She reads Polish crime novels on her Kindle and some British ones too, and listens to Polish radio and Radio 2 in the car.
- travel persona: Flies back to Poland twice a year, at summer and at Christmas or Easter, to see her parents and sister. Holidays are usually a week in a villa in Croatia or Portugal with another Polish family they're friends with. She gets anxious at airports, arrives very early, and keeps all the documents in one plastic folder.
