Week to week it's pasta bakes, chicken traybakes and soups. She bakes a good cheesecake (sernik) for work birthdays. She shops at Aldi and the Polish shop on the high street.
- hobbies and interests: Baking for friends and colleagues, Pilates, Lunchtime walks and weekend walks at the Basingstoke Canal or West Ham Park, Keeping the garden tidy, especially her hanging baskets, Polish crime fiction, Musicals, Organising family photo albums, which she still prints
- skills: Diary and travel management, Minute-taking and preparing board packs, Advanced Excel and PowerPoint formatting, Fluent Polish and English, Event and team-day organising, Calming down stressed colleagues, Budget tracking for household and office
- career goals: Happy where she is but would like to step up to Office Manager or Head of Executive Support if a role opens, ideally without the long hours. Job security matters more to her than a big title, and she wants to be home in time for Zosia's evenings.
- voice: Fluent, careful and polite, with a light Polish accent that shows mostly in her vowels and the occasional dropped 'the' when she's speaking quickly. Moderate pace that speeds up when she's nervous or talking about something she cares about. She uses 'erm' and 'sort of' naturally after years in British offices, says 'sorry' a lot, both as an apology and to correct herself ('it was Tuesday, sorry, Wednesday'), and ends things with 'you know?' or 'yeah?'. She might say 'I was shattered' or 'I was so chuffed'. She tends to fill silences with an apologetic laugh or a 'sorry, is that what you meant?' rather than leaving a gap.
- typing: Proper capitals and full stops, apostrophes almost always correct, and she rarely uses abbreviations other than 'e.g.' and 'etc.'. Answers are complete sentences, sometimes slightly longer than needed. There's an occasional small article slip ('I work in office in town') or a Polish-style comma before 'that'. She rereads before submitting.
- with strangers: Warm, friendly and slightly anxious to get things right. She asks whether her answers are useful, apologises for rambling, and opens up quickly if the other person seems kind. She is very polite and never interrupts.
- small things: Zosia's swimming lessons on Thursdays, The traffic on the Ringway in the morning, Her CFO's terrible handwriting, Baking a cheesecake for a colleague's leaving do, The Polish shop running out of good bread, Her hanging baskets not surviving the heatwave, Booking flights to Rzeszów before the prices go up
- deeper things: She worries constantly about her parents getting older and her being a two-hour flight away, The Brexit vote made her feel unwelcome for a while and she still remembers a comment from a neighbour, She and Tomasz tried for a second child for several years and it didn't happen, Her faith helps her when she gets anxious, and she prays more than she lets on, She sometimes feels she has never quite belonged fully in either country
- webcam photo: Laptop webcam at roughly eye level, slightly off-centre, framing her from mid-chest up. Soft daylight from a window to her left lights one side of her face, with a warm ceiling light on behind. She has a round, fair face with light freckles, blue-grey eyes and a polite, slightly self-conscious smile. Her shoulder-length dark blonde hair is tucked behind one ear, and she wears small gold stud earrings and a thin gold chain with a small cross. No glasses. She is wearing a navy round-neck knit jumper. Behind her is a white-painted wall in a small spare room used as an office: a framed print of Kraków's market square, a wall calendar with handwritten entries, a pinboard with a child's drawing and a school letter pinned to it, and the edge of a white bookshelf holding ring binders, a few paperbacks and a small potted orchid.

P137 (Annelies; transcript label: Annelies):
- first name: Annelies
- age: 56
- lives in: Sheffield, Yorkshire and The Humber
- occupation: Senior executive assistant to the head of a faculty at a Sheffield university. She manages the diary, committee papers and correspondence, and coordinates two junior administrators. Full-time, roughly 37 to 40 hours a week, mostly on campus with one day working from home.
- education detail: Completed a Dutch higher vocational diploma (HBO) in secretarial and management support in Utrecht. Later took a part-time CIPD Level 3 certificate in HR support and several in-house project coordination courses after moving to the UK.
- household: Lives with her husband Graham, 58, a recently semi-retired secondary school geography teacher, in a stone-built Victorian semi in Nether Edge. Their two adult children have left home: a son in Leeds and a daughter in Bristol. There is an elderly tabby cat called Maarten.
- cultural background: Born and raised in Amersfoort in the Netherlands, in a Protestant family. She met Graham on a walking holiday in the Lake District in her early twenties and moved to Sheffield at 25. She has lived in England for over thirty years and speaks fluent, idiomatic English. She still keeps Dutch habits like cycling when the hills allow, eating hagelslag on toast and phoning her sister in Utrecht every Sunday. She attends a local Anglican parish church most Sundays, quietly rather than as a committee type. Her faith is real but private.
- professional persona: Very trusted and very discreet. She is the person who knows where everything is and never gossips about what crosses her desk. She is efficient without being rigid, though she sometimes leaves things later than she'd like and then worries about them. She dislikes office politics and avoids open conflict, but she will say plainly when something is unfair. Colleagues describe her as calm, though inside she often isn't.
- sports persona: Not sporty in a competitive sense. She walks in the Peak District with Graham most weekends, swims lengths at a local leisure centre early on a Wednesday because it's quiet, and cycles to the shops when the weather is decent. She half-follows Dutch football during tournaments, mainly out of loyalty.
- arts persona: A keen reader of literary fiction and translated novels, and she belongs to a small book group of five women that meets monthly. She visits the Millennium Gallery and the Hepworth Wakefield, and loves Dutch Golden Age paintings and quiet landscape art. She does watercolour sketches in a notebook on walks but would never call herself an artist. She listens to Radio 3 and choral music, and cries easily at films and concerts.
- travel persona: Goes back to the Netherlands at least twice a year by the Hull–Rotterdam ferry, because she gets very anxious about flying. She researches everything in advance and books accommodation early to avoid uncertainty.
- culinary persona: Cooks a sensible weekday tea, often soup, stamppot in winter, or a vegetable curry from a well-thumbed cookbook. She bakes appeltaart for church events and birthdays. She enjoys trying new recipes from library cookbooks but gets flustered cooking for big groups. She drinks a lot of tea and a little white wine at weekends.
- hobbies and interests: hill walking in the Peak District, monthly book group, watercolour sketching in a field notebook, baking, especially Dutch apple cake, birdwatching from the kitchen window and at RSPB reserves, choral music and Radio 3, visiting small galleries, allotment-style vegetable growing in the back garden
- skills: complex diary and meeting management, minute-taking and drafting formal correspondence, fluent Dutch and good German, Excel and university finance systems, confidential handling of HR matters, baking, map reading and route planning
- career goals: No great ambition to climb further. She would like to stay in her role until about 62, possibly moving to four days a week in the next couple of years, then retire somewhere near the hills. Her main wish is to keep the job manageable and her team happy, and to leave things in good order for whoever follows her.
- voice: Softly spoken, measured and a little slow to start, as though she is checking the words before she says them. Her English is near-native with a faint Dutch edge: slightly clipped consonants, and the occasional sentence structure that sounds just a touch formal. Thirty years in Sheffield show lightly. She calls the evening meal 'tea', says 'love' to shop assistants, and uses 'knackered' and 'chuffed' naturally. She uses 'erm' when she hesitates and 'sort of' as a hedge. She apologises quickly ('sorry, I mean...') when she corrects herself. She doesn't fill silences herself. She waits, then gives a careful, honest answer, sometimes with a small nervous laugh. If a question touches on something emotional, her voice can go a bit tight.

Annelies: A robin, lately. He comes every morning about half seven, while I'm having my tea. Sorry, my cup of tea, I mean, not my meal. I've been in Yorkshire too long.
Joanne: No, I'm the same, I say tea and dinner and nobody knows what I'm on about. Where are you from originally?
Annelies: The Netherlands. Amersfoort. More than thirty years ago now.
Joanne: Gosh. Do you still have family over there?
Annelies: My sister. And my mother. She's in the early stages of dementia, erm, so I go over when I can. It's not easy, being on the ferry every time something happens.
Joanne: Oh, love. My mum's starting with it too. Little things, you know, she put the kettle in the fridge last month and laughed it off, but I could see she was frightened. And I'm only forty minutes away and I still feel like I'm not doing enough. So goodness knows how you manage it from another country.
Annelies: Badly, some weeks. I feel guilty a lot. My sister does most of it.
Joanne: I don't think you should feel guilty. You're ringing, you're going over. That's not nothing. Sorry, I don't mean to tell you how to feel.
Annelies: No, it's kind. Thank you. It's nice to hear it from someone who knows.
Joanne: Do you go to church at all? Sorry, that's a nosy one. It's just it helps me, sort of, sitting there.
Annelies: Yes, most Sundays. I don't say much about it. But I think it helps me too.
Joanne: Same. I'm on the flower rota, which is mostly an excuse for coffee and gossip, if I'm honest.
Annelies: I bake for ours. A Dutch apple cake. It disappears very quickly.
Joanne: Oh, I'd love that recipe! I do traybakes. Lemon drizzle, millionaire's shortbread. I take them to choir and all.
Annelies: You sing?
Joanne: Community choir. Pop, musicals. Nothing like the proper stuff.
Annelies: I listen to choral music on Radio 3. I cry at it, which is embarrassing.
Joanne: Oh, I cry at Strictly results, so you're doing better than me!
Annelies: I think we're nearly finished. It went fast.
Joanne: It did. You take care of yourself, won't you?

=== CALL C0288 ===
Agnieszka: Hello! Hi, can you hear me okay?
Shahida: Yes. I thought last one was finished, then another one comes.
Agnieszka: Oh, sorry! I think it's four rounds. I'm Agnieszka, I'm in Basingstoke.
Shahida: Shahida. Ilford.
Agnieszka: Nice to meet you. How has it been, the calls?
Shahida: Ok. Everybody very polite. The mechanic, he doesn't eat properly.
Agnieszka: Oh, Lee! He helped me with my car, actually. A noise in the front. He said it's a drop link, I wrote it down.
Shahida: Good. Free advice, that's the best kind.
Agnieszka: Exactly! Normally the garage, they charge you just to look.
Shahida: Everything costs now. You do your shopping where?
Agnieszka: Aldi, mostly. And there is Polish shop on the high street, for bread, sausage, things from home. But they keep running out of the good bread, it's so annoying.
Shahida: New Lidl near me, very cheap. Fruit, veg, good price. Meat I don't buy there, only from my butcher.
Agnieszka: Yes, I understand, you have your butcher you trust. My mum is the same in Rzeszów, thirty years the same man.
Shahida: Correct. Same man, he knows me, he doesn't give me rubbish.
Agnieszka: Do you cook every day?
Shahida: Every day. Roti fresh. Daal, karahi. My grandchildren, two days a week, I feed them.
Agnieszka: Oh, that's lovely. I have a daughter, Zosia, she's nine. I cook most evenings, but simple. Pasta bake, soup. When my mum visits, we make pierogi together, hundreds, and I freeze them.
Shahida: Pierogi, what is it?
Agnieszka: Sort of dumplings. Dough, and inside potato and cheese, or cabbage, or meat. You boil them, then fry with onion.
Shahida: Like samosa, but boiled. Ok. Freezing is clever. I also freeze, parathas, keema, ready for the week.
Agnieszka: Yes! Then on a busy day, you have something proper, you know?
Shahida: Better than takeaway. You live in house or flat?
Agnieszka: House, a semi. We bought in 2015, on a newer estate. Still mortgage, of course.
Shahida: We finished ours long time ago. Own outright. My husband wanted new car, I said no, house first.
Agnieszka: That's very wise. That's what I want also, security. More than anything, really, after Brexit and everything. Sorry, that's a big topic.
Shahida: Hm. People say things. You have your house, your job, your passport. Then they can say what they like.
Agnieszka: Yes. That's true. I got citizenship in 2019, for that reason. Peace of mind.
Shahida: Good. Paper is important. That's it.
Agnieszka: I bake also, cheesecake, for work. Do you bake?
Shahida: No. Diabetes. Doctor says no sugar, so I don't make sweet things now. Only for Eid.
Agnieszka: Oh, sorry. Only for Eid is fair, I think.
Shahida: Acha. Time is finishing, I think.

=== CALL C0289 ===
Joanne: Hiya! Oh, finally, it's you! I've been hoping I'd get you. Can you hear me alright?
Agnieszka: Yes! Hello! I was hoping also, honestly. I saw your photo at the beginning and I thought, she looks so friendly.

Agnieszka: Agnieszka, Basingstoke. Lee said you were nice, actually. He told me about his drop links.
Joanne: Ha! Did he fix your car over the video? He's a good lad, that one, bit grumpy about his boss, mind.
Agnieszka: He diagnosed it in thirty seconds. I wrote it down for my husband.
Joanne: Oh, that's brilliant. So what do you do, then? I'm guessing something organised, with that calendar behind you.

Joanne: Oh, I'd be the same. I used to do the rota at the practice, I was head vet nurse before my back went, and I'd lie awake thinking, have I put two people on the Saturday? Erm, I'm not working now, three years, I just help at a cat rescue. And I keep thinking about a little part-time job, reception or something, but then I think, oh, they won't want me, I'm out of the loop. Sorry, I've said that to about four people today!
Agnieszka: But you should go for it! You know animals, you know people. And reception, honestly, it's mostly being calm when someone is panicking. That's half my job too.
Joanne: That's what Shahida said! Well, sort of, she was a bit sterner about it.
Agnieszka: Ha, yes, she's very direct. I liked her.
Joanne: Oh, me too, in the end. Have you got children?
Agnieszka: One, Zosia, she's nine. Swimming Thursdays, Polish school Saturdays.
Joanne: Oh, busy girl. Mine are grown up now, twenty-two and nineteen. Ellie's at uni in Cardiff and I worry about her constantly, living in a city, walking home at night, all that. She rings when she wants money and I'm just relieved she's alive!
Agnieszka: I think I will be the same. Already I worry and she's only nine.
Joanne: Oh, it doesn't stop, love. Do you do anything for yourself?
Agnieszka: Pilates, Tuesday evenings, with a friend from work. And walking at lunchtime.
Joanne: No! I do Pilates on a Tuesday! Mornings, though. I'm always shattered after.

Helen: Hello. Yes, I think this is the last. I'm Helen.

req.text:
You write transcripts of realistic video calls between strangers for a fully synthetic research dataset set in the UK. The study, in order (from its published design): a short puzzle task done alone; first impressions of the others' webcam photos; then a series of three-minute, one-on-one video calls in rounds, each person meeting the others in their group; after each call a short survey.

Call shape (from the original study's numbers): a call is cut off by a three-minute timer. A typical call has about 30 turns (most between 20 and 39) and about 570 words in total (most between 440 and 682); half of all turns are 12 words or fewer, and a quarter are 24 or more. Short acknowledgements ("yeah", "mm") count as turns too. So aim for about 570 words in about 30 turns: alongside the quick back-and-forth, people often talk in longer stretches (explaining their job, telling a story), and those long turns carry much of the call.

Guide to British conversational English (use it for how people talk; it is a description of speech, not a script):
How British people talk in casual conversation. This is a paraphrase of published descriptions of spoken British English; sources are in SOURCES.md. Use these features lightly and only where they fit the person. Never use them as a caricature.

- **Fillers.** British speakers hesitate with "erm" and "er". Women and younger speakers lean towards "erm".
- **Hedges.** "Sort of" is everywhere and steady. "Kind of" is spreading, and younger speakers use it more.
- **Politeness words.** "Please", "thank you", "thanks" and "sorry" mostly mean what they say. "Sorry" also works as a repair word (to correct yourself, or to ask someone to repeat) and can be ironic.
- **Tags at the end of a sentence.** "You know", "right", "okay", "yeah", "do you know what I mean". Among young Londoners, "innit" and "you get me" are rising. Tags depend on age and region only, never on ethnicity.
- **Echoing.** In an engaged conversation people pick up and re-use parts of each other's words.
- **Regional words and grammar** (from a recent dialect survey):
  - A bread roll is a "barm" in the North West (Manchester to Liverpool and western Lancashire), a "cob" around Nottinghamshire, a "bap" in Staffordshire, the West Midlands and North Wales, and a "batch" in Liverpool and Coventry.
  - Around Liverpool an ice lolly can be a "lolly ice".
  - The evening meal is "tea" in the North West, North East and Yorkshire, and "dinner" in the South East and London. Some people say both.
  - "Yous" or "youse" for plural "you" is common in the North East (Newcastle, Teesside), Liverpool and Scotland, less so in Manchester, and rare in York, Leeds and Sheffield.
  - "Give it me" is normal in the North West and West Midlands and widely accepted in Sheffield and York; it fades south of Birmingham, Coventry and Leicester.
  - "You was" is widely used, historically Northern and now found as far south as London.
- **Everyday British words** to draw on where they fit, without assigning them to regions: knackered or shattered, chuffed or made up, skint or brassic, mardy or stroppy, mum or mam, mate or pal, settee, sofa or couch.

The group (session S34). Persona cards, including the webcam photo each person was rated on:

P179 (Kerry; transcript label: Kerry):
- first name: Kerry
- age: 38
- lives in: Chatham, Kent, South East England
- occupation: Salon manager and co-owner of a small four-chair hair salon on a parade of shops in Walderslade; still does her own clients three days a week
- education detail: Left secondary school in Gillingham at 16 with a handful of GCSEs, did an NVQ Level 2 and 3 in Hairdressing at college in Rochester through an apprenticeship, and later did a short business and bookkeeping course at the local adult education centre when she took on the salon
- household: Lives with her husband Darren (41, a self-employed electrician) in a three-bed ex-council semi they bought about eight years ago, with their two Cockapoos, Bonnie and Alfie. No children.
- cultural background: White British, born and raised in the Medway towns, from a big, close family that all still lives within twenty minutes of each other. Her mum was a dinner lady and her dad drove for a builders' merchant. Sunday dinners at her mum's are still a fixture. Religion isn't something she talks about. She was christened, but she'd only go to church for weddings and funerals.
- professional persona: Warm, chatty and good at making clients feel looked after, which is why her column is always booked. She took over managing the salon when the previous owner retired and went half-and-half on it with a friend from college. She is better with people than with spreadsheets, and does the rota, ordering and staff stuff on instinct rather than with systems. She worries more than she lets on about bills and whether the juniors are happy.
- sports persona: Not sporty herself, but she goes to a Zumba class at the community centre on Tuesday nights with her sister. She'll watch the football when England are in a tournament, mostly for the atmosphere down the pub. She walks the dogs at Capstone Farm Country Park most mornings before work.
- arts persona: Loves a big night out at a musical. She has seen Mamma Mia! three times and goes up to the West End for a show for birthdays. Telly is reality and comfort viewing: Strictly, Love Island, Gogglebox, and anything with a murder in it on a Sunday night. Not one for galleries or anything she'd call 'arty'.
- travel persona: A creature of habit. It's an all-inclusive week in Tenerife or Lanzarote most summers with Darren, sometimes with her sister's family too, plus a caravan weekend in Camber Sands or at a holiday park in Norfolk. She likes knowing where everything is and gets a bit anxious about flights and transfers. She doesn't fancy anywhere 'too different'.
- culinary persona: A plain, generous home cook: spag bol, chicken fajitas, roasts, a big shepherd's pie. She calls the evening meal 'dinner'. Friday is takeaway night, usually Chinese or a kebab from the place on the high street. She's not adventurous with food and will order the same thing every time at Nando's. She does a mean Victoria sponge for birthdays at the salon.
- hobbies and interests: Walking the dogs at Capstone Park, Zumba with her sister on Tuesdays, Watching Strictly and Love Island and messaging the family group chat about it, Nights out with the girls, usually cocktails in Rochester, Sorting and decorating the house, mainly scrolling home accounts on Instagram and doing bits from B&M and Dunelm, Following a couple of hair and colour educators online
- skills: Cutting, colouring and balayage, Putting nervous people at ease, Running a staff rota and keeping a small team happy, Basic bookkeeping and stock ordering, Remembering everyone's names, kids and holiday plans, Baking cakes for occasions
- career goals: Wants to keep the salon steady and maybe take on another apprentice, and eventually do fewer days on the floor herself. She has vaguely thought about a second site, but the risk makes her nervous. Mostly she wants to stop worrying about money every January.
- voice: Friendly, quick and a bit breathless when she gets going. She has a light Kent/Medway accent: dropped t's in words like 'bottle' and 'a lot of', and some glottal stops, but nothing exaggerated. She uses 'erm' a fair amount when she's thinking, plus 'sort of' and 'to be fair' as softeners. She ends points with 'you know?' or 'd'you know what I mean?'. She says 'knackered', 'mate' and 'mum'. She laughs easily and often echoes the interviewer's words back ('Oh, routine, yeah, I love a routine'). She hates silence and will fill a pause with a little story or an apologetic 'sorry, I'm rambling now'. She sometimes uses 'sorry?' to ask for a question to be repeated if the line's bad.
- typing: Types fast on her phone, mostly lower case with the odd capital at the start. She skips full stops at the end and uses lots of commas or '...' instead. Apostrophes come and go ('dont', 'im', but 'it's' sometimes). She uses 'lol' and the occasional 'x' out of habit, then deletes it. Spelling is generally fine, with occasional autocorrect slips. Answers are short unless she cares about the topic, then she writes a chatty paragraph.
- with strangers: Comes across as instantly warm and easy to talk to, the kind of person who asks you questions back. She's a bit eager to give the 'right' answer and may check whether she's doing it properly. She opens up quickly about everyday life but gets visibly flustered if something feels like a test or if she's put on the spot about things she doesn't know.
- small things: The dogs got into the bin again, Darren's van broke down and he's been knackered all week, Booked Tenerife for September, One of her regulars just had a baby, Prices at the wholesaler for colour have gone up again, Watching last night's Love Island, The parking on her road is a nightmare, Her mum's Sunday roast potatoes
- deeper things: She and Darren tried for a baby for a few years and it didn't happen; she's mostly made peace with it, but it still catches her at christenings, She gets anxious at night about the salon's finances and lies awake doing sums, She worries about her dad's health since his heart scare two years ago, She sometimes feels she missed out by not doing more at school and is a bit self-conscious around 'clever' people, She had a falling-out with her business partner last year that still feels fragile
- webcam photo: Laptop webcam shot from slightly below eye level, with the laptop resting on a kitchen table. Afternoon daylight comes from a window to her left, mixed with warm overhead spotlights, so the left side of her face is brighter. She's centred, framed from mid-chest up, leaning forward a little and smiling with her mouth slightly open as if mid-sentence. Her hair is shoulder-length and blonde with a soft balayage, darker at the roots, blow-dried with loose waves and tucked behind one ear. She wears neat, defined eyebrows, light makeup with mascara, and small gold hoop earrings. She has no glasses. She's in a black short-sleeved salon tunic with a small embroidered logo on the chest. Behind her is a grey gloss kitchen with a white quartz-effect worktop. On it sit a Nespresso machine, a wooden 'Home' sign, a fruit bowl with two bananas, and a stack of post. A wall calendar with dog photos hangs on the cupboard end. Through an open doorway on the right, part of a grey velvet sofa is visible with a beige dog curled up on a cushion.

P180 (Leanne; transcript label: Leanne):
- first name: Leanne
- age: 34
- lives in: Whittlesey, near Peterborough, East of England
- occupation: Director and office manager of her dad's small heating and plumbing firm (three engineers). She does the books, invoicing, scheduling and supplier orders, about 12 hours a week, mostly mornings.
- education detail: GCSEs at the local secondary school, then AAT Level 3 in accounting at Peterborough Regional College. She did not go to university and has never felt she missed out.
- household: Lives with her mum and dad, who have been married nearly 40 years, in their three-bed semi on the edge of town. She moved back at 29 after a long relationship ended and a rented flat in Peterborough fell through. She has the back bedroom and the box room as an office. There is also an elderly Staffordshire bull terrier called Bella.
- cultural background: White British, born and raised in the Fens. The family has been in and around Whittlesey and March for generations. She has no religion and the family isn't churchy, though they go to the carol service most years out of habit. Her outlook is solidly local and practical, and she is wary of anything that sounds pretentious.
- professional persona: Precise about money and dates but not a natural organiser beyond what the job needs. She is good at chasing late payers and doesn't mind being blunt with them. She gets stressed when the engineers change plans without telling her, and she will say so. She was made a director mainly for tax and succession reasons and finds the title slightly embarrassing.
- sports persona: Not sporty. She walks Bella round the same route along the river most evenings and watches the darts with her dad. She did a Couch to 5K once and stopped at week six when her knee twinged.
- arts persona: Watches the same handful of shows: crime dramas, Gogglebox, re-runs of Gavin & Stacey. She likes a few artists from her teens and won't really try new music. She has been to the theatre in Peterborough for a panto with her niece and that's about it.
- travel persona: Holidays mean a caravan at Hunstanton or Great Yarmouth with her mum, or occasionally a week in Tenerife at the same hotel as last time. Flying makes her anxious, and she gets to the airport very early.
- culinary persona: Plain home cooking. Her mum does most of the dinners and Leanne does a roast some Sundays. She likes a chippy tea on Friday, which she still calls dinner, and sticks to the same Chinese takeaway order. Spicy food is not for her.
- hobbies and interests: walking the dog on the same riverside loop, diamond painting kits, watching true crime documentaries, the Whittlesey Straw Bear festival (watches, doesn't take part), doing her niece's hair for school events, online shopping for home bits she then often returns
- skills: bookkeeping and VAT returns, Xero and Excel, chasing unpaid invoices, scheduling engineer jobs, knowing every regular customer's boiler history by heart
- career goals: Keep the business ticking over and take on more of the running of it when her dad retires in the next five or so years. She worries about whether she could actually manage the engineers. She would like to get her own place eventually but doesn't want to be far from her mum.
- voice: Quiet, fairly flat Fenland/East Anglian accent with some dropped t's. She speaks at a measured pace and gives short answers unless asked something she has an opinion on, then she can be quite sharp. She uses 'erm' a lot at the start of answers and 'sort of' as a hedge, with the occasional 'do you know what I mean'. Says 'yeah, no' and 'to be fair'. Silence makes her uncomfortable but she won't fill it chattily; she'll say 'I don't really know what else to say about that' or ask 'is that what you meant?'
- typing: Mostly lowercase, sometimes a capital at the start. Few full stops, commas used loosely. Apostrophes often missing ('dont', 'im'). Uses 'tbh' and 'idk', and sometimes ends with 'lol' when unsure. Answers are brief.
- with strangers: Reserved and a bit guarded at first, polite but not warm. She doesn't do much small talk and can come across as curt. She may visibly worry about whether she's answering 'right'. She warms up slightly if the other person is straightforward, and gets prickly if she thinks she's being patronised.
- small things: Bella's arthritis and her vet bills, the A605 roadworks, customers who don't pay on time, the weather making the river path muddy, what's on telly tonight, her mum's latest diet, Friday chippy tea
- deeper things: The end of an eight-year relationship at 29 and moving back home, which she's still a bit embarrassed about, Anxiety that flares up at night, especially about money and her parents getting older, Uncertainty about whether she wants kids and feeling time pressure from others, Feeling she's 'just doing the books' and not really a proper director, A fallout with her older sister over how much she helps their parents
- webcam photo: Laptop webcam at a slight upward angle, framing her from mid-chest up, slightly off-centre to the left. Daytime light comes from a window to her right, so one side of her face is brighter and the other a little shadowed. She has a fair complexion, a round face, light freckles, minimal makeup and a neutral, slightly wary half-smile. Her shoulder-length mousy brown hair is pulled back into a low ponytail with a few strands loose. She wears a grey zip-up hoodie over a black T-shirt and no glasses. Behind her is the box-room office: a white flat-pack shelving unit with lever-arch files labelled by year, a wall calendar with handwritten job bookings, a framed photo of a Staffie, and a half-open door showing part of a beige landing carpet.

P181 (Ffion; transcript label: Ffion):
- first name: Ffion
- age: 23
- lives in: Wrexham, North Wales
- occupation: Full-time final-year occupational therapy student; part-time kitchen assistant at a café in Wrexham town centre (Saturday shifts, about 10 to 12 hours a week: washing up, prepping salad, clearing tables)
- education detail: Third year of a BSc in Occupational Therapy at Wrexham University. Before that, A-levels in Biology, Psychology and Sociology at a sixth form college in Wrexham. She started a physiotherapy degree in Liverpool at 19 but left after one term because she was homesick and anxious, worked at the café full-time for most of a year, then reapplied closer to home.
- household: Lives with her mum, Karen (50, a senior pharmacist at the Wrexham Maelor hospital), her younger brother Owen (17, doing A-levels), and the family's elderly Jack Russell, Bonnie. It's a three-bed semi on an estate on the edge of town. Her parents split up when she was 12. Her dad lives in Chester with his new partner and she sees him every few weeks for Sunday lunch.
- cultural background: White Welsh, born and raised in Wrexham. The family speak English at home. She did Welsh to GCSE and can manage 'diolch' and a few phrases from placement, but she isn't confident with it. No religion. Her nan used to take her to chapel at Christmas, and she still likes carol services for the nostalgia. She thinks of herself as Welsh, gets properly emotional at the rugby anthem, and sees the border towns like Chester and Liverpool as part of her normal world.
- professional persona: Conscientious enough to get by. She keeps her placement paperwork mostly up to date but sometimes leaves reflective logs until the night before and then panics. On placement she is good with older patients because she is gentle and patient, but she dreads presenting in team meetings and rehearses what she'll say in the car. At the café she is reliable and quiet, prefers the back kitchen to the till, and gets flustered when it's busy.
- sports persona: Not sporty. She played netball at school until Year 10, then stopped because she hated being shouted at in matches. Now she walks Bonnie round the park most evenings and sometimes goes on the cross-trainer at the uni gym when she feels guilty. She watches Wales in the Six Nations with her mum and Owen, mostly for the atmosphere.

req.text:
You write transcripts of realistic video calls between strangers for a fully synthetic research dataset set in the UK. The study, in order (from its published design): a short puzzle task done alone; first impressions of the others' webcam photos; then a series of three-minute, one-on-one video calls in rounds, each person meeting the others in their group; after each call a short survey.

Call shape (from the original study's numbers): a call is cut off by a three-minute timer. A typical call has about 30 turns (most between 20 and 39) and about 570 words in total (most between 440 and 682); half of all turns are 12 words or fewer, and a quarter are 24 or more. Short acknowledgements ("yeah", "mm") count as turns too. So aim for about 570 words in about 30 turns: alongside the quick back-and-forth, people often talk in longer stretches (explaining their job, telling a story), and those long turns carry much of the call.

Guide to British conversational English (use it for how people talk; it is a description of speech, not a script):
How British people talk in casual conversation. This is a paraphrase of published descriptions of spoken British English; sources are in SOURCES.md. Use these features lightly and only where they fit the person. Never use them as a caricature.

- **Fillers.** British speakers hesitate with "erm" and "er". Women and younger speakers lean towards "erm".
- **Hedges.** "Sort of" is everywhere and steady. "Kind of" is spreading, and younger speakers use it more.
- **Politeness words.** "Please", "thank you", "thanks" and "sorry" mostly mean what they say. "Sorry" also works as a repair word (to correct yourself, or to ask someone to repeat) and can be ironic.
- **Tags at the end of a sentence.** "You know", "right", "okay", "yeah", "do you know what I mean". Among young Londoners, "innit" and "you get me" are rising. Tags depend on age and region only, never on ethnicity.
- **Echoing.** In an engaged conversation people pick up and re-use parts of each other's words.
- **Regional words and grammar** (from a recent dialect survey):
  - A bread roll is a "barm" in the North West (Manchester to Liverpool and western Lancashire), a "cob" around Nottinghamshire, a "bap" in Staffordshire, the West Midlands and North Wales, and a "batch" in Liverpool and Coventry.
  - Around Liverpool an ice lolly can be a "lolly ice".
  - The evening meal is "tea" in the North West, North East and Yorkshire, and "dinner" in the South East and London. Some people say both.
  - "Yous" or "youse" for plural "you" is common in the North East (Newcastle, Teesside), Liverpool and Scotland, less so in Manchester, and rare in York, Leeds and Sheffield.
  - "Give it me" is normal in the North West and West Midlands and widely accepted in Sheffield and York; it fades south of Birmingham, Coventry and Leicester.
  - "You was" is widely used, historically Northern and now found as far south as London.
- **Everyday British words** to draw on where they fit, without assigning them to regions: knackered or shattered, chuffed or made up, skint or brassic, mardy or stroppy, mum or mam, mate or pal, settee, sofa or couch.

req.text:
You write transcripts of realistic video calls between strangers for a fully synthetic research dataset set in the UK. The study, in order (from its published design): a short puzzle task done alone; first impressions of the others' webcam photos; then a series of three-minute, one-on-one video calls in rounds, each person meeting the others in their group; after each call a short survey.

Call shape (from the original study's numbers): a call is cut off by a three-minute timer. A typical call has about 30 turns (most between 20 and 39) and about 570 words in total (most between 440 and 682); half of all turns are 12 words or fewer, and a quarter are 24 or more. Short acknowledgements ("yeah", "mm") count as turns too. So aim for about 570 words in about 30 turns: alongside the quick back-and-forth, people often talk in longer stretches (explaining their job, telling a story), and those long turns carry much of the call.

Guide to British conversational English (use it for how people talk; it is a description of speech, not a script):
How British people talk in casual conversation. This is a paraphrase of published descriptions of spoken British English; sources are in SOURCES.md. Use these features lightly and only where they fit the person. Never use them as a caricature.

- **Fillers.** British speakers hesitate with "erm" and "er". Women and younger speakers lean towards "erm".
- **Hedges.** "Sort of" is everywhere and steady. "Kind of" is spreading, and younger speakers use it more.
- **Politeness words.** "Please", "thank you", "thanks" and "sorry" mostly mean what they say. "Sorry" also works as a repair word (to correct yourself, or to ask someone to repeat) and can be ironic.
- **Tags at the end of a sentence.** "You know", "right", "okay", "yeah", "do you know what I mean". Among young Londoners, "innit" and "you get me" are rising. Tags depend on age and region only, never on ethnicity.
- **Echoing.** In an engaged conversation people pick up and re-use parts of each other's words.
- **Regional words and grammar** (from a recent dialect survey):
  - A bread roll is a "barm" in the North West (Manchester to Liverpool and western Lancashire), a "cob" around Nottinghamshire, a "bap" in Staffordshire, the West Midlands and North Wales, and a "batch" in Liverpool and Coventry.
  - Around Liverpool an ice lolly can be a "lolly ice".
  - The evening meal is "tea" in the North West, North East and Yorkshire, and "dinner" in the South East and London. Some people say both.
  - "Yous" or "youse" for plural "you" is common in the North East (Newcastle, Teesside), Liverpool and Scotland, less so in Manchester, and rare in York, Leeds and Sheffield.
  - "Give it me" is normal in the North West and West Midlands and widely accepted in Sheffield and York; it fades south of Birmingham, Coventry and Leicester.
  - "You was" is widely used, historically Northern and now found as far south as London.
- **Everyday British words** to draw on where they fit, without assigning them to regions: knackered or shattered, chuffed or made up, skint or brassic, mardy or stroppy, mum or mam, mate or pal, settee, sofa or couch.

req.text:
You write transcripts of realistic video calls between strangers for a fully synthetic research dataset set in the UK. The study, in order (from its published design): a short puzzle task done alone; first impressions of the others' webcam photos; then a series of three-minute, one-on-one video calls in rounds, each person meeting the others in their group; after each call a short survey.

Call shape (from the original study's numbers): a call is cut off by a three-minute timer. A typical call has about 30 turns (most between 20 and 39) and about 570 words in total (most between 440 and 682); half of all turns are 12 words or fewer, and a quarter are 24 or more. Short acknowledgements ("yeah", "mm") count as turns too. So aim for about 570 words in about 30 turns: alongside the quick back-and-forth, people often talk in longer stretches (explaining their job, telling a story), and those long turns carry much of the call.

Guide to British conversational English (use it for how people talk; it is a description of speech, not a script):
How British people talk in casual conversation. This is a paraphrase of published descriptions of spoken British English; sources are in SOURCES.md. Use these features lightly and only where they fit the person. Never use them as a caricature.

- **Fillers.** British speakers hesitate with "erm" and "er". Women and younger speakers lean towards "erm".
- **Hedges.** "Sort of" is everywhere and steady. "Kind of" is spreading, and younger speakers use it more.
- **Politeness words.** "Please", "thank you", "thanks" and "sorry" mostly mean what they say. "Sorry" also works as a repair word (to correct yourself, or to ask someone to repeat) and can be ironic.
- **Tags at the end of a sentence.** "You know", "right", "okay", "yeah", "do you know what I mean". Among young Londoners, "innit" and "you get me" are rising. Tags depend on age and region only, never on ethnicity.
- **Echoing.** In an engaged conversation people pick up and re-use parts of each other's words.
- **Regional words and grammar** (from a recent dialect survey):
  - A bread roll is a "barm" in the North West (Manchester to Liverpool and western Lancashire), a "cob" around Nottinghamshire, a "bap" in Staffordshire, the West Midlands and North Wales, and a "batch" in Liverpool and Coventry.
  - Around Liverpool an ice lolly can be a "lolly ice".
  - The evening meal is "tea" in the North West, North East and Yorkshire, and "dinner" in the South East and London. Some people say both.
  - "Yous" or "youse" for plural "you" is common in the North East (Newcastle, Teesside), Liverpool and Scotland, less so in Manchester, and rare in York, Leeds and Sheffield.
  - "Give it me" is normal in the North West and West Midlands and widely accepted in Sheffield and York; it fades south of Birmingham, Coventry and Leicester.
  - "You was" is widely used, historically Northern and now found as far south as London.
- **Everyday British words** to draw on where they fit, without assigning them to regions: knackered or shattered, chuffed or made up, skint or brassic, mardy or stroppy, mum or mam, mate or pal, settee, sofa or couch.

req.text:
You write transcripts of realistic video calls between strangers for a fully synthetic research dataset set in the UK. The study, in order (from its published design): a short puzzle task done alone; first impressions of the others' webcam photos; then a series of three-minute, one-on-one video calls in rounds, each person meeting the others in their group; after each call a short survey.

Call shape (from the original study's numbers): a call is cut off by a three-minute timer. A typical call has about 30 turns (most between 20 and 39) and about 570 words in total (most between 440 and 682); half of all turns are 12 words or fewer, and a quarter are 24 or more. Short acknowledgements ("yeah", "mm") count as turns too. So aim for about 570 words in about 30 turns: alongside the quick back-and-forth, people often talk in longer stretches (explaining their job, telling a story), and those long turns carry much of the call.

Guide to British conversational English (use it for how people talk; it is a description of speech, not a script):
How British people talk in casual conversation. This is a paraphrase of published descriptions of spoken British English; sources are in SOURCES.md. Use these features lightly and only where they fit the person. Never use them as a caricature.

- **Fillers.** British speakers hesitate with "erm" and "er". Women and younger speakers lean towards "erm".
- **Hedges.** "Sort of" is everywhere and steady. "Kind of" is spreading, and younger speakers use it more.
- **Politeness words.** "Please", "thank you", "thanks" and "sorry" mostly mean what they say. "Sorry" also works as a repair word (to correct yourself, or to ask someone to repeat) and can be ironic.
- **Tags at the end of a sentence.** "You know", "right", "okay", "yeah", "do you know what I mean". Among young Londoners, "innit" and "you get me" are rising. Tags depend on age and region only, never on ethnicity.
- **Echoing.** In an engaged conversation people pick up and re-use parts of each other's words.
- **Regional words and grammar** (from a recent dialect survey):
  - A bread roll is a "barm" in the North West (Manchester to Liverpool and western Lancashire), a "cob" around Nottinghamshire, a "bap" in Staffordshire, the West Midlands and North Wales, and a "batch" in Liverpool and Coventry.
  - Around Liverpool an ice lolly can be a "lolly ice".
  - The evening meal is "tea" in the North West, North East and Yorkshire, and "dinner" in the South East and London. Some people say both.
  - "Yous" or "youse" for plural "you" is common in the North East (Newcastle, Teesside), Liverpool and Scotland, less so in Manchester, and rare in York, Leeds and Sheffield.
  - "Give it me" is normal in the North West and West Midlands and widely accepted in Sheffield and York; it fades south of Birmingham, Coventry and Leicester.
  - "You was" is widely used, historically Northern and now found as far south as London.
- **Everyday British words** to draw on where they fit, without assigning them to regions: knackered or shattered, chuffed or made up, skint or brassic, mardy or stroppy, mum or mam, mate or pal, settee, sofa or couch.

The group (session S35). Persona cards, including the webcam photo each person was rated on:

P184 (Gary; transcript label: Gary):
- first name: Gary
- age: 56
- lives in: Bridgwater, South West England
- occupation: Not currently working. Former forklift and warehouse operative at a food distribution depot on the edge of town for 19 years. Signed off just over two years ago with a lower back problem (a prolapsed disc and sciatica down his left leg). Now on benefits and doing a few hours a week volunteering.
- education detail: Left the local comprehensive at 16 with a handful of CSEs and one O level in woodwork. Did a YTS placement at a builders' merchant. Holds a counterbalance forklift licence (lapsed, but he keeps the card) and a food hygiene certificate from his depot days.
- household: Lives alone in a two-bedroom ex-council terraced house he rents from a housing association. Divorced from Karen eleven years ago after 20 years of marriage, and they are on civil terms. Has one grown-up daughter, Leanne (29), who lives in Taunton with her partner and his granddaughter Poppy (4). The second bedroom is kept made up for when Poppy stays.
- cultural background: White British, born and raised in Bridgwater. His dad worked at the cellophane factory and his mum did school dinners. Grew up on the same estate he lives near now. Not religious, though he went to Sunday school as a kid and still goes to the Remembrance service. Carnival season matters to him: his uncle was in a carnival club and Gary helped build carts in his twenties.
- professional persona: Was the reliable one on the shift: never late, kept the paperwork straight, knew everyone's name including the agency lads, and was the person the supervisor asked to show new starters round. Still talks about the depot as if he's going back. He'd like something part-time and not too heavy if his back allows, like a caretaker, a car park attendant or a meet-and-greet job.
- sports persona: Follows football loosely and supports Bristol City out of family habit, mostly watching highlights. Used to play skittles for a pub team and still goes along on league nights to score and socialise, even though he can't bowl much now. Walks every day on the physio's orders, usually along the river or the canal path.
- arts persona: Not much of a cultural outing person. Likes the carnival, the odd tribute band at the social club, and a film if Leanne drags him along. Watches quiz shows, Bargain Hunt and old episodes of Only Fools and Horses. Has no interest in galleries or the theatre and would say so cheerfully.
- travel persona: Hasn't been abroad since a family package holiday to Majorca about fifteen years ago, and his passport's expired. Prefers a static caravan at Brean or a week in Devon. Doesn't drive much now because his back stiffens up, so he relies on buses and Leanne's car.
- culinary persona: Plain, regular meals at set times. Batch-cooks a cottage pie or a stew on Sundays and portions it into labelled tubs for the week. Likes a fry-up on a Saturday, fish and chips on a Friday and a pasty when he's out. Doesn't like anything too spicy. Drinks tea all day and the odd pint of cider at the club.
- hobbies and interests: Volunteering two mornings a week at a community food bank, sorting stock and chatting to people in the queue, Skittles league nights (scoring rather than bowling these days), Doing the crossword in the local paper, Keeping his small back garden tidy: bedding plants and a couple of tomato pots, Pub quiz on Thursdays with the same three mates, Sorting out bits for neighbours, like fixing a gate or putting up a shelf, when his back's good
- skills: Forklift and warehouse stock handling, Very organised: lists, calendars, labelled boxes, Basic DIY and carpentry, Getting on with anyone and remembering names, Reliable timekeeping, Showing new people the ropes
- career goals: To get his back to a point where he can do 16 hours a week somewhere sociable without being in pain. He's been talking to a work coach about it. He doesn't want a career, just a routine, a bit of extra money and people to talk to. He worries about what happens if he can't go back to work.
- voice: Warm, chatty and quick to fill the gap, with a soft Somerset accent. He has a slight burr on his r's, says 'alright?' as a greeting and now and then uses 'my love' or 'mate'. Speaks fairly fast, with a lot of 'you know' and 'sort of', and 'er' when he's thinking. Tells little stories to answer simple questions and then says 'anyway, sorry, I'm going off on one'. Hates silence and will fill it, often by asking the interviewer something back, like 'where are you based then?'. Says 'thank you' and 'cheers' a lot and means it.
- typing: Types carefully with two fingers, so his answers are short. Capitalises the first word and names, mostly ends with a full stop and usually gets apostrophes right because he's careful. Sometimes types in all caps by accident and corrects it. No abbreviations beyond 'ok'. Might add 'Thanks' at the end of a free-text answer.
- with strangers: Instantly friendly and open, and treats a stranger like a new starter on shift. Asks how your day's going and makes self-deprecating jokes about his back and his age. Very honest, sometimes more than he needs to be. Keen to do things properly and checks he's answered what you actually asked. Can come across as a bit anxious to please.
- small things: His granddaughter Poppy's latest saying, The bus being late again, Who won at the skittles, The weather and whether he can get out in the garden, What came in at the food bank this week, His physio exercises and his new walking route, Getting the crossword done before lunch
- deeper things: He felt like he'd lost a part of himself when he stopped working, and the first year was very low, He's lonely in the evenings since the divorce and keeps busy to avoid it, He regrets working so many night shifts when Leanne was little, He's worried about money and the next benefits review, His dad died of a stroke at 64, and he thinks about that more than he lets on, He cried at Poppy's nursery nativity and was embarrassed about it
- webcam photo: A slightly low-angle laptop webcam shot from a dining table, with Gary centred and a bit too close to the screen. Daylight comes from a window to his right, so one side of his face is brighter. He has a broad, ruddy face with a big open grin and crow's feet. His hair is short, grey and thinning on top, and he has light stubble. He wears reading glasses with thin black frames pushed up slightly, and a navy fleece zipped halfway over a grey T-shirt. Behind him is a magnolia wall with a framed photo of a small girl in a fairy costume and a wall calendar with appointments written in biro. A neat shelf holds a skittles trophy, a row of DVDs and a carriage clock. A mug on a coaster is just visible at the bottom of the frame.

P185 (Bethany; transcript label: Bethany):
- first name: Bethany
- age: 25
- lives in: Basingstoke, South East England
- occupation: IT service desk analyst (second-line support) at an insurance company's regional office, full-time, about 37.5 hours a week plus the odd late shift
- education detail: A levels in Computing, Maths and Psychology at a sixth form college in Basingstoke. Started a Computer Science degree at Southampton but left after first year. Later picked up CompTIA A+ and ITIL Foundation certificates through work.
- household: Rents a two-bed terraced house in South Ham with her partner Dan (27), a warehouse shift manager she has been with for about a year and a half. They have a rescue cat called Biscuit. Her divorce from her first husband, who she married at 21, was finalised just over a year ago.
- cultural background: Grew up in Basingstoke. Her mum is a teaching assistant and her dad is a self-employed electrician, and she has a younger brother at uni. She was raised Church of England and went to Sunday school and youth group. Her faith still matters to her but she keeps it quiet. She goes to a local Anglican church every few weeks, more often around Easter and Christmas, and sits near the back.
- professional persona: Reliable on tickets and very good with frustrated users on the phone. She is patient and never makes people feel stupid. Her paperwork and ticket notes lag behind, and her manager has nudged her about closing tickets properly. She hates being put forward in team meetings and would rather fix things than talk about fixing them. She tells you straight if she broke something.
- sports persona: Not sporty. Does a Couch to 5K app in fits and starts and has restarted week three about four times. Walks along the canal path at weekends. Will watch the Women's Euros if Dan puts it on.
- arts persona: Reads a lot of fantasy and cosy mystery on her Kindle, often well past midnight. Likes indie folk and listens to the same few albums on repeat. Draws a bit in a sketchbook she never shows anyone.
- travel persona: Hasn't travelled much. Went to Cornwall most summers as a kid and to Lanzarote on her honeymoon. She and Dan did a long weekend in Edinburgh last year, which she loved because it was walking, bookshops and nobody needing her to talk. She keeps meaning to renew her passport.
- culinary persona: Cooks simple things like pasta bakes, fajitas and jacket potatoes. Batch-cooks with good intentions and then orders a Domino's on Fridays. Calls the evening meal dinner. Makes a decent Victoria sponge, taught by her nan.

=== CALL C0377 ===
Gary: Alright? Can you hear me okay? I'm Gary.
Bożena: Hello, yes, I can hear you very well. I am Bożena. Nice to meet you.
Gary: Lovely to meet you, my love. Where are you based then?
Bożena: Southampton. Bitterne, if you know it, on the east side.
Gary: Oh, I know Southampton a bit. I went down the boat show years ago with a lad from work, never bought a boat mind. I'm in Bridgwater, Somerset. Born and bred, never really left, you know. How did you get on with that puzzle thing at the start? I was hopeless. I sat there turning it round like a muppet.
Bożena: The puzzle? Erm, I think I did okay, but I check everything twice, so it took me very long time. My husband says I would check the sky is still blue.
Gary: Ha! No, that's good, that's proper. So what do you do then, Bożena, are you working?
Bożena: Not at the moment, no. I was pharmacy technician, eleven years at a pharmacy in Shirley, and then the branch closed, in 2023. So, sort of, I am looking for something part-time. Maybe a GP surgery, or hospital, somewhere more steady than the high street.
Gary: Oh, that's a shame. Were you there long? Sorry, you just said, eleven years. That's a good stretch. You'd miss the regulars, I bet.
Bożena: Yes, the regulars, exactly. People used to ask for me by name. "Is the Polish lady in?" I miss that more than the work, I think.
Gary: Funny, that, innit. I'm the same. I was nineteen years at a food depot, driving a forklift, doing the paperwork, showing the new lads round. Then my back went, a disc, and the sciatica down my leg, and I've been signed off two year now. And it's not the lifting I miss, it's the people. You'd have a laugh on nights, you know, a bacon roll at three in the morning. Anyway, sorry, I'm going off on one.
Bożena: No, no, it's okay. I understand. When the pharmacy closed it was, erm, how you say, I felt a little bit lost.
Gary: Yeah. Lost, that's the word. Are you keeping busy, though?
Bożena: Oh yes, very busy. I walk by the river every day, I help at the church coffee morning, and I am knitting a jumper for my grandson with a dinosaur on it.
Gary: A dinosaur! He'll love that. How old is he?
Bożena: He is five. And my granddaughter is seven. Do you have grandchildren? I saw a little girl in a fairy costume, in your photo.
Gary: That's Poppy, she's four. My daughter Leanne's little one, they're over in Taunton. She stays with me some weekends, I keep the spare room made up. Her latest thing is she calls me "Grumpa" when I won't let her have another biscuit. Cheeky madam.
Bożena: Grumpa! That is very good.
Gary: I'm not even grumpy, I'm a soft touch. She had her nativity at nursery at Christmas and I was a right mess, tissues out and everything. Leanne still takes the mick.
Bożena: My daughter is a teacher, primary school, and she says the grandparents always cry at nativity. So you are normal, Gary.
Gary: Well, that's a relief, cheers. And what about you, do you get back to Poland much?
Bożena: Once or twice a year. My mother is eighty-four, still in Olsztyn, and my sister looks after her. It is, erm, sometimes difficult, being so far away.
Gary: Yeah, I bet. My dad went at sixty-four, a stroke, so I know how you think about it, you know. You want to be near.
Bożena: Yes. I am sorry about your father.
Gary: Ah, it's a long time ago now. You've got a very kind face, you know, you remind me of my sister, she's a worrier too, checks the door three times before bed.
Bożena: Then I think I would like your sister. Is this enough talking, or should I...
Gary: No, you're grand, keep going, we've got ages yet, haven't we? I think...

Jurgita: Exactly.
Bethany: Yeah.

Jurgita: Once a year, two weeks in summer. And Tenerife sometimes, all-inclusive. Pool, nothing else.
Bethany: That sounds nice, actually. I really need to renew my passport, I keep saying I will.
Jurgita: Do it on the internet, is quick. And you know, I got new bag in the sale last week, TK Maxx, Michael Kors, forty pound. Proper bargain.
Bethany: Forty? That's really good. I never find anything in TK Maxx, I just sort of wander round.
Jurgita: You have to go Tuesday, when they put new stock out. Tuesday morning, before—

req.text:
You write transcripts of realistic video calls between strangers for a fully synthetic research dataset set in the UK. The study, in order (from its published design): a short puzzle task done alone; first impressions of the others' webcam photos; then a series of three-minute, one-on-one video calls in rounds, each person meeting the others in their group; after each call a short survey.

Call shape (from the original study's numbers): a call is cut off by a three-minute timer. A typical call has about 30 turns (most between 20 and 39) and about 570 words in total (most between 440 and 682); half of all turns are 12 words or fewer, and a quarter are 24 or more. Short acknowledgements ("yeah", "mm") count as turns too. So aim for about 570 words in about 30 turns: alongside the quick back-and-forth, people often talk in longer stretches (explaining their job, telling a story), and those long turns carry much of the call.

Guide to British conversational English (use it for how people talk; it is a description of speech, not a script):
How British people talk in casual conversation. This is a paraphrase of published descriptions of spoken British English; sources are in SOURCES.md. Use these features lightly and only where they fit the person. Never use them as a caricature.

- **Fillers.** British speakers hesitate with "erm" and "er". Women and younger speakers lean towards "erm".
- **Hedges.** "Sort of" is everywhere and steady. "Kind of" is spreading, and younger speakers use it more.
- **Politeness words.** "Please", "thank you", "thanks" and "sorry" mostly mean what they say. "Sorry" also works as a repair word (to correct yourself, or to ask someone to repeat) and can be ironic.
- **Tags at the end of a sentence.** "You know", "right", "okay", "yeah", "do you know what I mean". Among young Londoners, "innit" and "you get me" are rising. Tags depend on age and region only, never on ethnicity.
- **Echoing.** In an engaged conversation people pick up and re-use parts of each other's words.
- **Regional words and grammar** (from a recent dialect survey):
  - A bread roll is a "barm" in the North West (Manchester to Liverpool and western Lancashire), a "cob" around Nottinghamshire, a "bap" in Staffordshire, the West Midlands and North Wales, and a "batch" in Liverpool and Coventry.
  - Around Liverpool an ice lolly can be a "lolly ice".
  - The evening meal is "tea" in the North West, North East and Yorkshire, and "dinner" in the South East and London. Some people say both.
  - "Yous" or "youse" for plural "you" is common in the North East (Newcastle, Teesside), Liverpool and Scotland, less so in Manchester, and rare in York, Leeds and Sheffield.
  - "Give it me" is normal in the North West and West Midlands and widely accepted in Sheffield and York; it fades south of Birmingham, Coventry and Leicester.
  - "You was" is widely used, historically Northern and now found as far south as London.
- **Everyday British words** to draw on where they fit, without assigning them to regions: knackered or shattered, chuffed or made up, skint or brassic, mardy or stroppy, mum or mam, mate or pal, settee, sofa or couch.

Alison: Hello. Can you hear me alright?
Joanne: Yes, hello, sorry. I wasn't sure if it had started or not.
Alison: I think it just starts. There's a little timer in the corner, which is slightly ominous.
Joanne: Oh, yes, I see it. Erm, I'm Joanne. Jo. I don't really know what we're meant to talk about, sorry.

Alison: I abandoned one halfway, which is what I do with the crossword most mornings, so it felt quite normal.
Joanne: Oh, you do the crossword? The proper one?
Alison: The cryptic, yes. Badly. My husband says I only do it so I can complain about the setter.
Joanne: I do word searches. They're more my level, if that makes sense. I do them on my break at work.
Alison: What do you do?
Joanne: I'm a domestic at the hospital. On the wards, cleaning. I've been there eleven years now. I'm on earlies, so I'm up at half five, which is why I look like this, sorry.

Joanne: The general in Basingstoke. I've lived there all my life, really. I've never gone more than about five miles, Gary says.
Alison: There's a lot to be said for that. I'm in Tonbridge. I work for the council, planning, so I spend all day reading about people wanting to put extensions where they shouldn't.
Joanne: Oh, that sounds very clever. I'd worry about getting it wrong.
Alison: It's mostly reading. And sitting in meetings while people shout at you. You sort of learn not to take it personally. I imagine you get a bit of that too.
Joanne: Not shouting, really. The patients are mostly lovely. The elderly ones especially, they get frightened, you know, and you just have a little chat while you're doing round their bed. Some of them know me by name. Sorry, I'm going on.
Alison: No, you're not. That's the bit that actually matters, isn't it? The talking.
Joanne: I think so. The nurses haven't always got time, so. Erm, have you got a dog? I saw a lead in your picture.

Joanne: No! My cat's called Biscuit.
Alison: Is it really?
Joanne: She's nineteen. She's getting a bit doddery now, she sort of walks into the table leg.

Joanne: My daughter named her. Kirsty. She was about ten. She's twenty-nine now and she's got a little boy, he's just started saying Nanny Jo.
Alison: Oh, that's lovely. Mine are thirty-two and twenty-nine, no grandchildren yet. I'm not holding my breath. My daughter's in south London, so I get the train up and we have lunch and she tells me what I'm doing wrong.
Joanne: Kirsty does that. Mostly about my phone.
