req.text:
You write transcripts of realistic video calls between strangers for a fully synthetic research dataset set in the UK. The study, in order (from its published design): a short puzzle task done alone; first impressions of the others' webcam photos; then a series of three-minute, one-on-one video calls in rounds, each person meeting the others in their group; after each call a short survey.

Call shape (from the original study's numbers): a call is cut off by a three-minute timer. A typical call has about 30 turns (most between 20 and 39) and about 570 words in total (most between 440 and 682); half of all turns are 12 words or fewer, and a quarter are 24 or more. Short acknowledgements ("yeah", "mm") count as turns too. So aim for about 570 words in about 30 turns: alongside the quick back-and-forth, people often talk in longer stretches (explaining their job, telling a story), and those long turns carry much of the call.

Guide to British conversational English (use it for how people talk; it is a description of speech, not a script):
How British people talk in casual conversation. This is a paraphrase of published descriptions of spoken British English; sources are in SOURCES.md. Use these features lightly and only where they fit the person. Never use them as a caricature.

- **Fillers.** British speakers hesitate with "erm" and "er". Women and younger speakers lean towards "erm".
- **Hedges.** "Sort of" is everywhere and steady. "Kind of" is spreading, and younger speakers use it more.
- **Politeness words.** "Please", "thank you", "thanks" and "sorry" mostly mean what they say. "Sorry" also works as a repair word (to correct yourself, or to ask someone to repeat) and can be ironic.
- **Tags at the end of a sentence.** "You know", "right", "okay", "yeah", "do you know what I mean". Among young Londoners, "innit" and "you get me" are rising. Tags depend on age and region only, never on ethnicity.
- **Echoing.** In an engaged conversation people pick up and re-use parts of each other's words.
- **Regional words and grammar** (from a recent dialect survey):
  - A bread roll is a "barm" in the North West (Manchester to Liverpool and western Lancashire), a "cob" around Nottinghamshire, a "bap" in Staffordshire, the West Midlands and North Wales, and a "batch" in Liverpool and Coventry.
  - Around Liverpool an ice lolly can be a "lolly ice".
  - The evening meal is "tea" in the North West, North East and Yorkshire, and "dinner" in the South East and London. Some people say both.
  - "Yous" or "youse" for plural "you" is common in the North East (Newcastle, Teesside), Liverpool and Scotland, less so in Manchester, and rare in York, Leeds and Sheffield.
  - "Give it me" is normal in the North West and West Midlands and widely accepted in Sheffield and York; it fades south of Birmingham, Coventry and Leicester.
  - "You was" is widely used, historically Northern and now found as far south as London.
- **Everyday British words** to draw on where they fit, without assigning them to regions: knackered or shattered, chuffed or made up, skint or brassic, mardy or stroppy, mum or mam, mate or pal, settee, sofa or couch.

The group (session S28). Persona cards, including the webcam photo each person was rated on:

P147 (Craig; transcript label: Craig):
- first name: Craig
- age: 35
- lives in: Hartlepool, North East England
- occupation: Bricklayer by trade, currently out of work. He was signed off with a lower back problem about eighteen months ago, is now on Universal Credit, and does online panel surveys for a bit of extra money.
- education detail: Left secondary school in Hartlepool at 16 with a handful of GCSEs, the best a C in maths. Did a Level 2 NVQ in bricklaying at the local college while on an apprenticeship with a small building firm, and later a CSCS card and a short first aid course through work.
- household: Lives with his mam (62, works part-time at a supermarket) and his younger brother Lee (29, warehouse shifts) in the terraced council house he grew up in. He moved back in after the divorce four years ago. His daughter Ellie, 9, stays over every other weekend and sleeps in the box room.
- cultural background: White British, born and raised in Hartlepool in a working-class family. His dad was a welder and passed away when Craig was in his twenties. Not religious, although he went to a Church of England primary school. Very rooted in the town; most of his mates are lads he went to school with.
- professional persona: Practical, steady and well liked on site. He was the one who kept the peace and never moaned about the weather. He took pride in a neat, level wall. Since the back trouble he has felt a bit at a loss without the routine of work. He is honest about what he can and can't do and would rather not overpromise.
- sports persona: Lifelong Hartlepool United fan. He used to have a season ticket and now goes when money allows, watching the rest down the pub or on his phone. He played Sunday league football until his late twenties. These days the most he does is walk the seafront on the physio's advice.
- arts persona: Not really into arts. He watches telly with his mam in the evenings: quiz shows, Gogglebox, the odd crime drama. He listens to whatever is on local radio or old Oasis and Arctic Monkeys in the car. He hasn't been to a gallery since a school trip.
- travel persona: He has been abroad a few times, to Spain and once to Turkey, all package holidays with his ex-wife. Since then it's been the odd caravan weekend at Whitby or in Northumberland with Ellie. He is happy enough close to home and isn't bothered about seeing the world.
- culinary persona: Plain, filling food. His mam does most of the cooking, and he has his tea around half five: mince and dumplings, a Sunday dinner, chips from the chippy on a Friday. He can do a fry-up and spag bol when Ellie is over. Not adventurous, and he wouldn't order something he can't pronounce.
- hobbies and interests: Following Hartlepool United, Walking along the seafront and the Headland, Fishing off the pier with his brother now and then, FIFA/EA FC on the PlayStation, Doing small DIY jobs for his mam and neighbours when his back allows, Taking his daughter to the park and the cinema
- skills: Bricklaying and blockwork, Reading basic building plans, General DIY: tiling, fixing fences, putting up shelves, Getting on with pretty much anyone, Keeping calm when other people are wound up
- career goals: He wants to get back into work but knows full-time bricklaying might be off the cards for his back. He's been half-thinking about a site supervisor or building maintenance role, or a CSCS-related course through the job centre. Mostly he wants something steady so he can get his own place and have Ellie over more.
- voice: Friendly, unhurried and fairly quiet at first, with a light Hartlepool/Teesside accent. Says 'mam', 'aye' now and then, occasionally 'yous' when talking about a group, and 'tea' for his evening meal. Uses 'er' and 'sort of' a fair bit, and ends things with 'you know' or 'like'. Answers are short to begin with and he warms up once he's comfortable. If there's a silence he'll fill it with a 'yeah... er' or a small laugh rather than leave it hanging. He tends to agree with the interviewer and say 'aye, fair enough' even when he's only half sure.
- typing: Mostly lowercase and rarely capitalises 'i'. Few full stops, with sentences run together with commas or nothing. Drops apostrophes ('dont', 'im', 'cant'). Short answers, sometimes 'not sure tbh' or 'yeah its alright'. Spelling is mostly fine, with the odd slip he doesn't go back and fix.
- with strangers: Polite and a bit reserved at first, a touch self-conscious about being out of work. He's easy-going and keen not to cause bother, so he goes along with things and apologises if he thinks he's given the 'wrong' answer. Once he relaxes he's warm and chatty, with a dry, self-deprecating sense of humour.
- small things: The weather coming in off the sea, How Pools are getting on this season, His mam's Sunday dinner, His back playing up after sitting too long, Ellie's school stuff or what film they last saw, The price of a pint going up, Lee coming in late off his shifts
- deeper things: Feeling a bit embarrassed to be 35 and back in his childhood bedroom, Worrying he won't be able to lay bricks again and not knowing what else he's good for, Missing his dad, especially at the football, The divorce being nobody's fault really. They just drifted, and he still gets on with his ex for Ellie's sake, Being skint most months and not wanting his mam to carry him, Occasional low days since the injury that he doesn't really talk about
- webcam photo: Laptop webcam at a slightly low angle, so the image looks up a little at his chin. Head and shoulders, slightly off-centre to the left. Light comes from a window to his right, leaving one side of his face a bit shadowed, plus the warm yellow glow of a ceiling light. Pale skin with a bit of redness on the cheeks, short dark brown hair clipped at the sides and slightly longer on top, and a few days' stubble. Brown eyes, no glasses. A slightly awkward, polite half-smile. He wears a plain navy hooded sweatshirt with the drawstrings uneven. Behind him is a magnolia living room wall with a framed school photo of a smiling girl in a red jumper and a small mirror. Part of a brown leather settee is visible, with a folded grey throw on the arm. A blue and white Hartlepool United scarf is draped over the top of a door just out of focus on the right.

P148 (Kerry; transcript label: Kerry):
- first name: Kerry
- age: 42
- lives in: Taunton, South West England
- occupation: Diagnostic radiographer at a large NHS hospital, mostly general X-ray and some CT shifts. Full-time, about 37.5 hours a week plus the odd on-call weekend.
- education detail: GCSEs and A-levels (Biology, Chemistry, PE) at a comprehensive and sixth form in Bridgwater; BSc (Hons) Diagnostic Radiography from a university in the South West, finished in 2003. Has since done in-house CT training and a short course in clinical supervision of students.
- household: Lives with her husband Darren (44, an electrician who runs his own small business) in a three-bed semi on a 1990s estate on the edge of Taunton. They have no children. They have a ten-year-old springer spaniel called Moss. Her mum lives about fifteen minutes away in Bridgwater, and Kerry pops round most Sundays.
- cultural background: White British, born and raised in Somerset. Her dad was a postman and her mum worked in a school kitchen. She was the first in her family to go to university, though she doesn't make a thing of it. She isn't religious and never really was, apart from school nativities. She is rooted in the area: most of her friends are from school, netball or work, and she has no real interest in moving anywhere else.
- professional persona: Calm, efficient and reliable. She is the one who gets the department list moving on a busy Monday. She is good with anxious or confused patients, chatty without wasting time. She is straight with colleagues and doesn't play politics, and she would rather tell a manager directly that a rota won't work than moan about it in the staff room. She supervises student radiographers and is known for being firm but fair, with checklists for everything. She likes protocols and gets quietly irritated when people cut corners.
- sports persona: Plays goal defence in a local women's netball league on Tuesday nights and has done on and off since her twenties. She does the Saturday parkrun most weeks, more for the coffee and chat afterwards than for her time, though she does keep a note of it. She watches the rugby with Darren, mostly Bath and the Six Nations, and is fairly loud about it.
- arts persona: Not really an arts person, and she'd say so. She likes a good crime drama on telly, anything with Line of Duty energy, and the odd big musical if a mate organises a trip to Bristol Hippodrome. She reads a bit on holiday, usually a thriller someone has lent her. She listens to Heart or Radio 2 in the car.
- travel persona: Creature of habit. They go to the same campsite near Bude most summers with friends, and have a week somewhere warm in Spain or the Canaries in the autumn, usually a place they've been before. She organises everything well in advance, with a spreadsheet for the packing list. She isn't bothered about city breaks or 'finding herself', and calls a good holiday 'sun, a pool and someone else cooking'.
- culinary persona: Plain, decent home cooking. She batch-cooks chilli and spag bol on a Sunday so there's dinner ready after long shifts. She does a roast most weekends, sometimes at her mum's. She isn't adventurous: she'll have a curry on a Friday from the same takeaway and always orders the same thing. Darren does the barbecue. She likes a cream tea, jam first because she's from this side of the Tamar, and will defend it.
- hobbies and interests: Netball league, Saturday parkrun, Walking the dog on the Quantocks, Watching rugby, Crime dramas and quiz shows, Pub quiz with the netball girls once a month, Keeping the garden tidy
- skills: Patient positioning and image quality checks, Calming nervous patients, Organising rotas and lists, Training and supervising students, Keeping cool under pressure, Planning trips and events for friends, Basic DIY (learned from Darren)
- career goals: Would like to move up to a Band 7 lead or superintendent radiographer post in the next few years, ideally running the general X-ray team. She has no interest in leaving clinical work entirely for management, or in changing career. She is happy to stay at the same hospital until she retires if the job's right.
- voice: Warm, quick and confident, with a fairly mild Somerset accent. It's mostly in the vowels and the odd rolled 'r', and gets stronger when she's laughing or talking about home. She occasionally says 'proper' as an intensifier ('it was proper busy') or 'lush' about food, but nothing exaggerated. She says 'dinner' for the evening meal. She uses 'erm' a bit when thinking but usually gets to the point fast, with tags like 'you know' and 'yeah'. She answers questions directly and sometimes jokes. Silence doesn't bother her much, but she tends to fill it with a quick 'is that what you're after?' or 'sorry, do you want more on that?'
- typing: Quick and practical. She mostly uses capitals at the start of sentences and full stops, sometimes skipping the final one. Apostrophes are usually right. She uses the odd 'tbh' or 'x' habit from texting, but not in a form. Answers are short and to the point. She won't write paragraphs unless asked, and might use a dash or two.
- with strangers: Friendly and easy to talk to, quick to put people at ease, likely to make a light joke early on. Open about everyday stuff but not oversharing. Honest and unpretentious, she'll say 'I don't really know much about that' rather than bluff. Comes across as capable, grounded and a bit no-nonsense.
- small things: Moss rolled in something on the Quantocks again, The hospital car park is a nightmare, Netball team lost by two goals on Tuesday, Got a PB at parkrun, only by eight seconds, Darren's van needs an MOT, Planning the Bude camping trip with friends, Watching the latest crime series everyone's on about, Her mum's knee is playing up
- deeper things: She and Darren tried for children for a few years in their thirties, then decided to stop. She's mostly at peace with it but doesn't talk about it often., Her dad died suddenly when she was twenty-nine, and she still thinks about how she took over sorting everything for her mum., She sometimes worries about burnout in her department and about staff shortages., Being the first in her family to go to uni still means more to her than she lets on.
- webcam photo: Head-and-shoulders shot from a laptop on a kitchen table, camera slightly below eye level. Soft daylight from a window to her left lights her face, with the right side in slight shadow. She has fair skin, light freckles, a few fine lines round her eyes, and an open, friendly half-smile, looking straight at the camera. Her shoulder-length dark blonde hair, with darker roots showing, is tucked behind one ear. She wears a navy hoodie with a small netball club logo, no glasses, and small silver studs. Behind her is a white kitchen with grey cabinets. On the counter are a kettle, a toaster and a fruit bowl with bananas. A wall calendar with handwritten shifts hangs by the fridge. A dog lead hangs on a hook by the back door, and a corner of a dog bed is just visible on the floor.

- first name: Gareth
- age: 47
- lives in: Basingstoke, South East England (Hampshire)
- occupation: Senior structural engineer at a mid-sized engineering consultancy in Basingstoke, mostly working on commercial and light-industrial buildings such as warehouses, retail units and the odd school extension. Hybrid: three days in the office, two at home.

Joanne rents a flat in Reading and has the kids every other weekend and one evening a week. The arrangement mostly works, though she organises more of it than he does.
- cultural background: White British, born in Andover. His father was a telecoms engineer for BT and his mother worked part-time in a building society. He has one older sister in Salisbury. - hobbies and interests: Watching Southampton FC, Walking the family's Labrador cross, Bonnie, Fiddling about with the car, mostly basic maintenance, Fantasy Premier League in a work mini-league, though he often forgets to change his team, The odd bike ride along the Basingstoke Canal, A quiet pint at his local on a Thursday when the kids are at their mum's
- skills: Structural analysis and design calcs (steel and concrete frames), Using structural design software such as Tekla and Robot, Reading and marking up drawings, Staying calm when things go wrong on site, Basic car maintenance, Batch-cooking a chilli that lasts three days
- career goals: Nothing ambitious. He would like to stay where he is, keep the hybrid days, and maybe make associate eventually if it comes to him without having to push. Mostly he wants work to stay steady while the kids get through school.
- voice: Quiet, low and fairly flat, with a neutral southern accent from Hampshire and a bit of glottal stop on words like 'bit' and 'lot'. Answers are short, often just 'yeah' or 'not really', and he rarely elaborates unless asked a direct follow-up. He uses 'er' before answering and 'sort of' as a hedge ('it's sort of fine, yeah'). He occasionally ends with 'you know' but doesn't pile up tags. Silence doesn't bother him at all. He'll let a pause sit rather than fill it, which can make interviewers jump in first. He says 'sorry, say that again?' if the line is bad. He isn't unfriendly, just economical.
- typing: Mostly lowercase, often no capital at the start. Short answers, sometimes just a few words. Full stops are inconsistent and he usually leaves the last one off. Apostrophes are often dropped ('dont', 'its'). The occasional 'tbh' or 'n/a', and the odd typo he doesn't go back to fix. Example: 'not really, i just do the big shop on a sunday mostly tesco'
- with strangers: Reserved and a bit hard to read at first. He is polite and answers what he's asked, but offers little and doesn't ask questions back. He comes across as calm, unflustered and a little closed. People sometimes mistake his flatness for boredom. He warms up slightly if the topic turns to football, the kids or something practical.
- small things: Bonnie the dog needing walking before it gets dark, Callum's GCSE options and whether he's actually revising, The A33 traffic and the roadworks near Chineham, Saints' last result, Forgetting it was non-uniform day at Ellie's school, The boiler making a noise he keeps meaning to get looked at, Friday takeaway being the highlight of the week
- deeper things: He and Joanne drifted apart over years, and he admits he wasn't really paying attention until she said she was going, Being the main parent wasn't something he expected, and he worries he's doing the bare minimum with the kids rather than doing it well, Neither of them has started the divorce, and he isn't sure whether that's practicality or him avoiding it, He sometimes feels he coasted through his career and got chartered late because he just didn't get round to it, His dad's health is getting worse and his sister handles most of it, which he feels a bit guilty about
- webcam photo: Laptop webcam on a kitchen-diner table, angled slightly upward so the frame catches his chin and the ceiling edge. He is lit mostly by the overhead kitchen spotlights, which give a flat, slightly yellow light with a faint shine on his forehead. He is a white man in his late forties with a broad face, light stubble and short, thinning mid-brown hair going grey at the sides, cut fairly short. No glasses. His expression is neutral, a little tired, mouth closed, looking just below the camera at the screen. He wears a navy crew-neck sweatshirt over a grey T-shirt. Behind him on the left is a white fridge-freezer covered in school letters, a takeaway menu and a Southampton FC fixtures magnet. To the right is a laminate worktop with a kettle, a toaster, a stack of post and a dog lead hanging on a cupboard handle. A clothes airer with school shirts on it stands partly in shot at the back near patio doors, and the doors show darkness outside.

- occupation: General manager of a mid-sized bar and live music venue in Manchester's Northern Quarter, running a team of about 18 bar staff, two duty managers and the booking side

Ryan: I wasn't going to say Cardiff! I was going to say I've been to Swansea once for a gig. Sin City, is it still going?
Aleena: Oh my god, yeah, my friends go there all the time. That's so random.
Ryan: Small world. Is this your first one of these calls?
Aleena: Yeah, first one. Was your last one alright?
Ryan: Yeah, he was sound. Man of few words, like. I reckon I did about ninety percent of the talking.
Aleena: *(laughs)* I can believe that, ngl.
Ryan: Cheeky! Go on then, what do you do?
Aleena: First year at Swansea Uni, Business Management. And I work Saturdays in a sports shop in the Quadrant, and I flip trainers on Vinted on the side. I sold a pair of Air Forces last week for double what I paid. Double.
Ryan: That's quality, that. That's proper business, that's better than the degree, honestly. I left uni after a year and I'm doing alright.
Aleena: What do you do, then?
Ryan: I run a bar and a music venue in the Northern Quarter, in Manchester. About eighteen staff, I do the booking, the bands, licensing, all of it. And I'm opening my own place in the next few years. Small bar, basement for gigs. I've got a mate with money, we're talking about it.
Aleena: Wait, that's actually tidy. Do you get people on the guest list and that?
Ryan: All the time. You'd be on it. You'd have to come up to Manchester, mind.
Aleena: I'm moving to Manchester or London after uni anyway. That's where the money is. I want to go into sales or recruitment, somewhere with commission and a company car.
Ryan: Nah, not recruitment. I've got mates in recruitment, mate, it's soul-destroying. Ringing people up all day who don't want to talk to you.
Aleena: No, that's a bit of a stupid thing to say, you don't even know me. I'm brilliant at it. I'm the top seller on add-ons at work. I can get anyone to buy socks.
Ryan: *(laughs)* Fair enough, fair enough, I'll give you that. Socks is hard. Nobody wants socks.
Aleena: Nobody wants socks! But they buy them off me.
Ryan: You should do the festival side. Ticketing, sponsorship, that sort of thing. You'd smash it, you've got the gob for it.
Aleena: Thank you, I think? *(laughs)* Is that a compliment?
Ryan: It's a compliment! What do you listen to, then? Go on, judge yourself.
Aleena: UK rap, Afrobeats, whatever's on TikTok. And Malayalam film songs when my mum's driving, but that's not my choice.
Ryan: We do an Afrobeat night once a month, it's rammed, it's one of the best nights we do. Whose turntable do you reckon that is behind me?
Aleena: Yours, obviously. Do you DJ, then?
Ryan: At mates' parties, yeah. I'm decent, to be fair. Better than most of the lads they book.
Aleena: Everyone says that, though.
Ryan: Not everyone's right, though, are they? I am.
Aleena: Okay, go on then, what's the last thing you—

=== CALL C0309 ===
Kerry: Hiya! Oh, there you are. Can you hear me okay?
Gareth: Yeah. Hi.
Kerry: Great. I'm Kerry, I'm down in Taunton. Somerset.
Gareth: Gareth. Basingstoke.
Kerry: Ooh, Basingstoke. I've only ever seen it from the M3, to be honest. Is that a dog lead on your cupboard there?
Gareth: Er, yeah. Bonnie. Labrador cross.
Kerry: Snap, look, mine's on the back door. Moss, springer spaniel, he's ten. Went up the Quantocks on Sunday and he rolled in something absolutely disgusting, had to hose him down in the garden. Darren was not impressed.
Gareth: Bonnie does that. Fox, usually.
Kerry: Fox is the worst, isn't it? You can't get the smell off. So what do you do, Gareth?
Gareth: Structural engineer. Warehouses, retail units, that sort of thing.
Kerry: Oh, right. I'm a radiographer, so I suppose we both sort of look inside things to check they're not broken.
Gareth: *(pause)* Yeah. Sort of, yeah.
Kerry: Sorry, that was a terrible joke. Is that what you'd call it, checking they're not broken?
Gareth: More checking they won't break. Before they're built.
Kerry: Ah, see, I only get them after. People come in having fallen off a ladder, and I'm there going, right, arm up for me, my love. It's mostly general X-ray, a bit of CT. And the car park's a nightmare, that's the main thing about my job really. Twenty minutes going round some mornings.
Gareth: Sorry, say that again? You cut out a bit.
Kerry: The car park. Nightmare. Twenty minutes.
Gareth: Ah. The A33's like that for me. Roadworks.
Kerry: Do you drive in every day?
Gareth: Three days. Home the other two. Suits me with the kids.
Kerry: How many have you got?
Gareth: Two. Fifteen and twelve. Callum and Ellie.
Kerry: Oh, lovely. Busy, then.
Gareth: Yeah. I forgot it was non-uniform day last week. Ellie went in in her uniform and everyone else was in their own clothes.
Kerry: Oh no! *(laughs)* Was she furious?
Gareth: Pretty furious, yeah. I'm on my own with them most of the week, so it's sort of on me now.
Kerry: Well, honestly, I'd forget too. That's why I have the calendar on the wall there, everything goes on it, all my shifts, Darren's jobs, the dog's jabs. And I do a spreadsheet for the camping. We go to Bude every summer with friends and I do the packing list for everyone. They take the mick, but nobody's ever forgotten a tent peg.
Gareth: I took the kids to a caravan in Devon once. I forgot the bedding.
Kerry: All the bedding?
Gareth: All of it.
Kerry: *(laughs)* Oh, Gareth. You need me. Did you at least have a cream tea while you were down there?
Gareth: Yeah, think so.
Kerry: Jam first or cream first?
Gareth: Er. Didn't really think about it.
Kerry: Well, you're in Devon, they'd have done cream first, which is wrong. Jam first, always. I'll die on that hill.
Gareth: Fair enough. I just eat it.
Kerry: That's the most dangerous answer you could've given. Sorry, am I going on? Do you get to watch much football with all that?
Gareth: Saints, yeah. On the telly mostly. I go a couple of times a—

Round 3. These calls happen at the same time:

=== CALL C0310 ===
Ryan: Alright, mate! Can you hear me?
Craig: Aye, yeah, hiya. I'm Craig.
Ryan: Ryan. Stockport. Here, is that a Pools scarf on your door?
Craig: *(laughs)* Aye, Hartlepool. Didn't think anyone'd spot that.
Ryan: Mate, I spot scarves. I've got County on the shelf here, look. Stockport County. Season ticket.
Craig: Oh, aye, I saw that on your photo. Yous were in the National League with us for a bit, weren't you?
Ryan: We were, yeah, dark times. Dark times, Craig. Do you still go?
Craig: Er, when money allows, like. I had a season ticket for years. Me and me dad used to go every home game, from when I was about six. He's passed now, so it's sort of not the same. I watch most of 'em down the pub now, or on me phone.
Ryan: Ah, sorry, mate. That's rough.
Craig: Nah, it's alright. It's a long time ago now. Still miss him at the football, mind.
Ryan: Yeah. My dad had a heart scare a couple of years back, and it properly shook me, honestly. He's fine now, he's back moaning about the ref. But you think, don't you.
Craig: Aye. You do.
Ryan: Anyway! What do you do for work, then?
Craig: Er, I'm a brickie. Well, I was. Done me back about eighteen month ago, so I'm off at the minute. Universal Credit and that. Bit embarrassing, to be honest.
Ryan: Nah, don't be daft, that's not embarrassing. Backs go. Half my five-a-side lads have got a dodgy back and they still play, which is worse. What would you do instead, like, if you couldn't go back on the bricks?
Craig: I've been sort of thinking site supervisor, maybe. Or building maintenance. Something where I'm not lifting blocks all day. There's a course through the job centre I might look at.
Ryan: You'd be good at that, you. You've got the calm face. Supervisors need the calm face. I haven't got it, my staff say I'm blunt. I am blunt, to be fair.
Craig: *(laughs)* Aye, I was always the one keeping the peace on site, like. Someone'd be kicking off about the weather and I'd just crack on.
Ryan: See? That's a skill, that. I'm a manager, I run a bar in Manchester, and half the job's just stopping people kicking off. I'd hire you tomorrow.
Craig: Ha, I'd be no good behind a bar, I'd drop everything.
Ryan: You'd be on the door, mate. Here, I'm going to be honest, I'm living in my sister's spare room at the minute. Since the divorce. Thirty-seven, in a single bed. So you're not the only one.
Craig: No way. I'm back at me mam's. Same bedroom I had when I was a kid. Divorce and all.
Ryan: Ha! Look at us. The lads' club.
Craig: Aye. It's alright, though. Me mam does me tea, half five, mince and dumplings. Can't complain.
Ryan: My sister does tea and all. Best thing about it. Do you have kids?
Craig: Me daughter, Ellie, she's nine. Every other weekend. That's her on the wall there.
Ryan: Ah, she's got a cracking smile. Does she go to the match with you?
Craig: She's been once. She spent the whole game asking for chips.
Ryan: That's the proper football experience, that. My nephew was the same, now he's correcting my stats in the car. Give it a couple of years, she'll be—

=== CALL C0311 ===
Gemma: Hiya. Erm, can you hear me?
Gareth: Yeah. Hi.
Gemma: I'm Gemma.
Gareth: Gareth.
Gemma: *(pause)* Where are you, then?
Gareth: Basingstoke.
Gemma: Oh, right. I'm Walsall. Bloxwich.
Gareth: Right.
Gemma: *(laughs)* Sorry, I'm not very good at these.
Gareth: No, me neither. That's fine.
Gemma: Have you done many?
Gareth: This is the third. The last two did most of the talking, to be honest.
Gemma: Same. Well, my first one was nice, he was easy. Erm. What do you do?
Gareth: Structural engineer. Warehouses mainly.
Gemma: Oh, I work in one. Well, a depot. Parcel sorting, off the M6. I run the late shift.
Gareth: Big shed? Steel portal frame, probably.
Gemma: I don't know, to be fair. It's big. It's got a big roof. *(laughs)*
Gareth: Yeah, that'll be it. Most of them are. I've probably done one like it. You spend weeks on the calcs and then you drive past it and it's just a big grey box.
Gemma: Does it not feel weird, though? Like, you know it's your one?
Gareth: Bit, yeah. The kids don't care. I point and they don't look up.
Gemma: How old are they?
Gareth: Fifteen and twelve.
Gemma: Is that their school shirts behind you? On the airer?
Gareth: *(laughs)* Yeah. Ironing's not happening.
Gemma: Mine's the same, I just hang stuff up and hope. Craig does most of the tea on my shift days, my husband. I do four long shifts a week, so by the end I'm knackered, I can't even think.
Gareth: Late finish?
Gemma: Gone eleven, sometimes later. And then I can't sleep straight after, so I'm sat up with Dolly. That's her, the ear in the corner.
Gareth: Ah. What is she?
Gemma: Staffie. She's twelve, her hips have gone a bit. The vet bills, honestly.
Gareth: Yeah. Bonnie's getting there. Labrador cross. She was the kids' dog really, but it's me walks her.
Gemma: That's always how it goes, isn't it.
Gareth: Pretty much, yeah. *(pause)* I'm on my own with them, mostly. Their mum's in Reading.
Gemma: Oh. That's a lot on you, though, with work as well.
Gareth: Sort of, yeah. I muddle through. Forgot non-uniform day last week.
Gemma: *(laughs)* Oh no. My mum did that to me once and I've never let her forget it.
Gareth: Ellie won't let me forget it either.
Gemma: Ellie, that's funny, the bloke I just spoke to, his daughter's called Ellie.
Gareth: Popular one. *(pause)* Do you like it, then? Running the shift?
Gemma: Erm. I like the people, most of them. I don't like the paperwork. Or when you have to let someone go, I lie awake over that. Sorry, does that answer it?
Gareth: Yeah. I'm the same with paperwork. Timesheets.
Gemma: My team leader chases mine, to be fair. I'd be lost without her.
Gareth: Probably need one of those.
Gemma: Everyone needs one of those. *(laughs)* Would you go back to the office full-time, if they—

Gareth: Yeah. Fixtures. You're Hartlepool, then? Saw the scarf.

Craig: Ah, that's nice, that. I used to go with me dad every home game. He's gone now, so. You want to keep doing that with him, you know.

Craig: Oh, aye? I'm a brickie. Well, was. Done me back. So I've probably built the walls you've drawn, like.
Gareth: *(laughs)* Probably, yeah. Blockwork infill on a portal frame, that's half my drawings.
Craig: That's half me working life, that. Laying blocks in the rain off some drawing an engineer did in a warm office.
Gareth: Sorry about that.
Craig: Nah, you're alright. I'm thinking of going for site supervisor, maybe. If me back holds up.

Craig: Aye, I'm not a shouter. Is it—

=== CALL C0313 ===
Kerry: Hiya! There we go. Can you hear me?
Ryan: Loud and clear. Ryan, Stockport. You're Kerry, yeah? I said in the photo bit you look exactly like my sister. The calendar, the kettle, all of it.
Kerry: *(laughs)* Is that a good thing?
Ryan: It's a great thing. She's a machine, she organises everyone. I live in her spare room at the minute, so I'm biased.
Kerry: Oh, she sounds like my kind of woman. Taunton, by the way. Somerset.
Ryan: Somerset! Cider. That's all I know about Somerset, mate. Cider and Glastonbury.
Kerry: That's about right, to be fair. What do you do, then?
Ryan: I run a bar and music venue, Northern Quarter in Manchester. Eighteen staff, booking, licensing. And you're the NHS, I'm guessing? You've got the shifts on the calendar.
Kerry: Radiographer. X-ray, some CT. And yes, that calendar runs my life.
Ryan: See, I'd be useless at that. I just turn up. My rotas get done, but they get done at the last minute, do you know what I mean.
Kerry: Oh, that would drive me mad. Proper mad. I do the students' rotas at work and if someone sends me a swap the night before, I'm, no. Sorry. No.
Ryan: *(laughs)* You'd sack me.
Kerry: I wouldn't sack you, I'd just give you a checklist. Several checklists.
Ryan: I'd lose them.
Kerry: I'd laminate them.
Ryan: Ha! Okay, you win. What do you do for fun, then, when you're not laminating?
Kerry: Netball on a Tuesday, goal defence. Parkrun on a Saturday. Mostly for the coffee after, but I got a PB last week. Eight seconds.
Ryan: Eight seconds is eight seconds. I've got into padel. Have you played padel? It's like tennis but—
Kerry: In a cage, yeah, my husband's mates keep going on about it.
Ryan: It's brilliant, though! Honestly, you'd love it, you're competitive, I can tell. Goal defence, that's a competitive position, that.
Kerry: *(laughs)* Fair. I'm fairly loud watching the rugby as well. Bath, mostly. Darren just sits there and I'm up off the sofa.
Ryan: I'm the same at County. I'm the one shouting at the ref. Here, what do you do for food down there? I'm always looking for places.
Kerry: Oh, I'm not the one to ask. Same curry house every Friday, same order. Chicken tikka masala and a peshwari naan, it's lush, why change it?
Ryan: Nah, Kerry, you've got to branch out. There's a Vietnamese place round the corner from work, I've told everyone today about it, I'm like a stuck record.
Kerry: You can tell me, I'm still having the tikka masala.
Ryan: *(laughs)* Same with holidays, I bet. Same place every year?
Kerry: Bude every summer, camping with friends. Spain in the autumn, somewhere we've been before. Sun, a pool and someone else cooking. That's a holiday.
Ryan: I went to Mexico City on my own last year. Didn't book a thing. Just turned up, found the bar where the locals go.
Kerry: See, that's my nightmare. Is that what you're after, someone to tell you you're brave?
Ryan: *(laughs)* Bit, yeah. Bit—

=== CALL C0314 ===
Aleena: Hiya! Oh, there's your dog, I can see the ear. That's so cute.
Gemma: *(laughs)* Hiya. Yeah, that's Dolly. She won't get off me.
Aleena: I'm Aleena, I'm in Swansea. Not Cardiff.
Gemma: Gemma. Walsall. Erm, I wouldn't have said Cardiff.
Aleena: Everyone does, it's my thing now. Have you had Ryan yet? The Manchester one?
Gemma: No. I've had... Craig, and Gareth.
Aleena: Oh my god, he's so loud. He's nice, though. He told me recruitment was soul-destroying and I was like, you don't even know me. *(laughs)* So what do you do?
Gemma: I run a shift. At a parcel depot. Off the M6.
Aleena: Wait, parcels? Like Evri and stuff?
Gemma: Sort of, yeah. Couriers, that kind of thing.
Aleena: Stop. I sell on Vinted. I'm probably sending you stuff every week. Do you see the parcels, like, actually?
Gemma: *(laughs)* Erm, thousands of them, yeah. They come off the belt and the lads scan them. What do you send?
Aleena: Trainers, mostly. Clothes. I sold some Air Forces last week for double what I paid.
Gemma: Double? That's good, that.
Aleena: I know! So if a box of trainers goes missing, that's you, yeah?
Gemma: *(laughs)* It's not me, I promise. Usually it's a label that won't scan. You'd be surprised how many people write the postcode wrong.
Aleena: People are actually so stupid. Sorry, no, that's mean. Some people are.
Gemma: No, to be fair, some of them are. *(laughs)* Erm, are you at uni, then?
Aleena: First year, Business Management. And I work Saturdays in a sports shop. I'm the top seller on add-ons, socks and that.
Gemma: Socks. *(laughs)* I always get talked into socks.
Aleena: That's me. I'm the one doing it to you. Do you like your job, though?
Gemma: Erm. Most days. I started on the belt at nineteen, scanning, and just sort of worked up. I'm not really a manager, do you know what I mean, I just run a shift.
Aleena: No, that's literally a manager though. How many people?
Gemma: About forty.
Aleena: Forty! That's more than my whole shop. You should be saying that, not "I just run a shift". If I had forty people I'd be telling everyone.
Gemma: *(laughs)* I can tell.
Aleena: Rude! *(laughs)* No, but true. Do you have, like, holidays and stuff? Where do you go?
Gemma: Erm, Tenerife usually. Quiet all-inclusive. Booked last minute 'cause we never get round to it.
Aleena: I did Tenerife after A-levels with the girls! Not quiet, though. I want Ibiza next summer.
Gemma: I get stressed in the airport. I print everything out and then I lose it.
Aleena: Just put it on your phone. Sorry, that's obvious.
Gemma: Craig says that. My husband. I still print it.
Aleena: That's actually kind of sweet, ngl. Do you have kids, or—
Gemma: Erm, no. Not yet. Just Dolly.
Aleena: Dolly's enough, look at her. Is she—

PRIVATE, for CALL C0316 only: during this call one non-verbal thing happens on Ryan's side that Gemma sees or hears on the video, for example something visible in Ryan's room (their webcam description helps), a change in Ryan's face, a long silence, a silent laugh, a sigh, their voice catching, someone appearing behind them, or them glancing away repeatedly. It must NOT appear in the transcript in any way: no stage directions or brackets, nobody mentions it, reacts to it in words, or hints at it, and the talk carries on as if it hadn't happened. After that call's transcript, add a block '=== EVENT C0316 ===' with JSON only: {"turn": <number of the transcript line it happens at, counting that call's lines from 1>, "line_text": "<that line's text>", "who": "Ryan", "what": "<what a camera or microphone would show>"}.

text:
=== CALL C0315 ===
Aleena: Hiya! Can you hear me? I'm Aleena, I'm in Swansea.
Gareth: Yeah. Gareth. Basingstoke.
Aleena: Okay, nice. Is this your last one?
Gareth: Er, I thought the last one was. Apparently not.
Aleena: *(laughs)* Sorry to disappoint. Did you do the puzzle thing at the start, the shapes? I'm pretty sure I got them all. I was quick as well.
Gareth: Yeah. That one was alright.
Aleena: Just alright? Okay. What do you do, then?
Gareth: Structural engineer.
Aleena: Like bridges?
Gareth: Warehouses mostly. Retail units. Steel frames.
Aleena: Okay, so is that good money? Sorry, that's blunt, I just always ask. I'm doing Business, so I'm nosy about it.
Gareth: *(pause)* It's alright. Better once you're chartered. I did that late.
Aleena: Why late?
Gareth: Didn't get round to the paperwork. For a few years.
Aleena: Oh my god, years? I'd have done it in a week. I'd be like, give me the money. Sorry. Is that, like, normal for engineers?
Gareth: Not really. Just me.
Aleena: *(laughs)* Fair. I'm at Swansea Uni, first year. My dad's a nurse and my mum's a pharmacy tech, so they wanted me to do nursing or pharmacy, and I was like, no, it's not happening. I want sales. Commission, company car, Manchester or London, where the money is, do you know what I mean.
Gareth: My lad's got his GCSEs next year. He doesn't know what he wants either.
Aleena: Is he revising?
Gareth: Says he is.
Aleena: He's not. I said I was revising for two years and I was on TikTok the whole time. Still got an A in Business, though. Tell him flashcards the night before, that's what I did.
Gareth: *(laughs)* I'll pass that on. Probably not what his teachers want him hearing.
Aleena: Teachers don't know anything. Sorry, no, mine were fine actually. What's he into?
Gareth: Football, mainly. Saints. We go to St Mary's a couple of times a season, me and him.
Aleena: My dad and my brother watch the Swans. I go sometimes, but honestly, I'm there for the chips and the people-watching.
Gareth: Chips are the best bit at St Mary's too, to be fair.
Aleena: See! Is that a school shirt on the airer thing? Have you got another one?
Gareth: Yeah. Ellie. Twelve. She's on TikTok all the time, it's all she talks about.
Aleena: Okay, she's got taste. What's she watching? If she says Love Island, I'll be proud of her.
Gareth: Er, no idea, honestly. Dancing, I think. Something with a dog.
Aleena: You need to find out, that's literally dad homework. Like, ask her tonight. She'll think you're being weird, but she'll secretly love it, yeah?
Gareth: Yeah. Fair. I probably should, to be honest.
Aleena: Do you think you'd—

=== CALL C0316 ===
Ryan: Alright! Gemma, is it? Can you hear me?
Gemma: Hiya. Yeah. Yeah, I can hear you.
Ryan: Sound. Ryan, Stockport. You're my last one, so no pressure, you've got to be the best.
Gemma: *(laughs)* Oh no.
Ryan: I'm joking. Everyone's been sound. Where are you, then?
Gemma: Walsall. Bloxwich.
Ryan: Black Country! Is it true you lot say "yam yam"?
Gemma: Erm, some people say it. My granddad did. I don't really.
Ryan: Fair enough. What do you do?
Gemma: I run a shift. Parcel depot, off the M6. Late shift.
Ryan: Late shift, so you know the knackered feeling. I do lock-up at two some nights and I'm getting a cab home, costs me a fortune. How many people have you got?
Gemma: About forty.
Ryan: Forty, that's more than me. I've got eighteen and they're a nightmare. Do you get people not turning up? That's my whole life. Lads ringing in at four o'clock, "I've got a migraine." You haven't got a migraine, mate, you've got Leeds Fest tickets.
Gemma: *(laughs)* Yeah. Every Monday. Somebody's nan's always poorly.
Ryan: The nan! Classic. How do you deal with it? Do you go in hard? 'Cause I go in hard, I'm blunt, me.
Gemma: Erm, not really. I sort of try and talk to them first. Sometimes there's something going on, do you know what I mean. Had a lad last year, kept being late, and it turned out his mum was ill and he was doing everything at home. So you can't just go in hard on that.
Ryan: Yeah. No, that's fair, that. That's a better way of doing it than mine, to be honest. My sister says I've got no tact.
Gemma: Sorry, I didn't mean you were doing it wrong.

req.text:
You write transcripts of realistic video calls between strangers for a fully synthetic research dataset set in the UK. The study, in order (from its published design): a short puzzle task done alone; first impressions of the others' webcam photos; then a series of three-minute, one-on-one video calls in rounds, each person meeting the others in their group; after each call a short survey.

Call shape (from the original study's numbers): a call is cut off by a three-minute timer. A typical call has about 30 turns (most between 20 and 39) and about 570 words in total (most between 440 and 682); half of all turns are 12 words or fewer, and a quarter are 24 or more. Short acknowledgements ("yeah", "mm") count as turns too. So aim for about 570 words in about 30 turns: alongside the quick back-and-forth, people often talk in longer stretches (explaining their job, telling a story), and those long turns carry much of the call.

Guide to British conversational English (use it for how people talk; it is a description of speech, not a script):
How British people talk in casual conversation. This is a paraphrase of published descriptions of spoken British English; sources are in SOURCES.md. Use these features lightly and only where they fit the person. Never use them as a caricature.

- **Fillers.** British speakers hesitate with "erm" and "er". Women and younger speakers lean towards "erm".
- **Hedges.** "Sort of" is everywhere and steady. "Kind of" is spreading, and younger speakers use it more.
- **Politeness words.** "Please", "thank you", "thanks" and "sorry" mostly mean what they say. "Sorry" also works as a repair word (to correct yourself, or to ask someone to repeat) and can be ironic.
- **Tags at the end of a sentence.** "You know", "right", "okay", "yeah", "do you know what I mean". Among young Londoners, "innit" and "you get me" are rising. Tags depend on age and region only, never on ethnicity.
- **Echoing.** In an engaged conversation people pick up and re-use parts of each other's words.
- **Regional words and grammar** (from a recent dialect survey):
  - A bread roll is a "barm" in the North West (Manchester to Liverpool and western Lancashire), a "cob" around Nottinghamshire, a "bap" in Staffordshire, the West Midlands and North Wales, and a "batch" in Liverpool and Coventry.
  - Around Liverpool an ice lolly can be a "lolly ice".
  - The evening meal is "tea" in the North West, North East and Yorkshire, and "dinner" in the South East and London. Some people say both.
  - "Yous" or "youse" for plural "you" is common in the North East (Newcastle, Teesside), Liverpool and Scotland, less so in Manchester, and rare in York, Leeds and Sheffield.
  - "Give it me" is normal in the North West and West Midlands and widely accepted in Sheffield and York; it fades south of Birmingham, Coventry and Leicester.
  - "You was" is widely used, historically Northern and now found as far south as London.
- **Everyday British words** to draw on where they fit, without assigning them to regions: knackered or shattered, chuffed or made up, skint or brassic, mardy or stroppy, mum or mam, mate or pal, settee, sofa or couch.

req.text:
You write transcripts of realistic video calls between strangers for a fully synthetic research dataset set in the UK. The study, in order (from its published design): a short puzzle task done alone; first impressions of the others' webcam photos; then a series of three-minute, one-on-one video calls in rounds, each person meeting the others in their group; after each call a short survey.

Call shape (from the original study's numbers): a call is cut off by a three-minute timer. A typical call has about 30 turns (most between 20 and 39) and about 570 words in total (most between 440 and 682); half of all turns are 12 words or fewer, and a quarter are 24 or more. Short acknowledgements ("yeah", "mm") count as turns too. So aim for about 570 words in about 30 turns: alongside the quick back-and-forth, people often talk in longer stretches (explaining their job, telling a story), and those long turns carry much of the call.

Guide to British conversational English (use it for how people talk; it is a description of speech, not a script):
How British people talk in casual conversation. This is a paraphrase of published descriptions of spoken British English; sources are in SOURCES.md. Use these features lightly and only where they fit the person. Never use them as a caricature.

- **Fillers.** British speakers hesitate with "erm" and "er". Women and younger speakers lean towards "erm".
- **Hedges.** "Sort of" is everywhere and steady. "Kind of" is spreading, and younger speakers use it more.
- **Politeness words.** "Please", "thank you", "thanks" and "sorry" mostly mean what they say. "Sorry" also works as a repair word (to correct yourself, or to ask someone to repeat) and can be ironic.
- **Tags at the end of a sentence.** "You know", "right", "okay", "yeah", "do you know what I mean". Among young Londoners, "innit" and "you get me" are rising. Tags depend on age and region only, never on ethnicity.
- **Echoing.** In an engaged conversation people pick up and re-use parts of each other's words.
- **Regional words and grammar** (from a recent dialect survey):
  - A bread roll is a "barm" in the North West (Manchester to Liverpool and western Lancashire), a "cob" around Nottinghamshire, a "bap" in Staffordshire, the West Midlands and North Wales, and a "batch" in Liverpool and Coventry.
  - Around Liverpool an ice lolly can be a "lolly ice".
  - The evening meal is "tea" in the North West, North East and Yorkshire, and "dinner" in the South East and London. Some people say both.
  - "Yous" or "youse" for plural "you" is common in the North East (Newcastle, Teesside), Liverpool and Scotland, less so in Manchester, and rare in York, Leeds and Sheffield.
  - "Give it me" is normal in the North West and West Midlands and widely accepted in Sheffield and York; it fades south of Birmingham, Coventry and Leicester.
  - "You was" is widely used, historically Northern and now found as far south as London.
- **Everyday British words** to draw on where they fit, without assigning them to regions: knackered or shattered, chuffed or made up, skint or brassic, mardy or stroppy, mum or mam, mate or pal, settee, sofa or couch.

The group (session S39). Persona cards, including the webcam photo each person was rated on:

P204 (Sana; transcript label: Sana):
- first name: Sana
- age: 27
- lives in: Bolton, North West England
- occupation: Part-time packing operative at an online fashion distribution warehouse on an industrial estate near Bolton. She works about 24 hours a week over three or four shifts, picking, packing and labelling parcels.
- education detail: Finished intermediate (FA) at a girls' college in Lahore and started a BA but left when she got married. After moving to the UK she did ESOL courses up to Level 1 at Bolton College. She started a beauty and lash course online last year and has not finished it.
- household: Lives with her husband Imran (31, a Bolton-born multi-drop delivery driver) in a rented two-bed terraced house in Daubhill. There are no children yet. They moved out of his parents' house, a few streets away, about eighteen months ago, and she still goes round there most days.
- cultural background: Born and raised in Lahore, Pakistan, in a big, lively family with three sisters. She married Imran, a cousin of a family friend, at 20 and came to the UK on a spouse visa at 21. She has now been in Bolton six years and holds settled status. She is Muslim and fairly observant in a relaxed way. She wears a hijab, prays when she can, and fasts in Ramadan, though she admits she's not the most regular. Weddings, Eid and family gatherings are the high points of her year. She speaks Punjabi and Urdu at home and with family, and English at work and with friends.
- professional persona: Sees the warehouse job as money, not a career. She likes the women she works with and spends shifts chatting rather than chasing pick rates, and she has had a couple of warnings about being late and about her phone. She's good at getting people on side, swapping shifts, and talking her way out of trouble with supervisors. She has rung in sick on days she wasn't, and doesn't feel bad about it.
- sports persona: Not sporty at all. She joined a ladies-only gym with a friend, went about five times, and kept the membership going for months before cancelling. She walks a fair bit, to the shops, to her mother-in-law's and round Queen's Park in summer, and is naturally healthy without trying.
- arts persona: Not interested in galleries, theatre or books. She watches Pakistani dramas on YouTube and loves Bollywood films and Punjabi songs. She is on TikTok and Instagram constantly, mostly makeup, fashion and wedding content. She does mehndi designs for friends and family before weddings and is proud of it.
- travel persona: Goes back to Lahore every couple of years for a month or so, usually around a family wedding, and takes suitcases full of gifts and clothes. She went to Dubai once with Imran and his sister and still talks about the malls. She wants to go to Turkey or the Maldives mainly for the photos, but money and Imran's work keep putting it off.
- culinary persona: Cooks Pakistani food most days because Imran expects it: chicken karahi, daal, aloo gobi, roti. She learned more from her mother-in-law than from her own mum. She gets bored of cooking and pushes for takeaways, Nando's or a dessert parlour on Derby Street. She says 'tea' for the evening meal now like everyone at work, and has picked up 'barm' for a bread roll.
- hobbies and interests: watching Pakistani dramas on YouTube, TikTok and Instagram (makeup, modest fashion, wedding content), doing mehndi for weddings and Eid, shopping at the Trafford Centre and Asian clothes shops in Bolton and Rusholme, makeup and lashes, going round to friends' and sisters-in-law's houses, voice notes and long phone calls with her sisters in Lahore
- skills: fluent Punjabi and Urdu, conversational English, mehndi application, makeup and lash application (self-taught, partly trained), fast parcel packing when she's bothered, chatting to anyone and making friends quickly, haggling and finding deals on designer-looking clothes and bags
- career goals: Vague and changeable. She talks about finishing her lash course and running a home beauty and mehndi business from Instagram, with 'proper' bookings and a nice room set up for clients. She wants to earn enough to buy branded handbags without Imran moaning. She has no real plan or timeline and tends to start things and drop them.
- voice: Warm, chatty and quick. She talks a lot and laughs easily. Her English is fluent for everyday things but clearly second-language, with a Pakistani accent, Urdu or Punjabi words dropped in when she's excited ('acha', 'yaar'), and occasional grammar slips like 'he was telling me yesterday' or 'you was there'. She has picked up a few Bolton bits from work, such as 'tea' for the evening meal, 'knackered' and 'love', but nothing broad. She says 'erm' and 'you know' a lot, and 'sort of' sometimes. If she doesn't understand a question she says 'sorry, what?' and laughs it off. She can't stand silence and fills it with stories, often going off on a tangent about her sister-in-law or a wedding. She can get flustered and anxious if a question feels like a test.
- typing: Mostly lowercase, little punctuation, apostrophes usually missing (dont, im, its). Uses 'u', 'ur', 'ok', 'lol', 'tbh' and the odd emoji if allowed. Answers are short and sometimes misspelled, typed fast on her phone. She skims instructions and sometimes answers the question she thinks is being asked.
- with strangers: Friendly and open straight away, complimentary, and keen to be liked. She asks the other person questions and shares quite a lot quite fast. She likes to come across as a bit more comfortable and well-off than she is, and will say whatever seems to please. Underneath she can be nervous about getting things 'wrong'.
- small things: her shift got changed again and she's knackered, a new lip liner she got from TikTok Shop, a cousin's wedding coming up and what she's wearing, Imran working late on deliveries, her mother-in-law's karahi being better than hers, the weather being rubbish compared to Lahore, a Pakistani drama everyone at work is watching
- deeper things: pressure from her in-laws about when they're having children, and her own worry because it hasn't happened yet, missing her mum and sisters badly, and crying after video calls, feeling she married young and didn't get to finish her degree, money arguments with Imran about her spending and credit card, feeling lonely in her first years in Bolton, when her English wasn't good, worrying that people at work look down on her
- webcam photo: Phone propped on a stand at chest height, angled slightly upward, in the evening. Her face is lit by a small ring light, which shows as a circle in her pupils, with a warm table lamp off to the right. She is a young South Asian woman with full makeup: winged eyeliner, false lashes, contoured cheeks and a nude-brown lip. She is smiling widely with her head tilted slightly. She wears a dusty pink chiffon hijab wrapped loosely and pinned at the side, and a cream knitted jumper. No glasses. Behind her is a grey crushed-velvet sofa with silver cushions and a fluffy white throw. On the magnolia wall above it hangs a large mirror with a crystal-effect frame and a framed gold Arabic calligraphy print of Ayat al-Kursi. A glimpse of a doorway on the left shows a hallway with a coat on a hook.

P205 (Joanne; transcript label: Joanne):
- first name: Joanne
- age: 55
- lives in: Arnold, Nottinghamshire, East Midlands
- occupation: Part-time school office administrator at a primary school (about 25 hours a week, term-time, mornings and early afternoons)
- education detail: Left a local comprehensive in 1986 with five O-levels, including English and maths. Did an RSA typing certificate at evening college, then an NVQ Level 3 in Business Administration through work in her thirties. She has also done in-house first aid and safeguarding training at the school.
- household: Lives with her husband Steve, 57, a self-employed electrician, in a three-bed semi they've owned since 1998. Their daughter Becky, 28, lives in Leeds and their son Liam, 25, rents a flat in Derby. Both visit most weekends or every other weekend. They have an elderly Border terrier called Pickle.
- cultural background: White British, born and raised in Nottingham. Her dad worked at Raleigh and her mum was a dinner lady. Not religious, though the kids went to a C of E primary and she still enjoys the Christmas carol service there. She is very much a Nottingham person: she goes to Goose Fair every October, has strong opinions on Forest, and still calls the city centre 'town'.
- professional persona: She's the first face parents see in the morning and the one who knows where everything is. She deals with dinner money, absence calls, the photocopier, and the odd upset Year 2 child who needs a plaster and a chat. She's chatty and warm but straight with people. If a parent is being unreasonable she'll tell them kindly but plainly. She's well organised for the things that matter, like registers and safeguarding paperwork, but her desk is a bit of a mess and she runs on sticky notes.
- sports persona: A casual Nottingham Forest fan who goes to the City Ground a few times a season with Steve and Liam. She did Couch to 5K a few years back and now does parkrun at Colwick Park most Saturdays, chatting all the way round rather than chasing times. She walks Pickle every evening.
- arts persona: She likes a good night out more than anything highbrow. She goes to musicals at the Theatre Royal with her sister, comedy at the Royal Concert Hall, and the odd tribute act at a local pub. She reads crime thrillers on holiday and watches Strictly, Gogglebox and whatever drama everyone at work is talking about.
- travel persona: Mostly a week in the sun, often Tenerife or the Algarve, plus long weekends in a cottage or caravan in Norfolk, Skegness or the Peak District. She and Steve did a two-week trip to New York and Boston for their 25th anniversary and she still talks about it. She'd like to do a Canadian Rockies trip once Steve slows down with work.
- culinary persona: A solid, unfussy home cook. Her repertoire is shepherd's pie, chilli, a roast on Sundays when the kids come, and a big pan of soup in winter. Friday is chippy tea. She buys cobs from the bakery on Front Street, and a pork pie and mushy peas at Goose Fair is non-negotiable. She's tried a couple of air fryer recipes off Facebook with mixed results.
- hobbies and interests: Saturday parkrun at Colwick, Walking the dog around Arnot Hill Park, Pub quiz on Thursdays with a group of friends, Musicals and comedy nights, Watching Forest, Organising the school staff night out and Christmas do, Gardening, mainly hanging baskets and pots
- skills: Fast, accurate typing, Microsoft Office and school management systems (Arbor, previously SIMS), Calming down upset children and stressed parents, First aid, Remembering names and faces, Organising events and collections, Handling awkward phone calls
- career goals: Not chasing promotion. She turned down the school business manager job because she didn't want full-time hours or budget headaches. She wants to keep her part-time role until she's about 62, maybe drop a day, and help out with the PTA after that. She'd like to stay healthy and active enough to enjoy retirement with Steve.
- voice: Warm, quick and talkative, with a moderate Nottingham accent. She drops the odd 'h', says 'me' for 'my' now and again, and uses 'duck' occasionally with people she's warming to, but not every sentence. She says 'erm' when she's thinking and uses 'sort of' a lot. She ends points with 'you know' or 'do you know what I mean'. 'Mardy' and 'knackered' are natural words for her. She laughs easily, including at herself. She doesn't like silence and will fill it, often with a joke or 'sorry, I'm rambling'. She'll ask the interviewer how their day's going. She's honest even when it's unflattering, for example: 'no, I didn't do that, if I'm honest'.
- typing: Types quickly and doesn't go back to fix much. She capitalises the start of sentences most of the time but not always. She uses apostrophes properly but sometimes forgets full stops at the end. She likes exclamation marks and the odd 'lol' or 'haha'. Abbreviations are limited to 'tbh' and '&'. Her answers run longer than the form needs, e.g. 'Mostly by car tbh, the bus is ok but its every 20 mins & I'm usually running late haha'.
- with strangers: Instantly friendly and easy to talk to. She'll have told you about the dog and her daughter's new job within five minutes. She's genuinely interested in other people and asks questions back. She's unpretentious and doesn't try to impress or give the 'right' answer, and she will happily admit she doesn't know something. She isn't easily rattled; tech glitches or awkward pauses just get a laugh.
- small things: Pickle the Border terrier has gone a bit deaf and only hears the treat tin, The photocopier at work jams every Monday without fail, Her Saturday parkrun and the coffee afterwards, Thursday pub quiz, where her team always loses on the sport round, Getting cobs from the bakery on Front Street, Goose Fair and whether it's gone too expensive, Steve's van parked across the drive, Whatever's on Strictly
- deeper things: Her mum has early-stage dementia and Joanne goes round three times a week. She's practical about it but it does wear her down, She had a breast cancer scare at 50 that turned out fine, which is partly why she started running, She sometimes wonders if she undersold herself by staying in admin, but mostly she's content, She misses having the kids at home more than she lets on, She and Steve went through a rough patch in their early forties and came out of it stronger
- webcam photo: Head-and-shoulders shot from a laptop on a kitchen table, camera angled slightly upwards. The main light is daylight from a window to her left, so the right side of her face is a little shadowed. She is a white woman in her mid-fifties with a round, cheerful face, light freckles and laughter lines, smiling with her teeth showing and leaning slightly towards the screen. Her hair is shoulder-length, highlighted ash blonde with darker roots, tucked behind one ear. She wears red-framed reading glasses pushed up on her head, small gold hoop earrings, and a navy and white striped long-sleeved top. Behind her is a fitted cream kitchen with a wooden worktop. On the worktop are a kettle, a toaster and a mug tree. On the wall is a calendar with handwritten entries, and a fridge door covered in magnets holds a school newsletter and a photo of two young adults. A dog lead hangs on a hook by the back door, partly visible at the right edge of the frame.

P206 (Gareth; transcript label: Gareth):
- first name: Gareth
- age: 39
- lives in: Taunton, South West England
- occupation: Not currently working (long-term sick, on home haemodialysis). Formerly a chartered civil engineer specialising in drainage and flood defence schemes for a regional consultancy.
- education detail: A-levels in Maths, Physics and Geography at a sixth form college in Yeovil; BEng in Civil Engineering from the University of Bath; later became chartered (CEng, MICE) through his employer's training scheme in his late twenties.
- household: Lives with his partner of eleven years, Hannah, a primary school SENCo, in a three-bed semi on the edge of town that they bought together. They've never married ('always meant to, then the kidneys happened'). No children. They have an elderly Border terrier called Biscuit. The spare room has been turned into his dialysis room.
- cultural background: White British, grew up in a village near Yeovil. Dad was a farm machinery mechanic, mum worked in a GP surgery reception. Christened and confirmed Church of England, went to church as a kid; now goes to the local parish church at Christmas and Easter and the odd Sunday when he's up to it. Calls himself Christian 'in the C of E way, quietly'. First in his family to go to university.
- professional persona: Was a methodical, highly organised engineer who liked owning a project end to end: hydraulic models, planning submissions, site meetings in wellies. Known for immaculate spreadsheets and never missing a deadline. Diagnosed with IgA nephropathy at 31, managed to keep working until his kidneys failed at 36, then had to stop. Still keeps his CEng membership up and reads the trade magazine. Fairly unsentimental about the job itself but misses the status of it and being the person people came to.
- sports persona: Used to play five-a-side and cycle the Quantocks at weekends. Now his energy is too unpredictable, so he does gentle walks with the dog and physio exercises. Follows Somerset cricket closely, listens to county matches on the radio during dialysis sessions, and watches rugby with Bath as his team. Will happily talk about cricket stats for longer than anyone wants.
- arts persona: Not very arty. Likes long-form podcasts, history documentaries and the occasional crime drama with Hannah. Reads non-fiction, mostly engineering disasters, military history and biographies. Has a soft spot for brass band music from his granddad playing in one.
- travel persona: Travel is complicated now because he has to arrange holiday dialysis in advance. They've done a few UK breaks to Cornwall and the Lake District, booked around a dialysis unit. Before he got ill he liked city breaks: Amsterdam, Copenhagen, Berlin, where he'd mostly look at the canals and bridges. Pragmatic about it: 'If it's not near a unit, we don't go.'
- culinary persona: On a strict renal diet, so he's become very precise about potassium, phosphate and fluid. Weighs things, logs everything in an app. Does most of the cooking on good days, batch-cooks and labels the freezer. Misses proper cheddar and crisps. Calls the evening meal 'dinner', sometimes 'tea' when talking about his mum's.
- hobbies and interests: Following Somerset County Cricket, Building and painting model railway scenery in the garage, Walking Biscuit along the Bridgwater and Taunton canal, Podcasts on engineering failures and history, Tracking his blood results in a self-made spreadsheet, Bargain-hunting for tools and kit on eBay and Facebook Marketplace, Pub quizzes when he's well enough
- skills: Hydraulic modelling and flood risk assessment, Project and budget management, Excel to a frankly unnecessary level, Running his own home haemodialysis machine, DIY and basic plumbing, Negotiating with suppliers and getting a discount, Staying calm in a crisis
- career goals: Waiting for a kidney transplant (been on the list about two years). If it happens and goes well, he wants to get back into engineering, probably part-time or as a freelance consultant reviewing flood risk assessments from home. Has quietly thought about whether he could charge more freelance than he ever earned salaried. Realistic that it might not happen.
- voice: Steady, mid-paced, fairly low-key. Light Somerset accent: soft 'r' after vowels, 'alright' as a greeting, the odd 'proper' as in 'proper knackered'. Not broad. Uses 'sort of' a lot and the occasional 'erm' when thinking through a number or a date. Ends points with 'you know' or 'yeah'. Talks about his illness matter-of-factly, almost like a project update, and can get dry about it. Comfortable with silence. He'll just wait, or fill it with a practical question. Polite and says 'cheers' and 'sorry' easily, and will correct himself mid-sentence ('three years, sorry, two and a half') because he likes accuracy.
- typing: Proper capitals and full stops, apostrophes correct. Short, efficient answers. Gives exact figures where he can ('approx 4 hrs, 5x a week'). Uses 'approx', 'hrs', 'etc' and occasionally 'tbh'. No emojis. Rarely makes typos and goes back to fix them if he does.
- with strangers: Friendly, easygoing and accommodating. Lets the other person lead, agrees readily, doesn't argue. Comes across as calm and capable, maybe a little guarded about money, but will chat openly about his health if asked. There's a faint sense he likes to be seen as competent and can drop in his old job title. Not much fussed about awkwardness.
- small things: Biscuit refusing to walk in the rain, Somerset's batting order, Having to pause the call if the dialysis machine alarms, Being dry all day because of the fluid limit and craving a cold pint, A new bit of track for the model railway he got cheap, Hannah's school marking taking over the kitchen table, The A358 roadworks, His mum ringing every evening at the same time
- deeper things: The fear, which he rarely admits, that a transplant won't come or won't last, Feeling diminished going from chartered engineer to 'on benefits' and how much the status loss stings, Guilt that Hannah has become partly a carer and they never got round to the wedding, That he's not sure what he believes about God but finds the church building calming, A falling out with his younger brother, who was tested as a donor and wasn't a match. He suspects his brother didn't really want to be one., That he's become quite good at working the benefits and NHS systems and isn't entirely sorry about it
- webcam photo: Laptop webcam at desk height, slightly below eye level, angled up a touch. Daylight from a window to the left, with a cool cast and the right side of his face a bit shadowed. A man in his late thirties with a pale, slightly sallow complexion, faint grey shadows under his eyes, and a short, neatly trimmed brown beard flecked with grey. Short mousy-brown hair, thinning at the temples, combed to the side. No glasses. A small, polite, closed-mouth smile and a steady gaze at the camera. He's wearing a navy quarter-zip fleece over a grey T-shirt, the left sleeve pushed up, and a thin strip of surgical tape is just visible on his forearm. Behind him is a magnolia-painted spare bedroom: on the left, part of a grey home dialysis machine on a wheeled stand. On the right, a white flat-pack shelving unit holding labelled plastic storage boxes of medical supplies, a framed Institution of Civil Engineers certificate and a small Somerset CCC mug. Above the shelves is a wall calendar with handwritten entries. The corner of a dog bed is visible on the floor.

P207 (Martijn; transcript label: Martijn):
- first name: Martijn
- age: 47
- lives in: Walthamstow, London (East London)
- occupation: Associate Director and chartered structural engineer at a mid-sized engineering consultancy in Farringdon, working mainly on residential and mixed-use buildings
- education detail: MSc in Civil Engineering from TU Delft in the Netherlands; Chartered Engineer (CEng) and Member of the Institution of Structural Engineers, qualified after moving to the UK
- household: Lives alone in a two-bedroom ground-floor flat in a converted Victorian terrace, bought after his divorce six years ago. His 14-year-old daughter stays every other weekend and one night midweek, so the second bedroom is hers.

Junior engineers find him demanding but fair, and he never takes credit for their work. He regularly works 50 to 55 hours a week, mostly because he won't hand over drawings he isn't happy with. He has little patience for long meetings or for vague answers dressed up as positivity.

Gareth: Alright? Can you hear me okay?

Gareth: Do you go back much?

For the second pair, Gareth and Martijn are both engineers—Gareth in civil drainage work, Martijn in structural—and Martijn notices Gareth's ICE certificate in the background.
