18: Alison offers up that thirty-odd years of marriage hasn't made things calmer either, noting Graham's retired and started a half-finished hallway project since spring. She's 61 with a 32-year-old child.

19-23: Tendai jokes that Graham's in the same club as every other tradesperson's house, never finished, recalling how another woman mentioned her electrician partner's got a switch hanging off the wall. Alison finds it reassuring she's not alone in this. They swap notes on kids—her two grown and scattered between Bristol and south London, his stepson Kai, thirteen, whom he's raised since age four and who's just outgrown another pair of football boots.

24-29: They laugh about kids growing too fast and not listening, then Tendai shares his family's spread out too—sister in Leicester, mum still in Harare, visited every few years, staying close through WhatsApp and gospel songs. Alison reflects that even when her own mother was only forty minutes away, she didn't visit enough, concluding distance isn't really what keeps people apart.

30: Tendai asks about holidays, and Alison mentions cottages in Pembrokeshire and Northumberland, somewhere quiet with a good pub.

31: Tendai starts describing their caravan trips to Devon, noting it's far from peaceful with Kai around.

req.text:
You write transcripts of realistic video calls between strangers for a fully synthetic research dataset set in the UK. The study, in order (from its published design): a short puzzle task done alone; first impressions of the others' webcam photos; then a series of three-minute, one-on-one video calls in rounds, each person meeting the others in their group; after each call a short survey.

Call shape (from the original study's numbers): a call is cut off by a three-minute timer. A typical call has about 30 turns (most between 20 and 39) and about 570 words in total (most between 440 and 682); half of all turns are 12 words or fewer, and a quarter are 24 or more. Short acknowledgements ("yeah", "mm") count as turns too. So aim for about 570 words in about 30 turns: alongside the quick back-and-forth, people often talk in longer stretches (explaining their job, telling a story), and those long turns carry much of the call.

Guide to British conversational English (use it for how people talk; it is a description of speech, not a script):
How British people talk in casual conversation. This is a paraphrase of published descriptions of spoken British English; sources are in SOURCES.md. Use these features lightly and only where they fit the person. Never use them as a caricature.

- **Fillers.** British speakers hesitate with "erm" and "er". Women and younger speakers lean towards "erm".
- **Hedges.** "Sort of" is everywhere and steady. "Kind of" is spreading, and younger speakers use it more.
- **Politeness words.** "Please", "thank you", "thanks" and "sorry" mostly mean what they say. "Sorry" also works as a repair word (to correct yourself, or to ask someone to repeat) and can be ironic.
- **Tags at the end of a sentence.** "You know", "right", "okay", "yeah", "do you know what I mean". Among young Londoners, "innit" and "you get me" are rising. Tags depend on age and region only, never on ethnicity.
- **Echoing.** In an engaged conversation people pick up and re-use parts of each other's words.
- **Regional words and grammar** (from a recent dialect survey):
  - A bread roll is a "barm" in the North West (Manchester to Liverpool and western Lancashire), a "cob" around Nottinghamshire, a "bap" in Staffordshire, the West Midlands and North Wales, and a "batch" in Liverpool and Coventry.
  - Around Liverpool an ice lolly can be a "lolly ice".
  - The evening meal is "tea" in the North West, North East and Yorkshire, and "dinner" in the South East and London. Some people say both.
  - "Yous" or "youse" for plural "you" is common in the North East (Newcastle, Teesside), Liverpool and Scotland, less so in Manchester, and rare in York, Leeds and Sheffield.
  - "Give it me" is normal in the North West and West Midlands and widely accepted in Sheffield and York; it fades south of Birmingham, Coventry and Leicester.
  - "You was" is widely used, historically Northern and now found as far south as London.
- **Everyday British words** to draw on where they fit, without assigning them to regions: knackered or shattered, chuffed or made up, skint or brassic, mardy or stroppy, mum or mam, mate or pal, settee, sofa or couch.

The group (session S42). Persona cards, including the webcam photo each person was rated on:

P221 (Darren; transcript label: Darren):
- first name: Darren
- age: 50
- lives in: Basingstoke, South East
- occupation: Branch manager at a builders' merchants (timber, plumbing and heavy-side supplies), running a yard and trade counter with about 14 staff
- education detail: Left a comprehensive in Basingstoke at 16 with a handful of GCSEs. He started a BTEC in business at the local college but dropped out after a year to take a job on a trade counter. He has done a few in-house management courses over the years and says 'I'm more learn-on-the-job, me.'
- household: Lives in a four-bed 1990s detached house on an estate on the edge of town with his wife Nicola (48, part-time receptionist at a dental practice) and their daughter Ellie (16, doing GCSEs). Their son Jake (19) is at university in Nottingham and comes home for holidays. There is a black Labrador called Murphy.
- cultural background: White British, born and raised in Basingstoke. His dad sold cars and his mum worked in a bank branch. He is not religious and never has been. It doesn't come up, and he finds it a bit odd when people make a big thing of it either way. His outlook is conventional, comfortable home-counties working-to-middle class. He reads the news on his phone, mostly headlines and the sport.
- professional persona: A confident, talk-first manager who is good with trade customers and likes being the face of the branch. He has been with the same merchant chain for over 20 years. He enjoys the perks: the company Audi, the fuel card and the regional awards dinner. He is quietly pleased when his branch beats others on the league table. He is weaker on admin and leans heavily on his assistant manager for rotas, compliance paperwork and stock audits. He tends to leave reports to the last minute. He is not above rounding numbers in his favour or bending a returns policy for a good account. He doesn't lose his head when a delivery goes wrong or a customer kicks off.
- sports persona: A lifelong Southampton fan who watches most games on TV or at the pub and goes to St Mary's a few times a season with a mate. He played five-a-side until his early forties. Now he plays golf at a pay-and-play course roughly once a month, badly, and enjoys the bar afterwards more than the round. He follows the Grand Prix casually.
- arts persona: Not really his thing. He watches whatever crime drama or reality show Nicola has on, likes a big action film, and listens to Heart or Absolute 80s in the car. His last gig was a tribute act at the local pub. He hasn't been to a museum since the kids were small and doesn't feel he's missing out.
- travel persona: A creature of habit. He goes on a week or two in an all-inclusive in Spain, the Canaries or the Algarve most summers, sometimes back to the same hotel. He prefers a pool and a decent bar to sightseeing. He has been on a couple of lads' golf weekends in Portugal, and once went to Florida with the kids, which he still talks about. He isn't keen on anywhere 'too foreign' or a hassle to get to.
- culinary persona: Meat-and-two-veg. He calls the evening meal 'dinner'. He likes a steak, a Sunday roast at the pub and a takeaway curry on a Friday. He cooks on the barbecue in summer and not much otherwise. He drinks lager and the odd red with a steak, and won't try anything he can't pronounce.
- hobbies and interests: Watching Southampton, Occasional golf, Cars, especially browsing what he'll get as his next company car, Pub quiz night now and then with mates, Walking the dog, mostly at weekends, Barbecues in the summer, Fantasy Premier League with work lads
- skills: Dealing with trade customers and smoothing over complaints, Negotiating with suppliers and reps, Staying calm in a crisis on the yard, Forklift licence (lapsed), Knowing building materials and pricing inside out, Talking up a good result to head office
- career goals: He'd like an area manager role before he's 55, mainly for the money, the status and a better car. He's been overlooked once and reckons it was politics. If that doesn't happen, he's happy enough to see it out at the branch, pay the mortgage off and retire early-ish somewhere with a golf course.
- voice: Relaxed, fairly loud and chatty, with a mild southern accent: dropped t's in words like 'bottle' and 'a lot of', and 'yeah' as a default response. He talks at a steady clip and often over-explains with work anecdotes. He uses 'mate' with men, says 'sort of' a lot and the odd 'er' when thinking. He tags sentences with 'you know' or 'right'. He fills silences himself rather than waiting, usually with a joke or 'anyway, yeah'. He is not bothered by awkwardness.
- typing: Quick and careless. Mostly lowercase with no full stop at the end, and apostrophes often missed ('dont', 'its'). The occasional 'tbh' or 'lol'. Short answers like 'yeah fine' or 'not really bothered'. He doesn't reread before submitting, so the odd typo stays in.
- with strangers: Friendly and easy to talk to straight away, with a bit of a salesman's confidence. He jokes early and asks a couple of questions back, though he steers the conversation to his own stories. He comes across as likeable and unflappable, if a little pleased with himself, and he gets bored quickly if things get too abstract.
- small things: The dog ate a tea towel last week, Traffic on the M3 has been a nightmare with the roadworks, Saints were rubbish on Saturday, Thinking about getting a hot tub for the garden, His daughter's mocks are coming up, A rep took him out for a steak lunch, Fuel prices, Got done by a speed camera on the A33 again
- deeper things: Being passed over for area manager two years ago still annoys him more than he lets on, His dad walked out when he was 14 and they barely speak; he doesn't feel much about it either way and says so, His mum is in a care home in Eastbourne, and he knows he doesn't visit as often as he should, He sometimes wonders whether he and Nicola have much to talk about once Ellie leaves home, Money's tighter than the car and holidays suggest, and he's put a bit more on credit cards than Nicola knows
- webcam photo: Laptop webcam at a slightly low angle, so the camera looks up at him a little. He sits at a dining table, framed from mid-chest up, a bit off-centre to the left. He is a broad-faced white man with short, greying brown hair clipped at the sides and thinning on top, light stubble, and a slight sunburn on his nose and forehead. He wears no glasses. He has an easy half-smile and is looking just above the camera. He is wearing a navy quarter-zip fleet jumper with a small embroidered company logo on the chest. The lighting is evening ceiling light, warm and a bit flat, with some glare on his forehead. Behind him is an open-plan kitchen-diner: grey gloss kitchen units, a large black American-style fridge freezer with a calendar and takeaway menus held on by magnets, a kettle and a toaster on the worktop, a bowl with keys and a car fob in it, and a dog lead hanging off a cupboard handle. Part of a black Labrador's back is visible on a dog bed in the bottom right corner.

P222 (Donna; transcript label: Donna):
- first name: Donna
- age: 45
- lives in: Plumstead, south-east London
- occupation: Not currently working. Last job was an early-morning office cleaner on a contract in Woolwich, which ended about eight months ago. She is on Universal Credit and supposed to be looking for cleaning or kitchen porter work, though she isn't looking very hard.
- education detail: Left a comprehensive in Woolwich at 16 with four GCSEs at low grades and no further qualifications. She started a college catering course at 17 and dropped out in the first term. She did a mandatory food hygiene certificate through a job years ago and has no idea where the paperwork is.
- household: Lives in a two-bedroom housing association flat on an estate with her son Kyle (16, in Year 11) and her daughter Mia (11, just started secondary). Never married. The kids have different dads. One sends money irregularly and the other doesn't, and she has stopped chasing him. Her mum lives fifteen minutes away in Abbey Wood and helps out with Mia sometimes.
- cultural background: White British, born and raised in south-east London. Her family are Woolwich and Plumstead going back a couple of generations, and her grandad worked at the Arsenal before it shut. She has no religion and only ever went to church for weddings and funerals. She sees herself as ordinary London working class and doesn't think about it beyond that.
- professional persona: A reliable enough worker once she's actually there, but bad at the admin around a job. She misses texts about shift changes, loses payslips and forgets to sign things. She doesn't get on with supervisors who micromanage and has walked out of one job after a row. She is honest to a fault and will tell you straight if she's broken something or hasn't done it. She prefers early shifts on her own with headphones in, away from people.
- sports persona: Doesn't do sport and never has. She walks everywhere because she doesn't drive and the buses annoy her, so she's on her feet a lot and is fit without trying. She will half-watch football if Kyle has it on and nominally supports Charlton because her dad did.
- arts persona: Watches the soaps (EastEnders mainly) and reality TV like Married at First Sight or Gogglebox, usually with her phone in her hand. She listens to Magic FM or old garage and R&B from when she was young. She hasn't read a book since school and hasn't been to a museum or a show in years. She isn't against it, it just isn't for her.
- travel persona: Hardly travels. A caravan in Kent or Camber Sands a couple of times when the kids were small, and one trip to Benidorm with a mate about twelve years ago. She doesn't have a valid passport. Money is the main reason, but she also isn't bothered. She likes knowing where things are.
- culinary persona: Cooks the same handful of things: spag bol, chicken and chips, fish fingers, jacket potatoes, beans on toast. She does a big shop at Lidl when she remembers and the Co-op the rest of the time. Some weeks it's a lot of oven food. She treats herself to a Chinese takeaway on a Friday if money allows and always calls the evening meal dinner.
- hobbies and interests: soaps and reality TV, scrolling TikTok and local Facebook groups, walking, mostly out of necessity, scratchcards now and then, sitting in the garden at her mum's in summer, online research studies and surveys for a bit of extra money
- skills: cleaning quickly and thoroughly when she's in the zone, stretching a small budget, though not with any system, dealing with the council and the school without being fobbed off, honest, straight talking, being calm and practical in an actual emergency
- career goals: No real career plan. She'd like a steady early-morning cleaning or school kitchen job, ideally term-time, so she's home when Mia is. She's vaguely thought about redoing the food hygiene certificate and keeps not doing it. Her main goal is just being less skint.
- voice: London accent, ordinary south-east London rather than broad. Short answers, a fairly flat delivery and not much small talk. She starts things with 'erm' and uses 'sort of' and 'do you know what I mean' now and then, and sometimes says 'you was' without thinking. She says 'yeah, no' and 'to be fair'. If she doesn't get a question she'll say 'sorry, what was that?' rather than guess. She is comfortable with silence and will just wait for you to carry on rather than fill it. She can be blunt, for example 'no, I don't really do that'. She warms up slightly if you ask about her kids.
- typing: Mostly lowercase and doesn't bother capitalising 'i'. Few or no apostrophes ('dont', 'im', 'its'). Short answers, sometimes one word, with commas instead of full stops or no punctuation at all. Uses 'n' for 'and' and 'cos'. Occasional typos she doesn't correct. No emojis on a form.
- with strangers: Guarded and a bit closed. She's polite enough, but doesn't smile much or ask anything back, and can come across as uninterested or slightly prickly. She doesn't put on a front or exaggerate. If she thinks a question is stupid her tone shows it. She is straightforward and won't pretend to be more than she is, which people tend to find refreshing once they get past the flatness.
- small things: the 53 bus being late again, Mia losing her blazer already, Kyle being on his PlayStation till all hours, the lift in the block being broken, how much the electric's gone up, what happened on EastEnders, her mum ringing her five times a day, forgetting a Jobcentre appointment and having to rearrange
- deeper things: worrying about Kyle's GCSEs and him drifting, because she wants him to do better than she did, feeling embarrassed about being on Universal Credit when she's always worked, still being angry with Mia's dad for walking off and never paying anything, knowing she's disorganised and feeling bad about it, but not knowing how to change, being lonely sometimes since most of her old mates moved out to Kent or Essex, her dad dying six years ago and not really talking about it
- webcam photo: A slightly low-angled shot from a laptop on a kitchen table, so the ceiling is partly in frame. Daytime, lit flatly by a window off to the left plus an overhead light, which makes her face a bit washed out. A white woman in her mid-forties with a pale complexion and light freckles. Dark blonde hair with grown-out lighter ends, scraped back in a claw clip with loose bits at the front. No glasses. Little or no makeup, slight shadows under her eyes. Neutral, slightly guarded expression, mouth closed, looking just below the camera. She wears a grey zip-up hoodie over a black T-shirt and small gold hoop earrings. Behind her is an open-plan kitchen-living area: a white kitchen cupboard with one door not quite shut, a kettle and a cluttered worktop with a bread bag, a few unopened envelopes and a school letter. Part of a grey fabric sofa with a crumpled throw is visible, along with a radiator with a school polo shirt drying on it and a framed school photo of two children on the wall, slightly crooked.

P223 (Joanne; transcript label: Joanne):
- first name: Joanne
- age: 46
- lives in: Crawley, South East England
- occupation: Not currently in paid work. Previously an accounts and purchase-ledger administrator for 17 years at a builders' merchants near Gatwick, made redundant in early 2023 when the firm was bought out and moved its back office to Milton Keynes.
- education detail: Left Hazelwick-type local comprehensive at 16 with GCSEs, did a one-year BTEC in Business Administration at the local college, later completed an AAT Level 2 bookkeeping certificate through work in her late twenties.
- household: Lives with her parents, Pauline (73) and Roy (76), who have been married 50 years, in their three-bed ex-council semi in Tilgate. She has the back bedroom she moved back into in her mid-thirties after a long relationship ended, and she never moved out again. Her older brother lives in Horsham with his family. There's an elderly Jack Russell called Bobby.
- cultural background: White British, born at Crawley Hospital, family originally from south London and moved out to the new town in the 1960s. Goes with her mum to a small Spiritualist church on a Wednesday evening most weeks. She was brought up in it, believes in it quietly and doesn't like discussing it with people who'd take the mickey.
- professional persona: Reliable, private, prefers to be left alone to get on with it. Good with invoices, supplier statements and chasing payments by email rather than phone. Found the redundancy a real shock and has been applying for admin roles on Indeed in fits and starts, but dreads interviews and has turned down a couple of agency temp offers because they meant phones and reception work. Does the online research panel for a bit of money and something to do.
- sports persona: Not sporty. Walks Bobby round Tilgate Park most mornings, same route. Will have the snooker on in the background with her dad. No interest in football and finds the noise of it irritating.
- arts persona: Watches a lot of TV: Coronation Street, Emmerdale, repeats of Midsomer Murders, and true-crime documentaries she says she shouldn't watch because they keep her up. Listens to Heart or Magic FM. Reads the odd Martina Cole or Peter James paperback from the charity shop. Doesn't see the point of galleries or theatre.
- travel persona: Hasn't been abroad since a Majorca holiday in 2014 that she didn't enjoy (too hot, upset stomach). Goes with her parents to the same caravan park on the Isle of Wight every September. Gets anxious about travelling and plans everything in advance. Hates the idea of flying even though she lives next to Gatwick.
- culinary persona: Plain home cooking. Her mum does most of the dinners and Joanne helps: shepherd's pie, roast on Sunday, fish on Friday from the chippy. Doesn't like spicy food or 'anything fancy'. Will eat a mild chicken korma at a push. Bakes a Victoria sponge for birthdays. Drinks a lot of tea, and a glass of rosé on a Saturday.
- hobbies and interests: Dog walking in Tilgate Park, Word searches and the puzzles in her mum's magazines, Watching soaps and crime dramas, Spiritualist church on Wednesdays, Facebook groups about Crawley local news and Jack Russells, Online survey and research panels
- skills: Purchase and sales ledger, reconciling statements, Sage accounting software and Excel basics, Accurate data entry and careful with figures, Keeping on top of household bills and paperwork for her parents, Baking
- career goals: Wants another back-office admin or accounts job, ideally part-time, local, and with a small team where she wouldn't have to be on the phones much. Not ambitious beyond that. Mostly she wants to feel she's earning her keep again and not be asked by relatives what she's 'doing with herself'.
- voice: Quiet, fairly flat South East accent with some glottal stops ('a bi' of'), nothing broad. Speaks slowly and briefly, and often answers in a sentence then stops. Uses 'erm' a lot at the start of answers and 'sort of' as a hedge. Says 'dinner' for the evening meal, 'knackered', and 'mum'. Apologises when she's misheard something ('sorry, what was that?'). Doesn't fill silences, so she'll wait for the next question rather than elaborate. If pushed on something she disagrees with, she can be a bit curt ('No, I don't think so, really.'). Sighs or laughs nervously when a question is personal.
- typing: Types properly from her office years: capital at the start, full stops, apostrophes mostly right. Answers are short, often one line. Occasionally 'dont' slips through when rushing. No emojis, no text-speak apart from the odd 'etc'. Will write 'Not really sure' or 'Prefer not to say' rather than explain.
- with strangers: Reserved and a bit guarded at first. She can seem cool or unfriendly, but it's mostly nerves. Gives minimal answers, doesn't ask questions back, and is quick to notice if she thinks she's being patronised. Warms up slightly if the topic is something practical or about the dog, but never really chatty. Gets flustered if technology goes wrong on the call.
- small things: Bobby the dog's dodgy back leg and the vet bills, The planes from Gatwick being louder lately, Parking around the hospital being a nightmare, What's happening on Corrie, Her dad's allotment tomatoes, Prices at the big Tesco going up, Being knackered after a bad night's sleep
- deeper things: The redundancy knocked her confidence badly and she worries she'll never get another job at her age, Embarrassment about living with her parents at 46, and fear of what happens when they're gone, A nine-year relationship that ended when she was 35. He married someone else within two years, Her nan's death and the comfort she took from a medium's message at church, Panic attacks she's had since her twenties, which she's never seen anyone about, Feeling her brother gets the credit while she does the caring
- webcam photo: Laptop webcam shot from slightly below, with the laptop on a dressing table in a small bedroom. Joanne is centred, framed from mid-chest up, leaning a little away from the screen. Light comes from a window to her left, so one side of her face is brighter and there's a faint grey cast from the overcast day. She has a pale, slightly round face with fine lines around the eyes and a closed-mouth, polite but tight smile. Her shoulder-length mid-brown hair has some grey at the parting and is tucked behind one ear. No glasses. She's wearing a navy fleece zipped halfway over a lilac T-shirt and a thin gold chain. Behind her is a magnolia wall with a framed photo of a Jack Russell and a small print of a guardian angel. The edge of a single bed shows with a floral duvet and two cushions, plus a white wardrobe door with a dressing gown hanging on a hook. A plastic storage box with folders sits on top of the wardrobe.

P224 (Gareth; transcript label: Gareth):
- first name: Gareth
- age: 47
- lives in: Andover, Hampshire, South East England
- occupation: Operations Director at a regional warehousing and distribution company with three sites along the M3/A303 corridor, responsible for about 180 staff, the shift rota, health and safety, and the fleet contract.
- education detail: A-levels in Maths, Economics and Geography at a sixth-form college in Basingstoke, then a BSc in Business Management at a polytechnic-turned-university in the Midlands. Later did an IOSH Managing Safely course and a company-funded CMI Level 5 certificate in his thirties. He considers the CMI one 'mostly box-ticking'.
- household: Lives with his wife Karen (46), who works part-time as a practice manager at a GP surgery, and their son Josh (16), who is doing his GCSEs. Their daughter Ellie (19) is at university in Southampton and comes home most holidays. A four-bedroom 1990s detached house on an estate on the edge of town, with a mortgage about ten years from being paid off. No pets since the family dog died two years ago.
- cultural background: White British, born in Basingstoke to a father who was a heating engineer and a mother who worked in a building society branch. Raised Church of England. He still counts himself a Christian and goes to the local parish church at Christmas, Easter and the odd family service, more because Karen goes than from strong conviction, but he wouldn't describe himself as anything else. Grew up comfortable but not well-off, and is a bit uneasy being described as 'senior management'.
- professional persona: Joined the company 19 years ago as a shift manager and worked up. He is known for being straight and hard to flannel: he will tell a supplier or a director to their face that something won't work. Staff find him fair but not warm. He doesn't do 'motivational' talks and gets visibly impatient in long meetings and with consultants. He regularly does 50 to 55 hours: in early for the handover, a walk round the floor most days, and emails at night. He doesn't take credit he hasn't earned and has turned down a company car upgrade because he thought it looked bad during a pay freeze.
- sports persona: Watches football, a lifelong Southampton supporter. He has a season ticket he uses about half the time, and goes with an old school friend rather than a big group. Runs three or four times a week before work, usually the same 5k or 8k route, and does the odd local 10k but isn't bothered about times. Played five-a-side until his late thirties. Watches the cricket highlights in summer.
- arts persona: Very little interest. He goes to the cinema a couple of times a year when Karen or Josh picks something, usually an action film. He has no time for galleries or theatre and will say so, though he went to Ellie's school productions without complaint. Listens to the same music he did at 20 (Oasis, Ocean Colour Scene, some Springsteen) on the drive to work. Reads the occasional military history or sports autobiography.
- travel persona: Creature of habit. Most summers it's two weeks at the same family-run villa complex in the Algarve they've been going to for about eight years, plus a week in Cornwall or Devon at half-term. He doesn't see the point of 'doing' a city break and finds airports a hassle. Has been to the US once, Florida with the kids, and found it 'too much'. Drives everywhere in the UK rather than taking trains.
- culinary persona: Plain eater. He likes a roast on Sunday, which he usually cooks himself and is quietly proud of, along with steak, chilli and a decent curry from the same takeaway. He's suspicious of anything with 'foam' or 'jus' on the menu. Calls the evening meal 'dinner'. Drinks bitter or a lager at the pub, a glass of red at home on a Friday, rarely more. Takes a packed lunch to work most days because the canteen is 'a rip-off'.
- hobbies and interests: Running the same routes before work, Following Southampton FC and listening to football phone-ins in the car, Keeping the garden and lawn tidy, with mild obsession about the edges, DIY around the house: shelves, fence panels, tiling the downstairs loo, Washing and looking after his car at weekends, Watching war documentaries and Top Gear-type programmes, The occasional pint at a local pub with one or two old friends
- skills: Shift planning and staff rostering, Health and safety management and incident investigation, Negotiating with hauliers and suppliers, Reading a P&L and spotting where money is leaking, Forklift-licensed from his early days, Basic plumbing and carpentry, Cooking a reliable Sunday roast
- career goals: Not chasing much more. He'd like to see the third site's new racking project through and keep his team intact. He has been sounded out about a group-level role, but it would mean more travel and more politics, and he isn't keen. He wants to pay off the mortgage, help both kids through university, and maybe step down to four days a week in his mid-fifties. Says he'd 'rather be good at this job than average at a bigger one'.
- voice: Southern English, Hampshire, fairly neutral middle-class with a slightly flat, clipped delivery. He speaks at a measured pace and keeps answers short. He pauses with 'er' while he thinks rather than filling every gap, and is comfortable with silence. He'll just wait if the interviewer pauses. Uses 'sort of' now and then, and occasionally ends with 'you know' or 'to be honest'. Says 'mate' to men he knows, rarely to strangers. Can be blunt: 'No, I don't really see the point of that.' Uses 'sorry' mainly as repair: 'Sorry, say that again?' or 'Sorry, I mean the Basingstoke site.' He gets a bit more animated on football or on something at work he thinks is badly run.
- typing: Quick and functional. He usually capitalises the first word and proper nouns, uses full stops but few commas, and gets apostrophes mostly right with the odd slip like 'its'. Answers are short, sometimes just a few words. He doesn't use emojis or text abbreviations beyond 'etc' and occasionally 'n/a'. If a question annoys him he might type something like 'Depends what you mean by that.'
- with strangers: Reserved and a bit guarded at first. He's polite but doesn't make small talk for its own sake and can come across as curt or unimpressed. He answers what's asked, honestly and without exaggeration, and won't pretend to have opinions he doesn't have. He warms up slightly if the conversation is practical or about something he knows. req.text:
You write transcripts of realistic video calls between strangers for a fully synthetic research dataset set in the UK. The study, in order (from its published design): a short puzzle task done alone; first impressions of the others' webcam photos; then a series of three-minute, one-on-one video calls in rounds, each person meeting the others in their group; after each call a short survey.

Call shape (from the original study's numbers): a call is cut off by a three-minute timer. A typical call has about 30 turns (most between 20 and 39) and about 570 words in total (most between 440 and 682); half of all turns are 12 words or fewer, and a quarter are 24 or more. Short acknowledgements ("yeah", "mm") count as turns too. So aim for about 570 words in about 30 turns: alongside the quick back-and-forth, people often talk in longer stretches (explaining their job, telling a story), and those long turns carry much of the call.

Guide to British conversational English (use it for how people talk; it is a description of speech, not a script):
How British people talk in casual conversation. This is a paraphrase of published descriptions of spoken British English; sources are in SOURCES.md. Use these features lightly and only where they fit the person. Never use them as a caricature.

- **Fillers.** British speakers hesitate with "erm" and "er". Women and younger speakers lean towards "erm".
- **Hedges.** "Sort of" is everywhere and steady. "Kind of" is spreading, and younger speakers use it more.
- **Politeness words.** "Please", "thank you", "thanks" and "sorry" mostly mean what they say. "Sorry" also works as a repair word (to correct yourself, or to ask someone to repeat) and can be ironic.
- **Tags at the end of a sentence.** "You know", "right", "okay", "yeah", "do you know what I mean". Among young Londoners, "innit" and "you get me" are rising. Tags depend on age and region only, never on ethnicity.
- **Echoing.** In an engaged conversation people pick up and re-use parts of each other's words.
- **Regional words and grammar** (from a recent dialect survey):
  - A bread roll is a "barm" in the North West (Manchester to Liverpool and western Lancashire), a "cob" around Nottinghamshire, a "bap" in Staffordshire, the West Midlands and North Wales, and a "batch" in Liverpool and Coventry.
  - Around Liverpool an ice lolly can be a "lolly ice".
  - The evening meal is "tea" in the North West, North East and Yorkshire, and "dinner" in the South East and London. Some people say both.
  - "Yous" or "youse" for plural "you" is common in the North East (Newcastle, Teesside), Liverpool and Scotland, less so in Manchester, and rare in York, Leeds and Sheffield.
  - "Give it me" is normal in the North West and West Midlands and widely accepted in Sheffield and York; it fades south of Birmingham, Coventry and Leicester.
  - "You was" is widely used, historically Northern and now found as far south as London.
- **Everyday British words** to draw on where they fit, without assigning them to regions: knackered or shattered, chuffed or made up, skint or brassic, mardy or stroppy, mum or mam, mate or pal, settee, sofa or couch.

req.text:
You write transcripts of realistic video calls between strangers for a fully synthetic research dataset set in the UK. The study, in order (from its published design): a short puzzle task done alone; first impressions of the others' webcam photos; then a series of three-minute, one-on-one video calls in rounds, each person meeting the others in their group; after each call a short survey.

Call shape (from the original study's numbers): a call is cut off by a three-minute timer. A typical call has about 30 turns (most between 20 and 39) and about 570 words in total (most between 440 and 682); half of all turns are 12 words or fewer, and a quarter are 24 or more. Short acknowledgements ("yeah", "mm") count as turns too. So aim for about 570 words in about 30 turns: alongside the quick back-and-forth, people often talk in longer stretches (explaining their job, telling a story), and those long turns carry much of the call.

Guide to British conversational English (use it for how people talk; it is a description of speech, not a script):
How British people talk in casual conversation. This is a paraphrase of published descriptions of spoken British English; sources are in SOURCES.md. Use these features lightly and only where they fit the person. Never use them as a caricature.

- **Fillers.** British speakers hesitate with "erm" and "er". Women and younger speakers lean towards "erm".
- **Hedges.** "Sort of" is everywhere and steady. "Kind of" is spreading, and younger speakers use it more.
- **Politeness words.** "Please", "thank you", "thanks" and "sorry" mostly mean what they say. "Sorry" also works as a repair word (to correct yourself, or to ask someone to repeat) and can be ironic.
- **Tags at the end of a sentence.** "You know", "right", "okay", "yeah", "do you know what I mean". Among young Londoners, "innit" and "you get me" are rising. Tags depend on age and region only, never on ethnicity.
- **Echoing.** In an engaged conversation people pick up and re-use parts of each other's words.
- **Regional words and grammar** (from a recent dialect survey):
  - A bread roll is a "barm" in the North West (Manchester to Liverpool and western Lancashire), a "cob" around Nottinghamshire, a "bap" in Staffordshire, the West Midlands and North Wales, and a "batch" in Liverpool and Coventry.
  - Around Liverpool an ice lolly can be a "lolly ice".
  - The evening meal is "tea" in the North West, North East and Yorkshire, and "dinner" in the South East and London. Some people say both.
  - "Yous" or "youse" for plural "you" is common in the North East (Newcastle, Teesside), Liverpool and Scotland, less so in Manchester, and rare in York, Leeds and Sheffield.
  - "Give it me" is normal in the North West and West Midlands and widely accepted in Sheffield and York; it fades south of Birmingham, Coventry and Leicester.
  - "You was" is widely used, historically Northern and now found as far south as London.
- **Everyday British words** to draw on where they fit, without assigning them to regions: knackered or shattered, chuffed or made up, skint or brassic, mardy or stroppy, mum or mam, mate or pal, settee, sofa or couch.

req.text:
You write transcripts of realistic video calls between strangers for a fully synthetic research dataset set in the UK. The study, in order (from its published design): a short puzzle task done alone; first impressions of the others' webcam photos; then a series of three-minute, one-on-one video calls in rounds, each person meeting the others in their group; after each call a short survey.

Call shape (from the original study's numbers): a call is cut off by a three-minute timer. A typical call has about 30 turns (most between 20 and 39) and about 570 words in total (most between 440 and 682); half of all turns are 12 words or fewer, and a quarter are 24 or more. Short acknowledgements ("yeah", "mm") count as turns too. So aim for about 570 words in about 30 turns: alongside the quick back-and-forth, people often talk in longer stretches (explaining their job, telling a story), and those long turns carry much of the call.

Guide to British conversational English (use it for how people talk; it is a description of speech, not a script):
How British people talk in casual conversation. This is a paraphrase of published descriptions of spoken British English; sources are in SOURCES.md. Use these features lightly and only where they fit the person. Never use them as a caricature.

- **Fillers.** British speakers hesitate with "erm" and "er". Women and younger speakers lean towards "erm".
- **Hedges.** "Sort of" is everywhere and steady. "Kind of" is spreading, and younger speakers use it more.
- **Politeness words.** "Please", "thank you", "thanks" and "sorry" mostly mean what they say. "Sorry" also works as a repair word (to correct yourself, or to ask someone to repeat) and can be ironic.
- **Tags at the end of a sentence.** "You know", "right", "okay", "yeah", "do you know what I mean". Among young Londoners, "innit" and "you get me" are rising. Tags depend on age and region only, never on ethnicity.
- **Echoing.** In an engaged conversation people pick up and re-use parts of each other's words.
- **Regional words and grammar** (from a recent dialect survey):
  - A bread roll is a "barm" in the North West (Manchester to Liverpool and western Lancashire), a "cob" around Nottinghamshire, a "bap" in Staffordshire, the West Midlands and North Wales, and a "batch" in Liverpool and Coventry.
  - Around Liverpool an ice lolly can be a "lolly ice".
  - The evening meal is "tea" in the North West, North East and Yorkshire, and "dinner" in the South East and London. Some people say both.
  - "Yous" or "youse" for plural "you" is common in the North East (Newcastle, Teesside), Liverpool and Scotland, less so in Manchester, and rare in York, Leeds and Sheffield.
  - "Give it me" is normal in the North West and West Midlands and widely accepted in Sheffield and York; it fades south of Birmingham, Coventry and Leicester.
  - "You was" is widely used, historically Northern and now found as far south as London.
- **Everyday British words** to draw on where they fit, without assigning them to regions: knackered or shattered, chuffed or made up, skint or brassic, mardy or stroppy, mum or mam, mate or pal, settee, sofa or couch.

P210 (Jaspal; transcript label: Jaspal):
- first name: Jaspal
- age: 41

- occupation: Business Studies and Economics teacher at a sixth form college on the edge of Derby

- household: Rents a three-bed semi in Littleover with his partner Gemma, 38, a physiotherapist at the Royal Derby. They have been together nine years and are not married. Gemma's ageing cocker spaniel, Biscuit, lives with them. No children so far, and they go back and forth on it.

His family left in the early 1990s during the civil war, spent about a year in Delhi, then settled in Derby when he was nine, where an uncle already had a shop. On forms he writes 'Afghan Sikh' because neither 'Indian' nor 'Asian' quite fits. He grew up speaking Punjabi and some Dari at home, and English is now his strongest language. He cut his hair at university, which caused a huge row at the time, but he still wears a kara. His classroom energy is high and his paperwork is chaotic. He marks late, wings lessons he has taught before, and charms his way out of deadline emails from his head of department. He is good at selling the college at open evenings and knows it. He likes being seen as the go-to person and will quietly take credit for a group project's success.

He occasionally fantasises about leaving teaching to do something in finance or start a business, and has a half-built idea for a tutoring company.

He talks fast and laughs easily, says 'you know' and 'to be fair' a lot, and uses 'sort of' as a hedge. He drops in 'mate', 'mardy' and 'knackered' naturally. He goes 'er' when thinking and will often answer a question with a story. He doesn't like silence and fills it with a joke or by asking the interviewer something back. - typing: Fast and mostly lowercase, with a capital only on the odd name. Apostrophes are frequently missing (dont, im, its). He uses commas instead of full stops and sometimes 'lol' or 'tbh'. Answers are short and a bit casual, and he occasionally leaves a typo uncorrected, e.g. 'tbh i think its fine, depends on the day really'.

He seems relaxed and unflappable, and is happy to share opinions. He may present himself in a slightly better light than strictly accurate, rounding up his achievements or downplaying things he hasn't got round to.

Late-afternoon daylight comes from a window to his left, with the overhead light on, giving fairly even but slightly warm lighting. A South Asian man in his early forties with a short neat beard going grey at the chin and short dark hair faded at the sides. He is mid-laugh with a broad open smile, looking just past the camera. No glasses. He wears a navy quarter-zip jumper over a white collar, and a steel kara is visible on his right wrist as he gestures. Behind him: a magnolia wall with a framed Derby County shirt, a cheap white bookshelf with A-level economics textbooks, a stack of unmarked exercise books, a Funko-style figure and a small framed photo of an older couple. req.text:
You write transcripts of realistic video calls between strangers for a fully synthetic research dataset set in the UK. The study, in order (from its published design): a short puzzle task done alone; first impressions of the others' webcam photos; then a series of three-minute, one-on-one video calls in rounds, each person meeting the others in their group; after each call a short survey.

Call shape (from the original study's numbers): a call is cut off by a three-minute timer. A typical call has about 30 turns (most between 20 and 39) and about 570 words in total (most between 440 and 682); half of all turns are 12 words or fewer, and a quarter are 24 or more. Short acknowledgements ("yeah", "mm") count as turns too. So aim for about 570 words in about 30 turns: alongside the quick back-and-forth, people often talk in longer stretches (explaining their job, telling a story), and those long turns carry much of the call.

Guide to British conversational English (use it for how people talk; it is a description of speech, not a script):
How British people talk in casual conversation. This is a paraphrase of published descriptions of spoken British English; sources are in SOURCES.md. Use these features lightly and only where they fit the person. Never use them as a caricature.

- **Fillers.** British speakers hesitate with "erm" and "er". Women and younger speakers lean towards "erm".
- **Hedges.** "Sort of" is everywhere and steady. "Kind of" is spreading, and younger speakers use it more.
- **Politeness words.** "Please", "thank you", "thanks" and "sorry" mostly mean what they say. "Sorry" also works as a repair word (to correct yourself, or to ask someone to repeat) and can be ironic.
- **Tags at the end of a sentence.** "You know", "right", "okay", "yeah", "do you know what I mean". Among young Londoners, "innit" and "you get me" are rising. Tags depend on age and region only, never on ethnicity.
- **Echoing.** In an engaged conversation people pick up and re-use parts of each other's words.
- **Regional words and grammar** (from a recent dialect survey):
  - A bread roll is a "barm" in the North West (Manchester to Liverpool and western Lancashire), a "cob" around Nottinghamshire, a "bap" in Staffordshire, the West Midlands and North Wales, and a "batch" in Liverpool and Coventry.
  - Around Liverpool an ice lolly can be a "lolly ice".
  - The evening meal is "tea" in the North West, North East and Yorkshire, and "dinner" in the South East and London. Some people say both.
  - "Yous" or "youse" for plural "you" is common in the North East (Newcastle, Teesside), Liverpool and Scotland, less so in Manchester, and rare in York, Leeds and Sheffield.
  - "Give it me" is normal in the North West and West Midlands and widely accepted in Sheffield and York; it fades south of Birmingham, Coventry and Leicester.
  - "You was" is widely used, historically Northern and now found as far south as London.
- **Everyday British words** to draw on where they fit, without assigning them to regions: knackered or shattered, chuffed or made up, skint or brassic, mardy or stroppy, mum or mam, mate or pal, settee, sofa or couch.

A typical call has about 30 turns (most between 20 and 39) and about 570 words in total (most between 440 and 682); half of all turns are 12 words or fewer, and a quarter are 24 or more. Short acknowledgements ("yeah", "mm") count as turns too. So aim for about 570 words in about 30 turns: alongside the quick back-and-forth, people often talk in longer stretches (explaining their job, telling a story), and those long turns carry much of the call.

Guide to British conversational English (use it for how people talk; it is a description of speech, not a script):
How British people talk in casual conversation. This is a paraphrase of published descriptions of spoken British English; sources are in SOURCES.md. Use these features lightly and only where they fit the person. Never use them as a caricature.

- **Fillers.** British speakers hesitate with "erm" and "er". Women and younger speakers lean towards "erm".
- **Hedges.** "Sort of" is everywhere and steady. "Kind of" is spreading, and younger speakers use it more.
- **Politeness words.** "Please", "thank you", "thanks" and "sorry" mostly mean what they say. "Sorry" also works as a repair word (to correct yourself, or to ask someone to repeat) and can be ironic.
- **Tags at the end of a sentence.** "You know", "right", "okay", "yeah", "do you know what I mean". Among young Londoners, "innit" and "you get me" are rising. Tags depend on age and region only, never on ethnicity.
- **Echoing.** In an engaged conversation people pick up and re-use parts of each other's words.
- **Regional words and grammar** (from a recent dialect survey):
  - A bread roll is a "barm" in the North West (Manchester to Liverpool and western Lancashire), a "cob" around Nottinghamshire, a "bap" in Staffordshire, the West Midlands and North Wales, and a "batch" in Liverpool and Coventry.
  - Around Liverpool an ice lolly can be a "lolly ice".
  - The evening meal is "tea" in the North West, North East and Yorkshire, and "dinner" in the South East and London. Some people say both.
  - "Yous" or "youse" for plural "you" is common in the North East (Newcastle, Teesside), Liverpool and Scotland, less so in Manchester, and rare in York, Leeds and Sheffield.
  - "Give it me" is normal in the North West and West Midlands and widely accepted in Sheffield and York; it fades south of Birmingham, Coventry and Leicester.
  - "You was" is widely used, historically Northern and now found as far south as London.
- **Everyday British words** to draw on where they fit, without assigning them to regions: knackered or shattered, chuffed or made up, skint or brassic, mardy or stroppy, mum or mam, mate or pal, settee, sofa or couch.

Nicola: Hiya! Can you hear me alright, love?
Darren: Yeah, loud and clear. Hello. I'm Darren.

Nicola: Oh, bless you. What do you do, then?
Darren: Gas engineer. Boilers, mainly. Got my own business, one van, about fourteen years now.
Nicola: Ooh, I could do with you. Mine makes this horrible banging noise when the heating first comes on. The housing association sent someone and he said it was normal.
Darren: Banging? Could be air in the system, or a bit of sludge in the pipes. It's not dangerous usually, but it's not normal either. I'd get them back out, if I'm honest.

Nicola: Oh, do you miss your Jess?
Darren: Erm, yeah. More than I'd tell her, to be fair. She's round most Sundays, though, for a roast.

Darren: No, you're alright. I think that's us nearly done, actually.

req.text:
You write transcripts of realistic video calls between strangers for a fully synthetic research dataset set in the UK. The study, in order (from its published design): a short puzzle task done alone; first impressions of the others' webcam photos; then a series of three-minute, one-on-one video calls in rounds, each person meeting the others in their group; after each call a short survey.

Call shape (from the original study's numbers): a call is cut off by a three-minute timer. A typical call has about 30 turns (most between 20 and 39) and about 570 words in total (most between 440 and 682); half of all turns are 12 words or fewer, and a quarter are 24 or more. Short acknowledgements ("yeah", "mm") count as turns too. So aim for about 570 words in about 30 turns: alongside the quick back-and-forth, people often talk in longer stretches (explaining their job, telling a story), and those long turns carry much of the call.

Guide to British conversational English (use it for how people talk; it is a description of speech, not a script):
How British people talk in casual conversation. This is a paraphrase of published descriptions of spoken British English; sources are in SOURCES.md. Use these features lightly and only where they fit the person. Never use them as a caricature.

- **Fillers.** British speakers hesitate with "erm" and "er". Women and younger speakers lean towards "erm".
- **Hedges.** "Sort of" is everywhere and steady. "Kind of" is spreading, and younger speakers use it more.
- **Politeness words.** "Please", "thank you", "thanks" and "sorry" mostly mean what they say. "Sorry" also works as a repair word (to correct yourself, or to ask someone to repeat) and can be ironic.
- **Tags at the end of a sentence.** "You know", "right", "okay", "yeah", "do you know what I mean". Among young Londoners, "innit" and "you get me" are rising. Tags depend on age and region only, never on ethnicity.
- **Echoing.** In an engaged conversation people pick up and re-use parts of each other's words.
- **Regional words and grammar** (from a recent dialect survey):
  - A bread roll is a "barm" in the North West (Manchester to Liverpool and western Lancashire), a "cob" around Nottinghamshire, a "bap" in Staffordshire, the West Midlands and North Wales, and a "batch" in Liverpool and Coventry.
  - Around Liverpool an ice lolly can be a "lolly ice".
  - The evening meal is "tea" in the North West, North East and Yorkshire, and "dinner" in the South East and London. Some people say both.
  - "Yous" or "youse" for plural "you" is common in the North East (Newcastle, Teesside), Liverpool and Scotland, less so in Manchester, and rare in York, Leeds and Sheffield.
  - "Give it me" is normal in the North West and West Midlands and widely accepted in Sheffield and York; it fades south of Birmingham, Coventry and Leicester.
  - "You was" is widely used, historically Northern and now found as far south as London.
- **Everyday British words** to draw on where they fit, without assigning them to regions: knackered or shattered, chuffed or made up, skint or brassic, mardy or stroppy, mum or mam, mate or pal, settee, sofa or couch.

Gemma: Yeah, we've got a couple of them. HCAs on their phones in the sluice.
Joanne: In the sluice! See, I'd have something to say about that.
Gemma: I did. Got told to soften how I say things. Again.
Joanne: No, that's rubbish, to be honest. If someone's not doing their job, you tell them. I'm the same. Some of the younger ones find me hard work, you know, but the managers don't mind.
Gemma: That's sort of what my mentor says. Good on the hands-on stuff, bad on documentation.
Joanne: Oh, documentation. I keep a paper notebook as well as the electronic records, 'cause I don't trust the system not to go down. It went down for a whole morning in March, and guess who had everything written down.
Gemma: Fair. Our e-obs freezes on nights all the time.
Joanne: There you go. What do you want to do when you qualify, then?
Gemma: Band 5 on a medical ward or A&E. Probably the same trust. Band 6 eventually. Not management.
Joanne: No, I get that. I'm doing my Level 3 leadership diploma, the home's paying for it, 'cause I want deputy manager when ours retires. But not registered manager. No way. I'm worrying weeks before a CQC inspection as it is.
Gemma: What's the diploma like? The writing bits?
Joanne: Erm, it's alright. Slow. I do it on my days off in between batch cooking. Sorry, am I going on?
Gemma: No, it's fine. I've got an essay due Friday I haven't started, so I'm not judging.
Joanne: Friday! Gemma!
Gemma: I know. I always do them the night before.
Joanne: My daughter was like that. Ellie. She's twenty, she's in Peterborough now with her boyfriend.
Gemma: Is that alright?
Joanne: ...Yeah. Sort of. She's an adult, isn't she. You can't tell them. Anyway. Is it London you're in?
Gemma: Catford. One-bed above a dry cleaner's with my husband.
Joanne: Do you get a proper dinner when you get in, or is it toast?
Gemma: Dean does most of the cooking. On nights it's a meal deal and a Twix.
Joanne: Oh, don't. I batch-cook so there's always something in the freezer, otherwise Callum, my son, would live on crisps. He's seventeen. Never puts a plate in the dishwasher, ever.
Gemma: Sounds about right.
Joanne: Do you get much time off, on placement? Do you—

Kayleigh: No, that's alright, that. You did that?
Darren: Yeah, years ago. Did a year of art at college then packed it in.
Kayleigh: I did a year of hair and beauty and packed that in. I do nails now, on the side, like.
Darren: Yeah? Gemma'd love that, she's always—

req.text:
You write transcripts of realistic video calls between strangers for a fully synthetic research dataset set in the UK. The study, in order (from its published design): a short puzzle task done alone; first impressions of the others' webcam photos; then a series of three-minute, one-on-one video calls in rounds, each person meeting the others in their group; after each call a short survey.

Call shape (from the original study's numbers): a call is cut off by a three-minute timer. A typical call has about 30 turns (most between 20 and 39) and about 570 words in total (most between 440 and 682); half of all turns are 12 words or fewer, and a quarter are 24 or more. Short acknowledgements ("yeah", "mm") count as turns too. So aim for about 570 words in about 30 turns: alongside the quick back-and-forth, people often talk in longer stretches (explaining their job, telling a story), and those long turns carry much of the call.

Guide to British conversational English (use it for how people talk; it is a description of speech, not a script):
How British people talk in casual conversation. This is a paraphrase of published descriptions of spoken British English; sources are in SOURCES.md. Use these features lightly and only where they fit the person. Never use them as a caricature.

- **Fillers.** British speakers hesitate with "erm" and "er". Women and younger speakers lean towards "erm".
- **Hedges.** "Sort of" is everywhere and steady. "Kind of" is spreading, and younger speakers use it more.
- **Politeness words.** "Please", "thank you", "thanks" and "sorry" mostly mean what they say. "Sorry" also works as a repair word (to correct yourself, or to ask someone to repeat) and can be ironic.
- **Tags at the end of a sentence.** "You know", "right", "okay", "yeah", "do you know what I mean". Among young Londoners, "innit" and "you get me" are rising. Tags depend on age and region only, never on ethnicity.
- **Echoing.** In an engaged conversation people pick up and re-use parts of each other's words.
- **Regional words and grammar** (from a recent dialect survey):
  - A bread roll is a "barm" in the North West (Manchester to Liverpool and western Lancashire), a "cob" around Nottinghamshire, a "bap" in Staffordshire, the West Midlands and North Wales, and a "batch" in Liverpool and Coventry.
  - Around Liverpool an ice lolly can be a "lolly ice".
  - The evening meal is "tea" in the North West, North East and Yorkshire, and "dinner" in the South East and London. Some people say both.
  - "Yous" or "youse" for plural "you" is common in the North East (Newcastle, Teesside), Liverpool and Scotland, less so in Manchester, and rare in York, Leeds and Sheffield.
  - "Give it me" is normal in the North West and West Midlands and widely accepted in Sheffield and York; it fades south of Birmingham, Coventry and Leicester.
  - "You was" is widely used, historically Northern and now found as far south as London.
- **Everyday British words** to draw on where they fit, without assigning them to regions: knackered or shattered, chuffed or made up, skint or brassic, mardy or stroppy, mum or mam, mate or pal, settee, sofa or couch.

P200 (Alison; transcript label: Alison):
- first name: Alison
- age: 61
- lives in: Tonbridge, South East England (Kent)
- occupation: Principal Planning Officer at a borough council in West Kent, mainly handling larger residential applications and appeals; works about 37 hours a week, two days in the office and three from home
- education detail: Grammar school in Kent, then a BA in Geography at the University of Sheffield and a postgraduate diploma in Town and Country Planning at Oxford Polytechnic (now Oxford Brookes). Chartered member of the RTPI since her late twenties.
- household: Lives with her husband Graham, 64, a retired building surveyor, in a 1930s semi-detached house on the edge of town. Their two children, a son of 32 in Bristol and a daughter of 29 in south London, have both moved out. They have an elderly, rather lazy Labrador cross called Biscuit.
- cultural background: White British, born in Maidstone to a father who was a bank clerk and a mother who was a primary school secretary. Brought up Church of England and still goes to the parish church, mostly at Christmas, Easter and the odd harvest festival. She'd call herself Christian without fuss and doesn't talk about it much. Very much Home Counties middle class, though she doesn't think of herself in those terms.
- professional persona: She is respected at work for being unflappable. Furious residents at committee meetings and aggressive developers' agents don't rattle her, and she's known for giving straight, fair assessments without playing politics. She has turned down a head-of-service role twice because she didn't want the meetings or the profile. Her weakness is admin. Her inbox is chaotic, she leaves reports until close to the deadline, and her desk notes are a mess. She gets away with it because her judgement is good and she's quick once she starts.
- sports persona: Not sporty. She walks Biscuit most mornings along the Medway towpath and has a half-hearted swimming habit at the leisure centre that comes and goes. She'll watch Wimbledon on the telly and pays very little attention to football.
- arts persona: Reads a lot, mostly crime fiction and the occasional big historical novel, often several at once and never quite finishing some of them. Listens to Radio 4 and some 1970s and 80s music. She and Graham go to the theatre in Tunbridge Wells or London a couple of times a year, usually because Graham booked it.
- travel persona: Prefers quiet trips to busy ones. They go to Pembrokeshire, Northumberland or the Norfolk coast in a rented cottage, plus the odd week in France or northern Spain. She's relaxed about travel to the point of being disorganised. Graham does the bookings and packing lists, and she's been known to forget her phone charger and her walking boots on the same trip.
- culinary persona: A competent but improvisational cook who never follows a recipe exactly. Dinner is usually something like a tray bake, a risotto or a curry made from whatever's in the fridge. She likes a glass of red with dinner, buys decent cheese, and has no interest in fancy restaurants. A good pub lunch is her idea of eating out.
- hobbies and interests: Dog walking along the river, Crime novels and the occasional literary prize shortlist, Radio 4, especially the panel shows and From Our Own Correspondent, Pottering in the garden without much of a plan, Cryptic crossword in the paper, abandoned halfway as often as not, Looking at old buildings and village layouts on holiday, which Graham teases her about
- skills: Reading and interpreting planning policy and site plans quickly, Staying calm in heated public meetings, Writing clear, plain-English reports (eventually), Negotiating with developers without getting drawn in, Knows the local geography of West Kent in great detail, Reasonable cook without a recipe
- career goals: Not much ambition left in the climbing sense. She wants to see out a few more years doing casework she finds interesting, possibly go down to four days a week at 63 or so, and retire around 66. She's vaguely considered doing some part-time consultancy or volunteering with a local heritage trust afterwards but hasn't done anything about it.
- voice: Southern English, educated and fairly neutral, with a slight Kentish flatness on some vowels. Speaks at a steady, unhurried pace and doesn't fill gaps. If she's thinking she'll just pause, or say 'erm' once and then carry on. Uses 'sort of' quite a lot as a softener ('it's sort of a compromise site') and finishes some points with 'you know'. Her humour is dry and understated and she doesn't oversell anything. She'll say 'sorry, say that again?' if she misses a question, with no embarrassment. Says 'dinner' for the evening meal and 'sofa'. Occasionally 'knackered' after a long committee night. Answers are honest and sometimes blunter than people expect, delivered without any edge.
- typing: Quick and a bit careless. She mostly starts with a capital letter but often drops the full stop at the end. Apostrophes are hit and miss: she knows the rules but doesn't always bother ('dont', 'its fine'). There are occasional typos she doesn't go back to fix. No emojis and few abbreviations beyond 'etc' and the odd 'tbh' picked up from her daughter. Short answers, often one line, unless the question genuinely interests her.
- with strangers: Pleasant, a little reserved and hard to read at first. She doesn't do much small talk and won't perform enthusiasm, but she's not cold. She answers what's asked, honestly, and doesn't try to impress. Comes across as calm and slightly wry. Some people take her quietness for disinterest until she says something sharp and funny. She never name-drops or mentions her job title unless asked.
- small things: Biscuit refusing to walk in the rain, The roadworks on the high street, Having left a mug of tea somewhere and found it cold an hour later, The crossword clue she couldn't get, Graham's latest DIY project that's been half-finished since spring, A new crime series she's started on the telly, Getting the train up to London to see her daughter
- deeper things: Her mother's dementia in her last years and the guilt of not visiting as often as her brother did, A quiet sense that she coasted a bit in her career and could have done more, which she doesn't actually regret much, Her faith is less certain than it was, though she still finds the church comforting, mainly for the building and the ritual, Worry about her son, who has struggled with his mental health, which she handles practically rather than emotionally, Being told by more than one person over the years that she seems not to feel things, which she thinks is unfair and slightly true
- webcam photo: Head-and-shoulders shot from a laptop on a kitchen table, camera slightly below eye level so it looks up a little at her chin. Soft, greyish daylight comes from a window off to her left, leaving the right side of her face in mild shadow. She is a 61-year-old white woman with a fairly lined, fair-skinned face, light freckling and a calm, neutral expression with a faint half-smile. Her chin-length hair is grey with some remaining mousy-brown, tucked behind one ear and a bit untidy. She wears tortoiseshell reading glasses pushed slightly down her nose and a navy crew-neck jumper over a pale blue collared shirt. Behind her is a cream-painted kitchen wall with a wall calendar from a local vet still showing last month, a cork noticeboard crammed with overlapping letters, a takeaway menu and a postcard of St Davids. At the right edge is the end of a wooden dresser holding a stack of mismatched mugs, a fruit bowl with two bananas, and a dog lead hanging from a hook.

Leanne: Obviously. I listen to it while I'm printing.
Jodie: It gives me anxiety but I can't stop. I watch it, then I'm checking the back door.
Leanne: That's the point of it, isn't it. Reminds you you've locked up. Anyway, I'm having my tea after this, Gavin's doing chilli.
Jodie: Ryan's on early starts so I do tea, which means chippy on Friday. Or a bap from the cafe if I'm at uni.
Leanne: A bap. Bless you. It's a barm.
Jodie: It's a bap, mate. Don't —

=== CALL C0409 ===
Tendai: Alright! Hello, can you hear me?
Joanne: Yes, hello. Sorry, I'm Joanne.
Tendai: Tendai. How you doing, Joanne? You've done a couple of these now, yeah?
Joanne: Two. I'm still not sure I'm doing it right.
Tendai: Ah, there's no right. It's just a chat, you know. Like at the bus stop.
Joanne: I don't really talk at bus stops.
Tendai: Ha! Me, I talk to everybody. Natalie says I'll talk to a lamppost. So where are you?
Joanne: Basingstoke. I clean on the wards at the hospital. Early shifts.
Tendai: Ah, respect. Proper hard work, that. Honestly. When I first came over, I did nights in care homes. Years. Nobody looks at you, you know? You're just the one in the tabard. So I know that job is hard.
Joanne: It can be like that. The patients notice you, though. The nurses do. Some of them know my name.
Tendai: That's the thing, yeah. The old ones, they'd just want somebody to sit down for a minute.
Joanne: They do. You have a little chat while you're doing their table. Sorry. What do you do now?
Tendai: Electrician. Self-employed, in Gloucester. Rewires, kitchens. My van's outside, the heater's broken, so I'm freezing every morning. Hey, the lady I spoke to before, Alison, she told me her dog's called Biscuit.
Joanne: Oh, I know! My cat's called Biscuit. We worked that out in the first one.
Tendai: Two Biscuits! That's a sign. Of what, I don't know. Do you have kids?
Joanne: Two, grown up. Kirsty's got a little boy, he's two. He's just started saying Nanny Jo.
Tendai: Ahh, Nanny Jo! That's lovely, man.
Joanne: I have him on my days off. He's into everything. Sorry, I'm going on.
Tendai: No, go on! I've got Kai, my partner's boy, he's thirteen. He eats everything in the fridge and grows out of his boots every two months. Third pair this year.
Joanne: Liam was like that. He's in Reading now. Twenty-five. I still think he's about twelve.
Tendai: They're always twelve, you know. My mum's in Zimbabwe, I'm forty and she still asks if I'm eating properly.
Joanne: Are you?
Tendai: Ha! Meal deal from the Co-op. So no. But on Sunday I make sadza, beef stew. Kai loves it now. First time, he looked at it like it was, er, like it was wallpaper paste.
Joanne: I don't know what that is, sorry.
Tendai: Like a thick maize porridge, you eat it with your hands with the stew. Proper comfort food.
Joanne: Oh, that sounds nice. I'm not very adventurous. Shepherd's pie, spag bol. A roast on Sundays.
Tendai: A roast is perfect, man. Nothing wrong with that. Hey, did you see the car park prices, at hospitals? I did a job at one, I paid nine pound.
Joanne: They've gone up again for us as well. Staff. It's not right.
Tendai: That's not right, no. You're there cleaning for them —
Joanne: That's what I said to Gary.
