req.text:
You write transcripts of realistic video calls between strangers for a fully synthetic research dataset set in the UK. The study, in order (from its published design): a short puzzle task done alone; first impressions of the others' webcam photos; then a series of three-minute, one-on-one video calls in rounds, each person meeting the others in their group; after each call a short survey.

Call shape (from the original study's numbers): a call is cut off by a three-minute timer. A typical call has about 30 turns (most between 20 and 39) and about 570 words in total (most between 440 and 682); half of all turns are 12 words or fewer, and a quarter are 24 or more. Short acknowledgements ("yeah", "mm") count as turns too. So aim for about 570 words in about 30 turns: alongside the quick back-and-forth, people often talk in longer stretches (explaining their job, telling a story), and those long turns carry much of the call.

Guide to British conversational English (use it for how people talk; it is a description of speech, not a script):
How British people talk in casual conversation. This is a paraphrase of published descriptions of spoken British English; sources are in SOURCES.md. Use these features lightly and only where they fit the person. Never use them as a caricature.

- **Fillers.** British speakers hesitate with "erm" and "er". Women and younger speakers lean towards "erm".
- **Hedges.** "Sort of" is everywhere and steady. "Kind of" is spreading, and younger speakers use it more.
- **Politeness words.** "Please", "thank you", "thanks" and "sorry" mostly mean what they say. "Sorry" also works as a repair word (to correct yourself, or to ask someone to repeat) and can be ironic.
- **Tags at the end of a sentence.** "You know", "right", "okay", "yeah", "do you know what I mean". Among young Londoners, "innit" and "you get me" are rising. Tags depend on age and region only, never on ethnicity.
- **Echoing.** In an engaged conversation people pick up and re-use parts of each other's words.
- **Regional words and grammar** (from a recent dialect survey):
  - A bread roll is a "barm" in the North West (Manchester to Liverpool and western Lancashire), a "cob" around Nottinghamshire, a "bap" in Staffordshire, the West Midlands and North Wales, and a "batch" in Liverpool and Coventry.
  - Around Liverpool an ice lolly can be a "lolly ice".
  - The evening meal is "tea" in the North West, North East and Yorkshire, and "dinner" in the South East and London. Some people say both.
  - "Yous" or "youse" for plural "you" is common in the North East (Newcastle, Teesside), Liverpool and Scotland, less so in Manchester, and rare in York, Leeds and Sheffield.
  - "Give it me" is normal in the North West and West Midlands and widely accepted in Sheffield and York; it fades south of Birmingham, Coventry and Leicester.
  - "You was" is widely used, historically Northern and now found as far south as London.
- **Everyday British words** to draw on where they fit, without assigning them to regions: knackered or shattered, chuffed or made up, skint or brassic, mardy or stroppy, mum or mam, mate or pal, settee, sofa or couch.

The group (session S43). Persona cards, including the webcam photo each person was rated on:

P225 (Tracey; transcript label: Tracey):
- first name: Tracey
- age: 51
- lives in: Dagenham, East London
- occupation: Kitchen assistant in a primary school canteen, about 25 hours a week, term-time only. She preps veg, serves at the hatch, washes up and does the end-of-service clean.
- education detail: Left a local comprehensive at 16 in 1989 with a handful of GCSEs (English, Maths at a low grade, Home Economics). Has a Level 2 Food Hygiene certificate through work and did a short first-aid course years ago. No further qualifications.
- household: Lives with her husband Steve (54), a van driver for a builders' merchant, in a two-bedroom ex-council terraced house they bought under right-to-buy from his late mum. Their son Dean (27) moved out three years ago to a flat in Romford with his girlfriend. There's no pet since their old Staffie died last year.
- cultural background: White British, born at Barking hospital and raised on the Becontree estate. Her dad worked at the Ford plant until it wound down and her mum did cleaning jobs. She isn't religious and only goes in a church for weddings and funerals. Her outlook is solidly working-class East London: family nearby, a mistrust of anyone who 'thinks they're better', and some nostalgia for how the area used to be, which she knows isn't the whole story.
- professional persona: Reliable and honest to a fault. She'd never take food home that she wasn't supposed to and she gets annoyed when others do. She isn't one for workplace chat or getting along for the sake of it, and she has fallen out with a previous cook over corners being cut. She gets on with the job, says what she thinks to the catering manager, and worries afterwards about whether she went too far.
- sports persona: Not sporty herself. She walks to work and around Parsloes Park when the weather's decent. She watches West Ham with Steve on telly and moans about them, and puts the big tournaments on in the summer when England are playing.
- arts persona: Watches a lot of telly: soaps, Gogglebox, crime dramas and true-crime documentaries that she says give her the creeps. She reads the odd paperback thriller on holiday. She went to see a West End musical for her 50th, which Dean paid for, and still talks about it.
- travel persona: A week in Spain or Turkey most summers when money allows, usually all-inclusive, plus a caravan weekend in Clacton or Great Yarmouth. She doesn't like flying much and gets anxious at airports. She's never wanted to go anywhere 'too far or too foreign'.
- culinary persona: Plain home cooking: roast on a Sunday, shepherd's pie, spag bol, sausage and mash. She calls the evening meal 'dinner'. She does a big Aldi shop and is careful with money. She has a soft spot for pie and mash from the shop in Barking and has a takeaway on Fridays.
- hobbies and interests: Walking in Parsloes Park, Watching crime documentaries and soaps, Word searches and the puzzle pages in magazines, Looking after her hanging baskets and small back garden, Facebook groups about old Dagenham photos, Seeing her sister and her mum on Sundays
- skills: Food prep and safe kitchen hygiene, Working fast under pressure at the serving hatch, Budgeting a tight household income, Keeping a house spotless, Spotting when someone's trying it on
- career goals: Nothing ambitious. She'd like to stay at the school until she can afford to stop. She thought about going for the cook's job once but didn't fancy the responsibility or the stress. She mainly hopes her back and knees hold out.
- voice: Estuary/East London accent, fairly quick once she gets going but guarded at first. Says 'erm' when she's thinking, and uses 'sort of' and 'you know' a fair bit. Sometimes she says 'you was' in passing. She's blunt: she'll say 'no, that's not right' or 'I don't agree with that' without dressing it up, then add 'sorry, but it's not' if she thinks it came out sharp. She uses ordinary words like 'knackered' and 'skint'. Silences make her a bit uneasy, and she'll either ask 'is that what you wanted?' or just wait for the next question rather than fill it.
- typing: Mostly lowercase with a capital at the start sometimes. Short answers with minimal punctuation and the odd full stop missing at the end. Apostrophes are hit and miss (dont, its, I'm). Occasional 'cos' and 'tbh', no emojis. Mild typos she doesn't go back to fix.
- with strangers: A bit wary and reserved at first. She'll answer honestly but won't flatter or pretend to agree. She can come across as a little prickly or short, especially if a question seems daft or nosey. Underneath she's anxious about saying the wrong thing. She warms up if the other person is straightforward with her.
- small things: The school ran out of jacket potatoes again, Steve's van broke down on the A13, Her hanging baskets are doing well this year, Prices in Aldi have gone up, Can't stand the new self-checkouts, Watched a documentary that kept her up at night
- deeper things: Worries a lot about her mum, who is 78 and getting forgetful, Her dad died of a heart attack at 60 and she frets about Steve's health, Still upset about a falling out with her sister-in-law that's lasted years, Felt lonely and a bit lost when Dean moved out, Gets anxious about money and lies awake over bills, Feels she never had the chances to do more with her life, but doesn't like to dwell on it
- webcam photo: Head-and-shoulders shot from a laptop on a kitchen table, angled slightly upward so the ceiling light is visible at the top edge. Daylight comes from a window to her left, lighting one side of her face more than the other. She has fair skin with some redness on the cheeks and faint lines around the eyes. Her shoulder-length hair is highlighted blonde with darker roots, pulled back in a claw clip with a few loose strands. No glasses. She wears a navy fleece zipped halfway over a grey T-shirt and small gold hoop earrings. Her expression is neutral and slightly wary, mouth closed, eyebrows a little raised. Behind her is a white-tiled kitchen wall with a kettle, a toaster and a stack of post on the counter, a calendar from a local Chinese takeaway pinned up, and a tea towel hanging off the oven door.

P226 (Gemma; transcript label: Gemma):
- first name: Gemma
- age: 37
- lives in: Wigan, North West England
- occupation: Primary school teacher (Year 4 class teacher and maths lead) at a Church of England primary school in Wigan
- education detail: Went to a local comprehensive and sixth form college in Wigan, then a BA in Primary Education with QTS at Edge Hill University in Ormskirk, commuting from home for most of it. She has done in-house CPD on maths mastery and took on the maths lead role three years ago.
- household: Lives with her daughter Lily (11, in Year 6 at a different primary) in a three-bed semi on an estate in Standish that she bought after renting for years. Lily's dad was a long-term boyfriend. They never married and split when Lily was two. He lives in Leigh and has Lily every other weekend. Gemma's mum lives ten minutes away and does school pick-ups on the days Gemma has staff meetings.
- cultural background: White British, born and raised in Wigan, from a working-class family that has become more comfortable. Her dad was an electrician (now retired) and her mum was a dinner lady and then a teaching assistant. She was brought up Church of England and still goes to the parish church most Sundays with her mum, and she helps at the Christmas and harvest services. Her faith is practical and unshowy: it is more about community and doing right by people than doctrine. Her family is Wigan Warriors through and through.
- professional persona: Well liked by staff and parents, and known as the teacher who will cover a playground duty without being asked. She is organised enough to get everything done but not a perfectionist: her planning is solid rather than beautifully laminated. She likes the structure of the school year and sticks to approaches she knows work, and she is a bit sceptical of every new initiative that comes down from the trust. She is straight with parents, kind but honest, and doesn't flannel. She is good in a crisis and rarely rattled when a child kicks off or an Ofsted call comes in.
- sports persona: Plays goal defence for a back-to-netball team on Tuesday nights and does the Haigh Woodland parkrun most Saturdays when Lily is at her dad's. She is not fast and not bothered about times, and she's mainly there for the chat and the coffee after. She goes to a few Wigan Warriors home games a season with her dad and Lily and watches the Grand Final at her parents' house.
- arts persona: Not really an arts person. She watches whatever is on telly on a Saturday night, such as Strictly, Gogglebox and the odd crime drama, and sometimes falls asleep halfway through. She listens to Radio 2 and 2000s pop in the car. Once a year or so she goes to a big arena gig at the AO Arena in Manchester with friends, and she reliably goes to the panto with Lily. She reads the occasional paperback on holiday, usually a thriller someone has lent her.
- travel persona: Prefers what she knows. She takes a week in an all-inclusive in Tenerife or Majorca every summer holiday with Lily and sometimes her mum, often at the same resort as before. In the October half-term they do a caravan break at Haven in North Wales or the Lake District. She has no real urge to backpack or 'see the world' and finds the idea a bit stressful logistically.
- culinary persona: Cooks plain, reliable family teas: spag bol, chicken fajitas, a roast on Sunday, and a pie barm from the bakery on a Friday as a treat. She batch-cooks a chilli on Sundays to get through the week. She will try a new restaurant if friends book it but usually orders something safe. She has a soft spot for a Greggs sausage roll and a proper brew, and she drinks prosecco on a night out.
- hobbies and interests: Tuesday night netball, Parkrun on child-free Saturdays, Wigan Warriors rugby league, Helping with church coffee mornings and the harvest service, Pub quiz once a month with old school friends, Walking the dog (a cockapoo called Bramble) round Haigh Hall, Strictly Come Dancing with her mum and Lily
- skills: Classroom behaviour management, Explaining maths simply, Calming down upset children and parents, Organising school trips and residentials, Getting on with almost anyone, Basic Excel for tracking pupil data, Cooking for a crowd on a budget
- career goals: Probably wants to move to assistant head in the next few years, ideally at her current school or nearby so she doesn't have to commute. She isn't desperate to be a head because she'd miss being in the classroom. Mostly she wants a manageable workload and enough income to keep the house and the holidays going while Lily is at high school.
- voice: Warm, chatty and quick, with a clear Wigan accent: flat vowels, 'book' with a short northern 'oo', and dropped 'h's when she's relaxed. Her register is casual but polite, and she says 'please' and 'thank you' naturally. Her filler is mostly 'erm', and she hedges with 'sort of' and the odd 'kind of'. She tags sentences with 'you know' or 'yeah' rather than heavier tags. She uses local words naturally but not constantly: 'tea' for the evening meal, 'barm', 'give it me', 'made up', 'knackered', 'our Lily'. She doesn't mind silence on a call and will fill it with a light joke or a 'sorry, go on' if she thinks she's talked over someone. She answers straight and doesn't overthink questions.
- typing: Quick and practical. She mostly uses capitals at the start of sentences and usually gets apostrophes right because she's a teacher, though she sometimes skips them when rushing. She often finishes with no full stop or a single exclamation mark. She uses a few abbreviations like 'tbh' and 'x' habits from texting, but drops the kisses on forms. Answers are short and to the point, e.g. 'Yes I'd say so, mostly on weekdays tho'.
- with strangers: Friendly and open straight away, and easy to talk to. She asks people how they are and actually listens to the answer, laughs readily and makes people feel at ease. She's honest even when it would be easier to say what people want to hear, but she says it kindly. She doesn't come across as nervous and is happy to just get on with whatever is asked of her.
- small things: Bramble the cockapoo rolling in something on the walk, Lily starting high school in September and the uniform costing a fortune, Marking a pile of maths books at the kitchen table, The netball team losing again but having a laugh, Wigan Warriors' last result, Her mum doing the school run on Wednesdays, Getting a brew and a pie barm on a Friday, Booking the summer all-inclusive before prices go up
- deeper things: Doing it mostly on her own since Lily was two and being proud she bought the house herself, Sometimes feeling lonely on the weekends Lily is at her dad's, Not really wanting to date again but wondering if she should, Her dad's heart scare a couple of years ago and how it made her lean on her faith, Worrying about how much she relies on her mum and what happens as her parents get older, Feeling a bit stretched between being a good teacher and being there for Lily
- webcam photo: Head-and-shoulders framing from a laptop webcam set slightly below eye level, so the angle looks up a little. Lighting comes from a window to her left, making that side of her face brighter, with a warm ceiling light behind. She has a round, friendly face, light freckles and minimal make-up, and is smiling with teeth showing as if mid-laugh. Her shoulder-length light brown hair has blonde highlights growing out and is pulled back loosely with a claw clip, with a few strands loose. She wears a navy quarter-zip fleece over a white T-shirt and no glasses, plus small gold stud earrings. Behind her is a kitchen-diner: a white fridge with a school calendar, a child's drawing and a Wigan Warriors magnet on the door; a grey worktop with a kettle, a stack of exercise books and a fruit bowl with bananas; and a dog lead hanging on a hook by a back door with a frosted glass panel.

P227 (Carys; transcript label: Carys):
- first name: Carys
- age: 51
- lives in: Mold, Flintshire, North Wales
- occupation: Senior civil engineer (chartered) at a mid-sized engineering consultancy, specialising in flood risk and drainage schemes for local authorities across North Wales and Cheshire
- education detail: Comprehensive school in Flintshire, A-levels in Maths, Physics and Geography; BEng in Civil Engineering from Cardiff University; later became chartered with the Institution of Civil Engineers in her early thirties
- household: Lives with her son Rhys, 16, who is in the sixth form doing A-levels, in a three-bed semi on the edge of town. She and Rhys's dad were together for nine years but never married; they split when Rhys was four. His dad lives in Chester, and Rhys sees him most Sunday afternoons. There's an elderly cat called Moss.
- cultural background: Born and raised in Flintshire to a mum who was a school secretary and a dad who worked at the Shotton steelworks until it scaled down. Welsh was a school subject rather than a home language; she understands a fair bit and can get through basic conversation, but would never claim to be fluent. Rhys went to an English-medium school but is better at Welsh than she is, which he enjoys pointing out. She doesn't talk about religion and would rather leave that box blank.
- professional persona: Thorough, quietly competent and trusted with the awkward schemes: culverts that flood every winter, estates built on old floodplain. She works long hours, often 50-plus a week, mostly hybrid with two or three days in the office in Chester, plus site visits. She's happier with a spreadsheet, a hydraulic model and a site walkover than with a big stakeholder meeting, but she's learned to handle public consultation evenings by preparing heavily. Junior engineers come to her because she explains things without making them feel stupid.
- sports persona: Not sporty in a team sense, but very fit. She walks the Clwydian hills most weekends, Moel Famau being the default, and swims lengths at the leisure centre early on Tuesday and Thursday mornings before work. She'll watch Wales in the Six Nations with Rhys and get more invested than she'd admit.
- arts persona: Reads a lot, mostly crime fiction and the odd nonfiction book about rivers or landscape. She listens to Radio 4 and podcasts in the car. She'll go to Theatr Clwyd a couple of times a year, usually for a play rather than a musical, and prefers going on her own or with one friend.
- travel persona: Prefers quiet, walkable places. She's done the Lake District, Pembrokeshire and the west coast of Scotland. Abroad, she likes northern Spain and once did a walking holiday in the Dolomites with a friend from university. Holidays are planned around Rhys's school terms, and she always books well ahead.
- culinary persona: A practical, batch-cooking sort of cook because of her hours: chilli, stews and a big tray bake on a Sunday that does two nights. She calls a bread roll a bap. Evening meal is 'tea' or 'dinner' depending on her mood. She enjoys a proper Sunday roast when there's time and is partial to a good bakery Welsh cake. Not a foodie, but she won't eat badly.
- hobbies and interests: Hill walking in the Clwydian Range, Early-morning swimming, Cryptic crosswords, usually the Saturday one, Small back-garden vegetable patch, mostly runner beans and tomatoes, Crime novels, Following the weather and river levels more closely than most people would
- skills: Hydraulic modelling and drainage design, Writing clear technical reports, Managing a project budget and programme, Mentoring graduate engineers, Navigation with a map and compass, Basic Welsh, Keeping a teenage boy fed on a tight schedule
- career goals: She'd like to be made an associate director within the next few years, mainly for the recognition and the pension, but she doesn't want to drift so far into management that she stops doing actual engineering. Longer term, once Rhys has left home, she's thought about cutting back to four days and maybe doing some volunteering with a community flood group.
- voice: Calm, measured and a bit reserved at first. She speaks at a steady pace and thinks before answering, often with a soft 'erm' or a short pause while she gets it straight. Her accent is North-east Wales, softer and more Cheshire-edged than people expect from 'Welsh'. There's a slight lilt and the odd 'yeah, no' or 'to be fair'. She hedges with 'sort of' when she's being careful about accuracy, not out of nerves. She's comfortable with silence and won't rush to fill it, though she might say 'sorry, can you say that again?' if a question is vague. When she warms up she gets drier and funnier.
- typing: Types properly even in a quick form: capital letters, full stops, correct apostrophes. Answers are short and precise, sometimes a single complete sentence. She uses 'e.g.' and the occasional bracket for clarification and almost never uses emojis or text-speak. If a question is ambiguous, she might note her interpretation in brackets.
- with strangers: Polite, a little guarded and slightly formal to begin with. She answers what's asked without over-sharing and doesn't do much small talk. She comes across as sensible and reliable rather than chatty. Given a bit of time, and a sense that the other person is genuine, she relaxes and shows a wry sense of humour.
- small things: Rhys has his mocks coming up and is 'very relaxed about it, unlike me', The A55 roadworks are making her commute a nightmare, She got up Moel Famau on Saturday before the cloud came in, The cat has started yowling at five in the morning, She's finally finished a crossword clue that bugged her all week, The leisure centre changed the pool timetable again
- deeper things: Being a lone parent working long hours has meant a lot of guilt about missed parents' evenings, and she leans on her mum more than she'd like, She worries about Rhys leaving for university and the house going very quiet, She sometimes wonders whether she should have tried harder to make things work with Rhys's dad, though she knows they were better apart, Her dad's redundancy from the steelworks shaped how much she values job security, She hasn't really dated in years and has mixed feelings about whether she wants to
- webcam photo: Head-and-shoulders shot from a laptop on a kitchen table, camera angled slightly upward. Daylight from a window to her left lights one side of her face, with the other side a little shadowed. She has a fair, lightly freckled complexion, a few lines around her eyes and a neutral but attentive expression with the hint of a polite smile. Her hair is shoulder-length, mid-brown with some grey at the temples, tucked behind one ear. She wears rectangular dark-framed glasses and a navy crew-neck jumper over a pale blue collared shirt. Behind her are white kitchen wall units, a kettle and a bread bin on the worktop, a calendar with handwritten entries pinned to the side of a cupboard, and a pair of walking boots just visible on the floor by the back door.

P228 (Callum; transcript label: Callum):
- first name: Callum
- age: 23
- lives in: Wolverhampton, West Midlands
- occupation: Full-time undergraduate student (second year, BSc Computer Science) at the University of Wolverhampton. Picks up the odd Saturday shift at a mate's dad's tyre place in Bilston when he's skint.
- education detail: Left school in Wednesfield with mostly 4s and 5s at GCSE. Did a BTEC in IT at college and passed, though not with distinction. Worked two years on nights in a distribution warehouse off the M6, then applied to uni through Clearing at 21. He's coasting on a 2:2 average. Coursework tends to go in on the deadline day, sometimes an hour before.
- household: Rents a one-bedroom flat above a takeaway in Whitmore Reans with his girlfriend Jade, 24, who works as a care assistant. They've been together four years and have lived together for two. No kids, no pets. The landlord won't allow them.
- cultural background: White British, Black Country born and bred. Mum works in a school kitchen. Dad drives a van for a parcel firm. He has an older sister in Dudley with two kids. Nobody in the family has been to uni before him, which his nan brings up more than he'd like. Not religious. He hasn't been in a church since a cousin's christening.
- professional persona: Practical rather than academic. He likes getting something to actually work and gets bored by theory and write-ups. He's good in group projects at the bit where code has to run, and not interested in the meetings. He'll tell a lecturer straight if he thinks a module is pointless. He doesn't sweat about grades and thinks the degree is mostly a box to tick to get out of warehouse work.
- sports persona: Wolves fan through his dad. He watches most games in a pub on the Dudley Road rather than paying for a season ticket. Plays five-a-side on Thursday nights when enough of the lads turn up. Fairly competitive and quick to have a go at someone for not tracking back. Doesn't go to the gym anymore.
- arts persona: Not much. Mostly YouTube and Twitch, plus whatever Jade puts on Netflix. He'll sit through crime documentaries. He listens to UK rap and a bit of old Arctic Monkeys on Spotify. He hasn't been to a gig since a Wolverhampton Civic show a couple of years ago.
- travel persona: He's been abroad a handful of times: Tenerife and Magaluf with mates, and a cheap week in Turkey with Jade. Doesn't plan anything. Jade books it and he turns up. He'd like to do Japan one day but hasn't saved a penny towards it.
- culinary persona: Can do the basics: pasta bake, fajitas, a fry-up. Jade does most of the proper cooking. He eats a lot of chicken and rice and grabs a bacon bap from the café near campus most mornings he's in. The takeaway downstairs is a temptation, and they give in about twice a week.
- hobbies and interests: PC gaming, mainly FIFA/EA FC and Call of Duty with the same group of mates, Five-a-side football on Thursdays, Watching Wolves, Messing about building cheap PCs for people from second-hand parts, Reddit and tech YouTube
- skills: Python and some Java from his course, Building and fixing PCs, Forklift licence (counterbalance) from the warehouse, Stays calm when stuff goes wrong, Getting things done last-minute under pressure

Gemma: Hiya! Can you hear me okay?
Yusuf: Yeah, loud and clear. Hiya, I'm Yusuf. Gemma, is it?
Gemma: That's me, yeah. Nice to meet you. How are you doing?
Yusuf: Not bad, not bad. Bit knackered, I went gym before this, which was a mistake, my legs are gone. How about you?
Gemma: Oh I'm alright, thanks. I've just got through a pile of maths books at the kitchen table, so I'm feeling quite smug actually.
Yusuf: Maths books. Teacher, then?
Gemma: Yeah, primary. Year 4 in Wigan. And I'm maths lead as well, which sounds dead fancy but mostly it means I get the emails nobody else wants.
Yusuf: Ha, I know that feeling, mate. Erm, so I'm an exec assistant, I work for two directors at a property consultancy in Birmingham. Basically I keep two grown men's diaries alive. Client lunches, travel, board minutes, all that. If I'm off sick for a day, honestly, the whole place just stops. I'm not even joking.
Gemma: So it's like having two Year 4s then.
Yusuf: Do you know what, Year 4s are probably better behaved. At least yours can tell the time.
Gemma: You'd be surprised. We're doing analogue clocks at the minute and it's carnage.
Yusuf: Carnage, I bet. So did you do that puzzle thing at the start? How'd you get on?
Gemma: Erm, alright I think? I did the first bit really quick and then just sort of stared at the last one for ages. You?
Yusuf: Same, same. I reckon I got most of them. I'm saying most. Couldn't swear to it.
Gemma: That's the spirit.
Yusuf: Is that a Warriors magnet on your fridge? I can see it behind you.
Gemma: Oh, it is, yeah! Well spotted. My family are Wigan Warriors through and through, my dad's been taking me since I was little and now I take our Lily as well, she's eleven. We go to a few home games a season and watch the Grand Final at my mum and dad's. Do you follow rugby at all?
Yusuf: Not really, I'm football. Villa, all day. I get to a few home games when a client's got a spare hospitality seat, which, I'm not gonna lie, is the best way to watch it. Free food.
Gemma: Free food is always the best way to do anything.
Yusuf: Exactly. Exactly that. You got any holidays sorted this year?
Gemma: Tenerife, same place as last year. I always go back to the same resort with Lily and sometimes my mum. All-inclusive, kids' club, done. I need to book it before the prices go up, actually, you've reminded me.
Yusuf: See, I couldn't do the same place twice. I always want somewhere new. Last year was Marrakech with my girlfriend, before that Dubai. I like a nice hotel, bit beyond my budget, if I'm honest.
Gemma: I'd find all that a bit stressful, to be fair. The planning and that. I like knowing where the pool is and where they do the chips.
Yusuf: No, that's fair, that's fair. Different strokes.
Gemma: And to be honest, with an eleven-year-old you just want an easy life. She's starting high school in September and the uniform alone has cost me a fortune.
Yusuf: Oh, the blazer and everything? My mum used to moan about that with all four of us.
Gemma: The blazer, the PE kit, the special socks with the logo on. Socks! I said to the lady, they're socks.
Yusuf: Mate, they got you. That's a racket, that.
Gemma: It is. Anyway, my treat to myself is a pie barm on a Friday from the bakery, so that keeps me going.
Yusuf: A pie barm? Sorry, what's a barm?
Gemma: A bread roll! A barm cake. Pie inside a barm. Don't look at me like that.
Yusuf: A pie in a bap? That's mad. That's carbs in carbs.
Gemma: It's a Wigan thing, it's beautiful, you'd love it.

=== CALL C0456 ===
Carys: Hello. Can you hear me all right?
Callum: Yeah, fine. You alright?
Carys: Fine, thanks. I'm Carys.
Callum: Callum.
Carys: Right. Erm, so I suppose we just chat. What do you do, Callum?
Callum: Student. Computer science at Wolverhampton, second year. Do the odd Saturday at a tyre place when I'm skint.
Carys: Oh, okay. And do you enjoy it? The course, I mean, not the tyres.
Callum: Bits of it. The coding's alright, getting stuff to actually run. The theory and the write-ups I could do without, to be honest. Half the modules feel like they're just there to fill the timetable, do you know what I mean.
Carys: Yeah, I remember some of those. Mine was civil engineering, a long time ago now.
Callum: That what you do then?
Carys: It is, yeah. I'm a civil engineer at a consultancy, I do flood risk and drainage mostly. So, councils across North Wales and Cheshire come to us with, erm, say an estate that floods every winter, or a culvert that can't cope, and I model how the water moves and work out what we can actually do about it.
Callum: Like the floods you see on the news, people in canoes down the high street.
Carys: Sort of, yeah. Hopefully I'm the reason you don't see it on the news. That's the idea, anyway.
Callum: Fair. Sounds more useful than half of what I do.
Carys: Well, someone's got to write the software for the models, to be fair. Did you do the puzzle at the start?
Callum: Yeah. Rubbish at it. Rushed the last two cos I got bored.
Carys: I quite liked it, actually. I do the Saturday cryptic, so I'm used to staring at things until they give in.
Callum: Cryptic crosswords. My nan does them. Well, she does the easy ones.
Carys: There's no shame in the easy ones. So what are you thinking of doing after? Have you got a placement year?
Callum: Nah. Not yet. My tutor keeps on at me about it. Something'll turn up.
Carys: Hm. That's exactly what my son says about his mocks.
Callum: How old's he?
Carys: Sixteen. He's very relaxed about it. Unlike me.
Callum: Sounds about right, yeah.
Carys: I'll be honest with you though, I mentor graduates at work, and the ones who got placements sorted early had a much easier time. I'm not nagging. Well, I am a bit.
Callum: No, you're probably right, I know I'm leaving it late. I just can't get myself bothered till it's urgent. Did two years on nights in a warehouse before uni, so I'm not exactly panicking, if that makes sense. Anything's better than nights.
Carys: That makes sense, yeah. My dad was at the steelworks, so I understand wanting something steady.
Callum: Yeah. That's it really.
Carys: Is that a Wolves scarf behind you?
Callum: Yeah, through my dad. Watch most of them down the pub. You into football?
Carys: Not really. Rugby, for the Six Nations. My son and I watch Wales and I get more worked up than I should.
Callum: Never got rugby, mate. Too many stoppages.
Carys: Yeah, no, I've heard that one before.

You write transcripts of realistic video calls between strangers for a fully synthetic research dataset set in the UK. The study, in order (from its published design): a short puzzle task done alone; first impressions of the others' webcam photos; then a series of three-minute, one-on-one video calls in rounds, each person meeting the others in their group; after each call a short survey.

Call shape (from the original study's numbers): a call is cut off by a three-minute timer. A typical call has about 30 turns (most between 20 and 39) and about 570 words in total (most between 440 and 682); half of all turns are 12 words or fewer, and a quarter are 24 or more. Short acknowledgements ("yeah", "mm") count as turns too. So aim for about 570 words in about 30 turns: alongside the quick back-and-forth, people often talk in longer stretches (explaining their job, telling a story), and those long turns carry much of the call.

Guide to British conversational English (use it for how people talk; it is a description of speech, not a script):
How British people talk in casual conversation. This is a paraphrase of published descriptions of spoken British English; sources are in SOURCES.md. Use these features lightly and only where they fit the person. Never use them as a caricature.

- **Fillers.** British speakers hesitate with "erm" and "er". Women and younger speakers lean towards "erm".
- **Hedges.** "Sort of" is everywhere and steady. "Kind of" is spreading, and younger speakers use it more.
- **Politeness words.** "Please", "thank you", "thanks" and "sorry" mostly mean what they say. "Sorry" also works as a repair word (to correct yourself, or to ask someone to repeat) and can be ironic.
- **Tags at the end of a sentence.** "You know", "right", "okay", "yeah", "do you know what I mean". Among young Londoners, "innit" and "you get me" are rising. Tags depend on age and region only, never on ethnicity.
- **Echoing.** In an engaged conversation people pick up and re-use parts of each other's words.
- **Regional words and grammar** (from a recent dialect survey):
  - A bread roll is a "barm" in the North West (Manchester to Liverpool and western Lancashire), a "cob" around Nottinghamshire, a "bap" in Staffordshire, the West Midlands and North Wales, and a "batch" in Liverpool and Coventry.
  - Around Liverpool an ice lolly can be a "lolly ice".
  - The evening meal is "tea" in the North West, North East and Yorkshire, and "dinner" in the South East and London. Some people say both.
  - "Yous" or "youse" for plural "you" is common in the North East (Newcastle, Teesside), Liverpool and Scotland, less so in Manchester, and rare in York, Leeds and Sheffield.
  - "Give it me" is normal in the North West and West Midlands and widely accepted in Sheffield and York; it fades south of Birmingham, Coventry and Leicester.
  - "You was" is widely used, historically Northern and now found as far south as London.
- **Everyday British words** to draw on where they fit, without assigning them to regions: knackered or shattered, chuffed or made up, skint or brassic, mardy or stroppy, mum or mam, mate or pal, settee, sofa or couch.

The group (session S35). Persona cards, including the webcam photo each person was rated on:

P184 (Gary; transcript label: Gary):
- first name: Gary
- age: 56
- lives in: Bridgwater, South West England
- occupation: Not currently working. Former forklift and warehouse operative at a food distribution depot on the edge of town for 19 years. Signed off just over two years ago with a lower back problem (a prolapsed disc and sciatica down his left leg). Now on benefits and doing a few hours a week volunteering.
- education detail: Left the local comprehensive at 16 with a handful of CSEs and one O level in woodwork. Did a YTS placement at a builders' merchant. Holds a counterbalance forklift licence (lapsed, but he keeps the card) and a food hygiene certificate from his depot days.
- household: Lives alone in a two-bedroom ex-council terraced house he rents from a housing association. Divorced from Karen eleven years ago after 20 years of marriage, and they are on civil terms. Has one grown-up daughter, Leanne (29), who lives in Taunton with her partner and his granddaughter Poppy (4). The second bedroom is kept made up for when Poppy stays.
- cultural background: White British, born and raised in Bridgwater. His dad worked at the cellophane factory and his mum did school dinners. Grew up on the same estate he lives near now. Not religious, though he went to Sunday school as a kid and still goes to the Remembrance service. Carnival season matters to him: his uncle was in a carnival club and Gary helped build carts in his twenties.
- professional persona: Was the reliable one on the shift: never late, kept the paperwork straight, knew everyone's name including the agency lads, and was the person the supervisor asked to show new starters round. Still talks about the depot as if he's going back. He'd like something part-time and not too heavy if his back allows, like a caretaker, a car park attendant or a meet-and-greet job.
- sports persona: Follows football loosely and supports Bristol City out of family habit, mostly watching highlights. Used to play skittles for a pub team and still goes along on league nights to score and socialise, even though he can't bowl much now. Walks every day on the physio's orders, usually along the river or the canal path.
- arts persona: Not much of a cultural outing person. Likes the carnival, the odd tribute band at the social club, and a film if Leanne drags him along. Watches quiz shows, Bargain Hunt and old episodes of Only Fools and Horses. Has no interest in galleries or the theatre and would say so cheerfully.
- travel persona: Hasn't been abroad since a family package holiday to Majorca about fifteen years ago, and his passport's expired. Prefers a static caravan at Brean or a week in Devon. Doesn't drive much now because his back stiffens up, so he relies on buses and Leanne's car.
- culinary persona: Plain, regular meals at set times. Batch-cooks a cottage pie or a stew on Sundays and portions it into labelled tubs for the week. Likes a fry-up on a Saturday, fish and chips on a Friday and a pasty when he's out. Doesn't like anything too spicy. Drinks tea all day and the odd pint of cider at the club.
- hobbies and interests: Volunteering two mornings a week at a community food bank, sorting stock and chatting to people in the queue, Skittles league nights (scoring rather than bowling these days), Doing the crossword in the local paper, Keeping his small back garden tidy: bedding plants and a couple of tomato pots, Pub quiz on Thursdays with the same three mates, Sorting out bits for neighbours, like fixing a gate or putting up a shelf, when his back's good
- skills: Forklift and warehouse stock handling, Very organised: lists, calendars, labelled boxes, Basic DIY and carpentry, Getting on with anyone and remembering names, Reliable timekeeping, Showing new people the ropes
- career goals: To get his back to a point where he can do 16 hours a week somewhere sociable without being in pain. He's been talking to a work coach about it. He doesn't want a career, just a routine, a bit of extra money and people to talk to. He worries about what happens if he can't go back to work.
- voice: Warm, chatty and quick to fill the gap, with a soft Somerset accent. He has a slight burr on his r's, says 'alright?' as a greeting and now and then uses 'my love' or 'mate'. Speaks fairly fast, with a lot of 'you know' and 'sort of', and 'er' when he's thinking. Tells little stories to answer simple questions and then says 'anyway, sorry, I'm going off on one'. Hates silence and will fill it, often by asking the interviewer something back, like 'where are you based then?'. Says 'thank you' and 'cheers' a lot and means it.
- typing: Types carefully with two fingers, so his answers are short. Capitalises the first word and names, mostly ends with a full stop and usually gets apostrophes right because he's careful. Sometimes types in all caps by accident and corrects it. No abbreviations beyond 'ok'. Might add 'Thanks' at the end of a free-text answer.
- with strangers: Instantly friendly and open, and treats a stranger like a new starter on shift. Asks how your day's going and makes self-deprecating jokes about his back and his age. Very honest, sometimes more than he needs to be. Keen to do things properly and checks he's answered what you actually asked. Can come across as a bit anxious to please.
- small things: His granddaughter Poppy's latest saying, The bus being late again, Who won at the skittles, The weather and whether he can get out in the garden, What came in at the food bank this week, His physio exercises and his new walking route, Getting the crossword done before lunch
- deeper things: He felt like he'd lost a part of himself when he stopped working, and the first year was very low, He's lonely in the evenings since the divorce and keeps busy to avoid it, He regrets working so many night shifts when Leanne was little, He's worried about money and the next benefits review, His dad died of a stroke at 64, and he thinks about that more than he lets on, He cried at Poppy's nursery nativity and was embarrassed about it
- webcam photo: A slightly low-angle laptop webcam shot from a dining table, with Gary centred and a bit too close to the screen. Daylight comes from a window to his right, so one side of his face is brighter. He has a broad, ruddy face with a big open grin and crow's feet. His hair is short, grey and thinning on top, and he has light stubble. He wears reading glasses with thin black frames pushed up slightly, and a navy fleece zipped halfway over a grey T-shirt. Behind him is a magnolia wall with a framed photo of a small girl in a fairy costume and a wall calendar with appointments written in biro. A neat shelf holds a skittles trophy, a row of DVDs and a carriage clock. A mug on a coaster is just visible at the bottom of the frame.

P185 (Bethany; transcript label: Bethany):
- first name: Bethany
- age: 25
- lives in: Basingstoke, South East England
- occupation: IT service desk analyst (second-line support) at an insurance company's regional office, full-time, about 37.5 hours a week plus the odd late shift
- education detail: A levels in Computing, Maths and Psychology at a sixth form college in Basingstoke. Started a Computer Science degree at Southampton but left after first year. Later picked up CompTIA A+ and ITIL Foundation certificates through work.
- household: Rents a two-bed terraced house in South Ham with her partner Dan (27), a warehouse shift manager she has been with for about a year and a half. They have a rescue cat called Biscuit. Her divorce from her first husband, who she married at 21, was finalised just over a year ago.
- cultural background: Grew up in Basingstoke. Her mum is a teaching assistant and her dad is a self-employed electrician, and she has a younger brother at uni. She was raised Church of England and went to Sunday school and youth group. Her faith still matters to her but she keeps it quiet. She goes to a local Anglican church every few weeks, more often around Easter and Christmas, and sits near the back.
- professional persona: Reliable on tickets and very good with frustrated users on the phone. She is patient and never makes people feel stupid. Her paperwork and ticket notes lag behind, and her manager has nudged her about closing tickets properly. She hates being put forward in team meetings and would rather fix things than talk about fixing them. She tells you straight if she broke something.
- sports persona: Not sporty. Does a Couch to 5K app in fits and starts and has restarted week three about four times. Walks along the canal path at weekends. Will watch the Women's Euros if Dan puts it on.
- arts persona: Reads a lot of fantasy and cosy mystery on her Kindle, often well past midnight. Likes indie folk and listens to the same few albums on repeat. Draws a bit in a sketchbook she never shows anyone.
- travel persona: Hasn't travelled much. Went to Cornwall most summers as a kid and to Lanzarote on her honeymoon. She and Dan did a long weekend in Edinburgh last year, which she loved because it was walking, bookshops and nobody needing her to talk. She keeps meaning to renew her passport.
- culinary persona: Cooks simple things like pasta bakes, fajitas and jacket potatoes. Batch-cooks with good intentions and then orders a Domino's on Fridays. Calls the evening meal dinner. Makes a decent Victoria sponge, taught by her nan.
- hobbies and interests: reading fantasy and mystery novels, cosy video games like Stardew Valley and Animal Crossing, sketching, canal walks, jigsaws, fostering kittens occasionally through a local cat rescue
- skills: troubleshooting Windows and Microsoft 365 issues, Active Directory account admin, calming down stressed people on the phone, baking, patient, careful explaining
- career goals: Wants to move into a quieter, more technical role, maybe infrastructure or Microsoft 365 administration. She's been 'about to start' the Azure fundamentals course for six months. She isn't chasing management and would hate it.
- voice: Soft, fairly quiet southern English with no strong accent. Pace is slow-to-medium. She often starts answers with 'erm' and hedges with 'sort of' and 'kind of'. She ends thoughts with 'yeah' or 'I don't know'. If you've asked something vague she'll repair with 'sorry, do you mean...'. She gives short answers at first and opens up if you echo something back or show interest. She doesn't fill silences. She'll wait, then say something like 'yeah, that's sort of it really'. She laughs a little nervously when talking about herself.
- typing: Mostly lowercase and doesn't bother capitalising 'i' in quick answers. Uses few full stops and separates thoughts with commas or line breaks. Usually keeps apostrophes in (dont slips through sometimes). Uses 'tbh', 'idk' and occasionally 'lol'. Answers are short and honest. She'll type 'not sure' rather than guess.
- with strangers: Reserved and polite. She can seem a bit flat or shy at first. She answers what's asked without embellishing and won't pretend to know things she doesn't. She warms up slowly and comes across as genuine, modest and slightly awkward, and says 'sorry' more than she needs to.
- small things: Biscuit keeps walking across her keyboard, the trains into work being rubbish, a book series she's halfway through, forgetting to defrost something for dinner, her nan's cake recipes, Dan's shift patterns, the Festival Place shops
- deeper things: She married her school boyfriend at 21 because it felt like the right, grown-up thing, and it fell apart within two years, She felt awkward at her old church after the divorce and switched to a different one, She still feels a bit like she failed at her first try at being an adult, Dropping out of uni still bothers her, though she rarely says so, She and Dan have talked about marriage and she's not sure she wants to do it again
- webcam photo: Laptop webcam at a slight upward angle, framing her from mid-chest up, a little off-centre to the left. Lighting is a warm ceiling light plus cooler daylight from a window to her right, so one side of her face is brighter. She is a pale-skinned young woman with light brown, shoulder-length hair tied in a loose low ponytail, a few strands escaping. No makeup apart from a bit of mascara. She has a small, polite closed-mouth smile and her eyes are looking slightly below the camera at the screen. She wears an oversized sage green knitted jumper and a thin gold chain with a small cross. No glasses. Behind her is a magnolia wall with a cheap white bookshelf crammed with paperbacks, some stacked sideways, a small potted pothos on top and a jigsaw box leaning against it. To the right, half out of frame, is a clothes airer with a couple of T-shirts on it. A ginger cat is curled on the arm of a grey sofa just visible at the bottom left.

P186 (Callum; transcript label: Callum):
- first name: Callum
- age: 28
- lives in: Swindon, South West England
- occupation: Currently out of work. Until about four months ago he was assistant manager at a branch of a national sports and outdoor retail chain at a retail park in Swindon. He took redundancy when the branch was restructured and has been half-heartedly applying for supervisory retail and warehouse roles since.
- education detail: Went to a comprehensive in Swindon and got a handful of GCSEs including English and maths. Started a BTEC in Business at the local college but didn't finish the second year. He has worked in retail since he was 18, moving up from sales assistant to supervisor to assistant manager.
- household: Rents a two-bed terraced house in the Rodbourne area with his girlfriend of six years, Jess, who works as a dental nurse. They aren't married and have no children. Jess handles most of the bills and admin, which is a quiet sore point now that he isn't earning.
- cultural background: White British, born and raised in Swindon. His dad worked at the Honda plant until it closed and his mum works part-time in a school office. He has no religion and never really thinks about it. His family is ordinary and close-ish: Sunday dinner at his mum's once a month or so, and a younger sister in Chippenham.
- professional persona: He was a decent but unflashy assistant manager. He was good at the practical side of running a shop floor and calm with difficult customers, but bad at paperwork, rota deadlines and anything that needed planning ahead. He got the job mostly by being reliable at turning up and knowing the stock, not through ambition. He didn't enjoy the team briefings or the 'motivating staff' part.
- sports persona: Watches football on the telly, mainly Premier League highlights and the odd Swindon Town result he checks on his phone, though he rarely goes to the County Ground any more. Used to play five-a-side but drifted off when the group's organiser moved away. Goes for walks with Jess at Coate Water sometimes.
- arts persona: Not really interested. He watches whatever's on Netflix or Prime, usually crime series or stuff Jess has picked, and rewatches comedy he already knows. He listens to Spotify playlists in the car without paying much attention to who the artists are. He hasn't been to a gig or the theatre in years.
- travel persona: Not bothered about travel. They've had a week in Tenerife twice and once went to a mate's stag in Newquay. He'd happily go back to the same all-inclusive place again. Doesn't have a current passport, because it expired and he hasn't got round to renewing it.
- culinary persona: Plain eater. Pasta, chicken, oven chips, Friday takeaway (usually a Chinese or a kebab). Jess does most of the cooking. He can do a fry-up and that's about it. Calls the evening meal 'tea' or 'dinner' interchangeably.
- hobbies and interests: Playing FIFA/EA FC and Call of Duty on the PlayStation, often late into the night, Watching football highlights, Scrolling YouTube and Reddit, The occasional pint at the local with one or two old school mates, Walks at Coate Water when Jess suggests it
- skills: Handling stock and deliveries, Dealing calmly with awkward customers, Cashing up and basic till systems, Knows the ins and outs of trainers and sports kit, Decent at video games
- career goals: Vague. He'd like another assistant manager or supervisor job, ideally somewhere with a regular rota and no weekend lates, maybe a warehouse at one of the distribution centres off the M4. He doesn't have a long-term plan and doesn't like being asked about one.
- voice: Quiet and fairly flat, low energy, with short answers unless he's asked about something he knows well. He has a light Swindon/Wiltshire accent: some rhotic 'r's, and occasionally 'we was' or 'you was'. Uses 'erm', 'sort of' and 'I dunno' a lot, and ends things with 'yeah' or 'so, yeah'. Says 'mate' if he's relaxed. He doesn't fill silences himself; he waits for the next question and might say 'that's it really'.
- typing: All lowercase, minimal punctuation, often no full stop at the end. Apostrophes are usually missing ('dont', 'im'). Short answers, sometimes just a few words. Uses 'idk', 'tbh' and 'n/a'. Typos are left uncorrected.
- with strangers: Polite but reserved and a bit hard to draw out. He comes across as easy-going rather than unfriendly, gives minimal answers at first, and warms up slightly if the topic is football, games or work stories. He doesn't ask questions back.
- small things: The PS5 controller drifting and him meaning to buy a new one, Swindon Town having another rubbish season, Jess's shifts at the dental practice, Roadworks on the Magic Roundabout, Getting a Greggs on the way back from the job centre, The house being cold because they're trying not to put the heating on
- deeper things: Feels a bit embarrassed about being out of work while Jess carries the bills, Knows he puts things off and that it's caused problems, like late applications and the expired passport, Jess has started hinting about getting engaged and buying a place, and he feels unready, Misses the routine and the people at the old shop more than he expected, Worries a little that he's 'just drifting' compared with his sister
- webcam photo: Laptop webcam at a slightly low angle, so the frame cuts off just above his head. Lit mainly by the laptop screen and a ceiling light behind him, so his face is a bit washed out and bluish. A white man in his late twenties with short brown hair, clippered at the sides and slightly messy on top, a couple of days of stubble, and a neutral, slightly tired expression, looking just below the camera. No glasses. He's wearing a grey Nike hoodie. Behind him is a magnolia living room wall with a large TV on a black stand, a PS5 and controller, a beige fabric settee with a crumpled throw, and a door half-open to a hallway with coats on hooks.

P187 (Daniel; transcript label: Daniel):
- first name: Daniel
- age: 36
- lives in: Peterborough, East of England
- occupation: Operations manager at a regional distribution centre for a national homeware and DIY retailer, responsible for about 140 warehouse staff across three shifts
- education detail: A-levels in Business Studies, Geography and PE at a sixth form college in Huntingdon; BA (Hons) Business Management from Anglia Ruskin University in Cambridge (2:1); later completed a CMI Level 5 diploma in Management and Leadership, paid for by his employer
- household: Lives with his wife Sophie, a primary school teacher, in a four-bedroom new-build semi in Hampton on the southern edge of Peterborough, which they bought in 2019. No children yet, though they've talked about it. They have a cocker spaniel called Bramble.
- cultural background: White British, born and raised in Huntingdon, Cambridgeshire. His dad was a lorry driver and later a transport planner, and his mum worked in a GP surgery reception. He has one younger sister in St Neots. Not religious and wasn't brought up going to church beyond school nativities. He's the first in his family to go to university, which he mentions matter-of-factly rather than as a big deal.
- professional persona: Started as a graduate trainee shift supervisor at 22 and worked his way up. He's known as a visible manager who walks the floor rather than sitting in the office, and he remembers people's names and their kids' names. He is organised to the point of colour-coded rotas, and he doesn't flap when a lorry's late or a system goes down. He's straight with people about targets and won't fudge numbers to look good upwards, which has occasionally irritated his regional boss. He isn't a pushover, but he doesn't play politics.
- sports persona: Plays five-a-side on Wednesday nights with a group from work and old uni mates, and does the Peterborough parkrun at Ferry Meadows most Saturdays, with a PB just under 22 minutes. He's had a Peterborough United season ticket on and off for years and goes with his dad when he can. He watches the cricket in the summer if it's on in the background.
- arts persona: Not a big arts person but not dismissive of it. He likes stand-up comedy and has been to see a few big names in Cambridge and at the Corn Exchange, and he listens to podcasts on the commute, mostly football, comedy and the odd true-crime series. Sophie drags him to the occasional West End musical, and he admits he usually enjoys it.
- travel persona: Likes a mix of a proper week in the sun, usually the Algarve or Majorca, and UK breaks with the dog: the Norfolk coast, the Peak District, the Lake District. He did a lads' trip to Berlin a few years back and a honeymoon in Croatia. He plans trips well in advance with a spreadsheet, which Sophie teases him about.
- culinary persona: Does most of the cooking at weekends: barbecues as soon as it's vaguely warm, a Sunday roast, and a decent chilli or curry. Weeknight dinners are quick and practical, often something Sophie's batch-cooked. He enjoys a pint of real ale or a lager at the pub but isn't a heavy drinker, and he's cut back since getting into running.
- hobbies and interests: five-a-side football, parkrun at Ferry Meadows, following Peterborough United, walking the dog, barbecuing, comedy podcasts, pub quizzes, DIY and sorting the garden
- skills: workforce planning and shift rota management, staying calm in operational crises, coaching and developing supervisors, Excel and warehouse management systems, health and safety compliance (IOSH Managing Safely), plain-speaking communication with staff at all levels, basic plumbing and flat-pack assembly
- career goals: Wants to move up to site general manager within the next few years, ideally without relocating out of the Peterborough area. He's thought about an MBA but isn't sure it's worth the money compared with experience. Long term he'd like a role where he's mentoring newer managers, because that's the part of the job he enjoys most.
- voice: Friendly, confident and fairly quick, with a neutral East of England accent: slightly flattened vowels and a few dropped t's ('a bi' of'), nothing strong. He talks in a conversational, managerial way and is comfortable explaining things. He uses 'er' when thinking and 'sort of' a lot as a hedge, and ends points with 'you know' or 'yeah'. He says 'mate' when relaxed and 'knackered' after a long shift week. He calls the evening meal 'dinner'. Silences don't bother him. He'll usually fill one with a quick 'er, what else' or a light joke, but if he's thinking he'll just say 'hang on, let me think about that' and take a second.
- typing: Quick and mostly correct, with capitals at the start of sentences and usually full stops. Apostrophes are mostly right because he types work emails all day. He'll use 'e.g.' and 'etc' and sometimes 'tbh', but no emojis. Short answers are practical, like 'Yes, a couple of times a week mainly for work stuff.' Spelling is accurate and he doesn't over-explain.
- with strangers: Warm and easy from the first minute. He asks the other person a question back and makes them feel at ease. He's chatty without dominating, and he's honest even when the answer is a bit dull ('to be honest I don't really think about it much'). He doesn't show off about his job title and is more likely to downplay it.
- small things: the dog getting muddy at Ferry Meadows, Posh's latest result, the A1 and the A14 roadworks, peak season at the warehouse before Christmas, his parkrun time, a new barbecue he's eyeing up, Sophie's school holidays versus his annual leave, the new-build estate's snagging issues
- deeper things: he and Sophie have been trying for a baby for over a year and it's starting to weigh on them, he sometimes feels he's drifting away from mates back in Huntingdon who didn't go to uni, his dad had a heart scare two years ago, which is partly why he started running, he once reported a colleague for fiddling timesheets and lost a friendship over it, but would do it again, he worries he's defined himself too much by work
- webcam photo: Laptop webcam at slightly below eye level, so the frame looks a touch upward at him. He sits centred, with head and shoulders filling the lower two-thirds of the frame. The lighting is soft daylight from a window to his left, leaving the right side of his face a little shadowed. He has a broad, clean-shaven face with light stubble along the jaw, short brown hair cut close at the sides and a bit longer on top, and a relaxed half-smile with slight crow's feet. No glasses. He wears a navy quarter-zip fleece over a white T-shirt collar. Behind him is a pale grey wall in a small home office (the box room). A white IKEA shelving unit holds box files, a few paperbacks, a framed wedding photo and a small Peterborough United mug holding pens. A cork board with a printed calendar and a parkrun barcode keyring hanging from a pin is partly visible on the right edge. Part of a dog bed shows in the bottom left corner.

P188 (Jurgita; transcript label: Jurgita):
- first name: Jurgita
- age: 37
- lives in: Wakefield, Yorkshire and The Humber
- occupation: Senior care assistant at a privately run residential care home for older people. She works mostly 12-hour day shifts, about 40 hours a week, and picks up extra shifts when the overtime rate is good.
- education detail: Finished secondary school in Šiauliai, Lithuania, then did one year of a vocational course in hospitality that she didn't complete. In the UK she has an NVQ Level 3 in Health and Social Care, done through work, plus the usual mandatory training certificates: manual handling, medication administration and first aid.
- household: Lives with her husband Darius, 39, also Lithuanian, who drives a forklift at a distribution warehouse off the M62. No children. They rent a two-bed terraced house and have talked for years about saving for a deposit, without getting very far.
- cultural background: Born and raised in Šiauliai, Lithuania. Came to the UK in 2008 aged 21, first to a food-packing job in Grimsby through an agency, then to Wakefield in 2011 when Darius got work nearby. Raised Catholic. She goes to the Polish-Lithuanian Mass in Leeds at Christmas and Easter and occasionally otherwise, mostly to please her mum when she phones. She speaks Lithuanian at home and English at work. She has settled status and has never really considered going back for good, though she says she might 'when old'.
- professional persona: Competent and quick with residents and good at getting them washed, dressed and fed. Less keen on the paperwork side and often finishes care notes in a rush at the end of shift. She knows which shifts pay best and which managers will let things slide, and she works that to her advantage. She is not especially warm with colleagues but gets on with them. She has opinions about who pulls their weight, usually that she does and others don't.
- sports persona: Not sporty. Walks a lot on shift and says that's enough exercise. Darius watches basketball, the Lithuanian league and the NBA, and she half-watches with him. She tried a gym membership once and stopped going after about three weeks.
- arts persona: Very little interest. Watches reality TV and the odd crime drama on Netflix, and scrolls TikTok and Facebook. Has never been to a gallery in the UK and doesn't see the point. Listens to whatever is on the radio in the car.
- travel persona: Goes back to Lithuania once a year, usually in summer, for two weeks to see her mum and sister. She likes a week in Tenerife or Turkey, all-inclusive, by the pool. Not interested in sightseeing or trying new places. She prefers somewhere she's been before and knows is good.
- culinary persona: Cooks simple food: potatoes, meat, soups, and cepelinai only at Christmas or when her mum visits. Buys Lithuanian sausage and bread from the Eastern European shop on Kirkgate. Says 'tea' for the evening meal like her colleagues do. Gets takeaway more than she means to, often a Chinese or a Domino's after a long shift.
- hobbies and interests: Watching reality TV, especially Love Island and Married at First Sight, Shopping for handbags and perfume, including from TK Maxx and Vinted, Getting her nails and lashes done, Scrolling TikTok, Video-calling her sister in Lithuania, Online surveys for a bit of extra money
- skills: Personal care and moving and handling, Administering medication on a MAR chart, Calming confused residents with dementia, Speaks Lithuanian, decent Russian and good working English, Finding a bargain online, Working long shifts without complaining much
- career goals: Nothing very ambitious. She'd like a small pay rise or a move to a care home closer to home with better rotas. She has thought about becoming a team leader but doesn't fancy the extra paperwork and responsibility. Mostly she wants more money for the same work and to buy a house eventually.
- voice: Lithuanian accent, clearly not native but fluent after years here. She sometimes drops articles ('I was on shift whole weekend') and occasionally mixes up tenses. req.text:
You write transcripts of realistic video calls between strangers for a fully synthetic research dataset set in the UK. The study, in order (from its published design): a short puzzle task done alone; first impressions of the others' webcam photos; then a series of three-minute, one-on-one video calls in rounds, each person meeting the others in their group; after each call a short survey.

Call shape (from the original study's numbers): a call is cut off by a three-minute timer. A typical call has about 30 turns (most between 20 and 39) and about 570 words in total (most between 440 and 682); half of all turns are 12 words or fewer, and a quarter are 24 or more. Short acknowledgements ("yeah", "mm") count as turns too. So aim for about 570 words in about 30 turns: alongside the quick back-and-forth, people often talk in longer stretches (explaining their job, telling a story), and those long turns carry much of the call.

Guide to British conversational English (use it for how people talk; it is a description of speech, not a script):
How British people talk in casual conversation. This is a paraphrase of published descriptions of spoken British English; sources are in SOURCES.md. Use these features lightly and only where they fit the person. Never use them as a caricature.

- **Fillers.** British speakers hesitate with "erm" and "er". Women and younger speakers lean towards "erm".
- **Hedges.** "Sort of" is everywhere and steady. "Kind of" is spreading, and younger speakers use it more.
- **Politeness words.** "Please", "thank you", "thanks" and "sorry" mostly mean what they say. "Sorry" also works as a repair word (to correct yourself, or to ask someone to repeat) and can be ironic.
- **Tags at the end of a sentence.** "You know", "right", "okay", "yeah", "do you know what I mean". Among young Londoners, "innit" and "you get me" are rising. Tags depend on age and region only, never on ethnicity.
- **Echoing.** In an engaged conversation people pick up and re-use parts of each other's words.
- **Regional words and grammar** (from a recent dialect survey):
  - A bread roll is a "barm" in the North West (Manchester to Liverpool and western Lancashire), a "cob" around Nottinghamshire, a "bap" in Staffordshire, the West Midlands and North Wales, and a "batch" in Liverpool and Coventry.
  - Around Liverpool an ice lolly can be a "lolly ice".
  - The evening meal is "tea" in the North West, North East and Yorkshire, and "dinner" in the South East and London. Some people say both.
  - "Yous" or "youse" for plural "you" is common in the North East (Newcastle, Teesside), Liverpool and Scotland, less so in Manchester, and rare in York, Leeds and Sheffield.
  - "Give it me" is normal in the North West and West Midlands and widely accepted in Sheffield and York; it fades south of Birmingham, Coventry and Leicester.
  - "You was" is widely used, historically Northern and now found as far south as London.
- **Everyday British words** to draw on where they fit, without assigning them to regions: knackered or shattered, chuffed or made up, skint or brassic, mardy or stroppy, mum or mam, mate or pal, settee, sofa or couch.
