req.text:
You write transcripts of realistic video calls between strangers for a fully synthetic research dataset set in the UK. The study, in order (from its published design): a short puzzle task done alone; first impressions of the others' webcam photos; then a series of three-minute, one-on-one video calls in rounds, each person meeting the others in their group; after each call a short survey.

Call shape (from the original study's numbers): a call is cut off by a three-minute timer. A typical call has about 30 turns (most between 20 and 39) and about 570 words in total (most between 440 and 682); half of all turns are 12 words or fewer, and a quarter are 24 or more. Short acknowledgements ("yeah", "mm") count as turns too. So aim for about 570 words in about 30 turns: alongside the quick back-and-forth, people often talk in longer stretches (explaining their job, telling a story), and those long turns carry much of the call.

Guide to British conversational English (use it for how people talk; it is a description of speech, not a script):
How British people talk in casual conversation. This is a paraphrase of published descriptions of spoken British English; sources are in SOURCES.md. Use these features lightly and only where they fit the person. Never use them as a caricature.

- **Fillers.** British speakers hesitate with "erm" and "er". Women and younger speakers lean towards "erm".
- **Hedges.** "Sort of" is everywhere and steady. "Kind of" is spreading, and younger speakers use it more.
- **Politeness words.** "Please", "thank you", "thanks" and "sorry" mostly mean what they say. "Sorry" also works as a repair word (to correct yourself, or to ask someone to repeat) and can be ironic.
- **Tags at the end of a sentence.** "You know", "right", "okay", "yeah", "do you know what I mean". Among young Londoners, "innit" and "you get me" are rising. Tags depend on age and region only, never on ethnicity.
- **Echoing.** In an engaged conversation people pick up and re-use parts of each other's words.
- **Regional words and grammar** (from a recent dialect survey):
  - A bread roll is a "barm" in the North West (Manchester to Liverpool and western Lancashire), a "cob" around Nottinghamshire, a "bap" in Staffordshire, the West Midlands and North Wales, and a "batch" in Liverpool and Coventry.
  - Around Liverpool an ice lolly can be a "lolly ice".
  - The evening meal is "tea" in the North West, North East and Yorkshire, and "dinner" in the South East and London. Some people say both.
  - "Yous" or "youse" for plural "you" is common in the North East (Newcastle, Teesside), Liverpool and Scotland, less so in Manchester, and rare in York, Leeds and Sheffield.
  - "Give it me" is normal in the North West and West Midlands and widely accepted in Sheffield and York; it fades south of Birmingham, Coventry and Leicester.
  - "You was" is widely used, historically Northern and now found as far south as London.
- **Everyday British words** to draw on where they fit, without assigning them to regions: knackered or shattered, chuffed or made up, skint or brassic, mardy or stroppy, mum or mam, mate or pal, settee, sofa or couch.

The group (session S39). Persona cards, including the webcam photo each person was rated on:

P204 (Sana; transcript label: Sana):
- first name: Sana
- age: 27
- lives in: Bolton, North West England
- occupation: Part-time packing operative at an online fashion distribution warehouse on an industrial estate near Bolton. She works about 24 hours a week over three or four shifts, picking, packing and labelling parcels.
- education detail: Finished intermediate (FA) at a girls' college in Lahore and started a BA but left when she got married. After moving to the UK she did ESOL courses up to Level 1 at Bolton College. She started a beauty and lash course online last year and has not finished it.
- household: Lives with her husband Imran (31, a Bolton-born multi-drop delivery driver) in a rented two-bed terraced house in Daubhill. There are no children yet. They moved out of his parents' house, a few streets away, about eighteen months ago, and she still goes round there most days.
- cultural background: Born and raised in Lahore, Pakistan, in a big, lively family with three sisters. She married Imran, a cousin of a family friend, at 20 and came to the UK on a spouse visa at 21. She has now been in Bolton six years and holds settled status. She is Muslim and fairly observant in a relaxed way. She wears a hijab, prays when she can, and fasts in Ramadan, though she admits she's not the most regular. Weddings, Eid and family gatherings are the high points of her year. She speaks Punjabi and Urdu at home and with family, and English at work and with friends.
- professional persona: Sees the warehouse job as money, not a career. She likes the women she works with and spends shifts chatting rather than chasing pick rates, and she has had a couple of warnings about being late and about her phone. She's good at getting people on side, swapping shifts, and talking her way out of trouble with supervisors. She has rung in sick on days she wasn't, and doesn't feel bad about it.
- sports persona: Not sporty at all. She joined a ladies-only gym with a friend, went about five times, and kept the membership going for months before cancelling. She walks a fair bit, to the shops, to her mother-in-law's and round Queen's Park in summer, and is naturally healthy without trying.
- arts persona: Not interested in galleries, theatre or books. She watches Pakistani dramas on YouTube and loves Bollywood films and Punjabi songs. She is on TikTok and Instagram constantly, mostly makeup, fashion and wedding content. She does mehndi designs for friends and family before weddings and is proud of it.
- travel persona: Goes back to Lahore every couple of years for a month or so, usually around a family wedding, and takes suitcases full of gifts and clothes. She went to Dubai once with Imran and his sister and still talks about the malls. She wants to go to Turkey or the Maldives mainly for the photos, but money and Imran's work keep putting it off.
- culinary persona: Cooks Pakistani food most days because Imran expects it: chicken karahi, daal, aloo gobi, roti. She learned more from her mother-in-law than from her own mum. She gets bored of cooking and pushes for takeaways, Nando's or a dessert parlour on Derby Street. She says 'tea' for the evening meal now like everyone at work, and has picked up 'barm' for a bread roll.
- hobbies and interests: watching Pakistani dramas on YouTube, TikTok and Instagram (makeup, modest fashion, wedding content), doing mehndi for weddings and Eid, shopping at the Trafford Centre and Asian clothes shops in Bolton and Rusholme, makeup and lashes, going round to friends' and sisters-in-law's houses, voice notes and long phone calls with her sisters in Lahore
- skills: fluent Punjabi and Urdu, conversational English, mehndi application, makeup and lash application (self-taught, partly trained), fast parcel packing when she's bothered, chatting to anyone and making friends quickly, haggling and finding deals on designer-looking clothes and bags
- career goals: Vague and changeable. She talks about finishing her lash course and running a home beauty and mehndi business from Instagram, with 'proper' bookings and a nice room set up for clients. She wants to earn enough to buy branded handbags without Imran moaning. She has no real plan or timeline and tends to start things and drop them.
- voice: Warm, chatty and quick. She talks a lot and laughs easily. Her English is fluent for everyday things but clearly second-language, with a Pakistani accent, Urdu or Punjabi words dropped in when she's excited ('acha', 'yaar'), and occasional grammar slips like 'he was telling me yesterday' or 'you was there'. She has picked up a few Bolton bits from work, such as 'tea' for the evening meal, 'knackered' and 'love', but nothing broad. She says 'erm' and 'you know' a lot, and 'sort of' sometimes. If she doesn't understand a question she says 'sorry, what?' and laughs it off. She can't stand silence and fills it with stories, often going off on a tangent about her sister-in-law or a wedding. She can get flustered and anxious if a question feels like a test.
- typing: Mostly lowercase, little punctuation, apostrophes usually missing (dont, im, its). Uses 'u', 'ur', 'ok', 'lol', 'tbh' and the odd emoji if allowed. Answers are short and sometimes misspelled, typed fast on her phone. She skims instructions and sometimes answers the question she thinks is being asked.
- with strangers: Friendly and open straight away, complimentary, and keen to be liked. She asks the other person questions and shares quite a lot quite fast. She likes to come across as a bit more comfortable and well-off than she is, and will say whatever seems to please. Underneath she can be nervous about getting things 'wrong'.
- small things: her shift got changed again and she's knackered, a new lip liner she got from TikTok Shop, a cousin's wedding coming up and what she's wearing, Imran working late on deliveries, her mother-in-law's karahi being better than hers, the weather being rubbish compared to Lahore, a Pakistani drama everyone at work is watching
- deeper things: pressure from her in-laws about when they're having children, and her own worry because it hasn't happened yet, missing her mum and sisters badly, and crying after video calls, feeling she married young and didn't get to finish her degree, money arguments with Imran about her spending and credit card, feeling lonely in her first years in Bolton, when her English wasn't good, worrying that people at work look down on her
- webcam photo: Phone propped on a stand at chest height, angled slightly upward, in the evening. Her face is lit by a small ring light, which shows as a circle in her pupils, with a warm table lamp off to the right. She is a young South Asian woman with full makeup: winged eyeliner, false lashes, contoured cheeks and a nude-brown lip. She is smiling widely with her head tilted slightly. She wears a dusty pink chiffon hijab wrapped loosely and pinned at the side, and a cream knitted jumper. No glasses. Behind her is a grey crushed-velvet sofa with silver cushions and a fluffy white throw. On the magnolia wall above it hangs a large mirror with a crystal-effect frame and a framed gold Arabic calligraphy print of Ayat al-Kursi. A glimpse of a doorway on the left shows a hallway with a coat on a hook.

P205 (Joanne; transcript label: Joanne):
- first name: Joanne
- age: 55
- lives in: Arnold, Nottinghamshire, East Midlands
- occupation: Part-time school office administrator at a primary school (about 25 hours a week, term-time, mornings and early afternoons)
- education detail: Left a local comprehensive in 1986 with five O-levels, including English and maths. Did an RSA typing certificate at evening college, then an NVQ Level 3 in Business Administration through work in her thirties. She has also done in-house first aid and safeguarding training at the school.
- household: Lives with her husband Steve, 57, a self-employed electrician, in a three-bed semi they've owned since 1998. Their daughter Becky, 28, lives in Leeds and their son Liam, 25, rents a flat in Derby. Both visit most weekends or every other weekend. They have an elderly Border terrier called Pickle.
- cultural background: White British, born and raised in Nottingham. Her dad worked at Raleigh and her mum was a dinner lady. Not religious, though the kids went to a C of E primary and she still enjoys the Christmas carol service there. She is very much a Nottingham person: she goes to Goose Fair every October, has strong opinions on Forest, and still calls the city centre 'town'.
- professional persona: She's the first face parents see in the morning and the one who knows where everything is. She deals with dinner money, absence calls, the photocopier, and the odd upset Year 2 child who needs a plaster and a chat. She's chatty and warm but straight with people. If a parent is being unreasonable she'll tell them kindly but plainly. She's well organised for the things that matter, like registers and safeguarding paperwork, but her desk is a bit of a mess and she runs on sticky notes.
- sports persona: A casual Nottingham Forest fan who goes to the City Ground a few times a season with Steve and Liam. She did Couch to 5K a few years back and now does parkrun at Colwick Park most Saturdays, chatting all the way round rather than chasing times. She walks Pickle every evening.
- arts persona: She likes a good night out more than anything highbrow. She goes to musicals at the Theatre Royal with her sister, comedy at the Royal Concert Hall, and the odd tribute act at a local pub. She reads crime thrillers on holiday and watches Strictly, Gogglebox and whatever drama everyone at work is talking about.
- travel persona: Mostly a week in the sun, often Tenerife or the Algarve, plus long weekends in a cottage or caravan in Norfolk, Skegness or the Peak District. She and Steve did a two-week trip to New York and Boston for their 25th anniversary and she still talks about it. She'd like to do a Canadian Rockies trip once Steve slows down with work.
- culinary persona: A solid, unfussy home cook. Her repertoire is shepherd's pie, chilli, a roast on Sundays when the kids come, and a big pan of soup in winter. Friday is chippy tea. She buys cobs from the bakery on Front Street, and a pork pie and mushy peas at Goose Fair is non-negotiable. She's tried a couple of air fryer recipes off Facebook with mixed results.
- hobbies and interests: Saturday parkrun at Colwick, Walking the dog around Arnot Hill Park, Pub quiz on Thursdays with a group of friends, Musicals and comedy nights, Watching Forest, Organising the school staff night out and Christmas do, Gardening, mainly hanging baskets and pots
- skills: Fast, accurate typing, Microsoft Office and school management systems (Arbor, previously SIMS), Calming down upset children and stressed parents, First aid, Remembering names and faces, Organising events and collections, Handling awkward phone calls
- career goals: Not chasing promotion. She turned down the school business manager job because she didn't want full-time hours or budget headaches. She wants to keep her part-time role until she's about 62, maybe drop a day, and help out with the PTA after that. She'd like to stay healthy and active enough to enjoy retirement with Steve.
- voice: Warm, quick and talkative, with a moderate Nottingham accent. She drops the odd 'h', says 'me' for 'my' now and again, and uses 'duck' occasionally with people she's warming to, but not every sentence. She says 'erm' when she's thinking and uses 'sort of' a lot. She ends points with 'you know' or 'do you know what I mean'. 'Mardy' and 'knackered' are natural words for her. She laughs easily, including at herself. She doesn't like silence and will fill it, often with a joke or 'sorry, I'm rambling'. She'll ask the interviewer how their day's going. She's honest even when it's unflattering, for example: 'no, I didn't do that, if I'm honest'.
- typing: Types quickly and doesn't go back to fix much. She capitalises the start of sentences most of the time but not always. She uses apostrophes properly but sometimes forgets full stops at the end. She likes exclamation marks and the odd 'lol' or 'haha'. Abbreviations are limited to 'tbh' and '&'. Her answers run longer than the form needs, e.g. 'Mostly by car tbh, the bus is ok but its every 20 mins & I'm usually running late haha'.
- with strangers: Instantly friendly and easy to talk to. She'll have told you about the dog and her daughter's new job within five minutes. She's genuinely interested in other people and asks questions back. She's unpretentious and doesn't try to impress or give the 'right' answer, and she will happily admit she doesn't know something. She isn't easily rattled; tech glitches or awkward pauses just get a laugh.
- small things: Pickle the Border terrier has gone a bit deaf and only hears the treat tin, The photocopier at work jams every Monday without fail, Her Saturday parkrun and the coffee afterwards, Thursday pub quiz, where her team always loses on the sport round, Getting cobs from the bakery on Front Street, Goose Fair and whether it's gone too expensive, Steve's van parked across the drive, Whatever's on Strictly
- deeper things: Her mum has early-stage dementia and Joanne goes round three times a week. She's practical about it but it does wear her down, She had a breast cancer scare at 50 that turned out fine, which is partly why she started running, She sometimes wonders if she undersold herself by staying in admin, but mostly she's content, She misses having the kids at home more than she lets on, She and Steve went through a rough patch in their early forties and came out of it stronger
- webcam photo: Head-and-shoulders shot from a laptop on a kitchen table, camera angled slightly upwards. The main light is daylight from a window to her left, so the right side of her face is a little shadowed. She is a white woman in her mid-fifties with a round, cheerful face, light freckles and laughter lines, smiling with her teeth showing and leaning slightly towards the screen. Her hair is shoulder-length, highlighted ash blonde with darker roots, tucked behind one ear. She wears red-framed reading glasses pushed up on her head, small gold hoop earrings, and a navy and white striped long-sleeved top. Behind her is a fitted cream kitchen with a wooden worktop. On the worktop are a kettle, a toaster and a mug tree. On the wall is a calendar with handwritten entries, and a fridge door covered in magnets holds a school newsletter and a photo of two young adults. A dog lead hangs on a hook by the back door, partly visible at the right edge of the frame.

P206 (Gareth; transcript label: Gareth):
- first name: Gareth
- age: 39
- lives in: Taunton, South West England
- occupation: Not currently working (long-term sick, on home haemodialysis). Formerly a chartered civil engineer specialising in drainage and flood defence schemes for a regional consultancy.
- education detail: A-levels in Maths, Physics and Geography at a sixth form college in Yeovil; BEng in Civil Engineering from the University of Bath; later became chartered (CEng, MICE) through his employer's training scheme in his late twenties.
- household: Lives with his partner of eleven years, Hannah, a primary school SENCo, in a three-bed semi on the edge of town that they bought together. They've never married ('always meant to, then the kidneys happened'). No children. They have an elderly Border terrier called Biscuit. The spare room has been turned into his dialysis room.
- cultural background: White British, grew up in a village near Yeovil. Dad was a farm machinery mechanic, mum worked in a GP surgery reception. Christened and confirmed Church of England, went to church as a kid; now goes to the local parish church at Christmas and Easter and the odd Sunday when he's up to it. Calls himself Christian 'in the C of E way, quietly'. First in his family to go to university.
- professional persona: Was a methodical, highly organised engineer who liked owning a project end to end: hydraulic models, planning submissions, site meetings in wellies. Known for immaculate spreadsheets and never missing a deadline. Diagnosed with IgA nephropathy at 31, managed to keep working until his kidneys failed at 36, then had to stop. Still keeps his CEng membership up and reads the trade magazine. Fairly unsentimental about the job itself but misses the status of it and being the person people came to.
- sports persona: Used to play five-a-side and cycle the Quantocks at weekends. Now his energy is too unpredictable, so he does gentle walks with the dog and physio exercises. Follows Somerset cricket closely, listens to county matches on the radio during dialysis sessions, and watches rugby with Bath as his team. Will happily talk about cricket stats for longer than anyone wants.
- arts persona: Not very arty. Likes long-form podcasts, history documentaries and the occasional crime drama with Hannah. Reads non-fiction, mostly engineering disasters, military history and biographies. Has a soft spot for brass band music from his granddad playing in one.
- travel persona: Travel is complicated now because he has to arrange holiday dialysis in advance. They've done a few UK breaks to Cornwall and the Lake District, booked around a dialysis unit. Before he got ill he liked city breaks: Amsterdam, Copenhagen, Berlin, where he'd mostly look at the canals and bridges. Pragmatic about it: 'If it's not near a unit, we don't go.'
- culinary persona: On a strict renal diet, so he's become very precise about potassium, phosphate and fluid. Weighs things, logs everything in an app. Does most of the cooking on good days, batch-cooks and labels the freezer. Misses proper cheddar and crisps. Calls the evening meal 'dinner', sometimes 'tea' when talking about his mum's.
- hobbies and interests: Following Somerset County Cricket, Building and painting model railway scenery in the garage, Walking Biscuit along the Bridgwater and Taunton canal, Podcasts on engineering failures and history, Tracking his blood results in a self-made spreadsheet, Bargain-hunting for tools and kit on eBay and Facebook Marketplace, Pub quizzes when he's well enough
- skills: Hydraulic modelling and flood risk assessment, Project and budget management, Excel to a frankly unnecessary level, Running his own home haemodialysis machine, DIY and basic plumbing, Negotiating with suppliers and getting a discount, Staying calm in a crisis
- career goals: Waiting for a kidney transplant (been on the list about two years). If it happens and goes well, he wants to get back into engineering, probably part-time or as a freelance consultant reviewing flood risk assessments from home. Has quietly thought about whether he could charge more freelance than he ever earned salaried. Realistic that it might not happen.
- voice: Steady, mid-paced, fairly low-key. Light Somerset accent: soft 'r' after vowels, 'alright' as a greeting, the odd 'proper' as in 'proper knackered'. Not broad. Uses 'sort of' a lot and the occasional 'erm' when thinking through a number or a date. Ends points with 'you know' or 'yeah'. === CALL C0418 ===
Sana: Hiya! Can you hear me okay?
Martijn: Yes. Martijn. Walthamstow.
Sana: I'm Sana, from Bolton. Erm, nice to meet you. Your room looks very, like, professional. Is that a hard hat?

Sana: Acha, okay. That sounds hard. I was rubbish at maths at college. I do packing in a warehouse, online fashion. Part-time.
Martijn: What does packing involve, exactly?
Sana: Erm, you get the order on the scanner, you go and pick the item, like a dress or whatever, you put it in the bag, label, and it goes on the belt. They count how many you do an hour. Pick rate. Mine is not... it's okay. [laughs]
Martijn: What's the target?
Sana: Sorry, what?
Martijn: The rate. How many an hour are you supposed to do?
Sana: Oh, erm, I think it's like ninety? Something like that. I don't really look, to be honest. The supervisor looks. I'm chatting with the girls, that's the best bit.
Martijn: Ninety an hour is fast.
Sana: It is! That's what I say! [laughs] Did you do that puzzle at the start?
Martijn: Yes. One question was wrong. It had two answers.
Sana: Oh, thank God, I thought it was only me who was confused. So, is that your daughter, in the photo, on the beach?
Martijn: Yes. She's fourteen. That's Zeeland, in the Netherlands. We go every summer, same place.
Sana: Aww, she's so pretty. Same place every year? You don't want to try somewhere new? I want to go Maldives, or Turkey, for the photos, you know, the water villas.
Martijn: No. She likes it, I know where everything is, and we take the train. I don't like flying.
Sana: Oh, I love flying! Well, not the flying, the airport, the duty free. We went Dubai once, me and my husband and his sister. The malls, oh my God, so big you need a car inside. [laughs]
Martijn: I've heard. Too big for me.
Sana: Does your daughter like makeup and that? Because fourteen, all the girls are on TikTok doing the routines.
Martijn: Er, yes. More than before. I don't really know what she's watching. She doesn't tell me much now.
Sana: That's normal, honestly. My little sister was like that, she wouldn't talk to my mum for like a whole year. Now they're best friends. You should ask her to show you her makeup stuff, girls love that, explaining everything. My sister made me watch a forty-minute video about skincare once.
Martijn: Forty minutes.
Sana: Yeah! But it made her happy, you know.
Martijn: That's a sensible idea, actually. I'll try it.
Sana: Really? [laughs] Okay! Tell her a girl from Bolton said.
Martijn: Do you have children?
Sana: No, not yet. Erm... not yet. Everyone asks. My mother-in-law asks every day nearly. [laughs]
Martijn: Sorry. I didn't mean to pry.
Sana: No, no, it's fine! It's a normal question.

Gareth: Very. Low potassium, low phosphate, and I can only drink about a litre a day. I weigh everything and log it on an app. Bit obsessive, but it works.
Agnieszka: Potassium, so no tomatoes? Oh no. I grow tomatoes, this year so many, I was going to say I send you some.

Agnieszka: That's hard. My husband, he can't go two hours without tea.
Gareth: It does sort of focus the mind. I'm on the transplant list, two years now, so that's the hope.
Agnieszka: Family can't give, like a brother or something?
Gareth: My brother got tested. Wasn't a match. So, erm, it's the list.
Agnieszka: Okay. I hope it comes soon. I mean it.
Gareth: Cheers. Appreciate that. What about you, you've been here a while? I'm guessing Poland?
Agnieszka: Yeah, Łódź. Since 2006. First two years I was cleaning offices, then college, bookkeeping, then the school. Now is eighteen years, my kids grew up here. My son is at uni in Leeds, my daughter doing A-levels.
Gareth: That's a proper journey. Do you get back much?
Agnieszka: Once, twice a year, my mum is there. I drive sometimes, sometimes fly from Birmingham. I don't mind long drives.
Gareth: Lucky. Travel's a whole spreadsheet for me now. I have to book dialysis at a unit wherever we go, so it's Cornwall, the Lakes. If it's not near a unit, we don't go.
Agnieszka: But you still go. That's the important thing.
Gareth: Yeah, that's how Hannah puts it. And we take the dog. Biscuit, old Border terrier. Refuses to walk if it's raining, so not much use in the Lakes.
Agnieszka: [laughs] Clever dog. He knows.
Gareth: He does. Sits down on the canal path and just looks at me.

=== CALL C0420 ===
Joanne: Hiya! Oh, there you are. I'm Joanne, I'm in Arnold, just outside Nottingham. How's your day going?
Abena: Abena. Thornton Heath. It's okay. I'm off today.
Joanne: Oh, lovely, a day off. I thought you looked like you'd just come off shift in your photo. Uniform and that.
Abena: That photo was after a twelve-hour day. I'm a senior care assistant, care home for older people.
Joanne: Twelve hours, bless you. I do part-time in a primary school office, mornings mostly, so I've got no right to moan, but I do anyway. [laughs] Photocopier jams every Monday, without fail.
Abena: Hm. Everybody's photocopier jams.
Joanne: [laughs] Universal truth, that. So what are you doing with your day off then?
Abena: Cooking. Light soup, goat, for the week. And I have a damp problem in my bathroom, my landlord won't fix it. One of the men on this study, the Dutch engineer, told me to hold toilet paper to the fan, see if it pulls. So I'm going to do that.
Joanne: Oh, that's a good tip! I'm going to try that, our fan's been rattling for months. Steve's an electrician and he still hasn't looked at it. Cobbler's children, isn't it.
Abena: Same everywhere.
Joanne: Can I ask you something, being in care? My mum's got early dementia. I go round three times a week. Some days she's fine, and some days she gets really agitated in the afternoon and accuses me of moving her things. I never know what to do.
Abena: Afternoons are common. We call it sundowning. Don't argue with her about the things. Even if you know you didn't move them. You say, okay, let's look together. Then you find it, or you make a tea, and she forgets.
Joanne: See, I always argue. I go, Mum, I didn't touch your purse, it's where you left it.
Abena: You are right, but being right doesn't help her. Also, lights on early, curtains closed before it gets dark. Shadows upset them. And a routine. Same time, same things.
Joanne: That's really helpful, honestly. Nobody's told me any of that. The GP just gives you leaflets.
Abena: Leaflets. [laughs] Yes. The families who do best are the ones who stop correcting.
Joanne: I'll try that. It does wear you down, you know, I'm practical about it but some days I drive home and just sit in the car for ten minutes.
Abena: That's normal. You have to look after yourself also. You have help? Brothers, sisters?
Joanne: My sister helps a bit. And Steve's good. The kids are grown up, Leeds and Derby, so they're not round the corner.
Abena: My son is in Leicester. Near you, no?
Joanne: Oh, not far at all, duck! Forty minutes down the M1. Does he come down to London much?
Abena: Christmas. He phones on Sundays. That's enough. He has his life.
Joanne: Yeah. I miss mine more than I let on, if I'm honest. House is too quiet.
Abena: Mm. Quiet is not so bad. You get used to it.

req.text:
You write transcripts of realistic video calls between strangers for a fully synthetic research dataset set in the UK. The study, in order (from its published design): a short puzzle task done alone; first impressions of the others' webcam photos; then a series of three-minute, one-on-one video calls in rounds, each person meeting the others in their group; after each call a short survey.

Call shape (from the original study's numbers): a call is cut off by a three-minute timer. A typical call has about 30 turns (most between 20 and 39) and about 570 words in total (most between 440 and 682); half of all turns are 12 words or fewer, and a quarter are 24 or more. Short acknowledgements ("yeah", "mm") count as turns too. So aim for about 570 words in about 30 turns: alongside the quick back-and-forth, people often talk in longer stretches (explaining their job, telling a story), and those long turns carry much of the call.

Guide to British conversational English (use it for how people talk; it is a description of speech, not a script):
How British people talk in casual conversation. This is a paraphrase of published descriptions of spoken British English; sources are in SOURCES.md. Use these features lightly and only where they fit the person. Never use them as a caricature.

- **Fillers.** British speakers hesitate with "erm" and "er". Women and younger speakers lean towards "erm".
- **Hedges.** "Sort of" is everywhere and steady. "Kind of" is spreading, and younger speakers use it more.
- **Politeness words.** "Please", "thank you", "thanks" and "sorry" mostly mean what they say. "Sorry" also works as a repair word (to correct yourself, or to ask someone to repeat) and can be ironic.
- **Tags at the end of a sentence.** "You know", "right", "okay", "yeah", "do you know what I mean". Among young Londoners, "innit" and "you get me" are rising. Tags depend on age and region only, never on ethnicity.
- **Echoing.** In an engaged conversation people pick up and re-use parts of each other's words.
- **Regional words and grammar** (from a recent dialect survey):
  - A bread roll is a "barm" in the North West (Manchester to Liverpool and western Lancashire), a "cob" around Nottinghamshire, a "bap" in Staffordshire, the West Midlands and North Wales, and a "batch" in Liverpool and Coventry.
  - Around Liverpool an ice lolly can be a "lolly ice".
  - The evening meal is "tea" in the North West, North East and Yorkshire, and "dinner" in the South East and London. Some people say both.
  - "Yous" or "youse" for plural "you" is common in the North East (Newcastle, Teesside), Liverpool and Scotland, less so in Manchester, and rare in York, Leeds and Sheffield.
  - "Give it me" is normal in the North West and West Midlands and widely accepted in Sheffield and York; it fades south of Birmingham, Coventry and Leicester.
  - "You was" is widely used, historically Northern and now found as far south as London.
- **Everyday British words** to draw on where they fit, without assigning them to regions: knackered or shattered, chuffed or made up, skint or brassic, mardy or stroppy, mum or mam, mate or pal, settee, sofa or couch.

You write transcripts of realistic video calls between strangers for a fully synthetic research dataset set in the UK. The study, in order (from its published design): a short puzzle task done alone; first impressions of the others' webcam photos; then a series of three-minute, one-on-one video calls in rounds, each person meeting the others in their group; after each call a short survey.

Call shape (from the original study's numbers): a call is cut off by a three-minute timer. A typical call has about 30 turns (most between 20 and 39) and about 570 words in total (most between 440 and 682); half of all turns are 12 words or fewer, and a quarter are 24 or more. Short acknowledgements ("yeah", "mm") count as turns too. So aim for about 570 words in about 30 turns: alongside the quick back-and-forth, people often talk in longer stretches (explaining their job, telling a story), and those long turns carry much of the call.

Guide to British conversational English (use it for how people talk; it is a description of speech, not a script):
How British people talk in casual conversation. This is a paraphrase of published descriptions of spoken British English; sources are in SOURCES.md. Use these features lightly and only where they fit the person. Never use them as a caricature.

- **Fillers.** British speakers hesitate with "erm" and "er". Women and younger speakers lean towards "erm".
- **Hedges.** "Sort of" is everywhere and steady. "Kind of" is spreading, and younger speakers use it more.
- **Politeness words.** "Please", "thank you", "thanks" and "sorry" mostly mean what they say. "Sorry" also works as a repair word (to correct yourself, or to ask someone to repeat) and can be ironic.
- **Tags at the end of a sentence.** "You know", "right", "okay", "yeah", "do you know what I mean". Among young Londoners, "innit" and "you get me" are rising. Tags depend on age and region only, never on ethnicity.
- **Echoing.** In an engaged conversation people pick up and re-use parts of each other's words.
- **Regional words and grammar** (from a recent dialect survey):
  - A bread roll is a "barm" in the North West (Manchester to Liverpool and western Lancashire), a "cob" around Nottinghamshire, a "bap" in Staffordshire, the West Midlands and North Wales, and a "batch" in Liverpool and Coventry.
  - Around Liverpool an ice lolly can be a "lolly ice".
  - The evening meal is "tea" in the North West, North East and Yorkshire, and "dinner" in the South East and London. Some people say both.
  - "Yous" or "youse" for plural "you" is common in the North East (Newcastle, Teesside), Liverpool and Scotland, less so in Manchester, and rare in York, Leeds and Sheffield.
  - "Give it me" is normal in the North West and West Midlands and widely accepted in Sheffield and York; it fades south of Birmingham, Coventry and Leicester.
  - "You was" is widely used, historically Northern and now found as far south as London.
- **Everyday British words** to draw on where they fit, without assigning them to regions: knackered or shattered, chuffed or made up, skint or brassic, mardy or stroppy, mum or mam, mate or pal, settee, sofa or couch.

req.text:
You write transcripts of realistic video calls between strangers for a fully synthetic research dataset set in the UK. The study, in order (from its published design): a short puzzle task done alone; first impressions of the others' webcam photos; then a series of three-minute, one-on-one video calls in rounds, each person meeting the others in their group; after each call a short survey.

Call shape (from the original study's numbers): a call is cut off by a three-minute timer. A typical call has about 30 turns (most between 20 and 39) and about 570 words in total (most between 440 and 682); half of all turns are 12 words or fewer, and a quarter are 24 or more. Short acknowledgements ("yeah", "mm") count as turns too. So aim for about 570 words in about 30 turns: alongside the quick back-and-forth, people often talk in longer stretches (explaining their job, telling a story), and those long turns carry much of the call.

Guide to British conversational English (use it for how people talk; it is a description of speech, not a script):
How British people talk in casual conversation. This is a paraphrase of published descriptions of spoken British English; sources are in SOURCES.md. Use these features lightly and only where they fit the person. Never use them as a caricature.

- **Fillers.** British speakers hesitate with "erm" and "er". Women and younger speakers lean towards "erm".
- **Hedges.** "Sort of" is everywhere and steady. "Kind of" is spreading, and younger speakers use it more.
- **Politeness words.** "Please", "thank you", "thanks" and "sorry" mostly mean what they say. "Sorry" also works as a repair word (to correct yourself, or to ask someone to repeat) and can be ironic.
- **Tags at the end of a sentence.** "You know", "right", "okay", "yeah", "do you know what I mean". Among young Londoners, "innit" and "you get me" are rising. Tags depend on age and region only, never on ethnicity.
- **Echoing.** In an engaged conversation people pick up and re-use parts of each other's words.
- **Regional words and grammar** (from a recent dialect survey):
  - A bread roll is a "barm" in the North West (Manchester to Liverpool and western Lancashire), a "cob" around Nottinghamshire, a "bap" in Staffordshire, the West Midlands and North Wales, and a "batch" in Liverpool and Coventry.
  - Around Liverpool an ice lolly can be a "lolly ice".
  - The evening meal is "tea" in the North West, North East and Yorkshire, and "dinner" in the South East and London. Some people say both.
  - "Yous" or "youse" for plural "you" is common in the North East (Newcastle, Teesside), Liverpool and Scotland, less so in Manchester, and rare in York, Leeds and Sheffield.
  - "Give it me" is normal in the North West and West Midlands and widely accepted in Sheffield and York; it fades south of Birmingham, Coventry and Leicester.
  - "You was" is widely used, historically Northern and now found as far south as London.
- **Everyday British words** to draw on where they fit, without assigning them to regions: knackered or shattered, chuffed or made up, skint or brassic, mardy or stroppy, mum or mam, mate or pal, settee, sofa or couch.

- first name: Joanne
- age: 45
- lives in: Huntingdon, East of England
- occupation: Senior care assistant and shift lead at a 40-bed residential care home on the edge of Huntingdon. She runs the day shift, does medication rounds, handles handovers and keeps the staff rota
- education detail: Left secondary school in St Neots at 16 with GCSEs, including a C in English and a D in maths that she later retook. Started an NVQ Level 2 in Health and Social Care at 23 and went on to Level 3. She has done the in-house medication administration and safeguarding courses, and is currently halfway through a Level 3 Diploma in Leading and Managing in Adult Care that the home is paying for
- household: Lives in a three-bed semi on a 1990s estate with her husband Darren (47), a delivery driver for a builders' merchant, and their son Callum (17), who is doing a plumbing course at the college in Huntingdon. Their daughter Ellie (20) moved to Peterborough last year to live with her boyfriend. There is also an elderly Staffordshire bull terrier called Bella
- cultural background: White British, born in Bedford and raised in St Neots by a mum who worked in a school kitchen and a dad who was a forklift driver. Christened and confirmed Church of England. She goes to the parish church at Christmas, at Easter and for the occasional Remembrance Sunday, and she prays privately when she's worried, which is often. She had both children christened at the same church she was married in. Her family is close and local: her mum is still in St Neots and her sister lives in Godmanchester
- professional persona: Organised, reliable and quietly proud that the day shift runs properly when she's on. She keeps a paper notebook alongside the electronic care records because she doesn't trust the system not to go down. She is very fond of certain residents and gets genuinely upset when one deteriorates or dies. She can be sharp with colleagues who cut corners, turn up late or are always on their phones, and she doesn't really hide it. Some of the younger staff find her hard work, and the managers trust her completely. She worries about CQC inspections weeks in advance
- sports persona: Not sporty. She walks Bella round the estate and along the river at Hinchingbrooke Country Park most days. She did a Couch to 5K a few years ago and stopped when her knee started playing up. Darren watches the football (Peterborough United, loosely), and she will have it on in the background but isn't bothered
- arts persona: Doesn't go in for galleries or theatre much. She enjoys a pantomime at Christmas, which started when the kids were small and continues now as a habit. She watches a lot of telly: Coronation Street, Strictly, Gogglebox and crime dramas, although true crime makes her too anxious so she avoids it. Her music is whatever's on Heart radio in the car, and she still loves Take That
- travel persona: Prefers somewhere she knows. Most years it's a week in a caravan at Hunstanton or Great Yarmouth, and every couple of years a package holiday to Majorca or Tenerife. She gets nervous flying and checks the passports about five times. She has never been further than the Canaries and doesn't feel any need to
- culinary persona: Plain home cooking with a weekly meal plan written on the fridge whiteboard: spag bol, chicken pie, jacket potatoes, a roast on Sunday. Calls the evening meal dinner. She batch-cooks on her days off because of shift work. She isn't keen on spicy food and has the same order from the Chinese takeaway every time. Her treat is a Colin the Caterpillar cake on birthdays
- hobbies and interests: Walking the dog along the Great Ouse, Watching soaps and Strictly with a cup of tea, Keeping the garden tidy, mostly hanging baskets and tubs, Word searches and the puzzle magazines she buys at Tesco, Facebook, mainly local community groups and family photos, Sunday dinner at her mum's once a month
- skills: Medication administration and care planning, Writing staff rotas and covering sickness at short notice, Calming distressed residents with dementia, Spotting when something's not right with someone's health, Household budgeting to the pound, Batch cooking and freezer organisation
- career goals: To finish her Level 3 leadership diploma and become deputy manager at the home when the current deputy retires, which is expected in the next year or two. She doesn't want to be the registered manager because of the stress and accountability. She just wants the deputy role and the pay rise that comes with it, and she wants to stay somewhere she knows
- voice: Mild East of England, close to Estuary: some glottal stops, and 'yeah' rather than 'yes'. She speaks at a medium-quick pace and speeds up when she's anxious or annoyed. She uses 'erm' quite a lot when she's thinking and says 'sort of' often ('it's sort of a team leader thing'). Tags are mostly 'you know' and 'yeah'. She'll call herself 'knackered' after a long shift. She is direct, sometimes blunt, and gives opinions without much softening ('No, that's rubbish, to be honest'). She doesn't like long silences and fills them with a quick 'is that what you wanted?' or 'sorry, am I going on?'
- typing: Proper capitals at the start of sentences, full stops and apostrophes mostly correct. Her answers are fairly short but complete. She sometimes uses '...' to trail off and the odd 'tbh'. She occasionally uses a double exclamation mark when she feels strongly. She rereads her answers before submitting and quite often goes back to fix a typo
- with strangers: Polite but a bit guarded at first, and quick to worry about whether she's doing it 'right'. She warms up once she's talking about work or her family. She doesn't do flattery or small talk for its own sake. If a question seems pointless she'll say so, and she isn't shy about disagreeing
- small things: Bella the staffie is getting old and has a dodgy hip, She's just done three twelve-hour shifts in a row and is shattered, Callum never puts his plates in the dishwasher, The A14 roadworks are a nightmare, Her hanging baskets did really well this year, She's started doing a big Tesco shop online to save time, She has Strictly on every Saturday without fail
- deeper things: She lies awake worrying about Ellie living with a boyfriend she isn't sure about, Her dad died of dementia six years ago, and that is partly why she does the job. She still finds some residents hard because of it, She has had periods of anxiety and was on sertraline for a year after her dad died, She feels guilty that she sometimes loses her temper with Darren after a bad shift, She worries about money more than she lets on, especially with energy bills, She prays at night when something's worrying her but would feel awkward telling most people that
- webcam photo: Laptop webcam at a slightly low angle, so the image looks a little up at her, framed from the chest up and slightly off-centre to the left. The light is mixed, cool daylight from a window on her right and a warm overhead kitchen light, which leaves a faint shine on her forehead. She is a white woman in her mid-forties with a round face, light freckles, fair skin a little flushed at the cheeks, and a polite closed-mouth smile with slightly raised eyebrows that makes her look a bit unsure. Her shoulder-length dark blonde hair, with grown-out highlights, is scraped back into a low clip and has a few loose strands at the front. She is wearing a navy fleece zipped halfway over a grey T-shirt, with small gold stud earrings and no glasses. Behind her is a kitchen with white gloss cupboards, a fridge with a whiteboard meal plan and a few magnets on it, a kettle, and a tub of dog treats on the worktop. A wall calendar is pinned up showing shifts marked in different coloured pens. In the bottom corner of the frame, a stair gate is propped against the wall by the back door.

P217 (Kayleigh; transcript label: Kayleigh):
- first name: Kayleigh
- age: 34
- lives in: Bridgwater, South West England
- occupation: Care assistant at a privately run residential care home for older people, mostly on twelve-hour day shifts, about 40 hours a week
- education detail: Left a local comprehensive at 16 with five GCSEs, including a C in English and a D in maths that she later resat and passed at college. Did a year of a hair and beauty course at Bridgwater college and dropped out. Has an NVQ Level 2 in Health and Social Care through work. Started the Level 3 Diploma twice and hasn't finished either time, because she fell behind on the written units.
- household: Rents a two-bed ex-council terrace with her partner Craig, 37, a delivery driver she has been with for seven years but never married, and her daughter Lacey, 10, from a previous relationship. Craig's 15-year-old son stays every other weekend on a camp bed in Lacey's room, which causes rows.
- cultural background: White British, born and raised in Somerset. Her mum's family is from Bridgwater and her dad's from Burnham-on-Sea. She was christened Church of England and ticks 'Christian' on forms. Lacey goes to a C of E primary. Kayleigh only goes to church for christenings, funerals and the school carol service, but she does pray, privately, when she's frightened about something. She is close to her mum, who lives ten minutes away and does most of the school pick-ups.
- professional persona: Good with the residents she likes and quietly offhand with the ones she doesn't. She's warm with the confused ladies and impatient with the 'demanding' ones and their families. Often late for handover. Swaps shifts at short notice and isn't above ringing in sick when she's had enough. Resents the senior carers and the manager, and thinks the place is badly run and the pay is a joke, which isn't wrong. She'd move to an agency for an extra pound an hour without a second thought. Very upset when a resident she was fond of dies, though she wouldn't necessarily show it at work.
- sports persona: Not sporty. Has a gym membership she pays for and barely uses. Walks a lot on shift and says that counts. Watches the odd England match in the pub if there's a group going, mainly for the atmosphere.
- arts persona: Reality TV and true crime: Love Island, Married at First Sight, Netflix murder documentaries. Listens to a mix of 2000s R&B and whatever's on Heart in the car. Goes to Bridgwater Carnival every November and is genuinely proud of it, though she'd never be on a cart herself.
- travel persona: Holidays are a week in Tenerife or Turkey, all-inclusive, booked on finance or a buy-now-pay-later plan, which she then complains about paying off. Otherwise caravan weekends at Brean. Gets anxious flying and has a couple of drinks at the airport to cope.
- culinary persona: Cooks quick and cheap: pasta bakes, fajita kits, chicken nuggets for Lacey, Chinese takeaway on Fridays. Calls the evening meal tea, sometimes dinner. Lives on meal deals and energy drinks at work. Picks at food when she's stressed rather than sitting down to eat properly.
- hobbies and interests: Doing her own nails and occasionally friends' for cash, Scrolling TikTok and Facebook local groups, and arguing in the comments, True crime documentaries and podcasts, Online shopping for clothes and handbags, lots of it returned, Scratch cards and the odd go on bingo apps, Bridgwater Carnival
- skills: Personal care, hoisting and moving residents safely, Calming distressed residents with dementia, Gel and acrylic nails, Spotting when someone is about to kick off, Finding the cheapest deal on anything, Talking her way out of a late payment fee
- career goals: Vague. She wants more money without much more responsibility. She talks about either getting senior carer or going agency, and sometimes about doing nails full-time from home, but she hasn't done anything concrete about any of it. Mainly she wants to stop doing twelve-hour shifts.
- voice: Quiet and a bit flat at first, with short answers and a soft Somerset accent: slightly rolled r's and a rounded 'ar' sound, nothing exaggerated. Uses 'erm' and 'like' a lot, 'sort of' and 'kind of' as hedges, and ends things with 'yeah' or 'do you know what I mean'. Says 'to be fair' and 'I'm not being funny but'. Speeds up and gets sharper when talking about something that annoys her, like work, her ex or Craig's son. Uses words like 'knackered' and 'skint' naturally. In a silence she won't fill it. She'll wait, or say 'dunno really' and leave it at that.
- typing: Mostly lower case, no full stops at the end, few or no apostrophes (dont, im, its). Abbreviations like 'tbh', 'idk', 'cba' now and then. Short answers unless she's annoyed, then one long run-on sentence with commas. Occasional typos she doesn't fix.
- with strangers: Guarded and a bit unimpressed at first, as if she's working out what you want from her. She doesn't do much small talk. She's polite enough on the surface and says sorry and thanks, but can be blunt or slightly sarcastic if a question seems pointless. Warms up if you get her onto something she has opinions about, and then she's quite frank. She is clearly doing the study for the payment and may say so.
- small things: Being knackered after a run of long days, Lacey's school asking for money for something again, The price of petrol and her car needing an MOT, Something mad that happened on Love Island, Her mum having Lacey after school, The parking at work being a nightmare, A parcel she needs to send back before the deadline
- deeper things: She worries constantly about money and has credit card and catalogue debt Craig doesn't fully know about, She's had anxiety since her early twenties, has been on sertraline on and off, and gets panicky at night, She isn't sure she and Craig will last, and she resents his son being around, Lacey's dad isn't involved and doesn't pay regularly, and she still gets angry about it, A resident she was close to died last year and she cried in her car for a week, She prays sometimes when she's scared, which she'd find embarrassing to admit, She feels she never got a fair chance and that other people have it easier
- webcam photo: Laptop webcam at a slight upward angle, so the shot is a little under the chin. Head and shoulders are centred but slightly too close. Lighting comes from a ceiling bulb and the cool glow of the screen, with a yellowish tint and a faint shadow under her eyes. She's a white woman in her mid-thirties with a round face, light freckles, pencilled-in brows and the remains of mascara. Her expression is neutral and a little tired, mouth closed, eyes looking just below the camera. Her dyed dark blonde hair has darker roots and is scraped up into a messy bun. She's wearing a grey hoodie over a navy care home tunic, with a lanyard just visible at the collar. No glasses. Small gold hoop earrings and long almond-shaped nails, painted nude, show where one hand rests near her cheek. Behind her is a living room with a grey fabric corner sofa piled with throws and a pink unicorn cushion. A clothes airer stands beside it, draped with school polo shirts. Above the sofa hangs a canvas print that says 'Live Laugh Love', slightly off-centre. A white wall and a radiator show to the left, and the edge of a large TV is visible on the right.

P218 (Darren; transcript label: Darren):
- first name: Darren
- age: 40
- lives in: Sutton-in-Ashfield, East Midlands
- occupation: Warehouse operative (picker and loader) at a large distribution centre off the M1, working four long shifts a week plus regular overtime, usually 50 to 55 hours
- education detail: Left a comprehensive school in Ashfield at 16 with five GCSEs, including a B in Art and a C in English. Started a BTEC in Art and Design at a local college but dropped out after the first year to earn money. Holds a counterbalance forklift licence through work and a lapsed CSCS card from a spell labouring.
- household: Rents a two-bed terraced house with his partner Gemma (37), a care assistant at a residential home. They have been together nine years and have never married. Neither of them sees the point, though her mum brings it up. They have an elderly Staffordshire bull terrier cross called Mabel.
- cultural background: White British, born and raised in the old mining towns of north Nottinghamshire. His grandad worked at a local pit and his dad drove lorries. Not religious; the family were nominally C of E but nobody went. He is proud of the area's history and gets prickly when people from outside sneer at it.
- professional persona: Fast and capable on the warehouse floor when he is in the mood, but he hates being micromanaged and has had more than one run-in with team leaders over pick-rate targets and being timed on breaks. Works the hours because they need the money, not out of any love for the place. He is the one who questions the new process rather than the one who quietly follows it. Turns up, but he is often only just on time.
- sports persona: Follows Mansfield Town loosely, mostly checking scores on his phone, and goes to a few home games a season if he isn't working. Not sporty himself. He walks Mabel a lot and gets out on his bike on the old railway trails when the weather's decent. Watched the darts religiously for a few years, then lost interest.
- arts persona: The arty one in his family and slightly self-conscious about it. Sketches in biros and cheap pads, mostly buildings, old pit headstocks and the dog. Listens to a lot of music: Britpop he grew up on, plus whatever odd stuff he finds through podcasts and YouTube, like ambient, old folk recordings and film soundtracks. Watches documentaries about history, space and art forgery late into the night.
- travel persona: Hasn't been abroad much: a couple of package holidays to Spain and one long weekend in Amsterdam with mates in his twenties. Would love to see Iceland or Rome but money and time never line up. More likely to do day trips to the Peak District, Lincoln Cathedral or Whitby, where he will happily wander round old churches and graveyards.
- culinary persona: Simple food mostly, because they're both knackered after shifts. A cob with chips or bacon, curries from the takeaway on a Friday, and Gemma does a proper roast when they're both off. He'll try anything new if someone else is cooking, and occasionally gets ambitious with a recipe off YouTube, makes a mess of the kitchen, and leaves the washing up.
- hobbies and interests: Sketching buildings and old industrial sites, Local mining history and old photos of the area, Space and astronomy documentaries, Cycling the old railway trails, Walking the dog, Collecting secondhand vinyl from charity shops, Late-night history podcasts
- skills: Forklift operation, Drawing and quick sketching, Basic DIY and fixing bikes, Knows the local area and its history inside out, Spotting when a work process is daft and saying so
- career goals: Doesn't really have a plan, which bothers him more than he admits. Half-wants to get off the warehouse floor before his back goes, maybe into something like signwriting or tattoo work. He has looked into a tattoo apprenticeship but thinks he's too old. More realistically he'd take a team leader role for the money, though he knows he'd clash with management.
- voice: Low, fairly flat East Midlands accent, not broad. Speaks in quickish bursts and then trails off. Uses 'erm' and 'sort of' a fair bit, and ends things with 'you know' or 'do you know what I mean'. Says 'cob' for a bread roll and 'tea' for the evening meal, and might call a moody manager 'mardy'. Swears mildly when he forgets himself, then says sorry. Uncomfortable with silence at first and fills it, but can go short and clipped if a question annoys him or feels pointless.
- typing: Mostly lower case, with a capital only at the start now and then. Hardly any full stops, uses commas or just runs sentences on. Drops apostrophes ('dont', 'im', 'its'). Uses 'tbh', 'idk' and the occasional 'lol'. Quick and a bit careless with typos he doesn't go back and fix. Gives short answers unless the topic interests him, then writes a surprisingly long ramble.
- with strangers: Guarded and slightly dry at first, with blunt opinions he doesn't soften much, so he can come across as a bit grumpy. Warms up quickly if the conversation goes somewhere interesting, like history, music or something odd. Gets a bit nervy if he thinks he's being judged or tested. Will tell you straight if he thinks a question is stupid.
- small things: Mabel the dog's latest antics, How many hours he's done this week, Found a decent record in a charity shop, The weather ruining his bike ride, A documentary he watched till 2am, Mansfield's result at the weekend, Fuel prices
- deeper things: Worries a lot about money and about Gemma's health, as she has a bad back from lifting at work, Regrets dropping out of the art course and wonders what might have been, His dad died four years ago and he still gets upset about it, especially when he hears certain songs, Feels a bit stuck and anxious about being 40 and still doing the same job, Gets low in winter when he's working nights and never sees daylight, Isn't sure whether he and Gemma want kids and they avoid talking about it
- webcam photo: A slightly low-angle shot from a laptop resting on his knees, framing his head and shoulders a little off-centre to the left. Lit by a ceiling light and the laptop screen, giving his face a faint bluish cast. He has a broad face with a few days' dark stubble going grey at the chin, short dark brown hair clipped at the sides and slightly messy on top, and tired eyes with a neutral, faintly wary half-smile. No glasses. He wears a faded navy hoodie over a grey T-shirt. Behind him is a magnolia wall with a cheap clip frame holding a pencil drawing of a pit headstock, and part of a brown fabric settee with a crumpled fleece throw. A shelf on the right holds a stack of vinyl records leaning sideways, a mug, and a phone charger cable dangling down.

P219 (Gareth; transcript label: Gareth):
- first name: Gareth
- age: 41
- lives in: Maidstone, South East England
- occupation: Secondary school geography teacher and Head of Year 9 at a mixed comprehensive academy in Maidstone
- education detail: A-levels at a sixth form college in Ashford; BSc in Geography from the University of Southampton; PGCE from Canterbury Christ Church University. Has done in-house pastoral leadership training but no master's.
- household: Lives in a three-bed 1930s semi on the edge of town with his wife Rachel (39, part-time practice manager at a GP surgery) and their two children, Isla (11) and Theo (8). There's also an elderly, fairly lazy Labrador called Biscuit.
- cultural background: Grew up in Ashford, Kent, the younger of two boys. His dad was a postman and his mum a teaching assistant, and he was the first in the family to go to university. Not religious, and his parents weren't really either beyond Christmas carol services. Thoroughly Kentish and suburban: Sunday roasts, school fetes, the odd trip up to London.
- professional persona: Has taught for about seventeen years and has been at the same school for eleven. Kids and staff see him as the calm one. He doesn't get rattled when a corridor kicks off or Ofsted turns up, and he's the person colleagues come to for a chat when they're stressed. He's good with difficult students because he doesn't take things personally and genuinely likes teenagers. His paperwork is fine rather than impeccable. He gets it done, sometimes on a Sunday night. He runs the Year 9 Duke of Edinburgh Bronze expedition every year and loves it.
- sports persona: Plays five-a-side on Wednesday evenings with a group of dads and a couple of other teachers, and organises the WhatsApp group. Supports Gillingham out of family loyalty and goes to a handful of home games a season with his brother. Watches the cricket when it's on, mostly as background noise. Took up parkrun a couple of years ago and goes most Saturdays with Theo, who usually beats him.
- arts persona: Not a big arts person, but he enjoys a good live gig and will go to anything if a mate has a spare ticket. Listens to Britpop and indie from his teens (Blur, Supergrass, Arctic Monkeys) and whatever's on Radio X in the car. He and Rachel watch crime dramas and the occasional panel show. He has done the school staff panto three years running and hams it up shamelessly.
- travel persona: Family holidays are usually a gîte or campsite in France, driven down via the tunnel, or a week in Cornwall. Did a gap summer in his twenties travelling round Australia and still talks about it. He'd like to take the kids to Canada one day. Not fussy, and happy to chat to whoever's at the next pitch.
- culinary persona: He's the household's barbecue enthusiast and does a reliable Sunday roast. Otherwise the cooking is fairly evenly split with Rachel, mostly pasta, curries and fajitas. Friday night is takeaway night, usually Indian. Likes a pint of something local from a Kent brewery and is partial to a pub lunch after a country walk.
- hobbies and interests: five-a-side football, parkrun with his son, barbecuing, pub quizzes (he's the geography and sport guy on the team), walking the North Downs Way in sections, following Gillingham FC, staff panto, pottering in the garden, under supervision
- skills: calming down tense situations, talking to just about anyone, organising group trips and expeditions, map reading and outdoor navigation, basic first aid (renewed for DofE), explaining things simply, running a barbecue for twenty people
- career goals: He's been nudged towards applying for assistant head and is thinking about it, though he's a bit wary of losing classroom time and the pastoral side he enjoys. Realistically he expects to go for it within the next couple of years, probably at his current school.
- voice: Warm, chatty and quick to laugh. Speaks at a fairly brisk pace with a mild Kent/South East accent. Glottal stops on words like 'bit of' and 'got it', but nothing heavy. Uses 'er' when he's thinking and leans on 'sort of' and 'you know'. Says 'mate' easily, even to people he's only just met. Calls the evening meal 'dinner'. Fills silences without any awkwardness, often with a light joke or 'sorry, I'm rambling a bit there'. Tends to echo the interviewer's words back ('yeah, the balance thing, definitely'). Sounds relaxed even on tricky questions.
- typing: Quick and casual. Usually starts with a capital but doesn't always bother with full stops at the end. Uses apostrophes correctly out of teacherly habit, though they slip sometimes when he's in a hurry. The odd 'tbh' or 'lol', and occasionally a smiley ':)'. Answers tend to be a sentence or two, friendly in tone, with commas doing a lot of the work.
- with strangers: Instantly friendly and easy to talk to. He'll ask how your day's going and mean it. Comes across as open, upbeat and unflappable, the kind of person who makes small talk feel effortless. He's generous with his time and patient if a question is confusing, and he wouldn't get snippy about technical glitches. He might overshare a funny anecdote or two before getting to the point.
- small things: Theo beat his parkrun time again on Saturday, the five-a-side lot are trying to get a team shirt made, Biscuit ate half a loaf off the kitchen counter, marking mock exams at the kitchen table, the M20 being a nightmare again, planning this year's DofE route, Gillingham's latest dodgy result, the new barbecue he's been eyeing up
- deeper things: his dad had a stroke a couple of years ago and he drives to Ashford most weekends to help his mum, a former student of his was killed in a car crash a few years back, and it stayed with him more than he lets on, he sometimes wonders whether he's ambitious enough, or just comfortable, he and Rachel went through a rough patch when the kids were little and came out of it stronger, he worries a bit about Isla starting secondary school and phones and social media
- webcam photo: Head-and-shoulders shot from a laptop webcam set slightly below eye level, so the camera looks up a little at his chin. Lit mostly by a window off to the left, which leaves the right side of his face a touch shadowed. A white man in his early forties with short, slightly thinning light brown hair, a bit of grey at the temples and a day's stubble. He's mid-smile with crinkles around his eyes, looking straight at the screen. No glasses. He's wearing a navy quarter-zip fleece over a grey t-shirt. Behind him is the dining area of a family kitchen: a pale wall with a large framed Ordnance Survey map of the Kent Downs, a wall calendar covered in scribbles, a fruit bowl and a stack of exercise books on a sideboard, and part of a fridge door with children's drawings and a Gillingham FC fixture magnet. A corner of a dog bed is just visible at the bottom right of the frame.

P220 (Gemma; transcript label: Gemma):
- first name: Gemma
- age: 28
- lives in: Catford, south-east London
- occupation: Student nurse (final year, MSc Adult Nursing pre-registration) currently on full-time hospital placement on an acute medical ward
- education detail: Went to a comprehensive in Bexleyheath and did A-levels in PE, Biology and Business. Took a BSc in Sport and Exercise Science at a university in Kent and got a 2:1. Worked three years as a healthcare assistant, then started a two-year graduate-entry MSc in Adult Nursing at a London university. Placements run 37.5-hour weeks of long days and nights, so she's a full-time student who works full-time hours.
- household: Rents a one-bedroom flat above a dry cleaner's with her husband Dean, 31, a gas engineer. They married two years ago at a registry office with a pub do afterwards. No kids and no pets, though Dean keeps talking about getting a dog and she keeps saying no.
- cultural background: White British. Grew up in Bexleyheath with a mum who's a school receptionist, a dad who drives for a building supplies firm, and a younger brother. Not religious, and neither were her parents beyond weddings and funerals. A fairly typical outer-south-east-London upbringing: Saturday football, family holidays in Kent and Spain, Sunday roasts at Nan's.
- professional persona: Practical and quick on the ward, and good in a crisis because she doesn't overthink. She is blunt with colleagues and has been told more than once to soften how she says things. She will always own up to a mistake straight away and won't fudge a chart. Her paperwork is often late, and she leaves her reflective essays until the night before. Mentors rate her clinical hands-on care and nag her about documentation.
- sports persona: Played netball through school and university and still does Tuesday nights in a casual league when the rota allows. Watches Charlton with her dad and brother occasionally. She would rather play than watch, and the gym membership mostly goes unused.
- arts persona: Not really into it. Watches whatever's on: reality TV, Gogglebox, the odd crime drama Dean picks. She has no interest in galleries or theatre and says so. Listens to Capital or a playlist of the same 2010s pop she's had for years.
- travel persona: Likes the same things every time: a week all-inclusive in Tenerife or Majorca, sunbed, pool, done. They went to Lanzarote for the honeymoon. She finds city breaks tiring. Long-haul doesn't appeal and it isn't affordable on a student budget anyway.
- culinary persona: Plain eater. Spag bol, fajitas from a kit, chicken and chips, a roast on Sundays if she isn't on shift. Dean does most of the cooking. On nights she lives on meal deals and a Twix from the vending machine. She won't try anything too spicy and isn't bothered about restaurants beyond Nando's or a Wetherspoons breakfast.
- hobbies and interests: netball in a casual league, reality TV, Sunday roasts at her mum's, pub quiz with Dean's mates now and then, scrolling TikTok on breaks
- skills: cannulation and basic clinical observations, staying calm in emergencies, handling difficult patients and relatives, netball (goal defence), driving (has a licence but rarely uses it in London)
- career goals: Qualify, get her NMC PIN and a Band 5 job on an acute medical or A&E ward, probably at the same trust where she's placed. Eventually she'd like to move to a Band 6 role. She has no plans to go into management or research. She wants decent pay, a stable rota, and to save for a deposit somewhere cheaper, maybe back towards Bexley.
- voice: South-east London accent, unremarkable to most Londoners. She talks at a brisk pace and gives short, direct answers. Says 'erm' when thinking and uses 'sort of' and 'kind of' a fair bit. Sometimes ends a point with 'yeah?' or 'you know', and 'innit' occasionally slips out with friends but rarely with strangers. The study, in order (from its published design): a short puzzle task done alone; first impressions of the others' webcam photos; then a series of three-minute, one-on-one video calls in rounds, each person meeting the others in their group; after each call a short survey.

Call shape (from the original study's numbers): a call is cut off by a three-minute timer. A typical call has about 30 turns (most between 20 and 39) and about 570 words in total (most between 440 and 682); half of all turns are 12 words or fewer, and a quarter are 24 or more. Short acknowledgements ("yeah", "mm") count as turns too. So aim for about 570 words in about 30 turns: alongside the quick back-and-forth, people often talk in longer stretches (explaining their job, telling a story), and those long turns carry much of the call.

Guide to British conversational English (use it for how people talk; it is a description of speech, not a script):
How British people talk in casual conversation. This is a paraphrase of published descriptions of spoken British English; sources are in SOURCES.md. Use these features lightly and only where they fit the person. Never use them as a caricature.

- **Fillers.** British speakers hesitate with "erm" and "er". Women and younger speakers lean towards "erm".
- **Hedges.** "Sort of" is everywhere and steady. "Kind of" is spreading, and younger speakers use it more.
- **Politeness words.** "Please", "thank you", "thanks" and "sorry" mostly mean what they say. "Sorry" also works as a repair word (to correct yourself, or to ask someone to repeat) and can be ironic.
- **Tags at the end of a sentence.** "You know", "right", "okay", "yeah", "do you know what I mean". Among young Londoners, "innit" and "you get me" are rising. Tags depend on age and region only, never on ethnicity.
- **Echoing.** In an engaged conversation people pick up and re-use parts of each other's words.
- **Regional words and grammar** (from a recent dialect survey):
  - A bread roll is a "barm" in the North West (Manchester to Liverpool and western Lancashire), a "cob" around Nottinghamshire, a "bap" in Staffordshire, the West Midlands and North Wales, and a "batch" in Liverpool and Coventry.
  - Around Liverpool an ice lolly can be a "lolly ice".
  - The evening meal is "tea" in the North West, North East and Yorkshire, and "dinner" in the South East and London. Some people say both.
  - "Yous" or "youse" for plural "you" is common in the North East (Newcastle, Teesside), Liverpool and Scotland, less so in Manchester, and rare in York, Leeds and Sheffield.
  - "Give it me" is normal in the North West and West Midlands and widely accepted in Sheffield and York; it fades south of Birmingham, Coventry and Leicester.
  - "You was" is widely used, historically Northern and now found as far south as London.
- **Everyday British words** to draw on where they fit, without assigning them to regions: knackered or shattered, chuffed or made up, skint or brassic, mardy or stroppy, mum or mam, mate or pal, settee, sofa or couch.

req.text:
You write transcripts of realistic video calls between strangers for a fully synthetic research dataset set in the UK. The study, in order (from its published design): a short puzzle task done alone; first impressions of the others' webcam photos; then a series of three-minute, one-on-one video calls in rounds, each person meeting the others in their group; after each call a short survey.

Call shape (from the original study's numbers): a call is cut off by a three-minute timer. A typical call has about 30 turns (most between 20 and 39) and about 570 words in total (most between 440 and 682); half of all turns are 12 words or fewer, and a quarter are 24 or more. Short acknowledgements ("yeah", "mm") count as turns too. So aim for about 570 words in about 30 turns: alongside the quick back-and-forth, people often talk in longer stretches (explaining their job, telling a story), and those long turns carry much of the call.

Guide to British conversational English (use it for how people talk; it is a description of speech, not a script):
How British people talk in casual conversation. This is a paraphrase of published descriptions of spoken British English; sources are in SOURCES.md. Use these features lightly and only where they fit the person. Never use them as a caricature.

- **Fillers.** British speakers hesitate with "erm" and "er". Women and younger speakers lean towards "erm".
- **Hedges.** "Sort of" is everywhere and steady. "Kind of" is spreading, and younger speakers use it more.
- **Politeness words.** "Please", "thank you", "thanks" and "sorry" mostly mean what they say. "Sorry" also works as a repair word (to correct yourself, or to ask someone to repeat) and can be ironic.
- **Tags at the end of a sentence.** "You know", "right", "okay", "yeah", "do you know what I mean". Among young Londoners, "innit" and "you get me" are rising. Tags depend on age and region only, never on ethnicity.
- **Echoing.** In an engaged conversation people pick up and re-use parts of each other's words.
- **Regional words and grammar** (from a recent dialect survey):
  - A bread roll is a "barm" in the North West (Manchester to Liverpool and western Lancashire), a "cob" around Nottinghamshire, a "bap" in Staffordshire, the West Midlands and North Wales, and a "batch" in Liverpool and Coventry.
  - Around Liverpool an ice lolly can be a "lolly ice".
  - The evening meal is "tea" in the North West, North East and Yorkshire, and "dinner" in the South East and London. Some people say both.
  - "Yous" or "youse" for plural "you" is common in the North East (Newcastle, Teesside), Liverpool and Scotland, less so in Manchester, and rare in York, Leeds and Sheffield.
  - "Give it me" is normal in the North West and West Midlands and widely accepted in Sheffield and York; it fades south of Birmingham, Coventry and Leicester.
  - "You was" is widely used, historically Northern and now found as far south as London.
- **Everyday British words** to draw on where they fit, without assigning them to regions: knackered or shattered, chuffed or made up, skint or brassic, mardy or stroppy, mum or mam, mate or pal, settee, sofa or couch.

- first name: Alison
- age: 61
- lives in: Tonbridge, South East England (Kent)
- occupation: Principal Planning Officer at a borough council in West Kent, mainly handling larger residential applications and appeals; works about 37 hours a week, two days in the office and three from home
- education detail: Grammar school in Kent, then a BA in Geography at the University of Sheffield and a postgraduate diploma in Town and Country Planning at Oxford Polytechnic (now Oxford Brookes). Chartered member of the RTPI since her late twenties.
