P210 (Jaspal; transcript label: Jaspal):
- first name: Jaspal
- age: 41
- lives in: Derby, East Midlands
- occupation: Business Studies and Economics teacher at a sixth form college on the edge of Derby
- education detail: A-levels at a Derby comprehensive, then a BA in Business and Economics at the University of Derby, followed by a PGCE at Nottingham Trent. Has talked for years about doing a master's in education leadership but has never filled in the application.
- household: Rents a three-bed semi in Littleover with his partner Gemma, 38, a physiotherapist at the Royal Derby. They have been together nine years and are not married. Gemma's ageing cocker spaniel, Biscuit, lives with them. No children so far, and they go back and forth on it.
- cultural background: Afghan Sikh, born in Kabul. His family left in the early 1990s during the civil war, spent about a year in Delhi, then settled in Derby when he was nine, where an uncle already had a shop. On forms he writes 'Afghan Sikh' because neither 'Indian' nor 'Asian' quite fits. He grew up speaking Punjabi and some Dari at home, and English is now his strongest language. He cut his hair at university, which caused a huge row at the time, but he still wears a kara. He goes to the gurdwara on Stanhope Street for weddings, Vaisakhi and family occasions, and occasionally with his mum. Faith for him is more about family and community than daily practice.
- professional persona: Popular with students. He is the teacher who runs the Young Enterprise group and gets kids talking about mortgages and crypto scams. His classroom energy is high and his paperwork is chaotic. He marks late, wings lessons he has taught before, and charms his way out of deadline emails from his head of department. He is good at selling the college at open evenings and knows it. He likes being seen as the go-to person and will quietly take credit for a group project's success.
- sports persona: A massive Derby County fan who goes to Pride Park a handful of times a season with his cousin and moans about the board all the way home. He plays five-a-side on Wednesday nights at a leisure centre, mostly for the pint afterwards. He watches cricket when India or Afghanistan are playing and enjoys winding up mates about which side he is backing.
- arts persona: Not a gallery person. He likes stand-up comedy and has been to Nottingham's Glee Club a few times. He listens to old bhangra, 90s garage and whatever's on Radio 1Xtra in the car. He binge-watches crime dramas with Gemma and will happily argue about the endings.
- travel persona: Prefers easy, sociable holidays: a stag-style long weekend in Benidorm with mates, or a villa in Portugal with Gemma's family. He went to Amritsar with his parents a few years ago and found it more moving than he expected. He has never been back to Afghanistan and does not expect to.
- culinary persona: Makes a decent chicken karahi and lets everyone know about it. Otherwise he is a lazy cook who leans on Gemma or takeaway. He loves his mum's food, especially Afghan-style bolani and rice dishes, and comes back from her house with tubs. He will grab a bacon cob from the van near college, which his mum doesn't need to know about. He calls the evening meal tea or dinner depending on who he's with.
- hobbies and interests: five-a-side football, Derby County, stand-up comedy nights, fantasy football league he runs for staff, dabbling in shares and crypto on an app, playing FIFA/EA FC online with cousins, walking Biscuit in Markeaton Park, reluctantly
- skills: public speaking and working a room, explaining money stuff in plain terms, Punjabi conversation, some Dari, talking his way out of tight spots, organising nights out (though not paying the deposit on time)
- career goals: He wants to be head of sixth form or head of department, mainly for the status and the pay bump, but he resents the admin that comes with it. He occasionally fantasises about leaving teaching to do something in finance or start a business, and has a half-built idea for a tutoring company.
- voice: Warm, quick and chatty Derby English with a light East Midlands flatness. There is a faint trace of his family's Punjabi in a few vowels, but you'd mostly place him as local. He talks fast and laughs easily, says 'you know' and 'to be fair' a lot, and uses 'sort of' as a hedge. He drops in 'mate', 'mardy' and 'knackered' naturally. He goes 'er' when thinking and will often answer a question with a story. He doesn't like silence and fills it with a joke or by asking the interviewer something back. He echoes the question before answering ('what would I change? honestly...'). He sometimes says 'sorry, go on' when he realises he's talked over someone.
- typing: Fast and mostly lowercase, with a capital only on the odd name. Apostrophes are frequently missing (dont, im, its). He uses commas instead of full stops and sometimes 'lol' or 'tbh'. Answers are short and a bit casual, and he occasionally leaves a typo uncorrected, e.g. 'tbh i think its fine, depends on the day really'.
- with strangers: Instantly friendly and comes across as confident, funny and easy to talk to. He builds rapport fast, sometimes with mild flattery. He seems relaxed and unflappable, and is happy to share opinions. He may present himself in a slightly better light than strictly accurate, rounding up his achievements or downplaying things he hasn't got round to.
- small things: Biscuit the dog eating a sock again, the Derby score at the weekend, parking at college being a nightmare, Gemma's shifts at the hospital, a staff fantasy football rivalry, fancying a new car, probably on finance, his mum sending him home with food
- deeper things: Barely remembers Kabul but remembers the sound of shelling and the flight out, Guilt about cutting his hair and how much it hurt his dad, His dad's health declining and family expectations that he'll be the one to step up, Pressure from relatives to marry, and the fact Gemma isn't Sikh, Not being sure he wants kids, and not having told Gemma that clearly, A nagging sense he's coasted on charm and hasn't fully done the work
- webcam photo: Laptop webcam at slightly below eye level, angled up a little, in a spare bedroom used as an office. Late-afternoon daylight comes from a window to his left, with the overhead light on, giving fairly even but slightly warm lighting. A South Asian man in his early forties with a short neat beard going grey at the chin and short dark hair faded at the sides. He is mid-laugh with a broad open smile, looking just past the camera. No glasses. He wears a navy quarter-zip jumper over a white collar, and a steel kara is visible on his right wrist as he gestures. Behind him: a magnolia wall with a framed Derby County shirt, a cheap white bookshelf with A-level economics textbooks, a stack of unmarked exercise books, a Funko-style figure and a small framed photo of an older couple. An airer with towels on it stands half in shot in the corner, and a dog's tail is just visible at the bottom right edge.

- first name: Joel
- age: 26
- lives in: Levenshulme, Manchester, North West
- occupation: Newly qualified solicitor in the corporate team of a mid-sized commercial law firm in Manchester city centre, working mainly on business sales, share purchases and shareholder agreements for owner-managed companies across the North West

His dad is a plumbing and heating engineer who runs his own small firm, his mum is a primary school teaching assistant, and his younger sister is training as a nurse in Liverpool. He doesn't get rattled when a completion runs to midnight or a partner rewrites his draft, and juniors tend to come to him because he's approachable. A big trip to Japan is on the list for when work calms down, if it ever does.

He takes pride in doing a proper Sunday roast when they host. On busy weeks it's meal deals at his desk and too many takeaways. A bacon barm from the café near the office is his treat after a late completion. He likes the Levenshulme food scene and the independent spots on Stockport Road.
- hobbies and interests: Wednesday night five-a-side, Warrington Wolves rugby league, Saturday parkrun, gigs and comedy nights in Manchester, pub quizzes at the local, fantasy football league with uni mates, DIY on the rented house that the landlord technically allows, planning a Japan trip
- skills: Drafting and negotiating share purchase agreements, Explaining legal stuff to clients in plain English, Staying calm under deadline pressure, Getting on with pretty much anyone, Basic plumbing and tiling learned from working with his dad in summers, Organising group trips and stag dos, Cooking a roast for eight
- career goals: Wants to make senior associate within four or five years and eventually partner, ideally staying in Manchester rather than going to London. He's open to an in-house role at a big Northern business if the hours stay brutal. He'd like to be able to buy a house with Hannah in the next couple of years, probably further out towards Stockport or Heaton Moor.

He uses 'er' and the occasional 'erm' while thinking, hedges with 'sort of' and 'kind of', and ends points with 'you know' or 'yeah'. He says 'tea' for the evening meal, 'barm' for a roll, and 'made up' when he's pleased. He calls people 'mate' fairly often. He isn't bothered by silence and fills it with a joke or a 'yeah, no, good question' rather than looking awkward. He tends to echo the interviewer's words back to show he's following.

He sometimes drops the final full stop and uses 'tbh' and the odd 'etc'. Answers are short and to the point, maybe two sentences, occasionally with a dash for an aside.
- with strangers: Warm and open straight away. He asks questions back, laughs easily, and makes people feel at ease. He comes across as a confident, sociable lad who's good at his job without making a thing of it. He isn't guarded, but he doesn't overshare either; he keeps it light until there's a bit of rapport.
- small things: Five-a-side got rained off again, The 192 bus being a nightmare into town, Warrington's chances this season, Hannah wanting a dog and him slowly giving in, Trying a new Lebanese place on Stockport Road, Being knackered after a late completion, His dad still asking when he's going to get a proper trade, The fantasy football league he's losing

- webcam photo: Evening shot from a laptop webcam set slightly below eye level on a small white desk, so the image looks up a little at his chin. The light comes mostly from a warm desk lamp to his left, with some cooler glow from the laptop screen on his face. Joel is white, with a clean-shaven, slightly broad face and a relaxed half-smile showing a bit of teeth. He has short light-brown hair, faded at the sides and a bit longer on top, pushed loosely to one side. No glasses. He's wearing a navy quarter-zip jumper over a white T-shirt collar. Behind him is a magnolia wall in a small spare room. A clothes airer with a couple of shirts on it stands in the right corner, and the front wheel and handlebars of a road bike lean against the wall. A framed Warrington Wolves shirt hangs slightly crooked above a radiator, and a closed IKEA wardrobe door is visible on the left edge of the frame.

P212 (Gemma; transcript label: Gemma):
- first name: Gemma
- age: 32
- lives in: Beeston, Nottinghamshire (East Midlands)
- occupation: Band 6 musculoskeletal physiotherapist in an NHS outpatient department in Nottingham, plus cash-in-hand sports massage on some Saturdays
- education detail: A-levels in Biology, PE and Psychology at a sixth form college in Derby; BSc (Hons) Physiotherapy from a university in the Midlands, graduated at 22; various short CPD courses since, including acupuncture/dry needling and a weekend course in sports taping

req.text:
You write transcripts of realistic video calls between strangers for a fully synthetic research dataset set in the UK. The study, in order (from its published design): a short puzzle task done alone; first impressions of the others' webcam photos; then a series of three-minute, one-on-one video calls in rounds, each person meeting the others in their group; after each call a short survey.

Call shape (from the original study's numbers): a call is cut off by a three-minute timer. A typical call has about 30 turns (most between 20 and 39) and about 570 words in total (most between 440 and 682); half of all turns are 12 words or fewer, and a quarter are 24 or more. Short acknowledgements ("yeah", "mm") count as turns too. So aim for about 570 words in about 30 turns: alongside the quick back-and-forth, people often talk in longer stretches (explaining their job, telling a story), and those long turns carry much of the call.

Guide to British conversational English (use it for how people talk; it is a description of speech, not a script):
How British people talk in casual conversation. This is a paraphrase of published descriptions of spoken British English; sources are in SOURCES.md. Use these features lightly and only where they fit the person. Never use them as a caricature.

- **Fillers.** British speakers hesitate with "erm" and "er". Women and younger speakers lean towards "erm".
- **Hedges.** "Sort of" is everywhere and steady. "Kind of" is spreading, and younger speakers use it more.
- **Politeness words.** "Please", "thank you", "thanks" and "sorry" mostly mean what they say. "Sorry" also works as a repair word (to correct yourself, or to ask someone to repeat) and can be ironic.
- **Tags at the end of a sentence.** "You know", "right", "okay", "yeah", "do you know what I mean". Among young Londoners, "innit" and "you get me" are rising. Tags depend on age and region only, never on ethnicity.
- **Echoing.** In an engaged conversation people pick up and re-use parts of each other's words.
- **Regional words and grammar** (from a recent dialect survey):
  - A bread roll is a "barm" in the North West (Manchester to Liverpool and western Lancashire), a "cob" around Nottinghamshire, a "bap" in Staffordshire, the West Midlands and North Wales, and a "batch" in Liverpool and Coventry.
  - Around Liverpool an ice lolly can be a "lolly ice".
  - The evening meal is "tea" in the North West, North East and Yorkshire, and "dinner" in the South East and London. Some people say both.
  - "Yous" or "youse" for plural "you" is common in the North East (Newcastle, Teesside), Liverpool and Scotland, less so in Manchester, and rare in York, Leeds and Sheffield.
  - "Give it me" is normal in the North West and West Midlands and widely accepted in Sheffield and York; it fades south of Birmingham, Coventry and Leicester.
  - "You was" is widely used, historically Northern and now found as far south as London.
- **Everyday British words** to draw on where they fit, without assigning them to regions: knackered or shattered, chuffed or made up, skint or brassic, mardy or stroppy, mum or mam, mate or pal, settee, sofa or couch.

The group (session S41). Persona cards, including the webcam photo each person was rated on:

req.text:
You write transcripts of realistic video calls between strangers for a fully synthetic research dataset set in the UK. The study, in order (from its published design): a short puzzle task done alone; first impressions of the others' webcam photos; then a series of three-minute, one-on-one video calls in rounds, each person meeting the others in their group; after each call a short survey.

Call shape (from the original study's numbers): a call is cut off by a three-minute timer. A typical call has about 30 turns (most between 20 and 39) and about 570 words in total (most between 440 and 682); half of all turns are 12 words or fewer, and a quarter are 24 or more. Short acknowledgements ("yeah", "mm") count as turns too. So aim for about 570 words in about 30 turns: alongside the quick back-and-forth, people often talk in longer stretches (explaining their job, telling a story), and those long turns carry much of the call.

Guide to British conversational English (use it for how people talk; it is a description of speech, not a script):
How British people talk in casual conversation. This is a paraphrase of published descriptions of spoken British English; sources are in SOURCES.md. Use these features lightly and only where they fit the person. Never use them as a caricature.

- **Fillers.** British speakers hesitate with "erm" and "er". Women and younger speakers lean towards "erm".
- **Hedges.** "Sort of" is everywhere and steady. "Kind of" is spreading, and younger speakers use it more.
- **Politeness words.** "Please", "thank you", "thanks" and "sorry" mostly mean what they say. "Sorry" also works as a repair word (to correct yourself, or to ask someone to repeat) and can be ironic.
- **Tags at the end of a sentence.** "You know", "right", "okay", "yeah", "do you know what I mean". Among young Londoners, "innit" and "you get me" are rising. Tags depend on age and region only, never on ethnicity.
- **Echoing.** In an engaged conversation people pick up and re-use parts of each other's words.
- **Regional words and grammar** (from a recent dialect survey):
  - A bread roll is a "barm" in the North West (Manchester to Liverpool and western Lancashire), a "cob" around Nottinghamshire, a "bap" in Staffordshire, the West Midlands and North Wales, and a "batch" in Liverpool and Coventry.
  - Around Liverpool an ice lolly can be a "lolly ice".
  - The evening meal is "tea" in the North West, North East and Yorkshire, and "dinner" in the South East and London. Some people say both.
  - "Yous" or "youse" for plural "you" is common in the North East (Newcastle, Teesside), Liverpool and Scotland, less so in Manchester, and rare in York, Leeds and Sheffield.
  - "Give it me" is normal in the North West and West Midlands and widely accepted in Sheffield and York; it fades south of Birmingham, Coventry and Leicester.
  - "You was" is widely used, historically Northern and now found as far south as London.
- **Everyday British words** to draw on where they fit, without assigning them to regions: knackered or shattered, chuffed or made up, skint or brassic, mardy or stroppy, mum or mam, mate or pal, settee, sofa or couch.

The group (session S35). Persona cards, including the webcam photo each person was rated on:

P184 (Gary; transcript label: Gary):
- first name: Gary
- age: 56
- lives in: Bridgwater, South West England
- occupation: Not currently working. Former forklift and warehouse operative at a food distribution depot on the edge of town for 19 years. Signed off just over two years ago with a lower back problem (a prolapsed disc and sciatica down his left leg). Now on benefits and doing a few hours a week volunteering.
- education detail: Left the local comprehensive at 16 with a handful of CSEs and one O level in woodwork. Did a YTS placement at a builders' merchant. Holds a counterbalance forklift licence (lapsed, but he keeps the card) and a food hygiene certificate from his depot days.
- household: Lives alone in a two-bedroom ex-council terraced house he rents from a housing association. Divorced from Karen eleven years ago after 20 years of marriage, and they are on civil terms. Has one grown-up daughter, Leanne (29), who lives in Taunton with her partner and his granddaughter Poppy (4). The second bedroom is kept made up for when Poppy stays.
- cultural background: White British, born and raised in Bridgwater. His dad worked at the cellophane factory and his mum did school dinners. Grew up on the same estate he lives near now. Not religious, though he went to Sunday school as a kid and still goes to the Remembrance service. Carnival season matters to him: his uncle was in a carnival club and Gary helped build carts in his twenties.
- professional persona: Was the reliable one on the shift: never late, kept the paperwork straight, knew everyone's name including the agency lads, and was the person the supervisor asked to show new starters round. Still talks about the depot as if he's going back. He'd like something part-time and not too heavy if his back allows, like a caretaker, a car park attendant or a meet-and-greet job.
- sports persona: Follows football loosely and supports Bristol City out of family habit, mostly watching highlights. Used to play skittles for a pub team and still goes along on league nights to score and socialise, even though he can't bowl much now. Walks every day on the physio's orders, usually along the river or the canal path.
- arts persona: Not much of a cultural outing person. Likes the carnival, the odd tribute band at the social club, and a film if Leanne drags him along. Watches quiz shows, Bargain Hunt and old episodes of Only Fools and Horses. Has no interest in galleries or the theatre and would say so cheerfully.
- travel persona: Hasn't been abroad since a family package holiday to Majorca about fifteen years ago, and his passport's expired. Prefers a static caravan at Brean or a week in Devon. Doesn't drive much now because his back stiffens up, so he relies on buses and Leanne's car.
- culinary persona: Plain, regular meals at set times. Batch-cooks a cottage pie or a stew on Sundays and portions it into labelled tubs for the week. Likes a fry-up on a Saturday, fish and chips on a Friday and a pasty when he's out. Doesn't like anything too spicy. Drinks tea all day and the odd pint of cider at the club.
- hobbies and interests: Volunteering two mornings a week at a community food bank, sorting stock and chatting to people in the queue, Skittles league nights (scoring rather than bowling these days), Doing the crossword in the local paper, Keeping his small back garden tidy: bedding plants and a couple of tomato pots, Pub quiz on Thursdays with the same three mates, Sorting out bits for neighbours, like fixing a gate or putting up a shelf, when his back's good
- skills: Forklift and warehouse stock handling, Very organised: lists, calendars, labelled boxes, Basic DIY and carpentry, Getting on with anyone and remembering names, Reliable timekeeping, Showing new people the ropes
- career goals: To get his back to a point where he can do 16 hours a week somewhere sociable without being in pain. He's been talking to a work coach about it. He doesn't want a career, just a routine, a bit of extra money and people to talk to. He worries about what happens if he can't go back to work.
- voice: Warm, chatty and quick to fill the gap, with a soft Somerset accent. He has a slight burr on his r's, says 'alright?' as a greeting and now and then uses 'my love' or 'mate'. Speaks fairly fast, with a lot of 'you know' and 'sort of', and 'er' when he's thinking. Tells little stories to answer simple questions and then says 'anyway, sorry, I'm going off on one'. Hates silence and will fill it, often by asking the interviewer something back, like 'where are you based then?'. Says 'thank you' and 'cheers' a lot and means it.
- typing: Types carefully with two fingers, so his answers are short. Capitalises the first word and names, mostly ends with a full stop and usually gets apostrophes right because he's careful. Sometimes types in all caps by accident and corrects it. No abbreviations beyond 'ok'. Might add 'Thanks' at the end of a free-text answer.
- with strangers: Instantly friendly and open, and treats a stranger like a new starter on shift. Asks how your day's going and makes self-deprecating jokes about his back and his age. Very honest, sometimes more than he needs to be. Keen to do things properly and checks he's answered what you actually asked. Can come across as a bit anxious to please.
- small things: His granddaughter Poppy's latest saying, The bus being late again, Who won at the skittles, The weather and whether he can get out in the garden, What came in at the food bank this week, His physio exercises and his new walking route, Getting the crossword done before lunch
- deeper things: He felt like he'd lost a part of himself when he stopped working, and the first year was very low, He's lonely in the evenings since the divorce and keeps busy to avoid it, He regrets working so many night shifts when Leanne was little, He's worried about money and the next benefits review, His dad died of a stroke at 64, and he thinks about that more than he lets on, He cried at Poppy's nursery nativity and was embarrassed about it
- webcam photo: A slightly low-angle laptop webcam shot from a dining table, with Gary centred and a bit too close to the screen. Daylight comes from a window to his right, so one side of his face is brighter. He has a broad, ruddy face with a big open grin and crow's feet. His hair is short, grey and thinning on top, and he has light stubble. He wears reading glasses with thin black frames pushed up slightly, and a navy fleece zipped halfway over a grey T-shirt. Behind him is a magnolia wall with a framed photo of a small girl in a fairy costume and a wall calendar with appointments written in biro. A neat shelf holds a skittles trophy, a row of DVDs and a carriage clock. A mug on a coaster is just visible at the bottom of the frame.

P185 (Bethany; transcript label: Bethany):
- first name: Bethany
- age: 25
- lives in: Basingstoke, South East England
- occupation: IT service desk analyst (second-line support) at an insurance company's regional office, full-time, about 37.5 hours a week plus the odd late shift
- education detail: A levels in Computing, Maths and Psychology at a sixth form college in Basingstoke. Started a Computer Science degree at Southampton but left after first year. Later picked up CompTIA A+ and ITIL Foundation certificates through work.
- household: Rents a two-bed terraced house in South Ham with her partner Dan (27), a warehouse shift manager she has been with for about a year and a half. They have a rescue cat called Biscuit. Her divorce from her first husband, who she married at 21, was finalised just over a year ago.
- cultural background: Grew up in Basingstoke. Her mum is a teaching assistant and her dad is a self-employed electrician, and she has a younger brother at uni. She was raised Church of England and went to Sunday school and youth group. Her faith still matters to her but she keeps it quiet. She goes to a local Anglican church every few weeks, more often around Easter and Christmas, and sits near the back.
- professional persona: Reliable on tickets and very good with frustrated users on the phone. She is patient and never makes people feel stupid. Her paperwork and ticket notes lag behind, and her manager has nudged her about closing tickets properly. req.text:
You write transcripts of realistic video calls between strangers for a fully synthetic research dataset set in the UK. The study, in order (from its published design): a short puzzle task done alone; first impressions of the others' webcam photos; then a series of three-minute, one-on-one video calls in rounds, each person meeting the others in their group; after each call a short survey.

Call shape (from the original study's numbers): a call is cut off by a three-minute timer. A typical call has about 30 turns (most between 20 and 39) and about 570 words in total (most between 440 and 682); half of all turns are 12 words or fewer, and a quarter are 24 or more. Short acknowledgements ("yeah", "mm") count as turns too. So aim for about 570 words in about 30 turns: alongside the quick back-and-forth, people often talk in longer stretches (explaining their job, telling a story), and those long turns carry much of the call.

Guide to British conversational English (use it for how people talk; it is a description of speech, not a script):
How British people talk in casual conversation. This is a paraphrase of published descriptions of spoken British English; sources are in SOURCES.md. Use these features lightly and only where they fit the person. Never use them as a caricature.

- **Fillers.** British speakers hesitate with "erm" and "er". Women and younger speakers lean towards "erm".
- **Hedges.** "Sort of" is everywhere and steady. "Kind of" is spreading, and younger speakers use it more.
- **Politeness words.** "Please", "thank you", "thanks" and "sorry" mostly mean what they say. "Sorry" also works as a repair word (to correct yourself, or to ask someone to repeat) and can be ironic.
- **Tags at the end of a sentence.** "You know", "right", "okay", "yeah", "do you know what I mean". Among young Londoners, "innit" and "you get me" are rising. Tags depend on age and region only, never on ethnicity.
- **Echoing.** In an engaged conversation people pick up and re-use parts of each other's words.
- **Regional words and grammar** (from a recent dialect survey):
  - A bread roll is a "barm" in the North West (Manchester to Liverpool and western Lancashire), a "cob" around Nottinghamshire, a "bap" in Staffordshire, the West Midlands and North Wales, and a "batch" in Liverpool and Coventry.
  - Around Liverpool an ice lolly can be a "lolly ice".
  - The evening meal is "tea" in the North West, North East and Yorkshire, and "dinner" in the South East and London. Some people say both.
  - "Yous" or "youse" for plural "you" is common in the North East (Newcastle, Teesside), Liverpool and Scotland, less so in Manchester, and rare in York, Leeds and Sheffield.
  - "Give it me" is normal in the North West and West Midlands and widely accepted in Sheffield and York; it fades south of Birmingham, Coventry and Leicester.
  - "You was" is widely used, historically Northern and now found as far south as London.
- **Everyday British words** to draw on where they fit, without assigning them to regions: knackered or shattered, chuffed or made up, skint or brassic, mardy or stroppy, mum or mam, mate or pal, settee, sofa or couch.

P231 (Tomasz; transcript label: Tomasz):
- first name: Tomasz

- occupation: Full-time student, BSc Construction Management at the University of Reading (second year). Previously worked six years as a shift team leader at a distribution warehouse near Theale. He keeps a few weekend shifts there over the summer.
- education detail: Finished technical secondary school (technikum) in Poland with a qualification in building technology. In the UK he did a forklift licence, an Access to HE course and a Level 3 in supervisory management through work. He started his degree at 31 with a student loan and savings.
- household: Lives with his wife Agnieszka (32), a dental nurse at a practice in Wokingham, in a rented two-bedroom flat in Earley. The second bedroom is his study room. They have no children yet, though they have talked about it for after he graduates.
- cultural background: Born and raised in Rzeszów, south-east Poland. He moved to the UK at 19 to join an older cousin in Reading and has stayed since. He is Roman Catholic and goes to Mass at the Polish church in Reading most Sundays, more from habit and family expectation than strong feeling. He speaks Polish at home and with family, and English everywhere else. He has pre-settled-then-settled status and has not bothered with citizenship yet, though he says he will 'when there is time'.
- professional persona: Organised and exact. At the warehouse he was known for keeping a tight rota and not tolerating excuses. At university he submits work early, keeps a spreadsheet of every deadline and finds group projects frustrating when others are vague. He wants clear briefs and measurable results, and he is not interested in networking events.
- sports persona: Runs 5k three mornings a week on a fixed route around Maiden Erlegh Lake and records times on a watch. He watches Ekstraklasa and Premier League football results rather than full matches, and has a casual attachment to Stal Rzeszów. He does not play team sports any more.

He says 'dinner' for the evening meal and 'mate' with colleagues, and occasionally 'knackered'. He doesn't mind silence at all and will just wait. - webcam photo: Laptop webcam at slightly below eye level, framing his head and shoulders, with the light coming from a window to his left and a ceiling light on. He has a lean face, short dark-blond hair clipped at the sides and light stubble. His grey-blue eyes look directly at the camera, his mouth is neutral and slightly tight, and he is not smiling. He wears no glasses, and he has on a plain navy quarter-zip jumper over a white T-shirt collar. Behind him is a white wall with a large printed academic year planner pinned up, marked with coloured highlighter. A narrow pine bookshelf holds construction textbooks, a hard hat on the top shelf and a framed wedding photo. A small wooden crucifix hangs high on the wall to the right of the frame.

req.text:
You write transcripts of realistic video calls between strangers for a fully synthetic research dataset set in the UK. The study, in order (from its published design): a short puzzle task done alone; first impressions of the others' webcam photos; then a series of three-minute, one-on-one video calls in rounds, each person meeting the others in their group; after each call a short survey.

Call shape (from the original study's numbers): a call is cut off by a three-minute timer. A typical call has about 30 turns (most between 20 and 39) and about 570 words in total (most between 440 and 682); half of all turns are 12 words or fewer, and a quarter are 24 or more. Short acknowledgements ("yeah", "mm") count as turns too. So aim for about 570 words in about 30 turns: alongside the quick back-and-forth, people often talk in longer stretches (explaining their job, telling a story), and those long turns carry much of the call.

Guide to British conversational English (use it for how people talk; it is a description of speech, not a script):
How British people talk in casual conversation. This is a paraphrase of published descriptions of spoken British English; sources are in SOURCES.md. Use these features lightly and only where they fit the person. Never use them as a caricature.

- **Fillers.** British speakers hesitate with "erm" and "er". Women and younger speakers lean towards "erm".
- **Hedges.** "Sort of" is everywhere and steady. "Kind of" is spreading, and younger speakers use it more.
- **Politeness words.** "Please", "thank you", "thanks" and "sorry" mostly mean what they say. "Sorry" also works as a repair word (to correct yourself, or to ask someone to repeat) and can be ironic.
- **Tags at the end of a sentence.** "You know", "right", "okay", "yeah", "do you know what I mean". Among young Londoners, "innit" and "you get me" are rising. Tags depend on age and region only, never on ethnicity.
- **Echoing.** In an engaged conversation people pick up and re-use parts of each other's words.
- **Regional words and grammar** (from a recent dialect survey):
  - A bread roll is a "barm" in the North West (Manchester to Liverpool and western Lancashire), a "cob" around Nottinghamshire, a "bap" in Staffordshire, the West Midlands and North Wales, and a "batch" in Liverpool and Coventry.
  - Around Liverpool an ice lolly can be a "lolly ice".
  - The evening meal is "tea" in the North West, North East and Yorkshire, and "dinner" in the South East and London. Some people say both.
  - "Yous" or "youse" for plural "you" is common in the North East (Newcastle, Teesside), Liverpool and Scotland, less so in Manchester, and rare in York, Leeds and Sheffield.
  - "Give it me" is normal in the North West and West Midlands and widely accepted in Sheffield and York; it fades south of Birmingham, Coventry and Leicester.
  - "You was" is widely used, historically Northern and now found as far south as London.
- **Everyday British words** to draw on where they fit, without assigning them to regions: knackered or shattered, chuffed or made up, skint or brassic, mardy or stroppy, mum or mam, mate or pal, settee, sofa or couch.

Darren: Baggies. Always have been.
Gareth: Blues.

Gareth: Half-season share with a mate. Don't make as many as I should. Owners don't help.

Gareth: Not a bad way to do it. You can turn it off when they're losing.
Darren: That's about it really.
Gareth: Booked next year's holiday yet? I've done ours already. January's when the deals are.
Darren: Same caravan park near Tenby, every summer. Booked it the week we got back.
Gareth: Can't beat knowing what you're getting.
Darren: That's what I keep telling Claire.

Nasreen defends receptionists, noting the system itself causes the backlog, and says she enjoyed the role because she liked talking to people and calming them down.

Rhys describes his own job stocking shelves at a supermarket, waking up at five for early "replenishment" shifts, admitting he keeps meaning to take a course but never does. Nasreen reassures him he's young and has time, and he mentions still living at home hearing the same advice from his mum, which prompts Nasreen to compare him to her own son, Zain.

Nasreen laughs, saying her partner's the same — always promising to fix things and never doing it. She mentions he drives a taxi nights and is sleeping now, though she waves off Rhys's worry about keeping quiet. I'm thinking about having his mam appear in the doorway behind him around here, maybe timed to a different line than the obvious one.

Continuing the count through the rest of the dialogue, down to Rhys's line about being on the shelves, and I'm making sure line 19's text is captured exactly for matching.

req.text:
You write transcripts of realistic video calls between strangers for a fully synthetic research dataset set in the UK. The study, in order (from its published design): a short puzzle task done alone; first impressions of the others' webcam photos; then a series of three-minute, one-on-one video calls in rounds, each person meeting the others in their group; after each call a short survey.

Call shape (from the original study's numbers): a call is cut off by a three-minute timer. A typical call has about 30 turns (most between 20 and 39) and about 570 words in total (most between 440 and 682); half of all turns are 12 words or fewer, and a quarter are 24 or more. Short acknowledgements ("yeah", "mm") count as turns too. So aim for about 570 words in about 30 turns: alongside the quick back-and-forth, people often talk in longer stretches (explaining their job, telling a story), and those long turns carry much of the call.

Guide to British conversational English (use it for how people talk; it is a description of speech, not a script):
How British people talk in casual conversation. This is a paraphrase of published descriptions of spoken British English; sources are in SOURCES.md. Use these features lightly and only where they fit the person. Never use them as a caricature.

- **Fillers.** British speakers hesitate with "erm" and "er". Women and younger speakers lean towards "erm".
- **Hedges.** "Sort of" is everywhere and steady. "Kind of" is spreading, and younger speakers use it more.
- **Politeness words.** "Please", "thank you", "thanks" and "sorry" mostly mean what they say. "Sorry" also works as a repair word (to correct yourself, or to ask someone to repeat) and can be ironic.
- **Tags at the end of a sentence.** "You know", "right", "okay", "yeah", "do you know what I mean". Among young Londoners, "innit" and "you get me" are rising. Tags depend on age and region only, never on ethnicity.
- **Echoing.** In an engaged conversation people pick up and re-use parts of each other's words.
- **Regional words and grammar** (from a recent dialect survey):
  - A bread roll is a "barm" in the North West (Manchester to Liverpool and western Lancashire), a "cob" around Nottinghamshire, a "bap" in Staffordshire, the West Midlands and North Wales, and a "batch" in Liverpool and Coventry.
  - Around Liverpool an ice lolly can be a "lolly ice".
  - The evening meal is "tea" in the North West, North East and Yorkshire, and "dinner" in the South East and London. Some people say both.
  - "Yous" or "youse" for plural "you" is common in the North East (Newcastle, Teesside), Liverpool and Scotland, less so in Manchester, and rare in York, Leeds and Sheffield.
  - "Give it me" is normal in the North West and West Midlands and widely accepted in Sheffield and York; it fades south of Birmingham, Coventry and Leicester.
  - "You was" is widely used, historically Northern and now found as far south as London.
- **Everyday British words** to draw on where they fit, without assigning them to regions: knackered or shattered, chuffed or made up, skint or brassic, mardy or stroppy, mum or mam, mate or pal, settee, sofa or couch.

The group (session S47). Persona cards, including the webcam photo each person was rated on:

P246 (Kirsty; transcript label: Kirsty):
- first name: Kirsty
- age: 36
- lives in: Burnley, North West England
- occupation: Not currently in paid work. She was a packing operative on the line at a food factory on the edge of town for nine years and was made redundant about fourteen months ago when the site cut a shift. She is on Universal Credit, applies for warehouse, retail and cleaning jobs, and does the occasional study on an online research panel for a bit of extra money.
- education detail: Left a local comprehensive with five GCSEs, including a B in Art and a C in English. She started a BTEC National in Art and Design at Burnley College but left partway through the second year when she needed to earn. She has since done a free online short course in local history and a Level 1 food hygiene certificate through work.
- household: Lives alone in a one-bedroom housing association flat on the first floor of a small block near the canal. She has an elderly cat called Moss. Her mum lives about ten minutes' walk away and her younger brother lives in Blackburn with his partner and kids.
- cultural background: White British, born and raised in Burnley to a working-class family. Her dad worked in a tyre depot and died when she was 24, and her mum was a dinner lady. She was brought up Church of England. She still believes and goes to a quiet early Sunday service at the parish church most weeks, sitting near the back, but avoids the social side like the coffee mornings. She is Lancashire through and through but not loud about it.
- professional persona: A steady, reliable worker who preferred jobs where she could get her head down and not have to make small talk. On the line she was quick and careful and was trusted to train new starters one at a time, which she found nerve-racking but managed. Job interviews make her very anxious and she over-prepares for them. She would rather email than phone an employer.
- sports persona: Not sporty. She walks a lot, mostly along the Leeds and Liverpool Canal towpath and up towards the moors when the weather's decent. She follows Burnley FC loosely because her dad did, and puts the radio on for scores, but she has not been to Turf Moor in years because the crowds are too much.
- arts persona: This is where she lights up, quietly. She sketches in pencil and fineliner: old mill chimneys, canal locks, her cat, bits of terraced streets. She posts some of it anonymously on an Instagram account with about 200 followers. She loves folk music and old ballads, reads a lot of library books, from historical fiction to odd nonfiction about folklore and witch trials (the Pendle witches fascinate her), and watches arthouse films on free streaming services late at night.
- travel persona: Hasn't been abroad since a school trip to France and a single week in Majorca with friends at 21. She likes day trips on the train or bus: Clitheroe, Hebden Bridge, Lancaster, sometimes the Lakes on a cheap advance ticket. She would love to see Brittany or the west coast of Ireland one day but money and nerves stop her. She plans trips in detail so there are no surprises.
- culinary persona: Cooks cheap and simple: big pans of stew or chilli frozen in portions, beans on toast, jacket potatoes. A barm with chips from the chippy is a Friday treat when she can afford it. Tea is around half five. She bakes when she's stressed, mostly flapjacks and banana bread, and drops some round to her mum's.
- hobbies and interests: pencil and pen sketching, long walks on the canal towpath and moors, local history and Pendle folklore, folk music and old ballads, reading library books, arthouse and foreign films, baking, doing online research studies, looking after her cat
- skills: careful, accurate manual work, drawing and observation, budgeting on a tight income, baking, patient one-to-one training of new starters, researching things thoroughly online, basic food hygiene
- career goals: Short term, a stable job with predictable hours and not too much customer contact, such as warehouse, stockroom or a back-of-house kitchen. Privately she would like to do something with art or heritage, like working in a museum shop, a framing workshop or as a volunteer-turned-staff at a local heritage site. She has looked at an Access to HE course in art but keeps putting off applying in case she's not good enough.
- voice: Quiet and a bit hesitant, especially at the start. She talks at a slowish pace with a soft Lancashire accent: flat vowels, 'bath' with a short a, and some dropped t's and h's. She uses 'erm' a lot and 'sort of' and 'I don't know' as hedges, and says 'sorry' when she loses her thread or mishears ('sorry, what was that?'). Northern usage comes out naturally rather than for show: 'tea' for the evening meal, 'barm', 'give it me', the odd 'our kid' for her brother, 'me mam' now and then, 'knackered', 'made up'. She doesn't fill silences herself. She waits, sometimes too long, then says 'erm, is that okay?' or 'I don't know if that's what you meant.' When a topic she cares about comes up, like drawing, the canal or old local stories, she speeds up a little and gives longer, more vivid answers before catching herself: 'sorry, I'm going on.'
- typing: Mostly lowercase with a capital at the start sometimes. Light punctuation: commas run things together and there's rarely a full stop at the end. Apostrophes are often dropped ('dont', 'im', 'its') but spelling is otherwise good. She writes 'idk' occasionally and 'tbh' quite a lot. Answers are short unless it's about something she's interested in, then they get surprisingly detailed. Example: 'not working at the min, got made redundant last year tbh its been hard'
- with strangers: Reserved and polite. She can come across as shy or a bit flat at first, with short answers and lots of 'yeah' and 'I think so'. She is obviously nervous about getting things 'wrong' and asks for reassurance. Underneath she is thoughtful and observant, and if the other person is patient and kind she warms up and shows a dry, gentle sense of humour. She never pushes herself forward and is careful not to complain too much.
- small things: her cat Moss knocking things off the windowsill, the canal being full of geese again, the price of a loaf at the corner shop, what she had for tea, a library book she's halfway through, the bus being late or cancelled, Burnley's results because her mum asks her, a sketch she did of the mill chimney near her, it raining again, having a good walk up by Pendle Hill at the weekend
- deeper things: losing her dad at 24 and still missing him, especially at church, how much the redundancy knocked her confidence and that some days she doesn't go out, anxiety that's never been formally diagnosed, and dreading the Jobcentre appointments, feeling she let herself down by leaving the art course, being lonely living on her own but also finding people exhausting, quietly wanting a partner but never quite knowing how to meet anyone, her faith being a private comfort rather than something she talks about, worry about her mum getting older and who'll look after her
- webcam photo: A laptop webcam shot taken from slightly below eye level, framed from the chest up, with her face a little off-centre to the left. Lighting comes mainly from a window to her right, giving soft daylight on one side of her face and leaving the other side slightly shadowed. She is a white woman in her mid-thirties with a pale complexion, light freckles across her nose, grey-blue eyes and a small, tentative closed-mouth smile. Her mid-brown hair is shoulder length and pulled back into a low, slightly loose ponytail, with a few strands falling by her face. She wears a dark green hooded sweatshirt with the hood down and small silver stud earrings, and no glasses. Behind her is a magnolia-painted wall with a cheap pine bookshelf holding a row of library books with plastic covers, a jar of pencils and fineliners, and a sketchbook lying flat. A small framed pencil drawing of a canal lock hangs on the wall beside the shelf. The arm of a grey fabric settee with a knitted throw over it is visible at the bottom right, and a grey-and-white cat's ear and back are just in frame on the cushion.

P247 (Neil; transcript label: Neil):
- first name: Neil
- age: 45
- lives in: Halifax, Yorkshire and The Humber
- occupation: Stonemason (banker and fixer) for a small heritage restoration firm based in Calderdale, working mostly on listed churches, mills and chapels across West Yorkshire
- education detail: Left school at 16 with GCSEs, a B in Art and Cs in most else. Did a three-year stonemasonry apprenticeship with an NVQ Level 3 through a college in Leeds. Later took a short accredited course in conservation of historic masonry and lime mortars. Has done a couple of free online courses in architectural history for his own interest.
- household: Lives alone in a two-up two-down stone terrace he bought after the divorce, about eight years ago. His daughter Ellie (16) lives with her mum in Brighouse and stays with him some weekends, less often now she's older. No pets, though he feeds a neighbour's cat when they're away.
- cultural background: White British, born and raised in Halifax. Dad was a bus driver, mum worked in a building society. Baptised Church of England and still calls himself Christian, though he's more of an occasional attender than a believer in any strict sense. He'll go to evensong at the Minster now and then, mainly for the choir and the building, and he's fairly private about what he actually believes. Grew up on rugby league, Saturday markets and his grandad's stories about the mills.
- professional persona: Twenty-plus years in the trade and good at it. Known for precise carving and for knowing his lime mortars properly. Blunt with clients and site managers when he thinks a spec is wrong, especially cement repointing on old stone, which he regards as vandalism. Doesn't do small talk on site but is reliable and turns up. Gets on with older craftsmen and architects who know their stuff, and has little patience for project managers who don't. Would rather work alone on a carved piece than run a gang.
- sports persona: Watches Halifax Panthers when he can and follows rugby league generally, but isn't fanatical. Does a lot of fell walking on his own, Calderdale Way, the Dales. Swims outdoors in reservoirs and the river most of the year without making a fuss about it. Stopped five-a-side years ago after a knee tweak and doesn't miss it.
- arts persona: Far more into the arts than people expect. Sketches buildings and carvings in a notebook, drawing being half the job anyway. Listens to a lot of jazz and some early church music, and will go to a concert at the Piece Hall or Leeds Town Hall on his own. Reads widely: history, a bit of philosophy, translated novels. Watches subtitled films and has opinions about them. Goes to the Hepworth in Wakefield and Yorkshire Sculpture Park a few times a year.
- travel persona: Travels alone, cheaply, and with a purpose, usually to look at buildings. Has done Rome, Florence, Barcelona, Lisbon, and a week walking in the Picos de Europa. Wants to see the cathedrals in northern France and the stone villages in Puglia. Not bothered about beach holidays. Happy to work out transport and food in places where he doesn't speak the language.
- culinary persona: Cooks properly for himself most nights, usually something like a stew, a curry or pasta, and has his tea around half six. Got into Italian cooking after Florence and makes his own pasta on Sundays occasionally. Still likes a pie and peas at a match, and a proper chippy tea on a Friday. Drinks real ale, not much, and has started on red wine. Doesn't like fussy restaurants.
- hobbies and interests: Sketching buildings and carved details, Fell walking and wild swimming, Jazz and choral music, Reading history and translated fiction, Learning Italian on an app, badly, Visiting churches and old mills, Cooking Italian food, Subtitled films
- skills: Stone carving and letter cutting, Lime mortar mixing and repointing, Reading architectural drawings, Freehand drawing, Basic Italian, Map reading and navigation on the fells, Fixing most things around the house
- career goals: Wants to do more carving and conservation and less basic rebuilding work. He's thinking about going self-employed in the next few years and taking on church and heritage commissions directly. He'd like to pass on the trade properly to an apprentice, as long as it's someone who actually cares. He has no interest in management.
- voice: Flat West Yorkshire accent, not heavy. Speaks fairly slowly and plainly, and says exactly what he thinks, sometimes more bluntly than is comfortable. Uses 'tea' for his evening meal, 'owt' and 'nowt' now and then, and 'love' or 'mate' occasionally. Says 'er' rather than 'erm' when thinking, and uses 'sort of' as a hedge, though not often. Will say 'nah, I don't think that's right, actually' without softening it. Comfortable with silence. He'll just stop talking when he's finished and not fill the gap, and he'll take his time before answering a question he finds interesting. Gets noticeably more animated about buildings, books or music.
- typing: Mostly lowercase, with a capital at the start only sometimes. Short sentences with full stops and the odd comma, and no exclamation marks. Usually keeps the apostrophes in 'don't' and 'it's' but doesn't fuss. Avoids text-speak apart from 'tbh' now and again. Answers are brief unless the question interests him, in which case he writes a proper paragraph.
- with strangers: Reserved but not shy. Polite enough at first and then quite direct. He can come across as a bit gruff or unimpressed, and won't laugh at things he doesn't find funny. If the conversation turns to something he's into, he opens up and asks good questions. Doesn't flatter people and doesn't need to be liked, which some find refreshing and others find hard work.
- small things: Had to redo someone else's cement pointing on a chapel last week, Swam at Gaddings Dam on Sunday, water was freezing, Reading a book about Brunelleschi's dome, Halifax lost again, Made a ragù that took four hours and was worth it, His van's due its MOT, Found a carved mason's mark on a job that he reckons is 1700s
- deeper things: The divorce was mostly his fault. He admits he was distant and wrapped up in work and his own interests., He worries less than he probably should, and his ex used to say that came across as not caring, He feels he's missing out on Ellie growing up and doesn't really know how to talk to her now, He goes to evensong partly because it's the only time he sits still with other people, He sometimes wonders if he should have gone to art school, His dad died a few years ago and he didn't cry at the funeral, which bothers his mum more than it bothers him
- webcam photo: Head-and-shoulders shot from a laptop on a kitchen table, angled slightly up so the ceiling and a light fitting are visible at the top of the frame. Daylight from a window to his left lights one side of his face, and the other side is in mild shadow. White man in his mid-forties with a broad, weathered face, short greying brown hair cut close at the sides, and a couple of days' stubble, mostly grey at the chin. No glasses. Neutral expression, looking at the screen rather than the lens, mouth closed, faintly sceptical. Wearing a faded navy crew-neck sweatshirt with a small paint mark near the collar. Behind him is a whitewashed exposed stone wall with a wooden shelf holding a row of cookbooks, a Moka pot and a jar of wooden spoons. A framed pencil sketch of a church window hangs slightly off-centre. To the right, part of a door frame is visible, with a hi-vis jacket hanging on a hook.

P248 (Kulwinder; transcript label: Kulwinder):
- first name: Kulwinder
- age: 50
- lives in: Hayes, West London (London Borough of Hillingdon)
- occupation: Not currently in paid work. Trained as a tailor and alterations machinist and worked in garment workrooms and a dry-cleaner's alterations counter for over 20 years. Stopped about three years ago because of arthritis in her hands and lower back pain, and her caring load as a lone parent.
- education detail: Left a comprehensive school in Hayes with GCSEs. Did a City & Guilds in fashion and textiles (garment making) at a local further education college, then learned most of the trade on the job in a workroom in Southall.
- household: Lives in a three-bedroom ex-council terraced house with her two children, a son of 19 doing an apprenticeship and a daughter of 15 doing her GCSEs. Separated from her husband for about four years. They are still legally married and haven't sorted out the divorce, partly because of the house and partly because of family. Her widowed mother lives ten minutes away and comes round most days.
- cultural background: British-born Punjabi Sikh. Her parents came from Jalandhar district in the late 1960s and her dad worked at Heathrow. She grew up in Hayes and Southall and speaks English at home with the kids and Punjabi with her mum and the aunties. She goes to the gurdwara in Hayes most Sundays and for gurpurabs, and does sewa in the langar kitchen when her back allows. Faith matters to her quietly and practically rather than as something she talks about a lot. The separation is a sore point with some relatives, and she has stopped going to certain family functions.
- professional persona: Precise, fast and fussy about finish when she was working. She took pride in hems that sat right and never cut corners even when the shop was rushed. She was honest with customers to the point of bluntness, telling people straight if a garment wasn't worth altering. She didn't suffer lazy colleagues and could be short with managers she felt were taking the mick. She was reliable, never late, and kept her own notebook of every job.
- sports persona: Not sporty. She walks to the shops and round Lake Farm Country Park when her back is okay, and has a physio sheet of exercises she does fairly religiously. She half-watches the cricket when India are playing because her son puts it on.
- arts persona: Not one for galleries or theatre and finds most of it a bit pretentious. Watches Indian dramas on Sony and Zee with her mum, Coronation Street, and the odd Bake Off. Likes old Punjabi songs from her parents' era, and kirtan on in the kitchen in the mornings.
- travel persona: Doesn't travel much and doesn't miss it. Went to Punjab for a relative's wedding about six years ago and found the heat and the crowds hard going. Prefers a day trip to Brighton or Windsor. Worries about flying and about money, so holidays have mostly stopped since the separation.
- culinary persona: Cooks dinner from scratch every night: dal, sabzi, rotis, and chicken curry on Fridays. Makes things the way her mum does and isn't keen on 'fusion' anything. Batch-cooks on Sundays. Her daughter wants pasta more often, which is an ongoing negotiation. Buys from the Indian grocer on the Uxbridge Road and does the big shop at Asda.
- hobbies and interests: Still sews for family: salwar kameez alterations, school uniform hems, curtains, Watching Indian TV dramas with her mum, Gurdwara and langar sewa, Keeping the house spotless, Growing chillies, mint and tomatoes in pots in the back garden, Doing online survey panels for a bit of extra money
- skills: Pattern adjustment and garment alterations, Industrial and domestic sewing machines, Hand finishing and invisible hemming, Running a tight household budget, Cooking for large numbers in a langar kitchen, Fluent spoken Punjabi, basic Gurmukhi reading, Dealing with council and benefits paperwork
- career goals: Would like to take in alterations from home a few days a week once her hands are managed better, word of mouth through the gurdwara and the school. She doesn't want to go back to a workroom or work for anyone else. Mainly wants to get her daughter through school and her son settled, and to get the house and divorce sorted without losing out.
- voice: West London accent, ordinary and fairly quick when she's sure of something, slower and more careful when a question is personal. Says 'erm' when thinking and 'sort of' a lot, with the odd 'you know' or 'do you know what I mean' at the end. Calls the evening meal dinner. Occasionally drops a Punjabi word ('haan', 'chalo') without thinking, then carries on. Answers directly, even curtly, if she thinks a question is daft. Doesn't fill silences much. She'll wait for you to ask the next thing rather than chat on. Says 'sorry, what was that?' if the line is bad, and apologises if her mum talks in the background.
- typing: Types properly: capital at the start, full stops, apostrophes mostly right. Short, plain answers. No emojis or text-speak, though she'll use 'etc' and sometimes '...' when she trails off. Occasionally an autocorrect slip because she types on her phone.
- with strangers: Polite but a bit guarded at first, and not warm in a gushing way. Wants to know what something is for and who will see her answers. Once she trusts that it's genuine she is very straight and honest, even about things that don't flatter her. Can come across as a bit sharp or unimpressed, especially if she feels she's being talked down to. Nervous about getting things 'wrong' on a study and will double-check instructions.
- small things: Her daughter's mock exams coming up, The 140 bus being late again, Her mum not taking her blood pressure tablets, Heathrow planes over the house, Asda putting prices up, Her son finally passing his driving theory, The boiler making a noise, Langar at the gurdwara last Sunday
- deeper things: Still being legally married and not knowing how to finish it without a fight over the house, Some relatives quietly blaming her for the separation, Worrying a lot at night about money and her health, Grief that her hands won't let her work like she used to, because sewing was who she was, Feeling she has to be both parents and not being allowed to be tired, Her dad dying before the kids really knew him
- webcam photo: Laptop on a kitchen table, camera slightly below eye level so it looks a little up at her. Daylight from a window to her left, with an overhead light on giving a slightly yellow cast. A South Asian woman of 50 with a round face, faint lines round the eyes and a polite, slightly wary closed-mouth smile. Shoulder-length black hair with grey at the parting, pulled back in a low clip. Thin rectangular reading glasses pushed up on her head. Wearing a plum-coloured knitted cardigan over a plain black top, with a thin steel kara on her right wrist resting near the keyboard. Behind her: a white fitted kitchen with a kettle, a bread bin and a jar of utensils on the worktop, a wall calendar from a local Indian grocer with dates written on it in biro, and a small framed picture of Guru Nanak on a shelf beside a spider plant. A school blazer hangs on the back of a chair at the edge of the frame.

P249 (Gemma; transcript label: Gemma):
- first name: Gemma
- age: 30
- lives in: Taunton, South West England
- occupation: Registered adult nurse on a surgical ward at the county hospital, Band 6 since last spring, working mostly long days on a rota
- education detail: GCSEs and A levels (Biology, Psychology, Sociology) at a sixth form college in Bridgwater; BSc (Hons) Adult Nursing from the University of Plymouth, graduated 2016; has since done a mentorship module and an in-house course on wound care
- household: Rents a two-bedroom terraced house on the edge of town with her partner Liam (32), an electrician who works for a local firm. They've been together seven years and living together for five. No children yet. They're not married and have no firm plans, though it comes up at family dos. Liam's van is usually parked outside.
- cultural background: White British, born and raised in Somerset. Her dad was a mechanic and her mum worked school dinners and later as a teaching assistant. First in the family to go to university. Christened Church of England and went to Brownies at the church hall. Now she would say she's Christian but not really a churchgoer: she goes at Christmas, for weddings and christenings, and occasionally with her mum on Mothering Sunday. Close to her parents and her younger brother, who all live within half an hour.
- professional persona: Competent, steady and practical. She's not the loudest on the ward but she's reliable, and newly qualified nurses tend to end up shadowing her. She is good at handovers and keeps on top of her paperwork, though she'll admit it slips at the end of a bad shift. She gets frustrated about staffing and bed pressures but doesn't dwell on it at home. She's had a couple of moments of thinking about leaving nursing, like most of her cohort, and stayed.
- sports persona: Goes to a parkrun at Vivary Park most Saturdays she isn't working and does the odd 10k for charity, with times that are fine but nothing special. She had a gym membership and cancelled it. She watches the rugby with Liam and his mates, mostly Six Nations and sometimes a Bath game, but she's more into the atmosphere than the rules.
- arts persona: Mostly TV and podcasts: crime dramas, Bake Off, true crime on the drive in. She reads a few paperbacks a year, usually thrillers off the supermarket shelf or whatever her book-swap colleague passes on. She's been to Glastonbury twice when she was younger and still talks about it, and she goes to the Brewhouse Theatre panto with her niece at Christmas.
- travel persona: One week abroad a year if the rota allows. She and Liam have done Tenerife, Majorca and a long weekend in Lisbon. They like camping trips to Cornwall and Pembrokeshire in summer, and they were going to buy a campervan until they looked at the prices. She went interrailing for three weeks after uni and would like to do something like that again 'before kids, if there are kids'.
- culinary persona: Cooks most of the evening meals in her week off and batch-cooks for shift weeks: chilli, curries, a lot of pasta bakes. Liam does a decent Sunday roast. They like a Friday takeaway, usually Indian. She loves a cream tea and will argue jam-first, Cornish style, just to wind people up, though she's from Somerset. Drinks cider at the pub and prosecco at birthdays.
- hobbies and interests: parkrun on Saturday mornings, walking on the Quantocks with friends, true crime podcasts, pub quiz with work friends once a month, growing tomatoes and herbs in the small back garden, helping her mum at the church summer fete
- skills: clinical assessment and wound care, staying calm with distressed patients and relatives, organising a shift and prioritising tasks, mentoring student nurses, basic budgeting and keeping the household admin in order, can parallel park the van, which Liam can't stand
- career goals: Thinking about moving towards a specialist role, maybe tissue viability or surgical pre-assessment, partly for more regular hours. She might go for a ward sister post in a few years but isn't sure she wants the stress. She'd like to be on a more settled pattern before thinking about starting a family.
- voice: Friendly and fairly quick once she warms up, a bit more measured at first. Her accent is a soft West Country, noticeable mainly on some vowels and a light 'r' rather than anything strong. She says 'dinner' for the evening meal and uses 'proper' and 'lush' now and then, more when she's relaxed. Her fillers are 'erm' and 'like'. She hedges with 'sort of' and 'kind of' and ends sentences with 'yeah' or 'you know'. She'll say 'sorry, what was that?' if a question isn't clear. She's comfortable with a short silence, then usually fills it with a small joke or 'I don't know if that answers it'. She echoes the interviewer's wording when she's thinking.
- typing: Mostly lower case with a capital at the start if she remembers. She uses full stops sometimes but often just runs on with commas. Her apostrophes are usually right except when she's rushing on her phone. She abbreviates a bit ('tbh', 'w/', 'approx') and sometimes adds a 'lol' or 'haha' at the end of a jokey answer. req.text:
You write transcripts of realistic video calls between strangers for a fully synthetic research dataset set in the UK. The study, in order (from its published design): a short puzzle task done alone; first impressions of the others' webcam photos; then a series of three-minute, one-on-one video calls in rounds, each person meeting the others in their group; after each call a short survey.

Call shape (from the original study's numbers): a call is cut off by a three-minute timer. A typical call has about 30 turns (most between 20 and 39) and about 570 words in total (most between 440 and 682); half of all turns are 12 words or fewer, and a quarter are 24 or more. Short acknowledgements ("yeah", "mm") count as turns too. So aim for about 570 words in about 30 turns: alongside the quick back-and-forth, people often talk in longer stretches (explaining their job, telling a story), and those long turns carry much of the call.

Guide to British conversational English (use it for how people talk; it is a description of speech, not a script):
How British people talk in casual conversation. This is a paraphrase of published descriptions of spoken British English; sources are in SOURCES.md. Use these features lightly and only where they fit the person. Never use them as a caricature.

- **Fillers.** British speakers hesitate with "erm" and "er". Women and younger speakers lean towards "erm".
- **Hedges.** "Sort of" is everywhere and steady. "Kind of" is spreading, and younger speakers use it more.
- **Politeness words.** "Please", "thank you", "thanks" and "sorry" mostly mean what they say. "Sorry" also works as a repair word (to correct yourself, or to ask someone to repeat) and can be ironic.
- **Tags at the end of a sentence.** "You know", "right", "okay", "yeah", "do you know what I mean". Among young Londoners, "innit" and "you get me" are rising. Tags depend on age and region only, never on ethnicity.
- **Echoing.** In an engaged conversation people pick up and re-use parts of each other's words.
- **Regional words and grammar** (from a recent dialect survey):
  - A bread roll is a "barm" in the North West (Manchester to Liverpool and western Lancashire), a "cob" around Nottinghamshire, a "bap" in Staffordshire, the West Midlands and North Wales, and a "batch" in Liverpool and Coventry.
  - Around Liverpool an ice lolly can be a "lolly ice".
  - The evening meal is "tea" in the North West, North East and Yorkshire, and "dinner" in the South East and London. Some people say both.
  - "Yous" or "youse" for plural "you" is common in the North East (Newcastle, Teesside), Liverpool and Scotland, less so in Manchester, and rare in York, Leeds and Sheffield.
  - "Give it me" is normal in the North West and West Midlands and widely accepted in Sheffield and York; it fades south of Birmingham, Coventry and Leicester.
  - "You was" is widely used, historically Northern and now found as far south as London.
- **Everyday British words** to draw on where they fit, without assigning them to regions: knackered or shattered, chuffed or made up, skint or brassic, mardy or stroppy, mum or mam, mate or pal, settee, sofa or couch.

Gemma: Oh, that's dead interesting. We had a flood at school a couple of years ago, actually. The playground drain backed up and the whole Key Stage 1 bit was under water. The kids thought it was brilliant.
Carys: They always do. It was probably a blocked gully, or the drain was undersized for the area. A lot of school sites were built before anyone thought about it properly. Then they add a car park, all that hardstanding, and the water's got nowhere to go.
Gemma: That's exactly what happened, they'd just done the car park! You'd have sorted them out.
Carys: I'd have written them a very long report.
Gemma: Have you got kids?
Carys: One. Rhys, he's sixteen. Doing his mocks, very relaxed about them, unlike me.
Gemma: Ha. Lily's eleven, starting high school in September. It's just me and her, really. Her dad has her every other weekend.
Carys: Same here, more or less. Rhys's dad's in Chester, he has him Sundays.
Gemma: Oh, is it? It's hard work, isn't it. I don't know what I'd do without my mum, she does pick-ups on my staff meeting days.
Carys: Yes. Mine too. More than I'd like, if I'm honest.
Gemma: I worry about that a bit. What happens when they can't, you know.
Carys: Yeah. I try not to think about it too hard.
Gemma: Sorry, that's gone a bit deep for three minutes. What do you do for fun?
Carys: I walk. The Clwydian hills most weekends, Moel Famau usually. I got up on Saturday before the cloud came in.
Gemma: Oh, I'd be dead by the top. I do parkrun at Haigh Woodland when Lily's at her dad's, but I'm slow. I'm there for the coffee after, honestly.
Carys: That's the right reason to go.
Gemma: I've just been telling the lad from Birmingham about pie barms, and he looked at me like I'd said something awful.
Carys: Pie in a bap? I'd eat that.
Gemma: A bap! Oh, I'll let you off, you're Welsh.
Carys: Very generous of you.
Gemma: Have you got anything planned this summer?
Carys: Probably Pembrokeshire. Walking. I've already booked it, I always book ahead.
Gemma: See, you're organised. I still haven't booked Tenerife.

=== CALL C0460 ===
Tracey: Hello? Can you hear me?
Callum: Yeah. Alright. Callum.
Tracey: Tracey. Where are you then?
Callum: Wolverhampton. I'm a student, before you ask. Computer science.
Tracey: I wasn't gonna ask. You do look like a student though, sorry, but you do.
Callum: Is it the laundry basket?
Tracey: It's the laundry basket. My son's room was exactly like that till he moved out. Dean. He's twenty-seven now, lives in Romford with his girlfriend, and I bet her flat's spotless cos she won't have it.
Callum: Yeah, that's my girlfriend as well. Them folders on the shelf are hers. Them're the only tidy bit.
Tracey: Sounds about right. So what you gonna do with it, the computers?
Callum: IT support or testing, something like that. Birmingham or round here. Anything that's not nights. I did two years on nights at a warehouse off the M6 before uni and I'm not going back to that.
Tracey: No, I don't blame you. Nights ruin you. Steve, my husband, he did nights for a bit and he was like a zombie.
Callum: What do you do?
Tracey: Kitchen assistant. Primary school canteen.
Callum: My mum does that. School kitchen, in Wednesfield.
Tracey: Does she? Then she'll know all about it. Is her back alright?
Callum: Her feet, mostly. And the cook. She's always got something to say about the cook.
Tracey: There's always something with the cook. I fell out with one, cos she was reheating stuff she shouldn't, and I went to the manager. Then I lay awake half the night thinking I'd gone too far. But it's kids' food, you know, you can't have that. You can't.
Callum: Nah, fair. My mum'd say exactly the same.
Tracey: Tell her from me, she's right, whatever it is.
Callum: Ha. I will. She'll like that.
Tracey: And we ran out of jacket potatoes again this week. Every week. They don't order enough and it's me at the hatch getting the faces.
Callum: The kids give you faces?
Tracey: The kids and the teachers. The teachers are worse.
Callum: What's your husband do then?
Tracey: Van driver, builders' merchant. His van broke down on the A13 last week, so that was a lovely afternoon.
Callum: My dad drives a van. Parcels. His back's going a bit, to be honest.
Tracey: Oh, that's hard. You do worry about them, don't you.
Callum: Yeah. Anyway.
Tracey: Do you watch much telly?
Callum: Whatever Jade puts on. Crime documentaries, mostly. She loves them.
Tracey: Oh, me too. I watched one last week about a man in Essex and I didn't sleep. Steve said turn it off and I said no, I need to know what happened.
Callum: That's the thing with them, innit, you can't stop.
Tracey: You can't. Do yous eat proper, the two of you, or is it all takeaways?
Callum: Bit of both. We live above a takeaway, so the flat smells of chips every night, which doesn't help.
Tracey: I wouldn't mind that, I have a takeaway every Friday anyway.
Callum: It gets old, trust me.

=== CALL C0461 ===
Yusuf: Hiya! Can you hear me alright? Yusuf.
Carys: Yes, fine. I'm Carys.
Yusuf: Carys, nice. Are them walking boots behind you? By the door?
Carys: They are, yes. I'm in the hills most weekends. Moel Famau, usually.
Yusuf: Proper outdoorsy, then. I'm more gym, if I'm honest. Indoors, with air con.
Carys: That's fair. Less mud.
Yusuf: Way less mud. So what do you do?
Carys: Civil engineer. Flood risk and drainage, for local authorities mostly.
Yusuf: No way, so this is actually relevant to me. I'm an exec assistant at a commercial property consultancy in Birmingham, and every other board meeting I'm minuting, somebody's going on about a flood risk assessment holding up a site.
Carys: That'll be people like me holding it up, then.
Yusuf: Ha, so it's your fault! What actually goes in one of them?
Carys: Erm, you look at where the water comes from, river, surface water, sometimes groundwater, and what happens when you put buildings and car parks on top of it. Then you have to show you're not just pushing the problem onto the next street. Which developers sometimes try.
Yusuf: Mate, I believe that. Our lot would definitely try that.
Carys: Most do. It's usually fine once you show them the model.
Yusuf: I'm actually trying to move into business development, so I'm meant to be learning all this. I've mentioned it to one of my directors.
Carys: Good. Learn the boring bits properly, though. People can tell quite quickly if you're bluffing.
Yusuf: Yeah. Yeah, that's fair. Noted.
Carys: Sorry, that came out like a lecture. I mentor graduates, it's a habit.
Yusuf: No, no, it's good advice. Did you do the puzzle at the start? I reckon I got them all.
Carys: All of them?
Yusuf: Most. Most of them. Okay, I'm being generous to myself.
Carys: I thought you might be.
Yusuf: You've rumbled me. That's three people today. Holidays, anything nice?
Carys: Pembrokeshire this summer, walking. I did the Dolomites once with a university friend, that was the best one.
Yusuf: The mountains in Italy? That's the kind of place I'd go for the photos. I always want somewhere new, me, I never go back anywhere twice.
Carys: I'd go back. It took us four days to stop being lost.
Yusuf: Four days lost in Italy. That's a good story, that, you should tell it more.
Carys: I'd probably tell it worse than you would.

=== CALL C0462 ===
Gemma: Hiya! Can you hear me okay?
Craig: Yeah, fine. Craig. You alright?
Gemma: Gemma. I'm good thanks, last one of the round. Is that a Leigh scarf on your shelf?
Craig: It is, yeah. And you've got a Warriors magnet on your fridge, so this could go badly.
Gemma: Oh, it could. I'm from Wigan, my dad'd disown me if I was nice to you.
