req.text:
You write transcripts of realistic video calls between strangers for a fully synthetic research dataset set in the UK. The study, in order (from its published design): a short puzzle task done alone; first impressions of the others' webcam photos; then a series of three-minute, one-on-one video calls in rounds, each person meeting the others in their group; after each call a short survey.

Call shape (from the original study's numbers): a call is cut off by a three-minute timer. A typical call has about 30 turns (most between 20 and 39) and about 570 words in total (most between 440 and 682); half of all turns are 12 words or fewer, and a quarter are 24 or more. Short acknowledgements ("yeah", "mm") count as turns too. So aim for about 570 words in about 30 turns: alongside the quick back-and-forth, people often talk in longer stretches (explaining their job, telling a story), and those long turns carry much of the call.

Guide to British conversational English (use it for how people talk; it is a description of speech, not a script):
How British people talk in casual conversation. This is a paraphrase of published descriptions of spoken British English; sources are in SOURCES.md. Use these features lightly and only where they fit the person. Never use them as a caricature.

- **Fillers.** British speakers hesitate with "erm" and "er". Women and younger speakers lean towards "erm".
- **Hedges.** "Sort of" is everywhere and steady. "Kind of" is spreading, and younger speakers use it more.
- **Politeness words.** "Please", "thank you", "thanks" and "sorry" mostly mean what they say. "Sorry" also works as a repair word (to correct yourself, or to ask someone to repeat) and can be ironic.
- **Tags at the end of a sentence.** "You know", "right", "okay", "yeah", "do you know what I mean". Among young Londoners, "innit" and "you get me" are rising. Tags depend on age and region only, never on ethnicity.
- **Echoing.** In an engaged conversation people pick up and re-use parts of each other's words.
- **Regional words and grammar** (from a recent dialect survey):
  - A bread roll is a "barm" in the North West (Manchester to Liverpool and western Lancashire), a "cob" around Nottinghamshire, a "bap" in Staffordshire, the West Midlands and North Wales, and a "batch" in Liverpool and Coventry.
  - Around Liverpool an ice lolly can be a "lolly ice".
  - The evening meal is "tea" in the North West, North East and Yorkshire, and "dinner" in the South East and London. Some people say both.
  - "Yous" or "youse" for plural "you" is common in the North East (Newcastle, Teesside), Liverpool and Scotland, less so in Manchester, and rare in York, Leeds and Sheffield.
  - "Give it me" is normal in the North West and West Midlands and widely accepted in Sheffield and York; it fades south of Birmingham, Coventry and Leicester.
  - "You was" is widely used, historically Northern and now found as far south as London.
- **Everyday British words** to draw on where they fit, without assigning them to regions: knackered or shattered, chuffed or made up, skint or brassic, mardy or stroppy, mum or mam, mate or pal, settee, sofa or couch.

The group (session S46). Persona cards, including the webcam photo each person was rated on:

P242 (Andrew; transcript label: Andrew):
- first name: Andrew
- age: 39
- lives in: Beeston, Nottinghamshire, East Midlands
- occupation: Senior GIS (geographic information systems) analyst at a regional water utility, mapping pipe networks and flood-risk data. Hybrid working: three days at home, two at the office in Nottingham.
- education detail: A-levels at a sixth-form college in Mansfield. BSc Geography at the University of Leicester, then a part-time MSc in Geographic Information Science, completed while working in his mid-twenties.
- household: Lives with his wife Kate (38), a speech and language therapist with the NHS, in a 1930s semi-detached house near the canal. No children. They have an elderly tabby cat called Moss.
- cultural background: White British, born and raised in a former mining town in north Nottinghamshire. His dad was an electrician at the pit and later for the council, and his mum worked in a school office. He was the first in his family to go to university. Not religious, and neither were his parents in any active way. He still feels at home in the East Midlands and has never seriously wanted to move to London.
- professional persona: He is quietly relied upon. He is the person colleagues go to when a dataset doesn't make sense, and he would rather fix it properly than present it well. He dislikes office politics and overselling, and he is uncomfortable taking credit for team work. He is good at explaining technical things one-to-one, less keen on big presentations, but he does them when he has to.
- sports persona: Not a team-sports person. He cycles most weekends, usually long solo rides out towards the Vale of Belvoir or along the Trent. He goes to the occasional Notts County match with his dad, mostly for his dad's sake. He follows test cricket loosely on the radio.
- arts persona: A big reader of literary fiction and narrative non-fiction, especially landscape writing, history and translated novels. He likes ambient and post-rock music and listens on headphones while working. He goes to the cinema on his own on weekday evenings for foreign-language films. He has taken up linocut printing in a small way at a community art space.
- travel persona: Prefers quiet, walkable places over resorts. He and Kate have done the Lake District, Northumberland and the west of Ireland, plus a train trip through northern Spain. He enjoys planning routes on maps nearly as much as the trip itself. He would like to visit Iceland and Japan.
- culinary persona: Does most of the weekday cooking. Steady, practical dishes: curries from scratch, dal, risotto, a decent Sunday roast. He has been slowly working through a Middle Eastern cookbook. He eats less meat than he used to, mainly because of Kate. He still loves a cob with chips or a bacon cob from the café by the station.
- hobbies and interests: long-distance road cycling, reading fiction and nature writing, linocut printing, old Ordnance Survey maps and local history, birdwatching along the Trent and at Attenborough Nature Reserve, cooking from cookbooks, jigsaw puzzles with Kate in winter
- skills: GIS software and spatial data analysis, Python and SQL scripting, basic bike maintenance, map reading and route planning, cooking for a household, patient one-to-one explaining
- career goals: He wants to stay technical rather than move into management. He'd like to lead on climate and flood-modelling projects and maybe mentor junior analysts. He has thought vaguely about going freelance or into a research role at a university, but he values stability and isn't in a hurry.
- voice: Quiet, measured and fairly slow. He thinks before he answers and often starts with 'er' or 'erm, well'. His accent is a soft Nottinghamshire one, with flattened vowels and the odd dropped 'h'. Without making a thing of it he'll say 'cob', 'mardy', 'tea' for the evening meal, and 'mate' to men he knows. He uses 'sort of' a lot as a hedge and ends points with 'yeah' or 'I suppose'. He is comfortable with silence and won't rush to fill a pause. If asked something vague, he'll ask, 'Sorry, do you mean at work or just generally?'
- typing: Mostly lowercase with few capitals at the start. Proper apostrophes and spelling, because he finds sloppy spelling grating. Short sentences, full stops, sometimes no full stop on the last line. No emojis. Rarely abbreviates beyond 'e.g.' or 'approx'. Answers are brief but accurate, e.g. 'cycling mostly, and reading. some printmaking lately'
- with strangers: Reserved and polite. He gives short answers at first and can seem a bit flat or shy, but he is honest and doesn't exaggerate. He warms up if the conversation turns to something he knows, like maps, books or cycling routes, and then becomes more detailed and quietly funny. He doesn't ask many questions back unless he's interested. He never tries to impress.
- small things: the cat waking him at 5am for food, a new cycling route he tried at the weekend, the tram works and traffic in Beeston, a book he's halfway through, getting a decent bacon cob from the café, the weather ruining a planned ride, his dad's latest DIY project
- deeper things: he and Kate tried for children for a few years and have mostly made peace with it not happening, he sometimes feels distant from old school friends who stayed in his hometown, he worries about his dad's health since a minor heart scare last year, he finds big social events genuinely draining and has skipped work parties, climate change makes him quietly anxious, which is partly why he wanted to do flood work
- webcam photo: Head-and-shoulders shot from a laptop webcam slightly below eye level, so the angle looks a little up at him. Soft daylight comes from a window to his left, leaving the right side of his face a bit shadowed. He's a pale-skinned man with short, light brown hair, slightly thinning at the front, and a closely trimmed beard with some grey in it. He wears rectangular black-framed glasses. His expression is neutral, with a small, slightly awkward closed-mouth smile. He's wearing a plain navy crew-neck jumper over a grey T-shirt. Behind him is a spare-bedroom office: a white wall with a framed print of an old Ordnance Survey map of Nottinghamshire, a tall pine bookshelf crammed with paperbacks and a few cycling magazines, and a road bike hanging on a wall bracket to the right. On the edge of the frame is part of a radiator with a drying cycling jersey draped over it.

P243 (Prajakta; transcript label: Prajakta):
- first name: Prajakta
- age: 38
- lives in: Stevenage, Hertfordshire, East of England
- occupation: Quality control laboratory analyst at a contract pharmaceutical manufacturing site, testing raw materials and finished batches against specifications. Full-time, about 37.5 hours a week plus occasional overtime when batch release is backed up.
- education detail: BSc in Chemistry from a college affiliated to Savitribai Phule Pune University, then an MSc in Analytical Chemistry in Pune. After moving to the UK she completed a GMP and laboratory data integrity training course through her employer, and the company has trained her on HPLC and dissolution testing.
- household: Lives with her husband Nikhil (40, a software test lead at an insurance firm, mostly working from home) and their daughter Ira (7, in Year 2). They own a three-bedroom semi-detached house on an estate in the Great Ashby/Chells side of Stevenage, bought in 2017. Her mother-in-law stays for two or three months most years.
- cultural background: Born and raised in Pune, Maharashtra, in a middle-class Marathi-speaking Hindu family. Her father was a bank clerk and her mother was a school teacher, now retired. She came to the UK in 2012 at 26, shortly after an arranged-but-chosen marriage, because Nikhil already had a job here. She speaks Marathi at home, Hindi with some friends, and English at work. She keeps Ganesh Chaturthi and Diwali at home with a small shrine in the kitchen and goes to the temple in Luton or Hemel only for big occasions. She has British citizenship and feels settled, but she gets homesick in a sudden, physical way, usually around her mother's birthday or monsoon season.
- professional persona: Precise and fairly quick at the bench. She does not do much chatting in the lab. Colleagues see her as reliable but a bit sharp: she will point out a sloppy entry in someone's notebook without softening it, and she does not forget when someone leaves her to clean up their mess. She worries a lot about out-of-specification results and replays mistakes at night. She is competent rather than ambitious, keeps her paperwork in decent order, and does not enjoy team meetings or being asked to present.
- sports persona: Not sporty. She walks about 40 minutes most evenings around Fairlands Valley Park, partly for health and partly to get time alone. She did a beginners' badminton session at a leisure centre once and didn't go back because she didn't like the group. She watches cricket only when India are playing well, and only if Nikhil has it on.
- arts persona: Watches Marathi and Hindi films on streaming services, and some British crime dramas. She likes slow, sad films and will cry at them, which she finds slightly embarrassing. She used to sing classical (Hindustani) as a girl and still hums bhajans while cooking, but she would never perform. She reads short Marathi stories on her phone.
- travel persona: Goes back to Pune every year or eighteen months for three weeks, usually in December. She gets anxious about flying and about leaving her parents each time. Other trips are short and planned: Cornwall once, the Lake District once, and Paris for a long weekend, which she found tiring and overcrowded. She prefers a cottage to a hotel and does not like group tours.
- culinary persona: Cooks most evenings, mainly Maharashtrian home food: varan bhaat, poha for weekend breakfast, bhakri, usal, and modak at Ganesh Chaturthi. She is vegetarian at home and has eggs occasionally. She is fussy about spices and buys them from an Indian grocer in Hitchin rather than the supermarket. She calls the evening meal dinner. She has opinions about restaurant 'Indian food' and mostly avoids it.
- hobbies and interests: Evening walks on her own, Growing coriander, methi and chillies in pots in the back garden and a small greenhouse, Watching Marathi films and serials, Video calls with her mum on Sunday mornings, Doing Ira's reading and spelling homework with her, Tidying and reorganising the kitchen cupboards when stressed
- skills: HPLC and UV-Vis analysis, Dissolution testing, Writing and checking lab documentation to GMP standards, Spotting errors in data and paperwork, Cooking Maharashtrian food from memory, Fluent Marathi, Hindi and English
- career goals: She would like to move up to senior analyst or a reviewer role, where she would check other people's data rather than run endless samples. She does not want to manage a team. Sometimes she thinks about a quality assurance office job with steadier hours, mainly so she can do the school run more often. She worries she has left it too late to change direction.
- voice: Quiet, fairly low-pitched, measured. Her Pune English is softened after twelve years here, and some British habits have crept in: 'erm', 'sort of', 'yeah' as a tag, and 'shattered' after a long shift. She answers in short, complete sentences and does not elaborate unless asked again. She pauses before answering and is comfortable leaving a silence rather than filling it. When she disagrees she says so flatly, something like 'No, that's not really right', and does not soften it with a laugh. If she gets onto her daughter or her parents she speeds up and sounds a bit more anxious. She uses 'sorry?' to ask for a repeat when the line is bad.
- typing: Mostly correct capitals and full stops, because she types a lot of formal text at work. She is quicker and looser on her phone: sometimes no full stop at the end, 'ok' rather than 'okay', and apostrophes usually there. She rarely uses emojis or exclamation marks. She gives brief answers, sometimes just a few words, and occasionally adds a pointed clarification if she thinks a question was badly worded.
- with strangers: Reserved and a little guarded. She can come across as cool or unfriendly at first. She won't do small talk for long and may ask what the point of a question is. She is honest and won't exaggerate to please you. If she senses the person is patient and not judging her, she warms up a little and becomes more candid, especially about worries.
- small things: The traffic on the A1(M) when it rains, Ira's school sending last-minute emails about non-uniform days, Her methi plants getting eaten by slugs, Being shattered after a run of late batches, The Indian grocer in Hitchin running out of the brand of jaggery she likes, Nikhil being on calls all day so the house is never quiet
- deeper things: She worries constantly about her parents ageing in Pune and feels guilty for not being there, particularly since her father's heart scare two years ago, She gets health anxiety about Ira and has taken her to A&E more than once for things that turned out to be nothing, She found the first two or three years in England very lonely and still doesn't have many close friends here, She clashed badly with a previous team leader and still feels resentful about how it was handled, She sometimes feels she gave up a more promising career in India to follow her husband
- webcam photo: Laptop webcam at slightly below eye level, so the angle looks up a little. Head and shoulders are framed slightly left of centre. Light comes from a window to her right, out of shot, and lights that side of her face, with the left side a bit shadowed. She has a medium-brown complexion and dark brown eyes, with a neutral, slightly guarded expression and her lips closed. Her straight black hair is pulled back into a low ponytail, with a few loose strands at the front. She wears thin rectangular black-framed glasses, small gold stud earrings, and a thin black-bead mangalsutra just visible at the neckline. She has on a plain navy round-neck jumper. Behind her is a kitchen-diner: cream wall, a white wall clock, the edge of a tall fridge-freezer with a child's drawing held on by a magnet, and a wooden shelf with steel spice tins and a small brass Ganesh idol with a dried marigold beside it. A school book bag hangs on the back of a dining chair at the edge of the frame.

P244 (Leanne; transcript label: Leanne):
- first name: Leanne
- age: 38
- lives in: Normanton, West Yorkshire (Yorkshire and The Humber)
- occupation: Shift manager at a large third-party distribution warehouse off the M62, running the late shift for a team of around 40 pickers, loaders and two team leaders
- education detail: Left school at 16 with GCSEs (C in English, D in maths, resat and passed at college). NVQ Level 2 then Level 3 in Warehousing and Storage done on the job, and an ILM Level 3 in Leadership and Management that the company paid for when she was made up to shift manager at 33. She has also got her counterbalance and reach truck licences.
- household: Rents a three-bed semi on an estate in Normanton with her partner Dean (41, HGV driver, together 11 years, never bothered getting married) and their Staffordshire bull terrier, Bella. No children. Her mam lives ten minutes away in Altofts and Leanne goes round most Sundays.
- cultural background: White British, born at Pinderfields in Wakefield and grew up in Castleford. Her dad worked at the glassworks until it shut, and her mam did school dinners. It's a working family with a big extended clan locally. She ticks 'prefer not to say' on religion forms because she doesn't see what it's got to do with anyone. req.text:
You write transcripts of realistic video calls between strangers for a fully synthetic research dataset set in the UK. The study, in order (from its published design): a short puzzle task done alone; first impressions of the others' webcam photos; then a series of three-minute, one-on-one video calls in rounds, each person meeting the others in their group; after each call a short survey.

Call shape (from the original study's numbers): a call is cut off by a three-minute timer. A typical call has about 30 turns (most between 20 and 39) and about 570 words in total (most between 440 and 682); half of all turns are 12 words or fewer, and a quarter are 24 or more. Short acknowledgements ("yeah", "mm") count as turns too. So aim for about 570 words in about 30 turns: alongside the quick back-and-forth, people often talk in longer stretches (explaining their job, telling a story), and those long turns carry much of the call.

Guide to British conversational English (use it for how people talk; it is a description of speech, not a script):
How British people talk in casual conversation. This is a paraphrase of published descriptions of spoken British English; sources are in SOURCES.md. Use these features lightly and only where they fit the person. Never use them as a caricature.

- **Fillers.** British speakers hesitate with "erm" and "er". Women and younger speakers lean towards "erm".
- **Hedges.** "Sort of" is everywhere and steady. "Kind of" is spreading, and younger speakers use it more.
- **Politeness words.** "Please", "thank you", "thanks" and "sorry" mostly mean what they say. "Sorry" also works as a repair word (to correct yourself, or to ask someone to repeat) and can be ironic.
- **Tags at the end of a sentence.** "You know", "right", "okay", "yeah", "do you know what I mean". Among young Londoners, "innit" and "you get me" are rising. Tags depend on age and region only, never on ethnicity.
- **Echoing.** In an engaged conversation people pick up and re-use parts of each other's words.
- **Regional words and grammar** (from a recent dialect survey):
  - A bread roll is a "barm" in the North West (Manchester to Liverpool and western Lancashire), a "cob" around Nottinghamshire, a "bap" in Staffordshire, the West Midlands and North Wales, and a "batch" in Liverpool and Coventry.
  - Around Liverpool an ice lolly can be a "lolly ice".
  - The evening meal is "tea" in the North West, North East and Yorkshire, and "dinner" in the South East and London. Some people say both.
  - "Yous" or "youse" for plural "you" is common in the North East (Newcastle, Teesside), Liverpool and Scotland, less so in Manchester, and rare in York, Leeds and Sheffield.
  - "Give it me" is normal in the North West and West Midlands and widely accepted in Sheffield and York; it fades south of Birmingham, Coventry and Leicester.
  - "You was" is widely used, historically Northern and now found as far south as London.
- **Everyday British words** to draw on where they fit, without assigning them to regions: knackered or shattered, chuffed or made up, skint or brassic, mardy or stroppy, mum or mam, mate or pal, settee, sofa or couch.

- household: Lives with her husband Imran (31, a Bolton-born multi-drop delivery driver) in a rented two-bed terraced house in Daubhill. There are no children yet. They moved out of his parents' house, a few streets away, about eighteen months ago, and she still goes round there most days.

- age: 39
- lives in: Taunton, South West England

He suspects his brother didn't really want to be one., That he's become quite good at working the benefits and NHS systems and isn't entirely sorry about it

A man in his late thirties with a pale, slightly sallow complexion, faint grey shadows under his eyes, and a short, neatly trimmed brown beard flecked with grey. Short mousy-brown hair, thinning at the temples, combed to the side. No glasses. A small, polite, closed-mouth smile and a steady gaze at the camera. He's wearing a navy quarter-zip fleece over a grey T-shirt, the left sleeve pushed up, and a thin strip of surgical tape is just visible on his forearm. Behind him is a magnolia-painted spare bedroom: on the left, part of a grey home dialysis machine on a wheeled stand. On the right, a white flat-pack shelving unit holding labelled plastic storage boxes of medical supplies, a framed Institution of Civil Engineers certificate and a small Somerset CCC mug. Above the shelves is a wall calendar with handwritten entries. The corner of a dog bed is visible on the floor.

- occupation: Associate Director and chartered structural engineer at a mid-sized engineering consultancy in Farringdon, working mainly on residential and mixed-use buildings

- webcam photo: Head-and-shoulders shot from a laptop webcam on a desk, angled slightly upwards so the top of the frame shows a bit of ceiling. Daylight from a window to his left lights one side of his face, and the other side is a little shadowed. He has a long, lean face with light stubber, pale skin slightly reddened at the cheeks, and short, neatly cut sandy-brown hair greying at the temples. He wears thin rectangular metal-framed glasses and a plain navy crew-neck jumper over a white collared shirt. His expression is neutral and attentive, mouth closed, eyebrows slightly raised as if waiting for a question. Behind him is a white-painted wall with a tall pale wooden bookcase holding several thick ring binders labelled with project codes, a few engineering reference books, a folded high-vis vest and a white hard hat on the top shelf. To the right of the frame the rear wheel of a black bicycle hangs on a wall hook. A small framed photo of a teenage girl on a beach sits on the edge of the shelf.

- first name: Agnieszka

Agnieszka: Once, twice a year. I drive sometimes, two days. I don't mind. Podcasts, coffee, is fine.

Agnieszka: Good. You miss Dutch food?

req.text:
You write transcripts of realistic video calls between strangers for a fully synthetic research dataset set in the UK. The study, in order (from its published design): a short puzzle task done alone; first impressions of the others' webcam photos; then a series of three-minute, one-on-one video calls in rounds, each person meeting the others in their group; after each call a short survey.

Call shape (from the original study's numbers): a call is cut off by a three-minute timer. A typical call has about 30 turns (most between 20 and 39) and about 570 words in total (most between 440 and 682); half of all turns are 12 words or fewer, and a quarter are 24 or more. Short acknowledgements ("yeah", "mm") count as turns too. So aim for about 570 words in about 30 turns: alongside the quick back-and-forth, people often talk in longer stretches (explaining their job, telling a story), and those long turns carry much of the call.

Guide to British conversational English (use it for how people talk; it is a description of speech, not a script):
How British people talk in casual conversation. This is a paraphrase of published descriptions of spoken British English; sources are in SOURCES.md. Use these features lightly and only where they fit the person. Never use them as a caricature.

- **Fillers.** British speakers hesitate with "erm" and "er". Women and younger speakers lean towards "erm".
- **Hedges.** "Sort of" is everywhere and steady. "Kind of" is spreading, and younger speakers use it more.
- **Politeness words.** "Please", "thank you", "thanks" and "sorry" mostly mean what they say. "Sorry" also works as a repair word (to correct yourself, or to ask someone to repeat) and can be ironic.
- **Tags at the end of a sentence.** "You know", "right", "okay", "yeah", "do you know what I mean". Among young Londoners, "innit" and "you get me" are rising. Tags depend on age and region only, never on ethnicity.
- **Echoing.** In an engaged conversation people pick up and re-use parts of each other's words.
- **Regional words and grammar** (from a recent dialect survey):
  - A bread roll is a "barm" in the North West (Manchester to Liverpool and western Lancashire), a "cob" around Nottinghamshire, a "bap" in Staffordshire, the West Midlands and North Wales, and a "batch" in Liverpool and Coventry.
  - Around Liverpool an ice lolly can be a "lolly ice".
  - The evening meal is "tea" in the North West, North East and Yorkshire, and "dinner" in the South East and London. Some people say both.
  - "Yous" or "youse" for plural "you" is common in the North East (Newcastle, Teesside), Liverpool and Scotland, less so in Manchester, and rare in York, Leeds and Sheffield.
  - "Give it me" is normal in the North West and West Midlands and widely accepted in Sheffield and York; it fades south of Birmingham, Coventry and Leicester.
  - "You was" is widely used, historically Northern and now found as far south as London.
- **Everyday British words** to draw on where they fit, without assigning them to regions: knackered or shattered, chuffed or made up, skint or brassic, mardy or stroppy, mum or mam, mate or pal, settee, sofa or couch.

The group (session S44). Persona cards, including the webcam photo each person was rated on:

P231 (Tomasz; transcript label: Tomasz):
- first name: Tomasz
- age: 33
- lives in: Earley, Reading, South East England
- occupation: Full-time student, BSc Construction Management at the University of Reading (second year). Previously worked six years as a shift team leader at a distribution warehouse near Theale. He keeps a few weekend shifts there over the summer.
- education detail: Finished technical secondary school (technikum) in Poland with a qualification in building technology. In the UK he did a forklift licence, an Access to HE course and a Level 3 in supervisory management through work. He started his degree at 31 with a student loan and savings.
- household: Lives with his wife Agnieszka (32), a dental nurse at a practice in Wokingham, in a rented two-bedroom flat in Earley. The second bedroom is his study room. They have no children yet, though they have talked about it for after he graduates.
- cultural background: Born and raised in Rzeszów, south-east Poland. He moved to the UK at 19 to join an older cousin in Reading and has stayed since. He is Roman Catholic and goes to Mass at the Polish church in Reading most Sundays, more from habit and family expectation than strong feeling. He speaks Polish at home and with family, and English everywhere else. He has pre-settled-then-settled status and has not bothered with citizenship yet, though he says he will 'when there is time'.
- professional persona: Organised and exact. At the warehouse he was known for keeping a tight rota and not tolerating excuses. At university he submits work early, keeps a spreadsheet of every deadline and finds group projects frustrating when others are vague. He wants clear briefs and measurable results, and he is not interested in networking events.
- sports persona: Runs 5k three mornings a week on a fixed route around Maiden Erlegh Lake and records times on a watch. He watches Ekstraklasa and Premier League football results rather than full matches, and has a casual attachment to Stal Rzeszów. He does not play team sports any more.
- arts persona: Not much interest. He watches the occasional action film or a Polish crime series with Agnieszka and listens to the radio in the car. He has not been to a gallery or the theatre in years and sees little point in it.
- travel persona: Travels to Poland twice a year, at Christmas and in summer, usually by flying from Luton or Stansted to Rzeszów. He prefers going back to the same places and once did a week in Croatia because Agnieszka wanted it. He books early, compares prices carefully and dislikes disorganised trips.
- culinary persona: Eats simply and regularly. Agnieszka cooks more Polish food at weekends, such as pierogi and żurek at Easter. On weekdays he cooks chicken, rice and vegetables in batches. He shops at Lidl and the Polish shop on Oxford Road, drinks black coffee, and has a beer occasionally but not much.
- hobbies and interests: Running with tracked times, Fixing and maintaining his Skoda Octavia himself, Watching construction and engineering videos on YouTube, Keeping a household budget spreadsheet, Football results and transfer news
- skills: Shift scheduling and rota planning, Forklift operation (counterbalance and reach), Excel, including pivot tables and budgeting, Basic AutoCAD and quantity take-off from drawings, Car maintenance, Fluent Polish and English
- career goals: Graduate in 2026 and get onto a site manager or assistant project manager graduate scheme with a mid-size contractor in the Thames Valley. Long term he wants to become chartered with CIOB and earn enough to buy a house in Woodley or Wokingham.
- voice: Calm, fairly flat and a bit clipped. He speaks fluent English with a noticeable but light Polish accent, and his word stress is occasionally slightly off. He answers the question asked and stops, without padding. He uses 'er' as a hesitation sometimes and a fair bit of 'sort of' and 'to be honest', picked up from years at work. He says 'dinner' for the evening meal and 'mate' with colleagues, and occasionally 'knackered'. He doesn't mind silence at all and will just wait. If a question is unclear he says 'sorry, what do you mean exactly?' rather than guessing.
- typing: Proper capitals at the start of sentences and full stops, short sentences, mostly correct apostrophes. He rarely uses abbreviations other than 'e.g.' and 'etc'. He occasionally drops an article or uses a slightly odd preposition ('I am studying in second year'). He never uses emojis or exclamation marks.
- with strangers: Polite but reserved, and can come across as blunt or a little cold at first. He doesn't do much small talk and won't laugh at things he doesn't find funny. He is reliable and to the point, and he is clearly sceptical if something seems like a waste of time. He warms slightly if the conversation is practical.
- small things: His running time this week was 30 seconds slower because of the rain, The Oxford Road Polish shop has put prices up again, He needs to replace the brake pads on the Skoda, A group member hasn't done their part of the site report, The 17 bus is always late, He's been doing his reading at the library because the flat is cold
- deeper things: He worries that starting a degree at 31 means he is behind people his age, His father has a heart condition and he feels guilty being far away, He and Agnieszka are living mostly on her salary and it puts pressure on him, He sometimes feels neither fully Polish nor British any more, He goes to church more for his mother than for himself
- webcam photo: Laptop webcam at slightly below eye level, framing his head and shoulders, with the light coming from a window to his left and a ceiling light on. He has a lean face, short dark-blond hair clipped at the sides and light stubble. His grey-blue eyes look directly at the camera, his mouth is neutral and slightly tight, and he is not smiling. He wears no glasses, and he has on a plain navy quarter-zip jumper over a white T-shirt collar. Behind him is a white wall with a large printed academic year planner pinned up, marked with coloured highlighter. A narrow pine bookshelf holds construction textbooks, a hard hat on the top shelf and a framed wedding photo. A small wooden crucifix hangs high on the wall to the right of the frame.

P232 (Nadeesha; transcript label: Nadeesha):
- first name: Nadeesha
- age: 39
- lives in: Pontprennau, Cardiff, Wales
- occupation: Senior procurement officer for an NHS health board in South Wales, managing tenders and supplier contracts for medical consumables
- education detail: BSc in Business Management from a private university college in Colombo. She moved to the UK at 24 for an MSc in International Business at Cardiff Metropolitan University, and later earned the CIPS Level 4 Diploma in Procurement and Supply, which her employer funded.
- household: Lives with her husband Dilan, 41, a community pharmacist, and their daughter Sanuli, 8, in a four-bedroom new-build semi they bought in 2019. Her mother stays with them for about three months most winters.
- cultural background: Born and raised in Kandy, Sri Lanka, in a Sinhalese Buddhist family. Her father was a bank manager and her mother a schoolteacher. She has lived in Cardiff for fifteen years and holds British citizenship. She goes to a Sri Lankan Buddhist temple in Cardiff for Vesak, poya days when she can manage it, and family almsgivings. She speaks Sinhala at home some of the time and wants Sanuli to keep it up.
- professional persona: Organised enough, though she relies on deadlines rather than discipline. She is good at the negotiating side and likes being the person in the room who knows what the contract actually says. She is quite conscious of her grade and title. She is happy to let her manager assume a cost saving was mostly her own work, and she is careful about how she is seen by people above her.
- sports persona: Not sporty. She goes to a gym class twice a week at a chain gym near Cardiff Gate, mostly Body Pump, and walks round Roath Park Lake at weekends. She follows Sri Lankan cricket loosely and gets very tense watching it.
- arts persona: Watches Korean dramas and Tamil and Sinhala films on streaming apps. She occasionally goes to musicals at the Wales Millennium Centre, mostly when friends organise it, and enjoys dressing up for the evening as much as the show itself.
- travel persona: Goes back to Sri Lanka every other year for a month, splitting the time between family in Kandy and a few nights at a nice hotel down the south coast. She likes city breaks with a bit of luxury, such as Dubai on the way home, Barcelona, and Lisbon last year. She gets anxious about flights and connections and over-prepares.
- culinary persona: Cooks rice and curry most weeknights, usually dhal, a fish curry, and a mallung, plus pasta for Sanuli. She makes kiribath for New Year and special days. She likes trying new restaurants in Cardiff Bay and posting the food, and buys spices in bulk from an Asian grocer in Grangetown.
- hobbies and interests: Korean dramas, Instagram, mainly food and home interiors, Gardening in pots on the patio, including chillies and curry leaf that keep dying, Interior decorating and browsing for furniture, Temple events and Sri Lankan community gatherings, Online shopping and deal-hunting
- skills: Contract negotiation, Running tender evaluations and procurement frameworks, Excel, especially pivot tables and lookups, Fluent Sinhala and English, Cooking for large gatherings, Reading people in meetings
- career goals: She wants to reach head of category or procurement manager within three or four years, ideally at Band 8a. She is considering a move to the Welsh Government or a private-sector role if the money is noticeably better. She also wants to finish full MCIPS membership, mainly for the letters after her name.
- voice: Fluent, clear Sri Lankan English with a slight Cardiff softening picked up over fifteen years. She speaks at a medium-quick pace and speeds up when she's worried she's taking too long. She uses 'erm' a fair bit and 'sort of' as a hedge, and says 'actually' often. She tags sentences with 'no?' or 'you know' now and then. She says 'sorry' a lot, both to apologise and to correct herself ('it was March, sorry, April'). She fills silences quickly, sometimes laughs a little nervously, and asks 'is that okay, is that what you wanted?' if she isn't sure she's answered properly.
- typing: Mostly correct capitals and apostrophes, because she writes formal emails all day. In quick answers she drops the full stop at the end, sometimes uses 'tbh' or 'etc', and occasionally makes an autocorrect slip. She is a bit overlong when she's trying to give a good answer.
- with strangers: Warm and polite on the surface, chatty, and keen to come across as capable and well-off. She mentions her job title early and drops the odd detail about holidays or the house. She is underneath a bit guarded and will tailor what she says to what she thinks the other person wants to hear. She gets visibly flustered if something technical goes wrong on the call.
- small things: The school run and Sanuli's swimming lessons on Tuesdays, Feeling knackered after a week of supplier meetings, The price of rice and coconut milk going up, A new air fryer she's obsessed with, The rain in Cardiff, still, after fifteen years, Arguing with Dilan about whether to get a bigger car
- deeper things: Worrying constantly about her father's health back in Kandy and feeling guilty for being so far away, Two early miscarriages before Sanuli, which she rarely talks about, Feeling she has to work harder to be taken seriously at work and sometimes resenting colleagues who got on more easily, Being unsure whether she'll ever move back to Sri Lanka, and quietly knowing she probably won't, Anxiety that comes in waves, especially at night, which she has never seen a doctor about
- webcam photo: A laptop webcam shot from slightly below eye level, framing her head and shoulders a little left of centre. Soft daylight comes from a window to her right, so the right side of her face is brighter. She has a light brown complexion and long straight black hair tied back in a low ponytail, with a few strands loose at the front. She wears small gold stud earrings and a thin gold chain. She has no glasses and is smiling politely with her lips closed and her eyebrows slightly raised, as if waiting for the call to start. She wears a navy fitted blouse. Behind her is a light grey painted wall with a large framed canvas print of tea plantations in the hill country. A white shelf holds a small brass Buddha statue, a framed school photo of a girl in a purple jumper, and a tall green plant in a white pot. The edge of a grey fabric sofa with a mustard cushion is just visible at the bottom right of the frame.

- occupation: Part-time replenishment assistant (shelf-stacking and unloading deliveries) at a large supermarket in Brent Park, about 25 hours a week, mostly 9:30 to 2:30 so he can do the school runs

- skills: Stock rotation and managing deliveries, Fluent Gujarati, conversational Hindi, Basic home cooking, Gujarati and English, Budgeting tightly on a low income, Fixing small things round the flat (flat-pack, tap washers), Plaiting hair, which he learned from YouTube for school mornings

Typical lines: 'Yeah, it's alright, it's sort of just me and my daughter, so.' and 'Erm... I'd say I'm pretty organised, kind of have to be.'
- typing: Mostly lowercase and types on his phone, so autocorrect sometimes capitalises the first word. He uses few full stops and often drops apostrophes ('dont', 'im', 'its'). Answers are short, a phrase or one sentence. He occasionally uses 'tbh' or 'idk', and spells 'you' out rather than 'u'. Example: 'shelf stacking at a supermarket, part time cos of school runs'
- with strangers: Polite and a bit reserved. He doesn't do small talk well and can come across as shy or flat until he gets used to someone. He answers what's asked honestly but briefly. He warms up a little when the topic turns to his daughter or cricket, and might even crack a dry joke. He won't push his opinions and is happy to be agreeable.
- small things: School run was a nightmare in the rain this morning, Anaya wants a hamster and he's trying to hold out, The store changed the rota again, His mum sent him back with way too many theplas, Bus was late so he walked, India lost the last match and he was gutted, Found a decent kids' bike on Marketplace for twenty quid, Feeling knackered after a delivery day
- deeper things: He and Priya married young, at 22, partly because both families pushed it, and he's not sure either of them really chose it, They're still legally married and he doesn't know whether to start divorce proceedings, partly because of what his parents and the community would think, Being a dad doing it mostly on his own is lonely, and other parents at the school gate are friendly but he doesn't really fit in with the mums' chat, Money is tight and he worries about Anaya noticing what other kids have, He feels guilty that Anaya speaks almost no Gujarati, He sometimes wonders what his life would be if he'd finished the IT course
- webcam photo: Phone camera propped up against something on a kitchen table, angled slightly upward so the top of the frame cuts close to his head. Lighting comes mostly from a ceiling light and a bit of grey daylight from a window to the left, leaving one side of his face slightly shadowed. He has a slim face, short black hair with a fade at the sides that's growing out, light stubble, dark brown eyes, and a neutral expression with a faint, polite half-smile. No glasses. He is wearing a plain dark grey hoodie with the hood down. Behind him is a small kitchen with white cupboard doors and a fridge covered in children's drawings and a school letter held by magnets. Next to the fridge a narrow shelf holds a small framed picture of Krishna, a brass diya and a couple of incense sticks in a holder. A pink child's backpack hangs on the back of a chair, and a drying rack with small school polo shirts is partly visible at the right edge of the frame.

P234 (Gemma; transcript label: Gemma):
- first name: Gemma
- age: 41
- lives in: Maidstone, South East England (Kent)
- occupation: Branch manager at an independent lettings and estate agency in Maidstone town centre. She runs a team of five (two lettings negotiators, a property manager, an admin and a part-time valuer), oversees landlord accounts and handles escalated complaints.

- cultural background: Born and raised in Kent. Her mum was a dental receptionist and her dad was a lorry driver, and she grew up in a semi in Aylesford. White British with no religion. - hobbies and interests: Walking Biscuit round the estate and at Mote Park, Watching reality TV with her phone in hand, Bottomless brunches and nights out with her school friends, Home decor, particularly scrolling Instagram for living room ideas, Following local Facebook groups for Maidstone, mostly to read the arguments, Occasional parkrun
- skills: Managing a small team and setting targets, Negotiating with landlords and tenants, Handling complaints and difficult phone calls, Using property management software (Reapit) and Excel, Spotting a problem tenant early, Organising family logistics around school and work

She uses 'erm' a fair amount, especially when she's thinking, and 'sort of' as a hedge. She tends to end points with 'you know?' or 'yeah'. She says 'dinner' for the evening meal and 'mum'. She'll say she's 'knackered' or 'shattered' and that something 'did my head in'. She gets slightly faster and higher-pitched when anxious. She tends to fill silences herself, often with a nervous little laugh or 'sorry, am I going on?'. If she disagrees she says so fairly bluntly ('no, I don't really agree with that, to be honest').

req.text:
You write transcripts of realistic video calls between strangers for a fully synthetic research dataset set in the UK. The study, in order (from its published design): a short puzzle task done alone; first impressions of the others' webcam photos; then a series of three-minute, one-on-one video calls in rounds, each person meeting the others in their group; after each call a short survey.

Call shape (from the original study's numbers): a call is cut off by a three-minute timer. A typical call has about 30 turns (most between 20 and 39) and about 570 words in total (most between 440 and 682); half of all turns are 12 words or fewer, and a quarter are 24 or more. Short acknowledgements ("yeah", "mm") count as turns too. So aim for about 570 words in about 30 turns: alongside the quick back-and-forth, people often talk in longer stretches (explaining their job, telling a story), and those long turns carry much of the call.

Guide to British conversational English (use it for how people talk; it is a description of speech, not a script):
How British people talk in casual conversation. This is a paraphrase of published descriptions of spoken British English; sources are in SOURCES.md. Use these features lightly and only where they fit the person. Never use them as a caricature.

- **Fillers.** British speakers hesitate with "erm" and "er". Women and younger speakers lean towards "erm".
- **Hedges.** "Sort of" is everywhere and steady. "Kind of" is spreading, and younger speakers use it more.
- **Politeness words.** "Please", "thank you", "thanks" and "sorry" mostly mean what they say. "Sorry" also works as a repair word (to correct yourself, or to ask someone to repeat) and can be ironic.
- **Tags at the end of a sentence.** "You know", "right", "okay", "yeah", "do you know what I mean". Among young Londoners, "innit" and "you get me" are rising. Tags depend on age and region only, never on ethnicity.
- **Echoing.** In an engaged conversation people pick up and re-use parts of each other's words.
- **Regional words and grammar** (from a recent dialect survey):
  - A bread roll is a "barm" in the North West (Manchester to Liverpool and western Lancashire), a "cob" around Nottinghamshire, a "bap" in Staffordshire, the West Midlands and North Wales, and a "batch" in Liverpool and Coventry.
  - Around Liverpool an ice lolly can be a "lolly ice".
  - The evening meal is "tea" in the North West, North East and Yorkshire, and "dinner" in the South East and London. Some people say both.
  - "Yous" or "youse" for plural "you" is common in the North East (Newcastle, Teesside), Liverpool and Scotland, less so in Manchester, and rare in York, Leeds and Sheffield.
  - "Give it me" is normal in the North West and West Midlands and widely accepted in Sheffield and York; it fades south of Birmingham, Coventry and Leicester.
  - "You was" is widely used, historically Northern and now found as far south as London.
- **Everyday British words** to draw on where they fit, without assigning them to regions: knackered or shattered, chuffed or made up, skint or brassic, mardy or stroppy, mum or mam, mate or pal, settee, sofa or couch.

req.text:
You write transcripts of realistic video calls between strangers for a fully synthetic research dataset set in the UK. The study, in order (from its published design): a short puzzle task done alone; first impressions of the others' webcam photos; then a series of three-minute, one-on-one video calls in rounds, each person meeting the others in their group; after each call a short survey.

Call shape (from the original study's numbers): a call is cut off by a three-minute timer. A typical call has about 30 turns (most between 20 and 39) and about 570 words in total (most between 440 and 682); half of all turns are 12 words or fewer, and a quarter are 24 or more. Short acknowledgements ("yeah", "mm") count as turns too. So aim for about 570 words in about 30 turns: alongside the quick back-and-forth, people often talk in longer stretches (explaining their job, telling a story), and those long turns carry much of the call.

Guide to British conversational English (use it for how people talk; it is a description of speech, not a script):
How British people talk in casual conversation. This is a paraphrase of published descriptions of spoken British English; sources are in SOURCES.md. Use these features lightly and only where they fit the person. Never use them as a caricature.

- **Fillers.** British speakers hesitate with "erm" and "er". Women and younger speakers lean towards "erm".
- **Hedges.** "Sort of" is everywhere and steady. "Kind of" is spreading, and younger speakers use it more.
- **Politeness words.** "Please", "thank you", "thanks" and "sorry" mostly mean what they say. "Sorry" also works as a repair word (to correct yourself, or to ask someone to repeat) and can be ironic.
- **Tags at the end of a sentence.** "You know", "right", "okay", "yeah", "do you know what I mean". Among young Londoners, "innit" and "you get me" are rising. Tags depend on age and region only, never on ethnicity.
- **Echoing.** In an engaged conversation people pick up and re-use parts of each other's words.
- **Regional words and grammar** (from a recent dialect survey):
  - A bread roll is a "barm" in the North West (Manchester to Liverpool and western Lancashire), a "cob" around Nottinghamshire, a "bap" in Staffordshire, the West Midlands and North Wales, and a "batch" in Liverpool and Coventry.
  - Around Liverpool an ice lolly can be a "lolly ice".
  - The evening meal is "tea" in the North West, North East and Yorkshire, and "dinner" in the South East and London. Some people say both.
  - "Yous" or "youse" for plural "you" is common in the North East (Newcastle, Teesside), Liverpool and Scotland, less so in Manchester, and rare in York, Leeds and Sheffield.
  - "Give it me" is normal in the North West and West Midlands and widely accepted in Sheffield and York; it fades south of Birmingham, Coventry and Leicester.
  - "You was" is widely used, historically Northern and now found as far south as London.
- **Everyday British words** to draw on where they fit, without assigning them to regions: knackered or shattered, chuffed or made up, skint or brassic, mardy or stroppy, mum or mam, mate or pal, settee, sofa or couch.

You write transcripts of realistic video calls between strangers for a fully synthetic research dataset set in the UK. The study, in order (from its published design): a short puzzle task done alone; first impressions of the others' webcam photos; then a series of three-minute, one-on-one video calls in rounds, each person meeting the others in their group; after each call a short survey.

Call shape (from the original study's numbers): a call is cut off by a three-minute timer. A typical call has about 30 turns (most between 20 and 39) and about 570 words in total (most between 440 and 682); half of all turns are 12 words or fewer, and a quarter are 24 or more. Short acknowledgements ("yeah", "mm") count as turns too. So aim for about 570 words in about 30 turns: alongside the quick back-and-forth, people often talk in longer stretches (explaining their job, telling a story), and those long turns carry much of the call.

Guide to British conversational English (use it for how people talk; it is a description of speech, not a script):
How British people talk in casual conversation. This is a paraphrase of published descriptions of spoken British English; sources are in SOURCES.md. Use these features lightly and only where they fit the person. Never use them as a caricature.

- **Fillers.** British speakers hesitate with "erm" and "er". Women and younger speakers lean towards "erm".
- **Hedges.** "Sort of" is everywhere and steady. "Kind of" is spreading, and younger speakers use it more.
- **Politeness words.** "Please", "thank you", "thanks" and "sorry" mostly mean what they say. "Sorry" also works as a repair word (to correct yourself, or to ask someone to repeat) and can be ironic.
- **Tags at the end of a sentence.** "You know", "right", "okay", "yeah", "do you know what I mean". Among young Londoners, "innit" and "you get me" are rising. Tags depend on age and region only, never on ethnicity.
- **Echoing.** In an engaged conversation people pick up and re-use parts of each other's words.
- **Regional words and grammar** (from a recent dialect survey):
  - A bread roll is a "barm" in the North West (Manchester to Liverpool and western Lancashire), a "cob" around Nottinghamshire, a "bap" in Staffordshire, the West Midlands and North Wales, and a "batch" in Liverpool and Coventry.
  - Around Liverpool an ice lolly can be a "lolly ice".
  - The evening meal is "tea" in the North West, North East and Yorkshire, and "dinner" in the South East and London. Some people say both.
  - "Yous" or "youse" for plural "you" is common in the North East (Newcastle, Teesside), Liverpool and Scotland, less so in Manchester, and rare in York, Leeds and Sheffield.
  - "Give it me" is normal in the North West and West Midlands and widely accepted in Sheffield and York; it fades south of Birmingham, Coventry and Leicester.
  - "You was" is widely used, historically Northern and now found as far south as London.
- **Everyday British words** to draw on where they fit, without assigning them to regions: knackered or shattered, chuffed or made up, skint or brassic, mardy or stroppy, mum or mam, mate or pal, settee, sofa or couch.

req.text:
You write transcripts of realistic video calls between strangers for a fully synthetic research dataset set in the UK. The study, in order (from its published design): a short puzzle task done alone; first impressions of the others' webcam photos; then a series of three-minute, one-on-one video calls in rounds, each person meeting the others in their group; after each call a short survey.

Call shape (from the original study's numbers): a call is cut off by a three-minute timer. A typical call has about 30 turns (most between 20 and 39) and about 570 words in total (most between 440 and 682); half of all turns are 12 words or fewer, and a quarter are 24 or more. Short acknowledgements ("yeah", "mm") count as turns too. So aim for about 570 words in about 30 turns: alongside the quick back-and-forth, people often talk in longer stretches (explaining their job, telling a story), and those long turns carry much of the call.

Guide to British conversational English (use it for how people talk; it is a description of speech, not a script):
How British people talk in casual conversation. This is a paraphrase of published descriptions of spoken British English; sources are in SOURCES.md. Use these features lightly and only where they fit the person. Never use them as a caricature.

- **Fillers.** British speakers hesitate with "erm" and "er". Women and younger speakers lean towards "erm".
- **Hedges.** "Sort of" is everywhere and steady. "Kind of" is spreading, and younger speakers use it more.
- **Politeness words.** "Please", "thank you", "thanks" and "sorry" mostly mean what they say. "Sorry" also works as a repair word (to correct yourself, or to ask someone to repeat) and can be ironic.
- **Tags at the end of a sentence.** "You know", "right", "okay", "yeah", "do you know what I mean". Among young Londoners, "innit" and "you get me" are rising. Tags depend on age and region only, never on ethnicity.
- **Echoing.** In an engaged conversation people pick up and re-use parts of each other's words.
- **Regional words and grammar** (from a recent dialect survey):
  - A bread roll is a "barm" in the North West (Manchester to Liverpool and western Lancashire), a "cob" around Nottinghamshire, a "bap" in Staffordshire, the West Midlands and North Wales, and a "batch" in Liverpool and Coventry.
  - Around Liverpool an ice lolly can be a "lolly ice".
  - The evening meal is "tea" in the North West, North East and Yorkshire, and "dinner" in the South East and London. Some people say both.
  - "Yous" or "youse" for plural "you" is common in the North East (Newcastle, Teesside), Liverpool and Scotland, less so in Manchester, and rare in York, Leeds and Sheffield.
  - "Give it me" is normal in the North West and West Midlands and widely accepted in Sheffield and York; it fades south of Birmingham, Coventry and Leicester.
  - "You was" is widely used, historically Northern and now found as far south as London.
- **Everyday British words** to draw on where they fit, without assigning them to regions: knackered or shattered, chuffed or made up, skint or brassic, mardy or stroppy, mum or mam, mate or pal, settee, sofa or couch.

The group (session S48). Persona cards, including the webcam photo each person was rated on:

P252 (Agnieszka; transcript label: Agnieszka):
- first name: Agnieszka
- age: 45
- lives in: Southampton, South East England
- occupation: Part-time cleaner for a contract cleaning company. She works around 20 hours a week, early mornings and some evenings, cleaning offices and a GP surgery in the city centre.
- education detail: She finished a five-year technical secondary school (technikum) in south-east Poland with a vocational qualification in catering and food technology. She did an evening ESOL course in Southampton in 2007–2008 and has a few cleaning and food hygiene certificates from work. No university.
- household: She lives with her husband Marek (48), a van delivery driver, and their son Kacper (17), who is doing a plumbing course at college. They rent a three-bed terraced house in Shirley. Their older daughter Natalia (21) moved out last year to live with her boyfriend in Eastleigh and still comes for Sunday dinner most weeks.
- cultural background: Born and raised in a small town near Rzeszów in Poland. She came to the UK in 2006, a year after Marek, and has lived in Southampton ever since. She is a practising Catholic and goes to Mass most Sundays at the Polish Catholic mission. At home the family speaks Polish. With Kacper it's a mix, because he answers in English. She feels settled here but still thinks of Poland as 'home' when she talks about her mum. She has pre-settled, now settled, status. She keeps Polish traditions at Christmas and Easter very seriously.
- professional persona: Reliable and thorough. Supervisors know she will do the job properly and turn up on time. She likes a fixed rota and gets anxious when sites are changed at short notice. She is chatty with the reception staff and the other cleaners, and is often the one who remembers birthdays. Her rheumatoid arthritis means she can't do heavy floor machines on bad days, and she worries a lot about letting people down or losing hours because of it.
- sports persona: Not sporty herself. She walks when her joints allow, usually round Southampton Common with a friend from church. She watches ski jumping and volleyball with Marek when Poland is on, and gets very loud and emotional about it. She does gentle exercises the physio gave her, mostly faithfully.
- arts persona: Not interested in galleries, theatre or 'arty' films and would say so honestly. She likes Polish TV series and comedies on streaming, singalong Polish pop and disco polo at family parties, and the hymns at church, where she sings with real enthusiasm. She has never been to a museum in Southampton and sees no reason to.
- travel persona: Every summer she goes back to Poland for two or three weeks to see her mum and sister, usually flying from Luton or Stansted, or occasionally driving across with Marek. She has no real wish to go anywhere else. The one beach holiday in Spain was 'nice, but too hot, and the food, no'. She packs weeks early and checks the passports several times.
- culinary persona: A traditional Polish home cook who cooks most days. Rosół on Sunday, pierogi made in big batches and frozen, gołąbki, schabowy with potatoes and mizeria. She shops at the Polish shop on Shirley High Street and at Lidl. She doesn't trust very spicy food and rarely gets takeaway apart from the odd fish and chips. She calls the evening meal 'dinner' in English.
- hobbies and interests: Cooking for family and church events, Mass and helping with the church coffee morning, Long phone and video calls with her mum and sister, Growing tomatoes, cucumbers and dill in pots in the back garden, Polish TV series and family films, Facebook groups for Poles in Southampton, Baking for Easter and Christmas
- skills: Commercial cleaning to a high standard, Food hygiene and kitchen work, Traditional Polish cooking and baking, Organising family celebrations, Bilingual Polish–English for everyday matters, often helping newer arrivals with forms, Very good at keeping to schedules and routines
- career goals: Mainly to keep her hours and stay well enough to work. She would like to move to a cleaning job with a steady daytime pattern, maybe at a school, so she isn't out early in the cold, which is bad for her hands. No ambition to retrain. Security and the family come first.
- voice: Warm, fast and talkative, with a clear Polish accent and fluent but not always standard English. She sometimes drops articles ('I go to work at six') and occasionally uses Polish word order. She uses 'erm' a lot, 'you know', and a bit of 'sort of'. She has picked up local phrases like 'lovely', 'bless him', 'I'm knackered' and 'sorry, sorry, what was that?' when she hasn't heard. Her voice gets quick and a bit worried if she thinks she's answered wrong. She fills silences herself almost immediately, usually with a story about her family or work, and laughs easily.
- typing: Capital at the start, then mostly lowercase. Short sentences joined with commas, few full stops. Apostrophes often missing ('dont', 'its'). Occasional Polish-influenced spelling or missed article. She uses 'ok' and the odd exclamation mark, and sometimes adds a smiley ':)' at the end. She checks the answer before sending but doesn't fuss over grammar.
- with strangers: Friendly and open almost straight away. She asks how you are and means it, and quickly shares details about her children or her job. She apologises for her English even when it's fine. She can be a bit nervous at first about doing something 'official', and wants to be told clearly what to do. Once she relaxes she talks a lot and is very expressive.
- small things: The early bus in winter is freezing and always late, Kacper never tidies his room, Her tomatoes did really well this year, Making pierogi with Natalia on Saturday, The Polish shop now sells proper bread again, Marek works too many hours with the deliveries, The GP surgery where she cleans is always so busy, Watching the ski jumping on a Sunday
- deeper things: Her rheumatoid arthritis, diagnosed in 2019, which some mornings makes her hands too stiff to hold a cup, and her fear of it getting worse, Worry about her mum, who is in her seventies and alone in Poland since her dad died, Guilt about not being there for her dad's last months, Anxiety that comes in waves, which she has only recently mentioned to her GP, Missing Natalia in the house more than she admits, Feeling that after nearly twenty years she still isn't fully 'from here' or 'from there' any more
- webcam photo: A laptop webcam shot taken at a kitchen table in the evening, slightly from below, so the ceiling light is visible at the top edge and lights her face from above. She is a 45-year-old white woman with shoulder-length dyed dark-blonde hair pulled back in a loose clip, a few strands falling by her face, and light brown roots showing. Round face, light makeup, a little mascara. She is smiling broadly with slightly raised eyebrows, as if mid-greeting. She wears a pale pink fleece zip-up over a grey T-shirt, a small gold cross on a thin chain, and a wedding ring visible as one hand rests near the laptop. No glasses. Behind her are white kitchen wall units, a kettle and a toaster on a worktop, a wall calendar from a Polish shop with notes written on it, a small framed picture of the Virgin Mary on the wall next to the fridge, and fridge magnets including one from Kraków. A tea towel hangs over the oven door handle.

P253 (Liam; transcript label: Liam):
- first name: Liam
- age: 29
- lives in: Wakefield, Yorkshire and The Humber
- occupation: Technical sales executive for a commercial heating, ventilation and air-conditioning supplier based on an industrial estate near Junction 41 of the M1. He manages around 60 trade and contractor accounts across West Yorkshire, quotes for jobs, and is out on site visits two or three days a week.

They are saving for a deposit, though Liam's leased company-upgrade Audi eats into that more than Jess would like.
- cultural background: White British, born and raised in Wakefield. His mum works in a school office. His dad ran a small kitchen-fitting business that went under when Liam was about fourteen, and he now works for a bigger firm. He has an older sister in Leeds. He has no religion and no strong feelings about it. He is very much from a family where you were expected to graft and not make a fuss.
- professional persona: Organised to the point of being teased for it. His CRM is always up to date, he plans his route the night before, and he sends follow-up emails within the hour. He will tell a client what they want to hear if it closes a deal, he enjoys being seen as the top performer, and he is not above nudging his mileage claims a bit.

He took up golf last year, partly because clients play.

He has been to the Hepworth once, when family visited, and found it 'alright, bit odd'. He likes going to gigs at the First Direct Arena for big-name acts.
- travel persona: Two holidays a year, usually somewhere hot and a bit flash: Dubai last year, Marbella the year before. He did a lads' trip to Benidorm at 25 and a Krakow stag do. He likes a nice hotel he can post about and is not fussed about 'proper' culture. He books everything well in advance and keeps a spreadsheet of costs.
- culinary persona: Calls the evening meal tea. He meal-preps chicken, rice and veg on Sundays for work lunches. He likes a steakhouse or a Nando's, and a curry from the local takeaway on Friday. Jess cooks more than he does, but he does a decent Sunday roast and barbecues a lot in summer. He likes a nice bottle of red when out, partly for the look of it.
- hobbies and interests: five-a-side football, gym and fitness tracking, golf (beginner, keen), Leeds United, cars, especially German ones, business and self-improvement podcasts, walking the dog around Pugneys Country Park, watching the Champions League with mates
- skills: building rapport quickly, negotiating on price, planning and scheduling, reading technical spec sheets, Excel and CRM software, remembering names and personal details, staying calm with awkward customers
- career goals: Wants to be area sales manager within two years and earning 'proper money' by 35, ideally with a better car allowance. He has half an eye on moving to a bigger national distributor, and occasionally talks about setting up his own agency one day, though the memory of his dad's business makes him cautious.
- voice: Friendly, chatty and fairly quick, with a light West Yorkshire accent (short 'a' in 'bath', flat vowels) but nothing broad. He uses 'mate' a lot, says 'to be fair' and 'do you know what I mean' as tags, and puts in the odd 'sort of' or 'kind of' when he's thinking. He uses 'erm' only occasionally, because he tends to keep talking rather than pause. He hates dead air and will fill a silence with a joke or a 'yeah, no, definitely'. He echoes the other person's words back to show he is listening, a habit partly picked up from sales training. He sounds warm and slightly polished.
- typing: Tidy for a quick answer: capitals at the start, full stops mostly, apostrophes usually correct. He occasionally uses 'tbh' or 'etc' but otherwise writes in full sentences. He sometimes ends with 'Cheers' out of email habit and rarely makes typos because he rereads before submitting.
- with strangers: Instantly likeable. He is open, asks you questions back, remembers what you said and laughs easily. He comes across as eager to be helpful and keen to make a good impression, maybe a touch salesy. If something might make him look good, he will mention it early: the car, the Dubai trip, being top of the sales board.
- small things: Alfie the dog chewing his work shoes, the traffic on the M62 near Lofthouse, Leeds' latest result, his new driver for golf, hitting his step count, a Wetherspoons in Wakefield town centre, meal-prep Sundays, the car's lease coming up for renewal, Jess's shifts at the dental practice
- deeper things: Watching his dad's business fold and his parents struggle for money, which is why he cares so much about earning well and being seen to be doing alright, Feels some pressure about proposing to Jess, and knows she'd rather they saved than spent on holidays and the car, Admits he sometimes bends the truth with customers and on expenses, and justifies it as 'everyone does it', Worries that if he stopped hitting targets he wouldn't really know who he was, Is a bit competitive with his older sister, who has a better-paid job in Leeds
- webcam photo: Head-and-shoulders shot from a laptop webcam set slightly below eye level, so the angle looks up a little. Bright, slightly cool daylight comes from a window to the left, leaving the right side of his face a touch shadowed. He has a broad, clean-shaven face with a light tan, short brown hair faded at the sides and slightly longer and styled on top, and no glasses. He is smiling with teeth, mid-way through saying something. He wears a navy quarter-zip pullover with a small company logo on the chest, over a white T-shirt. Behind him is a pale grey wall in a spare-room home office. A white flat-pack shelving unit holds a few box files, a Leeds United mug and a framed photo of him and a woman on a beach. The edge of a golf bag shows in the corner, and a ring light, switched off, stands to the right.

She has light brown skin and long dark brown hair worn down, middle parting, ends lightly curled. She's wearing full but natural-looking makeup: groomed brows, winged eyeliner, nude lip. Behind her: the corner of a small living room with magnolia walls, an unmade grey fabric sofa with a pink throw bunched on it, a white IKEA shelf holding a pot plant that's seen better days, some perfume boxes and a framed photo of her and Josh. A clothes airer with jeans and tops on it is partly visible at the right edge.

You write transcripts of realistic video calls between strangers for a fully synthetic research dataset set in the UK. The study, in order (from its published design): a short puzzle task done alone; first impressions of the others' webcam photos; then a series of three-minute, one-on-one video calls in rounds, each person meeting the others in their group; after each call a short survey.

Call shape (from the original study's numbers): a call is cut off by a three-minute timer. A typical call has about 30 turns (most between 20 and 39) and about 570 words in total (most between 440 and 682); half of all turns are 12 words or fewer, and a quarter are 24 or more. Short acknowledgements ("yeah", "mm") count as turns too. So aim for about 570 words in about 30 turns: alongside the quick back-and-forth, people often talk in longer stretches (explaining their job, telling a story), and those long turns carry much of the call.

Guide to British conversational English (use it for how people talk; it is a description of speech, not a script):
How British people talk in casual conversation. This is a paraphrase of published descriptions of spoken British English; sources are in SOURCES.md. Use these features lightly and only where they fit the person. Never use them as a caricature.

- **Fillers.** British speakers hesitate with "erm" and "er". Women and younger speakers lean towards "erm".
- **Hedges.** "Sort of" is everywhere and steady. "Kind of" is spreading, and younger speakers use it more.
- **Politeness words.** "Please", "thank you", "thanks" and "sorry" mostly mean what they say. "Sorry" also works as a repair word (to correct yourself, or to ask someone to repeat) and can be ironic.
- **Tags at the end of a sentence.** "You know", "right", "okay", "yeah", "do you know what I mean". Among young Londoners, "innit" and "you get me" are rising. Tags depend on age and region only, never on ethnicity.
- **Echoing.** In an engaged conversation people pick up and re-use parts of each other's words.
- **Regional words and grammar** (from a recent dialect survey):
  - A bread roll is a "barm" in the North West (Manchester to Liverpool and western Lancashire), a "cob" around Nottinghamshire, a "bap" in Staffordshire, the West Midlands and North Wales, and a "batch" in Liverpool and Coventry.
  - Around Liverpool an ice lolly can be a "lolly ice".
  - The evening meal is "tea" in the North West, North East and Yorkshire, and "dinner" in the South East and London. Some people say both.
  - "Yous" or "youse" for plural "you" is common in the North East (Newcastle, Teesside), Liverpool and Scotland, less so in Manchester, and rare in York, Leeds and Sheffield.
  - "Give it me" is normal in the North West and West Midlands and widely accepted in Sheffield and York; it fades south of Birmingham, Coventry and Leicester.
  - "You was" is widely used, historically Northern and now found as far south as London.
- **Everyday British words** to draw on where they fit, without assigning them to regions: knackered or shattered, chuffed or made up, skint or brassic, mardy or stroppy, mum or mam, mate or pal, settee, sofa or couch.

req.text:
You write transcripts of realistic video calls between strangers for a fully synthetic research dataset set in the UK. The study, in order (from its published design): a short puzzle task done alone; first impressions of the others' webcam photos; then a series of three-minute, one-on-one video calls in rounds, each person meeting the others in their group; after each call a short survey.

Call shape (from the original study's numbers): a call is cut off by a three-minute timer. A typical call has about 30 turns (most between 20 and 39) and about 570 words in total (most between 440 and 682); half of all turns are 12 words or fewer, and a quarter are 24 or more. Short acknowledgements ("yeah", "mm") count as turns too. So aim for about 570 words in about 30 turns: alongside the quick back-and-forth, people often talk in longer stretches (explaining their job, telling a story), and those long turns carry much of the call.

Guide to British conversational English (use it for how people talk; it is a description of speech, not a script):
How British people talk in casual conversation. This is a paraphrase of published descriptions of spoken British English; sources are in SOURCES.md. Use these features lightly and only where they fit the person. Never use them as a caricature.

- **Fillers.** British speakers hesitate with "erm" and "er". Women and younger speakers lean towards "erm".
- **Hedges.** "Sort of" is everywhere and steady. "Kind of" is spreading, and younger speakers use it more.
- **Politeness words.** "Please", "thank you", "thanks" and "sorry" mostly mean what they say. "Sorry" also works as a repair word (to correct yourself, or to ask someone to repeat) and can be ironic.
- **Tags at the end of a sentence.** "You know", "right", "okay", "yeah", "do you know what I mean". Among young Londoners, "innit" and "you get me" are rising. Tags depend on age and region only, never on ethnicity.
- **Echoing.** In an engaged conversation people pick up and re-use parts of each other's words.
- **Regional words and grammar** (from a recent dialect survey):
  - A bread roll is a "barm" in the North West (Manchester to Liverpool and western Lancashire), a "cob" around Nottinghamshire, a "bap" in Staffordshire, the West Midlands and North Wales, and a "batch" in Liverpool and Coventry.
  - Around Liverpool an ice lolly can be a "lolly ice".
  - The evening meal is "tea" in the North West, North East and Yorkshire, and "dinner" in the South East and London. Some people say both.
  - "Yous" or "youse" for plural "you" is common in the North East (Newcastle, Teesside), Liverpool and Scotland, less so in Manchester, and rare in York, Leeds and Sheffield.
  - "Give it me" is normal in the North West and West Midlands and widely accepted in Sheffield and York; it fades south of Birmingham, Coventry and Leicester.
  - "You was" is widely used, historically Northern and now found as far south as London.
- **Everyday British words** to draw on where they fit, without assigning them to regions: knackered or shattered, chuffed or made up, skint or brassic, mardy or stroppy, mum or mam, mate or pal, settee, sofa or couch.
