Joanne comes across as flattering while sizing Liam up, who works in car sales with a partner named Jess, and I'm weaving in local details like Gary's van failing its MOT and traffic at the Bridge Foot roundabout, along with dialect words like "barm," "tea," "made up," and "dead" while being careful to avoid caricature. Now I'm starting on the first call.

req.text:
You write transcripts of realistic video calls between strangers for a fully synthetic research dataset set in the UK. The study, in order (from its published design): a short puzzle task done alone; first impressions of the others' webcam photos; then a series of three-minute, one-on-one video calls in rounds, each person meeting the others in their group; after each call a short survey.

Call shape (from the original study's numbers): a call is cut off by a three-minute timer. A typical call has about 30 turns (most between 20 and 39) and about 570 words in total (most between 440 and 682); half of all turns are 12 words or fewer, and a quarter are 24 or more. Short acknowledgements ("yeah", "mm") count as turns too. So aim for about 570 words in about 30 turns: alongside the quick back-and-forth, people often talk in longer stretches (explaining their job, telling a story), and those long turns carry much of the call.

Guide to British conversational English (use it for how people talk; it is a description of speech, not a script):
How British people talk in casual conversation. This is a paraphrase of published descriptions of spoken British English; sources are in SOURCES.md. Use these features lightly and only where they fit the person. Never use them as a caricature.

- **Fillers.** British speakers hesitate with "erm" and "er". Women and younger speakers lean towards "erm".
- **Hedges.** "Sort of" is everywhere and steady. "Kind of" is spreading, and younger speakers use it more.
- **Politeness words.** "Please", "thank you", "thanks" and "sorry" mostly mean what they say. "Sorry" also works as a repair word (to correct yourself, or to ask someone to repeat) and can be ironic.
- **Tags at the end of a sentence.** "You know", "right", "okay", "yeah", "do you know what I mean". Among young Londoners, "innit" and "you get me" are rising. Tags depend on age and region only, never on ethnicity.
- **Echoing.** In an engaged conversation people pick up and re-use parts of each other's words.
- **Regional words and grammar** (from a recent dialect survey):
  - A bread roll is a "barm" in the North West (Manchester to Liverpool and western Lancashire), a "cob" around Nottinghamshire, a "bap" in Staffordshire, the West Midlands and North Wales, and a "batch" in Liverpool and Coventry.
  - Around Liverpool an ice lolly can be a "lolly ice".
  - The evening meal is "tea" in the North West, North East and Yorkshire, and "dinner" in the South East and London. Some people say both.
  - "Yous" or "youse" for plural "you" is common in the North East (Newcastle, Teesside), Liverpool and Scotland, less so in Manchester, and rare in York, Leeds and Sheffield.
  - "Give it me" is normal in the North West and West Midlands and widely accepted in Sheffield and York; it fades south of Birmingham, Coventry and Leicester.
  - "You was" is widely used, historically Northern and now found as far south as London.
- **Everyday British words** to draw on where they fit, without assigning them to regions: knackered or shattered, chuffed or made up, skint or brassic, mardy or stroppy, mum or mam, mate or pal, settee, sofa or couch.

The group (session S53). Persona cards, including the webcam photo each person was rated on:

P277 (Graham; transcript label: Graham):
- first name: Graham
- age: 70
- lives in: Newark-on-Trent, East Midlands
- occupation: Solicitor and senior partner in a small high-street firm (wills, probate and residential conveyancing), still working full-time
- education detail: Grammar school in Grantham, then an LLB at the University of Sheffield (graduated 1976), followed by the Law Society Finals at the College of Law in Chester and articles with a Lincoln firm. Has done the required continuing professional development ever since, usually at the last possible moment.
- household: Lives with his wife Linda (68, a retired primary school teacher) in a detached 1970s house on the edge of town. Their two grown-up children live away, a son in Leeds and a daughter in Northampton, and there are three grandchildren. No pets since the old Labrador died two years ago.
- cultural background: White British, born and raised in Lincolnshire, and has lived in Nottinghamshire for over forty years. Church of England, and goes to the parish church most Sundays because Linda does and because he likes the people, though he wouldn't call himself devout. A middle-class professional of the sort known by half the town because he did their parents' wills.
- professional persona: Took over as senior partner when the founding partner retired, mostly because nobody else wanted it. Clients find him warm, patient and reassuring, and he's very good with bereaved families. He is also chronically behind. His desk is buried in files, he forgets to return calls, and he relies heavily on his long-serving secretary, Janet, and a younger associate to keep deadlines from slipping. He keeps meaning to retire but hasn't sorted out the succession, and full-time hours suit him better than he lets on.
- sports persona: Follows Nottingham Forest without much fuss: watches on telly, goes to the odd match with his son-in-law. Used to play cricket for a village side and now watches Test matches on the radio at work. Plays a slow, sociable round of golf now and then, and his handicap has drifted upwards for years.
- arts persona: Not really an arts person. He'll watch a costume drama if Linda puts it on and enjoys the carol service at Christmas, but galleries leave him cold. Likes brass band music and the sort of seventies rock he grew up with. Reads thrillers on holiday and rarely finishes one otherwise.
- travel persona: Creature of habit. They've gone to the same part of the Norfolk coast most summers for thirty years, plus a week somewhere warm in Spain or Portugal in autumn. Has no appetite for long-haul or adventure trips and gets mildly fretful at airports, mainly because he's usually forgotten something.
- culinary persona: Traditional tastes: Sunday roast, fish and chips on a Friday, a ham cob from the bakery at lunchtime. Linda does most of the cooking, and Graham does the barbecue in summer, badly but enthusiastically. Likes a pint of bitter at the pub and a glass of red with his tea, and is wary of anything too spicy.
- hobbies and interests: Pottering in the garden without much of a plan, Watching Forest and the cricket, Occasional golf with old friends, Quiz nights at the local pub, Seeing the grandchildren, Helping with the church fete, usually the tombola
- skills: Putting anxious or grieving people at ease, Explaining legal processes in plain English, Drafting wills and handling probate, Remembering family histories across generations of clients, Smoothing over disagreements in the office or the family
- career goals: Mostly to find someone to take over the firm so he can wind down to three days a week, which he has been saying for about five years. No ambitions beyond that. He'd like to leave the practice in decent hands and not let his clients down.
- voice: Unhurried, friendly, slightly rambling. A mild East Midlands accent, softened by years of professional life, so it shows mostly in the vowels and the odd 'duck' to someone he's warmed to. Says 'tea' for the evening meal and 'cob' for a bread roll without thinking about it. Hesitates with 'er' quite a lot and uses 'sort of' and 'you know' as padding. Polite to a fault, with plenty of 'sorry' and 'thank you'. He often loses his thread mid-answer ('where was I, sorry'). He's comfortable with silence and tends to fill it with a gentle anecdote rather than awkwardness.
- typing: Types with two fingers and doesn't proofread. Starts sentences with capitals most of the time but drops them partway through. Uses full stops and occasional commas, and often leaves out apostrophes ('dont', 'its'). Typos stay in. Answers are short and a bit vague, and he sometimes trails off with '...'. No text-speak, apart from the odd 'etc'.
- with strangers: Comes across as kindly, easy-going and a little disorganised: late joining, apologetic about it, then perfectly pleasant. Agrees readily and gives people the benefit of the doubt. Doesn't push his opinions, and he's more interested in being agreeable than in being precise.
- small things: The traffic on the A46, Forest's latest result, That the bakery's run out of cheese cobs again, The weather spoiling his golf, Janet having to find a file he swore he'd put back, The grandchildren's school plays, Needing to sort the guttering
- deeper things: Worries that he's let the firm drift and that it won't survive him, Quietly dreads retirement because he doesn't know who he'd be without the work, Lost his younger brother to a heart attack ten years ago and thinks about it more than he says, Knows Linda carries a lot of the household organisation and feels a bit guilty about it, Finds church comforting more for the community than for belief, and isn't sure what he thinks about God
- webcam photo: A slightly low-angled shot from a laptop on a desk, so the top of his head is close to the frame edge. Soft daylight comes from a window to his left, leaving the right side of his face a little shadowed. A 70-year-old man with a round, ruddy face, thinning grey hair combed back, and a short neat grey moustache. He's half-smiling, as if mid-apology. He wears reading glasses pushed slightly down his nose, a pale blue checked shirt open at the collar, and a navy V-neck jumper. Behind him is a cluttered home study: a bookcase with law reference books, some lying sideways, and a framed graduation photo. Stacks of manila files sit on top of a filing cabinet, a Nottingham Forest mug holds pens, and a wall calendar from a local garage is still turned to last month.

P278 (Alison; transcript label: Alison):
- first name: Alison
- age: 55
- lives in: Chester-le-Street, North East England
- occupation: Not currently in paid work. Spent about twenty years as an administrator, most recently in the office of a primary school in Durham. Left two years ago and hasn't gone back.
- education detail: Left a local comprehensive at 16 with O-levels and GCSEs (her year was the changeover). Did an RSA typing and office skills course at the tech college, and an NVQ Level 2 in Business Administration through work in her thirties.
- household: Lives with her husband Steve (57), a maintenance electrician at a manufacturing site near Washington, in a three-bed semi they've owned since the late nineties. Their two grown-up children have moved out. Their daughter is in Newcastle and their son is in Leeds. There's an elderly cat called Biscuit.
- cultural background: Born and raised in County Durham. Her dad was in the pits until the closures, then drove for a builders' merchant, and her mam worked in a school kitchen. She was brought up Methodist and still goes to the local chapel most Sundays, though she's quiet about it. She values family, neighbours and not getting above yourself.
- professional persona: A reliable, unshowy office person who liked being the one who knew where everything was. She was good with anxious parents on the phone. She never wanted to manage anyone. She left when the school merged its office into a trust-wide team, the job became mostly screens and targets, and she found it stressful. Steve's wage covers them, and she's said she 'might do something part-time eventually'.
- sports persona: Not sporty. She walks most days, often along the riverside by the cricket ground or round Lambton way. She half-follows Sunderland because Steve does and will ask the score. She did a couple of gentle swimming sessions a week for a while and keeps meaning to go back.
- arts persona: Likes a good TV drama, especially period pieces and gentle crime. She reads library paperbacks, mostly family sagas and the odd Catherine Cookson re-read. She sings in the chapel's small choir at Christmas and Easter but would never do a solo.
- travel persona: Prefers familiar places. They take a caravan week in Northumberland most summers, near Beadnell. They've done a few package holidays to Spain and one cruise for their 25th anniversary, which she enjoyed more than she expected. She gets nervous about flying and airports and likes to be there very early.
- culinary persona: Plain, home-cooked food. Tea is on the table about half five: mince and dumplings, a roast on Sundays, stotties from the bakery on a Saturday. She bakes for chapel coffee mornings, mostly scones, tray bakes and a lemon drizzle she's known for. She doesn't really go in for spicy food but will have a mild curry on a Friday.
- hobbies and interests: Daily walks, sometimes with a neighbour, Baking for chapel events and family, Knitting baby cardigans for the hospital and for friends' grandchildren, Gardening, mainly the front borders and a few tomato plants, Watching TV dramas with Steve in the evenings, Doing word searches and the crossword in the local paper
- skills: Accurate typing and data entry, Organising paperwork, rotas and diaries, Calming down upset people on the phone, Baking and plain cooking, Knitting, Basic Word, Excel and email
- career goals: No strong ambitions. She'd consider a few mornings a week in a quiet office, a GP surgery or a charity shop if the right thing came up, but doesn't want the pressure she had before. Mostly she wants to be useful, help her daughter if grandchildren come along, and keep well.
- voice: Soft, fairly quiet and unhurried, with a gentle County Durham accent. Her vowels are local but she isn't broad, and she smooths it a bit with strangers. She says 'erm' a lot when thinking and uses 'sort of' to soften opinions. Family words slip in naturally: 'me mam', 'our Laura', 'having me tea'. She'd say 'are yous both on?' if there were two researchers. She apologises easily ('sorry, I've gone off on one there'). Silences make her a bit uneasy, so she fills them with 'I don't know if that's what you're after' or a small laugh. She answers honestly, even when the answer is a bit dull, and won't exaggerate to sound interesting.
- typing: Mostly proper sentences with a capital at the start and a full stop, though she sometimes forgets the capital on short answers. Apostrophes are usually right. She doesn't use text-speak beyond the odd 'ok'. Answers are short and literal, sometimes with a polite add-on like 'hope that helps'. She types slowly and occasionally leaves a double space or a small typo she doesn't go back for.
- with strangers: Polite, warm but reserved, a little nervous at first. She worries about saying the wrong thing or not being 'what they wanted'. She doesn't talk herself up and will play down anything she's good at. She warms up if the other person is friendly and patient, and then she can be quite chatty about family and local things. She would never try to bluff an answer.
- small things: Biscuit the cat being fussy about his food, The weather ruining her washing, Needing to get to the bakery before the stotties go, A programme she and Steve are watching, The bus into Durham being late again, Making a tray bake for the chapel coffee morning
- deeper things: Leaving her job left her feeling a bit lost and less useful, and she sometimes wonders if she gave up too easily, She worries a lot about her son in Leeds, who had a hard time with his mental health a few years ago, Her mam died three years ago and she still finds Sundays hard, Her faith is quiet but real, and she prays when she's anxious, She'd love to be a grandma but tries not to put pressure on her daughter, She feels her dad's generation and the area were let down when the pits closed
- webcam photo: Head-and-shoulders shot from a laptop on a dining table, angled slightly upwards so the ceiling's edge is visible. Daylight from a window to her left lights one side of her face more than the other. She has shoulder-length, ash-blonde hair with grey coming through at the roots, tucked behind one ear. She wears thin silver-framed reading glasses and has a slightly uncertain, polite half-smile. She has a fair complexion with fine lines around her eyes and wears a navy cardigan over a pale pink top, with a small gold cross on a chain. Behind her is a magnolia wall with a framed family photo of a wedding group, a wooden clock, and a corner of a glass-fronted cabinet holding some ornaments and a stack of placemats. The arm of a beige settee is just visible in the right edge of the frame.

P279 (Callum; transcript label: Callum):
- first name: Callum
- age: 18
- lives in: Basingstoke, South East England
- occupation: Part-time sales assistant at a sports and trainer shop in the town centre shopping centre, working Saturday shifts and the odd Sunday, usually 10 to 14 hours a week
- education detail: In the second year of A-levels at a sixth form college in Basingstoke, studying Business, Economics and PE. GCSEs were mostly 6s and 7s, with a 5 in English that he still thinks was marked harshly.
- household: Lives in a three-bed semi on an estate on the edge of town with his mum and dad, who have been married about 22 years, and his 14-year-old sister. His dad is a site supervisor for a facilities management firm and his mum is an office manager at a dental practice. He has the box room and wants the bigger one, which his sister has.
- cultural background: White British, born and raised in Basingstoke, with grandparents in Reading and Andover. The family isn't religious and he's never thought about it much. He left the religion question blank because he didn't see why it was anyone's business. His upbringing was standard suburban South East: Sunday roasts at his nan's, holidays in Spain, his dad's football on the telly.
- professional persona: He's good on the shop floor when there's a sale to be made and noticeably less keen when there isn't. He knows the stock well, upsells socks and protection spray because it helps the store's numbers and gets him noticed, and isn't above telling a customer something 'runs small' to shift a size. He gets short with customers he thinks are wasting his time and has had a word from his manager about his tone more than once. He thinks he should be a supervisor already.
- sports persona: Played Sunday league football until he was 16 and stopped after falling out with the coach over playing time. He still plays five-a-side on Wednesday nights with lads from college and goes to the gym four times a week, mostly upper body. He supports Arsenal like his dad, but mostly through FIFA/EA FC and arguing about it in group chats.
- arts persona: Not much. He listens to UK rap and some drill on Spotify, watches a lot of YouTube (football content, finance and 'side hustle' channels, gym videos) and the occasional Netflix crime series. He thinks most art is pretentious and says so.
- travel persona: Family holidays to Tenerife and the Costa del Sol. He went to Magaluf for a week with mates in the summer after his GCSEs, lying about his age a bit. He wants to do Dubai at some point because it looks like money. He's never been further than Spain and isn't bothered about 'culture' trips.
- culinary persona: Eats a lot of chicken and rice for the gym and tracks protein on an app, then undoes it with a Nando's or a McDonald's after five-a-side. His mum cooks dinner most nights and he'll complain if it's something he doesn't like. He can do pasta, eggs and a stir fry. He drinks energy drinks more than he should.
- hobbies and interests: Gym and lifting, Five-a-side football, Reselling trainers bought with his staff discount or on release days, EA FC and Call of Duty online with mates, Watching finance and crypto YouTube, Learning to drive (he's failed his test once and blames the examiner)
- skills: Selling and upselling on the shop floor, Spotting fake trainers and pricing resale stock, Handling a till, returns and stock checks, Basic spreadsheets from Business A-level, Quick mental maths for margins and discounts
- career goals: Wants to get on a business or finance degree apprenticeship, ideally at a bank or a big company in London or Reading, rather than go to uni and 'pay nine grand to sit in a room'. Longer term he talks about running his own reselling or clothing business and earning more than his dad by 25. He's vague on the details but confident about the outcome.
- voice: Southern English with a fairly neutral Hampshire accent, slightly flattened by London-ish youth speech, with some glottal stops. He talks quickly, says 'like' and 'kind of' a lot and sometimes 'to be fair'. He uses 'erm' when he's actually thinking, which isn't often. Tags such as 'yeah', 'you know' and an occasional 'innit' are habit and not performance. He calls the evening meal dinner. Answers are short and a bit flat unless the topic is money, football or something he has an opinion on, and then he'll talk over you. He doesn't fill silences for your benefit. He'll just wait, or say 'is that it?' or 'what was the question, sorry?' He can sound bored or dismissive without quite meaning to.
- typing: All lowercase, little or no punctuation, no full stops at the end of answers. Apostrophes are mostly dropped (dont, im, its). He uses 'idk', 'tbh', 'ngl' and 'dunno'. Answers are as short as the form allows, often a few words. He'll write 'n/a' or 'not sure' to skip anything that looks like effort, and occasionally puts in something sarcastic if a question annoys him.
- with strangers: Guarded and slightly cocky at first. He answers what he's asked without warmth and doesn't ask anything back. He can come across as rude, mainly because he doesn't soften anything and openly treats a question as pointless if he thinks it is. He warms up a bit if you let him talk about something he knows, and gets competitive or argumentative if he feels talked down to. He's polite in a basic way ('yeah, thanks') but clearly mostly there for the payment.
- small things: He's doing the study for the panel money and is putting it towards driving lessons, Saturday shifts are dead until about eleven and then it's chaos, He thinks the new Arsenal kit is overpriced but will still buy it, His sister uses all the hot water in the mornings, He's on a bulk and trying to get up to 80 kilos, A pair of trainers he bought on release went for nearly double on resale, Wednesday five-a-side games always end in an argument about whether something was a foul
- deeper things: He's more worried about his A-level grades than he lets on, especially Economics, and his parents keep comparing him to his cousin who went to Exeter, He felt properly gutted when he got dropped from the football team and quitting was partly to save face, He gets annoyed at his dad for 'settling' but also wants his approval more than anyone's, He knows people at work and college think he's arrogant and tells himself he doesn't care, He has a few hundred quid in crypto that's down and hasn't told anyone
- webcam photo: Laptop webcam at desk height, angled slightly upwards, framing his head and shoulders a little off-centre to the left. The room is lit mainly by a blue LED strip along the top of the wall behind him and a ceiling light, which gives his face a slightly cool, flat cast. He's pale with a few spots on his chin and short dark-brown hair in a skin fade with a slightly longer textured fringe pushed forward. He has no glasses, light stubble on his upper lip, and a neutral, faintly bored expression with his mouth closed and eyebrows a bit raised as if waiting for something to start. He's wearing a plain black Nike hoodie with the hood down and a thin silver chain just visible at the neckline. Behind him is a white wall with a small framed Arsenal shirt, the back of a black and red gaming chair, a stack of five or six orange and black trainer boxes against the wall, a single bed with a grey duvet pushed to one side, and a pair of wireless headphones hanging on the corner of a shelf.

P280 (Joanne; transcript label: Joanne):
- first name: Joanne
- age: 45
- lives in: Taunton, South West England
- occupation: Customer service team leader at a home insurance contact centre on a business park on the edge of Taunton. She supervises a team of eleven call handlers, works full-time (about 37.5 hours, with one late shift a week), and still takes escalated calls herself.
- education detail: Went to a comprehensive in Taunton and left after GCSEs, with a C in maths she is quietly proud of. Did a BTEC First in Business at Somerset College, then went straight into work. Since then she has picked up an in-house Level 3 Team Leading qualification and an FCA-related customer treatment course through her employer.
- household: Lives in a three-bed ex-council semi in the Priorswood area with her daughter Ellie (15, doing GCSEs) and son Callum (12). Her ex-husband Darren lives in Bridgwater and has the kids every other weekend. They divorced six years ago. There is an elderly Jack Russell called Pip, who was Darren's idea but is now very much Joanne's.
- cultural background: White British, born and raised in Somerset. Her mum still lives in Wellington and her dad, a retired lorry driver, died four years ago. She was brought up loosely Church of England but doesn't believe in anything in particular now, and only goes to church for weddings and funerals. Her family is ordinary working Somerset: a sister in Minehead, cousins all over the county, and Sunday dinners at her mum's when the kids aren't at their dad's.
- professional persona: Steady, fair and trusted. She has been with the same company for fourteen years, joining as a call handler and getting promoted to team leader after eight. Her team like her because she doesn't play favourites and owns up when she's got something wrong. She hates the targets side of the job and worries about staff who are struggling, sometimes more than she should. She is good at calming down angry customers because she genuinely listens. She is not one for office politics, and she turned down a move to the Bristol site because of the kids.
- sports persona: Not sporty as such. She walks Pip every morning before work round the local fields and along the canal towpath at weekends. She played netball at school and did a Couch to 5K a few years back, then let it slide. She watches the odd England football match and Wimbledon, and goes to a Somerset cricket match once a year because her brother-in-law gets tickets.
- arts persona: Not really an arts person, and she'd say so. She likes a good crime drama on telly, Vera and Happy Valley especially, plus Strictly on Saturday nights with Ellie. Her music is mostly what she grew up with: Take That, Robbie Williams, Westlife on long drives. She goes to the pantomime at the Brewhouse with the kids most Christmases. She reads the odd paperback on holiday, usually something her sister has passed on.
- travel persona: Prefers somewhere familiar. Most summers it's a static caravan at a holiday park in Cornwall, near St Ives or Newquay, same week every year. She has been abroad a handful of times: Tenerife twice, and a girls' weekend in Benidorm for her friend's fortieth. She gets anxious about flying and about the kids getting lost. She'd like to take them to Spain once more before Ellie decides she's too old for family holidays.
- culinary persona: Plain, reliable home cooking on a budget. She does a weekly shop at Asda or Aldi and batch cooks spag bol, chilli and shepherd's pie. Fridays are a chippy tea from the place round the corner, which she calls 'dinner' or 'tea' depending on mood. She does a proper roast when it's her weekend with the kids. She isn't adventurous: she'll try a curry but sticks to a korma. Her guilty pleasure is a cream tea, jam first, which she'll defend.
- hobbies and interests: Walking the dog, Watching crime dramas and Strictly, Car boot sales on Sunday mornings, Doing the garden, mainly hanging baskets and pots, Quiz night at the local pub once a month with two friends from work, Word puzzles and Wordle
- skills: De-escalating difficult phone calls, Coaching and supporting new staff, Budgeting a household on one income, Organising rotas and shift cover, Reading people's moods quickly, Basic Excel and the company CRM systems
- career goals: Mostly wants security rather than climbing. She'd consider an operations manager role if one came up in Taunton, but not if it meant more hours away from the kids while they're still at school. She would quite like to move into the training and quality side eventually, because she enjoys helping new starters find their feet. Her main goal is paying off the mortgage and being there for Ellie's exams.
- voice: Warm, friendly and fairly quick once she relaxes. She has a soft Somerset accent with a slight rounded 'r', but uses no heavy dialect words, maybe the odd 'proper' as in 'proper knackered'. She says 'erm' a lot when thinking and uses 'sort of' as a softener. She ends points with 'you know?' or 'yeah'. She apologises a lot ('sorry, I'm waffling') and says 'sorry, what was that?' if she mishears. She will openly say 'I don't really know, to be honest' rather than bluff. Silence makes her a bit uneasy, so she tends to fill it, then catches herself and laughs. She tends to repeat back the interviewer's words when agreeing ('yeah, the cost of living, that's it exactly').
- typing: Mostly lowercase in quick answers, but capitalises names and the start of the first sentence out of habit from work emails. She uses apostrophes properly most of the time. Uses commas loosely and the occasional '...' when trailing off. Abbreviations are minimal, mainly 'tbh' and 'x' if it feels informal. She double-checks spelling if it's anything official. Example: 'Its been ok, bit stressful with work tbh but kids are good'.
- with strangers: Pleasant, a bit cautious at first, and very polite. She warms up quickly if the other person is friendly. She is modest to the point of underselling herself and quick to say she's 'nothing special'. She is honest even when it's not flattering to her, and she might get a little emotional if the conversation touches on her kids or her dad.
- small things: Pip the dog snoring under the table, Ellie's GCSE mocks coming up, The A358 roadworks making her late, Fuel prices, Strictly results from the weekend, Finding a good bargain at the car boot, The weather ruining her washing, Callum wanting a new games console
- deeper things: Still finds it hard being a single parent and feels guilty about working full time, Misses her dad a lot and sometimes gets upset at little reminders like his favourite songs, Worries about money even though she manages fine, Felt she lost a lot of confidence during her marriage and is slowly rebuilding it, Anxious about Ellie growing up and going off one day, Sometimes lonely in the evenings once the kids have gone to bed
- webcam photo: A laptop webcam shot taken at a kitchen table in the early evening, angled slightly upward so her chin is a little prominent. She is centre-left in frame, from the shoulders up, lit by a warm overhead ceiling light with some cooler daylight coming from a window to her right. She has a round, friendly face with a slightly tired smile and faint lines around the eyes, and she wears no glasses. Her shoulder-length dark blonde hair, with darker roots growing out, is pulled back loosely with a claw clip and has a few strands loose. She wears a navy fleece zipped halfway over a grey T-shirt. Behind her are white kitchen cupboards, a kettle and a toaster on the worktop, a calendar stuck to the fridge with magnets and a school letter, a hanging tea towel with a Cornish lighthouse print, and the edge of a dog bed visible on the floor in the corner.

Their first impressions of each other's photos (private):
Graham on Alison's photo: likable 6/7, friendly 6/7, would pair: yes; gut: reminds me quite a lot of linda actually, looks like a very nice lady who does her fair share for the parish etc.
Graham on Callum's photo: likable 3/7, friendly 3/7, would pair: no; gut: looks a bit like my grandson when he cant get the internet to work, bit grumpy but probably just needs a proper tea.
Graham on Joanne's photo: likable 6/7, friendly 6/7, would pair: yes; gut: very friendly sort of face, looks like shes busy with the family and the dog... salt of the earth type.

You write transcripts of realistic video calls between strangers for a fully synthetic research dataset set in the UK. The study, in order (from its published design): a short puzzle task done alone; first impressions of the others' webcam photos; then a series of three-minute, one-on-one video calls in rounds, each person meeting the others in their group; after each call a short survey.

Call shape (from the original study's numbers): a call is cut off by a three-minute timer. A typical call has about 30 turns (most between 20 and 39) and about 570 words in total (most between 440 and 682); half of all turns are 12 words or fewer, and a quarter are 24 or more. Short acknowledgements ("yeah", "mm") count as turns too. So aim for about 570 words in about 30 turns: alongside the quick back-and-forth, people often talk in longer stretches (explaining their job, telling a story), and those long turns carry much of the call.

Guide to British conversational English (use it for how people talk; it is a description of speech, not a script):
How British people talk in casual conversation. This is a paraphrase of published descriptions of spoken British English; sources are in SOURCES.md. Use these features lightly and only where they fit the person. Never use them as a caricature.

- **Fillers.** British speakers hesitate with "erm" and "er". Women and younger speakers lean towards "erm".
- **Hedges.** "Sort of" is everywhere and steady. "Kind of" is spreading, and younger speakers use it more.
- **Politeness words.** "Please", "thank you", "thanks" and "sorry" mostly mean what they say. "Sorry" also works as a repair word (to correct yourself, or to ask someone to repeat) and can be ironic.
- **Tags at the end of a sentence.** "You know", "right", "okay", "yeah", "do you know what I mean". Among young Londoners, "innit" and "you get me" are rising. Tags depend on age and region only, never on ethnicity.
- **Echoing.** In an engaged conversation people pick up and re-use parts of each other's words.
- **Regional words and grammar** (from a recent dialect survey):
  - A bread roll is a "barm" in the North West (Manchester to Liverpool and western Lancashire), a "cob" around Nottinghamshire, a "bap" in Staffordshire, the West Midlands and North Wales, and a "batch" in Liverpool and Coventry.
  - Around Liverpool an ice lolly can be a "lolly ice".
  - The evening meal is "tea" in the North West, North East and Yorkshire, and "dinner" in the South East and London. Some people say both.
  - "Yous" or "youse" for plural "you" is common in the North East (Newcastle, Teesside), Liverpool and Scotland, less so in Manchester, and rare in York, Leeds and Sheffield.
  - "Give it me" is normal in the North West and West Midlands and widely accepted in Sheffield and York; it fades south of Birmingham, Coventry and Leicester.
  - "You was" is widely used, historically Northern and now found as far south as London.
- **Everyday British words** to draw on where they fit, without assigning them to regions: knackered or shattered, chuffed or made up, skint or brassic, mardy or stroppy, mum or mam, mate or pal, settee, sofa or couch.

req.text:
You write transcripts of realistic video calls between strangers for a fully synthetic research dataset set in the UK. The study, in order (from its published design): a short puzzle task done alone; first impressions of the others' webcam photos; then a series of three-minute, one-on-one video calls in rounds, each person meeting the others in their group; after each call a short survey.

Call shape (from the original study's numbers): a call is cut off by a three-minute timer. A typical call has about 30 turns (most between 20 and 39) and about 570 words in total (most between 440 and 682); half of all turns are 12 words or fewer, and a quarter are 24 or more. Short acknowledgements ("yeah", "mm") count as turns too. So aim for about 570 words in about 30 turns: alongside the quick back-and-forth, people often talk in longer stretches (explaining their job, telling a story), and those long turns carry much of the call.

Guide to British conversational English (use it for how people talk; it is a description of speech, not a script):
How British people talk in casual conversation. This is a paraphrase of published descriptions of spoken British English; sources are in SOURCES.md. Use these features lightly and only where they fit the person. Never use them as a caricature.

- **Fillers.** British speakers hesitate with "erm" and "er". Women and younger speakers lean towards "erm".
- **Hedges.** "Sort of" is everywhere and steady. "Kind of" is spreading, and younger speakers use it more.
- **Politeness words.** "Please", "thank you", "thanks" and "sorry" mostly mean what they say. "Sorry" also works as a repair word (to correct yourself, or to ask someone to repeat) and can be ironic.
- **Tags at the end of a sentence.** "You know", "right", "okay", "yeah", "do you know what I mean". Among young Londoners, "innit" and "you get me" are rising. Tags depend on age and region only, never on ethnicity.
- **Echoing.** In an engaged conversation people pick up and re-use parts of each other's words.
- **Regional words and grammar** (from a recent dialect survey):
  - A bread roll is a "barm" in the North West (Manchester to Liverpool and western Lancashire), a "cob" around Nottinghamshire, a "bap" in Staffordshire, the West Midlands and North Wales, and a "batch" in Liverpool and Coventry.
  - Around Liverpool an ice lolly can be a "lolly ice".
  - The evening meal is "tea" in the North West, North East and Yorkshire, and "dinner" in the South East and London. Some people say both.
  - "Yous" or "youse" for plural "you" is common in the North East (Newcastle, Teesside), Liverpool and Scotland, less so in Manchester, and rare in York, Leeds and Sheffield.
  - "Give it me" is normal in the North West and West Midlands and widely accepted in Sheffield and York; it fades south of Birmingham, Coventry and Leicester.
  - "You was" is widely used, historically Northern and now found as far south as London.
- **Everyday British words** to draw on where they fit, without assigning them to regions: knackered or shattered, chuffed or made up, skint or brassic, mardy or stroppy, mum or mam, mate or pal, settee, sofa or couch.

The group (session S49). Persona cards, including the webcam photo each person was rated on:

P256 (Leanne; transcript label: Leanne):
- first name: Leanne
- age: 40
- lives in: Walsall, West Midlands
- occupation: Practice nurse at a GP surgery in Bloxwich. She runs the long-term conditions clinics (asthma, diabetes reviews), does smears and childhood immunisations, and works four days a week
- education detail: GCSEs and A-levels (Biology, Psychology, English Language) at a sixth form college in Walsall. Adult Nursing BSc at the University of Wolverhampton, qualified at 23. She has since done short accredited courses in asthma and diabetes management and cervical screening
- household: Lives alone in a two-bedroom end-terrace she bought in 2016, about ten minutes' drive from her mum's. No pets, though she feeds next door's cat when they're away
- cultural background: Born and raised in Walsall. Her mum is white and from Darlaston, and her dad's family came from Jamaica in the early 1960s. Her parents separated when she was nine. She stayed close to her nan on her dad's side, who took her to a Methodist church as a child. She still goes to a Methodist church most Sundays, more for the people and the quiet than for any strong doctrine. She feels very much a local Black Country girl but says she always knew she was 'a bit of both'
- professional persona: Calm, thorough and good with nervous patients. She is the nurse colleagues send the anxious smear patients and the crying toddlers to. She keeps immaculate notes and hates rushing appointments, which puts her slightly at odds with ten-minute slots. She worries about getting things wrong more than she lets on, and double-checks vaccine batch numbers she's already checked
- sports persona: Not sporty. She walks most evenings round the Arboretum or along the canal towpath, and did a Couch to 5K a few years ago but never kept it up. She'll have the football on if Walsall are on the radio because her dad always did
- arts persona: Reads a lot, mostly crime novels and the odd family saga, borrowed from the library or bought on Kindle. She likes gentle telly: Gardeners' World, The Repair Shop, a long-running detective series. She sings in the church choir at Christmas and Easter and finds it nerve-wracking but lovely
- travel persona: Prefers familiar places. She has a yearly week in a cottage in Tenby or North Norfolk, sometimes with her mum. She went to Jamaica once at 30 with an aunt and cousins and found it emotional. She'd like to go back but finds the planning daunting. Not keen on flying or busy airports
- culinary persona: A decent, careful cook who batch-cooks on Sundays: chilli, curry goat when she has time (her nan's way, never quite as good), soups. Her weekday tea is often something simple. She takes a packed lunch to work, usually a bap and fruit. Saturday treat is a chippy tea
- hobbies and interests: evening walks on the canal towpath, crime novels and library visits, tending pots and a small raised bed in her back garden, church choir at Christmas and Easter, jigsaw puzzles in winter, family history research on her nan's side
- skills: clinical skills: immunisations, cervical screening, spirometry, wound care, putting anxious people at ease, meticulous record-keeping, batch cooking and budgeting, basic sewing and mending, patient, careful listening
- career goals: Not hungry for promotion. She'd like to do a nurse prescribing qualification so she can manage her asthma and diabetes patients more fully, and maybe eventually mentor student nurses. Mostly she wants to keep doing a job she's good at without burning out
- voice: Soft-spoken and measured, with a light Black Country/Walsall accent. It shows mainly in vowels and the odd 'give it me' or 'bap', never laid on thick. She speaks fairly slowly and chooses her words carefully. She uses 'erm' and 'sort of' a fair bit when she's thinking, and tags things with 'you know' or 'yeah'. She calls the evening meal 'tea' and says 'mom' rather than 'mum'. She apologises easily ('sorry, that's not what you asked') and often checks she's answered properly. She's comfortable with a pause and will let silence sit rather than fill it, but if it goes on she'll ask 'is that alright?'
- typing: Proper capitals and full stops, correct apostrophes, whole words. She rarely abbreviates beyond 'etc' or 'GP'. Answers are short but complete, and she sometimes adds a qualifier in brackets. She might add 'Thanks' at the end of a free-text box. She occasionally rereads and corrects typos before submitting
- with strangers: Polite, warm but reserved. She lets the other person lead and answers honestly without much self-promotion. She can seem a bit shy for the first few minutes, then relaxes once she feels she's being useful. She'd never exaggerate to sound more interesting
- small things: the surgery's phone lines being a nightmare on Monday mornings, next door's cat, Biscuit, sitting on her wheelie bin, what she's reading at the moment, her tomatoes not ripening this year, the traffic on the Wolverhampton Road, having a chippy tea on a Saturday, her mom ringing during Pointless
- deeper things: She sometimes feels lonely living alone and wonders if she 'missed the boat' on having a family, though she's mostly made peace with it, Her nan died in 2019 and she still misses her. Researching the family tree is partly a way of staying close to her, Growing up mixed-race in a mostly white estate, she sometimes felt she didn't fully fit in either side of the family, She had a long relationship in her late twenties that ended when he moved away for work. She didn't follow, and sometimes wonders if she should have, She gets anxious after difficult days at work and lies awake replaying conversations with patients
- webcam photo: Head-and-shoulders shot from a laptop on a dining table, camera slightly below eye level. Soft daylight comes from a window to her left, so the right side of her face is a little shadowed. She has light brown skin, a few faint freckles across her nose, and a small, slightly hesitant closed-mouth smile. Her eyebrows are raised as though she's just asked if she can be heard. Dark brown curly hair is pulled back in a low bun, with a few loose curls at her temples. She wears thin rectangular black-framed glasses, small gold stud earrings and a plain navy crew-neck jumper. Behind her is a magnolia wall with a framed print of a Welsh harbour and a narrow bookcase holding paperbacks, a jigsaw box and a small potted spider plant. A wall calendar from a local church hangs beside it, and a doorway on the right shows part of a hallway with a coat on a hook.

P257 (Kelly; transcript label: Kelly):
- first name: Kelly
- age: 44
- lives in: Walsall, West Midlands
- occupation: Part-time care assistant at a private residential care home for older people, about 24 hours a week on a mix of early shifts and the odd weekend
- education detail: Left a Walsall comprehensive at 16 with four GCSEs, including a C in English but not maths. Did a few months of a hairdressing course at college and dropped out. She goes to church for christenings, funerals and the Christmas carol service, and sometimes says a quiet prayer when things are bad, but she isn't a churchgoer. Very rooted locally. She has never lived more than a few miles from where she grew up and doesn't really want to.
- professional persona: Good with the residents she likes and can be warm and funny with them, especially the ones with dementia who need patience in the moment. She is less good with paperwork, rotas and managers. Care notes get written in a rush at the end of a shift. She is often five or ten minutes late and has had a couple of informal warnings. She swaps shifts when it suits her and doesn't always put herself out for colleagues in return. She says what she thinks to senior staff, which gets her a reputation as 'mouthy'. She is quietly tired of the low pay for a hard job.
- sports persona: Not sporty. She did a Couch to 5K app once and gave up in week three. She half-follows Walsall FC through her brother and will watch England in a tournament at the pub. She walks a fair bit because she doesn't drive, and that is about it. Her lower back plays up, which she blames on hoisting at work.
- arts persona: Watches a lot of telly: reality shows (Love Island, Married at First Sight Australia), soaps on and off, and true crime documentaries she then can't sleep after. She has been to a few tribute nights and a Take That concert in Birmingham years ago, which she still talks about.
- travel persona: Holidays are rare and money-dependent. She has done a handful of caravan breaks at Rhyl and Skegness with the kids, and one all-inclusive in Tenerife with a mate before the kids. She dreams of going back abroad but never manages to save for it. Day trips are to Birmingham city centre, Merry Hill or Drayton Manor when there's a deal on.
- culinary persona: Cooks quick and cheap: pasta bakes, chicken dippers and chips, fajita kits, a big pan of chilli when she can be bothered. She calls the evening meal 'tea' and a bread roll a 'bap'. The kids get takeaway on payday, usually a Chinese or a Saturday chippy. She snacks a lot when stressed and is always about to start a diet on Monday.
- hobbies and interests: Scrolling TikTok and Facebook local groups, and getting into arguments in the comments, Reality TV and true crime documentaries, Doing online surveys and panel studies for vouchers and a bit of extra money, Scratchcards and the odd tenner on bingo apps, Nails, lashes and keeping up with beauty trends when she can afford it, Going out with her friend Shaz for drinks a few times a year
- skills: Calming down distressed or confused older residents, Personal care and hoisting (manual handling trained), Stretching a small budget at the end of the month, Spotting a bargain or a freebie online, Doing her own and her friends' nails, Thinking on her feet in a crisis, even if she's disorganised the rest of the time
- career goals: No big plan. She'd like more money for the same or fewer hours and has vaguely thought about senior carer or doing her NVQ Level 3, but she hasn't got round to applying. Sometimes she talks about retraining as a nail technician and working from home. Mostly she wants things to stay manageable until Ellie-Mae is older.
- voice: Fairly quick and chatty once she's going, with a broad-ish Walsall/Black Country accent: 'yeah' comes out close to 'ar' sometimes, and she says 'mom' rather than 'mum'. Casual register throughout. She drops in 'give it me', 'you was' and 'bap' without thinking, plus 'shattered' and 'skint' a lot. Lots of 'erm' at the start of answers and 'do you know what I mean' or 'you know' tagged on the end. She can be blunt and a bit sarcastic ('well that's a stupid question, sorry, but it is'). She fills silences with a laugh or a side comment rather than waiting, and she gets visibly impatient if a question feels repetitive or pointless.
- typing: Mostly lowercase, with a capital only if her phone autocorrects one in. Very little punctuation: no full stops at the end, the odd comma, and '...' or 'lol' when she's unsure. She usually skips apostrophes ('dont', 'cant', 'im') and sometimes uses 'u' and 'ur'. Answers are short and to the point. She'll type 'not sure tbh' or 'depends' rather than writing much, and she rushes the open-text boxes to get to the end.
- with strangers: Friendly enough on the surface and quick to make a joke, but a bit guarded and ready to take offence if she thinks she's being judged or talked down to. She'll tell you if something's daft. She wants to know what she's getting out of the conversation, such as how long it'll take and when the payment comes through. She can come across as slightly prickly or rushed, but she warms up if you laugh with her.
- small things: The bus being late again, Ellie-Mae refusing to wear her school blazer, Kai eating everything in the fridge, Being shattered after an early shift, A resident at work who calls her by her nan's name, Her nails needing doing, Something mad she saw on the local Facebook group, Waiting on a voucher from another survey site
- deeper things: Darren hardly pays anything towards the kids, and she's still angry about it, She gets bad anxiety at night and has been on and off sertraline for years, She worries constantly about money and has a credit card and a catalogue account she's behind on, Her mom's health is getting worse and she dreads having to look after her as well, She sometimes feels she's wasted her life and gets jealous of friends who 'got out', She has fudged a few answers on screener questions to qualify for paid studies and feels a bit guilty about it, but not much
- webcam photo: Taken on a phone propped against something on a kitchen table, angled slightly upward so the frame shows her chin, face and shoulders with a bit of ceiling at the top. The evening light comes from a single overhead bulb, which makes the image a little yellow and slightly grainy, and there's a faint shine on her forehead. She's a white woman in her mid-forties with a round face, tired eyes, light freckles and minimal make-up apart from filled-in brows. Her expression is half-smiling but impatient, as if waiting for the call to start. Her dark blonde hair, with highlights growing out at the roots, is scraped into a messy bun with strands loose at the sides. No glasses. She's wearing a grey zip-up hoodie over a black vest top, and the hand near her face has long pink acrylic nails, one chipped. Behind her is a white fridge-freezer covered in magnets, school letters and a child's drawing. To the left, a clothes airer is loaded with school polo shirts and leggings. Beside it is a worktop with a kettle, a bread bin and a pile of post, and a doorway on the right leads into a dim hallway.

- voice: Relaxed, friendly and fairly quick. He talks like he's leaning on a counter. There's a mild Somerset burr on some vowels and a soft 'r', but he doesn't use broad dialect on a call. He calls the interviewer 'mate' once he's warmed up, sometimes within a couple of minutes. He isn't guarded and doesn't seem nervous. Answers questions straight and doesn't overthink them. He might go off on a tangent about work or the cricket and then cheerfully bring himself back.
- small things: Biscuit the dog has eaten another sock, The skittles team lost by two pins on Thursday, Traffic on the M5 at Junction 25, A builder who's been 'nearly finished' on the same extension for eight months, Trying to decide whether to book Tenerife or the Algarve, His fantasy football team is bottom of the work league, The new barbecue he bought with his bonus
- deeper things: His dad died of a heart attack at 61, which is part of why he gave up smoking and walks a lot. He says it matter-of-factly, He and Nicola tried for children in their thirties. It didn't happen and they decided not to go down the IVF route. He says he's made his peace with it, and mostly he has, His mum is in her late 70s in Bridgwater and starting to struggle, and he and his brother haven't worked out who'll step up, He sometimes wonders whether he should have stayed at college, but doesn't dwell on it, Nicola occasionally raises getting married for pension and inheritance reasons, and he knows he'll have to sort it eventually

He is a broad-shouldered white man in his mid-forties with a ruddy, outdoorsy complexion and a short-cropped beard going grey at the chin. His light brown hair is clipped short at the sides and thinning a little on top. He has no glasses. He's smiling with his mouth slightly open, as if mid-sentence, with crow's feet around his eyes. He wears a navy quarter-zip fleece with a small embroidered company logo on the chest. Behind him are a cream fitted kitchen with wooden worktops, a kettle, a toaster and a knife block, and a calendar from a local garage pinned to a cupboard door. A dog lead hangs on a hook by the back door, and the edge of a brown dog bed shows at the bottom right of the frame.

req.text:
You write transcripts of realistic video calls between strangers for a fully synthetic research dataset set in the UK. The study, in order (from its published design): a short puzzle task done alone; first impressions of the others' webcam photos; then a series of three-minute, one-on-one video calls in rounds, each person meeting the others in their group; after each call a short survey.

Call shape (from the original study's numbers): a call is cut off by a three-minute timer. A typical call has about 30 turns (most between 20 and 39) and about 570 words in total (most between 440 and 682); half of all turns are 12 words or fewer, and a quarter are 24 or more. Short acknowledgements ("yeah", "mm") count as turns too. So aim for about 570 words in about 30 turns: alongside the quick back-and-forth, people often talk in longer stretches (explaining their job, telling a story), and those long turns carry much of the call.

Guide to British conversational English (use it for how people talk; it is a description of speech, not a script):
How British people talk in casual conversation. This is a paraphrase of published descriptions of spoken British English; sources are in SOURCES.md. Use these features lightly and only where they fit the person. Never use them as a caricature.

- **Fillers.** British speakers hesitate with "erm" and "er". Women and younger speakers lean towards "erm".
- **Hedges.** "Sort of" is everywhere and steady. "Kind of" is spreading, and younger speakers use it more.
- **Politeness words.** "Please", "thank you", "thanks" and "sorry" mostly mean what they say. "Sorry" also works as a repair word (to correct yourself, or to ask someone to repeat) and can be ironic.
- **Tags at the end of a sentence.** "You know", "right", "okay", "yeah", "do you know what I mean". Among young Londoners, "innit" and "you get me" are rising. Tags depend on age and region only, never on ethnicity.
- **Echoing.** In an engaged conversation people pick up and re-use parts of each other's words.
- **Regional words and grammar** (from a recent dialect survey):
  - A bread roll is a "barm" in the North West (Manchester to Liverpool and western Lancashire), a "cob" around Nottinghamshire, a "bap" in Staffordshire, the West Midlands and North Wales, and a "batch" in Liverpool and Coventry.
  - Around Liverpool an ice lolly can be a "lolly ice".
  - The evening meal is "tea" in the North West, North East and Yorkshire, and "dinner" in the South East and London. Some people say both.
  - "Yous" or "youse" for plural "you" is common in the North East (Newcastle, Teesside), Liverpool and Scotland, less so in Manchester, and rare in York, Leeds and Sheffield.
  - "Give it me" is normal in the North West and West Midlands and widely accepted in Sheffield and York; it fades south of Birmingham, Coventry and Leicester.
  - "You was" is widely used, historically Northern and now found as far south as London.
- **Everyday British words** to draw on where they fit, without assigning them to regions: knackered or shattered, chuffed or made up, skint or brassic, mardy or stroppy, mum or mam, mate or pal, settee, sofa or couch.
