You write transcripts of realistic video calls between strangers for a fully synthetic research dataset set in the UK. The study, in order (from its published design): a short puzzle task done alone; first impressions of the others' webcam photos; then a series of three-minute, one-on-one video calls in rounds, each person meeting the others in their group; after each call a short survey.

Call shape (from the original study's numbers): a call is cut off by a three-minute timer. A typical call has about 30 turns (most between 20 and 39) and about 570 words in total (most between 440 and 682); half of all turns are 12 words or fewer, and a quarter are 24 or more. Short acknowledgements ("yeah", "mm") count as turns too. So aim for about 570 words in about 30 turns: alongside the quick back-and-forth, people often talk in longer stretches (explaining their job, telling a story), and those long turns carry much of the call.

Guide to British conversational English (use it for how people talk; it is a description of speech, not a script):
How British people talk in casual conversation. This is a paraphrase of published descriptions of spoken British English; sources are in SOURCES.md. Use these features lightly and only where they fit the person. Never use them as a caricature.

- **Fillers.** British speakers hesitate with "erm" and "er". Women and younger speakers lean towards "erm".
- **Hedges.** "Sort of" is everywhere and steady. "Kind of" is spreading, and younger speakers use it more.
- **Politeness words.** "Please", "thank you", "thanks" and "sorry" mostly mean what they say. "Sorry" also works as a repair word (to correct yourself, or to ask someone to repeat) and can be ironic.
- **Tags at the end of a sentence.** "You know", "right", "okay", "yeah", "do you know what I mean". Among young Londoners, "innit" and "you get me" are rising. Tags depend on age and region only, never on ethnicity.
- **Echoing.** In an engaged conversation people pick up and re-use parts of each other's words.
- **Regional words and grammar** (from a recent dialect survey):
  - A bread roll is a "barm" in the North West (Manchester to Liverpool and western Lancashire), a "cob" around Nottinghamshire, a "bap" in Staffordshire, the West Midlands and North Wales, and a "batch" in Liverpool and Coventry.
  - Around Liverpool an ice lolly can be a "lolly ice".
  - The evening meal is "tea" in the North West, North East and Yorkshire, and "dinner" in the South East and London. Some people say both.
  - "Yous" or "youse" for plural "you" is common in the North East (Newcastle, Teesside), Liverpool and Scotland, less so in Manchester, and rare in York, Leeds and Sheffield.
  - "Give it me" is normal in the North West and West Midlands and widely accepted in Sheffield and York; it fades south of Birmingham, Coventry and Leicester.
  - "You was" is widely used, historically Northern and now found as far south as London.
- **Everyday British words** to draw on where they fit, without assigning them to regions: knackered or shattered, chuffed or made up, skint or brassic, mardy or stroppy, mum or mam, mate or pal, settee, sofa or couch.

The group (session S48). Persona cards, including the webcam photo each person was rated on:

P252 (Agnieszka; transcript label: Agnieszka):
- first name: Agnieszka
- age: 45
- lives in: Southampton, South East England
- occupation: Part-time cleaner for a contract cleaning company. She works around 20 hours a week, early mornings and some evenings, cleaning offices and a GP surgery in the city centre.
- education detail: She finished a five-year technical secondary school (technikum) in south-east Poland with a vocational qualification in catering and food technology. She did an evening ESOL course in Southampton in 2007–2008 and has a few cleaning and food hygiene certificates from work. No university.
- household: She lives with her husband Marek (48), a van delivery driver, and their son Kacper (17), who is doing a plumbing course at college. They rent a three-bed terraced house in Shirley. Their older daughter Natalia (21) moved out last year to live with her boyfriend in Eastleigh and still comes for Sunday dinner most weeks.
- cultural background: Born and raised in a small town near Rzeszów in Poland. She came to the UK in 2006, a year after Marek, and has lived in Southampton ever since. She is a practising Catholic and goes to Mass most Sundays at the Polish Catholic mission. At home the family speaks Polish. With Kacper it's a mix, because he answers in English. She feels settled here but still thinks of Poland as 'home' when she talks about her mum. She has pre-settled, now settled, status. She keeps Polish traditions at Christmas and Easter very seriously.
- professional persona: Reliable and thorough. Supervisors know she will do the job properly and turn up on time. She likes a fixed rota and gets anxious when sites are changed at short notice. She is chatty with the reception staff and the other cleaners, and is often the one who remembers birthdays. Her rheumatoid arthritis means she can't do heavy floor machines on bad days, and she worries a lot about letting people down or losing hours because of it.
- sports persona: Not sporty herself. She walks when her joints allow, usually round Southampton Common with a friend from church. She watches ski jumping and volleyball with Marek when Poland is on, and gets very loud and emotional about it. She does gentle exercises the physio gave her, mostly faithfully.
- arts persona: Not interested in galleries, theatre or 'arty' films and would say so honestly. She likes Polish TV series and comedies on streaming, singalong Polish pop and disco polo at family parties, and the hymns at church, where she sings with real enthusiasm. She has never been to a museum in Southampton and sees no reason to.
- travel persona: Every summer she goes back to Poland for two or three weeks to see her mum and sister, usually flying from Luton or Stansted, or occasionally driving across with Marek. She has no real wish to go anywhere else. The one beach holiday in Spain was 'nice, but too hot, and the food, no'. She packs weeks early and checks the passports several times.
- culinary persona: A traditional Polish home cook who cooks most days. Rosół on Sunday, pierogi made in big batches and frozen, gołąbki, schabowy with potatoes and mizeria. She shops at the Polish shop on Shirley High Street and at Lidl. She doesn't trust very spicy food and rarely gets takeaway apart from the odd fish and chips. She calls the evening meal 'dinner' in English.
- hobbies and interests: Cooking for family and church events, Mass and helping with the church coffee morning, Long phone and video calls with her mum and sister, Growing tomatoes, cucumbers and dill in pots in the back garden, Polish TV series and family films, Facebook groups for Poles in Southampton, Baking for Easter and Christmas
- skills: Commercial cleaning to a high standard, Food hygiene and kitchen work, Traditional Polish cooking and baking, Organising family celebrations, Bilingual Polish–English for everyday matters, often helping newer arrivals with forms, Very good at keeping to schedules and routines
- career goals: Mainly to keep her hours and stay well enough to work. She would like to move to a cleaning job with a steady daytime pattern, maybe at a school, so she isn't out early in the cold, which is bad for her hands. No ambition to retrain. Security and the family come first.
- voice: Warm, fast and talkative, with a clear Polish accent and fluent but not always standard English. She sometimes drops articles ('I go to work at six') and occasionally uses Polish word order. She uses 'erm' a lot, 'you know', and a bit of 'sort of'. She has picked up local phrases like 'lovely', 'bless him', 'I'm knackered' and 'sorry, sorry, what was that?' when she hasn't heard. Her voice gets quick and a bit worried if she thinks she's answered wrong. She fills silences herself almost immediately, usually with a story about her family or work, and laughs easily.
- typing: Capital at the start, then mostly lowercase. Short sentences joined with commas, few full stops. Apostrophes often missing ('dont', 'its'). Occasional Polish-influenced spelling or missed article. She uses 'ok' and the odd exclamation mark, and sometimes adds a smiley ':)' at the end. She checks the answer before sending but doesn't fuss over grammar.
- with strangers: Friendly and open almost straight away. She asks how you are and means it, and quickly shares details about her children or her job. She apologises for her English even when it's fine. She can be a bit nervous at first about doing something 'official', and wants to be told clearly what to do. Once she relaxes she talks a lot and is very expressive.
- small things: The early bus in winter is freezing and always late, Kacper never tidies his room, Her tomatoes did really well this year, Making pierogi with Natalia on Saturday, The Polish shop now sells proper bread again, Marek works too many hours with the deliveries, The GP surgery where she cleans is always so busy, Watching the ski jumping on a Sunday
- deeper things: Her rheumatoid arthritis, diagnosed in 2019, which some mornings makes her hands too stiff to hold a cup, and her fear of it getting worse, Worry about her mum, who is in her seventies and alone in Poland since her dad died, Guilt about not being there for her dad's last months, Anxiety that comes in waves, which she has only recently mentioned to her GP, Missing Natalia in the house more than she admits, Feeling that after nearly twenty years she still isn't fully 'from here' or 'from there' any more
- webcam photo: A laptop webcam shot taken at a kitchen table in the evening, slightly from below, so the ceiling light is visible at the top edge and lights her face from above. She is a 45-year-old white woman with shoulder-length dyed dark-blonde hair pulled back in a loose clip, a few strands falling by her face, and light brown roots showing. Round face, light makeup, a little mascara. She is smiling broadly with slightly raised eyebrows, as if mid-greeting. She wears a pale pink fleece zip-up over a grey T-shirt, a small gold cross on a thin chain, and a wedding ring visible as one hand rests near the laptop. No glasses. Behind her are white kitchen wall units, a kettle and a toaster on a worktop, a wall calendar from a Polish shop with notes written on it, a small framed picture of the Virgin Mary on the wall next to the fridge, and fridge magnets including one from Kraków. A tea towel hangs over the oven door handle.

P253 (Liam; transcript label: Liam):
- first name: Liam
- age: 29
- lives in: Wakefield, Yorkshire and The Humber
- occupation: Technical sales executive for a commercial heating, ventilation and air-conditioning supplier based on an industrial estate near Junction 41 of the M1. He manages around 60 trade and contractor accounts across West Yorkshire, quotes for jobs, and is out on site visits two or three days a week.
- education detail: GCSEs and A-levels (Business, Geography, PE) at a sixth form college in Wakefield; BA (Hons) Business Management, 2:2, Sheffield Hallam University. He has since completed a company-funded certificate in HVAC product knowledge and a short course on negotiation.
- household: Rents a three-bed new-build semi in Outwood with his girlfriend of six years, Jess, who is a dental nurse. They are not married. They have a two-year-old cockapoo called Alfie. They are saving for a deposit, though Liam's leased company-upgrade Audi eats into that more than Jess would like.
- cultural background: White British, born and raised in Wakefield. His mum works in a school office. His dad ran a small kitchen-fitting business that went under when Liam was about fourteen, and he now works for a bigger firm. He has an older sister in Leeds. He has no religion and no strong feelings about it. He is very much from a family where you were expected to graft and not make a fuss.
- professional persona: Organised to the point of being teased for it. His CRM is always up to date, he plans his route the night before, and he sends follow-up emails within the hour. He is genuinely good with customers: patient, easygoing, and quick to forgive a late payment or a grumpy site manager. He is also very aware of commission and league tables. He will tell a client what they want to hear if it closes a deal, he enjoys being seen as the top performer, and he is not above nudging his mileage claims a bit.
- sports persona: Plays five-a-side on Wednesday nights at a 3G pitch in Wakefield and goes to the gym four mornings a week before work, tracking everything in an app. He follows Leeds United, watching on TV and going to Elland Road a few times a season, preferably with someone who can get hospitality tickets. He took up golf last year, partly because clients play.
- arts persona: Not big on the arts. He watches crime dramas and Netflix documentaries with Jess and listens to podcasts in the car, mostly business and self-improvement ones plus a football podcast. He has been to the Hepworth once, when family visited, and found it 'alright, bit odd'. He likes going to gigs at the First Direct Arena for big-name acts.
- travel persona: Two holidays a year, usually somewhere hot and a bit flash: Dubai last year, Marbella the year before. He did a lads' trip to Benidorm at 25 and a Krakow stag do. He likes a nice hotel he can post about and is not fussed about 'proper' culture. He books everything well in advance and keeps a spreadsheet of costs.
- culinary persona: Calls the evening meal tea. He meal-preps chicken, rice and veg on Sundays for work lunches. He likes a steakhouse or a Nando's, and a curry from the local takeaway on Friday. Jess cooks more than he does, but he does a decent Sunday roast and barbecues a lot in summer. He likes a nice bottle of red when out, partly for the look of it.
- hobbies and interests: five-a-side football, gym and fitness tracking, golf (beginner, keen), Leeds United, cars, especially German ones, business and self-improvement podcasts, walking the dog around Pugneys Country Park, watching the Champions League with mates
- skills: building rapport quickly, negotiating on price, planning and scheduling, reading technical spec sheets, Excel and CRM software, remembering names and personal details, staying calm with awkward customers
- career goals: Wants to be area sales manager within two years and earning 'proper money' by 35, ideally with a better car allowance. He has half an eye on moving to a bigger national distributor, and occasionally talks about setting up his own agency one day, though the memory of his dad's business makes him cautious.
- voice: Friendly, chatty and fairly quick, with a light West Yorkshire accent (short 'a' in 'bath', flat vowels) but nothing broad. He uses 'mate' a lot, says 'to be fair' and 'do you know what I mean' as tags, and puts in the odd 'sort of' or 'kind of' when he's thinking. He uses 'erm' only occasionally, because he tends to keep talking rather than pause. He hates dead air and will fill a silence with a joke or a 'yeah, no, definitely'. He echoes the other person's words back to show he is listening, a habit partly picked up from sales training. He sounds warm and slightly polished.
- typing: Tidy for a quick answer: capitals at the start, full stops mostly, apostrophes usually correct. He occasionally uses 'tbh' or 'etc' but otherwise writes in full sentences. He sometimes ends with 'Cheers' out of email habit and rarely makes typos because he rereads before submitting.
- with strangers: Instantly likeable. He is open, asks you questions back, remembers what you said and laughs easily. He comes across as eager to be helpful and keen to make a good impression, maybe a touch salesy. If something might make him look good, he will mention it early: the car, the Dubai trip, being top of the sales board.
- small things: Alfie the dog chewing his work shoes, the traffic on the M62 near Lofthouse, Leeds' latest result, his new driver for golf, hitting his step count, a Wetherspoons in Wakefield town centre, meal-prep Sundays, the car's lease coming up for renewal, Jess's shifts at the dental practice
- deeper things: Watching his dad's business fold and his parents struggle for money, which is why he cares so much about earning well and being seen to be doing alright, Feels some pressure about proposing to Jess, and knows she'd rather they saved than spent on holidays and the car, Admits he sometimes bends the truth with customers and on expenses, and justifies it as 'everyone does it', Worries that if he stopped hitting targets he wouldn't really know who he was, Is a bit competitive with his older sister, who has a better-paid job in Leeds
- webcam photo: Head-and-shoulders shot from a laptop webcam set slightly below eye level, so the angle looks up a little. Bright, slightly cool daylight comes from a window to the left, leaving the right side of his face a touch shadowed. He has a broad, clean-shaven face with a light tan, short brown hair faded at the sides and slightly longer and styled on top, and no glasses. He is smiling with teeth, mid-way through saying something. He wears a navy quarter-zip pullover with a small company logo on the chest, over a white T-shirt. Behind him is a pale grey wall in a spare-room home office. A white flat-pack shelving unit holds a few box files, a Leeds United mug and a framed photo of him and a woman on a beach. The edge of a golf bag shows in the corner, and a ring light, switched off, stands to the right.

P254 (Riya; transcript label: Riya):
- first name: Riya
- age: 21
- lives in: Leyton, East London
- occupation: Part-time receptionist and admin assistant at a private dental practice in Stratford, about 12 hours a week over two weekday shifts, alongside the final year of a university degree
- education detail: Final-year BSc Business Management student at Queen Mary University of London. Got A-levels in Business, Psychology and Sociology (A, B, B) at a sixth form in Harrow. Expected to finish with a 2:1 if she gets her dissertation in on time, which is a running joke between her and her boyfriend.
- household: Rents a one-bed flat above a dry cleaner's off Leyton High Road with her boyfriend Josh, 24, a junior data analyst at an insurance firm in the City. They moved in together eight months ago. Josh pays the larger share of the rent and they split bills. Her parents still live in the family semi in Harrow and she goes back most Sundays for food and to drop off laundry.
- cultural background: British-born, of Gujarati Indian heritage. Her grandparents came to London via Kenya in the early 1970s. Her dad is a community pharmacist and her mum is an accountant. She grew up in a comfortable, busy household with a younger brother who is doing his A-levels. She understands Gujarati well but replies in English. She goes to Diwali and family weddings and enjoys them, but keeps her own beliefs to herself and doesn't like ticking a box about religion.
- professional persona: Friendly and good at the front-desk side of the job: calming nervous patients, chatting, smoothing things over when the dentist runs late. She is less reliable on the back-office side. Recall letters pile up, she forgets to update the booking system, and she has been gently told off twice for being late to her shift. She sees the job mainly as decent money and something for the CV. She has been known to quietly take the nicer branded pens and the odd sample whitening kit home.
- sports persona: Not sporty. She has a gym membership she uses in bursts, mostly the treadmill and the occasional reformer Pilates class when there's a deal on. She walks a lot around London without counting it as exercise. She watches the big football tournaments with Josh for the atmosphere rather than the football.
- arts persona: Mostly screens. She binges reality TV (Love Island, The Traitors) and Netflix dramas, and follows a few makeup and fashion creators on TikTok. She has been to a couple of West End shows on birthday trips and liked them. She'll go to an exhibition if it's a good photo opportunity, like the immersive ones.
- travel persona: Loves a holiday but leaves planning to others. She has done girls' trips to Barcelona and Lisbon, and a family trip to Gujarat and Mumbai when she was 16. She would like to do Dubai or Bali 'properly', with a nice hotel and a pool, and is quietly a bit status-conscious about where she goes and what it looks like on Instagram.
- culinary persona: Can cook a few things: pasta, a basic dal her mum taught her, stir fries. She orders in more than she should. She calls the evening meal dinner. Brunch spots in Hackney and Walthamstow are her treat. She loves her mum's thepla and undhiyu and always comes back from Harrow with tubs of leftovers.
- hobbies and interests: reality TV and gossiping about it in group chats, makeup and skincare, especially trying new products, browsing Vinted and Depop for designer bits, brunch and cafés with friends, TikTok scrolling, getting dressed up for nights out in Shoreditch
- skills: putting people at ease on the phone and in person, basic Microsoft Office and dental booking software, talking her way out of minor trouble, doing other people's makeup for events, conversational understanding of Gujarati
- career goals: Vague. She likes the idea of working in marketing or brand partnerships for a beauty or fashion company, ideally somewhere with a nice office and perks. She's thinking about a graduate scheme but hasn't applied anywhere yet and keeps saying she'll 'sort it after the dissertation'. Partly she wants to earn enough not to rely on Josh or her parents.
- voice: Warm, chatty North-West-London-meets-East-London voice, fairly quick when she's comfortable. She uses 'like' and 'kind of' a lot, starts answers with 'erm' or 'oh my god, so', and throws in the occasional 'innit' or 'you know what I mean' with friends, less so with strangers. She says 'sorry, what was the question again?' when she's drifted off. She picks up the interviewer's words and echoes them back. With silence she tends to fill the gap with a laugh and a 'yeah, so, that's basically it'.
- typing: Mostly lowercase, capitals only when autocorrect does it. Few full stops, lots of commas or none. Drops apostrophes ('dont', 'im'), uses 'tbh', 'idk', 'ngl' and the odd 'lol'. Answers are short unless she's interested, then they run on. Occasional typos she doesn't bother fixing.
- with strangers: Comes across as friendly, easy-going and agreeable. She's quick to laugh, says 'no, totally' a lot and rarely pushes back. She can seem a bit performatively nice, and she'll steer answers towards what makes her look good. She's not shy, but not loud either.
- small things: the dentist she works for always running twenty minutes behind, the Central line being rammed, a skincare product she's obsessed with right now, what happened on last night's episode of whatever she's watching, going back to her mum's on Sunday and coming home with food, being skint before her student loan comes in, the dry cleaner downstairs starting the machines at 7am
- deeper things: she feels a bit behind her friends who already have graduate jobs lined up, and avoids thinking about it, she knows she leans on Josh financially and it sometimes makes her uneasy, even if she'd never say so to him, her parents assumed she'd do pharmacy or accounting like them and she senses mild disappointment, she hasn't fully told her extended family she lives with her boyfriend, she worries she's not very good at sticking at things
- webcam photo: Laptop webcam shot from slightly below, framing her head and shoulders, a little off-centre to the left. Soft warm light from a ring light out of shot on the right, with cooler grey daylight from a window behind her that slightly washes out the background. She has light brown skin and long dark brown hair worn down, middle parting, ends lightly curled. She's wearing full but natural-looking makeup: groomed brows, winged eyeliner, nude lip. Small gold hoop earrings. No glasses. She's in an oversized cream knitted jumper with the sleeves pulled over her hands, smiling with lips closed and eyebrows slightly raised, as if mid-'hi'. Behind her: the corner of a small living room with magnolia walls, an unmade grey fabric sofa with a pink throw bunched on it, a white IKEA shelf holding a pot plant that's seen better days, some perfume boxes and a framed photo of her and Josh. A clothes airer with jeans and tops on it is partly visible at the right edge.

P255 (Tariq; transcript label: Tariq):
- first name: Tariq
- age: 49
- lives in: Gants Hill, Ilford, East London
- occupation: Customer service team leader at a broadband and mobile provider's contact centre in Stratford. He supervises a team of eleven advisers handling retentions and upgrades, and does a share of the escalated calls himself.
- education detail: Intermediate (FSc) and a BCom from a university in Karachi. Since moving to the UK he has done a CIPD-style certificate in team leadership and several in-house sales and complaints-handling courses. He started an Open University module in art history in his forties, finished it, and didn't carry on.
- household: Lives in a three-bedroom semi he and his wife bought in 2011 and have extended at the back. His wife, Samina, works part-time as a pharmacy dispenser. Their son, 17, is doing A-levels and their daughter is 14. His mother-in-law visits for long stretches but doesn't live with them.
- cultural background: Born in Karachi to a Punjabi-speaking family who had moved down from Lahore. He came to London at 24 on a student visa, stayed on through work and marriage, and has held British citizenship for years. He is Sunni Muslim and practising in a steady, unshowy way. He goes to Friday prayers when his shift allows, fasts in Ramadan, and doesn't drink. He speaks Urdu and Punjabi at home with older relatives and English with his kids. He sees himself as a Londoner first when abroad and as Pakistani when he's in London.
- professional persona: Organised and results-focused. He keeps his team's stats in his own spreadsheet as well as the official dashboard because he likes to know before his manager does. He is good at retentions and knows exactly which offers can be pushed further than the script suggests. He isn't above nudging a customer onto a longer contract than they strictly need, or letting a colleague's mistake sit unmentioned if it makes his team look better. He is polished with senior managers and quietly calculating about who is worth his time. His staff find him fair enough and very reliable, though not warm.
- sports persona: Follows cricket closely, Pakistan first and England second, and will watch a Test match in full on catch-up. He watches some Premier League but isn't fussed about a team. He walks a lot on purpose, aiming for 10,000 steps, and does a Sunday morning circuit of Valentines Park. He played tape-ball cricket as a young man and now just bowls at his son in the garden now and then.
- arts persona: His most surprising side. He goes alone to the Tate Modern, the V&A and the Barbican, usually on a weekday off, and prefers modern art and Islamic architecture exhibitions. He reads Faiz and Ghalib in Urdu, and translated literature in English, recently Orhan Pamuk and some Borges. He watches subtitled films, especially Iranian and Turkish cinema. He has strong opinions about brutalist buildings and likes them, which his family finds baffling.
- travel persona: Goes to Pakistan every couple of years for family, which he sees as duty more than holiday. He loves going somewhere new and planning every detail: Istanbul, Granada for the Alhambra, Marrakech, and a long weekend in Rome he still talks about. He likes upgrading to a nicer hotel than they can really justify and enjoys mentioning it afterwards.
- culinary persona: Samina does most of the everyday cooking. He does weekend barbecues and an ambitious biryani for guests. He is curious about food and will try anything halal: Georgian, Ethiopian, Peruvian places in East London and beyond. He is particular about tea, drinking doodh patti at home and black coffee at work. The evening meal is 'dinner'.
- hobbies and interests: visiting galleries and architecture exhibitions on his own, reading Urdu poetry and translated novels, Test cricket, planning city breaks in obsessive detail, watches and fountain pens; he owns one good watch he talks about more than he should, documentaries on history and design, long walks with a podcast
- skills: handling difficult and escalated customers calmly, sales and retention negotiation, Excel and building his own tracking sheets, coaching new advisers on call structure, fluent Urdu and Punjabi, reading a room and working out who holds the power in it, trip planning and budgeting
- career goals: Wants to move up to operations manager within the next couple of years and has been positioning himself for it, volunteering for projects that senior people will notice. Privately he likes the idea of eventually running something of his own, possibly a small phone and accessories franchise, so that he answers to nobody. He wants the title and the car that come with it at least as much as the money.
- voice: Measured, fairly low-key and articulate, with a South Asian-accented London English that has softened over 25 years. Medium pace. He chooses his words and sometimes pauses mid-sentence to find a more precise one. He uses 'er' when thinking and 'sort of' a fair bit, and ends points with 'you know' or 'right?' in a checking way. He slips into his customer-facing manner when he wants something: 'Yeah, no, absolutely, I understand.' He isn't chatty, but he warms up and talks at length on topics he likes, such as art, cities and books. He is comfortable with silence and doesn't rush to fill it. He tends to wait for the other person.
- typing: Proper sentences with capital letters and full stops, mostly correct apostrophes. He keeps it brief and businesslike and sometimes uses work shorthand like 'approx', 'e.g.' or 'w/e'. No emojis. He occasionally types 'Thanks' or 'Regards' out of habit even in a web form.
- with strangers: Polite, reserved and slightly guarded at first. He comes across as competent and well-spoken, and is quick to work out what the other person wants from the conversation. He can be quietly charming when it suits him and drops in references to galleries or travel that subtly signal he is cultured. He won't overshare, and it takes a while before he says anything that isn't considered.
- small things: the Central line being rammed again, his team hitting their retention target for the month, a new exhibition he wants to see at the Barbican, his son's A-level revision, or the lack of it, the price of petrol and the ULEZ, a Turkish restaurant in Walthamstow he rates, the cricket score, his daughter rolling her eyes at his music
- deeper things: he sometimes feels he settled for a call centre career when he could have done something more intellectual, and he resents colleagues with degrees from here who he thinks are less sharp, he has bent the truth on sales calls more than he'd admit and has mostly made peace with it as 'how the industry works', his father died in Karachi while he was in London and he didn't make it back in time, he wants his children to do better than him and pushes his son hard, maybe too hard, he feels most like himself alone in a gallery, which he finds hard to explain to anyone at home, he enjoys the status of being the one in the family who made it in London and quietly likes being asked for help and money
- webcam photo: Laptop webcam at slightly below eye level, angled up a little. He sits centred, head and shoulders in frame, at a dining table. Soft daylight comes from a window to his left, with a warm ceiling light on behind him. He has a medium-brown complexion, a neatly trimmed short beard going grey at the chin, and short black hair receding slightly at the temples, combed back. He wears thin rectangular black-framed reading glasses. His expression is composed, with a slight closed-mouth smile and eyes looking directly at the screen. He wears a navy quarter-zip jumper over a white collared shirt and a steel watch visible on his left wrist. Behind him is a magnolia wall with a framed print of Islamic geometric tilework, and a low bookshelf holding a mix of Urdu and English paperbacks, a Tate exhibition catalogue lying flat, and a small brass vase. Part of a grey corner sofa with a folded throw is visible at the right edge of the frame.

Their first impressions of each other's photos (private):
Agnieszka on Liam's photo: likable 5/7, friendly 6/7, would pair: yes; gut: he looks very nice, reminds me of the managers at the office where i clean, very tidy office and he likes football like my Marek
Agnieszka on Riya's photo: likable 6/7, friendly 7/7, would pair: yes; gut: she is lovely girl, reminds me of my Natalia with her hair and makeup, but she needs to put the washing away properly :)

req.text:
You write transcripts of realistic video calls between strangers for a fully synthetic research dataset set in the UK. The study, in order (from its published design): a short puzzle task done alone; first impressions of the others' webcam photos; then a series of three-minute, one-on-one video calls in rounds, each person meeting the others in their group; after each call a short survey.

Call shape (from the original study's numbers): a call is cut off by a three-minute timer. A typical call has about 30 turns (most between 20 and 39) and about 570 words in total (most between 440 and 682); half of all turns are 12 words or fewer, and a quarter are 24 or more. Short acknowledgements ("yeah", "mm") count as turns too. So aim for about 570 words in about 30 turns: alongside the quick back-and-forth, people often talk in longer stretches (explaining their job, telling a story), and those long turns carry much of the call.

Guide to British conversational English (use it for how people talk; it is a description of speech, not a script):
How British people talk in casual conversation. This is a paraphrase of published descriptions of spoken British English; sources are in SOURCES.md. Use these features lightly and only where they fit the person. Never use them as a caricature.

- **Fillers.** British speakers hesitate with "erm" and "er". Women and younger speakers lean towards "erm".
- **Hedges.** "Sort of" is everywhere and steady. "Kind of" is spreading, and younger speakers use it more.
- **Politeness words.** "Please", "thank you", "thanks" and "sorry" mostly mean what they say. "Sorry" also works as a repair word (to correct yourself, or to ask someone to repeat) and can be ironic.
- **Tags at the end of a sentence.** "You know", "right", "okay", "yeah", "do you know what I mean". Among young Londoners, "innit" and "you get me" are rising. Tags depend on age and region only, never on ethnicity.
- **Echoing.** In an engaged conversation people pick up and re-use parts of each other's words.
- **Regional words and grammar** (from a recent dialect survey):
  - A bread roll is a "barm" in the North West (Manchester to Liverpool and western Lancashire), a "cob" around Nottinghamshire, a "bap" in Staffordshire, the West Midlands and North Wales, and a "batch" in Liverpool and Coventry.
  - Around Liverpool an ice lolly can be a "lolly ice".
  - The evening meal is "tea" in the North West, North East and Yorkshire, and "dinner" in the South East and London. Some people say both.
  - "Yous" or "youse" for plural "you" is common in the North East (Newcastle, Teesside), Liverpool and Scotland, less so in Manchester, and rare in York, Leeds and Sheffield.
  - "Give it me" is normal in the North West and West Midlands and widely accepted in Sheffield and York; it fades south of Birmingham, Coventry and Leicester.
  - "You was" is widely used, historically Northern and now found as far south as London.
- **Everyday British words** to draw on where they fit, without assigning them to regions: knackered or shattered, chuffed or made up, skint or brassic, mardy or stroppy, mum or mam, mate or pal, settee, sofa or couch.

You write transcripts of realistic video calls between strangers for a fully synthetic research dataset set in the UK. The study, in order (from its published design): a short puzzle task done alone; first impressions of the others' webcam photos; then a series of three-minute, one-on-one video calls in rounds, each person meeting the others in their group; after each call a short survey.

Call shape (from the original study's numbers): a call is cut off by a three-minute timer. A typical call has about 30 turns (most between 20 and 39) and about 570 words in total (most between 440 and 682); half of all turns are 12 words or fewer, and a quarter are 24 or more. Short acknowledgements ("yeah", "mm") count as turns too. So aim for about 570 words in about 30 turns: alongside the quick back-and-forth, people often talk in longer stretches (explaining their job, telling a story), and those long turns carry much of the call.

Guide to British conversational English (use it for how people talk; it is a description of speech, not a script):
How British people talk in casual conversation. This is a paraphrase of published descriptions of spoken British English; sources are in SOURCES.md. Use these features lightly and only where they fit the person. Never use them as a caricature.

- **Fillers.** British speakers hesitate with "erm" and "er". Women and younger speakers lean towards "erm".
- **Hedges.** "Sort of" is everywhere and steady. "Kind of" is spreading, and younger speakers use it more.
- **Politeness words.** "Please", "thank you", "thanks" and "sorry" mostly mean what they say. "Sorry" also works as a repair word (to correct yourself, or to ask someone to repeat) and can be ironic.
- **Tags at the end of a sentence.** "You know", "right", "okay", "yeah", "do you know what I mean". Among young Londoners, "innit" and "you get me" are rising. Tags depend on age and region only, never on ethnicity.
- **Echoing.** In an engaged conversation people pick up and re-use parts of each other's words.
- **Regional words and grammar** (from a recent dialect survey):
  - A bread roll is a "barm" in the North West (Manchester to Liverpool and western Lancashire), a "cob" around Nottinghamshire, a "bap" in Staffordshire, the West Midlands and North Wales, and a "batch" in Liverpool and Coventry.
  - Around Liverpool an ice lolly can be a "lolly ice".
  - The evening meal is "tea" in the North West, North East and Yorkshire, and "dinner" in the South East and London. Some people say both.
  - "Yous" or "youse" for plural "you" is common in the North East (Newcastle, Teesside), Liverpool and Scotland, less so in Manchester, and rare in York, Leeds and Sheffield.
  - "Give it me" is normal in the North West and West Midlands and widely accepted in Sheffield and York; it fades south of Birmingham, Coventry and Leicester.
  - "You was" is widely used, historically Northern and now found as far south as London.
- **Everyday British words** to draw on where they fit, without assigning them to regions: knackered or shattered, chuffed or made up, skint or brassic, mardy or stroppy, mum or mam, mate or pal, settee, sofa or couch.

You write transcripts of realistic video calls between strangers for a fully synthetic research dataset set in the UK. The study, in order (from its published design): a short puzzle task done alone; first impressions of the others' webcam photos; then a series of three-minute, one-on-one video calls in rounds, each person meeting the others in their group; after each call a short survey.

Call shape (from the original study's numbers): a call is cut off by a three-minute timer. A typical call has about 30 turns (most between 20 and 39) and about 570 words in total (most between 440 and 682); half of all turns are 12 words or fewer, and a quarter are 24 or more. Short acknowledgements ("yeah", "mm") count as turns too. So aim for about 570 words in about 30 turns: alongside the quick back-and-forth, people often talk in longer stretches (explaining their job, telling a story), and those long turns carry much of the call.

Guide to British conversational English (use it for how people talk; it is a description of speech, not a script):
How British people talk in casual conversation. This is a paraphrase of published descriptions of spoken British English; sources are in SOURCES.md. Use these features lightly and only where they fit the person. Never use them as a caricature.

- **Fillers.** British speakers hesitate with "erm" and "er". Women and younger speakers lean towards "erm".
- **Hedges.** "Sort of" is everywhere and steady. "Kind of" is spreading, and younger speakers use it more.
- **Politeness words.** "Please", "thank you", "thanks" and "sorry" mostly mean what they say. "Sorry" also works as a repair word (to correct yourself, or to ask someone to repeat) and can be ironic.
- **Tags at the end of a sentence.** "You know", "right", "okay", "yeah", "do you know what I mean". Among young Londoners, "innit" and "you get me" are rising. Tags depend on age and region only, never on ethnicity.
- **Echoing.** In an engaged conversation people pick up and re-use parts of each other's words.
- **Regional words and grammar** (from a recent dialect survey):
  - A bread roll is a "barm" in the North West (Manchester to Liverpool and western Lancashire), a "cob" around Nottinghamshire, a "bap" in Staffordshire, the West Midlands and North Wales, and a "batch" in Liverpool and Coventry.
  - Around Liverpool an ice lolly can be a "lolly ice".
  - The evening meal is "tea" in the North West, North East and Yorkshire, and "dinner" in the South East and London. Some people say both.
  - "Yous" or "youse" for plural "you" is common in the North East (Newcastle, Teesside), Liverpool and Scotland, less so in Manchester, and rare in York, Leeds and Sheffield.
  - "Give it me" is normal in the North West and West Midlands and widely accepted in Sheffield and York; it fades south of Birmingham, Coventry and Leicester.
  - "You was" is widely used, historically Northern and now found as far south as London.
- **Everyday British words** to draw on where they fit, without assigning them to regions: knackered or shattered, chuffed or made up, skint or brassic, mardy or stroppy, mum or mam, mate or pal, settee, sofa or couch.

=== CALL C0539 ===
Jade: Hiya! Can you hear me alright?
Megan: Hi! Yeah, yeah I can hear you. Sorry, I've never done one of these before, I'm a bit nervous, I don't know why.
Jade: Oh don't be, I'm the same. I'm Jade. I'm in Barnsley.
Megan: I'm Megan, I'm in Chelmsford, so like Essex. Erm, did you do the puzzle bit at the start?
Jade: Oh my god, the puzzle. I got about halfway and then I were just clicking things, honestly. Did you finish it?
Megan: Kind of? I ran out of time on the last one. I just kept staring at it, do you know what I mean? Like the shapes stopped looking like shapes.
Jade: Yeah! That's exactly it.
Megan: Erm, so what do you do? Sorry, is that, is that alright to ask?
Jade: No, it's fine. I'm a nail tech. Well, I were. The salon I worked at shut down about eight months ago, so I'm kind of between things at the minute. I'm meant to be setting up doing nails from home. I've bought half the kit for it and it's just sat in the spare room in boxes. Like I've got the lamps and that, I just need to sort insurance and a booking thing and I keep putting it off. Do you know what I mean?
Megan: Oh, I totally get that. That's like me with my coursework. Are those your nails now? They look really nice.
Jade: Yeah, did them myself last night. They're like a pinky almond. I were bored.
Megan: That's so cool. I couldn't do that, I can't even do nail varnish without getting it everywhere.
Jade: Everyone says that. It's just practice, honestly. What about you, are you at uni?
Megan: Yeah, second year. Wildlife, Ecology and Conservation Science, which is a bit of a mouthful. Erm, it's out at Writtle, just outside Chelmsford. Basically we do a lot of fieldwork, like bird surveys and pond dipping and trapping li'le mammals, voles and shrews, and then you let them go obviously. That's my favourite bit. The writing up, the stats, I'm not so good at. I kind of panic.
Jade: Aw, that sounds dead nice though. Is that a bird chart behind you?
Megan: Yeah! Sorry, it's a bit nerdy. It's just so I can learn them.
Jade: No it's not, it's cute. I wouldn't know a robin from a pigeon, me.
Megan: Honestly, you'd be surprised. Once you start looking you see them everywhere. I saw a kestrel this morning by the bus stop, just hovering over the verge.
Jade: Mm.
Megan: Have you got any pets? Sorry, random.
Jade: Yeah, we've got a Staffy, Bella. She's a nightmare. She chewed the remote again on Tuesday and Liam had to order a new one off Amazon. She's lovely though, she just thinks everything's a toy.
Megan: Aw, I love Staffies. We've got a guinea pig, Biscuit. He's a rescue. He squeaks every time the fridge opens because he thinks it's food.
Jade: Oh, that's so funny. Bless him.
Megan: Is Liam your boyfriend?
Jade: Husband, three years now. He's a sparky. He's working over Wakefield this week, so I've just been sat in with Bella watching Married at First Sight, like a proper sad case.
Megan: No, that sounds ideal, honestly. My boyfriend does deliveries so he's out all hours. I just read and do sketches and stuff.
Jade: You draw as well?
Megan: Erm, a bit. Birds and plants mostly. I don't really show anyone, it's kind of... it's just for me, do you know what I mean?
Jade: You should though. I bet they're well good. Like, I'm always putting my nails on Instagram and half of them are rubbish.
Megan: Maybe. Oh, I think we've only got like a minute left.
Jade: Is it? That's gone dead quick.
Megan: Sorry, I've been talking about birds the whole time.
Jade: Don't be daft, I've loved it.

Marijke: There you go, you should go and tell them.
Callum: Maybe.
Marijke: I'm a carer. Morning calls, washing, dressing, breakfast, make sure they take their tablets. Just part-time now, twelve hours. I finish by eleven and then the day is mine.
Callum: My mam's a care assistant. In a home, though.
Marijke: Oh, is she? Then she knows. It's hard on the body. My knees, I tell you, some of these houses have stairs like a lighthouse. And the parking, honestly, in the cul-de-sacs I go round and round. Last week I had to park by the shops and walk, and the lady I go to, she's ninety-one, she says, you're late, Marijke, and I say yes, I know, blame the man with the van. Callum: Mam says the same about her back.
Marijke: Everybody does. Do you live at home then?

Marijke: Very sensible. My son was the same, he stayed home till he was twenty-six, I couldn't get rid of him. Did you do that puzzle at the start? I was useless.
Callum: It was alright. Last one was a bit awkward.

Callum: Fair enough.
Marijke: So what are you going to do after? Building things?
Callum: Hopefully a graduate job round here. Drainage or highways. Then work towards chartership, then save for a house.
Marijke: You've got it all planned. Good for you. I never planned anything. I came on a coach holiday, met Keith, and that was that.
Callum: That's a bit different.
Marijke: Ha, a little bit. What else, erm... do you do anything for fun, or is it all books?
Callum: Gym mostly. Watch the Boro with my stepdad.
Marijke: Keith's football mad as well. All weekend, the telly. I just sit with my word search.

Then Jade asks if Megan's at uni, and Megan explains she's in her second year studying Wildlife, Ecology and Conservation Science at Writtle, describing fieldwork like bird surveys and small mammal trapping as her favorite part, though she struggles with the stats and writeups. Megan asks if Liam is Jade's boyfriend, learning they're actually married three years, with Liam working as an electrician currently away in Wakefield, leaving Jade home watching reality TV with Bella. Megan says that sounds nice compared to her own situation with a boyfriend doing deliveries at odd hours, mentioning she fills her time reading and sketching, which leads Jade to ask if she draws.

Megan admits she sketches birds and plants a bit, though she keeps it private rather than sharing it with others. Jade encourages her to post her art, comparing it to how she shares her nail designs on Instagram despite not loving all of them. They then realize their time is almost up, with Megan apologizing for talking about birds the whole call and Jade reassuring her she enjoyed it.

I'm settling on placing the event near the fleece blanket over the guinea pig cage shifting as the animal moves underneath, around the middle of the conversation. Now I'm sketching out the next pair, Marijke and Callum, with Callum keeping things brief and Marijke opening with some gentle joking about accents and age before getting into Callum's dissertation on drainage and her own stories about parking struggles and knee trouble.

Teesside. Marijke asks about bridges, but Callum explains his dissertation focuses on drainage for new housing estates, preventing flooding by managing rainwater runoff. Marijke relates this to flooded gardens near her in Sittingbourne, and Callum attributes it to poor soakaway design or clay ground, before Marijke mentions she works as a carer doing morning calls.

16 Callum mentions his mam works as a care assistant in a home. 17 Marijke sympathizes about the physical toll of the job, joking about tricky parking in cul-de-sacs and a ninety-one-year-old client who likes her porridge at half eight. 18 Callum starts to say his mam says something similar.

Marijke asks if he lives at home, and he confirms, mentioning he also works Saturdays at Morrisons to save on rent. She approves, comparing him to her own son who stayed home until twenty-six, then asks about the puzzle from earlier -- Callum thought it was fine though the last one felt a bit tricky, and Marijke jokes about just pressing buttons while her husband Keith teased her about it being "research." I'm flagging that Callum's line uses "were" instead of "was" -- not his dialect, so I should avoid that phrasing and correct it to "It was alright."

The conversation winds down: Callum talks about wanting a graduate job locally in drainage or highways, working toward chartership, and saving for a house, while Marijke contrasts this with her own unplanned life meeting Keith on a coach holiday. They touch on hobbies -- Callum's into the gym and watching Boro football with his stepdad, Marijke mentions Keith's similarly football-obsessed and she does word searches -- before Marijke signals the conversation is wrapping up.

Now moving to a new conversation, C0541, between Zain and Gemma, both from electrician households with Rob as the electrician figure. Zain mentions driving the M1 before asking about Gemma's job, and she explains she's a pharmacy technician at a Nottingham hospital, downplaying her role despite catching prescription errors on two wards. Zain pushes back on her modesty, calling it "proper important," and she concedes the point before asking about his work. Zain describes himself as a sparky doing domestic and commercial electrical work for a Manchester firm, mentioning EV chargers as the big growth area and an early start in Horwich that morning.

Zain shares the satisfying story of tracking down a tripping fault to a water-damaged outside socket in just forty minutes after others failed, pleasing the customer; Gemma reveals her husband Rob is also an electrician at a small local firm, which excites Zain and prompts him to send Rob solidarity over checking outside sockets. Zain then opens up about his plan to go self-employed in a couple of years with his own van, specializing in EV chargers and solar since that's where the money is, and Gemma starts responding enthusiastically before the thought cuts off.

The conversation continues naturally -- Gemma mentions Rob keeps talking about going self-employed but never does because the paperwork, tax, and insurance worry him, and Zain admits that's the part he'd outsource to someone else. They then shift to discussing a timed puzzle task, with Gemma admitting she overthought it by double-checking everything despite that being counterproductive under time pressure, while Zain just went with his gut and figures he got some wrong; they both agree his approach was probably smarter. The exchange ends with Zain noticing a dog in Gemma's photo and asking about it.

Good, that checks out with the dog detail mentioned earlier too, so I'm confident this is consistent and ready to finalize.

req.text:
You write transcripts of realistic video calls between strangers for a fully synthetic research dataset set in the UK. The study, in order (from its published design): a short puzzle task done alone; first impressions of the others' webcam photos; then a series of three-minute, one-on-one video calls in rounds, each person meeting the others in their group; after each call a short survey.

Call shape (from the original study's numbers): a call is cut off by a three-minute timer. A typical call has about 30 turns (most between 20 and 39) and about 570 words in total (most between 440 and 682); half of all turns are 12 words or fewer, and a quarter are 24 or more. Short acknowledgements ("yeah", "mm") count as turns too. So aim for about 570 words in about 30 turns: alongside the quick back-and-forth, people often talk in longer stretches (explaining their job, telling a story), and those long turns carry much of the call.

Guide to British conversational English (use it for how people talk; it is a description of speech, not a script):
How British people talk in casual conversation. This is a paraphrase of published descriptions of spoken British English; sources are in SOURCES.md. Use these features lightly and only where they fit the person. Never use them as a caricature.

- **Fillers.** British speakers hesitate with "erm" and "er". Women and younger speakers lean towards "erm".
- **Hedges.** "Sort of" is everywhere and steady. "Kind of" is spreading, and younger speakers use it more.
- **Politeness words.** "Please", "thank you", "thanks" and "sorry" mostly mean what they say. "Sorry" also works as a repair word (to correct yourself, or to ask someone to repeat) and can be ironic.
- **Tags at the end of a sentence.** "You know", "right", "okay", "yeah", "do you know what I mean". Among young Londoners, "innit" and "you get me" are rising. Tags depend on age and region only, never on ethnicity.
- **Echoing.** In an engaged conversation people pick up and re-use parts of each other's words.
- **Regional words and grammar** (from a recent dialect survey):
  - A bread roll is a "barm" in the North West (Manchester to Liverpool and western Lancashire), a "cob" around Nottinghamshire, a "bap" in Staffordshire, the West Midlands and North Wales, and a "batch" in Liverpool and Coventry.
  - Around Liverpool an ice lolly can be a "lolly ice".
  - The evening meal is "tea" in the North West, North East and Yorkshire, and "dinner" in the South East and London. Some people say both.
  - "Yous" or "youse" for plural "you" is common in the North East (Newcastle, Teesside), Liverpool and Scotland, less so in Manchester, and rare in York, Leeds and Sheffield.
  - "Give it me" is normal in the North West and West Midlands and widely accepted in Sheffield and York; it fades south of Birmingham, Coventry and Leicester.
  - "You was" is widely used, historically Northern and now found as far south as London.
- **Everyday British words** to draw on where they fit, without assigning them to regions: knackered or shattered, chuffed or made up, skint or brassic, mardy or stroppy, mum or mam, mate or pal, settee, sofa or couch.

The group (session S47). Persona cards, including the webcam photo each person was rated on:

P246 (Kirsty; transcript label: Kirsty):
- first name: Kirsty
- age: 36
- lives in: Burnley, North West England
- occupation: Not currently in paid work. She was a packing operative on the line at a food factory on the edge of town for nine years and was made redundant about fourteen months ago when the site cut a shift. She is on Universal Credit, applies for warehouse, retail and cleaning jobs, and does the occasional study on an online research panel for a bit of extra money.
- education detail: Left a local comprehensive with five GCSEs, including a B in Art and a C in English. She started a BTEC National in Art and Design at Burnley College but left partway through the second year when she needed to earn. She has since done a free online short course in local history and a Level 1 food hygiene certificate through work.
- household: Lives alone in a one-bedroom housing association flat on the first floor of a small block near the canal. She has an elderly cat called Moss. Her mum lives about ten minutes' walk away and her younger brother lives in Blackburn with his partner and kids.
- cultural background: White British, born and raised in Burnley to a working-class family. Her dad worked in a tyre depot and died when she was 24, and her mum was a dinner lady. She was brought up Church of England. She still believes and goes to a quiet early Sunday service at the parish church most weeks, sitting near the back, but avoids the social side like the coffee mornings. She is Lancashire through and through but not loud about it.
- professional persona: A steady, reliable worker who preferred jobs where she could get her head down and not have to make small talk. On the line she was quick and careful and was trusted to train new starters one at a time, which she found nerve-racking but managed. Job interviews make her very anxious and she over-prepares for them. She would rather email than phone an employer.
- sports persona: Not sporty. She walks a lot, mostly along the Leeds and Liverpool Canal towpath and up towards the moors when the weather's decent. She follows Burnley FC loosely because her dad did, and puts the radio on for scores, but she has not been to Turf Moor in years because the crowds are too much.
- arts persona: This is where she lights up, quietly. She sketches in pencil and fineliner: old mill chimneys, canal locks, her cat, bits of terraced streets. She posts some of it anonymously on an Instagram account with about 200 followers. She loves folk music and old ballads, reads a lot of library books, from historical fiction to odd nonfiction about folklore and witch trials (the Pendle witches fascinate her), and watches arthouse films on free streaming services late at night.
- travel persona: Hasn't been abroad since a school trip to France and a single week in Majorca with friends at 21. She likes day trips on the train or bus: Clitheroe, Hebden Bridge, Lancaster, sometimes the Lakes on a cheap advance ticket. She would love to see Brittany or the west coast of Ireland one day but money and nerves stop her. She plans trips in detail so there are no surprises.
- culinary persona: Cooks cheap and simple: big pans of stew or chilli frozen in portions, beans on toast, jacket potatoes. A barm with chips from the chippy is a Friday treat when she can afford it. Tea is around half five. She bakes when she's stressed, mostly flapjacks and banana bread, and drops some round to her mum's.
- hobbies and interests: pencil and pen sketching, long walks on the canal towpath and moors, local history and Pendle folklore, folk music and old ballads, reading library books, arthouse and foreign films, baking, doing online research studies, looking after her cat
- skills: careful, accurate manual work, drawing and observation, budgeting on a tight income, baking, patient one-to-one training of new starters, researching things thoroughly online, basic food hygiene
- career goals: Short term, a stable job with predictable hours and not too much customer contact, such as warehouse, stockroom or a back-of-house kitchen. Privately she would like to do something with art or heritage, like working in a museum shop, a framing workshop or as a volunteer-turned-staff at a local heritage site. She has looked at an Access to HE course in art but keeps putting off applying in case she's not good enough.
- voice: Quiet and a bit hesitant, especially at the start. She talks at a slowish pace with a soft Lancashire accent: flat vowels, 'bath' with a short a, and some dropped t's and h's. She uses 'erm' a lot and 'sort of' and 'I don't know' as hedges, and says 'sorry' when she loses her thread or mishears ('sorry, what was that?'). Northern usage comes out naturally rather than for show: 'tea' for the evening meal, 'barm', 'give it me', the odd 'our kid' for her brother, 'me mam' now and then, 'knackered', 'made up'. She doesn't fill silences herself. She waits, sometimes too long, then says 'erm, is that okay?' or 'I don't know if that's what you meant.' When a topic she cares about comes up, like drawing, the canal or old local stories, she speeds up a little and gives longer, more vivid answers before catching herself: 'sorry, I'm going on.'
- typing: Mostly lowercase with a capital at the start sometimes. Light punctuation: commas run things together and there's rarely a full stop at the end. Apostrophes are often dropped ('dont', 'im', 'its') but spelling is otherwise good. She writes 'idk' occasionally and 'tbh' quite a lot. Answers are short unless it's about something she's interested in, then they get surprisingly detailed. Example: 'not working at the min, got made redundant last year tbh its been hard'
- with strangers: Reserved and polite. She can come across as shy or a bit flat at first, with short answers and lots of 'yeah' and 'I think so'. She is obviously nervous about getting things 'wrong' and asks for reassurance. Underneath she is thoughtful and observant, and if the other person is patient and kind she warms up and shows a dry, gentle sense of humour. She never pushes herself forward and is careful not to complain too much.
- small things: her cat Moss knocking things off the windowsill, the canal being full of geese again, the price of a loaf at the corner shop, what she had for tea, a library book she's halfway through, the bus being late or cancelled, Burnley's results because her mum asks her, a sketch she did of the mill chimney near her, it raining again, having a good walk up by Pendle Hill at the weekend
- deeper things: losing her dad at 24 and still missing him, especially at church, how much the redundancy knocked her confidence and that some days she doesn't go out, anxiety that's never been formally diagnosed, and dreading the Jobcentre appointments, feeling she let herself down by leaving the art course, being lonely living on her own but also finding people exhausting, quietly wanting a partner but never quite knowing how to meet anyone, her faith being a private comfort rather than something she talks about, worry about her mum getting older and who'll look after her
- webcam photo: A laptop webcam shot taken from slightly below eye level, framed from the chest up, with her face a little off-centre to the left. Lighting comes mainly from a window to her right, giving soft daylight on one side of her face and leaving the other side slightly shadowed. She is a white woman in her mid-thirties with a pale complexion, light freckles across her nose, grey-blue eyes and a small, tentative closed-mouth smile. Her mid-brown hair is shoulder length and pulled back into a low, slightly loose ponytail, with a few strands falling by her face. She wears a dark green hooded sweatshirt with the hood down and small silver stud earrings, and no glasses. Behind her is a magnolia-painted wall with a cheap pine bookshelf holding a row of library books with plastic covers, a jar of pencils and fineliners, and a sketchbook lying flat. A small framed pencil drawing of a canal lock hangs on the wall beside the shelf. The arm of a grey fabric settee with a knitted throw over it is visible at the bottom right, and a grey-and-white cat's ear and back are just in frame on the cushion.

P247 (Neil; transcript label: Neil):
- first name: Neil
- age: 45
- lives in: Halifax, Yorkshire and The Humber
- occupation: Stonemason (banker and fixer) for a small heritage restoration firm based in Calderdale, working mostly on listed churches, mills and chapels across West Yorkshire
- education detail: Left school at 16 with GCSEs, a B in Art and Cs in most else. Did a three-year stonemasonry apprenticeship with an NVQ Level 3 through a college in Leeds. Later took a short accredited course in conservation of historic masonry and lime mortars. Has done a couple of free online courses in architectural history for his own interest.
- household: Lives alone in a two-up two-down stone terrace he bought after the divorce, about eight years ago. His daughter Ellie (16) lives with her mum in Brighouse and stays with him some weekends, less often now she's older. No pets, though he feeds a neighbour's cat when they're away.
- cultural background: White British, born and raised in Halifax. Dad was a bus driver, mum worked in a building society. Baptised Church of England and still calls himself Christian, though he's more of an occasional attender than a believer in any strict sense. He'll go to evensong at the Minster now and then, mainly for the choir and the building, and he's fairly private about what he actually believes. Grew up on rugby league, Saturday markets and his grandad's stories about the mills.
- professional persona: Twenty-plus years in the trade and good at it. Known for precise carving and for knowing his lime mortars properly. Blunt with clients and site managers when he thinks a spec is wrong, especially cement repointing on old stone, which he regards as vandalism. Doesn't do small talk on site but is reliable and turns up. Gets on with older craftsmen and architects who know their stuff, and has little patience for project managers who don't. Would rather work alone on a carved piece than run a gang.
- sports persona: Watches Halifax Panthers when he can and follows rugby league generally, but isn't fanatical. Does a lot of fell walking on his own, Calderdale Way, the Dales. Swims outdoors in reservoirs and the river most of the year without making a fuss about it. Stopped five-a-side years ago after a knee tweak and doesn't miss it.
- arts persona: Far more into the arts than people expect. Sketches buildings and carvings in a notebook, drawing being half the job anyway. Listens to a lot of jazz and some early church music, and will go to a concert at the Piece Hall or Leeds Town Hall on his own. Reads widely: history, a bit of philosophy, translated novels. Watches subtitled films and has opinions about them. Goes to the Hepworth in Wakefield and Yorkshire Sculpture Park a few times a year.
- travel persona: Travels alone, cheaply, and with a purpose, usually to look at buildings. Has done Rome, Florence, Barcelona, Lisbon, and a week walking in the Picos de Europa. Wants to see the cathedrals in northern France and the stone villages in Puglia. Not bothered about beach holidays. Happy to work out transport and food in places where he doesn't speak the language.
- culinary persona: Cooks properly for himself most nights, usually something like a stew, a curry or pasta, and has his tea around half six. Got into Italian cooking after Florence and makes his own pasta on Sundays occasionally. Still likes a pie and peas at a match, and a proper chippy tea on a Friday. Drinks real ale, not much, and has started on red wine. Doesn't like fussy restaurants.
- hobbies and interests: Sketching buildings and carved details, Fell walking and wild swimming, Jazz and choral music, Reading history and translated fiction, Learning Italian on an app, badly, Visiting churches and old mills, Cooking Italian food, Subtitled films
- skills: Stone carving and letter cutting, Lime mortar mixing and repointing, Reading architectural drawings, Freehand drawing, Basic Italian, Map reading and navigation on the fells, Fixing most things around the house
- career goals: Wants to do more carving and conservation and less basic rebuilding work. He's thinking about going self-employed in the next few years and taking on church and heritage commissions directly. He'd like to pass on the trade properly to an apprentice, as long as it's someone who actually cares. He has no interest in management.
- voice: Flat West Yorkshire accent, not heavy. Speaks fairly slowly and plainly, and says exactly what he thinks, sometimes more bluntly than is comfortable. Uses 'tea' for his evening meal, 'owt' and 'nowt' now and then, and 'love' or 'mate' occasionally. Says 'er' rather than 'erm' when thinking, and uses 'sort of' as a hedge, though not often. Will say 'nah, I don't think that's right, actually' without softening it. Comfortable with silence. He'll just stop talking when he's finished and not fill the gap, and he'll take his time before answering a question he finds interesting. Gets noticeably more animated about buildings, books or music.
- typing: Mostly lowercase, with a capital at the start only sometimes. Short sentences with full stops and the odd comma, and no exclamation marks. Usually keeps the apostrophes in 'don't' and 'it's' but doesn't fuss. Avoids text-speak apart from 'tbh' now and again. Answers are brief unless the question interests him, in which case he writes a proper paragraph.
- with strangers: Reserved but not shy. Polite enough at first and then quite direct. He can come across as a bit gruff or unimpressed, and won't laugh at things he doesn't find funny. If the conversation turns to something he's into, he opens up and asks good questions. Doesn't flatter people and doesn't need to be liked, which some find refreshing and others find hard work.
- small things: Had to redo someone else's cement pointing on a chapel last week, Swam at Gaddings Dam on Sunday, water was freezing, Reading a book about Brunelleschi's dome, Halifax lost again, Made a ragù that took four hours and was worth it, His van's due its MOT, Found a carved mason's mark on a job that he reckons is 1700s
- deeper things: The divorce was mostly his fault. He admits he was distant and wrapped up in work and his own interests., He worries less than he probably should, and his ex used to say that came across as not caring, He feels he's missing out on Ellie growing up and doesn't really know how to talk to her now, He goes to evensong partly because it's the only time he sits still with other people, He sometimes wonders if he should have gone to art school, His dad died a few years ago and he didn't cry at the funeral, which bothers his mum more than it bothers him
- webcam photo: Head-and-shoulders shot from a laptop on a kitchen table, angled slightly up so the ceiling and a light fitting are visible at the top of the frame. Daylight from a window to his left lights one side of his face, and the other side is in mild shadow. White man in his mid-forties with a broad, weathered face, short greying brown hair cut close at the sides, and a couple of days' stubble, mostly grey at the chin. No glasses. Neutral expression, looking at the screen rather than the lens, mouth closed, faintly sceptical. Wearing a faded navy crew-neck sweatshirt with a small paint mark near the collar. Behind him is a whitewashed exposed stone wall with a wooden shelf holding a row of cookbooks, a Moka pot and a jar of wooden spoons. A framed pencil sketch of a church window hangs slightly off-centre. To the right, part of a door frame is visible, with a hi-vis jacket hanging on a hook.

P248 (Kulwinder; transcript label: Kulwinder):
- first name: Kulwinder
- age: 50
- lives in: Hayes, West London (London Borough of Hillingdon)
- occupation: Not currently in paid work. Trained as a tailor and alterations machinist and worked in garment workrooms and a dry-cleaner's alterations counter for over 20 years. Stopped about three years ago because of arthritis in her hands and lower back pain, and her caring load as a lone parent.
- education detail: Left a comprehensive school in Hayes with GCSEs. Did a City & Guilds in fashion and textiles (garment making) at a local further education college, then learned most of the trade on the job in a workroom in Southall.
- household: Lives in a three-bedroom ex-council terraced house with her two children, a son of 19 doing an apprenticeship and a daughter of 15 doing her GCSEs. Separated from her husband for about four years. They are still legally married and haven't sorted out the divorce, partly because of the house and partly because of family. Her widowed mother lives ten minutes away and comes round most days.
- cultural background: British-born Punjabi Sikh. Her parents came from Jalandhar district in the late 1960s and her dad worked at Heathrow. She grew up in Hayes and Southall and speaks English at home with the kids and Punjabi with her mum and the aunties. She goes to the gurdwara in Hayes most Sundays and for gurpurabs, and does sewa in the langar kitchen when her back allows. Faith matters to her quietly and practically rather than as something she talks about a lot. The separation is a sore point with some relatives, and she has stopped going to certain family functions.
- professional persona: Precise, fast and fussy about finish when she was working. She took pride in hems that sat right and never cut corners even when the shop was rushed. She was honest with customers to the point of bluntness, telling people straight if a garment wasn't worth altering. She didn't suffer lazy colleagues and could be short with managers she felt were taking the mick. She was reliable, never late, and kept her own notebook of every job.
- sports persona: Not sporty. She walks to the shops and round Lake Farm Country Park when her back is okay, and has a physio sheet of exercises she does fairly religiously. She half-watches the cricket when India are playing because her son puts it on.
- arts persona: Not one for galleries or theatre and finds most of it a bit pretentious. Watches Indian dramas on Sony and Zee with her mum, Coronation Street, and the odd Bake Off. Likes old Punjabi songs from her parents' era, and kirtan on in the kitchen in the mornings.
- travel persona: Doesn't travel much and doesn't miss it. Went to Punjab for a relative's wedding about six years ago and found the heat and the crowds hard going. Prefers a day trip to Brighton or Windsor. Worries about flying and about money, so holidays have mostly stopped since the separation.
- culinary persona: Cooks dinner from scratch every night: dal, sabzi, rotis, and chicken curry on Fridays. Makes things the way her mum does and isn't keen on 'fusion' anything. Batch-cooks on Sundays. Her daughter wants pasta more often, which is an ongoing negotiation. Buys from the Indian grocer on the Uxbridge Road and does the big shop at Asda.
- hobbies and interests: Still sews for family: salwar kameez alterations, school uniform hems, curtains, Watching Indian TV dramas with her mum, Gurdwara and langar sewa, Keeping the house spotless, Growing chillies, mint and tomatoes in pots in the back garden, Doing online survey panels for a bit of extra money
- skills: Pattern adjustment and garment alterations, Industrial and domestic sewing machines, Hand finishing and invisible hemming, Running a tight household budget, Cooking for large numbers in a langar kitchen, Fluent spoken Punjabi, basic Gurmukhi reading, Dealing with council and benefits paperwork
- career goals: Would like to take in alterations from home a few days a week once her hands are managed better, word of mouth through the gurdwara and the school. She doesn't want to go back to a workroom or work for anyone else. Mainly wants to get her daughter through school and her son settled, and to get the house and divorce sorted without losing out.
- voice: West London accent, ordinary and fairly quick when she's sure of something, slower and more careful when a question is personal. Says 'erm' when thinking and 'sort of' a lot, with the odd 'you know' or 'do you know what I mean' at the end. Calls the evening meal dinner. Occasionally drops a Punjabi word ('haan', 'chalo') without thinking, then carries on. Answers directly, even curtly, if she thinks a question is daft. Doesn't fill silences much. She'll wait for you to ask the next thing rather than chat on. Says 'sorry, what was that?' if the line is bad, and apologises if her mum talks in the background.
- typing: Types properly: capital at the start, full stops, apostrophes mostly right. Short, plain answers. No emojis or text-speak, though she'll use 'etc' and sometimes '...' when she trails off. Occasionally an autocorrect slip because she types on her phone.
- with strangers: Polite but a bit guarded at first, and not warm in a gushing way. Wants to know what something is for and who will see her answers. Once she trusts that it's genuine she is very straight and honest, even about things that don't flatter her. Can come across as a bit sharp or unimpressed, especially if she feels she's being talked down to. Nervous about getting things 'wrong' on a study and will double-check instructions.
- small things: Her daughter's mock exams coming up, The 140 bus being late again, Her mum not taking her blood pressure tablets, Heathrow planes over the house, Asda putting prices up, Her son finally passing his driving theory, The boiler making a noise, Langar at the gurdwara last Sunday
- deeper things: Still being legally married and not knowing how to finish it without a fight over the house, Some relatives quietly blaming her for the separation, Worrying a lot at night about money and her health, Grief that her hands won't let her work like she used to, because sewing was who she was, Feeling she has to be both parents and not being allowed to be tired, Her dad dying before the kids really knew him
- webcam photo: Laptop on a kitchen table, camera slightly below eye level so it looks a little up at her. Daylight from a window to her left, with an overhead light on giving a slightly yellow cast. A South Asian woman of 50 with a round face, faint lines round the eyes and a polite, slightly wary closed-mouth smile. Shoulder-length black hair with grey at the parting, pulled back in a low clip. Thin rectangular reading glasses pushed up on her head. Wearing a plum-coloured knitted cardigan over a plain black top, with a thin steel kara on her right wrist resting near the keyboard. Behind her: a white fitted kitchen with a kettle, a bread bin and a jar of utensils on the worktop, a wall calendar from a local Indian grocer with dates written on it in biro, and a small framed picture of Guru Nanak on a shelf beside a spider plant. A school blazer hangs on the back of a chair at the edge of the frame.

P249 (Gemma; transcript label: Gemma):
- first name: Gemma
- age: 30
- lives in: Taunton, South West England
- occupation: Registered adult nurse on a surgical ward at the county hospital, Band 6 since last spring, working mostly long days on a rota
- education detail: GCSEs and A levels (Biology, Psychology, Sociology) at a sixth form college in Bridgwater; BSc (Hons) Adult Nursing from the University of Plymouth, graduated 2016; has since done a mentorship module and an in-house course on wound care
