P236 (Tomasz; transcript label: Tomasz):
- first name: Tomasz
- age: 38
- lives in: Ealing, London
- occupation: Sales executive at a premium German car dealership in Park Royal, west London. He sells new and approved used cars on a basic salary plus commission, and he is consistently near the top of the monthly league table.
- education detail: Bachelor's degree in economics and management from Wrocław University of Economics in Poland. He has done various manufacturer sales accreditation courses since joining the dealership, and he never took his English beyond what he picked up working in London.
- household: Rents a two-bedroom flat in a converted Victorian house near West Ealing with his partner of nine years, Hannah, a British-born community pharmacist. They are not married. Hannah raises it now and then and he deflects. No children, no pets. Hannah earns slightly more than him on paper, though his commission sometimes overtakes her in good months, and he likes to point that out.
- cultural background: Born and raised in Wrocław, Poland, in a working-class Catholic family. He came to London in 2008 at 22, initially to earn money for a year, and stayed. He calls himself Catholic but goes to Mass mainly at Christmas and Easter, usually at the Polish church in Ealing, and partly to keep his mum happy when she asks. He holds settled status and has thought about British citizenship mostly because it would make travel easier. He feels more Londoner than Pole day to day, but still watches Polish football and eats Polish food.
- professional persona: Confident, polished and very aware of how he comes across. He started on a phone sales floor selling broadband, then moved to a mid-range car dealer and then to the premium brand. He is good at reading what a customer wants to feel and selling them that. He is relaxed about stretching the truth on finance terms or a car's history if it gets a deal over the line, and he talks about colleagues who don't hit targets with open contempt. He is managed rather than liked by his sales manager, who tolerates him because the numbers are good.
- sports persona: Lifts weights four mornings a week at a mid-price gym on Ealing Broadway, mostly for appearance, and he will tell you his bench press if given half a chance. He watches the Premier League and supports Arsenal, an allegiance he picked up from flatmates in 2009. He also follows Śląsk Wrocław results online. He plays five-a-side occasionally with people from work and takes it too seriously.
- arts persona: Not much. He watches Netflix crime series and car shows with Hannah, and listens to house music and some Polish hip hop in the car. He has been to the theatre a handful of times because Hannah booked it, and he found musicals 'a bit much'. He follows a lot of car and watch accounts on Instagram.
- travel persona: Flies back to Wrocław two or three times a year to see his mum and sister. He prefers short, flashy holidays: Dubai, Marbella, a long weekend in Lisbon. He likes a decent hotel he can post about. Hannah prefers walking holidays in the Lake District, and they compromise badly.
- culinary persona: Cooks rarely; Hannah does most of it. He will make żurek or proper bigos when his mum's recipe comes up or when friends come round, and he is proud of it. Otherwise it's protein-heavy meals for the gym, Deliveroo, steak restaurants for celebrating a good month, and Polish deli runs for kabanos and twaróg. He calls the evening meal dinner.
- hobbies and interests: cars, especially performance models and car auctions, watches; he owns a second-hand Omega he is very pleased with, weightlifting, Arsenal and Polish football, poker nights with a few friends from the dealership, looking at property listings, mostly as a fantasy
- skills: closing a sale, reading people quickly, car finance and part-exchange negotiation, fluent Polish and fluent, accented English, basic Russian from school, getting tradespeople to knock money off
- career goals: Wants to become sales manager at the dealership within two years, then possibly move into a regional role or open his own used prestige car business with a friend. Mainly he wants more money and the visible signs of it: a bigger flat and a better car. He talks about buying a property in London 'before I'm forty', though he has not saved consistently towards it.
- voice: Fluent, quick and quite loud, with a clear Polish accent that has softened over sixteen years. Some vowels and the odd dropped article still give him away ('I went to gym this morning'). He has picked up London casual speech: 'mate', 'to be fair', 'you know what I mean', the occasional 'you was' without noticing. He uses 'sort of' and 'basically' a lot and hesitates with 'er' rather than 'erm', usually only when he is choosing a word in English. He doesn't like silence and fills it, often by turning the question back to something he has done or bought. He interrupts. When he disagrees he says so straight out: 'Nah, that's rubbish, to be honest.'
- typing: Fast and lowercase-heavy. He capitalises 'I' about half the time and skips most apostrophes ('dont', 'its', 'im'). He uses commas instead of full stops and runs sentences together. He writes 'tbh' and 'ok' and occasionally drops an article. He spells car and watch brands correctly and almost everything else roughly. No emojis in forms.

He can come across as cocky, and he name-drops prices and brands. If he decides you are not useful or not interesting, he gets noticeably shorter and more dismissive. He is happy to give strong opinions on anything.

- webcam photo: Head-and-shoulders shot from a laptop on a dining table, camera slightly below eye level so it looks a little up at him. Evening, lit mainly by a warm ceiling light overhead and the cool glow of the screen, which leaves faint shadows under his eyes. Broad-shouldered white man in his late thirties with short dark-blond hair, faded close at the sides and slightly longer and styled on top. Neatly trimmed short beard, light eyes, no glasses. He is half-smiling with one eyebrow slightly raised, leaning towards the camera. He wears a fitted black crew-neck T-shirt, and a steel watch is visible on his left wrist where his hand rests near his chin. Behind him: a light grey painted wall with a large framed black-and-white print of a vintage sports car, a tall green houseplant in a white pot in the corner, and part of a grey fabric sofa with a folded throw. On a shelf to the right sit a few cookery books, a small speaker and a framed photo too small to make out.

- first name: Gareth

- education detail: A-levels in Maths, Business Studies and Geography at a Solihull sixth form college; BSc in Quantity Surveying at Birmingham City University (2:1); chartered member of RICS since his late twenties, which the firm paid for and he made sure they did

=== CALL C0487 ===
Tomasz: Hello! Gareth, yeah? Tomasz. Finally, the last one.

Tomasz: Cars. Premium German, dealership in Park Royal. New and approved used. I'm usually top three on the league table every month.
Gareth: Right. Which brand?
Tomasz: I can't really say on this, mate, but you can guess. What do you drive?
Gareth: 5 Series. Leased. It's in for a service this week, actually.
Tomasz: Okay, nice. Good car. Which spec?
Gareth: M Sport.
Tomasz: Of course. Everybody wants M Sport. You lease through work or personal?
Gareth: Personal, for now. Car allowance comes with the next job up, hopefully.
Tomasz: Next job up, what is it, director?
Gareth: Commercial Director. Within five years, that's the plan. Here or somewhere bigger.
Tomasz: Same, same. I want sales manager in two years. Then maybe my own business, used prestige cars, with a friend. The manager now, honestly, he's not great. He's there because he's been there long time, you know what I mean.
Gareth: Yeah. There's a lot of that about.
Tomasz: You got it too? Old guys blocking the door?
Gareth: Something like that. I've gone for it twice. Didn't get it. Politics, mostly.
Tomasz: Politics. Always politics. You have to make numbers so big they can't ignore you, that's my thing. That's why I'm top. My manager doesn't like me, but he can't say nothing because of the numbers.
Gareth: That works until it doesn't.
Tomasz: Ha. Maybe. Nice watch, by the way, in your photo? No, wait, that was mine.
Gareth: Yours. I noticed it, to be fair. What is it?
Tomasz: Omega. Second-hand, but perfect condition, I got good price because the guy needed cash quick. Seamaster.
Gareth: Nice. What does one of them go for?
Tomasz: New, five, six grand. I paid much less. I always pay less. Same with builders, plumbers, I get them to knock off.
Gareth: That's most of my job, getting people to knock off.
Tomasz: See! Same job, different product. You play golf? You look like golf.
Gareth: Saturdays. Handicap fourteen. Eighty-seven last week.
Tomasz: I don't know if that's good, but it sounds good. I tried once in Marbella, I hit the ball into a swimming pool.
Gareth: That'll do it.
Tomasz: So, house, you own, yeah? Up there it's cheaper, everybody has house.
Gareth: Four-bed detached. New-build in Shirley.
Tomasz: Four-bed detached. Mate, in Ealing that's like three million. I'm still renting, honestly, but I want to buy before I'm forty. Two years, so—
Gareth: Better get saving, then.
Tomasz: Ha, yeah. Yeah, I know.

Rhys: It's Welsh. Means soon. Or never.

=== CALL C0489 ===
Darren: Hiya. Can you hear me alright?
Nasreen: Yes, hello. I'm Nasreen.
Darren: Darren. Nice to meet you.
Nasreen: You too. You are the last one for me.
Darren: Same here. Where are you?
Nasreen: Walsall.

Nasreen: Oh, not far.
Darren: No. What do you do?
Nasreen: Erm, I'm between jobs. Before, I was receptionist at a GP surgery.

Darren: That must be hard.
Nasreen: Yes. I talk to her every day, on the phone. But, you know.
Darren: Yeah.
Nasreen: You work with what?
Darren: Gas engineer. Boilers.
Nasreen: Oh. Our boiler, the house is rented, every winter it stops. The landlord sends somebody, he hits it, it works for one week.
Darren: Hits it?
Nasreen: Yes, with the hand. Like this.
Darren: That's not a repair, that. What's it doing, losing pressure?
Nasreen: I don't know. It says something, a number. F, something.
Darren: Fault code. Take a picture of it next time and give it to the landlord in writing. If it keeps going, he's got to get it properly sorted. You're entitled to heating.
Nasreen: Okay. Picture, then writing. Thank you.
Darren: No bother.
Nasreen: You have family?
Darren: Wife, two kids. And a spaniel, Bonnie.
Nasreen: Spaniel. The ones with the long ears?
Darren: That's her. Rolls in everything.
Nasreen: Ha. My son wants a dog. I said no, who will walk it?
Darren: That's what I said. Guess who walks it.
Nasreen: You?
Darren: Every morning, before work.

For the final round, everyone meets their last remaining partner: Tomasz-Gareth, Rhys-Ollie, Nasreen-Darren, with no private event this time. I'm aiming for roughly 30 turns and 570 words, staying true to each character's cards—Tomasz and Gareth will have a status-driven exchange, each subtly sizing the other up, with Gareth's BMW lease and Tomasz's premium German car sales giving them overlapping territory without needing to name the brand outright.

Gareth brings up upgrades and golf while Tomasz mentions his bench press and Omega watch, which Gareth notices and clocks as decent. Gareth stays calm and gives short answers throughout.

For Rhys and Ollie, I'm connecting them through five-a-side football on Wednesdays, with Rhys rating Ollie a 7/7, veering into Benidorm stories and nights out, while Ollie counters with parkrun and Watford talk—Rhys might bring up personal training, Ollie his running shop connection, both touching on FPL, with Ollie staying a bit guarded ("innit") around someone new.

Nasreen and Darren, both quieter and more reserved, need a slower pace with Darren comfortable in silence and Nasreen patient—I want to work in Black Country references like Walsall and Stourbridge, maybe her rented terrace's boiler, his mum's health, and her own mother, with Darren warming up over practical talk and a nice moment where he mentions sorting his mum's GP appointments and Nasreen offers a helpful tip about booking systems.

req.text:
You write transcripts of realistic video calls between strangers for a fully synthetic research dataset set in the UK. The study, in order (from its published design): a short puzzle task done alone; first impressions of the others' webcam photos; then a series of three-minute, one-on-one video calls in rounds, each person meeting the others in their group; after each call a short survey.

Call shape (from the original study's numbers): a call is cut off by a three-minute timer. A typical call has about 30 turns (most between 20 and 39) and about 570 words in total (most between 440 and 682); half of all turns are 12 words or fewer, and a quarter are 24 or more. Short acknowledgements ("yeah", "mm") count as turns too. So aim for about 570 words in about 30 turns: alongside the quick back-and-forth, people often talk in longer stretches (explaining their job, telling a story), and those long turns carry much of the call.

Guide to British conversational English (use it for how people talk; it is a description of speech, not a script):
How British people talk in casual conversation. This is a paraphrase of published descriptions of spoken British English; sources are in SOURCES.md. Use these features lightly and only where they fit the person. Never use them as a caricature.

- **Fillers.** British speakers hesitate with "erm" and "er". Women and younger speakers lean towards "erm".
- **Hedges.** "Sort of" is everywhere and steady. "Kind of" is spreading, and younger speakers use it more.
- **Politeness words.** "Please", "thank you", "thanks" and "sorry" mostly mean what they say. "Sorry" also works as a repair word (to correct yourself, or to ask someone to repeat) and can be ironic.
- **Tags at the end of a sentence.** "You know", "right", "okay", "yeah", "do you know what I mean". Among young Londoners, "innit" and "you get me" are rising. Tags depend on age and region only, never on ethnicity.
- **Echoing.** In an engaged conversation people pick up and re-use parts of each other's words.
- **Regional words and grammar** (from a recent dialect survey):
  - A bread roll is a "barm" in the North West (Manchester to Liverpool and western Lancashire), a "cob" around Nottinghamshire, a "bap" in Staffordshire, the West Midlands and North Wales, and a "batch" in Liverpool and Coventry.
  - Around Liverpool an ice lolly can be a "lolly ice".
  - The evening meal is "tea" in the North West, North East and Yorkshire, and "dinner" in the South East and London. Some people say both.
  - "Yous" or "youse" for plural "you" is common in the North East (Newcastle, Teesside), Liverpool and Scotland, less so in Manchester, and rare in York, Leeds and Sheffield.
  - "Give it me" is normal in the North West and West Midlands and widely accepted in Sheffield and York; it fades south of Birmingham, Coventry and Leicester.
  - "You was" is widely used, historically Northern and now found as far south as London.
- **Everyday British words** to draw on where they fit, without assigning them to regions: knackered or shattered, chuffed or made up, skint or brassic, mardy or stroppy, mum or mam, mate or pal, settee, sofa or couch.

req.text:
You write transcripts of realistic video calls between strangers for a fully synthetic research dataset set in the UK. The study, in order (from its published design): a short puzzle task done alone; first impressions of the others' webcam photos; then a series of three-minute, one-on-one video calls in rounds, each person meeting the others in their group; after each call a short survey.

Call shape (from the original study's numbers): a call is cut off by a three-minute timer. A typical call has about 30 turns (most between 20 and 39) and about 570 words in total (most between 440 and 682); half of all turns are 12 words or fewer, and a quarter are 24 or more. Short acknowledgements ("yeah", "mm") count as turns too. So aim for about 570 words in about 30 turns: alongside the quick back-and-forth, people often talk in longer stretches (explaining their job, telling a story), and those long turns carry much of the call.

Guide to British conversational English (use it for how people talk; it is a description of speech, not a script):
How British people talk in casual conversation. This is a paraphrase of published descriptions of spoken British English; sources are in SOURCES.md. Use these features lightly and only where they fit the person. Never use them as a caricature.

- **Fillers.** British speakers hesitate with "erm" and "er". Women and younger speakers lean towards "erm".
- **Hedges.** "Sort of" is everywhere and steady. "Kind of" is spreading, and younger speakers use it more.
- **Politeness words.** "Please", "thank you", "thanks" and "sorry" mostly mean what they say. "Sorry" also works as a repair word (to correct yourself, or to ask someone to repeat) and can be ironic.
- **Tags at the end of a sentence.** "You know", "right", "okay", "yeah", "do you know what I mean". Among young Londoners, "innit" and "you get me" are rising. Tags depend on age and region only, never on ethnicity.
- **Echoing.** In an engaged conversation people pick up and re-use parts of each other's words.
- **Regional words and grammar** (from a recent dialect survey):
  - A bread roll is a "barm" in the North West (Manchester to Liverpool and western Lancashire), a "cob" around Nottinghamshire, a "bap" in Staffordshire, the West Midlands and North Wales, and a "batch" in Liverpool and Coventry.
  - Around Liverpool an ice lolly can be a "lolly ice".
  - The evening meal is "tea" in the North West, North East and Yorkshire, and "dinner" in the South East and London. Some people say both.
  - "Yous" or "youse" for plural "you" is common in the North East (Newcastle, Teesside), Liverpool and Scotland, less so in Manchester, and rare in York, Leeds and Sheffield.
  - "Give it me" is normal in the North West and West Midlands and widely accepted in Sheffield and York; it fades south of Birmingham, Coventry and Leicester.
  - "You was" is widely used, historically Northern and now found as far south as London.
- **Everyday British words** to draw on where they fit, without assigning them to regions: knackered or shattered, chuffed or made up, skint or brassic, mardy or stroppy, mum or mam, mate or pal, settee, sofa or couch.

The group (session S50). Persona cards, including the webcam photo each person was rated on:

P261 (Gemma; transcript label: Gemma):
- first name: Gemma
- age: 38
- lives in: Huntingdon, East of England
- occupation: Site operations manager at a third-party logistics distribution centre near Alconbury, responsible for about 180 warehouse staff across three shifts
- education detail: Left school in St Neots with GCSEs and two A-levels (Business Studies and PE, mediocre grades). Started as a temp picker at 19, made shift supervisor at 23, and later did a part-funded CMI Level 5 in Management and Leadership through work. She never finished the written assignments on time but got through.
- household: Lives with her husband Craig, 41, a self-employed electrician, in a four-bed new-build on an estate on the edge of Huntingdon. They have one son, Alfie, aged 9, and a cockapoo called Biscuit. Craig does most of the school runs because Gemma's hours are unpredictable.
- cultural background: White British, born and raised in Cambridgeshire. Her dad was a lorry driver and her mum worked in a school kitchen. She was brought up without religion and doesn't think about it. She is the first in her family to be on a salary like hers and is quietly proud of that, though she would never say so in those words.
- professional persona: Direct, fast and short-tempered. She is good in a crisis: a missed trailer, an agency no-show, a client screaming about peak volumes. She is much worse at the steady paperwork side. Her inbox runs into the thousands, she forgets one-to-ones, and she leans heavily on her deputy, Priya, to keep the KPIs reporting and the audits tidy. Staff see her as fair but harsh. She doesn't sugar-coat, she has little patience for excuses, and she will tell a team leader in front of others that something is 'not good enough'. Her 50-60 hour weeks come more from firefighting than from planning.
- sports persona: Not sporty in any committed way. She used to play netball at school and has a gym membership she uses in fits and starts, usually after a comment about her weight or a holiday booking. She watches the football if Craig has it on (he supports Arsenal) but isn't fussed. She walks Biscuit round Hinchingbrooke Country Park at weekends.
- arts persona: Very little interest. She watches telly in the evenings: Gogglebox, Married at First Sight, the odd true-crime documentary, and whatever series everyone at work is talking about. She has been to a couple of musicals in London for hen dos and birthdays and enjoyed the drinks more than the show. She doesn't read books beyond a holiday paperback.
- travel persona: One big summer holiday a year, ideally somewhere hot and all-inclusive: Tenerife, Turkey, once Cancún. She likes a pool, a sunbed and not having to organise anything. Weekend breaks to Center Parcs with Alfie. Craig books everything because she leaves it too late. She has no real interest in sightseeing or 'finding the authentic bit'.
- culinary persona: Doesn't enjoy cooking and doesn't pretend to. Weeknight dinners are whatever Craig throws together, a ready meal, or a takeaway on Fridays (usually Indian or a Chinese from the place on the high street). She likes a roast at her mum's on Sundays. She drinks rosé or a gin and tonic and has a steady habit of coffee from the vending machine at work.
- hobbies and interests: Watching reality TV with a glass of wine, Walking the dog at Hinchingbrooke, Occasional nights out with old school friends in St Neots, Scrolling Facebook Marketplace for things she doesn't need, Following her son's football team on Saturday mornings, mostly from the car with a coffee
- skills: Managing large shift-based teams, Handling difficult clients and agency suppliers, Making quick operational decisions under pressure, Warehouse management systems and labour planning (at a practical level), Holding people to account, sometimes too bluntly, Forklift licence (lapsed)
- career goals: Wants to be a general manager running a bigger site, or a regional ops role, mainly for the money and so she doesn't have to answer to her current GM, whom she thinks is useless. She has no plan for how to get there beyond 'keep the numbers up and apply when something comes up'. She has turned down a move to Daventry because she won't relocate.
- voice: Mid-pace, slightly clipped, a fairly neutral south-east Midlands/East Anglian accent with dropped t's ('a lo' of'). Says 'dinner' for her evening meal, and 'mum'. Uses 'erm' when she's thinking and 'sort of' a fair bit, and ends points with 'yeah?' or 'you know'. She is blunt and will answer a question she finds silly with a flat 'Not really' or 'Dunno, never thought about it.' She doesn't fill silences to be nice; she waits for the next question or says 'Is that it?' She can be dryly funny, usually at someone else's expense, and says 'knackered' a lot.
- typing: Quick and careless. Mostly lowercase, drops apostrophes ('dont', 'im'), few full stops, and runs sentences together with commas. She uses 'tbh' and 'idk' and the occasional 'lol' when she's being sarcastic. Short answers, often a single line, and she won't go back to fix typos.
- with strangers: Polite enough on the surface but impatient. She wants to know what this is and how long it'll take. She can come across as cold or a bit dismissive at first, and doesn't do much small talk or warm agreement. Once she's decided you're not wasting her time she relaxes slightly and gets chattier, mostly complaining about work.
- small things: The dog has chewed another charging cable, Peak season at work is 'a nightmare every year, without fail', The A14 roadworks, Alfie's football kit always being muddy and never washed in time, Wanting to book Tenerife again, Being knackered after a run of night-shift cover
- deeper things: She feels like a worse mum than Craig and gets defensive about it, She knows people at work don't really like her and tells herself she doesn't care, Her dad's health has been going downhill, and she hasn't visited as much as she should, She sometimes wonders whether the long hours are really worth it, then shuts the thought down, She and Craig argue about money even though they're comfortable
- webcam photo: Laptop webcam at a slightly low angle, so the shot looks a little up at her chin. She's sitting at the kitchen island in the evening under bright overhead spotlights, with a slightly cold white cast. Head and shoulders are framed slightly off-centre to the left. She has a round face with light make-up worn off from the day, a faint frown and a flat, unimpressed expression with one eyebrow slightly raised. Her shoulder-length highlighted blonde hair is scraped back into a low claw clip, with darker roots showing. She wears a navy quarter-zip fleece with a small embroidered company logo on the chest, and no glasses. Behind her are grey gloss kitchen cabinets, a black kettle and a toaster, a half-full glass of rosé on the counter, a stack of post and a school letter held by a magnet on the American-style fridge, and the edge of a dog bed on the floor with part of a brown cockapoo visible.

P262 (Bethany; transcript label: Bethany):
- first name: Bethany
- age: 23
- lives in: Bridgwater, South West England
- occupation: Currently not in paid work and looking for a job. Her last job was a fixed-term seasonal contract on a packing line at a food warehouse, which ended over a year ago. She volunteers two mornings a week at a hospice charity shop in the town centre.
- education detail: Nine GCSEs from a local secondary, including a 7 in Art and a 6 in English. She then did a Level 3 Extended Diploma in Art and Design at Bridgwater & Taunton College. She thought about university but didn't want the debt and wasn't sure she'd cope living away. She has since done a free online Level 2 course in customer service.
- household: Lives with her boyfriend Kieran, 25, in a rented one-bedroom flat above a takeaway near the town centre. They've been together four years and lived together for two. Kieran works shifts as a forklift driver at a distribution centre off the M5, and his wage covers most of the rent. req.text:
You write transcripts of realistic video calls between strangers for a fully synthetic research dataset set in the UK. The study, in order (from its published design): a short puzzle task done alone; first impressions of the others' webcam photos; then a series of three-minute, one-on-one video calls in rounds, each person meeting the others in their group; after each call a short survey.

Call shape (from the original study's numbers): a call is cut off by a three-minute timer. A typical call has about 30 turns (most between 20 and 39) and about 570 words in total (most between 440 and 682); half of all turns are 12 words or fewer, and a quarter are 24 or more. Short acknowledgements ("yeah", "mm") count as turns too. So aim for about 570 words in about 30 turns: alongside the quick back-and-forth, people often talk in longer stretches (explaining their job, telling a story), and those long turns carry much of the call.

Guide to British conversational English (use it for how people talk; it is a description of speech, not a script):
How British people talk in casual conversation. This is a paraphrase of published descriptions of spoken British English; sources are in SOURCES.md. Use these features lightly and only where they fit the person. Never use them as a caricature.

- **Fillers.** British speakers hesitate with "erm" and "er". Women and younger speakers lean towards "erm".
- **Hedges.** "Sort of" is everywhere and steady. "Kind of" is spreading, and younger speakers use it more.
- **Politeness words.** "Please", "thank you", "thanks" and "sorry" mostly mean what they say. "Sorry" also works as a repair word (to correct yourself, or to ask someone to repeat) and can be ironic.
- **Tags at the end of a sentence.** "You know", "right", "okay", "yeah", "do you know what I mean". Among young Londoners, "innit" and "you get me" are rising. Tags depend on age and region only, never on ethnicity.
- **Echoing.** In an engaged conversation people pick up and re-use parts of each other's words.
- **Regional words and grammar** (from a recent dialect survey):
  - A bread roll is a "barm" in the North West (Manchester to Liverpool and western Lancashire), a "cob" around Nottinghamshire, a "bap" in Staffordshire, the West Midlands and North Wales, and a "batch" in Liverpool and Coventry.
  - Around Liverpool an ice lolly can be a "lolly ice".
  - The evening meal is "tea" in the North West, North East and Yorkshire, and "dinner" in the South East and London. Some people say both.
  - "Yous" or "youse" for plural "you" is common in the North East (Newcastle, Teesside), Liverpool and Scotland, less so in Manchester, and rare in York, Leeds and Sheffield.
  - "Give it me" is normal in the North West and West Midlands and widely accepted in Sheffield and York; it fades south of Birmingham, Coventry and Leicester.
  - "You was" is widely used, historically Northern and now found as far south as London.
- **Everyday British words** to draw on where they fit, without assigning them to regions: knackered or shattered, chuffed or made up, skint or brassic, mardy or stroppy, mum or mam, mate or pal, settee, sofa or couch.

Joanne: Oh, Kent. I nearly said when I saw your picture, you remind me of my sister Michelle. Sorry, is that a strange thing to say?

Tracey: Shelf stacking. Supermarket, early mornings. Up at quarter past four, start at five, done at eleven.

Joanne: Did she really? Oh, it's hard graft, isn't it, people don't realise. It's not just dishing up. You're doing the prep, you're watching for allergies, there's always one who's crying 'cause his yoghurt's the wrong colour, and then you're on your hands and knees wiping the hall down after. My knees aren't what they was.

Joanne: Ha! I'd like a rule like that. Is she still going, your mum?

Joanne: They do. Sorry, that's a bit heavy for three minutes, isn't it? I don't know if that's what you wanted.

=== CALL C0575 ===
Joanne: Hello, love, can you hear me? I'm Joanne, from Gosport.
Shazia: Yeah. Shazia. Walsall.
Joanne: Oh, the Midlands. Erm, I never know how to start these. What do you do, Shazia?
Shazia: Nothing at the minute. I'm at home with the kids. I used to pack at a warehouse but me back went.
Joanne: Oh, I'm sorry. Backs are awful. Mine's not brilliant either, and my knees. I'm a kitchen assistant at a primary school, have been for eleven years.
Shazia: School kitchen? That's what I was thinking of doing. Once my youngest goes up to secondary. Dinner lady or a TA, something in school hours.
Joanne: Oh, you'd be lovely at it! Honestly. It's term-time, so you get the holidays with your kids, that's the big thing.
Shazia: Is it hard on your back, though? To be honest that's what I'm worried about.
Joanne: Erm, I won't lie to you, love, it can be. It's the standing, and the lifting the big trays out of the oven, and then wiping all the tables in the hall after. Some days I go home and I can barely get up the stairs to my flat. But our cook's good, she'll swap me onto the till or the salad bit if I'm struggling. It depends on the school, really. I'd say ask them what the actual jobs are before you start. Sorry, I don't want to put you off.
Shazia: No, that's helpful. Better you say it.
Joanne: Have you got your food hygiene? That's the first thing they ask.
Shazia: Yeah, I done it online. And first aid.
Joanne: Well, there you go, you're halfway there already.
Shazia: I started a childcare NVQ years ago. Never finished it. Had my first.
Joanne: That's life, isn't it. How many have you got?
Shazia: Three. Seventeen, fourteen and nine.
Joanne: Oh, that's a houseful. I bet tea time's busy.
Shazia: It's every day. I do curry, daal, chapatis, then the kids moan they want fish fingers. So I'm making two teas. And my mother-in-law comes round most afternoons, so that's another one.
Joanne: Every afternoon?
Shazia: Most. She's alright. She just sits there and tells me how to do things, d'you know what I mean.
Joanne: Oh dear. Ha. My mum used to do that, God rest her. She'd stand at my cooker going "you want more salt in that".
Shazia: Yeah. That's her.
Joanne: Do you get a bit of time for yourself at all?
Shazia: Dramas. Pakistani dramas on YouTube, at night. I'm hooked on one now, she's just found out her husband's been lying about everything.
Joanne: Oh, I love a drama! I'm all crime ones and The Chase. And I do a bit of crochet, little hats for the baby unit at the hospital.
Shazia: That's nice, that.
Joanne: Thank you, love. I don't know if that's very interesting.
Shazia: It is. More useful than me watching YouTube.
Joanne: Oh no, we all need our telly. What do they eat at your house for a treat, then?
Shazia: Chips from the chippy on a Friday, in a bap. Hamza won't have it any other way.
Joanne: Friday fish and chips, same as me!

=== CALL C0576 ===
Chiamaka: Hello hello! Can you hear me okay? I'm Chiamaka, in Leeds.
Tracey: Yeah. Tracey. Sittingbourne, in Kent.
Chiamaka: Kent! The garden of England, they call it, right? So what do you do, Tracey?
Tracey: Shelf stacking. Early mornings at a supermarket. What about you, you're a nurse or something? I saw the top.
Chiamaka: Doctor, actually! Acute medicine. But honestly, the nurses run the place, I just get the credit, ha. I've just come off four nights so I'm a bit loopy.
Tracey: Four nights. I'm up at quarter past four and I moan about it.
Chiamaka: No, quarter past four is a proper night shift, that counts! You're on your feet the whole time as well, lifting, everything.
Tracey: Yeah. Quicker than most of them, to be honest. I just want it done so I can go home at eleven.
Chiamaka: I love that. Get in, get it done, go home. I wish I could do that, but there's always one more discharge summary.
Tracey: Can I ask you something, since you're a doctor?
Chiamaka: Go on, everyone does! My whole family WhatsApp asks me.
Tracey: My mum's getting forgetful. Like, leaving the gas on, asking the same thing three times. She's had the memory test at the GP and they've referred her, but it's been months. Is that normal, the wait?
Chiamaka: Erm. Honestly? Yeah, the memory clinic waits are long, it's not just you. What I'd say is, if something happens, like a fall, or she gets suddenly confused, really suddenly, over a day or two, that's different, that can be an infection, and you get her seen quickly. Don't wait on the clinic for that. And keep a little list of what you notice, dates and that, because when you finally get in, they'll ask, and you'll forget. Everyone forgets in the room.
Tracey: Right. That's useful. My sister's no help.
Chiamaka: It's always one daughter doing it, isn't it. I'm the eldest, I know. Even from Leeds I'm the one sorting everything back home in Nigeria.
Tracey: Do you get back much?
Chiamaka: About every eighteen months. Not enough, really.
Tracey: Long way, though.
Chiamaka: It is. My poor mum. Anyway! Do you go on holiday? Please say yes, I need to live through someone.
Tracey: Tenerife. Been four times. All-inclusive, sunbed, done.
Chiamaka: Tenerife! I've not done Tenerife. I did Dubai last year, and Barcelona, with my girls. Lots of dressing up, lots of photos.
Tracey: I don't do the photos. Dean takes one of me looking miserable by the pool and that's it.
Chiamaka: Ha! That's the real holiday photo, though. Mine are all fake, I'm standing there for twenty minutes.
Tracey: What d'you watch, then, after all them nights?
Chiamaka: Love Island. I'm not ashamed.
Tracey: I watch Gogglebox. Anything with people arguing, really.
Chiamaka: Yes! That's the best telly. Who's your favourite on Gogglebox?
Tracey: The ones that hate everything.
Chiamaka: Ha, of course. I think we'd get on, Tracey.
Tracey: Yeah, you're alright.

=== CALL C0577 ===
Gemma: Hi, can you hear me? I'm Gemma, Hornchurch.
Ryan: Yeah. Ryan. Castleford.
Gemma: Okay. So what do you do, Ryan?
Ryan: Mechanic. Independent garage. MOT tester an' all.
Gemma: Oh, useful. My husband's an electrician, so between us we'd be a whole trades directory. I'm a speech and language therapist.
Ryan: Right. Kids?
Gemma: Mostly children, yeah. Speech sounds, language delays. I'm self-employed.
Ryan: Fair enough.
Gemma: ...So, do you enjoy it? The garage?
Ryan: It's alright. I like the work. Don't like customers much.
Gemma: Ha. Honest. What's wrong with the customers?
Ryan: People argue about the quote. They think you're making it up. You show 'em the worn pads and they still say it's too much. I'd rather just be under the car.
Gemma: See, I get that, actually. I get parents who argue about my rates, and I've got ten years in the NHS behind me. I know what I'm worth. And then they don't do the home practice and wonder why nothing's changed.
Ryan: Same. Folk don't check their oil for three years then come in when it's seized.
Gemma: Exactly. That's exactly it. Erm, have you ever thought about going on your own? Self-employed?
Ryan: Bit. Mobile mechanic, maybe. Have a van. No boss.
Gemma: What's stopping you?
Ryan: Dunno. Money. Getting the van. Getting round to it.
Gemma: Sorry, can I be blunt? "Getting round to it" isn't really a reason. You need a plan. Costs, how many jobs a week you'd need, whether you'd keep some hours at the garage at first. That's what I did. I had a spreadsheet before I handed my notice in.
Ryan: Yeah. Probably.
Gemma: Sorry, I'm not having a go.
Ryan: No, it's fine. Chloe says the same.
Gemma: Chloe's your partner?
Ryan: Girlfriend. Works in a nursery.
Gemma: Well, she sounds sensible. Electric cars, is that something you'd have to learn?
Ryan: Yeah, if I wanted to stay in it long term. Garage might pay for the course. Haven't asked.
Gemma: Ask. Honestly. Worst case, they say no.
Ryan: Fair.
Gemma: What do you drive, then? Something flash, I imagine.
Ryan: Old Focus ST. Doing it up. Been waiting on a part for six week.
Gemma: Six weeks! Dean'd be climbing the walls. What's it for, the part?
Ryan: Turbo. Hard to get hold of.
Gemma: Right. I won't pretend I know what that means.
Ryan: Makes it go quicker.
Gemma: Ha. Fair enough.

req.text:
You write transcripts of realistic video calls between strangers for a fully synthetic research dataset set in the UK. The study, in order (from its published design): a short puzzle task done alone; first impressions of the others' webcam photos; then a series of three-minute, one-on-one video calls in rounds, each person meeting the others in their group; after each call a short survey.

Call shape (from the original study's numbers): a call is cut off by a three-minute timer. A typical call has about 30 turns (most between 20 and 39) and about 570 words in total (most between 440 and 682); half of all turns are 12 words or fewer, and a quarter are 24 or more. Short acknowledgements ("yeah", "mm") count as turns too. So aim for about 570 words in about 30 turns: alongside the quick back-and-forth, people often talk in longer stretches (explaining their job, telling a story), and those long turns carry much of the call.

Guide to British conversational English (use it for how people talk; it is a description of speech, not a script):
How British people talk in casual conversation. This is a paraphrase of published descriptions of spoken British English; sources are in SOURCES.md. Use these features lightly and only where they fit the person. Never use them as a caricature.

- **Fillers.** British speakers hesitate with "erm" and "er". Women and younger speakers lean towards "erm".
- **Hedges.** "Sort of" is everywhere and steady. "Kind of" is spreading, and younger speakers use it more.
- **Politeness words.** "Please", "thank you", "thanks" and "sorry" mostly mean what they say. "Sorry" also works as a repair word (to correct yourself, or to ask someone to repeat) and can be ironic.
- **Tags at the end of a sentence.** "You know", "right", "okay", "yeah", "do you know what I mean". Among young Londoners, "innit" and "you get me" are rising. Tags depend on age and region only, never on ethnicity.
- **Echoing.** In an engaged conversation people pick up and re-use parts of each other's words.
- **Regional words and grammar** (from a recent dialect survey):
  - A bread roll is a "barm" in the North West (Manchester to Liverpool and western Lancashire), a "cob" around Nottinghamshire, a "bap" in Staffordshire, the West Midlands and North Wales, and a "batch" in Liverpool and Coventry.
  - Around Liverpool an ice lolly can be a "lolly ice".
  - The evening meal is "tea" in the North West, North East and Yorkshire, and "dinner" in the South East and London. Some people say both.
  - "Yous" or "youse" for plural "you" is common in the North East (Newcastle, Teesside), Liverpool and Scotland, less so in Manchester, and rare in York, Leeds and Sheffield.
  - "Give it me" is normal in the North West and West Midlands and widely accepted in Sheffield and York; it fades south of Birmingham, Coventry and Leicester.
  - "You was" is widely used, historically Northern and now found as far south as London.
- **Everyday British words** to draw on where they fit, without assigning them to regions: knackered or shattered, chuffed or made up, skint or brassic, mardy or stroppy, mum or mam, mate or pal, settee, sofa or couch.

The group (session S52). Persona cards, including the webcam photo each person was rated on:

P271 (Megan; transcript label: Megan):
- first name: Megan
- age: 20
- lives in: Chelmsford, East of England
- occupation: Full-time student, second year of a BSc in Wildlife, Ecology and Conservation Science. No paid job during term at the moment. She gave up weekend shifts at a garden centre café to focus on coursework and placements.
- education detail: Did GCSEs at a comprehensive in Harlow, then A-levels in Biology, Geography and English Language at a sixth form college (B, B, C). Now in her second year at the Writtle campus outside Chelmsford, funded by a student loan and maintenance loan. She is the first in her immediate family to go to university.
- household: Lives with her boyfriend Jordan, 22, in a small rented one-bedroom flat above a row of shops on the edge of Chelmsford. Jordan works long shifts as a multi-drop delivery driver. Money is tight and they split bills down the middle. They have a rescue guinea pig called Biscuit. Her mum and younger brother live in Harlow, about forty minutes away, and she visits most Sundays.
- cultural background: Grew up in Harlow in a working-class family. Her mum is a school dinner lady and her dad left when she was nine. She sees him a few times a year. Her nan and her nan's allotment were a big part of her childhood and the reason she got into nature. The family isn't religious and doesn't do much ceremony beyond big family Christmases at her aunt's.
- professional persona: Conscientious enough to hand things in on time but often finishes at midnight the night before. She is happiest on fieldwork days doing bird transects, small mammal trapping or pond dipping, and less confident writing up stats. Tutors find her keen and kind. She is quick to help coursemates but worries a lot about grades and about saying the wrong thing in seminars.
- sports persona: Not sporty in a team sense. She walks a lot, both for fieldwork and for fun, and has started going to a beginners' yoga class at the leisure centre with a friend from her course. She'll watch the Women's Euros or the Lionesses if Jordan has the football on, but wouldn't seek it out.
- arts persona: Loves nature documentaries, especially anything with David Attenborough narrating, and cries at most of them. She reads fantasy and cosy romance novels from the library and keeps a sketchbook of birds and plants that she's a bit shy about showing anyone. Listens to Hozier, Phoebe Bridgers and Taylor Swift.
- travel persona: Hasn't travelled much. She had one family holiday to Majorca at fourteen, a few caravan weekends in Norfolk and Suffolk, and a residential field trip to Wales with her course. She dreams of volunteering on a turtle conservation project abroad but knows the cost puts it out of reach for now. Days out to Mersea Island and the Suffolk coast are her idea of a treat.
- culinary persona: Cooks cheap and simple: pasta bakes, jacket potatoes, stir-fries and a big pot of chilli that does three dinners. She's been mostly vegetarian for a year but eats chicken if Jordan cooks. Her treat is a Greggs vegan sausage roll or a Friday chippy tea when they've been paid. She bakes banana bread whenever bananas go brown.
- hobbies and interests: birdwatching with a secondhand pair of binoculars, sketching plants and birds, fantasy and romance novels, looking after Biscuit the guinea pig, beginners' yoga, helping on her nan's allotment, nature documentaries, charity shop browsing
- skills: bird identification by sight and some by song, basic species surveying and field notes, patient with animals and small children, budgeting on very little money, baking, good listener
- career goals: Wants to work as a ranger or education officer for a wildlife trust or the RSPB, ideally running sessions for kids. She is thinking about a placement year but worries about money. Longer term she'd love a small house near the coast with a garden and room for more rescue animals.
- voice: Soft, friendly, fairly quick when she's comfortable and slower and more careful when she isn't sure. Light Essex/South East accent with some dropped t's ('bo'le', 'li'le') and 'dinner' for the evening meal. Uses 'erm' a lot and 'kind of' more than 'sort of'. Ends sentences with 'yeah?' or 'do you know what I mean?'. Says 'sorry' often, to apologise, to correct herself ('sorry, I mean the second one') and when she's unsure she heard properly. Laughs nervously at awkward moments. In a silence she'll fill the gap by over-explaining or asking 'is that, erm, is that what you meant?'. Echoes the interviewer's words back when she's engaged.
- typing: Mostly lowercase, sometimes capitalises the first word. Light punctuation, often no full stop at the end, but uses commas. Apostrophes are hit and miss ('dont', 'im', but usually 'it's'). Uses 'tbh', 'idk' and occasionally 'x' out of habit before deleting it. Exclamation marks when being friendly. Answers are short but honest, sometimes with a slightly apologetic add-on like 'sorry if thats not very helpful'.
- with strangers: Warm, polite and eager to please, a little anxious at first. She smiles a lot and agrees readily, so she may need encouraging to give her real opinion. She gets noticeably more relaxed and chatty once the topic turns to animals, nature or her course. She is very unlikely to be rude or dismissive.
- small things: Biscuit squeaking when the fridge opens, spotting a kestrel on the walk to the bus stop, the bus to campus being late again, being knackered after a fieldwork day, what she's making for dinner, a book she's halfway through, her mum's new hairdo, the heating being too expensive to put on
- deeper things: She worries constantly about money and whether the degree will lead to a job., Her dad leaving still makes her anxious that people will leave her., She sometimes feels out of place next to coursemates from wealthier families., She has had periods of anxiety and saw a counsellor in sixth form., She feels guilty for moving away from her mum and brother., She and Jordan have talked about marriage, but she wants to finish her degree first.
- webcam photo: Laptop webcam at slightly below eye level, angled up a little, showing her head and shoulders. Lit mainly by a window to her left, so the left side of her face is brighter and the right slightly shadowed, with a warm lamp glow in the background. She has a round face with light freckles across her nose, minimal makeup and a small, slightly nervous closed-mouth smile. Shoulder-length mid-brown hair is pulled back loosely in a claw clip, with a few strands falling at the front. She wears a sage-green oversized hoodie with a small embroidered bee on the chest and silver stud earrings. No glasses. Behind her is a cream wall with a corkboard pinned with a printed bird ID chart, a couple of photos and a fieldwork timetable. Next to it is a narrow bookshelf holding paperback novels, a pair of binoculars and a potted spider plant. In the lower right corner the top of a guinea pig cage is just visible, with a fleece blanket draped over one end.

P272 (Marijke; transcript label: Marijke):
- first name: Marijke
- age: 64
- lives in: Sittingbourne, South East England
- occupation: Part-time domiciliary care worker, doing about 12 hours a week of morning calls (washing, dressing, breakfasts, medication prompts) for an agency covering Sittingbourne and the villages towards Faversham

Marijke: Yes, that was yours! I liked it. Bolton Wanderers. My husband Keith watches all the football, all weekend.
Zain: Who's he support?
Marijke: Gillingham, sort of. Mostly he watches whatever is on.
Zain: Respect. I'm a season ticket man in spirit, go to a handful of games with my cousins. What do you do, then?
Marijke: I'm a carer, mornings. I go to people's houses, wash, dress, breakfast, tablets. Done by eleven.
Zain: That's good, that. Proper important job. My mum worked in a school canteen, the old dears there were like that, looked after everyone.
Marijke: Ha, maybe I'll do dinner ladies next. What about you?
Zain: Electrician. EV chargers, rewires, all that. I'm going self-employed in a couple of years. Got it all planned in my head, van, logo, the lot.
Marijke: Ooh, a businessman. Can you come and look at my kitchen light? It flickers.
Zain: Could be the fitting, could be a loose connection. Get someone out, don't leave it, mind.
Marijke: Keith says it's fine. Keith says everything is fine.
Zain: Ha, every bloke says that. Have you been back to Holland lately? I've always wanted to go to Amsterdam, look at the old buildings.
Marijke: Once a year, to my sister. We drive and take the ferry. But I'm not from Amsterdam, near Arnhem. Amsterdam is all tourists.
Zain: Fair enough. I'm planning Japan, me. Been watching vlogs for months. Tokyo, Kyoto, the temples, the food. Found some decent flight deals as well.
Marijke: Japan! Too far for me. I've done my moving, I came to England, that's enough.
Zain: Ha, that's a big move, to be fair.
Marijke: It was. What else, erm... my sister sends me stroopwafels. You know them? Like a biscuit with syrup.
Zain: Yeah, had them in Istanbul, weirdly, at the airport. They're mint.
Marijke: Mint, yes. I keep them in a tin, I don't give the grandkids too many.
Zain: You've got grandkids?
Marijke: Three. Every weekend, chaos. I make the dinner, shepherd's pie, Dutch mash.
Zain: Dutch mash? What's that?
Marijke: Stamppot. Potatoes with kale, sausage. Nothing spicy, I can't do spicy.

text:
=== CALL C0545 ===
Gemma: Hiya, hello! Can you hear me alright?
Megan: Hi! Yeah, I can. Sorry, my internet's been a bit funny today. I'm Megan.
Gemma: I'm Gemma. Erm, I have to tell you, I think we've got something in common. Jade said your guinea pig's called Biscuit?
Megan: Oh my god, yeah! Is that your dog? Jade said there was another Biscuit but I thought she'd got muddled.
Gemma: No, she's right. Biscuit the greyhound. She's thirteen, and she's on the sofa behind me now, if you can see her ears.
Megan: I can! Aw, she's gorgeous. I love greyhounds. They just look so gentle, do you know what I mean?
Gemma: She is. She's frightened of absolutely everything, but she's gentle. Why Biscuit for yours?
Megan: Erm, he's kind of a light brown, like a digestive. And when we got him from the rescue he wouldn't stop eating, so. My boyfriend picked it, really.
Gemma: Ha, ours came with the name, from the rescue. We didn't want to confuse her at her age.
Megan: That's sweet. Erm, sorry, what do you do? I should've asked.
Gemma: Don't be sorry. I'm a pharmacy technician at a hospital in Nottingham. I do the medicines on two wards, so when someone comes in, I check what they were taking at home matches what's been written up. You'd be surprised how often it doesn't. Somebody's on the wrong dose, or a tablet's been missed off completely. It's sort of my job to catch it before it gets to them. And I look after a few junior techs.
Megan: That sounds really important. Like, really stressful.
Gemma: It can be. I do lie awake sometimes going over things, if I'm honest. But I like it. What about you? Jade mentioned birds?
Megan: Yeah, I'm at uni, second year, wildlife and conservation. So lots of fieldwork, which I love, and then writing up, which I don't. The stats bit, I just kind of freeze, and I'm always up till midnight the night before a deadline.
Gemma: Oh, I was exactly the same with stats. I started a degree, actually, biomedical science, and I left after the first year. I just didn't get on with it.
Megan: Oh really? Do you, erm, sorry, do you regret it?
Gemma: Sometimes, a bit. But I'd not be doing this if I'd stayed, and I'm good at this. So, you know. Stick with yours, though, it sounds like you love it.
Megan: I do. I just worry about getting a job at the end. I want to be a ranger, or do education stuff with kids, for a wildlife trust or the RSPB.
Gemma: You'd be brilliant with kids, I can tell. You've got that sort of patient voice.
Megan: Aw, thank you. My nan's got an allotment, and I used to help her when I was li'le, and that's kind of why I got into it all.
Gemma: That's lovely. I do tomatoes and sweet peas, that's my limit. My tomatoes were rubbish this year, though.
Megan: Were they? Did they get blight? My nan's did.
Gemma: I think so, the leaves went all brown. Sorry, I'm keeping you talking about tomatoes.
Megan: No, I love this. Honestly, it's the best bit.
Gemma: Do you get out much near you, nature-wise?
Megan: Mersea Island, when we can. And the Suffolk coast. That's like my treat day. Do you walk Biscuit somewhere nice?
Gemma: The canal, every day. There's a heron that stands in the same spot every morning. Biscuit's terrified of it.
Megan: Ha! Herons are terrifying, to be fair, they're like dinosaurs.
Gemma: That's exactly what Rob says. Oh, I think we're nearly out of time.
Megan: Aw. Give Biscuit a stroke from me.
Gemma: I will, and you give yours a bit of carrot.

=== CALL C0546 ===
Zain: Alright mate, how's it going?
Callum: Alright. Yeah, fine.
Zain: Zain, Bolton. You're the gym lad, aren't you? From the picture, the Gymshark top.
Callum: Callum. Stockton. Yeah, I go a fair bit.
Zain: Same, three times a week, weights. What you on?
Callum: Four mornings, before lectures. Trying to get a hundred and forty on deadlift.
Zain: A hundred and forty? Fair play. I'm nowhere near. I've been doing padel lately as well, mate from work dragged me along. Proper addictive. You ever tried it?
Callum: No. Not really my thing.
Zain: Fair enough. What you studying?
Callum: Civil engineering. Final year. Teesside.
Zain: Oh nice, I love all that. I'm a sparky, but I watch loads of stuff on YouTube about old mills getting converted. There's one in Bolton they've done flats in, kept all the brick and the iron columns. Proper nice.
Callum: Yeah, the cast iron ones are interesting. You've got to check them before you put load on, half of them weren't designed for what people want now.
Zain: See, that's the stuff I want to know. What you doing your dissertation on?
Callum: Drainage. New housing estates.
Zain: Drainage. Right.
Callum: It's more interesting than it sounds.
Zain: Go on then, sell it me.
Callum: Every new estate's adding roofs and tarmac, so the rain can't soak in. It all goes in the pipes at once and floods somewhere downstream. So you design it to hold back, ponds, swales, permeable paving, and let it out slowly. If you get it wrong, people's houses flood. If you get it right, nobody notices. That's it really.
Zain: Nah, that's mint, that. The nobody-notices bit. Same with wiring. Do a good job and no one thinks about you again.
Callum: Yeah. Pretty much.
Zain: You go to the football? I'm Wanderers.
Callum: Boro. Watch most of it on telly with my stepdad. Go to the Riverside a few times a season.
Zain: Same with me and my cousins. We've played yous a few times in pre-season and that. What d'you reckon to your manager?
Callum: Should've gone in October, to be honest.
Zain: Ha, blunt. I like it. Ours, I'd give him till the summer. You play at all?
Callum: Used to. Sunday league. Stopped.
Zain: How come?
Callum: Didn't like the lads' side of it. All the banter and that.
Zain: Ah, fair. Our five-a-side's bad for that, to be fair. There's one lad never passes and we never stop giving him stick. He deserves it, mind.
Callum: Probably.
Zain: What you doing after uni, then? Staying up there?
Callum: Yeah. Consultancy in the North East. Get chartered. Save for a house.
Zain: Sound. I'm going on my own, two years. Van, my name on the side, EV chargers and solar. That's where the money is.
Callum: You'll need someone good on the paperwork for that.
Zain: Ha, you're the second person to say that today. I'm on it, mate. Think the timer's about to go.
Callum: Yeah. Good luck with it.

=== CALL C0547 ===
Jade: Hiya! Oh, you look just like your picture, that's nice.
Marijke: Hello, love! Well, I didn't have time to change. I'm Marijke.
Jade: Jade. I'm in Barnsley. Is that, sorry, is it Dutch, your name?
Marijke: Yes, very good! I'm Dutch, but I've been in Kent forty years, so now I'm a bit of both. Neither, really. You'll hear the accent.
Jade: I love it, honestly. It's dead nice.
Marijke: You're kind. What do you do, Jade?
Jade: Erm, nothing at the minute, which sounds terrible. I were a nail tech, but the salon shut about eight months ago. I've been meaning to set up from home, I've got all the stuff, I just keep not doing it. Like I'll sit down to do the insurance form and then I'm on TikTok for two hours. Do you know what I mean?
Marijke: Oh, I know. My paperwork at work, the office is always chasing me. I'm a carer, mornings, and they want everything written in the app. I'm good with the ladies, the talking, the washing, but the typing, pff.
Jade: That's exactly me! I were brilliant with the clients, they all came back, but I'd forget to order stock and that.
Marijke: Well, the clients is the hard part. Anyone can do the forms. Let me see the nails.
Jade: Here. Pink almond. Did them myself.
Marijke: Ooh. They're very long. How do you do the washing up?
Jade: Ha! Everyone asks. You just get used to it. I could do you some, if you were up here.
Marijke: No, no, I can't, with my job. They'd be in someone's porridge. My granddaughter would love them, though. She's nine and she wants everything sparkly.
Jade: Aw, I used to do kids' parties sometimes, little pamper parties. They love the glitter.
Marijke: You see, there's a business. Pamper parties. Mums would pay.
Jade: Do you know what, that's actually a good idea.
Marijke: Course it is, I'm old, I know things. What else, erm... have you got children?
Jade: No, not yet. My mam keeps asking. Every Sunday dinner, it's when are you having a baby. I'm like, Mam, I can't even sort the spare room out.
Marijke: Ha! Mine were the same with my daughter. Tell her you'll let her know.
Jade: That's what I say. Have you got kids?
Marijke: Two, grown up, and three grandchildren. Every weekend. They love the hagelslag, it's like chocolate sprinkles, on toast. My sister sends it from Holland.
Jade: Chocolate sprinkles on toast? For breakfast?
Marijke: Every Dutch child. Very normal.
Jade: Oh my god, I'm moving to Holland.
Marijke: It rains just as much, love. Don't bother.
Jade: Ha! I think we're nearly done.
Marijke: Go and do your spare room. And the parties.
Jade: I will. Probably. Thank you, it's been lovely.

I want to keep the details consistent—Megan's guinea pig and Gemma's greyhound both named Biscuit, which Jade already picked up on, so Megan and Gemma could have their own moment discovering this coincidence. I should also keep Callum blunt and Zain chatty, and double check that odd line Marijke had about "a funny name for you" since it felt off.

For word choice, I'll have Gemma and Zain and Callum and Jade use "tea" and "mam" to sound natural for them, while Megan and Marijke use "dinner" instead, keeping the regional voice consistent.

req.text:
You write transcripts of realistic video calls between strangers for a fully synthetic research dataset set in the UK. The study, in order (from its published design): a short puzzle task done alone; first impressions of the others' webcam photos; then a series of three-minute, one-on-one video calls in rounds, each person meeting the others in their group; after each call a short survey.

Call shape (from the original study's numbers): a call is cut off by a three-minute timer. A typical call has about 30 turns (most between 20 and 39) and about 570 words in total (most between 440 and 682); half of all turns are 12 words or fewer, and a quarter are 24 or more. Short acknowledgements ("yeah", "mm") count as turns too. So aim for about 570 words in about 30 turns: alongside the quick back-and-forth, people often talk in longer stretches (explaining their job, telling a story), and those long turns carry much of the call.

Guide to British conversational English (use it for how people talk; it is a description of speech, not a script):
How British people talk in casual conversation. This is a paraphrase of published descriptions of spoken British English; sources are in SOURCES.md. Use these features lightly and only where they fit the person. Never use them as a caricature.

- **Fillers.** British speakers hesitate with "erm" and "er". Women and younger speakers lean towards "erm".
- **Hedges.** "Sort of" is everywhere and steady. "Kind of" is spreading, and younger speakers use it more.
- **Politeness words.** "Please", "thank you", "thanks" and "sorry" mostly mean what they say. "Sorry" also works as a repair word (to correct yourself, or to ask someone to repeat) and can be ironic.
- **Tags at the end of a sentence.** "You know", "right", "okay", "yeah", "do you know what I mean". Among young Londoners, "innit" and "you get me" are rising. Tags depend on age and region only, never on ethnicity.
- **Echoing.** In an engaged conversation people pick up and re-use parts of each other's words.
- **Regional words and grammar** (from a recent dialect survey):
  - A bread roll is a "barm" in the North West (Manchester to Liverpool and western Lancashire), a "cob" around Nottinghamshire, a "bap" in Staffordshire, the West Midlands and North Wales, and a "batch" in Liverpool and Coventry.
  - Around Liverpool an ice lolly can be a "lolly ice".
  - The evening meal is "tea" in the North West, North East and Yorkshire, and "dinner" in the South East and London. Some people say both.
  - "Yous" or "youse" for plural "you" is common in the North East (Newcastle, Teesside), Liverpool and Scotland, less so in Manchester, and rare in York, Leeds and Sheffield.
  - "Give it me" is normal in the North West and West Midlands and widely accepted in Sheffield and York; it fades south of Birmingham, Coventry and Leicester.
  - "You was" is widely used, historically Northern and now found as far south as London.
- **Everyday British words** to draw on where they fit, without assigning them to regions: knackered or shattered, chuffed or made up, skint or brassic, mardy or stroppy, mum or mam, mate or pal, settee, sofa or couch.

The group (session S54). Persona cards, including the webcam photo each person was rated on:

P281 (Liam; transcript label: Liam A):
- first name: Liam
- age: 30
- lives in: Ilkeston, East Midlands
- occupation: Electrician (domestic and light commercial), employed full-time by a small firm in Nottingham, about 40 hours a week plus the odd cash-in-hand weekend job
- education detail: Left school at 16 with GCSEs, mostly Cs and a B in art. Did a Level 3 electrical installation apprenticeship through a college in Nottingham, then got his NVQ and 18th Edition wiring regs. Has thought about an HNC but never enrolled.
- household: Lives back at his mum and dad's three-bed semi on the edge of Ilkeston. His parents have been married 34 years. He moved back two years ago after splitting up with his long-term girlfriend, and pays them board while he saves for a deposit. His older sister lives in Derby with her kids.
- cultural background: White British, born and raised in Erewash. Christened Church of England and ticks 'Christian' on forms. Goes to church for weddings, funerals and sometimes Christmas with his mum, but doesn't really think about it otherwise. His dad was a fitter at a factory that's long gone. The family is solidly working-class and proud of having a trade.
- professional persona: Quick, capable and confident on site, and he knows it. He likes the customer-facing side, chatting to homeowners and selling them on an upgrade they didn't know they wanted. He's impatient with slower lads and doesn't hide it, and has had a couple of run-ins with his boss over 'attitude'. He will round up hours or take a side job off the books without losing sleep. His work is tidy enough and he does it properly when it matters.
- sports persona: Nottingham Forest fan, goes to a few home games a season with mates and watches the rest in the pub. Plays five-a-side on Wednesday nights and is the one shouting at everyone, referee included. Goes to the gym three or four times a week, mostly weights. Got into bouldering last year at a climbing wall in Nottingham and loves it.
- arts persona: More into art than you'd guess and he enjoys surprising people with it. He follows street artists on Instagram, has been to Nottingham Contemporary a few times, and takes photos of graffiti and old industrial buildings on his phone. He listens to house and techno, goes to nights in Nottingham and the odd festival, and watches a lot of documentaries about anything from cults to architecture.
- travel persona: Loves a city break and goes for the buzz rather than the beach. Berlin was his favourite, for the clubs, the murals and the history. He has done Amsterdam, Budapest and Lisbon with mates. He likes to just turn up and wing it, and gets restless by day three if he's somewhere quiet. Wants to do Japan or Mexico City next.
- culinary persona: Lives on cobs and meal-deal stuff during the working week. He likes cooking big on a Sunday when his mum lets him have the kitchen, usually a curry from scratch or something he's seen on YouTube. He collects hot sauces and likes finding the spiciest thing on the menu and making a show of it. Calls the evening meal 'tea' at home and 'dinner' when he's out.
- hobbies and interests: bouldering, five-a-side football, weights at the gym, street art and urban photography, house and techno nights, Forest, true-crime and history documentaries, hot sauces, city breaks
- skills: domestic rewiring and fault-finding, consumer unit upgrades, EV charger and solar installs (learning), talking customers into extras, phone photography, cooking curries from scratch, reading a room fast
- career goals: Wants to go self-employed within a couple of years, ideally doing EV chargers and solar because that's where the money is. He'd like his own van with his name on it and eventually a lad or two working for him. He talks about it a lot and is a bit vague on the paperwork side.
- voice: Loud, fast and confident, and he warms up within seconds. He has a light East Midlands accent with flat vowels, says 'were' for 'was' now and then, and uses 'you was' casually. He says 'mate' a lot and drops in 'mardy' or 'me duck' only when he's joking or quoting his mum. His filler is 'er', not much, because he rarely pauses. He ends points with 'you know?' or 'yeah?' and sometimes 'do you know what I mean'. He uses 'sort of' when he's actually unsure, which isn't often. He hates silence and fills it immediately, often with a story or a counter-opinion. He interrupts without really noticing and will say 'nah, sorry, but...' before disagreeing outright.
- typing: Mostly lowercase and quick, with the odd capital at the start if autocorrect does it. Few apostrophes ('dont', 'im', 'thats'), and commas instead of full stops. Uses 'tbh', 'prob', 'lol' and sometimes 'haha'. Answers are short and blunt unless the question annoys him or interests him, and then he writes a proper rant. Occasional typo he doesn't bother fixing.
- with strangers: Instantly chatty and likeable at first, with lots of banter and a big laugh, and he makes himself the centre of the conversation. After a few minutes he gets opinionated and a bit cocky. He'll challenge what you say, tell you you're wrong, and brag a little about money he's made or places he's been. He's not nervous at all and doesn't do much small-talk flattery. Some people find him great fun, others find him a lot.
- small things: the van's heater being knackered, a job where the previous sparky had done 'cowboy' wiring, Forest's last result, a new hot sauce he's found, his mum doing his washing whether he wants her to or not, a mural he spotted in Sneinton, being shattered after climbing, his mate always being skint by the twentieth of the month
- deeper things: the break-up hit him harder than he lets on, and moving back home at 28 felt like going backwards, he thinks he's cleverer than school ever gave him credit for and sometimes wonders about doing an art course, he and his dad don't really talk beyond football and work, he knows he can be a bit of an arse with people and has lost a couple of mates over it, but tends to blame them, he'd like kids one day but doesn't say that out loud to his mates
- webcam photo: Head-and-shoulders shot from a laptop on a desk, angled slightly upward so the ceiling is just visible. Lighting comes from a window to his left, with a yellowish ceiling light on as well, so one side of his face is brighter. White man with a broad face, short faded brown hair, darker on top and pushed forward, and a few days of stubble. He's grinning with his head tilted, close to the screen. No glasses. He's wearing a grey hoodie with a small brand logo, and the edge of a tattoo is visible on his neck just above the collar. Behind him is a small bedroom with magnolia walls. There's a framed print of a colourful graffiti piece above a single bed with a navy duvet, a pull-up bar over the door frame, a pair of climbing shoes and a gym bag on the floor, a shelf with three or four hot sauce bottles and a Forest scarf draped over it, and a hi-vis jacket hanging on the back of the door.

P282 (Gemma; transcript label: Gemma):
- first name: Gemma
- age: 44
- lives in: Beeston, Nottinghamshire (East Midlands)
- occupation: Head of Maths at a large secondary academy on the west side of Nottingham. She teaches about two-thirds of a full timetable on top of running a department of nine, and regularly works 50 to 55 hours a week once marking, data deadlines and parents' evenings are counted.
- education detail: Went to the local comprehensive and sixth form in Long Eaton (A levels in Maths, Biology and Business Studies), then a BSc in Mathematics at Nottingham Trent University, followed by a PGCE at the University of Nottingham. Has since done the NPQML middle leadership qualification through the trust.
- household: Lives in a 1930s semi in Beeston with her husband Rob (46), a self-employed electrician, and their two children, Maisie (15, in Year 10 at a different school) and Josh (12, Year 7). They have a slightly overweight Border Terrier called Biscuit. Her mum lives ten minutes away in Chilwell and helps with school pick-ups.
- cultural background: White British, born and raised in the Long Eaton and Beeston area, from a close working-class family. Her dad was a fitter at a plant in Derby and her mum was a dinner lady and later a teaching assistant. She was the first in her family to go to university, which she's quietly proud of. Not religious, though she was christened and the kids went to a Church of England primary because it was nearest. Christmas, birthdays and Sunday dinners at her mum's matter a lot to her.
- professional persona: A warm, loud, visible presence in school. Kids know her as strict but fair and she remembers every name. She's good at the people side of leading a department: keeping morale up, defending her staff, smoothing things over with parents. She's less naturally good at the paperwork, and she gets things done in bursts close to deadlines. She worries a lot about exam results and about individual students, especially the vulnerable ones, and takes it home with her more than she'd like. She is suspicious of new initiatives the trust brings in every year and prefers methods she knows work.
- sports persona: Played netball at school and for a Sunday league team in her twenties. Now mostly walks Biscuit round the Attenborough Nature Reserve and does a Saturday morning parkrun at Colwick when she can drag herself out, usually with a friend from work. Not hugely into football herself, but Rob and Josh are Forest season-ticket holders, so she follows the results and knows when to keep her head down.
- arts persona: Not one for galleries or the theatre beyond the odd panto at the Theatre Royal with the kids and an occasional touring musical with her sister. Likes TV she can switch off to: Strictly, Bake Off, Gogglebox, Gavin & Stacey reruns, and whatever crime drama everyone at work is talking about. Listens to Heart or Capital in the car and has a soft spot for Take That and 90s pop. Cries at almost anything sad on telly and is teased for it.
- travel persona: Prefers the familiar. The family has gone to the same all-inclusive resort in Majorca three summers running, and there's usually a half-term caravan trip to Skegness or Mablethorpe with her mum. She gets anxious about flying and airport logistics, so she over-prepares, with printed boarding passes and lists. She has no real urge to go anywhere exotic and says she 'just wants a sunbed and a book'.
- culinary persona: Cooks plain, reliable family food: spag bol, chilli, roast chicken on a Sunday, a big batch of stew in winter. Still calls a bread roll a cob and the evening meal 'tea'. Friday is chippy tea or a takeaway from the Indian on the high street, where she always orders a chicken korma. Not adventurous and suspicious of anything too spicy. Bakes a lot, mostly Victoria sponges and traybakes for staff room birthdays and school fundraisers.
- hobbies and interests: walking the dog round Attenborough Nature Reserve, parkrun, on and off, baking traybakes and birthday cakes, watching Strictly and Bake Off with Maisie, WhatsApp group chats with old school friends, occasional quiz night at the local pub, Slimming World, on and off for years
- skills: explaining maths patiently to teenagers who think they can't do it, managing a team and keeping people's spirits up, dealing with angry parents calmly, at least on the outside, organising school trips and events, spreadsheets and pupil data tracking, baking for large numbers
- career goals: Has been nudged towards applying for assistant head and feels torn. She'd like the pay and the recognition, but she worries about losing classroom time and about the stress. She'd also feel guilty about being away from the kids even more. Most likely to stay as Head of Maths for a few more years, and might consider moving to a smaller school nearer home.
- voice: Chatty, warm and fairly quick, with a gentle East Midlands accent: short vowels and a dropped 'h' here and there. She'll occasionally say 'duck' when relaxed, but not with a stranger at first. Uses 'erm' when gathering her thoughts and 'sort of' quite a lot ('it's sort of hard to say'). Says 'do you know what I mean?' and 'yeah, no' a fair bit, and will echo the question back while she thinks ('what would I change? erm...'). Might call something 'mardy' or say she's 'shattered'. Uses a slightly clearer, more organised teacher voice if asked something formal. Uncomfortable with silence and fills it, sometimes over-explaining or apologising ('sorry, I'm rambling'). Laughs easily, including at herself.
- typing: Types quickly, mostly in proper sentences because of the job, with capitals at the start and apostrophes usually right. Gets looser when rushed: drops the final full stop, uses 'and' a lot, and adds the odd 'lol' or '!!' when something's funny. No text-speak abbreviations beyond 'tbh' occasionally. Sometimes writes more than the box needs.
- with strangers: Friendly and open almost straight away, and quick to find common ground or make a joke. Comes across as confident and sociable, though underneath she's a bit anxious about saying the 'wrong' thing or being judged, so she checks ('is that the kind of thing you mean?'). Shares fairly readily about family and work but keeps the genuinely worrying stuff back until she feels at ease.
- small things: Biscuit the dog has rolled in something again, the photocopier at school always jams on deadline day, Josh only eats beige food, her mum's Sunday dinners are better than hers, Forest results affecting the mood in the house, parkrun being too early on a Saturday, the price of the big shop at Asda going up, half-term can't come soon enough
- deeper things: She lies awake worrying about specific students, especially a few in care or with problems at home, her dad died of a heart attack when she was 30 and she still gets anxious about Rob's and her own health, she sometimes feels she's failing at both work and being a mum because of the hours, she's had a couple of spells of anxiety and saw her GP about it once but didn't take the tablets, she feels guilty she's not as close to her younger sister as she'd like, she worries about Maisie and social media
